en: Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

To the One who alone is able to awaken to and understand, without error or confusion, the most extremely difficult-to-know specific and general characteristics that pervade all phenomena— to this All-Knowing One, I now pay homage.
With words that are vast and accord with principle, I refute other schools to reveal my own fundamental meaning;
if the Master of the Sūtras speaks in accordance with reasoned teaching, I shall follow and record it without seeking fault.
Should there be even slight deviations from the intent of the Abhidharma and the Sūtras, I vow to investigate them thoroughly and eliminate them;
this treatise, titled *Nyāyānusāra* (Conformity with Correct Reasoning), is what those who delight in analytical investigation should study.
The textual exegesis is so vast and difficult to navigate that it cannot be understood without great exertion;
therefore, I have extracted the extensive writings to facilitate comprehension and composed this concise treatise titled *Xianzong* (Exposition of the Tenets).
I have preserved those verses as my ultimate refuge, pruning and streamlining them to provide extensive analysis within the framework of reason;
I offer this correct exposition to refute erroneous claims and reveal the true, wondrous meaning of our school’s tenets.
The treatise says:
Since he is not [merely] an omniscient one, how can he know?

This Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the All-Knowing One; he is able to awaken to the self-characteristics and common characteristics of all phenomena—among which there are those most difficult to know—without error or confusion.

Although it is not exhaustive knowledge, it is nonetheless capable of knowing; for by practicing according to the Buddha’s teachings, one will certainly attain the fruit. It is like a wise person who skillfully examines a skilled physician.

Suppose there is a physician in the world who first carefully investigates the source of a patient’s illness—whether it arises from wind, heat, or phlegm—and then accurately observes the two factors of nature and habit, as well as various differences such as age, season, and location, before prescribing a remedy and medicine to eliminate it.
When those who are ill are able to follow his instructions and take the medicine, their chronic ailments gradually subside and their physical well-being increases day by day.
The wise, observing these results, recognize him as a truly skilled physician who possesses pure and universal knowledge regarding all prescriptions and medicines.

In this way, the World-Honored One knows the sources of the diseases of affliction—such as greed, hatred, and delusion—in those to be converted; furthermore, he observes with perfect accuracy their innate nature, the cultivation and accumulation of the two types of wholesome seeds, their resolute inclinations (*adhimukti*), their latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and their capacity for self-perfection. Desiring to bring about their temporary and ultimate cessation, he expounds the methods and medicines of the two paths: subduing and eradication.

Those who are to be transformed are able to comply with and practice the medicinal remedies of the remedial paths, whether specific or general. As the afflictions—which have been habitually practiced since beginningless time, thus becoming increased, flourishing, and firm—are gradually dispelled, greed and the other [afflictions] are extinguished and attained; within one's own person, according to the depth of the path, they become increasingly superior and more excellent.
From this, by inference, one knows that our Great Teacher has extinguished all darkness and possesses all-encompassing wisdom; therefore, the one who offers praise extols the Buddha, saying:
"Who, like the Venerable One, can skillfully distinguish The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), their objects, and their specific and general characteristics?"
Through immeasurable and boundless varieties of teachings, one should teach as appropriate to benefit sentient beings.
Who, practicing in gradual succession, would not attain supreme benefit and happiness?
"Lacking wisdom, they cannot follow the Noble Teaching; how could the fault of failing to provide proof lie with the Tathāgata!

There are those who, possessing overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding their own analytical discernment, claim that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not omniscient because he provides various different answers to questions posed to him. They say:
"These various different answers should not have been given as 'unanswerable' (*avyākṛta*), for they arise from ignorance."

Furthermore, because he stated that the past limit (*pūrvānta*) is unknowable, this itself reveals his own ignorance; because he was not previously aware of the incident involving Sundarī and failed to restrain her associates from committing various evils; because he could not dispel the slanderous accusations leveled against the Brahmin woman Cañcā; because he previously granted Devadatta permission to go forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma; because he did not know in advance whether the life of the outsider Udraka would be preserved or end; because he did not preordain that such calamities would arise in the city of Pāṭaliputra; because he did not prophesy in advance that eighteen distinct schools would emerge within his own Buddha-dharma; and because he taught that there are karmic actions that are indeterminate (*aniyata*).
The heterodox teachers' slanderous words have been briefly recounted in this manner.

Those heterodox teachers remained obstinately attached to their views in their hearts; thus, although the Honored One of All-Knowledge employed various skillful means to guide them, he was unable to cause them to give rise to pure faith and understanding toward Perfectly Equal Enlightenment.
Only those who possess superior merit and wisdom and seek the ultimate truth can fathom the ocean of omniscience.
Now, with a courageous and vigorous mind of right effort, I have attained a slight awakening in accordance with the Dharma and as is appropriate.

To claim that one answers a question by distinguishing it—meaning to say, "This should not be answered"—and thus provide a distinct response based on ignorance, is unreasonable; for the reason (hetu) established therein is not definitive.
Furthermore, one should examine this in detail:
Is it because of ignorance that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, says he should not provide an answer to a question?

Or is it because he perceives that the questioner harbors pride in their own cleverness and cannot immediately be led to a correct understanding, such that although he fully comprehends the matter, he does not provide an answer?
For example, if someone were to ask with deceptive intent,
"Are the children of barren women black or white?
one would never provide an answer.
Could there be some other method capable of dispelling that ailment?

In this same way, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), clinging to the notion of a self as real, falsely inquire of the Tathāgata whether he exists or does not exist after death, and so forth; the World-Honored One replied:
"This is not to be answered."
The Buddha’s intention was that because a self does not truly exist, it should not be answered [as to its existence].
This demonstrates that if a phenomenon is entirely non-existent in reality, one should not pose a question regarding its specific distinctions.
Alternatively, it may be that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, did not provide a prediction for the sake of taming them through his skillful means;
this non-prediction is itself the cause of their taming, rather than being a divergent answer given out of ignorance.
Furthermore, one should not say that the Buddha lacks eloquence, for that which he was asked was not included within the scope of formal debate.
If what was asked had been included within formal debate, then the Buddha’s failure to provide an answer might imply a lack of eloquence.
In this matter, not even a slight degree of logical objection can be found; how, then, can it be claimed that the Buddha lacks eloquence?

Furthermore, because the listeners' minds were not earnest, because they clung to the view of a self, and because their faculties were not yet mature, there was no means by which the World-Honored One could cause them to attain faith and understanding. Therefore, he set aside and did not provide an answer to their questions. Thus, one should not conclude from his failure to answer that the Great Sage is not omniscient.

To say that it is "unknowable" because it was taught regarding the beginning [of time] is itself to reveal that one lacks knowledge; this too is irrational, for a non-existent thing cannot be the object of cognition.
If cognition does not arise regarding the objects of existence, one might say that the Tathāgata is not omniscient.
Yet, since there is no beginning in the fundamental state (*anādikāla*), what could cognition possibly know?
To not know because something does not exist—how could this constitute a lack of wisdom?
If that is so, why not simply say "non-existent"?
This statement does not allow for the further establishment of a reason.
If it is argued that one should establish the reason of "inapprehensibility," this is also incorrect, because it is not determinative.
Alternatively, although a phenomenon may exist, it is not known due to the deficiency of conditions; therefore, its unknowability does not imply that it lacks a cause.

If one were to posit "lack of nature" as the cause for its unknowability, there would be no possible similar example (sapakṣa) because such a thing would be absolutely non-existent; rather, it is said to be unknowable because it is possible for a cause to exist.
If it is argued that there is the fault of non-establishment because [the beginning] lacks a cause, this is unreasonable, for it is not unestablished.

If the initial limit of birth and death were definitely not non-existent, then the body at that initial limit would not arise without a cause; and if it were causeless at the beginning, it should likewise be causeless later, since there is no differing cause for the bodies of the earlier and later states.
If you were to grant this, then all performed actions—whether pure or impure—would necessarily be without fruit;
since you do not grant this, the previously established premise that there is no beginning is not an invalid reason.
If it is argued that because birth and death have no beginning, they must likewise have no end—just like space—this is also illogical, for the analogy with external seeds is the same.

Just as external grains such as rice or barley arise from preceding causes, and although they have no beginning, they are nonetheless permanently destroyed when they encounter conditions such as fire or water that burn or rot them.

In this way, the causes of birth, death, afflictions, and karma arise from one another in succession; although they have no beginning, through the power of repeatedly practicing the antidotes to greed, hatred, and delusion, the aggregates of birth and death ultimately cease to arise. This constitutes the "final limit" (paryanta), for since it is empty and non-arising, a final limit may indeed be said to exist.
Since birth-and-death involves actual arising, how could it lack a subsequent limit?
We observe that the nature of birth necessarily entails a time of cessation.

Since birth-and-death has already arisen, it must logically return to extinction; therefore, the statement that the prior limit is unknowable because it does not exist as a cause is well-established in meaning.
Therefore, one should not conclude that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not omniscient simply because he did not know the beginning of cyclic existence.
To claim that he was not previously aware of the circumstances regarding Sundarī or that he permitted her associates to commit various evils is likewise unreasonable.
Although he was aware of it beforehand, he did not reveal it himself in order to avoid many faults.

If the Buddha had first said, "I have done nothing of this kind; those who did so were others," then the malicious intent of his followers would have increased, and those of neutral disposition would all have come to harbor doubts.
As for such faults, do they belong to the Buddha or to that person?
Furthermore, the way of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*) is not to manifest the faults of others; since the Buddha is a Great Being, how could he ever proclaim the evils of another?
Moreover, to expose their faults would cause immeasurable people to harbor hatred toward and turn away from the World-Honored One, thereby obstructing their entry into the True Dharma.

Furthermore, the Buddha perceived that both his own body and the bodies of others possessed determinate karma that would invite slander and a short lifespan. Moreover, he sought to provide consolation to the bhikṣus of the final age; observing that the True Dharma was about to perish, he saw that among the many learned and precept-observing bhikṣus who were the hope of the multitude, few would avoid being slandered before they died.

Desiring to encourage them, he spoke these words of self-consolation: "I, the Great Sage, have forever uprooted all afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies; my fame is universally renowned, yet even when I reached the Akaniṣṭha heaven, I was still subjected to clamorous slander—how much more so for someone like me!"
Therefore, with a peaceful mind, he cultivated various wholesome deeds.
Because he had definitively discerned such gains and losses through contemplation, the World-Honored One did not first reveal [the truth] himself.

Furthermore, after seven days had passed, the matter manifested of its own accord, revealing the Buddha’s supreme dignity and showing that the fault lay with the non-Buddhists; thus, one should not conclude that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not omniscient on the grounds that he did not reveal it himself.
Precisely for this reason, it should be understood that the objection regarding Devadatta’s own rejection of the cause of slander has already been refuted.
There is a profound intention behind the permission granted for Devadatta to go forth as a monk within the Buddha-dharma.

The Buddha perceived that if this person did not go forth as a monk, he would certainly become a powerful wheel-turning monarch who would harm immeasurable people, destroy the Buddha-dharma, and fall into the evil realms from which it would be difficult to emerge.

By ordaining them, one plants deep roots of merit that those who have not left the household life cannot plant; furthermore, ordination is permitted for the sake of protecting many people so they may be free from harm, and to restrain various evils.
As for the claim that the non-Buddhist Udraka Rāmaputra did not previously know whether his own life would endure or perish, this too is irrational, because he did know it through mindfulness.
It is not the case that when another consciousness arises with respect to another object, one is thereby able to cognize the objects of other [past] consciousnesses.
The Buddha’s mind was previously occupied with the matter of preaching the Dharma and had not yet observed whether that person’s life remained or had ended.
Later, wishing to know this, as soon as he raised his mind, he knew according to reality that the person’s life had already passed.
If one were unable to know that which one desires to know, one could say that the Tathāgata is not omniscient.
To claim that he lacks knowledge simply because his mind is directed toward another object and has not yet apprehended this particular object is unreasonable.
To say that it was not predetermined that such a calamity would arise in Pāṭaliputra is also illogical, because it was secretly predetermined.
It was previously stated with intentional ambiguity (saṃdhāya-vākya) that if one is spared from one [calamity], another will subsequently be harmed by yet another.
This means that the Buddha, having first awakened, realized that if others were left unprotected, they would inevitably be harmed by others.
He therefore instructed each to guard themselves against the three types of hardships; since others could not then cause harm, he spoke with this underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
This is precisely the prediction that difficult matters will necessarily occur; how can it be said that the Blessed One is not omniscient?
To claim that he did not predict in advance that within his own Dharma there would be eighteen distinct schools of tenet-holders is also unreasonable, for he had already predicted this.

As it is said, there will be a community of bhikṣus in the future who do not properly understand the meaning of my words; they will give rise to sectarian attachments and compete with one another in mutual disparagement.

Regarding this, the Blessed One briefly explained two kinds of protection: the internal, which refers to the "Black Exposition" and the "Great Exposition," as manifested in the sūtras through the protection of contemplation;
and the external, which refers to the six "desirable qualities," as taught in the sūtras through the protection of withdrawal.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Saṃyuktāgama*:
"Within my Dharma, there shall be differing explanations: some say that only the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) can suddenly sever the afflictions;
some say that the two dharmas of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and nirvāṇa constitute its essence; others say it is dissociated (*viprayukta*)."
There is no separate substantial entity for "formation" (*saṃskāra*); some say that even manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) does not exist, let alone non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karman*);

some say that all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) have the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their essence; some say that similarity between preceding and succeeding moments constitutes the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);

some say that the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) has only visible color (*varṇa*) as its essence; and some say that the sense-sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) has only the primary elements as its essence.

Some say that only the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) possesses resistance; some say that both the sense-base of tangibles and the sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*) possess resistance;
some say that only the five external sense-bases possess resistance; some say that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is able to see; some say that the conjunction (*sāmagrī*) is able to see;
or some say that both the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*) are both permanent and impermanent. Or...
They assert that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are not momentary; or they assert that non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) endure for multiple moments;

or they assert that there is always a present mind during the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); or they assert that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) also extends to material phenomena;
or they assert that no material phenomenon has a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*); or they assert that there is matter born of maturation (*vipākaja-rūpa*).
Once severed, it may be reconnected; some say that animals, hungry ghosts, and those in the heavenly realms can also obtain the Pratimokṣa precepts;
some say that even with an undefiled mind, one may reconnect [the precepts]; some say that all reconnection occurs through craving or hatred;
some say that the vows of restraint and non-restraint may be received partially or in their entirety; some say [regarding] animals and hungry ghosts...

Regarding ghosts (*preta*), there is the karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*); or it is said that both the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) can sever all afflictions (*kleśa*);
or it is said that not all wholesome, out-flowing wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) constitutes "view" (*dṛṣṭi*);

or it is said that both the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and have objects belonging to other realms; or it is said that all afflictions are [unwholesome].
Some say there is neither pleasure nor equanimity; some say there is only the absence of equanimity;
some say that various forms also exist within the formless realm; some say that those who die in the Heaven of Non-conception all fall into the miserable destinies;
some say that no sentient being dies an untimely death; and some say that all untainted wisdoms have the nature of both knowledge and vision.
Some say that there is no past or future, and that all things exist only in the present, each described individually;
some say that matter and mind are not mutual simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*); some say that at the stage of the *kalala*, all material sense-faculties are already fully possessed;
some say that those who have attained the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) never fall into the evil destinies; and some speak of various wholesome and unwholesome karmas.

All of these can be overturned and refuted: some claim that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) lack a real substantial essence; some claim that mundane paths do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*);

some claim that only those born in Jambudvīpa can give rise to the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), the absence of contention (*araṇā*), the unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the triple samādhi;
and some claim that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) also take non-existent objects as their cognitive domain.

Regarding these various distinctions of contentious arguments, each school articulates its own tenets in numbers exceeding several thousand; these have been transmitted from master to disciple across hundreds of thousands of followers, who explain and extol them for both monastics and laypeople alike.

Within my Buddha-dharma, in future ages there shall be such disputes and disagreements, where for the sake of profit and fame, they will speak evil and grasp it wrongly, failing to realize the reality of the Dharma and manifesting it perversely.
Within this very school, there have likewise been such differences in dispute regarding the past, present, and future.
Although the Blessed One has thus clearly prophesied in advance, his disciples disregard the holy word and, each clinging to their own tenets, mutually revile one another.
The fault lies with the disciple; how could it belong to the World-Honored One?
One must not, on this basis, slander the words of the Omniscient One.

To say that the principle of karma being indeterminate is irrational is also incorrect; since such karma exists, one must necessarily admit the existence of the nature of karma whose maturation is indeterminate.
If this did not exist, then the cultivation of the path to sever the fetters would be in vain, because all karma would necessarily yield its fruit.
One should not, on account of these stated reasons or any other reasons, slander the Omniscient One.
The World-Honored One has accomplished inconceivable and rare merits and possesses a lofty and far-reaching reputation; to slander him unrighteously brings boundless transgression.
All wise people should place their faith in the Buddha, for he is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, and thus one should first pay him homage.

I pay homage to the Teacher of Reality, who has extinguished all darkness in every respect and has pulled sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death; I shall now expound the Abhidharmakośa Śāstra.
The Commentary says:
Although the various terms are general, they each have their specific objects of observation.
What are these specific objects of observation?
This means that the virtue of one's own benefit is fulfilled because of the perfection of wisdom and abandonment;
the virtue of benefiting others is fulfilled because of the completeness of beneficent qualities.

This is omniscience itself, capable of delivering sentient beings; for it possesses the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), as all darkness of every kind is eternally extinguished; it possesses the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), as the darkness regarding all objects of cognition is also eternally extinguished; and it possesses the perfection of the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), as it extends the hand of the True Dharma to pull sentient beings out from the mire of birth and death.
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have extinguished all darkness, because they have not utterly severed defiled ignorance, this is not in every respect;
and because they lack the sublime wisdom capable of eternally extinguishing undefiled ignorance, they do not possess all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
It cannot uproot the darkness of sentient beings; that is to say, just as cataracts can obscure the pure eye, so too does ignorance obstruct true vision.

Just as blinding delusion and gloom can screen off forms and images, so too does ignorance veil the true meaning. When the various superior paths of remedy arise, they cause [this darkness] never to arise again; therefore, it is called "cessation," meaning that all categories of darkness regarding objects are extinguished.

Regarding the statement that "all darknesses are extinguished in every way" and that [the Buddha] "uproots sentient beings from the mire of birth and death": because this birth and death is the place where all sentient beings have been submerged since beginningless time and is difficult to escape, it is likened to mud.

Sentient beings are submerged within this [samsara] without rescue; those who have perfected skillful wisdom and great compassion grant appropriate instruction to pull them out and provide salvation. I pay homage to such a Teacher of Reality (yathārtha-śāstṛ).

I bow my head to the Great Master who possesses the aforementioned virtues of benefit for oneself and others, and who can expound the sublime teaching of reality. Because they lack the requisite intention, latent tendencies, wisdom, and so forth, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not Teachers of Reality; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses such qualities.

The preceding general statement regarding the objects of observation is correct; in order to circulate the teachings he established, he first offers praise and homage to the Teacher who teaches according to reality.

Since the words of praise and homage eliminate all evil obstacles and manifest auspicious omens, he has signaled the commencement of his treatise and thus declares: "I shall now expound the Abhidharmakośa."
What is the Abhidharma?
The verse says:
Pure wisdom along with its attendants is called Abhidharma, as well as the wisdom and treatises that can attain it.
The treatise says:

"Pure" refers to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*); "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). This collectively subsumes the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*).
On what basis is it known that only untainted wisdom is designated as the Abhidharma?
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, permitted Śakra and others to pose their inquiries, as stated in the Sūtra:
"I possess profound Abhidharma and Vinaya; you may inquire of me as you please."
This grants permission for Śakra to inquire about the noble path and the meaning of the fruits realized by that noble path; the *Vatsagotra Sūtra* is likewise.
Furthermore, for what reason is only untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) designated as the Abhidharma?

Because one does not again become deluded after having thus realized the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), is it not the case that realization (*abhisamaya*) is not capable of being achieved by wisdom (*prajñā*) alone?

If that were so, then the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*) would likewise not be wisdom alone. Since the correct awakening to the truth of the [Four] Noble Truths is called realization, the function of realization belongs to wisdom alone and nothing else.
Furthermore, within the context of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is preeminent; because it possesses three capacities, it alone is designated as the Abhidharma.
Nevertheless, this Abhidharma does not exist independently of other factors; therefore, the mental concomitants that accompany wisdom are also called Abhidharma.
The retinue of wisdom is called "concomitants.
What constitutes this retinue?
It refers to the mental factors that arise concomitantly with wisdom—such as form, feeling, perception, and so forth—as well as the mind itself.
Thus, the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) taken collectively are called Abhidharma; this is the ultimate (paramārtha) Abhidharma.
If one speaks of conventional (saṃvṛti) Abhidharma, it refers to those various forms of wisdom and treatises by which this [ultimate Abhidharma] is attained.

This refers to the various types of wisdom—the previously attained untainted faculty of wisdom—which are capable of attaining the three worldly types of wisdom; that is, the superior worldly wisdoms of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), along with their concomitants.

The sequence of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) is explained based on the proximity or distance of their attainment; it is not possible to realize [the fruit] apart from such wisdom and its concomitant untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*). Because this [faculty] is the superior means for attaining this, it shares the name of the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-in-accordance-with-truth) with untainted wisdom, just as the means of loving-kindness (*maitrī-upāya*) is also called "loving-kindness" and so forth.

The treatises refer to these works such as the *Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna*, which are so called because they are the supreme provisions for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*); thus they are also termed "Abhidharma" (Dharma-in-accordance-with), just as the provisions for karma, maturation, outflows, and so forth are themselves termed "karma" and so on.

The aforementioned statement that "all wisdom" also includes innate wisdom (*upapattilābhika-prajñā*) is because it is only innate wisdom that can correctly recite and uphold the Abhidharma treatises; therefore, it is also called "Abhidharma.
But surely this treatise itself is also called "Abhidharma" because it is the supreme provision for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*); why then is it given this distinct name?
The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says:
"Because it summarizes that ultimate [Abhidharma] and relies upon it, this is established by the name *Abhidharmakośa*.
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) says:
"Storehouse" (*piṭaka*) means that which is solid and essential, just as the core of a tree; all the true meanings of the Abhidharma are subsumed within this.
This treatise is the storehouse of that Abhidharma; it is, in other words, the storehouse of the solid and essential meaning of the Abhidharma.

Alternatively, the "basis" (āśraya) is like a sword-sheath; that is, the Abhidharma is the basis for this [Abhidharmakośa], because this treatise was composed by drawing upon the meaning of that [Abhidharma].
Thus, this treatise takes that Abhidharma as its "sheath," which is to say that it takes the Abhidharma as its basis.
On what basis is it taught?
Who taught it first?

Although one should not inquire [in this manner] regarding the teacher of the Abhidharma—since the Buddha’s teaching relies on the Dharma and not on the person—one shall nonetheless reveal the reasons for teaching the Abhidharma, and the person who can teach it should also be made clear.
The verse says:
Apart from the discernment of phenomena, there is truly no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions.
Because of afflictions, the world drifts in the ocean of existence; therefore, for the sake of tranquility, the Great Teacher taught Abhidharma.
The treatise states:
Since there is no superior means other than the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) capable of extinguishing the afflictions that draw forth suffering in the world, the Blessed One said:
"If one has not fully realized or known even a single dharma, I do not say that one can rightly bring an end to suffering."
Because the afflictions have not yet been extinguished in the world, beings transmigrate through birth and death within the ocean of the three realms of existence.

To cause the world to cultivate the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) so that the afflictions—the causes of birth in the three realms—are forever stilled, the Great Teacher first himself expounded the Abhidharma.
If the Buddha did not teach it, even Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas would have been unable to correctly discern the characteristics of all phenomena through reasoned analysis.
Nevertheless, because the Teacher, the Buddha, takes into account the differences in the dispositions of those to be trained, he has taught this in various places in a scattered manner.

The venerable Kātyāyanīputra and other great śrāvakas, through their sublime knowledge of aspirations (*praṇidhijñāna*), examined the teachings and instructions spoken by past Buddhas and compiled them into a formal collection according to what was appropriate, just as the great venerable Kāśyapa and others had previously compiled the Vinaya and the Sūtras together.

The two piṭakas of Sūtra and Vinaya were compiled according to their literal texts, whereas the Abhidharma-piṭaka alone was compiled according to its underlying meaning; as it is said, regarding the compilation of meanings, the Abhidharma is superior to both the Vinaya and the Sūtras.
The Abhidharma was compiled in accordance with the Buddha’s holy teaching; thus, being permitted by the Buddha, it receives the name "the word of the Buddha.
What are the dharmas that are to be investigated?
Based upon what did the Blessed One teach the Abhidharma?
The verse says:
Contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena— With the exception of the Path,
all other conditioned phenomena Are called "contaminated" because contaminants increase in accordance with them.
The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena—namely, space and the two types of cessation. Among these, space is characterized by non-obstruction;
analytical cessation is defined as dissociation from fetters, which is distinct for each specific object of bondage.
That which ultimately obstructs what is to arise Attains separately the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The Commentary says:
It is taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are briefly of two kinds: first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), and second, those without outflows (*anāsrava*); this is the general statement.
Next, we shall explain this individually: conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), excluding the Noble Truth of the Path, are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
What, then, are these? They are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As it is said: "What is called the aggregate of grasping at form?
It refers to contaminated form that accords with various forms of grasping," and so on, up to consciousness, which is likewise.
For what reason is the aggregate of grasping termed "contaminated"?
Because the outflows increase therein,
the name "outflow" (āsrava) is applied to the various afflictions such as the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), because they cause the defiled mind to constantly leak and flow forth.
Because they are associated with the outflows (*āsrava*), have the outflows as their object, and increase (*anuśerate*) the outflows, they are called "outflow-increasing" (*āsravānuśaya*).
The meaning of "increasing" as "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) will be discussed extensively later.

From this, it should be understood that all latent tendencies of afflictions that belong to different realms or stages, as well as those that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, are excluded from being "outflow-increasing"; since these do not mutually increase one another, they are not established in relation to one another as such.
Regarding these two names, "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*), what further characteristics do they possess?
As the Blessed One said:

"Dharmas with outflows refer to all form (*rūpa*) that accords with the various graspings (*upādāna*), which serves to increase the sense of grasping at existence; this is explained in detail up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is likewise."
That which is the opposite of this is the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma.
Such, in brief, are the characteristics of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted.
Furthermore, that which is tainted is said to belong to the mundane world (*loka*), whereas that which transcends the mundane world is called untainted.

That which is comprised within the world is called "fallen into the world" (*loka-patita*); this means to abide in the world without emerging from it. The term "world" (*loka*) is established based on the essence of the Truth of Suffering;
therefore, a sutra says: "I shall now proclaim for you the world and the origin of the world."
Furthermore, the five aggregates of clinging are called "suffering" and "with outflows" (*sāsrava*); thus, we know that "with outflows" refers to that which falls within the mundane world (*loka*).
How do we know that all things falling within the mundane world are dharmas with outflows?
As the Blessed One said:
I shall now proclaim for you the phenomena that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*).

As for phenomena with outflows, they refer to all eyes, all forms, all eye-consciousnesses, and all eye-contact; and whatever internal feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arise conditioned by eye-contact.

In this way, it extends even to falling into worldly mind, falling into worldly phenomena, falling into worldly mental consciousness, and falling into worldly mental contact; as explained at length, these are called tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

As for untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), they refer to supramundane mind, supramundane mental objects, supramundane mental consciousness, and supramundane mind-contact; explained at length, these are termed untainted phenomena.
Based on this sacred teaching and through correct reasoning, one knows that all that falls within the world is contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Having already explained what is contaminated and the causes of contamination, what is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
The Noble Truth of the Path and the three unconditioned phenomena are termed "untainted" (anāsrava).
The Noble Truth of the Path refers to that which is not the five aggregates of tainted form and so forth.
The three unconditioned phenomena refer to space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation.
This space (*ākāśa*) and the noble truth of the path (*mārga-āryasatya*) are termed the untainted cause (*anāsrava-hetu*).
The path has already been explained previously; the noble truths shall be analyzed in detail later.

Among the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) briefly mentioned, space has non-obstruction as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because all phenomena appear therein with extreme clarity and without hindrance, it is called space.

This means that because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the collection of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are all incapable of universally covering or obstructing, or because [space] is neither that which is obstructed nor that which obstructs, it is said that the characteristic of space is non-obstruction.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has disjunction (*visamyoga*) as its intrinsic nature.

"Deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to the wisdom (*prajñā*) accomplished through effort in accordance with reality; because it involves the analytical discernment of the individual aspects of each of the four noble truths in accordance with reality, it is called "deliberation."

The state of permanent dissociation from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) obtained through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it certainly prevents the arising of the acquisition of those fetters (*bandhana*).
Alternatively, since there may be cessation that is not dissociation, the term "dissociation" is stated to distinguish it from such cases.
Some say: "All dharmas that are abandoned share the same analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because there is no distinction between them.
However, the great masters of the Abhidharma all say:
They differ according to the specific objects with which they are bound. Why is this so?
If these were one, there would be the fault that cultivating other remedial paths would be rendered useless.

If all that is to be abandoned shares the same analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), when the cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned by the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* is realized, is the cessation of other afflictions also realized?
If it were realized, then the cultivation of other remedial paths would be rendered useless.
If it were not realized, then one object would realize only a portion of itself and not the rest, which contradicts reason because it entails the fallacy of having parts.
Therefore, one must certainly admit that the entities of dissociation correspond in number to the entities of bondage; this does not contradict correct reasoning.

Regarding those without counterparts: this analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) itself has no similar cause (sabhāga-hetu), nor is it the cause of anything else; thus, it eternally obstructs future arising and constitutes non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Discrimination (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is precisely the wisdom established through correct reasoning as previously explained.
That which prevents the arising of future phenomena by means of this wisdom is called non-discrimination cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

For example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on one visible form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass away moment by moment; with respect to those [objects], the corresponding portions of the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) attain non-discrimination cessation. This is because the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) and a portion of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñānakāya*) can never arise again with respect to objects already ceased, since they take only simultaneous objects as their conditions.

Because the activity of arising is dependent upon its simultaneous basis and conditions, if a phenomenon can obstruct the activity of another phenomenon's arising, this [obstructing] phenomenon—being distinct from analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā*)—certainly prevents that [other] phenomenon from remaining in the future and never arising; therefore, it is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is not the case that a phenomenon will never arise again simply because its conditions were lacking; for when it later encounters conditions of a similar kind, it ought to arise once more.

That is to say, even if that phenomenon did not arise previously due to the absence of conditions, what obstacle could prevent it from arising when it subsequently encounters conditions of a similar kind?
It was previously stated that, with the exception of the Path, all other conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
What is meant by "conditioned"?
The verse says:
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena— namely the five aggregates such as form, and so forth—
are also called "paths of the world," "bases of speech," "possessing departure," "possessing objects," and so on.
The treatise says:
Because they are concealed, accumulated, impaired, and suppressed by various calamities such as old age, sickness, and death, they are called *skandhas* (aggregates).
To distinguish them from the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth, the term "form" (*rūpa*) and the others are used.

While the five aggregates beginning with ethical discipline cannot fully encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), the five aggregates beginning with form do fully encompass them; therefore, this specific designation is made. As for the term "conditioned," it is because they are produced through the collective operation of a multitude of causes and conditions.
The future has not yet arisen; how, then, can it be called conditioned?

Just as firewood is so called because it belongs to that category, so too do all dharmas that are not destined to arise not transcend that category; thus, although they never actually arise, they are still described as conditioned.
In various sūtras, the Blessed One has designated them by names such as "world-path" (*loka-vīthi*) according to their meaning. What, then, are they?

It is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are also called "world-paths. Because the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, and because they flow through the paths of the future, present, and past, or because they are devoured by impermanence, they are termed "world-paths."
Although various non-arising phenomena do not arise due to the deficiency of conditions, there is no error in establishing the name for them because they belong to that same category.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena are also called the "basis of names" (*nāma-āśraya*).

"Speech" refers to vocal sounds, or it is said to be that which can express; it is called the "basis" because it is that upon which the name depends, whether near or far. This is because both the meaning and the name are collectively said to depend on speech.
Since the name depends on the meaning and speech in turn depends on the name, speech as the basis collectively subsumes both name and meaning.
Thus, name and meaning together encompass the five aggregates.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"There are three bases for speech, not four, nor five."
Based on this excellent commentary on the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, it states that they are "designated in reliance upon" (*upādāya*) what is subsumed within the five aggregates.
Here, "reliance" (*upādāna*) carries the sense of a cause; since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack effects, they are not "designated in reliance upon."
Furthermore, if three factors are obtainable within a collection—namely, speech, its basis, and the designation based on meaning—it is called a "basis for designation.
Within a collection of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), there is only the meaning; because it lacks speech as its basis, it is not called a "basis for designation."

Some say that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) possesses both the basis and the meaning [of being a support for speech], but because it lacks the actual words, it is not called a "support for speech" (nāmanāśraya).
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena possess the sense of arising simultaneously with the entity that constitutes speech, whereas the unconditioned does not.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are also called "possessing departure" (*saniḥsāra*). "Departure" (*niḥsāra*) refers to eternal departure, which is precisely *nirvāṇa*; because once it is attained, one does not return to fall into birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are said to "possess departure" by virtue of having that departure.

One who possesses wealth is called "wealthy"; likewise, although this [noble path] is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not everything, because the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are excluded.

Furthermore, at the time of nirvāṇa, one also abandons the noble path; therefore, it is called "possessing detachment" (*saviyoga*), for it is taught that the noble path is like a raft and should also be relinquished.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are also called "possessing a basis" (*savastuka*); "basis" (*vastu*) refers to that which is the support or the locus, which is to say, it has the meaning of a cause.
The fruit depends upon the cause because it arises from the cause, just as a child depends upon its mother.
Alternatively, the fruit abides in the cause and is able to conceal the cause, just as a person sits upon a bed.
This signifies that the cause is obscured by the fruit; this is because the cause and fruit exist sequentially, and because they possess the natures of being subtle and gross, respectively.
Because these possess an object (*vastu*), they are said to be "with an object" (*savastuka*), as illustrated by the previous examples.
Such categories describe conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding the various distinctions among the names for these aforementioned conditioned phenomena, the verse says:
That which is with outflows is called the aggregates of grasping;
it is also described as being with contention, as well as suffering, the origin [of suffering], the world, the locus of views, the three realms of existence, and so forth.
The commentary says:
It was previously stated that, with the exception of the Path, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Having already analyzed their essential nature, I shall now restate this in order to clarify their differing designations and conceptual definitions, as well as their specific distinctions.

It has already been stated that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are called aggregates (*skandha*); now it is stated that those which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*). By this principle, those without outflows (*anāsrava*) receive the name "aggregate" alone.
The designation "clinging" (*upādāna*) is established exclusively for the outflows, because they are able to grasp at the three realms of existence;
or because they are able to maintain the karma that leads to future existence, those outflows are therefore called "clinging," and the five aggregates—form and the rest—arise from them.
Because they give rise to grasping (*upādāna*), they are called the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), like fire made of grass or chaff, or like a tree with flowers and fruit.

All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are also called "contentious" (*saraṇa*); that is to say, the term "contention" is established for the afflictions (*kleśa*) because they disturb wholesome qualities and cause harm to oneself and others.
The aggregates (skandha) coexist with conflict (raṇa), or they arise together with the aggregates of conflict; therefore, they are called "with-conflict" (saraṇa).
This meaning demonstrates that neither conflict nor the aggregates can arise if even one of them is missing.

The word "and" (*ca*) indicates other designations for that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*); that is to say, it may be called "suffering" (*duḥkha*), because the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are the locus upon which all forms of oppression depend, and because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is heavy and unstable.

It is sometimes called "origination" (*samudaya*), because that very category can act as a cause and can bring about accumulation; that is to say, from the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), the aggregates of grasping are accumulated. It is also called the "world" (*loka*), because it is subject to destruction.
As the Blessed One has said:
"That which is subject to destruction by nature is called the world (*loka*).

It is not that the nature of the noble paths (*āryamārga*) is subject to destruction and thus called the world; for within them, there is no counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) to bring about their destruction.

Alternatively, they are called "bases of views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), because the five views, such as the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, abide therein and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase accordingly.

Since those various views, with respect to all types of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), at all times and without distinction of aspect, persistently cling and remain unshakable while their latent tendencies increase, their essence and function become particularly intense; therefore, they are explained separately.
Greed and the others, as well as delusion and doubt, are not like this; for while greed and the others may exist in all aspects, they do not exist at all times.
Delusion exists at all times and is not without differentiation, whereas doubt, though lacking differentiation, does not involve firm adherence.
Therefore, the outflowing (sāsrava) states are not mentioned in that context.
Alternatively, they are called the "three existences" (trai-dhātu), because they are the cause of existence, the basis of existence, and are subsumed within the three existences.

The word "etc. is used to include those termed "defiled" (saṃkliṣṭa) and so forth; such categories as these are outflowing dharmas, possessing various specific names according to their respective meanings.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti*, Fascicle One;
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Two,
composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Two, Part Two: Discerning the Fundamental Bases. As stated above, the five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*), are termed conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is the aggregate of form?
The verse says:
Form consists solely of the five faculties, the five objects, and the unmanifest.
The treatise states:
Herein, the term "matter" (rūpa) signifies the aggregate of matter (rūpaskandha).
The five faculties refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five objects (*viṣaya*) are visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
They are called "objects" because they are what is apprehended by the eye and the other [senses].
Furthermore, "and the unmanifest" refers to the matter included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
"Only" means that only these ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base as thus revealed are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of these various forms?
The verse says:
That consciousness relies upon pure matter; these are called the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
The commentary states:
"That" refers to the aforementioned five faculties, beginning with the eye.
"Consciousness" refers to the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
"Basis" refers to that upon which these five consciousnesses depend.

Such a basis has pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as its essence; thus, it is revealed that the pure matter which serves as the basis for the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth is designated as the "eye-faculty" and the other faculties.
Therefore, the Bhagavān stated in the sūtras:
"The sense faculties, such as the eye, have pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as their characteristic.
The treatise (*śāstra*) likewise states:
What is the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?
Its nature is pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that serves as the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*).

Thus, it is explained at length in the various sacred teachings (*āgama*) that the faculties distinguish the consciousnesses, whereas the objects do not; therefore, we know that those words reveal the faculties and not the objects.
Some say: That [object] is an object-field (*viṣaya*) and not a sense-faculty (*indriya*), yet there is no consciousness [of it], because it takes form and so forth as its object.

The consciousnesses of form and so forth are named after their respective bases; thus, the designation "eye-consciousness" and so on would be erroneous, since they are distinguished by the term "pure matter" (*rūpaprasāda*).
Having already analyzed the characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*), one should now analyze the characteristics of their objects (*viṣaya*).
The verse says:
Visible form is of two kinds, or twenty; Sound has only two types.
Taste has six types; odor has four; and touch has eleven as its nature.
The treatise says:
"The term 'form' (rūpa) has two meanings," which refers to the two types of objects: namely, color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
Among these, there are twelve kinds of visible color (*varṇa*) and eight kinds of shape (*saṃsthāna*);
thus, they may total twenty. The twelve visible colors are: blue, yellow, red, white, smoke, cloud, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
Among the twelve [types of color], the four such as blue and so forth are the primary manifest colors, while the eight types such as clouds and so forth are their variations.
Those meanings that are obscure shall now be briefly explained.
The vapor rising from the earth and water is called mist (*nīhāra*).
When it obstructs the arising of light, the remaining colors visible therein are called shadows (*chāyā*);
the opposite of this is darkness (*andhakāra*).
The flame of the sun is called "light" (*āloka*).
The flames of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, precious gems, lightning, and so forth are called "clarity" (*ābhā*).
As for the eight types of shape (*saṃsthāna*), they are: long, short, square, round, high, low, regular, and irregular.
Among these, "regular" (samyak) refers to the equality of shape;
that which is unequal in shape is called "irregular" (asamyak).
Other forms are easy to understand, and therefore they are not explained here.
The sense base of form has already been explained; now the sense base of sound shall be explained.
It is called "sound" because it has the capacity to summon or call out, or simply because it is a resonance;
thus do the teachings of the Sugata universally declare.
Sound is the objective sphere apprehended by the auditory faculty; it is of the nature of derived matter produced from the four great elements.
This sound is of two kinds: namely, that which is appropriated (*upātta*) and that which is non-appropriated (*anupātta*).

With the primary elements as their cause, those that are appropriated consist of the great elements of present sentient beings—namely, those that are nourished, those that are outflows, and those that are maturations, such as the earth element;
those contrary to this are called non-appropriated. Sound is produced from these two types [of elements].
The same should be said for visible form and the other [sense objects].
However, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the sound-base (*śabda-āyatana*) is difficult to discern, it is described as being of two kinds solely with respect to its causes:

first, that which has the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—whether appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated—as its cause; and second, that which is the distinct result of each of the four great elements.
The two sets of the four great elements do not together produce a single result, for this would entail the fault of [the elements] being simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.

Although the two sets of great elements may strike against each other, they function as causes to produce sounds individually, based on their respective supports; thus, they do not constitute three entities.

Although there are two sounds produced by the cause of hands striking a drum, which compete with one another such that it is difficult to discern their distinct characteristics as they arise, for this reason, the sphere of sound (śabdāyatana) consists of only two types.
The sphere of sound has already been explained; now the sphere of taste shall be explained.
The reason for departing from the sequential order is to demonstrate that there is no fixed certainty regarding the arising of consciousness with respect to its objects.
"Taste" refers to that which is consumed; it carries the meaning of being something that can be tasted.
This [taste] is of six kinds, distinguished by the differences of sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland.
Having explained the sphere of taste (*rasāyatana*), the sphere of odor (*gandhāyatana*) shall now be explained.
Odor refers to that which is smelled; it is of four kinds, distinguished as pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and those that are both equal and unequal.
Regarding "equal" and "unequal": they differ because the physical bases upon which increase and decrease depend are distinct.
Some say they differ because of the distinction between the feeble and the intense.
The root treatise states:
There are three kinds of fragrance: pleasant fragrance, unpleasant fragrance, and neutral fragrance.
That which can nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements is called pleasant fragrance;
that which is contrary to this is called unpleasant fragrance.
That which lacks the first two functions is called "equal fragrance.
That which is produced through the predominance of superior meritorious karma is called "excellent fragrance.
If it is produced through the predominance of superior non-meritorious karma, it is called "unwholesome fragrance."
That which arises through the predominance of the four great elements is called "equal fragrance.
Having explained the sphere of fragrance, the sphere of tangibles shall now be explained.

Tangible objects refer to that which is touched; they have eleven as their nature, meaning that eleven real entities constitute their substance. These are the four great elements and the seven derivative tangibles: smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, and cold, hunger, and thirst, due to their distinct differences.
Among these, who are the "one that touches" and the "that which is touched"?

It should be understood that there is absolutely no "one that touches" or "that which is touched"; for if they were to touch, their nature would be lost due to their momentary character (*kṣaṇikatva*). Rather, the designation "contact" is established merely when the body-consciousness arises in immediate succession from its basis (*āśraya*) and its object (*ālambana*).
When the object is apprehended by this faculty-consciousness (indriya-vijñāna), it is conventionally said that "this faculty can touch that object.
Since contact (spraṣṭavya) is not the basis for body-consciousness, it is not said that "that contact can touch the body-faculty."
Because the tangible object and the body faculty are in immediate proximity, it is said that the tangible is what is touched and nothing else.
Although visible form and the other [objects] do not possess the nature of being tangible, they are nonetheless impaired when their basis is destroyed.
The characteristics of the objects have already been explained; now, the unmanifest (avijñapti) alone remains to be analyzed.
The verse says:
"Arising from volition and other minds, as well as being informative even when there is no mind."
That which is non-obstructive and derived [matter] is called non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes both informative action (*vijñapti*) and non-obstructive derived matter that is not informative; briefly, there are two types.
The first is based on manifestation (*vijñapti*), and the second is based on the mind (*citta*).

That which arises based on manifestation is further of two kinds: namely, that which evolves simultaneously with an action (*kriyā-sahabhū*), and that which evolves as a consequence of an action (*anu-vartaka*).
In order to encompass the essential characteristics of these various types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) without omission, the terms "action" (*kriyā*) and so forth are stated.

Regarding the phrase "other minds" (*cittāntara*), the term "and so forth" includes similar types of mind; that is, when a wholesome mind acts as the immediate cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*) or the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the unobstructed derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by it is wholesome. Minds that are unwholesome or neutral are termed "other minds," while the wholesome mind is termed "similar.

When an unwholesome mind acts as the immediate cause or the co-existent cause, the unobstructed derived form produced by it is unwholesome; minds that are wholesome or neutral are termed "other minds," while the unwholesome mind is termed "similar."

"Furthermore, for those without mind" refers to the state where the mind has ceased; that is, it is not in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) nor at birth (*upapatti*), because [the mind] is absent in the state of birth.

The word "furthermore" (*ca*) carries over from above and indicates that this applies to these cases and no others. Among the three states, this [non-restraint] may persist in accordance with the following: in the case of meditative absorption, it is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*); in the case of birth, it is unwholesome as well as other scattered wholesome states (*kuśala*), because it operates throughout all three states.
"Having a definition" (savijñapti) means being capable of being defined as either wholesome or unwholesome, because they belong to the categories of the agreeable and the disagreeable.
"Non-resistant" (apratigha) means not being composed of atoms (paramāṇu).
Regarding their being "derived" (bhautika), this does not exclude the primary elements (mahābhūta), because the nature of the primary elements is not non-resistant.
This merely excludes what is non-material; it reveals that this material nature is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) among the five aggregates.
"Is" refers to the various characteristics previously described; possessing those aforementioned characteristics is termed unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Having thus explained the characteristics of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*),
regarding what was stated therein— that it is "derived from the primary elements" (*bhūta-nirmita*)— what are these primary elements?
The verse says:
The great elements (mahābhūta) refer to the four realms: earth, water, fire, and wind.
They perform the functions of supporting and so forth, and possess the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
The commentary states:
For what reason are these primary elements (*mahābhūta*) called "elements" (*dhātu*)?
Because they are the source from which all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) arise, and because the primary elements themselves arise from the primary elements.
That which serves as the source of arising is termed an "element" in the world, just as gold ore is called a "gold element" and so forth.
Alternatively, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they are the source from which various kinds of suffering arise, as illustrated by the previous analogy.
Some say: they are called elements because they can maintain both the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
These various elements are also called "great primary elements" (*mahābhūta*). Why are they called "elements" (*bhūta*)?
Why are they called "great" (*mahat*)?
When various derivative forms (*upādāyarūpa*) arise in their diverse distinctions, these [primary elements] are able to give rise to each respective category; therefore, they are called "elements."
Due to the distinctions among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are distinctions among derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). Some say:
because the predominant influence of the karma of sentient beings has never been absent since beginningless time, it is therefore called a "seed" (*bīja*).

Because the general characteristics and categories of the four great elements are continuous and uninterrupted, or because when phenomena arise they are termed "existence" (*bhava*), and they cause the nature of existence to grow, they are therefore called "elements" (*dhātu*).

It is that which causes the existence-nature of all phenomena to grow and arise; or it has the sense of causing the bodies of sentient beings to grow and arise; or it is that which can manifest the ten kinds of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). For this reason, it is called "seed" (*bīja*), because those [phenomena] are manifested through its power.
That which is called "great" is so because it possesses great function.

As for "great function," it refers to the four kinds of superior operations within the fundamental matters of all sentient beings; based upon these, consciousness and emptiness are established, whereby they may be described as the foundation of sentient beings.
Furthermore, among the things that deceive and delude the foolish, these four are the most preeminent; therefore, they are called "great.
Just as among bridges and thieves, those whose activities are superior are distinguished from others and thus termed "great bridges" and "great thieves."
Furthermore, these four kinds serve as the universal basis for all other forms; they are called "great" because of their extensiveness.
Some say they are called "great" because solidity and the other qualities are fully present within every aggregate of form and so forth.

In the aggregate where wind predominates, visible form and the other [qualities] are absent; in the aggregate where fire predominates, darkness and the others are absent. In the various aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), odor and taste are entirely non-existent. Within an aggregate of blue and so forth, yellow and the others are absent; within an aggregate of smoothness and so forth, roughness and the others are absent. Since sound and the others are not fixed [in this manner], only these four are designated as "great" (*mahābhūta*).
Although these four great elements are always in combination and never separated from one another, they do not occupy the same location.
How is it known that they are never separated?
Because it is so stated in such texts as the *Garbhāvakrāntimahābhūta-sūtra*, and because it is also logically necessary.
What is the reasoning?

It is because within stones and other such objects, the three activities of cohesion, the generation of fire, and the increase of gravity are presently observable; therefore, one knows that water, fire, and wind are constantly inseparable therein.
Within a mass of water, the three activities of supporting a boat, possessing heat, and flowing can be observed; therefore, one knows that earth, fire, and wind are constantly inseparable from it.
Within the flame, the three activities of supporting, gathering, and vibrating are presently observable; therefore, one knows that earth, water, and wind are constantly inseparable within it.

Within the aggregate of wind, there are presently present the three functions of supporting, generating, and manifesting cold and warm tactile sensations; therefore, one knows that earth, water, and wind are constantly inseparable within it.
Furthermore, how is it known that these four elements exist?
It is because they constantly follow one another due to this causal condition, and because they are able to accomplish their respective functions, such as supporting.

That is to say, the elements of earth and so forth accomplish, respectively, the four types of activities: supporting, cohesion, maturation, and growth. Because of this causal condition, if the four activities of supporting and so forth are observed within any aggregate of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*), one knows that the elements of earth and so forth exist therein, mutually inseparable from one another.
It should be understood that the term "capable of extending" (*prasaraka*) here refers to being able to arrange or deploy. How does it arrange?
It means causing [the afflictions] to increase or to overflow.
Are the four functions, such as upholding and so forth, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the elements (*dhātu*)? No. Why is this so?
These four elements possess, respectively, solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion as their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It should be understood that here the "nature" (*prakṛti*) is mentioned to reveal the "substance" (*dravya*), in order to clarify that substance and nature are not mutually separable.
"Motion" refers to that which can lead the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) to arise in succession and reach another location.
Why is space not called a primary element?
Because the characteristics of a primary element are not established in it.
They are designated as "great elements" (mahābhūta) because they are capable of causing benefit or harm; space is not so, and therefore it is not a great element.
Alternatively, because their intrinsic nature does not differ during the states of arising and ceasing of all phenomena, it is not a great element.

We observe that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), through the transformation of their characteristics during stages such as the seed, serve as the conditions for the arising of sprouts and other subsequent states; it is only then that the various stages, such as the sprout, are able to come into existence.
Space (*ākāśa*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not like this; because their nature and characteristics are eternal, they possess no functional activity whatsoever.
Since it cannot produce anything, it is not a great element (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, the various great elements are neither unitary nor permanent; they possess manifold specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and their results are infinitely diverse.

Space, however, has a nature that is unitary and permanent, its characteristics are without differentiation, and it possesses no results at all. It is not the case that a distinct result can arise from a cause that lacks distinction; therefore, space is not called a great element.

If it is claimed that other causes possess distinctions that can assist space in producing distinct effects, then these distinct causes themselves are capable of producing those distinct effects; what need is there to insist upon this space as a cause?
Are the elements such as earth and so forth identical to earth and so forth? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
Earth refers to visible form and shape; names are established according to worldly convention.
Water and fire are likewise; wind is both an element and so too.
The treatise says:
The term "earth" (pṛthivī) expresses only the sense-fields of visible form and shape.
Since earth is not composed of four sense-fields in total, why is it said that only visible form and shape constitute earth?
Although odor, taste, and tangibility are present therein, this statement is made in accordance with worldly convention;
for when people in the world point out earth, they do so by indicating its color and shape.
Although people in the world also employ the term "earth" in reference to odors and so forth— saying, for example,
"I am now smelling the earth," "tasting the earth," or "touching the earth"—
it is because color and shape can universally represent the elements of earth, water, and fire that they are specifically mentioned here.
In the world, one does not commonly say, "I smell water," nor does one frequently say, "I smell or taste fire.

Although one speaks of touching earth and so forth, these are immediately the earth and other elements; therefore, although odors and so on exist within earth, because shape and color are predominant, they are mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, visible form and shape indicate that there is no difference between the two realms or the various levels; therefore, they are mentioned specifically.
If that were so, then since visible form and shape also indicate things such as clothing more clearly than odors and so forth, they should likewise be mentioned specifically [in those contexts].
Worldly designations and concepts lack any fixed certainty; therefore, they are spoken of according to worldly distinctions.

These names are established following the majority of worldly conceptions; since birth and so forth do not manifest as sounds or as continuities, they are not designated as "earth" or "cloth" and the like.
Just as earth has manifest color and shape as its essence, so too do water and fire; this is because they follow worldly convention.
Since people in the world commonly perceive water as blue, long, and so forth, it is said that manifest color and shape constitute the intrinsic nature of water.
In the world, fire is also perceived as being red, long, and so forth; therefore, it is said that color and shape constitute the intrinsic nature of fire.

However, when those very same [elements] undergo transformation through color and touch, they are termed "flame" or "charcoal. These are merely conventional designations and not real entities, because no single substantial entity can be apprehended by either the body or the eye. The distinction between the elements such as earth and their respective realms (*dhātu*) is likewise [conventional].
If wind is identical to the element (dhātu), it is because the world establishes the name "wind" based on movement; thus, wind and the wind-element are not distinct.
But is it not the case that the world also forms the conceptualization of "wind" with respect to visible form and shape?
Because the world currently manifests [these elements] through the appearance of black winds and whirlwinds, there is a response to this objection:
it is said that "manifestation" (saṃdarśana) has a meaning distinct from the [actual] elements (dhātu), such as earth and so forth.
The masters of antiquity all maintain this explanation:
it appears thus because the earth is interspersed therein; furthermore, the word "thus" is used again to demonstrate that this wind is indeed the wind element itself.
This refers to the definition.

Between these two explanations, the former is superior because there is no distinction between the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) and the *aśubha* (impurity), and because the *aśubha* takes only the objective sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object.
The verse says:
Herein, the faculties and their objects are precisely what are called the ten bases and elements (*āyatana* and *dhātu*).
The commentary says:

It has already been stated that the substantial entities of the sense faculties (*indriya*), their objects (*viṣaya*), and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) constitute the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Among these, the faculties and objects are also designated as the ten bases (*āyatana*) and the ten elements (*dhātu*).
Within the system of the bases (*āyatanamukha*), they are established as the ten bases, namely: the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*) and so forth.
