Within the classification of the *dhātus*, these are established as the ten *dhātus*, namely the eye-*dhātu* and so forth.

Having already explained the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) along with its establishment as bases (*āyatanas*) and elements (*dhātus*), we shall now explain the three aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*).
The verse says:
Feeling has the nature of experiencing; perception has the nature of grasping images;
the four remaining [aggregates] are called the aggregate of formations; thus are these three, beginning with feeling.
Together with the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these are called the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The treatise says:
That which arises following contact, and which experiences contact that is agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral, is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
"Appropriation" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of "that which experiences.
How does this feeling appropriate in accordance with contact?
It is because feeling is the immediate fruit of contact.

The term "conforming to contact" (*anuvyañjana*) is used here to indicate the sense of a cause, because it conforms to sensation, just as with the expression "conforming characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*).
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to that which manifests; that is, it is that which can display.
Since a cause can manifest its effect, the name "characteristic" is established.
This term "concomitant characteristic" (anulakṣaṇa) has the meaning of being "conducive to the cause.
Feeling (vedanā) is able to experience and is conducive to the cause of contact (sparśa); therefore, it is said that feeling experiences in accordance with contact.
As the Blessed One said:
There are contacts conducive to pleasant feeling, contacts conducive to painful feeling, and contacts conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
that is to say, they have the meaning of being conducive to the arising of pleasant feeling and so forth.

The experience that accords with the contact is called "feeling by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*); however, experiencing the object is also a characteristic of feeling. It is difficult to discern the distinct characteristics of feeling from other mental factors that share the same object, because all such factors are alike in their experience of the object.

When the mind and mental factors grasp an object, all of them are termed "experiencing their own respective objects. Therefore, it is said that the specific nature of feeling (*vedanā*) consists solely in experiencing the contact (*sparśa*), because its distinct characteristic is fixed.
The experience of an object is called "grasping-feeling" (*upādāna-vedanā*); this is not what is being discussed here, because its characteristics are indeterminate.
The distinctions between the two types of feeling should be understood as they are extensively analyzed in the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Pañcavastuka*.
These are generally stated as three, but specifically stated as six, because there are distinctions between the worlds and their bases.
Regarding the third aggregate, that of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): what is its essential nature? Its nature consists in the apprehension of images within objects of cognition.

That is to say, it apprehends—just as they appear—the objects of cognition, such as forms established according to their original designations as blue, long, and so forth; sounds such as those of lutes and conchs; fragrances such as those of lotuses; tastes such as bitter and pungent; tangibles such as smooth and rough; and phenomena such as arising and ceasing. Because it apprehends these according to their characteristics, it is called perception.
This perception is generally described as threefold from the perspective of the world, but is specifically described as sixfold when distinguished by their bases.
What is the essential nature of the fourth aggregate, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

It has as its nature the remaining formations other than those four; that is to say, with the exception of the three previously mentioned—form, feeling, and perception—and with the exception of consciousness, which will be discussed as the fourth, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called the aggregate of formations.
These consist of volition and so forth, as well as acquisition and so forth, which are respectively associated and dissociated [with the mind].
As for why the sūtra speaks only of the "six groups of volition," it is because they are the most preeminent.
Why is this so? Volition is the nature of karma;
as the cause that brings about its fruit, its power is the strongest.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
If one is able to perform that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called the aggregate of formations and grasping (*saṃskāra-upādānaskandha*).

One cannot say that volition (*cetanā*) alone constitutes the aggregate of formations, because it is established as a collective designation, just like the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) or the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

If it were otherwise, it would have to be designated simply as "volition" (*cetanā*), because it would be established as a single dharma, just like the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

The intention here is to clarify that, just as the term "dharma-sphere" (*dharmāyatana*)—the sixth external sphere—is established as a collective name and thus subsumes all eleven [factors], whereas the seventeen spheres and elements do not subsume many dharmas; so too, the term "volition" (*cetanā*) is established as a collective name and thus subsumes the four aggregates [of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness] without subsuming all formations. Therefore, one knows that the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is not merely volition.
Thus, because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) does not exhaust all bases, it is categorized into three types only by way of the time periods (*adhvan*).
Just as the essence of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) was previously analyzed, it is likewise established through the two gates of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
Having thus explained the essential natures of the three aggregates—feeling, perception, and formations—they should likewise be established as bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

That is to say, these three aggregates, together with unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), constitute seven factors that are established as the "base of mental objects" (*dharmāyatana*) within the system of bases, and as the "element of mental objects" (*dharmadhātu*) within the system of elements.
Regarding the fifth aggregate, consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), what are its intrinsic nature, bases, and elements?
The verse says:
"Consciousness is the respective discernment [of objects]; this is also called the mind-base (*manāyatana*)."
And one should know that the seven elements [are also included]; the six consciousnesses transform into the mind-element (*manas*).

The treatise says: "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to that which cognizes; this is the sense of merely grasping the general characteristics of an object. To grasp the general characteristics of various respective objects is called "individual cognition" (*prativijñapti*). That is to say, consciousness is only able to grasp the general characteristics of an object, and is not able to grasp the specific distinctions within those objective characteristics.
As the Blessed One said:
"That which cognizes is called consciousness. Other masters say:

The designation of an "agent" is applied to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) merely as a conventional expression, in order to preclude the notion that there is a cognizer existing apart from consciousness.
Where else, moreover, is such an agent seen to be designated merely upon the nature of phenomena?
It is observed that a shadow is said to be capable of movement;
although it lacks actual motion when it arises uninterruptedly in different locations, it is nonetheless described as an agent.

Consciousness is likewise: when it arises in a continuous succession across different objects, although it lacks actual motion, it is described as a cognizer, for it can indeed cognize its objects; thus, there is no fault in this.
How is this known to be so?
Because it is observed elsewhere that the agent is negated.
As the Blessed One told Potaliputra:
I never say that there is one who can fully comprehend it.
Furthermore, some say:
"The momentary [dharma] is called the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the continuity is called the agent."
This will be further demonstrated within the "Dependent Origination through the Intentional Establishment" (*abhiprāyika-pratītyasamutpāda*) that I have formulated.
This consciousness is generally described as threefold according to its temporal periods, and is divided into six types based on its respective supporting faculties (*indriya*).

It should be understood that this very aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) mentioned above is established as the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) within the system of bases (āyatana-mukha), and as seven elements (dhātu) within the system of elements (dhātu-mukha). Furthermore, by means of sound, the unity [of the aggregate] is revealed while being analyzed into two categories, thereby showing how each individual essence of consciousness is divided into bases and elements.
What are the seven elements?
They are the six consciousnesses and the mind, namely, from the visual-consciousness element up to the mental-consciousness element.
These very six consciousnesses, when they have ceased, become the mind element.
One should know that these distinct presentations of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) exhaustively encompass all phenomena.
Herein, one should reflect:

if the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is designated as the seven mind-elements (manodhātu), and it was previously stated that the aggregate of consciousness is divided into six based on its respective supporting faculties (indriya), then what further dharma, apart from the six consciousnesses, is here called the mind-element (manodhātu)?
There is no other distinct dharma; it is within this very context that the verse states:
"By means of the six groups of consciousness themselves, that which has ceased without interval constitutes the mind (manas)."
The treatise states:

It is precisely the six groups of consciousness that, having ceased without interval, are able to produce the subsequent consciousness; therefore, it is called the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*). There is no fault in establishing it as distinct because the temporal phases differ, just as a fruit is established as the seed of its father.
If that were so, the essential nature of the *dhātus* would consist of only seventeen or only twelve, because they mutually include one another.
For what reason, then, are eighteen *dhātus* established?
The verse says:
Because it establishes the sixth basis, the eighteen *dhātus* should be known.
The treatise says:

Just as the five consciousness-elements each have their respective bases in the five elements of the eye and so forth, the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has no separate basis. Just as consciousness cannot arise apart from its object (*ālambana*), it is likewise the case that it cannot arise apart from its basis; thus, consciousness would not be produced.
To establish this basis, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is taught.
Thus, one should understand that the bases, the faculties based upon them, and their objects each consist of six elements, thereby forming the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).
How can that which has already ceased be called the basis for present consciousness?
This manifestation-consciousness arises because of its proximity to its conditions.
Just as, although there is a visible form, visual consciousness must depend upon the eye to arise;
so too, although there is an objective sphere of perception, the subsequent consciousness arises depending upon the immediately preceding moment of mind that has just ceased.

Therefore, the aforementioned term "immediately preceding cessation" is intended to exclude the mind that ceases with an interval; for although the former [mind] had already vacated its place, it had not yet arisen.
Thus, the six consciousnesses that have already ceased without interval serve as the support for the present consciousness and are designated as the mental element (*manodhātu*).

Alternatively, while present consciousness currently functions as its support (āśraya), past consciousness has already become an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya), for it too is capable of taking up a fruit in the present.

Although [the present mind] arises in dependence upon that [past mind], it does not follow it; therefore, the mind is said to depend on the mind, but this is not called a mental factor (caitta), because the categories of mental factors necessarily follow the mind.

Having already explained the aggregates (*skandha*), the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*), one should now investigate their inclusive meanings within this context.

The aggregates collectively encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); the appropriated aggregates encompass only all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*); and the bases and elements collectively encompass all phenomena (*dharma*) without exception.
The five aggregates and the unconditioned are called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).
Having thus distinguished their individual inclusion, one should now analyze their collective inclusion.
The verse says:
All phenomena are subsumed by a single aggregate, sense-base, and element;
they are subsumed by their own intrinsic nature and not by others, because they are devoid of the nature of another.
The treatise says:
One aggregate is form; one base is the mind; one element is phenomena. These three collectively encompass the five aggregates and the unconditioned.
"Collectively" has the sense of aggregation.
The term "collectively" is employed so that one may understand them as a whole triad, rather than thinking they are each singular in isolation.
There is another school that maintains: "Inclusion" means including others, because it is stated in various places that "the remainder includes the remainder.
This position is irrational, as there is no definitive reason for it.
If there were a definitive reason, it would not be because of including others.

The masters of our own school maintain that [the inclusion] is by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This formulation of inclusion by intrinsic nature is the ultimate teaching, for it does not depend on anything else.
Inclusion that does not depend on causes is true inclusion, because all phenomena are at all times included within their own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, how is it known that [a phenomenon] does not include the nature of another?
Because all phenomena are devoid of the nature of others; that is to say, the nature of the eye-faculty is devoid of the nature of the ear-faculty and so forth.
To claim that something includes another when it is devoid of that other is logically impossible; therefore, one knows that all phenomena include only their own nature.

In this way, the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) comprises only the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), because its nature consists of the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana), the eye-element (cakṣur-dhātu), the truths of suffering and origin, and so forth;
it does not comprise the other aggregates, bases, or elements, because their natures are distinct from it.
Other dharmas should be considered accordingly.
Although the faculties of the eye, ear, and nose each rely on two locations, for what reason do the number of their elemental entities (*dhātu*) not become more than eighteen?
Because two are combined into one, there are only eighteen.
For what reason are two combined into a single element (*dhātu*)?
The verse says:
Because their type, object, and consciousness are the same, although there are two, the substance of the element is one.
The Treatise says:
Although the sense organs of the eye, ear, and nose each exist in two locations, they are combined into a single element (*dhātu*) because their categories and other attributes are identical.
"Identical in category" means that they are alike in being of the category of the eye.
Regarding the statement that their objects are the same: this is because they share the same object, namely visible form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the statement that their consciousnesses are the same: this is because they both rely upon visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The same applies to the ears and nose; therefore, they are established as a single element (*dhātu*).
Since the essential nature of the elements (*dhātu*) is one, for what reason are they located in two places?
The verse says:
However, in order to make [the body] beautiful, The eyes and so forth each arise as two.
The treatise says:
For the sake of making the physical body of the support (āśraya-deha) beautiful and dignified, although the essential nature (dhātu) of the sense organs is one, they arise in two locations.
If the sense organs of the eye and ear were to arise in only one location, and the nose had no two apertures, the body would not be dignified.
This explanation is incorrect; for how could there be any dignity in such ugliness as that of camels, cats, owls, and the like?
Therefore, the various sense faculties arise from distinct types, produced through such specific arrangements and differences.
These distinctions arise depending on causes and conditions; due to the presence of obstacles or the absence of such obstacles, they may not both arise.
As for the statement that two arise each for the sake of beauty, this has a specific meaning and does not refer to the adornment of the body.
This term "excellent" (*praśasta*) indicates the sense of superiority; it is called "excellent" because its function is superior.

If any one of the faculties, such as the eye, were missing, the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, and so forth would not be clear; only when each possesses both [the faculty and its object] does the clear function arise.
Therefore, each of the three faculties arises in two locations for the purpose of enhancing their superior function, not for the purpose of adorning the body.
For what reason did the World-Honored One teach the objects of knowledge by means of the three gateways of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)?
Because the meanings of these three gateways are each distinct,
what is the specific meaning of these aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)?
The verse says:
"Accumulation, door of arising, and lineage—these are the meanings of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
The treatise says:
the meaning of accumulation is the meaning of aggregate; the meaning of door of arising is the meaning of base; the meaning of lineage is the meaning of element.
On what grounds is it known that the meaning of "collection" (rāśi) is "aggregate" (skandha)?
It is because the Sūtra states:

"Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all such [form] taken together as a single collection is called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). This is explained at length for each up to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha)."
From this, it is known that the meaning of "collection" (*rāśi*) is what constitutes an "aggregate" (*skandha*).
If one were to explain the meaning of "aggregate" solely by means of the meaning of "collection," then the aggregate would not be real, because a collection is merely conventional (*prajñapti*).
This objection is not valid, because the term "collection" is established as a designation based upon the substratum of that collection.

That which is not an aggregate is precisely the meaning (*artha*); meaning is a real entity (*dravya*), whereas names are merely its distinctions. Since an aggregate is not a real entity, [it cannot be the meaning].
What is the meaning of "aggregate"? It refers to the sense of being an aggregation.
The meaning of "aggregation" (skandha) refers to that which serves as the basis for aggregation.

This explanation reveals that the sūtra possesses a profound significance: just as when one speaks of an "aggregation," apart from the basis of aggregation, no separate, substantially existent entity of an aggregation can be found.

Regarding this statement "I," one should not seek a real self-entity apart from the aggregates such as form; for the term "self" is a conventional designation applied within the continuity of the aggregates.
Just as a worldly collection is not substantially existent, if the aggregates were substantially existent, what meaning would the Sūtras be conveying?

It is not that those to be converted would know that the dharmas such as form have immeasurable distinctions across the three times and various categories, each of which constitutes an aggregate (*skandha*); for if the aggregates were thus infinite, they would become discouraged and withdraw, thinking, "How could I possibly fully know and forever abandon these infinite aggregates?"
To encourage them, although the aggregates (*skandha*) are infinite, they are spoken of collectively as one because they share the same nature.

Furthermore, since foolish worldlings give rise to the perception of a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍasaṃjñā*) regarding the many aggregates and thereby manifest the grasping of a self (*ātman*), it is said that a single aggregate contains numerous parts in order to eliminate that perception of a unified whole; it is not intended to demonstrate that the five aggregates—form (*rūpa*) and so forth—are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) formed by the synthesis of multiple dharmas rather than being real entities.

Furthermore, a single atom is comprised of the three time periods; when analyzed by wisdom, it is condensed into a single aggregate. Although an aggregate (*skandha*) is indeed a collection, its actual reality is established; the same applies to other phenomena. Therefore, the aggregates are not merely conventional designations.

Furthermore, since the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is also applied to each individual distinct phenomenon, the aggregates are certainly not merely nominal designations. For example, it is said that when they arise together, feeling is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), perception is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the others are explained as in the Sūtra.
Because they arise in combination at all times, although the aggregates (skandha) are distinct, the sense of a "collection" is established.
For what reason is the meaning of "gate" (āyatana) understood to be "base" (sthāna)?
It is by virtue of its etymological derivation (nirukti).
"Sphere" (*āyatana*) refers to a gateway of arising; because the mind and mental factors grow and arise therein, it is called a "sphere.
This signifies the sense of being able to produce and nourish them.
As stated in the Sūtra:
Brahmin, you should know that the eye serves as a gate solely for the purpose of seeing forms.
This sutra provides six proofs for the meaning of "gate" (*dvāra*); however, since the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) possess twelve gates, the *Sūtra* states:

"With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact (*sparśa*), which gives rise to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)," and so forth at length. For what reason is the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) understood to be "element" (*dhātu*)?
Because it shares a similar meaning with the term "lineage" (*gotra*) as used in the world.
For example, when a single mountain contains various lineages such as realgar, orpiment, red ochre, and *añjana*, it is called a "multitude of realms" (*anekadhātu*).
In this way, within a single body or a single continuum, there are eighteen categories; these various classes of phenomena are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
Just as realgar and other minerals are designated "classes" because their essential natures differ when compared with one another, so too are these called "classes."
In this way, because the eye and the other [faculties] differ in their essential nature when compared with one another, they are called "lineages" (*gotra*).
On the basis of this similarity in meaning, they can serve as a common example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If that were so, since the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has no distinct essential nature when compared to the six groups of consciousness, one should not establish them separately as the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*).
Because their essential natures and categories differ, there is no such fault.
For what reason did the Blessed One teach the threefold classification of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)?
Although the intent of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is difficult to discern, one should reflect upon it with careful consideration.
The verse says:
Because of the three factors—delusion, faculties, and so forth—the three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements are taught.
The commentary says:

Because the sentient beings to be converted differ in their delusions, faculties, and so forth—these three—the Buddha teaches the three categories of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) according to what is appropriate.
The word "and so forth" (ādi) is intended to clarify [the teaching of] the pleasures, states, faults, and diseases.
The three statements are made to show that each [of the three types of sentient beings] possesses three [aspects of delusion].

The delusions of the sentient beings to be converted are of three kinds: there are those who are deluded regarding mental factors and grasp them collectively as a self; those who are deluded regarding matter alone; and those who are deluded regarding both matter and mind.
The faculties (*indriya*) are also of three kinds: sharp, medium, and dull.
"Delight" (*ruci*) refers to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), which is likewise of three kinds: delight in the concise, the medium, and the extensive [text].

Furthermore, "stages" (*avasthā*) refer to the disciples (*śiṣya*), distinguished by the three stages of having transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*), having matured in practice (*caryā*), and being at the initial stage of undertaking the task (*karmasamārambha*).

The "faults" refer to the three distinct faults: sentient beings harboring the conceit of "I," adhering to the notion of "mine," and being deluded regarding the conditions upon which consciousness depends.
The "ailments" refer to the three distinct ailments: those to be converted relying on their life-span, wealth, or lineage, thereby giving rise to arrogance and indolence.
Based on these reasons, in their respective order, the Blessed One taught the three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements.
For what reason did the Blessed One establish feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) as two separate aggregates among all the mental factors (*caitta*)?
The verse says:
Because they are the roots of contention and the causes of birth and death, and because of the reason for their sequential order,
among all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*).
The Treatise says:
There are, in brief, two roots of worldly contention: namely, attachment to sensual desires and attachment to views.
The former arises from feeling (*vedanā*); the latter is produced by perception (*saṃjñā*).
Due to the power of sensation (*vedanā*), one becomes attached to various desires; due to the power of perverted perception (*saṃjñā*), one becomes attached to various views.

Furthermore, among the phenomena of birth and death, sensation and perception are the most predominant causes: because of indulging in pleasant sensations and because of clinging to perverted perceptions.
Those who act out of craving and views transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death due to these two causes.

Furthermore, because the sequential reasons for what will be explained later must be understood, one should know that feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately as aggregates; those sequential reasons shall be analyzed immediately hereafter.

Furthermore, the word "and" (ca) serves to indicate that among all mental factors (*caitasika*), only these two—feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)—are capable of acting as the roots for the arising of the two types of defilements (*saṃkleśa*): craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Moreover, each is designated individually by the name of a "station of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
Because the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is established based on the extinction of these two [aggregates].

For what reason, among such various categories of causes, is it said that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) exists within the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), but not within the aggregates (skandha)?
The verse says:
The aggregates do not include the unconditioned, because they are not consistent with the meaning [of "aggregate"].
The commentary says:

If all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) were said to be aggregates (*skandha*), whether established among the five or as a sixth, it would in every case be unreasonable, because it would contradict their essential meaning. Why is this so?
Since those [unconditioned phenomena] are neither form nor even consciousness, they do not exist within the five [aggregates].

"Aggregate" (skandha) has the meaning of a collection; since unconditioned phenomena are not like form and so forth—which possess distinctions of categories such as the past and so on that could be briefly summarized into a single aggregate called the "unconditioned aggregate"—they do not constitute a sixth [aggregate].

Furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are contrary to the meaning of being the basis for inversion and the means for its abandonment, the mention of the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) reveals the basis for inversion, while the mention of the uncontaminated aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) reveals the means for abandonment.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lacks both of these two meanings; since it does not correspond to these definitions, it is not established as an aggregate (*skandha*).
Having already explained the causes and conditions for the inclusion or exclusion of the aggregates, one should now explain their sequential order.
The verse says:
They are established in order according to their coarseness, defilement, vessel-like nature, and the distinctions of the realms.
The commentary says:
The five aggregates are established in their sequence according to their relative coarseness, their defilement, their function as a vessel and its contents, and their differentiation by realm.

Regarding establishment according to coarseness: among the five, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the coarsest because it possesses resistance and obstruction, because it is the basis for the five consciousnesses, and because it is the object of the six consciousnesses; thus, it is mentioned first among the five.

Among the four [aggregates], the most coarse is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); although it lacks physical form, its modes of activity and functions are easily understood, and thus it is mentioned first among the four.

Among the three [remaining aggregates], the most coarse is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); because its modes of activity, such as apprehending male or female, are easily understood, it is mentioned first among the three.

Among these two, that which is coarse is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); because its manifest aspects, such as greed and so forth, are distinct and easily discernible, it is mentioned first among the two.
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the most subtle; therefore, it is mentioned last.

Regarding the establishment [of the order] according to defilement: since beginningless saṃsāra, men and women have mutually felt defiled attachment toward each other's bodies due to the manifestation of form and so forth; therefore, "form" (rūpa) is mentioned first.
Thus, craving for form arises from indulging in the savoring of feeling; therefore, feeling is explained next.
This indulgence in the savoring of feeling arises from the perversion of perception; therefore, perception is explained next.
This perversion of perception arises through the power of the afflictions; therefore, formations are explained next.
The power of these afflictions depends on the production of consciousness that brings about future existence; therefore, consciousness is mentioned last.
Regarding "like a vessel and so forth": form is like a vessel, because it is the basis for feeling.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is like food and drink, for it increases or diminishes the body of sentient beings.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is like seasoning, because by grasping at enemies, friends, and neutral parties alike, it assists in the arising of feeling.
The formations are like a cook, because through the power of the karma and afflictions of volition, craving, and so forth, they produce various maturations such as the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Consciousness is likened to the eater, because it is the primary and most eminent factor within the fundamental constituent of sentient beings.
Consciousness is the foremost, because feeling and the other [mental factors] arise dependent upon it.
It is for this reason that, among the formations conducive to merit such as feeling, perception, and so forth, consciousness alone is described as being "conducive to merit."
Furthermore, by this same principle, it is said that "volitional formations condition consciousness.
For this reason, he further addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If consciousness were not present, it would not enter the mother's womb."
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is purified, sentient beings are purified.
In such sūtras, among the co-arising factors such as sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), only the primary consciousness is indicated.

Regarding the distinction according to the realms: in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpa*) is the most preeminent, because all forms of the sense faculties and their objects are fully present there.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), feeling (*vedanā*) is preeminent, because within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), all superior and sublime feelings can be obtained there.
Among the three formless realms, perception (*saṃjñā*) is supreme, because the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) is most distinct in those stages.
Within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), volition (*cetanā*) is supreme, because that volition can produce the greatest fruit.
This is precisely the station of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), wherein consciousness dwells.
This is illustrated by the analogy of the sequence of field and seed in the world;

therefore, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) is as it is. By this, the five aggregates are free from the fault of increase or decrease. Precisely because of these reasons for the sequence, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately among the mental factors (*caitta*). That is to say, among the mental factors, feeling and perception are coarser, give rise to defilement, share the same category of nutriment, and assist [consciousness] equally; they are powerful within the two realms (the desire realm and the form realm), and thus they are established as separate aggregates.

Having followed the root verses, we have thus explained the fourfold causes for the sequence according to the gate of progression (*pravṛtti-mukha*). Now, according to the gate of return (*nivṛtti-mukha*), one further type shall be explained.
That is to say, there are two essential gateways for entering the Buddha-dharma:
first, the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); second, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
The gateway of the contemplation of impurity contemplates derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), while the gateway of mindfulness of breathing contemplates the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Since these are the objects of focus for the essential gateways, matter is discussed first.
By the power of this contemplation, one analyzes the characteristics of matter, discerning the successive distinctions between moments and atoms.

When observing in this manner, because the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the mind experiences joy; therefore, sensation (*vedanā*) is explained next. Sensation, when conjoined with the body, inevitably results in either harm or benefit;

yet the notion that such harm or benefit pertains to a "self" (*ātman*) is logically untenable. Through this contemplative understanding, the conception of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) is extinguished and the conception of phenomena (*dharma-saṃjñā*) arises; therefore, perception (*saṃjñā*) is explained next.
Because of this perception, one realizes that there are only phenomena (*dharma*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise; therefore, "formations" (*saṃskāra*) are explained next.
Since afflictions have ceased, the mind abides in a state of pliancy and becomes capable of effective action; therefore, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is explained next.
The sequential order has already been explained; the reverse order should now be discussed.
Fearing that excessive detail would weary the reader, I shall cease for now.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Sarvāstivāda), Fascicle Two.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra, Volume Three.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
In the second part of the second chapter, "Discriminating the Fundamental Bases," the sequence of the aggregates has thus been explained.

Within the [classification of] elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), one should first explain the sequence of the six faculties; from this, the sequence of their respective objects and consciousnesses can be understood.
For what reason do the eye and the other [senses] follow this specific order?
The verse says:
The objects of the first five are only present; the objects of four are only derived matter.
The others function at a distance, with speed, and with clarity; or they follow the sequence of their respective locations.
The treatise says:
Among the six faculties, the first five—beginning with the eye—perceive only present objects; therefore, they are explained first.

The objective sphere (*ālambana*) is indeterminate; it may be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) across the three times, or one may apprehend only one, or two, three, or four. For this reason, it is explained later.
As for the determined object, its application is free from confusion and its characteristics are distinct; therefore, it is explained first.
Regarding the "unfixed objects," because their application is disordered and their characteristics are not distinct, they are explained later.

As for the statement that "the four objects consist only of the derived [elements]," this follows from what preceded; among the five, the first four objects consist only of the derived, and therefore they are explained first.
The body faculty has an indeterminate range of objects, as its objects consist of both primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); therefore, it is discussed later.

At times the body faculty perceives only the primary elements; at times it perceives only derived matter; and at times it perceives both kinds. Consequently, regarding body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), some say that at most it arises in dependence on five tangibles—namely, the four primary elements and any one of the [secondary qualities] such as smoothness;
others say that at most it arises in dependence on eleven.
The "others" refers to the first four [faculties].
They are mentioned first because they function over a distance, with speed, and with clarity, as appropriate.
That is to say, because the faculties of the eye and the ear apprehend distant objects, they are mentioned before the other two.

Between these two, the function of the eye is explained first because it reaches distant objects; for example, when a distant grove is struck by wind and so forth, one perceives its swaying but does not hear the sound.
Furthermore, the function of the eye is rapid, as one first sees from afar a person striking a bell or drum and only afterwards hears the sound.

The two faculties of nose and tongue both do not function at a distance; the nose is mentioned first because it is more rapid and clear. For example, when facing various fragrant foods and drinks, the nose smells the aroma first, while the tongue tastes the flavor afterward.
Thus, for the time being, the sequence of the faculties has been explained by distinguishing their objects as determinate or indeterminate, and by their functioning as remote, swift, or clear.
Alternatively, the sequence of the faculties is explained according to their spatial arrangement from top to bottom within the body, following the locations upon which they depend.
It is said that among the bases within the body, the eye-base is the most superior and is further manifested on the face; therefore, it is mentioned first.
The bases of the ear, nose, and tongue faculties are progressively lower, while the body-base is mostly below them.
The mind has no fixed location; as for its arising, it depends upon the five faculties. Therefore, it is mentioned last.

Is it not a matter of factual reality that the atoms of the olfactory faculty reside within the nasal cavity and do not dwell beneath the eyes? As it is said, the locations of these three faculties are arranged horizontally in rows without any elevation or depression, like a floral garland upon a crown.
In truth, it should indeed be so; however, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) intends to speak metaphorically in this way with respect to the locus of the sense faculties.
Alternatively, the Master may have intended this to apply to other interpretations as well; therefore, I shall now provide a separate verse on this point.
The functions of the first five arise first; among these five functions, the first two are distant, while the [first] three functions are clear in the first two.
Alternatively, they follow the order of their respective locations.

Among the six sense faculties, the first five—beginning with the eye—exert their functions toward objects such as visible forms prior to the arising of the mental faculty (*manas*); therefore, they are explained first.
As the treatise states:
"The five objects, such as form and so forth, are first perceived by the five consciousnesses and subsequently known by the mental consciousness.

One should understand that both [processes] are the functions of the eye and the other sense organs, serving as the supports for their respective consciousnesses and grasping their own specific objects."
Among the five faculties, the first two have a distant function because their objects do not come into contact with them; therefore, they are mentioned first.
Between these two, the function of the eye is even more distant than that of the ear, as illustrated by the examples given previously; for this reason, it is mentioned first.
Regarding the functions of the three organs beginning with the nose, the first two are more distinct; therefore, the nose is placed first, followed by the tongue, and then the body.
For example, while the nose can perceive subtle fragrances, the tongue is not so capable regarding sweetness or bitterness.
Just as the tongue can perceive subtle tastes, the body does not do so regarding cold and warmth.
The sequential explanation according to their respective locations is no different from what preceded.
Having thus explained the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), one should further investigate within this very context:
For what reason, when the entities of ten bases are all matter (*rūpa*), is the name "matter-base" (*rūpāyatana*) established for only one of them?
Furthermore, when the entities of twelve bases are all phenomena (*dharma*), why is the name "phenomena-base" (*dharmāyatana*) established for only one of them?
The verse says:
To distinguish them as most excellent, to include many superior dharmas,
one place is named "form" (rūpa), and one is named the "sphere of phenomena" (dharmāyatana).
The Treatise says:
Although all twelve bases (*āyatana*) and ten material phenomena (*rūpa*) are *dharma*, they are differentiated such that one general name is established for them.
What is meant by "differentiation" refers to their respective distinct bases.

If the name "aggregate" (skandha) were applied because the nature and characteristics of form (rūpa-dharma) are identical, then the names for the bases (āyatana) would likewise have to be either two or one.
Consequently, the disciples, relying on these collective names, would only understand them collectively and would not comprehend their individual specific characteristics.
In order to bring about an understanding of the various distinctions between objects (*viṣaya*) and subjects (*viṣayin*), distinct names are established.

Thus, the Tathāgata establishes specific conventional names for sounds and so forth, as well as for the eyes and so forth, upon the basis of form (*rūpa*); since the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) has no other specific conventional names, its general name itself serves as its particular name.

Just as various distinct names are established for the *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) to manifest specific meanings, so too does this [name] manifest a specific meaning and is thus a distinct designation; the same applies to the *dharmāyatana*.
Regarding the term "most excellent" (*pradhāna*), it is due to two causes and conditions that the characteristic of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) is most excellent specifically within the *rūpāyatana*:
First, because it is visible (*sanidarśana*), its distinctions as being "here" or "there" can be demonstrated;
second, because it is resistant (*sapratigha*), it undergoes transformation and decay when touched by the hand or other such objects.
Furthermore, because it is manifold and is the objective domain of the three types of eyes, the world collectively designates it with the name "form" (*rūpa*).
Therefore, because the great masters do not establish the designation "form" (rūpa) for sound and so forth, it is only [the first aggregate] that is called "form";
whereas, because the category of mental objects (dharmāyatana) subsumes numerous factors such as perception (saṃjñā) and others, it should be established with a general name.
If one were to exclude the general name, how could many distinct phenomena (dharma) be gathered together into a single locus?
Furthermore, because many categories are subsumed within this, it is called "all phenomena" (sarvadharma); thus, the name "phenomena" is established.

That is to say: the dharma of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), the dharma of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the dharma of knowledge (*jñāna-dharma*), the dharma of recollections (*anusmṛti-dharma*), the dharma of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda-dharma*), the dharma of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna-dharma*), the dharma of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid-dharma*), and the dharma of the jewels (*ratna-dharma*). Because there are immeasurable varieties of names for returning to these dharmas, and because all are subsumed within this category of "dharma," it is uniquely termed "dharma."
Furthermore, there is the preeminent dharma, namely *nirvāṇa*; because it is included herein, it alone is designated as "dharma.

Whatever other various aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*) with their respective names and designations are found in the various sūtras, they are all subsumed within these; this should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, to distinguish and subsume the names and designations of the remaining aggregates,
the verse says:
The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma;
Its essence is either speech or names; it is subsumed within the aggregates of form and formations.
The treatise says:

Some maintain that the Buddha’s teaching has speech as its intrinsic nature; they assert that the aggregates of dharma are all subsumed within the aggregate of form, because the function of speech has sound as its self-nature.

Some say that "Buddha-teaching" (buddha-vacana) is its own substantial entity (*svabhāva*). They maintain that the aggregates of dharma (*dharma-skandha*) are all subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), because their nature consists of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). [They argue:
"Speech" (*vāk*) and "teaching" (*deśanā*) are synonyms; thus, the teaching may well be speech. [But we ask:
If "name" (*nāman*) and "teaching" were distinct entities, how could the teaching be the name?
He offers this explanation:
it is only by virtue of having names that something is designated as "teaching"; therefore, the essence of the Buddha's teaching is precisely name. Why is this so?
Because it explains meanings according to reality, it is called "Buddha-teaching" (*buddha-śāsana*).
Since names are that which can explain meanings, the teaching consists of names.
Therefore, the Buddha-teaching definitely has names as its substance; by taking names as the primary element, one encompasses phrases and syllables.
How should one understand the extent of the aggregates of dharmas?
The verse says:
Some say that the extent of the aggregates of dharmas is as described in that treatise.
"Or following the [terms] 'aggregates' and so forth, / One practices the antidotes according to reality.
The treatise says:
Some masters state that each of the eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas* is equal in extent to the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*, meaning that each of them consists of six thousand stanzas.

As stated in the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* within the Abhidharma, the *dharmaskandhas*—according to the various enumerations such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), absence of contention (*araṇā*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—each distinct teaching door is designated as one *dharmaskandha*. Thus, there are eighty thousand such [teachings].

To speak according to reality: the sentient beings to be converted possess eighty thousand distinct modes of conduct, such as greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the view of a self-identity, and discursive thought. In order to counteract these eighty thousand modes of conduct, the Blessed One proclaimed eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*). That is to say, he taught various doors of antidotes, such as the meditation on impurity, loving-kindness and compassion, dependent origination, the perception of impermanence, emptiness, and mindfulness of breathing; this is what is meant by the expressions "following the aggregates" and so forth.
The statement that there are no aggregates and so forth was not spoken in vain as a remedy for the diseases of sentient beings' conduct;

rather, the eighty thousand dharma-aggregates (dharmaskandha) as they are described are all subsumed within two of these five aggregates. In the same way, the other aggregates, bases, and elements found elsewhere should be understood accordingly.
The verse says:
In this same way, the remaining aggregates and so forth are each subsumed within what has been previously explained as appropriate; one should carefully examine their specific characteristics.
The Commentary states:
The aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) mentioned in other sūtras are, as appropriate, subsumed within those previously explained.
One should carefully examine the individual specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of each of these aggregates and so forth as they are described in this treatise.

Furthermore, other five aggregates are taught in various sūtras, namely: the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), liberation (*vimukti-skandha*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*).
Among these, the aggregate of ethical discipline is subsumed within this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), because it consists of bodily and vocal actions and is not mental volition (*cetanā*).

The remaining four aggregates are subsumed within this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as they are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and are neither feeling (*vedanā*) nor perception (*saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, regarding the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth mentioned in various sūtras—the first eight spheres of totality and the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)—because their nature is non-attachment (*alobha*), they are subsumed within this sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

If including their associated mental factors (*sahāya*), they are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and are therefore subsumed within these very bases of mind (*manāyatana*) and phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

The latter two universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and the four formless bases (*ārūpyāyatana*), such as infinite space, being of the nature of the [upper] four aggregates, are likewise subsumed within these same bases of mind and phenomena.
Because the five bases of liberation (*pañca-vimukti-sthānāni*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
If accompanied by their associated factors (*sānucara*), they are subsumed under the spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects.

Furthermore, there are two other bases: the base of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva-āyatana*) and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The former base is subsumed under these ten bases, as it lacks odor and taste; [the latter is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects].
The latter category is subsumed within this very sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), because it lacks the nature of form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* speaks of sixty-two distinctions of elements (*dhātu*); one should know that these are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) according to their respective characteristics.

Furthermore, regarding the six elements taught in that sutra, the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind have already been explained; however, the characteristics of the two elements of space and consciousness have not yet been explained.
What are the characteristics of these two elements?
The verse says:
The space element refers to cavities; its essence is light and darkness.
The consciousness element consists of contaminated consciousness; it is the basis for the birth of sentient beings.
The treatise says:
The cavities and apertures, both internal and external, are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
What are these cavities?
This refers to light and darkness, namely the apertures and gaps of light and shadow such as windows and finger-slits.
The differentiation of visible color (*varṇa*) is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
One should know that the substance of this element is substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because it is described as being internal and external, just like the earth element and others.
This [space] exists as a distinct entity apart from emptiness; this principle is fully established by the sūtras. As a sūtra says:
"Emptiness is formless, invisible, and non-obstructive; upon what, then, could it depend?"
Nevertheless, it is by relying on light that space becomes manifest.
Furthermore, it is said that when one attains detachment from form (*rūpa*), the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*) is abandoned.
Therefore, we know that it exists as a distinct entity.
The element of space has already been explained.
All contaminated consciousnesses are called the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
Why, then, is uncontaminated consciousness not mentioned?

Because that [uncontaminated dharma] is not consistent with this meaning, and because uncontaminated dharmas function through distinctions such as severing, harming, and destroying the arising of sentient beings, they are not the basis for arising.
Thus, because these six elements function as distinct causes for the production, nourishment, and growth of sentient beings, they constitute the basis of birth.

The cause of production refers to the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), because it is the seed for the continuity of rebirth. The cause of nourishment refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because they provide the support for arising. The cause of growth refers to the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), because it provides room for birth. They are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they sustain the birth of sentient beings.

The six elements (*dhātu*) mentioned in that sūtra are subsumed within these nine elements; as for the remainder, their inclusion should be understood according to what is appropriate. Thus, all other elements are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).

Having thus explained that the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements are all contained herein, we shall now demonstrate how they are subsumed within the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Regarding the three categories of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), there are distinctions in their types and meanings based on gates such as "visible" and so forth.

Since the elements fully manifest the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, the types and meanings of these various gates are easily understood; therefore, for now, we shall analyze them by way of the eighteen elements.
By means of these aggregates and bases, their general categories have already been established.

Among the eighteen elements previously mentioned, how many are visible and how many are invisible; how many are resistant and how many are non-resistant; and how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
The verse says:
One is visible, namely form; ten are material and possess resistance.
Excluding form and sound, eight are indeterminate; the remaining three are of all three kinds.
The treatise says:
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), one is "visible," namely the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Why is this called "visible"?
This is due to two reasons.
First, this form is necessarily accompanied by seeing, and is therefore called "visible" (*sanidarśana*), because the form and the eye arise simultaneously, like having a companion.
Second, this form is called "visible" (*sanidarśana*) because it can be demonstrated; that is, it can be shown as being distinctively here or there, just like an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Some say that this form is called "visible and demonstrable" because an image (*pratibimba*) can appear within mirrors and the like; for just as that [original object] is so, this [image] is likewise.

It cannot be said that sound possesses qualities such as an echo and so forth, for it would follow that [sound] must be visible; however, this is not the case because they do not arise simultaneously.
By stating this characteristic, the fact that the other elements are invisible is established by implication.
Thus, having already explained what is visible and what is invisible, it is established that only the ten elements subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) are resistant (*sapratigha*).
"Resistance" (*pratigha*) has the meaning of obstruction; because this [element] obstructs that, it is therefore called "resistant."
This is further divided into three types based on the distinctions between objective sphere (*gocara*), focal object (*ālambana*), and obstruction (*pratighāta*).

Regarding "resistance by way of objective sphere" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*): this refers to the sense faculties such as the eye, as well as the mind and mental factors; when these various cognitive phenomena encounter and meet with objects such as visible forms, they are obstructed, and thus receive the name "possessing resistance."

Resistance regarding the object (*ālambana-pratighāta*) refers to the fact that the mind and mental factors encounter resistance when meeting their respective objects; thus they receive the name "possessing resistance.
What, then, is the difference between the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) and the object (*ālambana*)?
If this [cognition] possesses efficacy toward that object, then that object is said to be the sphere (gocara) of this cognition.
It is just as when a person possesses superior efficacy toward something, that thing is then said to be one's own sphere.
The mind and mental factors arise by grasping that [object]; thus, for the mind and its associates, that object is termed the "object-condition" (*ālambana*).

If a phenomenon possesses resistance with respect to its object-condition, it is necessarily a "resistance regarding the objective sphere" (*viṣayapratighāta*) for the mind and mental factors, because those mental states would certainly not function if they lacked the capacity to apprehend their object.

There are things that possess resistance with respect to their objective field (*viṣayāvaraṇa*) but do not possess resistance with respect to their cognitive object (*ālambanāvaraṇa*). This refers to the five material sense-faculties, which are not associated mental factors because they lack a cognitive object.
Why, then, are the eye and the other faculties said to be "obstructed" when they function toward their own respective fields and objects?
Because it does not function with respect to others beyond that;
or alternatively, "obstructing" (*āvaraṇa*) has the sense of "conjoining," meaning that dharmas such as the eye function by conjoining with their own respective domains and objects.
Some say that if a phenomenon functions only within a certain domain and cannot transcend it, it is therefore called "obstructive" (*sapratigha*).

Obstruction by resistance (*āvaraṇapratighata*) refers to the fact that conditioned matter (*rūpa*) itself is obstructed from arising in another location, such as when hands, stones, and so forth mutually obstruct one another.
Alternatively, it may obstruct the arising of others within its own location;
since only the matter of atoms (*paramāṇu*) can mutually obstruct one another, it can be called "obstructive resistance" (*pratigha-sapratigha*).
Here, only obstructive resistance is being discussed; therefore, only ten [bases] are mentioned, as the sense of "resistance" is predominant in their case.
What are the ten? They are the ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*) formed by atoms (*paramāṇu*), because they consist solely of matter.
The element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) encompasses both the material and the immaterial; that matter [within it] is invariably not composed of atoms.
Excluding these, the remaining ten are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*) because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
It is stated that these ten possessing form are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*); by implication, the others are said to be "without resistance" (*apratigha*).

Regarding the statement "possessing form" (*rūpin*): this refers to that which is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), excluding the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Because it is subject to transformation and resistance, it is called "form"; since it possesses the quality of being subject to transformation and resistance, it is termed "possessing form."
Some say that "form" (rūpa) refers to that which can be indicated by the words "here" or "there"; because it is designated by these terms, it is called "possessing form" (rūpin).

Others say that all forms possess their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and thus they are called "possessing form. Because it is easier to express in this way, the term "possessing form" is applied specifically to the substance of form itself.
Thus, having already explained the resistant (*sapratigha*) and the non-resistant (*apratigha*),
among these ten resistant elements previously mentioned, with the exception of visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*), the remaining eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
They are called "indeterminate" because they cannot be designated as either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Dharmas that should be praised or censured, and which can be definitively categorized within either the black or white category, are called "determined" (vyākṛta).
Those that are not accommodated by either of these two categories and whose nature is indistinct are called "undetermined" (avyākṛta) dharmas.

The remaining ten elements (dhātus) pertain to all three categories—wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth—namely, the seven mental elements, the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), the element of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), and the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*).
"Wholesome" means the relinquishing of evil; it carries the sense of being opposed to evil.

Alternatively, that which is wholesome is called "that which is embraced by wisdom" (*prajñā-parigṛhīta*); that is to say, if any phenomena are embraced by wisdom, or if they embrace wisdom, they are all termed wholesome.
Alternatively, "wholesome" (*kuśala*) signifies auspiciousness, as it can summon favorable omens, much like *maṅgala* grass.
The opposite of this explains the meaning of the term "unwholesome.

Within the two realms of form and sound, those [phenomena] arising simultaneously with a wholesome mind are termed wholesome; those arising simultaneously with an unwholesome mind are termed unwholesome; the remainder are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding the seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*), those associated with non-attachment and so forth are termed wholesome (*kuśala*); those associated with attachment and so forth are termed unwholesome (*akuśala*);

the remainder are termed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The categories subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) are manifold: those associated with the nature of non-attachment and so forth, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), are termed wholesome; those associated with the nature of attachment and so forth, as well as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), are termed unwholesome; the remainder are termed indeterminate.
The wholesome [dharmas] and so forth have already been explained.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The verse says:

Those bound to the desire realm are eighteen; those bound to the form realm are fourteen, excluding the two [objects] of odor and taste and the two [consciousnesses]; those bound to the formless realm are the final three.
The commentary says:
"Bound" (saṃyojana) means being attached, which carries the sense of being fettered.
Those bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) possess all eighteen [elements].
Those bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu) possess only fourteen types, excluding the objects of odor and taste, as well as the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses.
Odors and tastes are excluded because they are of the nature of substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); one can only be born there after having abandoned the desire for substantial food.
Furthermore, the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses are excluded because they lack their respective objects;
it is not the case that consciousness arises even slightly in the absence of its object.
If that were so, there would likewise be no touch (*spraṣṭavya*) in those [formless realms]; for touch that is not of the nature of nutriment cannot exist there.
While the element of touch does not function as nutriment in those realms, it does have other functions, namely, the formation of the body.

If it were not so, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) would be non-existent, and consequently, all derivative matter (*upādāyarūpa*) would also not exist; thus, it would be identical to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), so how could it be called the "form realm" (*rūpadhātu*)?
Furthermore, in that realm, tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) perform external functions, namely, they constitute palaces, clothing, and so forth.
Although the tangible has a distinct function apart from the desire for food, this is not the case for odor and flavor; therefore, they do not exist there.

In the realm associated with the formless (ārūpyadhātu), there are only the latter three: namely, the mind-element (manodhātu), the mental-object-element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu).

Because one must be free from attachment to form in order to be reborn there, the ten realms of form do not exist within the formless realm; since their bases and objects are absent, the five consciousnesses are likewise absent; therefore, only the final three [realms] are bound to the formless realm.
The bondage to the realms has already been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
The mind (*manas*), dharmas (*dharma*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are common to both; the remaining [elements] are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The treatise says:
The three immediately preceding—the mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness—all of them are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This means that, with the exception of the Truth of the Path and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the remaining three—the mind and so forth—are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Those comprised within the Truth of the Path and the three unconditioned phenomena are, as appropriate, all without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Only fifteen [of the eighteen elements] are exclusively associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), because they are not subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, the distinction between the outflowing and the non-outflowing has been explained.
Among the eighteen elements, how many are with vitarka and vicāra, how many are without vitarka and with vicāra only, and how many are without both vitarka and vicāra?
The verse says:
The five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra; the last three possess all three; the remainder have none.
The commentary says:

The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, possess both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), because they are always associated with vitarka and vicāra.

These five groups of consciousness are always associated with vitarka and vicāra because they exist only in those stages accompanied by vitarka and vicāra; they do not exist among the mind and mental factors of the desire realm or the first dhyāna.
Excluding vitarka and vicāra, there is one [element] that does not coexist with vitarka and vicāra.
The mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness are called the "last three" because they occupy the final positions among the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses respectively.

Thereafter, all three realms are common to the three grades. This includes the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the associated dharma-element (*samsṛṣṭadharmadhātu*), with the exception of vitarka and vicāra.

If one is in the desire realm or the first dhyāna, there is both vitarka and vicāra; in the intermediate dhyāna, there is no vitarka and only vicāra; from this point upward, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.

All non-associated dharmas within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as well as *vicāra* in the intermediate dhyāna, are likewise [without vitarka]. This is because in the stages above that there is neither vitarka nor vicāra; because they are non-associated; because those [higher stages] lack vitarka; and because a self-entity does not associate with itself.

At all times, *vitarka* (applied thought) is without *vitarka* and possesses only *vicāra* (sustained thought), because a factor cannot be associated with itself, and because this [state] is always associated with *vicāra*.

Although *vicāra* exists in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, it is not included within the three categories [of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral] and should therefore constitute a fourth; however, because such factors are few, they are not mentioned in the verse.
The remaining ten material elements (rūpa-dhātu) are entirely devoid of both vitarka and vicāra, because they are always dissociated from them.
In this context, one should further reflect on a related point:
if the five groups of sensory consciousness possess both vitarka and vicāra—and since vitarka is itself a form of conceptualization (vikalpa)—how can it be maintained that they are non-conceptual?
The verse says:
It is said that there are five types of non-conceptualization;
they consist of the discursive wisdom and the various mindfulnesses of the mental level, because they are [respectively] by way of calculation and recollection.

The treatise states: There are three types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*): first, conceptualization by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*); second, conceptualization through deliberation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*); and third, conceptualization through recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).

Although the five groups of sensory consciousness possess the first type, they lack the other two; therefore, they are said to be "without conceptualization. This is like calling a one-legged horse "legless"; thus, although one [type] exists, it is designated as "non-existent" [in respect to the others].
Is it not the case that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses only one type [of discrimination]?
It is associated with conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and because it relies upon the mental consciousness, it is said to possess all three types of discrimination in its general category.
The essence of intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāvavikalpa*) is exclusively vitarka; this will be explained in detail later among the mental factors (*caitta*).
The remaining two types of discrimination are, respectively, characterized by the nature of discursive wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) on the mental level (*manobhūmi*).

The term "discursive" excludes that which is associated with the mental consciousness in a state of meditative concentration; such discursive wisdom is termed "calculation discrimination" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), because within meditative concentration, one cannot calculate or deliberate upon objects.

The wisdom within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not function by conceptualizing its object in such-and-such a manner; therefore, in this context, "concentration" is excluded and "dispersion" is selected.

All mindfulness associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whether in a state of concentration or dispersion, is termed "discrimination of recollection" (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), because its function of clearly recording the object is equal in both states.

Although the five consciousnesses are associated with mindfulness and wisdom, because their functions of discernment and recollection are subtle, they are considered to consist solely of the mental faculty (*manas*).
As for "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), it refers to the mode of activity that investigates and seeks; therefore, *vitarka* (applied thought) is said to be its essential nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
Discrimination (*vikalpa*) is similar to vitarka in its aspect of discerning and recording; therefore, the term "discrimination" also applies to wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Because these three modes of activity—wisdom, mindfulness, and discrimination—collectively sustain the mind, they all cause it to operate with clarity regarding its object. Since discrimination prevents the arising of further discerning activity toward an object already apprehended, the term "discrimination" does not apply to perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because it cannot maintain a seal upon an object not yet fully understood, it is called "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*); this does not extend to "resolute determination" (*adhimokṣa*).
If it occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the first dhyāna, the indeterminate mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses all three types of conceptualization.
If the mental consciousness of the first dhyāna is in a state of meditative concentration, or if it is a distracted mind of a higher stage, each constitutes two types of discrimination.
If the mental consciousness of a higher stage is in a state of meditative concentration, or if it belongs to the five groups of sensory consciousness, each constitutes one type of discrimination.
Having thus explained those [factors] with vitarka and vicāra and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (dhātus), how many have an object (sālambana) and how many are without an object?
How many are appropriated (upātta) and how many are unappropriated?
The verse says:
Seven consciousnesses and half of the dharma-element possess objects; the rest do not.
The first eight elements and sound are non-appropriated; the rest are of both kinds.
The treatise states:

The six consciousnesses, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and the mental factors (*caitta*) subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are called "possessing an object" (*sālambana*). Because they possess an object, they are like a person who has a son.
The distinctions in meaning are as follows: those that have an object of cognition (*ālambana*), a sphere of activity (*gocara*), and a domain (*viṣaya*) are so named;
