the remaining ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*) and the non-associated factors (*viprayuktadharma*) subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are termed "without an object of cognition," as this is established by logical implication.

It should be understood that because the five consciousnesses are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), they take as their object the collection of real atoms (*paramāṇu*) and do not take a composite (*saṃghāta*) as their object.

A "composite" is not a distinct name for a few individual dharmas that could constitute an object apprehended by a non-conceptual consciousness; rather, it is called a "composite" because a single metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*) arises with respect to many dharmas, and linguistic expression proceeds based upon it.
The five consciousnesses do not take the "designation" (*adhivacana*) as their object; therefore, the synthesis [of name and form] is not the objective referent of the five.
Thus has been explained that which possesses an object and so forth.
Among the eighteen elements, nine are non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
What are these nine?

They are the seven previously mentioned types of objects that possess an objective referent (*sālambana*), together with the entire *dharmadhātu*; these eight, along with sound, are all non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
In the verse, the word "and" (*ca*) carries two meanings: [it connects the preceding items and indicates inclusion].
First, it reveals the general collection: that is, the eight [bases] and sound are collectively non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Second, it reveals alternative perspectives: that is, other masters state that sound which is not separated from the sense faculties is also appropriated.
The remaining nine are common to both [categories], namely: the five material sense-faculties (indriyas) and the objects of form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
How are they common to both?
The five faculties, such as the eye, when abiding in the present time, are termed "appropriated" (upātta); when past or future, they are termed "unappropriated" (anupātta).

The elements of form, odor, taste, and tangibility that abide in the present world and are not separated from the five sense organs are termed "appropriated" (*upātta*); those that are past, future, or abide in the present while being separated from the organs are termed "unappropriated" (*anupātta*). Therefore, nine elements each pertain to both categories.
What is defined as the characteristic of being appropriated (*upātta*)?
The *Śāstra* states that what is comprised within one's own body is called "appropriated.
What, then, does this mean?
This refers to that which the mind and mental factors grasp as their own;

that is, what is collectively grasped and maintained by the mind and mental factors, and is appropriated as a basis, is called "appropriated" (*sopādāna*), because benefit and harm are mutually transmitted between them.

If that were so, then matter (*rūpa*) and the like would necessarily be termed "unappropriated" (*anupātta*), because the mind and mental factors do not rely upon them and they lack the nature of sense organs (*indriya*).

This is not the case; for if matter and the like are not separated from the organs, although they are not the [direct] supports, they nonetheless assist the mind and its associates. Therefore, this fault does not arise.
Having thus explained what is appropriated and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are of the nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and how many are of the nature of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?
How many are accumulative, and how many are non-accumulative?
The verse says:
Within the element of tangibility there are two [types]; the remaining nine material [elements] are derived;
the same applies to one portion of the dharma-element; ten material elements are accumulative.
The treatise says:

The element of tangibility (spraṣṭavyadhātu) comprises two types: first, the primary elements (mahābhūta), and second, derived matter (upādāyarūpa). These two are as explained previously in the commentary on the eleven types of tangibility.

It is not that the element of tangibility is subsumed solely under the primary elements; for the *Prakaraṇapāda* Sūtra states that within the sphere of tangibility (spraṣṭavyāyatana), derived matter is also included.
The remaining nine material elements (*rūpadhātu*) are exclusively derived (*bhautika*); that is to say, the five sense organs and the objects of form, sound, odor, and taste.
A portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is likewise exclusively derived. What, then, is this?
That is to say, unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is called "derived" because it arises in dependence upon the primary elements (mahābhūta).
However, this is stated to clarify that there is certainly no single realm that consists exclusively of the nature of the primary elements.
The remaining seven mental realms and a portion of the dharma-realm—excluding unmanifest form—are neither of the two types [neither primary nor derived].

The principle has already been established: that there are derived elements (bhautika) existing separately from the primary elements (mahābhūta). The *Prakaraṇapāda* Sūtra, which treats them as distinct locations, serves as direct evidence.
Thus, the primary and derived elements have been explained.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the ten material elements—consisting of the five sense faculties and the five sense objects—are "accumulable" (*saṃcita*), because their substance consists of atoms (*paramāṇu*) that can be gathered together; thus they are called accumulable.
By logical extension, the remaining eight [elements] are not accumulative, because their substance is not composed of atoms and thus cannot be gathered together.
Having thus explained what is accumulative and so forth, [one may ask]:
among the eighteen elements, how many are capable of cutting and how many are cut; how many are capable of burning and how many are burned; how many are capable of weighing and how many are weighed?
Regarding these six questions, they should now be answered collectively.
The verse says:
It is said that only the four external elements are both that which cuts and that which is cut.
It is also that which is burned and that which weighs, as well as the dispute between that which burns and that which is weighed.
The treatise says:
Form, odor, taste, and tangibility constitute the axe, the firewood, and so forth; these are precisely what are termed "the cutter" and "the cut."
The term "only" (kevala) defines the scope, intending to show that cutting and so forth definitely pertain to the four external elements and nothing else.

The word "and" (ca) indicates that both the agent of cutting and the object being cut are common to all four elements; that is, when various aggregates of matter arise in close succession, and distinct conditions cause them to be separated so that they each continue to arise individually, these are termed the "agent" and "object" of cutting, because they are momentary in nature.
In reality, there is absolutely nothing that can cut nor anything that is cut.

Regarding this meaning of "being cut," the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and other such faculties cannot be divided by different conditions into two separate entities; they arise as a continuous stream, for if a limb were separated from the body, it would no longer possess the faculty.
Furthermore, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth are also not that which cuts, because they possess a pure and subtle nature, like the light of a jewel.
These meanings are expressed solely by words.

Just as the entities of that which cuts and that which is cut consist only of the four external elements, the same applies to the entities of that which burns and that which is weighed; that is to say, only the four external elements are termed "that which is burned" and "that which is weighed. Because the physical faculties such as the body possess a pure and subtle nature, they likewise do not constitute these two functions, being like the light of a jewel.
Sound does not arise in a continuous stream alongside [the other elements] such as form, because it is subject to interruption.
Regarding the six meanings, there is no capacity for burning or being weighed.
There is a divergent dispute: some say that the entities of the burner and the weighed are also, as before, merely the four external elements.
Furthermore, some say that only the fire element can be called "that which burns" and "that which is weighed," and it is only [the element of] heaviness.
Thus has been explained that which cuts and that which is cut, and so forth.

Among the eighteen elements, how many are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), how many are nurtured (*aupacayika*), how many are of uniform outflow (*naiṣyandika*), how many possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*), and how many are momentary (*ekakṣaṇika*)?
Regarding these five questions, they should now be answered collectively.
The verse says:
The five internal [bases] consist of the matured and the nurtured; Sound does not arise from maturation.
The eight [types of] unimpeded [speech] are of the nature of outflow and also of the nature of maturation;
the remaining three are substantially only dharmas; and in terms of moments, only the latter three [exist].
The commentary says:

The five internal [faculties] refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. Because they include those produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) and those nurtured by food (*aupacayika*), and exclude those of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), they are not mentioned [here].
Although the sense faculties such as the eye are also of the nature of outflow—since they possess homogeneous causes and are thus results of outflow—they are excluded for the reasons stated above.
Since there is no nature of outflow (niṣyanda) external to that which is produced by maturation (vipāka) or nurtured (aupacayika), it must be excluded.
Just as there is production from maturation apart from what is nurtured, and what is nurtured exists apart from production from maturation, there is no distinct outflow apart from these two.
To distinguish between different categories, the general discussion is set aside to treat specific cases.
"Ripening" (*vipāka*) means maturation; because it matures apart from its [immediate] cause, it is called "maturation.
When the essence of maturation arises, it is termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Alternatively, it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) because it is produced by a cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*);
this statement is made by omitting the intermediate term, just as one says "ox-cart.
Or, it is called "maturation" because when the karma that was performed reaches the time of its fruition, it transforms and becomes capable of ripening.
When a fruit arises from that [cause], it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).

Alternatively, the name of the fruit is metaphorically applied to the cause, just as the name of the cause is metaphorically applied to the fruit; for example, it is said that the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*) are themselves the karma that has been performed.
That which is benefited by superior conditions such as food, drink, rest, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called "nourished" (*aupacayika*).
Conditions such as food and drink can only maintain and protect the substance of maturation (*vipāka*); they cannot increase it.
There is another kind of augmentation called "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*).

It should be understood that within this context, the continuity of nourishment constantly protects and sustains the continuity of maturation (*vipāka*), just as an outer wall defends and supports an inner city.

Since it has been stated that the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*) is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*), it follows by implication that it is not without outflow (*naiṣyandika*) or nurtured (*aupacayika*).
For what reason is the sound-element not born of maturation?
Because it is repeatedly interrupted and then arises again.
Matter born of maturation (*vipākaja*) does not possess such a quality, for the fruit of maturation does not arise according to one's desire.
Sound arises according to desire; therefore, it is not maturation.

Regarding the eight unobstructed [realms], these consist of the seven mental elements and the mental-object element; they possess the nature of being both outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) and born of maturation.
If it is not produced by a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), or a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it is termed "of the nature of outflow" (*naiṣyandika*).
If it is produced by a ripening cause, it is termed "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).

The "remainder" refers to the other four—visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—all of which pertain to all three types: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those of uniform outflow (*naiṣyandika*), and those through nourishment (*aupacayika*).
As for "the real is only phenomena" (*dharma*): "real" refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it is firm and substantial.
Since these are subsumed within the dharma-dhātu, only the dharma-dhātu alone is said to possess substantial reality.
The mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness are called the "last three," because they are mentioned last among the three groups of six.

Only within these three realms is there a single moment, namely the category of the first untainted *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*; because it is not a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*), it is called a "single moment. This refers to its actual manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "nor is it a result of outflow" (*niṣyanda*): among other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there are none that are not results of outflow. Only the first moment of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) arises without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). Other conditioned phenomena do not possess such a quality; because the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is so strong, this [first moment] can arise even though the preceding cause is absent.

The samanantarapratyaya (immediately preceding condition) possesses a powerful force because its category is identical to that of the initial noble path, because it is nurtured by immeasurable wholesome dharmas, because its nature is equal to that of the initial noble path, and because it has been extensively cultivated through various preparatory practices for this purpose.

The mind associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) is called the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mental-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu); the other factors arising simultaneously are termed the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
Thus, the [categories] such as those born of maturation (vipākaja) have been explained.
Now one should reflect and investigate:
if the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) was previously unaccomplished and is now accomplished, is the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) likewise?
And if the eye-consciousness-element was previously unaccomplished and is now accomplished, is the eye-element likewise?
Regarding such questions as these, they shall now be answered briefly.
The verse says:
The eye and the eye-consciousness element Are acquired individually or together; they are not equal.
The treatise says:

Regarding "attaining alone," this refers to cases where the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is first achieved but the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not. This occurs, for example, when one born in the desire realm gradually attains the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), or when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages.

There are cases where visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) is first accomplished but the visual faculty (cakṣurindriya) is not; this refers to when visual consciousness arises while one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages, as well as at the time of passing away from those stages to be reborn in a lower stage.

Regarding "attaining both": this refers to cases where one who previously did not possess [the faculties] of two realms now attains possession of them; namely, when one dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).
"Neither" refers to the negation of both, meaning the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
"And so forth" (ādi) includes other meanings not yet mentioned. What, then, are these?

That is to say: if one accomplishes the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), does one also accomplish the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? This should be analyzed in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the first proposition: it refers to those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages whose eye-consciousness does not arise.
The second case refers to those born in the desire realm who have not yet obtained the eye faculty, or who have obtained it but subsequently lost it.

The third case refers to those born in the desire realm who have obtained the eye faculty and not lost it, as well as those born in the Brahma-world, or those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages when visual consciousness is manifest.
The fourth alternative refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.

In this manner, the relationship between the eye-element and the form-element, as well as between eye-consciousness and the form-element—regarding their acquisition (*prāpti*) and possession (*samanvāgama*)—should be considered according to reason.

By this line of reasoning, one should apply the same analysis to the latter five triads regarding their acquisition (*prāpti*), possession (*samanvāgama*), mutual relationship, and abandonment (*tyāga*). As extensively demonstrated in the *Vibhāṣā*, I shall not describe them here for fear of excessive prolixity.
Thus, the attainment of accomplishment and so forth have already been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are internal and how many are external?
The verse says:
The twelve internal [bases], such as the eye and so forth, and the six external [objects], such as form and so forth.
The Treatise says:
The six faculties and the six consciousnesses are termed the twelve internal [bases].
The external refers to the remaining six objects, such as visible form and so forth; although there is no real self, the internal sense-bases are established.
Having explained the internal and external, [one may ask]:
among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and how many are "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
The verse says:
Dharmas are of two types—homogeneous or otherwise—depending on whether they perform their own function or not.
The commentary says:
Regarding "dharmas that are *sabhāga* (homogeneous)": this refers to the single dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is exclusively *sabhāga*.
Now, one should first define the characteristics of objects that are *sabhāga*.

If an object is definitely taken as an objective support (*ālambana*) by consciousness—for instance, the dharma-realm is definitely taken as an objective support by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—because it is not shared [with other types of consciousness], then within that [realm], the consciousness has already arisen or is destined to arise; this objective support is called *sabhāga*, because the mind is able to take all objects as its range.

Within the objects of the three periods of time and that which is non-temporal, there is not a single element of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in which [consciousness] has not already arisen, is not currently arising, or will not arise; for the infinite mental consciousnesses—specifically those of two successive moments—are able to take all phenomena as their universal object. Consequently, the dharma-realm is always termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
The "remaining two" refers to the remaining seventeen elements (*dhātus*), all of which possess both the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
What are these termed "homogeneous" and "counter-homogeneous"?

It means performing one's own function and not performing one's own function: if it performs its own function, it is called homogeneous; if it does not perform its own function, it is called counter-homogeneous.
How are the eyes and other faculties described as "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and "counter-homogeneous" (tat-sabhāga)?
First, regarding the homogeneous eye, three types are taught: those that have seen, are seeing, or will see visible forms within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
That "homogeneous" eye is said to be of four kinds: namely, those that are the opposite of this [the non-homogeneous], and those that are of a nature not to arise.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and body; each should be explained according to its own object and its own function.
The mind-element (manodhātu) that is "homogeneous" (sabhāga) is said to be of three kinds: namely, that which has already cognized, is currently cognizing, or will cognize its object.
That which is "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) is of only one kind: namely, that which is of a nature not to arise.

The visual objects of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are of the same class (*sabhāga*) are said to be of three kinds: namely, those that have perished, those that are currently perishing, and those that will perish.

Those visual objects of the same class (*tatsabhāga-rūpa*) are said to be of four kinds: namely, the opposites of the aforementioned [three] and those dharmas that are not subject to arising (*anutpatti-dharma*).
To speak at length, this applies even to the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*); each should be explained according to its own faculty and its specific function.

Because the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are established as having two divisions based on whether their support arises or does not arise, they are to be explained in the same manner as the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
If the eye is sabhāga (homogeneous) with respect to one [object], it is sabhāga with respect to all others.
If it is tatsabhāga (non-homogeneous) with respect to one, it is tatsabhāga with respect to all others; this is explained in detail up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), which is likewise.
Form is not like this; it is "homogeneous" (sabhāga) for one who sees it and "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) for one who does not see it.
Furthermore, for what reason do you say that the eye's homogeneous and non-homogeneous states differ from those of form?
Many sentient beings may perceive the same visible form simultaneously; it would be useless for two sentient beings to observe with a single eye.
Sound is explained in the same way as visible form, because it is a common object.
The three—odor, taste, and tangible objects—are explained like the internal sense-bases, because they are not common objects.
However, based on conventional designations and conceptual notions, people in the world say:
"We all smell this same fragrance," "We all taste this same flavor," or "We all perceive this same tactile sensation.
What is the meaning of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) and "its homogeneity" (*tatsabhāgatā*)?
"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to mutual interaction; because they equally possess this part, it is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
What is meant by mutual interaction?
It refers to the mutual interaction between the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness; that is to say, the sense of successive conformity.

Alternatively, "part" (*bhāga*) refers to the mutual interaction of their own respective functions; thus it was previously stated that when they perform their own activity, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).

Alternatively, "part" refers to the contact (*sparśa*) that arises; because it is produced through the interaction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness, they all equally possess this part, and are therefore called "homogeneous. This signifies that they equally possess the function and equally possess contact.
That which is contrary to this is called "having a counterpart" (sabhāga).
Because it shares a commonality of type with that which is not its counterpart (tatsabhāga), it is named "having a counterpart.
In what way does it share a commonality of type with that?

This means that these and those share identical characteristics such as perception, occupy the same location and realm, and—because they serve as causes for one another, are mutually connected, and mutually induce one another—are identical in their classification and kind.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Three.
Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Four.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Two: Distinguishing the Fundamentals, Part Four. Having already explained *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous), among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aheya*)?
The verse says:
Fifteen are abandoned only by cultivation; the last three realms pertain to all three [types of abandonment].
Those that are non-defiled do not arise from the six [senses]; those of the form realm are certainly not abandoned by insight.
The treatise says:
Regarding the statement "fifteen," this refers to the ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*) and the five consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*).
"Only abandoned by cultivation" means that these fifteen elements are abandoned solely through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the "last three realms," these are the mind realm (*manodhātu*), the phenomena realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness realm (*manovijñānadhātu*), as they are taught last among the six triads.

Regarding their "pervasion of the three," each of these three pervades all three [categories]. The eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) along with their associated factors, their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*), and their co-existent factors such as arising and so forth, are all abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). All remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). All uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
To establish this meaning, it is further stated that they are "unafflicted.
That which is not produced by the six [consciousnesses] and is material (rūpa) is certainly not abandoned through seeing.
What is called "unafflicted" refers to contaminated wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states.
"Non-born from the sixth" refers to the sixth, which is the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*);
that which arises differently from this is called "non-born from the sixth.
This signifies arising from the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth; that is, the five consciousnesses and their associates.
Form refers to contaminated and non-contaminated form.
These three categories are certainly not abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).

Furthermore, as for non-contaminated phenomena and all form-phenomena that are not abandoned by insight, they are only designated as "abandoned" when the afflictions taking them as objects are ultimately severed.
What is the meaning of abandonment?
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, abandonment through detachment from bondage; second, abandonment through detachment from objects.
Regarding abandonment through detachment from bonds, as stated in a sutra:
"With respect to the absence of internal eye-fetters, one understands as it truly is: 'I have no internal eye-fetters.
Regarding abandonment through detachment from objects, as stated in a sutra:
"O bhikṣus, if you are able to sever craving for the eye, this is called the permanent abandonment of the eye.
The great masters of Abhidharma establish two kinds of abandonment based on that sequence: first, abandonment by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prahāṇa);
second, abandonment of the object (ālambana-prahāṇa)."
When the antidote arises for those phenomena that are fetters and share the same fruit, they are abandoned; this is called abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).

Because of that abandonment, one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*); it is not necessarily the case that non-possession (*aprāpti*) is attained with respect to it—this is called abandonment of the objective basis (*ālambana-prahāṇa*).

In this context, all non-defiled contaminated formless states, as well as contaminated forms and their various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and associated dharmas such as arising, are bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation that exist above them. When these fetters are gradually abandoned, and when the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises with respect to the distinct entities of each category, those fetters and their single fruit and so forth are all termed "abandoned."

At that time, the acquisitions of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) have not yet arisen with respect to those non-defiled, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) formless states, as well as outflow-tainted forms and their associated factors such as arising; therefore, they are not yet called "abandoned. This is because those dharmas are abandoned only by the final path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) of their respective stages, and it is not the case that the paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) can gradually effect detachment from desire according to the distinctions between the various stages.
How is it that those dharmas which are non-defiled and so forth, as well as those not produced by the six [consciousnesses], are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
Because they operate externally with respect to objects such as form (*rūpa*).
Thus has been explained what is abandoned by insight and so forth.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are "vision" (*darśana*) and how many are not?
The verse says:
The eye element and one part of the dharma element— these eight kinds are said to be vision.
The discernment (*prajñā*) co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), because it does not judge.
The eye sees form when it is of the same class (*sabhāga*), because it is the cause for the consciousness to see;
because there is no distinction in the category of consciousness; and because it does not perceive obstructed forms.
The Treatise says:
The eye faculty is entirely the seeing [aspect]; one part of the dharma-realm consists of eight types that are seeing, while all others are not seeing.
What are these eight?

That is to say: the five defiled views, such as the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), worldly right view, the right view of those in training (śaikṣa), and the right view of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Within the dharma-dhātu, these eight are "view" (dṛṣṭi);
all other parts of the dharma-dhātu and the remaining sixteen [bases] are not "view."

Among all phenomena, only two factors constitute the nature of seeing: among material phenomena, it is only the eye that sees; among immaterial phenomena, it is the clarity and sharpness of their mental modes.
The wisdom that functions within its own sphere through the process of inferential deliberation is "view" (dṛṣṭi), and nothing else.

Among these, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)—as previously explained—is designated as "seeing" because it is commonly understood by the world, because its nature is that of observation and illumination, because it is the opposite of darkness, and because its function is clear and sharp.
The five defiled views will be analyzed in their characteristics within the "Chapter on Latent Tendencies" (Anuśaya-nirdeśa).
Mundane right view refers to the superior, wholesome, and contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Right view of those in training refers to all untainted wisdom within the person of one in training.
Right view of those beyond training refers to the decisive, discerning untainted wisdom within the person of one beyond training.
The single term "right view" fully encompasses three types.

These three are distinguished separately in order to reveal the differences between the views of the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and furthermore, to demonstrate that they arise through gradual cultivation.
These various views, in their general categories, are fivefold:

first, the indeterminate category; second, the defiled category; third, the wholesome-with-outflows category; fourth, the category of those in training (śaikṣa); and fifth, the category of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Among the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) categories, the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is vision; all other faculties, such as the ear, and all non-obscured indeterminate wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*), etc., are not vision.

Among the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) categories, the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) are vision; all other defiled wisdom is not vision—namely, wisdom co-arising with greed, hatred, pride, unshared ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), and doubt—and other defiled dharmas are likewise not vision.
Among the categories of those in training (*śaikṣa*), there is no wisdom that is not vision; however, the remaining [wisdoms] are not vision.

Among the categories of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), as well as the remainder, are not vision; all other wisdoms of those beyond training are entirely vision.
Among the categories of wholesome contaminated [wisdom], only the wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); all others are not view.

Other masters state that there is also wholesome contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not view, namely: the wisdom induced by the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*), the wisdom that initiates manifest action (*vijñapti*), and the wisdom at the time of death.
Furthermore, among these wholesome contaminated categories, the wisdom (*prajñā*) co-arising with the five consciousnesses is also not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
For what reason are all such excluded forms of wisdom not considered views?

Because it lacks the capacity for decisive judgment (*niścaya*), only that which possesses the characteristics of wisdom (*prajñā*) as previously described constitutes the essence of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Specifically, wisdom that operates within the internal door—possessing clear and sharp modes of activity (*ākāra*) toward objects in the formless realm—is view and nothing else; only wisdom with these characteristics has the power of decisive judgment, as it functions through deliberation (*vicāra*) regarding its objective referents.
The wisdom that is not subject to obstruction is able to deliberate upon and determine its object; therefore, it is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
What is called "determination" refers to the final resolution following prior deliberation regarding an object.
The various forms of wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness cannot engage in thorough investigation regarding objects already cognized;
because they function by searching for and distinguishing between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, they are termed "determinative judgment" (*adhimokṣa*).

The wisdom within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can first engage in deliberation regarding its objects and ultimately achieve definitive discernment; therefore, it may be termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Because the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) lack such conceptual discrimination, the wisdom associated with them lacks this capacity and is therefore not termed "view."
If that is so, since the eye-faculty lacks these characteristics, it should not be called "seeing.

Is it not already stated that the eye is also called "seeing" because it is commonly understood by the world, because its nature is to observe and illuminate, because it is the opposite of darkness, and because its function is clear and sharp?
The Sūtra also states:
"The eye sees various forms"; therefore, it is said that the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is able to see various forms.
If it is the eye that sees, why does it not simultaneously apprehend all objects?
This fault does not apply, because it is admitted that a portion of the eye is capable of seeing visible forms.
What is this "portion"?
It refers to the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) eye, that is, the *sabhāga* visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
As previously stated, it is through the sustaining power of consciousness that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is established.
Since it is not the case that all sense faculties are simultaneously sustained by their respective individual consciousnesses, there is no such fault.
If that were so, then the consciousness which depends upon it would be the "seeing" and not the eye, because seeing occurs only when visual consciousness arises.
This is not the case, for it is through the sustaining power of visual consciousness that a superior function is produced [in the eye].

Just as fire arises depending on the superior power of fuel, if the function of seeing color were a phenomenon produced by consciousness, then this function of seeing color should arise even apart from the eye. Since consciousness nourishes the co-nascent primary elements (*mahābhūta*), causing the superior sense organ to arise and thereby enabling the perception of various forms, one should not say that it is the dependent consciousness that sees.
What wise person would speak thus:
"Whatever causes and conditions can produce discernment, such discernment is itself those causes and conditions"?
Consciousness is the cause of seeing; therefore, it is not the essence of seeing.

Furthermore, since the essence of visual consciousness is no different from that of auditory consciousness and the others, it certainly cannot be the essence of seeing. What distinction is there between visual consciousness and those other consciousnesses, such as the auditory, such that the former alone is called "seeing"? Therefore, the insistence that consciousness itself is seeing is certainly unreasonable.
Furthermore, other masters establish by another reasoning that visual consciousness is certainly not "seeing," because it cannot perceive objects obstructed by barriers.

We observe that when various forms are obstructed by walls and the like, they cannot be perceived; if it were consciousness that sees, then since consciousness is non-obstructive (*apratigha*), walls and such would not hinder it, and it should see the obstructed forms. Therefore, the principle that the eye and other faculties apprehend their respective objects is established—namely, that they are capable of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
Thus, the general characteristics of the function of seeing have already been established; now, one should further consider the specific characteristics of the function of seeing.
Regarding the visible forms that are seen, are they seen by one eye or by both eyes?
When one of the two eyes is closed or impaired, it does not cause the other eye to lose its capacity for vision; therefore, we know that even a single eye is capable of seeing forms.
If those two eyes are unimpaired and both open, then the two eye-faculties see forms simultaneously.
While the principle of one eye seeing form is manifest and easily established, the simultaneous seeing by both is difficult to establish; therefore, it should be analyzed and explained.
The verse says:
Or both eyes [function] simultaneously, because the perception of forms is clear.
The commentary says:
At times both eyes are able to see forms; by what means is this definitively known?
Because the vision is clear.
For when one eye is closed, the perception of forms is not clear; yet when both eyes are open, the perception of those very same forms is clear.
If the two eye-faculties were to see sequentially, then even when both eyes are open, there would be only a single act of seeing.
Just as the perception of forms is not clear when one eye is closed, it should likewise be so when both eyes are open.
Just as forms are seen clearly when both eyes are open, it should likewise be so when one eye is closed;
since this is not the case, we know for certain that there are times when both eyes see simultaneously, because their nature is one.
Even if there were a hundred thousand eyes, they would still give rise to only a single consciousness; how much more so when there are only two?
Regarding the various sense organs such as the eye, as described above, do they reach their objects when correctly perceiving them, or do they not?
For what reason does doubt arise regarding this?
Because two different explanations are seen within the sūtras.
As the Blessed One said:
The visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) of sentient beings is obstructed by pleasant and unpleasant forms (*rūpa*);
it is not that they do not reach one another, for the meaning of "obstruction" is thereby established.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
With his divine eye, he observes sentient beings— extensively described as being either far or near.
Since distance and proximity cannot be established for an object that is directly perceived,
doubt arises again because of these two [contradictory] statements.

The meaning of "the sense faculty and its object reaching one another" (*prāpti*) is not fixed. If "reaching" is defined in terms of functional efficacy—that is, reaching the object—then all sense faculties perceive only objects that are reached.
If, however, it is defined in terms of their physical characteristics, then "reaching" means being contiguous (*nirantara*).
The verse says:
The faculties of eye, ear, and mind, and their objects—these three are mutually contradictory regarding non-attainment (*aprāpti*).
The commentary says:
The faculties of the eye, ear, and mind apprehend objects that are not in direct contact. This is because the eye apprehends both distant and near objects simultaneously;

furthermore, it cannot apprehend an object that is immediately adjacent to it; moreover, it can apprehend forms obscured by substances such as rock crystal; and finally, there is doubt regarding what is seen.
Furthermore, because the eye has no capacity to reach distant objects, it apprehends non-contacted objects (*aprāptaviṣaya*).
The auditory faculty likewise apprehends only non-contacted objects, for sounds can be discerned regardless of whether they are located in the cardinal directions or at a distance or near.

Furthermore, because it perceives distant and near sounds as either distinct or indistinct, and because it perceives distant and near sounds with either hesitation or certainty, the mental faculty (*manas*) likewise apprehends only non-contiguous objects (*aprāptaviṣaya*), for it does not apprehend co-existent or associated phenomena (*sahabhū-saṃprayuktadharma*). Moreover, being formless (*arūpin*), it cannot possess contiguity.
Therefore, the faculty of mind (*manas*) apprehends objects that are not in contact (*aprāptaviṣaya*).
The other three—the nose and so forth—are the opposite of this; that is, the nose, tongue, and body apprehend only objects that are in contact (*prāptaviṣaya*).
But is it not the case that atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not touch one another?
If atoms were to touch one another in their entirety, there would be the fault of the substantial bodies intermingling; if they touched only in part, they would incur the loss of being partless.
How, then, do the nose and other [senses] perceive objects that have reached them?
Now, observing the ultimate meaning, it is said that an object can only be apprehended when it arises in immediate proximity to its respective sense faculty.
Based on this principle, it is taught that the nose, tongue, and body faculties apprehend only objects with which they are in contact.

As it is said, although the eye cannot see objects that have reached it—such as the eyelids or counting sticks—it is not the case that the eyelids and so forth must actually touch the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) to be designated as "reached. Rather, when the eyelids and so forth arise in proximity to the faculty, they are simply termed "reached."
Because one cannot see such [objects] as those that have reached the visual form, it is said that the eye-faculty apprehends objects not in contact with it.

Just as the eye and other faculties apprehend objects not in contact, yet cannot apprehend extremely distant objects, so too it is with the nose and the others; although they apprehend objects in contact, they cannot apprehend extremely proximate objects, for odors and the like must be adjacent to the faculty in order to arise.

Therefore, it is said that there is no fault in asserting that the three faculties grasp [their objects] by reaching them; however, this does not apply to the nose and its objects, such as odors, because the atoms of the faculty and the object do not touch one another, as they are not of a nature that can be touched.
Furthermore, since they possess the quality of resistance through obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), if they were to touch, it would entail a logical error.
To clarify this point, it should further be investigated.
Suppose someone were to raise this objection:
"If atoms do not touch one another, how can striking them produce sound?"
How could this possibly be the same as the position of the followers of Ulūka, who raise this objection that sound must arise only through the conjunction of qualities?
For since the principle of conjunction is not established at the time when objects meet, one should not admit that sound is produced by the conjunction of qualities.
If that is so, how can there be the production of sound?

Within this true system of the Noble Teaching, the terms "separation" and "conjunction" depend solely upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). That is to say, when two sets of the four primary elements arise in a state of separation or conjunction through their specific excellence, they receive those respective names.
In this stage, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause for the production of sound, and only the sound co-arising with them is the object of the auditory faculty.
What fault is there in this?
They do not accept it; I do not accept it either.
There is also a reason for this: since atoms do not actually touch one another, how could the meaning of the "conjunction" of their respective primary elements (mahābhūta) be established?
When they arise in immediate proximity, that itself is called conjunction; why wait for actual contact before they can be designated as conjoined?
Furthermore, you should not hesitate regarding this point: these and those primary elements (mahābhūta) certainly do not touch one another. Why is this?
Because they are that which is touched, and not that which touches.

Among all the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*), only the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) is designated as the "tangible," and only the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) is designated as the "tactile agent"; beyond this, the meaning of "tangibility" need not be further considered.

If it is argued that the object of touch is also capable of touching, then one must admit that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also an object of touch; in that case, there would be a confusion between the object and the subject.
If it is argued that there is no fault of such confusion because the focal object (*ālambana*) and the support (*āśraya*) of the body-consciousness are distinct, [we reply:]...
Does this not result in confusion?
For if the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) were also an object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), for what reason would it not become the object-condition (*ālambana*) of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*)?
And if the element of touch (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) were also capable of touching, for what reason would it not become the support-condition (*āśraya*) of body-consciousness?
Therefore, the statement that these and those primary elements (mahābhūta) certainly do not touch one another is logically established.
If this is so, how can the body-faculty (kāyendriya) and the tangible-object element (spraṣṭavyadhātu) function such that touching and being touched are established?
Because the sense organs and their objects arise in close proximity as atoms (paramāṇu), one might object:

"Since all nose, tongue, and body organs grasp only objects that reach them without distinction, should not the capacity to touch extend to the nose and tongue organs, and should the objects of touch not also include odors and tastes?"
This objection is unreasonable, for although they are equally proximate, there are distinctions among them.

Furthermore, since the world collectively applies the designation "tangible" (spraṣṭavya) to smoothness, roughness, and so forth, and designates the body-faculty (kāyendriya) as the "tactile agent" (spraṣṭṛ) in relation to them, there is no fault.
The detailed analysis of these points is as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Now, one should examine whether the sense faculties, such as the eye, perceive their respective objects by operating only upon objects of equal size and with extreme rapidity—thus seeing large mountains and the like, as in the case of a whirling firebrand.
Do they apprehend their own objects as being equal in size or unequal in size?
The verse says:
It should be known that the three beginning with the nose apprehend only objects of equal size.
The treatise states:
Regarding the previously mentioned [senses] that reach their objects, it should be understood that the three faculties—the nose and so forth—can only apprehend objects of equal magnitude.

For instance, just as the atoms of the faculties of the nose, tongue, and body are of a subtle measure, the atoms of the objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—are likewise; this is because the consciousnesses of the nose and so forth arise from the meeting of these corresponding [atoms].

Is it not the case that the atoms of the three faculties, such as the nose, sometimes cannot grasp odors and so forth in their entirety? Why, then, is it said that they grasp only what is equal in size?

It is because the atoms of the three faculties, such as the nose, do not grasp objects such as odors that exceed their own magnitude; therefore, it is said that they can only grasp objects of equal magnitude.

It is not the case that even a small portion of the atoms of the three faculties can apprehend only a small portion of the three objects; rather, according to the extent to which the minute measure of the object reaches the faculty—whether it be few or many atoms of the faculty—that many atoms of the faculty are able to perform their function.

The eye and the ear are indeterminate; that is to say, the eye sometimes perceives small forms, such as when seeing the tip of a hair; sometimes it perceives large forms, such as when momentarily opening one's eyes to see a great mountain and the like; and sometimes it perceives forms of equal size, such as when seeing grapes, jujubes, or similar fruits.
The auditory faculty also perceives the magnitude of sounds such as those of mosquitoes, thunder, and lutes, whether small or large.
Since the mental faculty lacks material obstruction, its distinctions in shape and magnitude cannot be discerned.

Within the verse, the term "should be known" (jñātavya) should be understood as also exhorting one to understand this meaning; now, taking advantage of this context, one should further investigate it.
What are the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the sense-faculties such as the eye?

Although their specific arrangement cannot be established because they are invisible, it must certainly be explained that there is a specific arrangement, since they possess resistance (*sapratigha*), occupy spatial locations, and arise through aggregation.

The atoms of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya-paramāṇu*) reside upon the pupil of the eye, facing their respective objects and arranged laterally; they are covered by a clear membrane, like a cumin flower, which prevents them from dispersing.
Some say that they abide in layers like pellets; because their substance is transparent, they do not obstruct one another, like an autumnal spring or pond.
The atoms of the auditory faculty reside within the ear cavity, arranged in a spiral, like a rolled birch bark.
The atoms of the olfactory faculty reside within the nasal bridge, facing backward and downward like a pair of fingernails.
These first three faculties are arranged horizontally in rows without any variation in height, resembling a crown or a floral garland.

The atoms of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed across the tongue; their shape is like a half-moon situated in the center of the tongue's form, measuring only the size of a hair-tip, and they do not pervade the entire surface of the tongue.
The atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are distributed throughout the entire body, corresponding to the dimensions of the physical form.
The atoms of the female faculty (*strīndriya*) are shaped like the head of a drum, and the atoms of the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) are shaped like a thumb.

The atoms of the eye faculty are sometimes all of the same class (sabhāga), sometimes all of the corresponding class (tatsabhāga), and sometimes some are of the corresponding class while the rest are of the same class; this applies likewise up to the atoms of the tongue faculty.

The atoms of the body-faculty (kāyendriya-paramāṇu) are certainly not all of them "functioning" (sabhāga); even in the Extremely Hot Hell (pratāpana-naraka), where the body is enveloped by fierce flames, there still exist infinite atoms of the body-faculty that are "non-functioning" (tatsabhāga).

Therefore, it is said as follows: even if consciousness were to arise from every [atom], the body would disintegrate, because no single atom of a sense faculty or object can serve as the support and objective condition capable of producing a body-consciousness.
The five consciousnesses necessarily accumulate many atoms (*paramāṇu*) before they can constitute their bases (*āśraya*), because their nature is that of an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
How, then, are the bases of the six consciousnesses established?

Is it the case that, just as the five consciousnesses take only the present as their object while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes all three times and the non-temporal as its objects, the same applies to their respective bases?
It is not so. Why? The verse says:
The latter rely solely on the past; the five consciousnesses rely either [on the past] or simultaneously.
The treatise says:

Because the six groups of consciousness, having ceased without interval, are all termed "mind" (*manas*), and this serves as the supporting faculty for the mental consciousness, the mental consciousness relies solely on the past eye-faculties and so forth.

The supports of the five consciousnesses are either simultaneous or, as the word "or" indicates, also past. That is to say, the five [faculties] such as the eye are the simultaneous supports, while the past support is the mental element (*manodhātu*).
Thus, the supports for the five consciousnesses are each twofold, while the support for the sixth mental consciousness is only one.
To clarify the distinctions in the meaning of "support" within the verse, one should further ask:
if something is the nature of the support for visual consciousness, is it also the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that visual consciousness?
If something is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for visual consciousness, is it also the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for that visual consciousness?
One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first alternative refers to the co-nascent eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
The second phrase refers to the mental factors (caitta-dharma) of the dharma-element that have just ceased without interval.
The third phrase refers to the past faculty of mind (manas).
The fourth phrase refers to everything other than what has been mentioned above.
The same applies up to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).

For each of these, one should state its own respective faculty (*indriya*). Regarding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one should provide an answer according to the "prior-phrase" formula (*pūrvapadaka*):
that which is the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for mental consciousness is necessarily the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for mental consciousness.

There exists that which serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), yet does not serve as its support (*āśraya*); this refers to the mental factors (*caitasikadharma*) of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that have ceased in the immediate past.

Furthermore, regarding the five consciousness-elements (*pañcavijñānadhātu*), while their supporting faculties (*indriya*) necessarily exist in both the present and the past, is it the same for their perceived objects (*ālambana*), or is there a difference?
There is certainly a distinction.
That which has already ceased and that which has not yet arisen are not the objects of the five consciousnesses. Why is this so?
Because it arises in a single object together with its basis, and because it does not arise based on what is not present before one's eyes;
for the Sūtra states:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises," and so forth, in detail.
For what reason is consciousness, which arises by depending on two conditions, given the name "basis" (āśraya) with respect to the sense organ and not the object?
The verse says:
Consciousness varies according to the transformation of the faculties; therefore, the eyes and so forth are called the "bases" (*āśraya*).
The treatise states:
The eyes and so forth are precisely the six elements (*dhātu*) of the eyes and so forth, because the faculties such as the eye undergo transformation.
The various consciousnesses undergo transformation and variation according to the increase or decrease of the sense organs, because they possess clarity or dullness.
It is not that the transformation of form and other objects causes the consciousness to differ, for consciousness follows the sense organs and does not follow the objects.
Based on their names, these [faculties] reside only in the eye and so forth, and not elsewhere.

If that were so, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would also shift according to the body; for when the body is afflicted by disorders such as wind-disease (*vāta*), the mental consciousness becomes disturbed, whereas when the body is in a state of tranquility, the mental consciousness is clear and lucid.
For what reason does that mental consciousness not take the body as its support?
Because it follows its own respective support, there is no such fault.

That is to say, when the body is afflicted by wind-disorders and the like, a body-consciousness associated with painful sensation arises; such a body-consciousness is termed a "disturbed mental element."
When this [feeling] perishes together with the painful feeling, it can cause the mental faculty (*manas*) to give rise to a distracted consciousness;
conversely, when it is contrary to this, the consciousness is clear. Therefore, consciousness follows its own basis.

The phrase "according to their respective bases" indicates the distinctions of increase or decrease, clarity or dullness; it does not indicate categories such as being determinate (*vyākṛta*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
For what reason is the name "consciousness" established based on the object that is cognized, rather than the sense organ?
It follows the faculties, not the objects.
The verse says:
"Because of those [faculties] and their unique causes, consciousness is said to follow the faculties."
The treatise says:

It is said that because the eyes and so forth were previously designated as "bases" (āśraya), the name "consciousness" (vijñāna) is established in accordance with the faculties rather than the objects; for the basis is predominant.
Regarding those that are "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*): this means that the eye is exclusively the support for its own visual consciousness.

Visible form, however, is also common to the visual consciousnesses of other bodies and is likewise apprehended by the mental consciousnesses of both oneself and others; it should be understood that this applies similarly to the body and tangible objects.
Is it not the case that because the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are not shared [with other senses], it should be called "dharma-consciousness"?

This objection is irrational, because the names "general" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*) regarding dharmas are shared but not universal, and because the objects [of the mental consciousness] do not possess the two aforementioned causes.

That is to say, the general designation "dharma" does not refer exclusively to that which is unique [to a specific consciousness], and the specific designation "dharmadhātu" does not universally encompass all consciousnesses.

Furthermore, although the specific dharmadhātu is not shared with others, it does not possess the nature of being the foundational faculty (*āśrayendriya*) for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, when a phenomenon is both the support for consciousness and its specific cause, consciousness is designated according to that phenomenon.
This is not the case with visible form and so forth; thus, consciousness is not designated as "consciousness of form" and so on, just as one speaks of the sound of a drum or the sprout of barley.
Furthermore, this verse has another meaning: it refers to the fact that [the eye and so forth] are followed by the consciousnesses of the eye and so on;
and as for "unshared," it means because the eye and so forth are unshared.

This means that while there may be one instance of a material form giving rise to four instances of visual consciousness, there is never a single instance of a visual faculty giving rise to two instances of visual consciousness, much less one capable of giving rise to four.

In this way, because the eyes of each distinct realm, destiny, class, and individual produce their own respective consciousnesses, they are called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*); the same applies extensively even to the body.
But would not the mental faculty (*manas*) of other beings also produce [consciousness]?
The mental consciousnesses of other sentient beings are not entirely non-arising; however, they do not arise simultaneously.

It is impossible for the mental consciousnesses of two sentient beings to arise at once in a single instance, as is the case with [material] forms and so forth. Therefore, it is said that there are not two, much less four.
Thus, because the visual consciousness and the others follow [their respective bases], they arise differently according to the realm (*dhātu*) and the destiny (*gati*);
for these two reasons, the consciousness follows the sense organ (*indriya*) and not the object (*viṣaya*).
When the eye sees a form while abiding in a particular body, are the levels (*bhūmi*) of the body, the eye, the form, and the consciousness the same or not?
One should say that these four are either different or the same.
Regarding what is meant by "the same": when one is born in the desire realm and sees forms of that same level with an eye of that same level, all four belong to the same level.

When one is born in the first dhyāna, seeing forms of that same level with the eye of that same level, all four factors belong to the same stage. This is not the case when one is born in another stage.

Regarding what is different: if one born in the desire realm sees a form of the desire realm with an eye of the first dhyāna, the body and the form belong to the desire realm, while the eye and the consciousness belong to the first dhyāna; thus, the body belongs to the desire realm, and the other three belong to the first dhyāna.

If one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to the desire realm, while the eye belongs to the second dhyāna and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna; when seeing forms of the first dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm and the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.

When visual consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna sees forms belonging to the second dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), both the eye and the forms belong to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.
In this same manner, it should be understood according to reason that when one uses an eye belonging to the third or fourth dhyāna stages to see forms of a lower stage or of one’s own stage.
Thus, if one is born in the stages of the four dhyānas, there are differences regarding these four matters, which should be considered according to reason.
The other realms should also be analyzed in this manner.
Now, I shall briefly explain the characteristics of this determination.
The verse says:
The eye is not inferior to the body; form and consciousness are not superior to the eye.
Form is [not inferior] to consciousness in all cases; the same applies to the other two in relation to the body.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear; the next three [faculties] belong to their own level;
body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower level; one should know that the mind is not fixed.
The treatise says:
The body, the eye, and visible forms all pertain to five stages—that is, they exist within the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
Eye-consciousness exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Among these, the eye faculty, in relation to the stage where the body is born, is either equal to or superior to it, but never inferior.
In relation to the eye, visual consciousness is equal to or inferior to it, but never superior.
The eye-faculty of a lower stage, having become habituated to perceiving coarse forms, lacks the functional capacity to perceive the subtle forms of a higher stage.
Furthermore, the eye-faculty of a lower stage possesses no superior efficacy.

The higher stages possess their own superior sense organs (*indriya*), and the lower stages possess their own visual consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore, the eyes of a lower stage are not the support for a consciousness of a higher stage.
As for visible forms (*rūpa*) in relation to consciousness, they may be equal to, or of a higher or lower level than, that consciousness.
The relationship of form-consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna*) to the body is like that of form to consciousness; that is, it may pertain to its own level, or to a higher or lower level.

Regarding consciousness in relation to the body, that which pertains to its own level occurs only when one is born in the Desire Realm or the First Dhyāna; that which pertains to a higher level occurs only when one is born in the Desire Realm; and that which pertains to a lower level occurs only when one is born in the Second, Third, or Fourth Dhyānas.

Regarding visible forms in relation to the body: those belonging to one's own level or a lower level are seen by eyes of a higher level; those belonging to a higher level are seen only by eyes of that same higher level.
Furthermore, by means of eyes belonging to one's own level, one sees only visible forms of one's own level or a lower level.

If one sees forms of one's own level or lower levels with the eye of a higher level, the detailed explanation for the auditory element (*śrotra-dhātu*) should be understood as being like that of the eye;

that is, the ear is not lower than the body, nor are sound and consciousness [lower than the body], while for the higher ear and sound, both [consciousness and object] are entirely [of the same or higher level].
The same applies to the body; it should be understood in detail according to its respective correspondence, as explained in the commentary on the eye.
The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are all generally of their own level (*svabhūmika*), because they mostly share this commonality.
This is because the consciousnesses of smell and taste belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and because the nose and tongue perceive only objects that have reached them.
Regarding the specific distinctions therein: the body and the tangible object must belong to the same level (*bhūmi*), because [the tactile consciousness] perceives objects that reach it.
As for the consciousness in relation to the tangible object and the body, it may be of its own level or of a lower level.
"Of its own level" refers to when one is born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna; "of a lower level" refers to when one is born in the three higher dhyānas.

It should be understood that the four factors of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are indeterminate: namely, the mind-element is sometimes co-existent with the body, consciousness, and mental objects in the same level (*bhūmi*), and sometimes it belongs to a higher or lower level.
The body exists only in five levels; the [other] three [consciousnesses] pervade all levels, yet they arise only within those five levels.
When the mind (*manas*) and its consciousness (*vijñāna*) take as their object a phenomenon belonging to their own level, it is said that the mind and the [three] are in the same level.

As for the case where the mind-element (*manodhātu*) belongs to a higher level: this refers to when one is practicing meditative absorption or has been born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet immediately after emerging from the first dhyāna, gives rise to a consciousness of the desire realm to cognize a phenomenon of the desire realm; in such a case, the mind belongs to the higher level while the [three] belong to the lower level.

Alternatively, when consciousnesses belonging to the first, second, or third dhyānas arise immediately after the second, third, or fourth dhyānas respectively, they cognize the dharmas of the first, second, or third dhyānas; in these cases, the mental faculty belongs to a higher stage while the three [consciousnesses] belong to lower stages.

In this way, when one is born into the first dhyāna or other higher realms and subsequently arises from them to descend to lower ones, it should be understood according to the principle that at the time of such rebirth, there is no mental consciousness (*manas*) belonging to a higher stage.
This is because, while relying on a body of a lower stage, it is impossible for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of that lower stage to cease, since one has received birth in a higher realm.
Furthermore, it is certain that there is no death while the mind abides in a different stage (*bhūmi*).
Thus, one should understand that there is no mental faculty (*manas*) of a lower stage based upon a body of a higher stage.

However, it is not contrary to reason for a body of a lower stage to be supported by a mental faculty of a higher stage; that is to say, when rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) first occurs in the Desire or Form Realms immediately following the mental element (*manodhātu*) of a higher stage, the mind belongs to the higher stage while the body and consciousness belong to the lower stage.
The phenomena perceived by that [consciousness] belong either to its own level, a higher level, or are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
It should be understood accordingly that it is not contrary to reason for a body of a higher level to be experienced by a mental faculty belonging to a lower level.

Regarding the time of wandering in meditative concentration, it is not contrary to reason that the mental faculty belonging to a lower stage may rely upon a body of a higher stage; that is to say, one born in a higher stage first gives rise to a transformative mind consisting of the consciousness-body of a lower stage.
This same principle regarding consciousness should also be explained in detail.

Furthermore, one should investigate: when an eye of the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm, or when an eye of the form realm sees forms of both realms, at that time, by how many kinds of visual consciousness can those forms be cognized?
Furthermore, how many kinds of discrimination arise therein?
In order to prevent confusion regarding this thesis, I shall first provide a general summary and subsequently offer a detailed explanation.

It should be understood that, for the time being, I will discuss the discriminative (abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa) and the indeterminate (aniyata) types, because the recollective (anusmaraṇa-vikalpa) pervades all stages.
Based on these two types, all visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

Furthermore, wholesome conceptualization (*kuśala-vikalpa*) is able to take as its objects those of its own level, the levels above, and the levels below; defiled conceptualization (*kliṣṭa-vikalpa*) takes as its objects those of its own level and the levels above; and neutral conceptualization (*avyākṛta-vikalpa*) takes as its objects those of its own level and the levels below.
As long as one has not abandoned the craving for the plane where one was born, one possesses all three types of conceptualization belonging to that plane.
If one has abandoned that craving, there remain only two types of conceptualization belonging to that plane—namely, excluding the defiled type—which do not arise on other planes.
There is the case where a wholesome eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) of the first dhyāna manifests, because it is necessarily bound to that specific birth.

Furthermore, one born in the first dhyāna cannot give rise to a wholesome eye-consciousness by relying on an eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) belonging to another stage; nor can one born in another stage cause a non-obscured, neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) discrimination of another stage to manifest, for this too is necessarily bound to that specific birth.

This is not the intended meaning here, which would be to speak only of the conceptualization arising in a single lifetime; for if one were speaking of a single lifetime, then when one is born in a higher realm, there should necessarily be no conceptualization belonging to lower realms.
For within this very life, it is impossible for those three types of discrimination to manifest;
furthermore, discrimination belonging to the higher stages would have to be exclusively wholesome rather than neutral, as the reason for this has already been stated previously.
It is generally taught that in all other births, these are fully possessed.
Having provided this general analysis, we shall now explain them individually.

When one who has severed the roots of goodness sees a form with the eye, that form is cognized by an eye-consciousness that is defiled or non-obscured-neutral; regarding this, three types of conceptualization arise, namely: wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured-neutral.

When one who has not severed the roots of goodness and is not yet free from craving sees a form with the eye, that form is cognized by the three types of visual consciousness, and in relation to it, three types of conceptualization arise.

If ordinary beings born in the desire realm have already abandoned craving for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned craving for the first dhyāna, when they see various forms with the eye of the desire realm, these forms are cognized by a wholesome or non-obscured-neutral visual consciousness, and in relation to them, they further give rise to conceptualization of the desire realm.

If one is of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), they possess all three types; if one is of the nature of not falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), they possess only two, namely, excluding the defiled.

When one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna, these forms are perceived solely by the visual consciousness, which is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); regarding this, the arising of further conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of the desire realm should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding this, there further arise two types of discrimination belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, namely, excluding the defiled.

When one sees forms of that stage with the eye of the first dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and neutral; regarding this, there further arises discrimination of the desire realm, which, for one subject to falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), is of two types, namely, excluding the non-obscured.
For one of non-retrogressive nature (*aparihāna-dharman*), there is only the wholesome (*kuśala*).

Within this, three types of discrimination (*vikalpa*) belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna arise again: when one who has abandoned craving for the first dhyāna but has not yet abandoned craving for the second dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Within this, discrimination of the desire realm arises again; for one of retrogressive nature, all three types are present, whereas for one of non-retrogressive nature, only two types exist—namely, excluding the defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Regarding this, the initial meditative absorption (*prathama-dhyāna*) is further distinguished: for one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇa-dharman*), there are two types—namely, excluding the defiled; for one of the "nature of non-falling away" (*aparihāṇa-dharman*), there is only the wholesome.
Regarding this, two further types of discrimination belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna arise, namely, excluding the defiled.

When one sees the forms of the first dhyāna with the eye of the second dhyāna, these forms are cognized solely by an eye-consciousness that is unobscured-neutral; regarding these, there further arises discrimination of the desire realm. For one who is subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types—excluding the unobscured; for one who is not subject to falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), it is exclusively wholesome.

Regarding this, there further arises a twofold distinction within the first dhyāna: for those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), all three types are present; for those of the nature of not falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), it is exclusively wholesome.
Regarding this, there further arises a twofold distinction within the stages of the [upper] three dhyānas, namely, with the exception of the defiled.
