When one sees the forms of the second dhyāna with the eye of the second dhyāna, these forms are perceived solely by an eye-consciousness that is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Regarding this, if a further conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of the desire realm arises, there are two possibilities for one of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*): namely, excluding the unobscured-neutral, both [the wholesome and the unwholesome] are present; however, for one of the "non-receding" type (*aparihāṇadharman*), there is only the wholesome.
It should be understood that the conceptualizations arising from the stage of the first dhyāna are likewise so.

Furthermore, regarding the three types of conceptualization arising from the stage of the second dhyāna, one should apply the principles of the specific explanations as stated here to each case: those who have abandoned craving for the second dhyāna but not yet abandoned craving for the third; those who have abandoned craving for the third but not yet abandoned craving for the fourth; and those who have abandoned craving for the fourth—all of these should be individually examined according to reason.

Just as it was explained regarding ordinary beings born in the desire realm, so too should it be explained in detail, as appropriate, for those born in the four dhyānas and for noble ones born in the five stages.

Nevertheless, there is a distinction: for all noble ones, whether subject to regression or not, there is no defiled discrimination directed toward higher realms, because universal [defilements] of other stages have already been abandoned and the virtues of the path of seeing are necessarily free from regression.
One should investigate by analogy according to this method.
Having completed the ancillary discussion on consciousnesses such as the ear-consciousness that hears sounds and their respective conceptualizations, one should now address the primary subject.

We shall now analyze: among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), which are included within the six consciousnesses; how many are cognized by each consciousness; how many are permanent and how many are impermanent; and how many are faculties (*indriya*) and how many are not faculties?
The verse says:
Five are external and cognized by two; the eternal is the unconditioned dharma-dhātu;
one portion of the dharmas is the faculties, as are the twelve internal elements.
The treatise states:

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the five elements beginning with form (*rūpa*) are, respectively, the objects of the five consciousnesses beginning with visual consciousness; furthermore, they are all collectively the objects of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Thus, these five elements are each cognized by two consciousnesses among the six consciousnesses.

By this principle, one should know that the remaining thirteen elements are all cognized solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because they are not the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), there is not a single element that is entirely permanent; only a portion of the dharma-element—the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is permanent. By extension, all other dharmas and all other elements are impermanent.

Within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) together with the twelve internal [elements] constitute the faculties (*indriya*), and nothing else. These are the five sensation-faculties (*vedanendriya*);

the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi*); the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) in its entirety; and a portion of each of the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), all of which are subsumed within the dharma-element.

The five faculties, beginning with the eye, are subsumed under their respective names. The female faculty and the male faculty are subsumed as a portion of the body element (*kāyadhātu*), as will be explained later.

The mental faculty (*manas*) is universally subsumed within the seven mind elements (*cittadhātu*); the final three [faculties] are partially subsumed within the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
By logical extension, the remaining five elements—form and so forth—and a portion of the dharma-element are all, by their very nature, not faculties (*indriya*).

The twenty-two faculties are as stated in the Sūtra: namely, the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, diligence faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
The Sūtras establish the sequence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and thus the mental faculty (*manas*) is taught immediately after the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).

However, the masters of the Abhidharma follow a sequence based on meaning; they teach the mental faculty only after the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because they explain it according to the order of those that are without objects (*anālambana*) followed by those with objects (*sālambana*), and because this facilitates clear understanding through various analytical categories.
*Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Four;
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.

Chapter Three: Distinguishing the Differences (Vibhāga-prakaraṇa), Part One. Having thus enumerated the faculties according to their elements, one should now further investigate this matter: for what reason did the Blessed One specifically designate them by the name "faculties" (*indriya*)?

The entire internal realm (*ādhyātmika-dhātu*) and a portion of the dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*) are designated as faculties (*indriya*) by virtue of their predominance (*adhipatya*), because they attain predominance over their respective objects.
Although the quality of predominance exists in all phenomena, the name "faculty" is established only for those that possess it to the highest degree.
In relation to whom does what serve as the supreme dominant condition?
The verse says:
The five faculties [are dominant] over four matters; the four faculties [are dominant] over two kinds.
Among the five [faculties] and the eight [pure faculties], each is preeminent within its own category of defilement or purity.
The treatise says:
It is not the case that all faculties collectively constitute the ultimate preeminence with respect to a single matter.

Each of the five faculties, such as the eye, exercises predominant influence over four matters: first, the adornment of the body; second, the guidance and nourishment of the body; third, the production of consciousness and so forth; and fourth, their unique function.
Adorning the body refers to the fact that if any one of the five sense faculties is lacking, the body becomes unsightly.
Sustaining and nourishing the body refers to avoiding dangers and difficulties through seeing and hearing, as well as being able to partake of solid food.
The three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—all constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). As a verse says:
"Just as a person with clear vision Can avoid present dangers, So too, those who possess intelligence in this world Can distance themselves from future suffering and evil."
"One who is learned can know the Dharma; one who is learned can leave behind evil;
through learning one abandons what is meaningless; through learning one attains Nirvāṇa.
The body subsists by means of food; life depends on food for its existence. Once fed, it causes the mind..."
"Appropriateness, pleasure, and tranquility.

Regarding "the arising of consciousnesses and so forth," this refers to the production of the five sensory consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, which vary in clarity or dullness according to the sense organs upon which they depend.
Regarding "their unique functions," this refers to the apprehension of their respective objects—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and discerning distinct objects.
Some say that the eyes and ears have predominant functions, respectively, in protecting the physical body and the Dharma-body; the two preceding verses serve as proof for this.

Some say that both the eye and the ear are able to protect the two bodies—the body of birth and the Dharma-body—because the eye and the ear each serve as a predominant condition for associating with virtuous persons and hearing the true Dharma.
The female, male, life, and mind faculties each possess predominant influence over two matters.
First, regarding the predominant influence of the female and male faculties: first, the differentiation of sentient beings; second, the differentiation of their distinctions.

Regarding the difference in sentient beings: at the beginning of the eon, the forms and types of sentient beings were all identical; only after the two sexual organs had arisen did the distinctions between female and male forms appear.
Regarding the difference in differentiation: this refers to the variations in the arrangement of movements, speech, breasts, topknots, and so forth.
Some say that because there are differences in courage and timidity, they are called "differences among sentient beings" (*sattva-viśeṣa*);
because there are differences in clothing and ornaments, they are called "differences in distinctions" (*vibhāga-viśeṣa*).

Others say that because these [factors] possess predominant power over both the defiled and pure categories, it is said they exist in both; and because they give rise to non-restraint, commit immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), and sever the roots of virtue, they are said to possess predominant power over the defiled category.

Because they are able to receive the vows (*saṃvara*), enter the Path, attain the fruits, and become free from desire, they possess superior power (*adhipatibala*) regarding the pure factors (*śukladharma*); eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others do not possess such qualities.

The life-faculty has predominance over two things: namely, it is by virtue of the life-faculty that the [other] faculties and their distinctions are established; for when this exists, that exists, and when this is absent, that is absent.

Alternatively, it is because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is required in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) for the continuity and maintenance of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), since it is only through the life-faculty that the place of rebirth is determined.
This is because when one gives rise to a wholesome or defiled mind of that same level, or gives rise to another mind, it does not constitute death.
The mental faculty (*manas*) exercises sovereignty over two aspects: namely, the ability to link to a subsequent existence and the capacity for autonomous functioning.
Regarding the linking to a subsequent existence, as the Blessed One told Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, would the semen and blood be able to form the *kalala*?"
"No, World-Honored One! ...
[and so on] as extensively explained."
Regarding "acting with mastery," as the sutra says:
"The mind leads the world; The mind thoroughly encompasses it.
Thus, this single dharma, the mind, Acts with mastery over all."
Some say that because the mental faculty (*manas*) possesses predominant power over both the defiled and purified categories, it is said to "pertain to both," as the Sūtra states:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is purified, sentient beings are purified."

The five sensations, such as pleasure, and the eight faculties, such as faith, possess sovereign power over both the defiled and the purified states; that is to say, the five sensations, such as pleasure, have sovereign power over the defiled because they serve as the basis for the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) such as attachment.

Some say that these [feelings] possess predominance over both the defiled and purified categories, because they are said to be the bases for worldly attachment (*gardha*) and renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).

Through pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated; suffering serves as the basis for faith; and the six [types of feeling] serve as the bases for joy, sorrow, and equanimity associated with renunciation.
Because it is stated in the sūtras, the eight faculties beginning with faith exercise sovereignty over purification, as the sūtra says:

"My noble disciples possess the ramparts and moats of faith, the power of diligence, the defense of mindfulness, a mind concentrated and liberated, and wisdom as their sword," and so forth, as explained at length.
Since these [three] include the latter three faculties, they certainly possess predominance (*adhipatya*) with respect to the pure category (*śukla-pakṣa*).

If a faculty is established on the basis of predominance, then among the afflictions of the categories of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*), the two factors of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) also exercise a predominant function; thus, perception should likewise be established as a faculty, just like feeling.

Furthermore, various afflictions possess predominant efficacy (*adhipatya*) in the destruction of wholesome factors (*kuśalapakṣa*) and so forth; thus, they should also constitute the nature of faculties (*indriya*).

Moreover, faculties are established on the basis of being preeminent (*pradhāna*); since among all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) nirvāṇa is the most preeminent, for what reason is nirvāṇa not established as a faculty?

Furthermore, the Kāpilas maintain that speech, the hands, and the anus are also established as faculties, because they possess predominance with respect to speaking, grasping and moving, and the act of excretion, respectively.

Such matters as these should not be established as faculties (*indriya*), because the characteristics of what is accepted as a faculty are as follows. The verse says: The basis of the mind, its differentiation, its maintenance, and its defilement; The commentary explains: Because the basis of the mind is distinct, and because of this [basis], there is its maintenance, its differentiation, and its defilement, these are established as faculties. Furthermore, because they are predominant in their respective functions, they are established as faculties. What are these? They are the five faculties beginning with the eye, the three faculties beginning with the life-faculty, the female and male faculties, the five feeling faculties, the faith faculty and so forth, the faculty of knowing what is unknown, and the faculty of one who has already known. This is the equipment, this is the purification; it is by virtue of these measures that the faculties are established.
The treatise says:
That upon which the mind relies consists of the six faculties, such as the eye; these six internal bases are the foundation of sentient beings.
These distinctions of characteristics arise from the male and female faculties (*puruṣa-strī-indriya*).
Furthermore, by means of the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*), this [existence] remains for a single period; by means of this, defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is established.

By means of the five feeling-faculties (*vedanā-indriya*), the equipment for purification (*viśuddhi-sambhāra*) is established; by means of the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), purification (*vyavadāna*) is established. By means of the final three faculties, the purpose of establishing the faculties is fully accomplished; therefore, one should not further establish perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth as faculties.
Among all afflictions, craving is the most grievous; therefore, only feeling is established as its root.
That the gravity of craving is paramount is because the Sūtra states that craving is the cause for the arising of the six sense bases.

Furthermore, one should consider that while non-seeing is not the cause for the arising of afflictions, once other causes have produced inverted views, false conceptualizations (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*) maintain them so that they continue in succession; because these cannot be severed or destroyed apart from the correct antidote, it is said that this perception serves as the cause for those [afflictions].
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the cause of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and both [feeling and craving] pertain to both types [of causes].
Because feeling is a particularly grave fault—being the cause of afflictions (*kleśa*) and serving as both types of causes—it is established independently as a faculty (*indriya*).
Other masters say:

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is not established as a faculty because it is eclipsed by other dharmas; that is to say, wholesome perceptions are eclipsed by right wisdom, while defiled perceptions are eclipsed by inversion. Since it does not possess predominance (*ādhipatya*), it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are also not predominant; since it is feeling (*vedanā*) that becomes predominant therein, only feeling can be established as a faculty (*indriya*).

Alternatively, how could that which harms the category of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*) and destroys the matter of pleasant results—being inferior, base, and impure—be established as a faculty?
The faculties (*indriya*) are called "sovereign dharmas" (*adhipati-dharma*) because they are predominant in the world.
Furthermore, although *nirvāṇa* is superior to all other dharmas, it is not established as a faculty because it brings about the cessation of the faculties.
It is like the breaking of various jars; the act of breaking is not itself the substance of the jar.
Furthermore, the vocal organs and so forth are not designated as faculties (*indriya*), because this would lead to the faults of being indeterminate, confused, and excessive.
Regarding the fault of indeterminacy: which vocal organ would be established as the faculty of speech?
That which is able to produce vocal sounds is called the organ of speech, and this is the tongue.

If that were so, then mental investigation (*vitarka*), analysis (*vicāra*), and other such factors, as well as the winds that can initiate vocal action, should also be established as faculties, because they too are able to produce speech.

This means that vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, depend on conditions such as the lips, teeth, palate, and throat to initiate speech and sound; they do not depend solely on the tongue, for there would otherwise be no distinction in their causes.

Furthermore, since vitarka, vicāra, and so forth are the primary causes for the production of speech and sound, and since various factors such as the hands, armpits, pipes, strings, and breath can all serve as causes for producing speech and sound, one ought not to establish the tongue alone as the faculty of speech (*vāgindriya*).
If it is argued that because the cognition of form also depends on speech, the eye should not be established as a faculty in its own right, this is necessarily unreasonable;
for those born blind, although they hear descriptions of form, do not perceive the distinct characteristics of blue and so forth.
The hands should not be designated as faculties (*indriya*) with respect to grasping, for the mouth and other parts are also capable of grasping objects.
The feet should not be designated as faculties with respect to locomotion, for classes of beings such as snakes and fish possess locomotion without relying on feet.
The excretory organ should not be called a faculty (*indriya*) because it performs the function of discarding; for the mouth and other organs are likewise capable of discarding.

As for the fault of confusion, the faculties established by that [opponent] would become confused, because the mouth is capable of both grasping and discarding, and because the hands and feet both possess the functions of grasping and moving. Such are the faults of confusion and so forth.
If there were such an excessive error, the sense-faculties established by them would be without limit.

If the tongue faculty were distinct from the speech faculty, one would have to admit that the nose faculty is distinct from the breath faculty, because the tongue can speak while the nose passes the breath.

If that which exerts even a slight efficacy toward something is established as a faculty (*indriya*), then the throat, teeth, lips, stomach, and so forth should also be established as faculties, because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) over such functions as swallowing, chewing, and containing food.
Alternatively, since all causes exercise sovereign influence (*adhipatitva*) over the production of their own respective effects, they should all be established as faculties (*indriya*).
Thus, the Kāpila system is like the play of a child; one should not grant the status of faculty to its speech organs and so forth.
Having already explained the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*) and the reasons for their establishment, we shall now explain the individual nature of each faculty.

Among these, from the eye faculty up to the male faculty, their characteristics were already analyzed in the preceding chapter; that is to say, those supports of consciousness consisting of five kinds of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) are called the eye and other faculties.
The two faculties of female and male are established based on specific distinctions within a single part of the body faculty.
Since the essence of the life faculty is dissociated from thought, it will be explained among the dissociated factors when we reach that section.
Since the essence of faith and the other [faculties] consists of mental factors (*caitta*), they will be analyzed when we reach the section on mental factors.
As for the five feelings such as pleasure and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), there is no other place where they are analyzed; therefore, they should be explained here.
The verse says:
Displeasure of the body is called suffering; that same [pleasure] is called happiness, as well as the mental pleasure of the three dhyānas. In other stages, this is termed joy.
Displeasure of mind is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*); the intermediate state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is undifferentiated from the two [others].
Based on the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, three faculties are established in relation to the nine stages.
The treatise says:
"Body" refers to bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*), so called because it depends on the material sense-faculties; that is, the sensation associated with the five consciousnesses.

"Displeasure" has the meaning of affliction or harm. Among the sensations experienced in conjunction with the five consciousnesses, those that are capable of causing affliction are termed the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

That which is called "pleasurable" (sukha) has the meaning of "beneficial. Specifically, among the feelings of contact experienced together with the five sensory consciousnesses, that which is internally beneficial is termed the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
Within the first dhyāna, the three sensory consciousnesses are accompanied by pleasure; these too are subsumed under this [faculty], as they belong to the same category.

In the third dhyāna, that feeling associated with the mental consciousness which is capable of providing benefit is also called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*); since there is no other body-consciousness in that stage, this very joy associated with the mind is established as the faculty of pleasure.

The pleasant sensation that arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness is of two kinds; in the third dhyāna it is called "pleasure" (*sukha*), because in that stage one is free from craving for joy (*prīti*).
Excluding the third dhyāna, in the three lower stages it is called the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*), because there is still craving for joy present.

These two states of mental joy (*cittaprīti*) are identical in their sense of gathering and benefiting; what difference is there in their modes of activity (*ākāra*) such that they are divided into joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*)?
It is because there is a distinction in the way their modes of activity proceed.
When a state of mental joy proceeds with a mode of activity characterized by tranquility, it is called the faculty of bliss (*sukhendriya*).
If there is a mental state that is joyful and characterized by coarse, active movement, it is termed the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Alternatively, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) possesses a superior power of benefit, whereas the benefit conferred by the faculty of joy is not like this.
Because of this pleasure of the third dhyāna stage, the Noble Ones describe it as a point of attachment.

The sensation that accompanies the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is capable of causing affliction is a lack of mental satisfaction, which is termed the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Having established four feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) based on the distinctions between the characteristics of experience—namely, whether they are pleasant or unpleasant for the body and mind—it is said that there is no distinction between "neutral equanimity" (*madhyopekṣā*) and the other two;
"neutral" (*madhya*) has the meaning of being neither pleasant nor unpleasant, which is precisely what is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) when it is neither suffering nor pleasure.
Regarding the feelings within body and mind, what feeling does this meditative concentration possess?
One should say that this feeling pertains to both body and mind.
For what reason are suffering and pleasure each divided into two [faculties], while neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is established as only a single faculty?
This is because there is no distinction between them in body and mind.
That is to say, mental pleasure and pain are for the most part restless, whereas pleasure and pain in the body are characterized by stability;
as for neither-pain-nor-pleasure, whether in the body or the mind, their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is without difference, consisting solely in stability.

Furthermore, mental suffering and pleasure arise mostly from conceptual discrimination, whereas those in the body do not; rather, they arise according to the power of the sensory objects, and thus they arise similarly for Arhats and others.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, exists in both body and mind without conceptual discrimination; its mode of activity arises spontaneously as it abides in the middle way.
Furthermore, painful and pleasant sensations, whether residing in the body or the mind, differ in their modes of manifestation toward enemies and toward loved ones;
neutral sensations, whether residing in the body or the mind, do not differ in their modes of manifestation toward objects that are neither [pleasant nor unpleasant].
Therefore, suffering and pleasure are each divided into two [roots], while neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is established as only one root.
Having already explained the essential nature of the various feeling-faculties such as pleasure, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) shall now be explained.
It is not possible to explain their essential natures individually; rather, they should be established collectively based on the nine faculties within the three paths.

These nine—the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—constitute the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) within the three paths. Specifically, when these nine factors, including the mental faculty and so forth, exist within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they constitute the essence of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvya-jñendriya*), because they function with the mode of activity of "I shall come to know what is not yet known."

If, during the path of cultivation, the nine factors such as the mental faculty (*manas*) constitute the second, the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*), it is because, in order to abandon the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one repeatedly and fully cognizes the objects already known.

The nine factors, beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*) in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), constitute the essence of the third faculty, the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). It is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it knows itself as knowing; that is, because through the cultivation of knowledge, it has become its very nature.
Alternatively, because they are capable of protecting and knowing, they are called "possessors of knowledge" (*ājñātāvin*).
Nine faculties are associated to constitute this state; therefore, the eight [faculties] beginning with volition also receive this name.

Thus, although there are twenty-two names for these faculties, their actual substance consists of only seventeen: the female and male faculties are subsumed within the body faculty, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are subsumed within nine faculties.
Having thus explained that the essential natures of the faculties differ, we shall now analyze their distinctions according to various categories.
Among these twenty-two faculties, how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:

Only the last three are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the material faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculties of grief and suffering should be known as exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*); the remaining nine faculties pertain to both.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the final three faculties mentioned immediately prior, their essence is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); this carries the meaning of being "stainless" (*vimala*). "Stain" (*mala*) and "taint" (*āsrava*) differ in name but are identical in substance.

The seven material faculties (rūpīndriya) are called "material" because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). These material faculties, along with the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the faculties of mental distress (daurmanasya) and physical pain (duḥkha), are exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava).

Regarding the nine that pertain to both [categories]: the nine faculties previously mentioned—consisting of the mind (manas) and the others—that are subsumed under the three untainted (anāsrava) states are called "untainted"; the remaining nine, such as the mind and others, are called "with-outflows."
Some say that faith and the other [faculties] are also exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is not reasonable, for as the Blessed One said:

"If I have not, regarding these five faculties such as faith, truly known them as they are—their origin, their passing away, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them—I am not yet able to transcend this world of gods and humans," and so forth at length, [stating that] they are not untainted dharmas.
One should perform such sequential observation in this manner.

Furthermore, before the Buddha turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma, he first surveyed the world universally with his Buddha-eye and perceived that among the various classes of sentient beings there were distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.
This detailed analysis is as set forth in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Having thus explained what is tainted (*sāsrava*) and what is untainted (*anāsrava*), [one may ask]:
among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are maturation (*vipāka*) and how many are not maturation?
The verse says:
Life is exclusively maturation; sorrow and the final eight are not.
The material faculties, the mind, and the remaining four sensations—each of these may be of either kind.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, among these various faculties, it is indistinguishable that only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is definitely a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
How can this life be considered indistinguishable?
Because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, this life-faculty is indeed a maturation, for it is the fruit of the volition (*cetanā*) of a monk who has attained the ultimate meditative absorption (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) and the fruit of arhatship, directed toward the Saṅgha or an individual: "May all my karmas capable of producing the maturation of wealth instead produce the maturation of longevity."
Because it was spoken by the Sage.

Some say that through the power of the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), one draws forth the lifespan produced by karma from a previous life that was to be experienced as indeterminate (*aniyata-vedanīya*) and causes it to be experienced in the present. Furthermore, others wish to have the power of the ultimate meditative concentration draw forth the remaining maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of karma from a previous life.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the subsequent eight faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), are all non-retribution (*avipāka*), because they are of a determinate nature (*vyākṛtatva*).
The Sūtra states that there is karma conducive to the experience of sorrow; this refers to its association with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*).
The statement is consistent and without fault, just as the statement that there is contact associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya*) and so forth.
For what reason is it definitively known that sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*)?
Because it does not continue to function in one who is free from desire and greed (*vītarāga*).
Retribution (vipāka) is not like this; therefore, it is not retribution.
How is it known for certain that sorrow does not persist in one who is free from sensual desire?

This is because sorrow is an outflow-result (niṣyanda-phala) of ignorance, and since Arhats and others have already abandoned all ignorance, and because those signs of enmity and hatred no longer exist for them.
For those Arhats who have abandoned sensual desire, because they have already severed all the calamities and afflictions of the desire realm, even the signs of enmity and aversion no longer exist.
Furthermore, because their mental continuity is largely filled with joy, sorrow does not follow after those who have abandoned sensual desire.

Thus, it is known that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) transcends the category of maturation (*vipāka*), while the remaining faculties pertain to both; this meaning is established by implication.
That is to say, the seven material faculties, the mental faculty (*manendriya*), and the four sensations other than sorrow—these twelve each pertain to both categories.
Regarding the seven material faculties, if they are nurtured (*aupacayika*), they are not maturation (*vipāka*); otherwise, they are all maturation.

As for the mental faculty and the four feelings, if they are wholesome or defiled, or if they belong to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), or transformative power (*nairmāṇika*), they are also not maturation as appropriate; otherwise, they are all maturation.
Having thus explained these [categories] such as maturation and so forth,
among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many have maturation and how many are without maturation?
The verse says:

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) definitely has maturation (*vipāka*); the first eight and the last three have none. The mental faculty (*manas*), the remaining [faculties], and the sensations such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth—each of these is common to both [types]. The Treatise says: The faculty of doubt (*vicikitsendriya*) necessarily possesses maturation. Among the faculties, the first eight—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, female, and male faculties—and the last three—the faculty of knowing what is not yet known, the faculty of perfect knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known—do not possess maturation. The mental faculty, the remaining [four] material faculties (excluding the five sensory organs), and the sensations of pleasure, pain, joy, and equanimity each pertain to both categories: they may either possess maturation or be without it. The Treatise says: [As for the statement that the first eight and the last three have no maturation: The first eight are without maturation because they are exclusively derived from the outflow of past karma (*niṣyanda*). As for the last three, they are without maturation because they are exclusively supramundane (*lokottara*). The mental faculty and the remaining [faculties] are common to both, because they can be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and because they can be either mundane or supramundane. Regarding the sensations, the sensation of equanimity is common to both because it is neither-painful-nor-pleasant; the other four sensations are common to both because they can be either contaminated or uncontaminated. Furthermore, the sensation of pleasure in the realm of desire is common to both because it can be either contaminated or uncontaminated. The sensation of pleasure in the first dhyāna is common to both because it can be either contaminated or uncontaminated. The sensation of pleasure in the second dhyāna and above is common to both because it is exclusively uncontaminated. The sensation of joy is common to both because it can be either contaminated or uncontaminated. The sensation of pain is common to both because it can be either contaminated or uncontaminated. Therefore, it is said that the mental faculty, the remaining [faculties], and the sensations such as pleasure and so forth each pertain to both categories. The rest is as previously explained. Thus, it is established that the faculty of doubt definitely has maturation, while the first eight and the last three have none. The mental faculty, the remaining [faculties], and the sensations such as pleasure and so forth each pertain to both. This concludes the section on the faculties. The following section concerns the faculties and their possession (*prāpti*). It asks: regarding the faculties, how many are possessed by which realms? How many are acquired through birth? How many are acquired through cultivation? And how many are acquired through detachment? The treatise states: "Possessed by all, except for two. This means that with the exception of the female and male faculties, the remaining twenty-two faculties are possessed by beings in all three realms. Why is this? Because the female and male faculties are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and do not exist in the formless realm. Furthermore, the faculty of knowing what is not yet known exists only in the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and does not exist in the subsequent stages. The faculty of perfect knowledge exists only in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and does not exist in the stage of the path of seeing. The faculty of one who has already known exists only in the stage of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) and does not exist in the preceding stages. Therefore, these three are not possessed by beings in all realms. The remaining twenty-two are possessed by beings in all three realms. However, there is a distinction between those who possess them and those who do not. Specifically, beings in the desire realm possess twenty-three faculties: the eleven faculties beginning with the eye, the five sensations, the life faculty, and the three faculties of the learner (*śaikṣa*). Beings in the form realm possess nineteen faculties: the eleven faculties beginning with the eye, the five sensations, the life faculty, and the three faculties of the learner. Beings in the formless realm possess eighteen faculties: the life faculty, the mental faculty, the sensation of equanimity, and the three faculties of the learner. Those in the stage of the path of seeing possess twenty-one faculties: the eleven faculties beginning with the eye, the five sensations, the life faculty, the mental faculty, and the faculty of knowing what is not yet known. Those in the stage of the path of cultivation possess nineteen faculties: the eleven faculties beginning with the eye, the five sensations, the life faculty, the mental faculty, and the faculty of perfect knowledge. Those in the stage of the path of no-more-learning possess eighteen faculties: the eleven faculties beginning with the eye, the five sensations, the life faculty, the mental faculty, and the faculty of one who has already known. The remaining faculties are not possessed by those in the aforementioned stages. This concludes the section on possession. Next, we shall discuss acquisition through birth. It asks: among the faculties, how many are acquired through birth? The treatise states: "Acquired through birth are ten. This means that ten faculties are acquired through birth: the five faculties beginning with the eye, the five sensations, and the life faculty. Why is this? Because these ten are acquired at the moment of conception. Furthermore, the life faculty is acquired through birth because it continues throughout the duration of the lifespan. The five faculties beginning with the eye and the five sensations are acquired through birth because they arise simultaneously with the body at the moment of conception. The remaining faculties are not acquired through birth. Why is this? Because the mental faculty, the sensation of pleasure, the sensation of joy, and the sensation of pain are acquired through cultivation. The female and male faculties are acquired through detachment. The faculty of knowing what is not yet known and the faculty of perfect knowledge are acquired through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, respectively. The faculty of one who has already known is acquired through the path of no-more-learning. Therefore, these are not acquired through birth. This concludes the section on acquisition through birth. Next, we shall discuss acquisition through cultivation. It asks: among the faculties, how many are acquired through cultivation? The treatise states: "Acquired through cultivation are seven. This means that seven faculties are acquired through cultivation: the five faculties beginning with the eye, the sensation of pleasure, and the sensation of joy. Why is this? Because these seven are acquired through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, the five faculties beginning with the eye and the sensation of pleasure are acquired through cultivation because they arise through the power of meditative concentration. The sensation of joy is acquired through cultivation because it arises through the power of meditative concentration. The remaining faculties are not acquired through cultivation. Why is this? Because the mental faculty, the sensation of equanimity, the sensation of pain, the life faculty, the female and male faculties, the faculty of knowing what is not yet known, the faculty of perfect knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known are not acquired through the power of meditative concentration. Therefore, these are not acquired through cultivation. This concludes the section on acquisition through cultivation. Next, we shall discuss acquisition through detachment. It asks: among the faculties, how many are acquired through detachment? The treatise states: "Acquired through detachment are two. This means that two faculties are acquired through detachment: the female and male faculties. Why is this? Because these two are acquired through the power of detachment from the desire realm. Furthermore, the female and male faculties are acquired through detachment because they are abandoned upon entering the form realm. The remaining faculties are not acquired through detachment. Why is this? Because the mental faculty, the sensation of equanimity, the sensation of pleasure, the sensation of joy, the sensation of pain, the life faculty, the five faculties beginning with the eye, the faculty of knowing what is not yet known, the faculty of perfect knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known are not acquired through the power of detachment. Therefore, these are not acquired through detachment. This concludes the section on acquisition through detachment. This concludes the chapter on the faculties. The following chapter concerns the powers (*bala*). It asks: regarding the powers, how many are there? What are their characteristics? The treatise states: "The powers are ten; they are the same as the faculties, but they are distinguished by the absence of obstruction. This means that the powers are ten in number, and their nature is the same as the faculties. However, they are distinguished by the fact that they are unobstructed. Why is this? Because the faculties are sometimes obstructed by the power of afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas the powers are never obstructed. Furthermore, the powers are unobstructed because they are the antidotes to the afflictions. This concludes the section on the powers. The following section concerns the faculties and the powers. It asks: regarding the faculties and the powers, how many are included in the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)? How many are included in the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)? The treatise states: "Included in form are nine; included in consciousness are seven. This means that nine faculties are included in the aggregate of form: the five faculties
Regarding the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) as previously described, one should know that it definitely possesses karmic maturation (vipāka).

The word "definitely" is intended to indicate that it exists exclusively [as such] and not otherwise; it excludes what is not maturation, because [the other types of sorrow] are either neutral (avyākṛta) or untainted (anāsrava).

The first eight faculties, beginning with the eye, and the final three—these eleven faculties are definitely without maturation (*vipāka*). This is because the eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and the three are untainted (*anāsrava*).

It is established by implication that all others pertain to both categories; namely, the mind faculty, the remaining four [feeling faculties], and faith and so forth—the term "and so forth" including the four faculties of diligence and the rest. Each of these eleven faculties pertains to both types.
The mental faculties of intention, joy, and equanimity, if they are unwholesome or wholesome with outflows, possess ripening; if they are neutral or without outflows, they do not possess ripening.
The faculty of suffering, if it is wholesome or unwholesome, possesses ripening; if it is neutral, it does not possess ripening.
If the five faculties beginning with faith are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they have maturation (*savipāka*); if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they have no maturation.
Thus has been explained [the distinction between] those with maturation and so forth.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:
Only the last eight faculties are exclusively wholesome; the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasya) pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
the mind faculty and the remaining sensations pertain to all three types; the first eight are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The treatise states:

The five faculties beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties are exclusively wholesome; the faculty of grief (daurmanasya) pertains only to the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome; the mental faculty and the four sensations (vedanā) all pertain to all three natures; and the eight faculties beginning with the eye are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Having thus explained the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, [one may ask]:

among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The verse says: In the desire, form, and formless realms, respectively, one excludes the last three [faculties],
as well as the female and male faculties, sorrow and suffering, and additionally, the other forms, joy, and pleasure.
The treatise states:

In the desire realm, the last three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are excluded, because those three faculties are exclusively non-bound (aniyata). By this analogy, it should be understood that there are nineteen remaining faculties bound to the desire realm.

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), as previously stated, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are excluded; furthermore, the four faculties of male, female, sorrow, and suffering are also excluded. By this analogy, it should be understood that fifteen faculties also pertain to the realm of form.

The faculties of male and female are excluded because beings in the realm of form have already transcended the phenomena of sexual desire, and there is no cause for them to experience these faculties.
Some say it is because this body is ugly;
however, this explanation is incorrect, for the concealment of the male organ is not ugliness. Nevertheless, the Buddha places them within the category of males.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"There is no possibility and no occasion for a female body to become a Brahmā; there is the possibility and occasion for a male to become a Brahmā, because his majesty and power, being free from desire, resemble those of a male."
As it is said in praise of the Great Brahmā King:
“The Great Brahmā is like a true man; Whatever was to be attained has already been attained.
Having abandoned desire, his path is majestic and fierce; Therefore, he is called a ‘true man.’”
Regarding the exclusion of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*): this is because in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) there is no occurrence of harm.
Suffering is harm, as it is the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma.
Some say it is because that body is extremely pure and sublime.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is excluded because that realm lacks the characteristic of enmity and aversion, and because the continuum is moistened by *śamatha*.
Some say that the form realm possesses the knowledge of detachment, whereas grief is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of ignorance.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as previously stated, one excludes the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the female and male faculties, the faculties of sorrow and suffering, as well as the faculties of joy, pleasure, and the five material faculties; by this analogy, it should be understood that the remaining eight faculties are associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Having thus explained those factors bound to the desire realm and so forth,

among the twenty-two faculties, how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
The verse says:
The mental [faculty] and the three feelings pertain to all three [categories]; Sorrow is abandoned through insight and cultivation;
Nine are abandoned only through cultivation; Five are abandoned through cultivation, while three are neither.
The Treatise says:
The faculties of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and joy (*sukha*) each pertain to all three [categories].
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*) pertains only to what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).

The seven material faculties, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) are abandoned only by cultivation; this is because they are material, are not defiled, are not produced from the six [consciousnesses], and are not untainted.

The five faculties beginning with faith are either to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) or are not to be abandoned (*aheya*), because they encompass both wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states.
The final three faculties are exclusively not to be abandoned, as they are entirely uncontaminated and free from fault.
However, a sutra states:
"One should know that the noble path is like a raft; even dharma should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharma.

This does not refer to what is abandoned by the two paths of seeing and cultivation; rather, it is called "abandoned" because it is relinquished at the stage of entering the realm of nirvana without remainder.

Having already explained the distinctions among the categories of the various doors, we shall now explain the initial acquisition of the various faculties (*indriya*) that are the result of maturation (*vipāka*).
How many faculties of maturation are initially acquired, and in which realm?
One must ask about the initial acquisition of the faculties of maturation in order to exclude the possibility that birth can be continued by a mind free from defilement (*akliṣṭa-citta*).
The verse says:
In the desire realm, those born from womb, egg, or moisture initially obtain two types of maturation;
those born by transformation obtain six, seven, or eight; in the form realm, there are six; in the higher realms, only life-faculty.
The Commentary states:
In the initial stage of receiving birth through the womb, egg, or moisture, one acquires only two ripening faculties (*vipāka-indriya*), namely the body faculty and the life faculty.
By mentioning the womb, egg, and moisture, it excludes miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), because the material faculties of those born miraculously do not arise gradually.
In this explanation of maturation (*vipāka*), mental equanimity (*upekṣā*) is not mentioned because at that time it is necessarily defiled and not a maturation.
Furthermore, although the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) are also acquired at that time, they are not maturations; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
This is explained by way of illustration and does not distinguish the three stages of birth.

Although at the stage of the *kalala* one acquires dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*) such as visible form and so forth, its substance is not yet a faculty (*indriya*); therefore, it is not mentioned here.
At the initial stage of birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), one acquires six, seven, or eight [faculties]. Those without gender acquire six;
as at the beginning of a kalpa, these six are the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life.
Those with one gender acquire seven, such as the various devas and so forth.
Those with both sexual organs obtain eight; it is possible for those in the evil destinies to be born by transformation with both organs.
Those in the first dhyāna of the form realm obtain six, as explained in the case of those born by transformation in the desire realm who lack organs.
"Above, there is only life" refers to the formless realm, which is called "above" because its birth and meditative attainment are superior to those below.
At that initial moment, they obtain only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as a result of maturation (*vipāka*); by this it is proven that the life-faculty truly exists.
If this did not exist, what faculty would one obtain such that one could be said to be "born in the formless realm"?
That which is neither virtuous nor defiled is termed "arising from the fruit of karma," because it has not yet undergone that birth and arises adventitiously.
Furthermore, a ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*) lacks the capacity for rebirth-continuation, as it is only admitted that a defiled mind can continue the process of rebirth.
For those who argue that the past and future do not exist, at that time the maturation (vipāka) of the three periods would be non-existent; upon what, then, could birth depend?
One must admit that the actual life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the basis for that birth, and thus it is designated as a faculty of maturation.
Having first explained those acquired at birth, one should now explain the faculties that are last to cease.
At the time of death in which realm do how many faculties cease last?
The verse says:
At the moment of death, the faculties cease: for those in the formless realm, three; for those in the three lower realms, eight;
in the desire realm, nineteen, eighteen, or eight, depending on whether death is sudden or gradual; for those of good rebirth, four, with five added in the case of a wholesome mind.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, regarding defiled and neutral minds, how many faculties (*indriya*) cease at the moment of death?

It is said that when one is about to die in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), three faculties—life, mind, and equanimity—cease last; for in the Formless Realm, there is only the feeling of equanimity and no others.
Furthermore, the term "formless" (ārūpya) excludes the possibility that they possess form. Other masters say:

since they do possess form, if one does not assert the existence of a substantial entity (dravya) called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), how could the cessation of such a maturation (vipāka) be designated as "death in the formless realm"?

If you say that one is called "dead" because the four aggregates of maturation (*vipāka*) have been severed, then one should also be called "dead" at the moment when a wholesome or defiled mind manifests.
If you say that the maturation experienced in that stage has not yet been exhausted, how could there be a time for its exhaustion without [the aggregates] being experienced?
When a wholesome or defiled mind is present, one should say that such a person experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of which karma?
It cannot be called "experiencing" [the result] if it is not presently manifest.
For a detailed determination of this, see the *Nyāyānusāra*.
At the time of death in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), eight faculties cease last: namely, the five beginning with the eye, as well as the first three [mental] faculties.
This is because the faculties of those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are never deficient at birth or death.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when dying suddenly, nineteen, eighteen, or eight faculties cease.
Those with both sexual organs cease ten faculties: namely, the female and male organs along with the eight previously mentioned.
Those with one sexual organ cease nine; those without sexual organs cease eight.
When dying gradually, the four faculties of body, life, mind, and equanimity are the last to cease; these four necessarily do not cease sequentially.
If one dies with a wholesome mind within the three realms, the number [of faculties] increases by five in each stage, because a wholesome mind necessarily possesses the faculties such as faith.
That is to say, in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) it increases to eight faculties, and so on down to the desire realm (kāmadhātu), where it gradually reaches nine.
Now, one should further consider:
how many faculties (*indriya*) are able to attain which fruit of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)?
Although the fruits of śramaṇaship can also be attained by means that are not faculties, since this discussion concerns the faculties, the question is restricted to them alone.
The verse says:
Nine attain the two extreme fruits; seven, eight, or nine attain the two intermediate fruits;
eleven attain arhatship; these are stated according to what is possible based on a single [type of] basis.
The treatise says:
The "extremes" refer to the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and arhatship; the "middle" refers to the fruits of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and non-returning (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, the fruit of stream-entry is attained by means of nine faculties: namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), the five faith-faculties (*śraddhādi*), and the first two untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*). Since this fruit and its preparatory stage (*prayoga*) are subsumed under the *anāgamya* level, there is only equanimity present.
How is this obtained by means of the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*)?
It is because the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises simultaneously with the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Although the path of liberation is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the fruit of śrāmaṇya, it is nonetheless associated with it and acts as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); therefore, there is no error in designating it as "obtained."

Alternatively, the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) may also serve as a homogeneous cause for attaining the fruit of stream-entry; that is to say, at the time of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), just as in the case of an Arhat, there is no fault in speaking of this possibility.

The fruit of arhatship is also attained through nine faculties: namely, the mental faculty, faith and the other [four] roots, the two untainted [faculties], and any one from among the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity. Since this fruit and its path (the stage leading toward it) are subsumed within nine stages, one takes any one of the three types of feeling accordingly.

The two intermediate fruits each pertain to both [the mundane and supramundane paths], as they may be attained through seven, eight, or nine faculties, depending on the distinction between gradual and leap-over realization.

First, regarding the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) realized through the gradual path: it is attained by means of the mundane path through seven faculties, namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
When attained by means of the supramundane path, it is acquired through eight faculties: namely, the aforementioned seven plus the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya).

For one who attains the fruit of a non-returner through the method of "leaping over" after having already abandoned double the amount of desire and greed, it should be understood that this is likewise attained through nine faculties, just as the fruit of a stream-enterer is.
Although this is the general rule, there are distinctions.
For one who attains transcendence by completely abandoning desire and greed, because they rely on different stages (*bhūmi*), any one of the three feelings may occur.

For one who attains it through the gradual path (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), if they enter the fundamental stage (*maula-bhūmi*) during the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they attain it by means of eight faculties (*indriya*) according to the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*), with joy (*saumanasya*) as the eighth.
According to the supramundane path, [the fruit] is attained by means of nine faculties, with the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) as the ninth.
If one were to claim that an Arhat is also attained by means of nine faculties, this would contradict the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
When asked how many faculties (indriya) one attains Arhatship with, the answer is eleven.
Since the three feelings (vedanā) are definitely absent because they do not arise simultaneously, one actually attains it by means of nine; however, it is said to be by means of eleven faculties.

According to what is possible, it is said that there may be a certain individual (*pudgala*) who, having repeatedly fallen back from the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), regains [the fruit] again and again through joy, equanimity, and renunciation.

The non-returner (anāgāmin) does not suffer from this same fault, because in the case of gradual attainment there is no possibility of obtaining the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), and in the case of leaping-over attainment (vyutkrāntaka) there is no possibility of falling away.
Now, one should investigate which faculties are possessed, and among those various faculties, how many are necessarily possessed.
The verse says:
One who possesses life, mind, or equanimity necessarily possesses three;
one who possesses pleasure or the body necessarily possesses four.
When the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as joy, are attained, each is necessarily accompanied by five faculties.
If one attains the faculty of suffering, one necessarily attains seven.
If one attains the female or male faculties, or the faculty of grief, or the faculties of faith and so forth, each is necessarily accompanied by eight.
Two are the eleven untainted [roots]; the first untainted consists of thirteen.
The treatise says:
Among life, mind, and equanimity, whichever one is achieved, those three roots are necessarily achieved.
There is no deficiency in the accomplishment of these three [faculties], as they pervade all stages (*bhūmi*) and all bases (*āśraya*).
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) pervade all stages, but do not pervade all bases.
The remaining fourteen faculties are not pervasive in either case;
therefore, the faculty of equanimity and the others necessarily possess only three [of these characteristics], while the remainder may or may not be possessed.
How does one possess the four faculties beginning with the eye?
The faculty of form (*rūpendriya*) is present throughout the entire realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and in a small portion of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

The body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is present throughout both the realms of desire and form. The female and male faculties (*strī- and puruṣendriya*) are present in a small portion of the realm of desire. The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is present in the lower three dhyānas of the realm of desire and in noble ones (*ārya*) born in higher realms. The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is present in the lower two dhyānas of the realm of desire and in noble ones born in higher realms.

If one is born in the entire Desire Realm, as long as one has not yet abandoned the desire-greed for sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) have not been severed, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) have already been attained and not yet lost—then in these respective states, one definitely possesses [these faculties]; in all other states, one definitely does not possess them.
If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four: namely, life (*jīvita*), mind (*manas*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and pleasure.
If one possesses the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*), one also necessarily possesses four: namely, life, mind, equanimity, and the body. As for the others, they may or may not be possessed.
If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses five: namely, the life, mind, equanimity, body, and eye faculties.
It should be known that for the ear, nose, and tongue faculties, there are likewise five; the first four are as in the case of the eye, and the fifth is the respective faculty itself.

If one accomplishes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily accomplishes five: namely, the life-faculty, the mental faculty, the equanimity faculty, the pleasure faculty, and the joy faculty.
When born in the second dhyāna, if one has not yet abandoned craving for it, one only accomplishes the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) feeling of pleasure belonging to the third dhyāna.
If one possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily possesses seven: namely, the faculties of body, life, mind, and four sensations, excluding that of sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
If one possesses the female faculty (*strīndriya*), one necessarily possesses eight: the seven as described for the faculty of suffering, with the eighth being the female faculty itself.
The male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) is also eightfold: seven are as explained for suffering, and the eighth is the male faculty itself.
The faculties of faith and so forth are also eightfold; that is, the life, mind, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
If both the female and male faculties are present, they necessarily constitute fifteen.

If one possesses the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), one necessarily possesses eleven: namely, the faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, life, mind, the five beginning with faith, and the faculty of one who has already known.
The same applies to the faculty of one who is currently knowing (*ājñendriya*); its own faculty is the eleventh.

If one possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), one necessarily possesses thirteen faculties: namely, the body, life, mind, the four sensations (excluding sorrow), the five faculties beginning with faith, and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
Regarding the stage of gradual death, it is traditionally taught that because of a profound mental revulsion toward birth and death, one is able to enter the Path of Seeing.

Having thus explained the definite accomplishment of the stages and the definite accomplishment of the *pudgala*, it shall now be explained how many faculties (*indriya*) those with the very minimum possess.
The verse says:
"At the very minimum, eight; lacking the wholesome, one possesses the faculties of sensation, body, mind, and life."
The fool born in the formless realm possesses wholesome life, mind, and equanimity.
The commentary states:
one who has already severed the roots of goodness is said to be "without goodness."

If one possesses the minimum number of faculties, they achieve eight: namely, the five feeling-faculties, the body-faculty, the life-faculty, and the mind-faculty. This refers to one who is gradually discarding their life until only the body-faculty remains.
"Fool" refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because they have not yet seen the Truths.

Those born in the formless realm also possess eight faculties: namely, the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as life, mind, and equanimity (*upekṣā*). This is because of the fixed number [of faculties] and because of the mention of "the deluded.
The term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) does not overlap with the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
How many faculties (*indriya*) do those who possess the maximum number achieve?
The verse says:
The maximum is nineteen; for those of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), three pure faculties are excluded.
The Noble One who has not yet abandoned desire possesses [all faculties], excluding two purities and one gender organ.
The commentary states:
Those with both sexual organs possess the eye and other organs; excluding the three untainted faculties, they possess the remaining nineteen.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) are called "pure" because they are free from the two bonds.

If a noble one in training (*śaikṣa*) has not yet abandoned desire and greed, even when possessing the maximum number, they still have nineteen, excluding the two untainted faculties and excluding one of the sexual organs.
The two untainted [faculties] refer to either one of the first two faculties preceding the faculty of one who has already known.
Regarding "one gender," it means there are neither two genders nor no gender at all, because one has attained the noble dharmas.
Having extensively analyzed the faculties following the differentiation of the elements, one should now investigate the co-arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Briefly stated, these conditioned phenomena are of two kinds: those with form (*rūpin*) and those without form (*arūpin*).
The formless has three types, namely: mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind.
The formed has two types, namely: the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) and that which is not the infinitesimal atom.
There are two types of atoms: first, those bound to the desire realm; second, those bound to the form realm.
Atoms of the desire realm are further divided into two kinds: first, aggregates without sense organs; second, aggregates with sense organs.
Herein, we shall first analyze the matter of the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The verse says:
In the desire realm, an atom-aggregate that lacks sound And lacks sense-faculties consists of eight substances.
The body-faculty consists of nine things; the remaining faculties consist of ten things.
The treatise says:
The final, most subtle division within obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), which can no longer be further analyzed, is called the atom (*paramāṇu*).

This means that this atom cannot be further analyzed into multiple [parts] by any other cognition of form; this is what is called the limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta*), and it is given the name "limit" because there are no further parts.
Just as a single *kṣaṇa* is the ultimate limit of time and cannot be further divided into half-*kṣaṇas*, so too is it with this:
when a multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*) are combined, they cannot be separated, and thus they are called an "atomic aggregate" (*saṃghātaparamāṇu*).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when there is no sound and no sense-faculties, these eight things arise together: namely, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the [four] derived qualities of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
If there is sound, they constitute nine things: the sound and the aforementioned eight.
The reason it is not mentioned [in that context] is to show that sound arises from the mutual impact of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), and is not like form and so forth, which exist at all times.

When there is no sound, there are either nine or ten faculties present. That is to say, in a cluster of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), nine things arise together: the eight as previously described, with the ninth being the body faculty itself.
In the remaining clusters of faculties, ten factors arise together; nine are as in the cluster of the body, with the addition of one—either the eye and so forth.
This is because the eye, ear, nose, and tongue are never separate from the body, as they function in dependence upon it.
The four sense organs arise sequentially and are separated from one another because their locations are distinct.
If sound arises within this cluster of organs, adding that produced sound results in ten or eleven [elements].

Because these have appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause, they arise inseparably from the sense faculties (*indriya*); the reason for this is not explicitly stated here, but should be understood as previously explained.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), with the exception of the two things—odor and taste—the rest is the same as in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and thus it is not described separately.

The explanations regarding the basis of the entity and the basis of the location are both without fault, because they are taught according to the distinctions between the basis and that which depends upon it, and the entity and its location.
Alternatively, there is no fault in relying solely on the entity, because [the existence of] the dependent is said to occur only when it is necessarily co-arisen with its basis.
The essence of shape, color, and so forth is not determinately existent, because they do not exist within light and other such phenomena.

Alternatively, there is no fault in regarding them as existing solely in dependence upon their location. To prevent various denials, the great elements (mahābhūta) are specifically mentioned: namely, to refute those who deny that the great elements and derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) have distinct intrinsic natures; or those who deny that there is a distinct body of derived matter within the sense-base of tangibles (spraṣṭavya-āyatana); or those who deny that every aggregate possesses all four great elements.
If one speaks of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) individually, these criticisms are all removed; yet they do not constitute a plurality, because they are spoken of in terms of their categories.
Having already explained that those with form (*rūpin*) necessarily arise together, I shall now explain the co-arising of those without form (*arūpin*).
The verse says:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; so too do the various formations, characteristics, or acquisitions.
The commentary says:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; if even one of them is absent, the others never arise.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are precisely these conditioned things, namely, those with form and those without form.

The phrase "necessarily concomitant" from the previous section should be understood as applying here as well; that is, when material and other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they necessarily arise together with the four characteristics, such as birth (*jāti*).
As for the mention of "or acquisition" (*prāpti*), this refers only to those phenomena pertaining to sentient beings, which arise simultaneously with acquisition.
Some say this indicates that [the definition] does not pervade all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Among the four types of conditioned things previously mentioned, while matter and mind have been extensively analyzed as explained in the preceding chapter, mental factors (*caitta*) and other such dharmas have not yet been extensively analyzed.
Now, first, we shall extensively analyze the various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
The verse says:
Mental factors are, for now, of five types, distinguished as the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*) and so forth.
The treatise says:
There are, for the time being, five categories of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), because there are distinctions such as those of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and so forth.
What are these five categories?

1. The universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), 2. the universal wholesome mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma), 3. the universal defiled mental factors (kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma), 4. the universal unwholesome mental factors (akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma), and 5. the limited defiled mental factors (parīttakleśabhūmika-dharma).
"Ground" (bhūmi) refers to a place of dwelling or a sphere of activity.
If one thing serves as the dwelling place or sphere of activity for another, then that [first] dharma is said to be the ground of that [second] dharma.
Because the ground (*bhūmi*) is the great ground of mind (*citta*), it is called the "great ground" (*mahābhūmi*).

Among these, those factors that belong to the great ground are termed "factors of the great ground" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); that is to say, those factors that arise universally together with every type of mind.
For this reason, mind is not a universal mental factor (mahābhūmika), because it does not arise simultaneously with [other] mental factors.
What are those factors?
The verse says:
Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and desire, Wisdom, mindfulness, and attention,
Resolve and concentration— These are present in all states of mind.
The Commentary says:
