Chapter Three: Differentiation of Characteristics, Part Three. Having thus explained the characteristics of the differentiation of acquisition (*prāpti*), what are the characteristics of the differentiation of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)?
The verse says:
Non-acquisition is pure and neutral; In the past and future, there are three types each.

The non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the three [types of] noble paths, which are not bound to the three realms, is designated as the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). It is abandoned through the attainment of the dharmas and by changing the stage (*bhūmi*).
The commentary says:
Regarding the distinction of nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*): all non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) are comprised exclusively within the category of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Regarding the distinction of time (*adhvan-viśeṣa*): past and future [non-acquisitions] each have three types; that is, for past dharmas and future dharmas, each has non-acquisition belonging to all three times.
As for present dharmas, there is only non-acquisition belonging to the past and the future.
It is certain that there is no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of a present dharma, because a present dharma does not coexist with its non-acquisition.
Some say that there is no present non-acquisition of a present dharma, because their natures are mutually contradictory.

A presently existing dharma that is capable of being attained must necessarily be accompanied by its acquisition (*prāpti*) and is definitely devoid of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); likewise, for a dharma that cannot be attained, non-acquisition also does not exist. Therefore, there is no present non-acquisition of a present dharma.

Regarding the distinction of realms: for dharmas bound to the three realms as well as unbound dharmas, there are three types of non-acquisition (aprāpti) each. That is to say, dharmas bound to the desire realm have non-acquisitions belonging to all three realms; the same applies to those bound to the form and formless realms, as well as to the unbound.
It is certainly not the case that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) can be untainted (*anāsrava*). Why is this?
Because it is accepted that the non-acquisition of the noble path (*āryamārga*) is designated as the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
As the treatise states:
"What is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*)."

Non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is merely another name for non-possession (*asamanvāgama*); how, then, could the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) be called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
Which noble dharma (*ārya-dharma*) is it that, through its non-attainment, one is termed an ordinary person?

Is it that one has not acquired all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) in their entirety, or is it only that one has not acquired the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)?
Some say that one has not acquired all noble dharmas.
If that were so, would it not follow that there are no non-ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), since there is not a single person who possesses all noble dharmas in their entirety?

If there is that which is not obtained and is unmixed with what is obtained, this constitutes the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); if it were mixed with what is obtained, it would not be the nature of an ordinary person. Therefore, there is no fault.
If that is so, the original treatise should have used the word "pure" (*kevala*).
This is not so, because there is the perception of the meaning apart from the words.

For example, when it is said that "this class [of beings] eats water" or "eats wind," although there is no explicit mention of "purely," one nevertheless understands that they eat only water or wind, unmixed with anything else.

Some say that it is the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*); however, one does not become a worldling (*pṛthagjana*) again upon later relinquishing [that receptivity], because its non-acquisition was already permanently destroyed previously.
For what reason is it known that there exists a distinct real dharma called "non-acquisition"?
This is because the sūtras speak of both "possession" (*samanvāgama*) and "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*).
As a sūtra says: "If one possesses six dharmas and does not possess the patient acceptance that accords with truth (*anulomikī kṣānti*), [these] six dharmas are as stated in the sūtra."

If it is claimed that the state of the continuity of those who have not yet produced the noble dharmas, such as the [noble] eye, is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*), this contradicts the sūtra.
As the Blessed One said:
"In this way, the follower by faith enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth, transcending the stage of an ordinary person."
This stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*) is itself the nature of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
For what reason is this known?
Because it is acquired and abandoned [in that manner].

Just as one is said to "enter" because of attaining distinct dharmas, one is said to "transcend" because of abandoning distinct dharmas; yet, at that time, it cannot be known that even a fraction of the previously attained dharmas, such as the eye-faculty and so forth, has been abandoned. Since this is like attaining noble dharmas never before attained, one cannot claim that the continuity of the eye-faculty and so forth belonging to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)—which has not yet produced noble dharmas—is itself the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). Therefore, it is logically certain that there exists a distinct dharma which belongs exclusively to ordinary persons, pervades all ordinary persons, and is the opposite of the attainment of the Noble Path; this is designated as the state of being an ordinary person. This principle is inevitable.
Is it not the case that just as the noble dharma is itself called the noble nature (*āryatva*), and one is named a "noble one" (*ārya*) because of having accomplished this nature;

so too, the dharma of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) should be the very nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and one is named an "ordinary person" because of having accomplished this nature?

This analogy does not hold; for while the dharmas of the noble ones exist only in noble beings and can thus be described as "noble nature" (*āryatva*), the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also exist in noble beings—how, then, could they be established as "ordinary being nature" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?

If the dharmas of an ordinary being were produced only by ordinary beings and existed throughout all states of being an ordinary being, they could constitute the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).

However, the miserable destinies, the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), and Uttarakuru do not pervade all states of being an ordinary being. Furthermore, although other factors such as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) do pervade all states of being an ordinary being, they also exist in noble ones (*ārya*).
The digression is concluded; we should now further consider this non-acquisition (*aprāpti*). At what time is this non-acquisition of a dharma abandoned?
When that dharma is acquired, or when one shifts to another stage (*bhūmi*), this non-acquisition is abandoned.

Just as the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the noble dharmas is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*), and one relinquishes the non-acquisition of the three realms at the moment of acquiring the noble dharmas;

so too, for one abiding in the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), through the successive stages up to one abiding in the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), they relinquish the respective non-attainments of all that belongs to an Arhat as they acquire those dharmas accordingly.

In this manner, up until the time one attains the fruit of arhatship as a "liberated at times" (samaya-vimukta) practitioner, regarding all the non-attainments (aprāpti) of the "liberated not at times" (asamaya-vimukta) arhat, when one attains these dharmas, one abandons those non-attainments.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of other dharmas should be understood in this same manner.
Furthermore, how is this non-acquisition said to be "abandoned"?
When the acquisition of non-acquisition is severed and the non-acquisition of non-acquisition arises, this is called the abandonment of non-acquisition.

Although acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) each have further acquisitions and non-acquisitions, these do not lead to an infinite regress. This is because the power of an acquisition brings about both the primary dharma and its own "acquisition-of-acquisition" (*prāptiprāpti*); then, the power of that acquisition-of-acquisition brings about the acquisition of the primary dharma. How, then, could this result in an infinite regress?
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) should also be examined according to reason.
Non-acquisition and its own non-acquisition necessarily do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, when one is born from a lower stage to a higher stage, all non-acquisitions of the lower stage are abandoned.
One should understand that the descent from a higher realm to a lower one follows this same principle, because non-acquisition (aprāpti) arises through the power of its basis (āśraya).
Thus has the characteristic of acquisition and non-acquisition been explained.
What, then, is the "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā)?
The verse says:
"Sabhāgatā is the equality among sentient beings.
The commentary says:

There exists a distinct, real entity called *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), which refers to the mutual similarity among sentient beings. The *Mūlaśāstra* designates this as *nikāyasabhāga* (group-homogeneity).

It is defined as the cause for the mutual resemblance in physical form, sensory faculties, functions, food, and so forth among all classes of sentient beings born within a single realm of existence (*gati*), as well as the cause for their mutual inclinations and desires; this is termed *nikāyasabhāga*.
Just as with a fresh and pure color, karma, the mind, and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are all its causes; therefore, the physical body and so forth are not caused by karma alone.

We observe that the physical body is a result induced by mutually similar karmas, because there are differences in the functions of the sense faculties, as well as in food, drink, and other such factors.
If it is argued that this differentiation arises because there are differences in the completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*), such reasoning is untenable.

Alternatively, there may be bodily forms that arise solely from similar projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), yet their functions and so forth differ because there are distinctions among their homogeneous classes (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
If the physical body and so forth were solely the fruit of karma, then activities such as abandoning or engaging in whatever actions one desires would not be possible.
In this context, because the physical body, its activities, and one's inclinations are mutually similar, they are termed "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*); this is the meaning of the term "cause."
There exists a distinct, substantial entity that serves as the cause for this similarity, and is therefore called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
Such homogeneity, the Blessed One taught, applies only to sentient beings and not to things such as grass or trees.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This is the commonality of these devas; this is the commonality of these humans," and so forth at length.
Thus, the reality of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous character) is established; it is not merely a designation for the mutual similarity of shape and color.

There are immeasurable kinds of *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) among sentient beings based on distinctions such as realm (*dhātu*), destiny (*gati*), birth (*upapatti*), place (*sthāna*), and body (*kāya*).

Furthermore, there is the *dharma-sabhāgatā*, which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); because these are the basis for the various types of homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāgatā*), they do not exist in non-sentient things.
The generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is abandoned at the time of entering the state free from birth;
the generic similarity of sentient beings is abandoned at the time of entering nirvāṇa.
Is it not the case that the nature of being an ordinary being is itself the generic similarity of ordinary beings?
This should not be so, because their functions differ.
That which serves as the mutual cause for similarity in physical form, function, and inclination is called *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity).
That which is contrary to the attainment of the Noble Path and serves as the cause for being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is called *pṛthagjanatva* (the state of being an ordinary person).

When entering the state of separation from birth (niyāmāvakrānti), one both relinquishes and acquires the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga); regarding the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva), one relinquishes it and does not acquire it again.
Since the homogeneous character is non-material (arūpa), how is it known?
There exists a functional capacity that gives rise to a distinct category of phenomena; because one perceives its fruit, one knows that it exists.
This is just as when one perceives the fruit obtained from present karma, one knows that there was karma previously created in a former life.
Furthermore, because it is directly realized by practitioners of meditation,
why not admit the existence of a "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) for non-sentient things?
One should not raise such an objection, for it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

You also admit that there are destinies such as humans and devas, and modes of birth such as the womb and the egg; why then do you not also admit that mangoes and the like have destinies and are born from mung beans and the like?
Furthermore, it is because the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, never taught this.
One should merely investigate: for what reason does the Blessed One speak of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) only with respect to sentient beings, and not with respect to grass and the like?
Furthermore, how is it known that such homogeneity exists as a real entity (dravya)?

Furthermore, I understand it in this way: because those grasses and so forth lack mutual functional activity or desire, and because they do not resemble one another, it is not said that there exists a distinct *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) among them.
Furthermore, because it arises only in dependence upon sentient beings, grass, and so forth, the term "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) is applied exclusively to sentient beings.
Moreover, this phenomenon arises due to both prior karma and present effort; since neither of these two conditions exists in the case of grass and such things, they lack homogeneity.
It is precisely by virtue of this fact that we can prove the existence of a real entity.

Furthermore, although images made of wood, clay, lacquer, or carved and painted materials, as well as their actual physical forms, possess color and shape that are mutually similar, they are nonetheless spoken of as being one and the same reality.

Therefore, it is not the case that one speaks of something as real merely upon seeing its similarity; rather, it is only with respect to distinct categories of similar things that the term "real" arises. Thus, we know that this distinct phenomenon truly exists, and it is from this phenomenon that such real discourse originates.
Furthermore, because it was stated previously. How was it stated?

It means that the physical form of the body is seen to be the result induced by mutually similar karma, because there are differences in the functions of the sense faculties, as well as in food, drink, and so forth.

Since these various *sabhāga* (homogeneous) categories differ from one another, how can there arise a cognition and designation of non-difference regarding them without further homogeneous categories?

Because these various *sabhāgas* serve as the common cause for things of the same class, they function as the cause for the cognition and designation of mutual similarity among those of the same class. This is just as the eye, ear, and so forth, although composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), constitute the nature of matter (*rūpatva*) by being derived from them; even though the primary elements themselves are not composed of other primary elements, their nature as matter is nonetheless established.
This should clarify and establish the categories of "universal" (sāmānya) and "particularity" (viśeṣa) as they are asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas.
If the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that these two categories are not of a single essence, are momentary and impermanent, lack a substratum, and are mutually distinct; [then...]

Even if we were to concede that this is the same as their position, it would not entail many faults; for it does not require the followers of the Śākya (Buddhists) to abandon their view—that the sense organs such as the eye can reach out to objects such as form—and instead adopt some other interpretation.
Therefore, that which he has criticized is merely partisan talk; those who seek the correct principle should not accept it.
Having already explained "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā), what is "non-conception" (asaṃjñin)?
The verse says:
In the state of non-conception, within non-conception, the mind and mental factors cease;
it is a karmic maturation and its inhabitants dwell in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
The treatise says:

If one is born among the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), there is a dharma capable of causing the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is termed "non-conception" (*asaṃjñi*).
This is a substantially existent entity that can obstruct future mind and mental factors so that they do not temporarily arise, just as a dam blocks a river.

This dharma is exclusively the maturation (*vipāka*) induced by the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); for within that heaven of non-conceptualizing beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), both non-conception and form are solely the maturation fruits induced by that attainment, since this attainment cannot project the generic similarity of the group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) or the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Because the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are exclusively the maturation (*vipāka*) produced by the fourth dhyāna that possesses mind, while the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) in that state are common maturations.

Although those born among the beings of the Heaven of Non-conceptualization possess minds for a long duration—namely, prior to entering the state of non-conception and after emerging from it—they are called the "Heaven of Non-conception" because the period of their mindlessness is extremely long.
Where do the non-conceptualizing sentient beings (asaṃjñisattva) reside?

They reside in the Bṛhatphala [heaven]. That is to say, within the Bṛhatphala heaven there is a superior and exalted place, which—just as the intermediate dhyāna is called the "Non-conceptualizing Heaven" (asaṃjñideva)—is named the Non-conceptualizing Heaven.

For them, karma and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) serve as the sustaining nutriment; that is to say, because past karma draws forth the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth, and because the mind at rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-citta*) and the mind immediately entering the fruit of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-phala*) provide the necessary attraction and assistance.
That [state] also possesses past contact and so forth as its sustaining nutriment.
In the state devoid of mind, only past contact and so forth serve as nutriment, while present nutriment is absent;
in the state possessed of mind, both types are present.

Because those sentient beings give rise to such thoughts, they pass away from that place; having passed away, they are certain to be reborn in the desire realm and nowhere else. This is because the power of the lifespan induced by their previous practice of meditative concentration has been exhausted, and they are no longer able to cultivate meditative concentration there—just as an arrow shot into the sky falls once its momentum is spent.
If sentient beings are to be born in those places, they must necessarily possess karma of the desire realm to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Just as those who are to be born in Uttarakuru must necessarily possess karma for rebirth in the heavens.
The state of non-perception has already been explained.
What are the two meditative attainments?
They are the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
First, regarding the nature of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
the verse says:
"Thus, the attainment of non-perception, is sought by those in the final dhyāna desiring liberation."
Wholesome, it is experienced only in the next life; non-noble ones attain it for one lifetime.
The commentary says:
As previously stated, there is a dharma that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is termed "non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*).
Furthermore, there is another distinct dharma capable of causing the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is called the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

The use of the term "thus" (*iti*) indicates that this attainment, in its cessation of the mind and mental factors, is identical to the state of non-conception; it is termed an "attainment" (*samāpatti*) because it is correctly accomplished or thoroughly perfected.
Other masters say:

It is called "concentration" (*samādhi*) because it causes the mental factors to proceed in accordance with the principle; that is, it causes the primary elements of the mind to proceed in equilibrium.

As for the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is either "non-perception within concentration" or "concentration of non-perception"; it is named thus because this attainment arises from the loathing and destruction of perception.
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to cultivate revulsion toward and destroy feelings (*vedanā*), because they enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by being attached to feelings.
In which stage does this absorption reside?
It resides in the subsequent dhyāna; that is, it is in the fourth dhyāna and not elsewhere.
This should not be said.
Why? Because this meditative absorption is certainly able to induce the maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).

It has already been stated that the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi-sattva) resides in the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala). Now it must be explained that the Heaven of Vast Fruit exists within the fourth dhyāna; however, could one cultivate its cause in other stages?
This objection is not valid, for there is no such teaching. Nowhere has it ever been stated that the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is the cause of the state of non-conception.

Is it not the case that the previous verse states that non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) is a maturation (*vipāka*), yet in its commentary it is said to be the fruit of the meditative attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?
This is also not so; for never before has a verse stated such a thing, and it is only now that this [interpretation] is established.
Why is this meditative absorption called the "absorption of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-samādhi*)?
It is because they cultivate this absorption seeking liberation.

They hold that non-conception (*asaṃjñi*) is true liberation and regard the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as the path to deliverance; thus, they cultivate this absorption in order to realize non-conception.

Since no noble being (ārya) clings to that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) as true liberation or true transcendence, this meditative absorption is called the "absorption of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-samādhi*).

Because it was previously stated that the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), its inclusion within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is established without needing to be explicitly stated.

Now, since the attainment of non-conception is invariably wholesome, is it not the case that because it is a cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), its inclusion within the category of wholesomeness is established without needing to be stated?
This serves as the cause for summoning the maturation of the five aggregates among the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception.
Not so, for this has not yet been stated in the verse.
Furthermore, who could possibly prevent it from being defiled or neutral?
If that were the case, one should have said here that it is "exclusively wholesome."

This is not so; for there exists the realization of the meaning apart from words. This should be explained according to the preceding discussion on the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), or it may be that the term "wholesome" alone already excludes all others.
Since this concentration is by nature a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), what kind of feeling does it accord with?

"It is exclusively karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and not karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), in future lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), or at an indefinite time (*aniyatavedanīya*).
A certain class of masters maintains this fixed position, yet it is logically consistent that it may also be karma to be experienced in the next life and at an indefinite time.
Why is this so? One who has accomplished this meditative absorption may also enter the state of rightness and departure from birth;
yet once having entered that state, there is absolutely no possibility of manifesting this absorption.

The state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is called the "dhyāna of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-dhyāna*) with respect to its actual manifestation, not with respect to its possession (*prāpti*).

Furthermore, it is admitted that this dhyāna is common to both those within this Dharma and external ordinary beings who have attained it, as it is not [the dhyāna] of the noble ones (*ārya*); for all noble ones, regarding the state of non-ideation, do not delight in entering it, viewing it as if it were a deep pit.

Since the verse already states the phrase "seeking liberation," it clearly indicates that this meditative absorption belongs exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); thus, to further state that it does not belong to noble ones (*ārya*) would be redundant.
When this is first attained, how many time periods (*adhvan*) are acquired?

In these various stages, just as the *prātimokṣa* vows are acquired anew with every moment because they have not been previously attained, at the first moment one does not acquire the past [vows], since there is no mind [to sustain them]; nor does one cultivate the future, therefore at the time of initial acquisition, one acquires only one period—namely, the present.

From the second moment until one has not yet emerged from the state, they also become past; once emerged, until they are relinquished, they remain only past. This is like the divine eye and ear, which lack cultivation of the future; they are acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Next, regarding the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), what are its characteristics?
The verse says:
The attainment of cessation is likewise; it is for the sake of dwelling in tranquility at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The two wholesome [faculties] and the two indeterminate [faculties] are acquired through application by the noble ones;
they are not acquired prior to becoming a Buddha, because it takes thirty-four moments of thought.
The Commentary says:
As with the previously mentioned attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), so too is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

That is to say, just as for one who has already become free from craving for the third dhyāna, there is a state that can cause the mind and mental factors to cease, which is called the attainment of non-conception.

Thus, for one who has already abandoned craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there is a state that can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors, which is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Regarding the distinguishing characteristics of these two attainments: the former, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), is entered by first applying the mental attention of the perception of renunciation, as one seeks liberation through the repudiation of perception.

Now, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is entered upon by first applying the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of stillness, out of a desire for tranquil abiding and a distaste for agitation.

Whereas the aforementioned attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) belongs to the peripheral regions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this attainment of cessation belongs to the peripheral region of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because the body born therein in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is drawn forth by the most supreme karma.

It is called the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*); alternatively, it is called the Peak of Existence because it is the ultimate limit of existence, just as the very top of a tree is called the "top of the tree.
Since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) exists only in this stage, for what reason does this attainment not exist in the lower stages?
Because one can only attain this supreme liberation by turning away from all states of mind and by the cessation of the final state of mind.
That is to say, this liberation is established based on two conditions:
first, the turning away from all states of mind; and second, the temporary cessation of the final state of mind.

If this meditative absorption were present in the lower stages, it would not constitute a mind that is weary of and averse to all types of states, because one would not yet have become weary of the minds of the higher stages.
Furthermore, it could not be called the "ultimate severance of the mind," because the minds of the higher stages would still remain unsevered.
It should be called "aversion toward a portion of all minds," and it should also be called "the severance of the mind at the middle limit.
Among the three natures, both the preceding state and this concentration are exclusively wholesome; they are neither defiled nor indeterminate.
The noble ones do not take aversion toward or fear of mental distraction, nor do they grasp at defiled or neutral states as a peaceful dwelling.

While the previously mentioned attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) conduces only to feeling experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) or to indeterminate feeling (*aniyata-vedanīya*), the present attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) conduces to feeling experienced in the next life, in subsequent lives, or is indeterminate. This means that regarding its maturation (*vipāka*), it may be experienced in the next life, in subsequent lives, or be indeterminate; or it may not be experienced at all. That is to say, if one has arisen from this meditative state in a lower realm and does not take birth in a higher realm but instead attains parinirvāṇa, this attainment of cessation brings about the maturation of the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

The aforementioned attainment of non-ideation is attained only by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whereas this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*). Ordinary beings are incapable of giving rise to the attainment of cessation because they have not yet abandoned the obstacles to arising in that attainment which belong to their own level; furthermore, as they have not transcended the afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they lack any capacity whatsoever to give rise to the attainment of cessation.

Since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to transcend the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), only noble ones (*ārya*) attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Do all noble ones who reach the Peak of Existence necessarily attain such an absorption of cessation?

One should say that it is not obtained [by detachment from defilements], because this concentration is certainly not obtained through the separation from passions (*vairāgya*). By what, then, is it obtained?
It is obtained through application (*prayoga*), for it must be realized only by means of application.
Just as when the attainment of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is first realized, one attains only the present and not the past;
nor does one cultivate the future, because cultivation can only occur through the power of the mind.
The second moment and those following it, as long as they have not been relinquished, also constitute the past.
Does the Blessed One also acquire [these] through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)? No.
How so? It is attained at the time of attaining Buddhahood; that is to say, it is attained by the World-Honored One at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

Would it not be the case that even the knowledge of exhaustion is not said to be "attained" at the time of attaining Buddhoadhood, let alone the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

When Bodhisattvas abide in the *vajropama-samādhi*, they are said to have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because it is at the moment the essence [of that samādhi] arises that attainment is defined.

At the time of attaining Buddhahood, one should say that the knowledge of exhaustion manifests without the need for further application (*prayoga*), because when the mere aspiration to do so momentarily arises, all perfections (*saṃpanna-guṇa*) arise in accordance with that aspiration.

The merits possessed within the Buddha’s body are not acquired at the moment of attaining Buddhahood; how, then, could it be said that the Buddha acquires the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) at the time of his knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?

Because the Bodhisattva, while still a bodhisattva, was already eternally free from the defilement of all afflictions (*kleśa*), this enabled the merits within the Buddha’s body to arise. Therefore, it is said that all the merits of the Tathāgata are attained through freedom from defilement.
Therefore, what they have said also contains errors.

To provide an interpretation that accords with the circumstances: it is a case of using a distant term to refer to something proximate; or, because one will certainly attain Buddhahood at the time of the Vajra-like Samādhi, one is also called "attained to Buddhahood," since one is certain to become a Buddha in the immediately following moment.
Setting this matter aside for a moment:

when the Blessed One had not yet arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) at the moment he attained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), how did he become one liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta)?

Because he was permanently freed from the hindrances of meditative absorption (samāpattyāvaraṇa), because he abandoned non-accomplishment, and because he attained mastery over the arising of the attainment of cessation, he became one liberated in both ways just like one who has already emerged from it.
The masters of the West say that a bodhisattva in the stage of training first gives rise to this meditative absorption and subsequently attains enlightenment.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:
It is not the case that the meditative attainment of cessation arises first and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises only later.

For what reason do the Vaibhāṣika masters of this land know that the meditative attainment of cessation has not arisen prior to the knowledge of exhaustion? Why do they not also question the origin [of the attainment] according to the Westerners?
Furthermore, we of Kaśmīra maintain that enlightenment is attained in thirty-four moments of thought.

This is because it is certain that Bodhisattvas must first become free from attachment to the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) before entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); they no longer need to abandon the afflictions of the lower levels.

One attains great enlightenment in thirty-four moments of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*). Within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there are sixteen moments of thought; for one who is free from craving for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are eighteen moments of thought, namely, nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions of the Peak of Existence.

Thus, the eighteen [mental states] added to the preceding sixteen constitute thirty-four; since there is no room for a dissimilar type of mind to arise during this interval, it is certain that the attainment of cessation cannot arise at these prior stages.
If one were to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) during the preceding stage, one would thereby transgress the resolve regarding the time limit.

However, because Bodhisattvas are determined never to transgress their formal resolve, it is thus well established that awakening is attained in thirty-four moments of thought; therefore, [the attainment of cessation] is not a prior cause.
Although it has already been stated that the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) possess many common and differing characteristics, there are further similarities and differences among them.
The verse says:
The two attainments depend on the desire and form realms; The attainment of cessation first arises among humans.
The treatise states:
Regarding the two meditative attainments, these refer to the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation; both of these arise manifest based upon the two realms of desire and form.
However, regarding this, some say that one enters the attainment of non-conception only in the three lower dhyānas, not in the fourth, lest cause and effect be too closely proximate.

Some say that one may also enter the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in the fourth dhyāna, with the exception of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), because one experiences its fruit upon being born in that heaven.
Other masters say:
one enters the attainment of non-conception only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
That contradicts the treatise, for the treatise states:
"There may be that which is form-existence (rūpabhava), yet this existence does not consist of the five aggregates.

This refers to sentient beings of the realm of form who are either born in the heavens of those possessing perception while abiding in a dissimilar state of mind, or have entered the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), or have entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), or are born in the heaven of non-perception."
Having already attained entry into the state of non-perception, this is called "form existence" (*rūpabhava*); yet this existence does not consist of the five aggregates.
From this it is proven that both of these meditative attainments arise based upon the realms of desire and form; this is termed their common characteristic.

Regarding the "distinctive characteristics": it is said that the attainment of the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) can first arise in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); however, the first arising of the cessation absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*) occurs only among humans.

That is to say, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) can first be cultivated and arisen only among humans; it exists only within the human realm.

Regarding the teacher and the commentator, because they possess the power of intense preparatory application (*prayoga*), there are those who, having first attained it while among humans, subsequently fall away from it before being born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); once established in a body of the form realm, they then cultivate and give rise to it once again.
One cannot enter the meditative attainment of cessation while in the formless realm, because there is no basis for it.

The life-faculty necessarily functions in dependence upon both matter and mind; if one were to enter the attainment of cessation in the formless realm, both matter and mind would be absent, and the life-faculty would consequently be severed.
Since the aggregates exist in mutual dependence upon one another, there is no sentient being that possesses only a single aggregate.
Furthermore, because the mind and mental factors are inseparable, there is also no sentient being that possesses only three aggregates.
For what reason is it known that there is falling away from the attainment of cessation?
It is because of the meaning of the Udāyin Sūtra.
The Sūtra says:
"Venerable ones!

It is possible that there are bhikṣus who, having previously in this very place been endowed with pure ethical discipline (śīla), endowed with concentration (samādhi), and endowed with wisdom (prajñā), are able to repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti)."

One should know this as it truly is: that in the present life, or at the point of death, they were unable to diligently practice so as to bring their liberation to fulfillment; yet, upon the dissolution of this body, they will transcend the heavens of those who subsist on physical food and, according to their merit, take birth in the body of a mind-made deity in one of those realms. Having been born there, it is also possible that they will repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

One should know this as it truly is: the Buddha taught that this body of the *manomaya-kāya* devas is the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), existing only at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
If one who has attained this attainment were never to fall away from it, they should not be able to go to be reborn in the form realm.

Thus, the detailed explanation of the distinct characteristics of these two meditative attainments comprises six categories in total: namely, differences in terms of their level (*bhūmi*), preparatory application (*prayoga*), continuity (*saṃtati*), maturation (*vipāka*), experience (*vedanīya*), and initial arising (*prathamotpāda*).

Now, one should investigate this: since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) extinguishes all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) without exception, for what reason is it specifically called the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*)?

It is because one gives rise to this attainment by being weary of and repelled by those two; that is to say, perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) serve as the basis for the defilements of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and thus they are particularly reviled.

These two factors involve many faults and afflictions, as has been extensively analyzed in the *Skandha-prakaraṇa*; therefore, one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) out of particular aversion toward them.
In this state of cessation, there is definitely no mind, because all minds arise and perish simultaneously with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
As stated in the Sūtra:

"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact, which arises simultaneously with feeling, perception, and volition," and so forth, as explained at length.
Nowhere has it been stated that there is a seventh consciousness which could be held to arise apart from feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).

This sutra speaks of them together to demonstrate their simultaneous arising, for it employs the metaphor of bundles of reeds leaning against one another and explains the conditions for the arising of the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta).
It is not that only perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā) cease within this meditative absorption; for it is also stated therein that mental formations (manas-saṃskāra) cease.
If the mind did not cease in this absorption, then both perception and feeling would likewise not cease, as the contact (sparśa) capable of producing them would still be present.
For this reason, there is necessarily no mind within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Nevertheless, that the mind arises again after the attainment is due to its being drawn forth and sustained by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the mind prior to the attainment, and because it was projected by the force of the formal resolve made during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
One should know that the essence of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) truly exists, because it is capable of obstructing the mind and preventing it from arising.
If one were to claim that the mind prior to the attainment obstructs subsequent minds, then subsequent minds would never arise at all.
If it were claimed that the body possessing sense faculties can give rise to other minds, then all consciousnesses should arise simultaneously at all times.

As for the claim that subsequent minds arise in dependence on preceding minds, this is because there is no second immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); thus, even though there are simultaneous supports and objects, consciousnesses of all objects do not arise simultaneously.

If one maintains that consciousness arises in dependence upon the body possessing sense faculties, without depending on causes and conditions of its own kind, then for all states and all objects, what factor would act as an obstruction such that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously?
Therefore, it must be that [the mind] arises solely in dependence upon the preceding mind;
the power of the preceding meditative concentration (*samādhi*) cannot obstruct other minds.

From this, we know that apart from the preceding mind, there must exist a distinct factor capable of obstructing the mind. Because of this factor, although the causes for the mind exist during the state of non-mentation (*acittaka*), the mind does not arise; this distinct factor is precisely what is called the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Its essence is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is real rather than provisional.

Because it is induced by the power of the vows and aspirations of the preceding mind during meditative cultivation, the force of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) gradually diminishes until, reaching the stage of total exhaustion, it no longer possesses the function of obstruction; then, with mental objects (*dharma*) as conditions, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises once more.

Based on this, the previously mentioned state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) have been explained accordingly. Having thus analyzed these two attainments,
what is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
The verse says:
The essence of the life-faculty is longevity; it is able to sustain warmth and consciousness.
The commentary says:
The essence of life is itself longevity.
Therefore, the Root Treatise asks:
"What is the life-faculty?"
This refers to the life-span of the three realms.
Although its synonyms are thus stated, its essential nature remains unexplained and should therefore be further specified.
What dharma is called "life-span" (āyus)?
It refers to a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is called "life-force" (*āyus*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Life-force, warmth, and consciousness—when these three dharmas abandon the body..."
"The discarded body lies prostrate, like a piece of wood without thought or sensation.
If this is so, what dharma is able to sustain this life-force?

I say that it is karma which sustains this life-force, because it is exclusively the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of karma and because it constantly persists throughout the course of a single lifetime.
Heat (*ūṣman*) is not exclusively the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of karma;

consciousness (*vijñāna*) is neither of the two. Although there is a location where it constantly accompanies [the person] throughout a single lifetime, it is not invariably the maturation of karma; therefore, one cannot say that consciousness is sustained by karma.
Therefore, it is said that life-force (*āyus*) can sustain warmth (*uṣman*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and this is not something not produced by karma.

Within the flow of consciousness, karma possesses a slight capacity for the function of sustaining; when the maturation-born consciousness (*vipākaja-vijñāna*) is severed within a single homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and subsequently re-continues, it is sustained solely by the power of life-force.
Furthermore, how is it known that vitality (*āyus*) can sustain heat (*uṣman*)?
It is because heat exists only where there is vitality; yet, those who lack heat are also seen to possess vitality. Therefore, we know that the essence of vitality is not sustained by heat.

From this, it is known that there exists a distinct real dharma whose power is able to sustain the warmth and consciousness of sentient beings; this is called "life-span" (*āyus*), which is precisely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Thus, the life-faculty does not depend solely upon the body, for it exists even in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*);
nor does it depend solely upon the mind, for it exists even during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
If that is so, upon what do they depend?
They depend on past karma and the present *nikāyasabhāga*; the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is also to be understood according to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
What is the difference between the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and the formations of longevity (*āyus-saṃskāra*)?

If the life-force (*jīvita*) of phenomena that are subject to arising is called the "formations of vitality" (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), the life-force of phenomena that are not subject to arising is said to be the "formation of longevity" (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*). Some say:
that which is not to be relinquished is called the formation of vitality, while that which is to be relinquished is called the formation of longevity.
Furthermore, some say:

if that which is the fruit of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is called the "volitional formation of life" (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), then that which is the fruit of prior karma is called the "volitional formation of lifespan" (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).

Others say: if birth governed by the predominance of clarity (*vidyā*) is called the "volitional formation of life," then birth governed by the predominance of ignorance (*avidyā*) is called the "volitional formation of lifespan."

Some say that only what is obtained within the continuum of one who is free from desire is called the formations of life (*āyusaṃskāra*), whereas that which is obtained within the continuum of one who still possesses desire is called the formations of longevity (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
This is the distinction between the formations of life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and the formations of longevity (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).
Having already explained the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
what are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?
There are four of these.
What are the four?
The verse says:
"Characteristics" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), namely the natures of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
The commentary states:

These four kinds are the characteristics of the conditioned; because they manifest that nature, they receive the name "characteristics. Based on these, it is said that there are various categories of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding "that which arises therein," this refers to a distinct dharma that serves as the unobstructed, predominant cause for the state of arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because it is capable of inducing and drawing them forth.
As for "inducing and drawing forth," it means that at the time those [phenomena] arise, this dharma acts as their predominant condition (*pratyaya*).

Although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that arise may be termed "birth," this specific designation of "birth" is established based on the unobstructed, predominant cause at the stage when those phenomena arise. These phenomena necessarily arise by depending on the power of preceding, co-arising, and homogeneous or heterogeneous conditions; this shall be demonstrated in detail within the investigation of cause and effect.

Among the previously mentioned similar and dissimilar conditions (*sabhāga* and *visabhāga-pratyaya*), the similar condition is predominant because [the result] arises in accordance with it; therefore, among the co-nascent conditions (*sahabhū-pratyaya*), there is no similar condition. Among the dissimilar conditions, however, there may be one that is particularly dominant, as is explained in the case of the arising of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) conditioned by the eye and visible forms (*rūpa*), where the eye is designated as the cause (*hetu*) and visible form as the nature of the condition (*pratyaya*).

Although visual consciousness does not arise if even one [of its conditions] is missing, the arising of visual consciousness follows the eye rather than the object, because the eye possesses the nature of being a proximate condition; therefore, it is designated as the cause.
Among all dharmas that arise simultaneously with visual consciousness and share a single fruit, those that assist the consciousness are superior in power, whereas the eye is not.

Furthermore, among those dharmas that arise simultaneously and share a single fruit, there may be one whose power to produce [the others] is particularly predominant; for example, wind in relation to fire, where the wind assists the power of the fire, causing it to blaze intensely, as is universally established in the world.

We observe that within a heterogeneous collection, wind is particularly conducive to fire; therefore, by analogy, it can be inferred that this is necessarily the case within a homogeneous collection. Thus, among the various formations (*saṃskāra*) that arise simultaneously, those whose internal generative power is predominant are specifically designated by the term "arising" (*jāti*).
The functional capacity produced by this [attainment] manifests most clearly at the very first moment of its arising among all the untainted factors it acquires.
Since such superior capacity is observed in this instance, one may infer that it likewise exists in other cases; thus, it should be understood that it is present there as well.

"Abiding" (sthiti) refers to a distinct dharma; it is the superior cause that, being unobstructed, draws forth its own fruit among those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that have already arisen but not yet perished.

Just as the arising of conditioned phenomena necessarily depends on a distinct dharma as a superior cause to assist in the superior function of drawing forth their fruit, so too must they necessarily depend on a distinct dharma as their cause.

The Abhidharmikas do not accept that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) exist as entities for even a moment while depending on various causes and conditions; rather, the masters of Abhidharma describe them as "present" and also say they possess "duration," because at that time, the conditioned phenomena project their own effects.
Furthermore, it is precisely in this regard that [the capacity for] activity is established.
The Blessed One also said:
"All conditioned phenomena abide only momentarily."
Furthermore, it is said that all material forms (*rūpa*) possess the stages of arising and abiding.

This cannot be said to refer to a continuum (*saṃtāna*), because even within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) they have the nature of suffering, and a continuum is necessarily constituted by the succession of moments.

The various characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) can only be established based on the continuity of preceding and succeeding moments; however, such a principle is necessarily untenable. Therefore, there must be a distinct dharma that serves as the immediate cause for the unimpeded activity of projecting effects for all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); the masters of the Abhidharma (*Abhidharmika*) designate this dharma as "duration" (*sthiti*).

"Difference" refers to a distinct dharma that constitutes the continuity of its own kind among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). It is impossible for a subsequent state to differ from its preceding cause without a cause; for it is logically untenable that there should be transformation without a cause, as this would imply that a single stream of consciousness could possess a prior and subsequent continuity while undergoing change spontaneously.

In those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the continuity of feeling (*vedanā*) and other factors undergoes transformation moment by moment; this function is most manifest there, and one can observe that the formless realm possesses distinct superior capacities, from which it may be inferred that other [faculties] likewise exist.
Cessation is a distinct dharma that arises simultaneously with conditioned formations; it is the supreme cause for their momentary destruction and non-obstruction.

One must not insist that cessation is an unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) entity, for such a view is logically untenable as it would lack arising from conditions, nor should one say that it possesses birth and cessation.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"One should know that arising and ceasing depend upon the absence of objects and cognition.
Since this principle necessarily implies non-existence, it cannot be said that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) possesses the characteristic of cessation.
Furthermore, just as phenomena that arise do so through a distinct arising, phenomena that cease should likewise do so through a distinct cessation.
Regarding the term "nature" (*svabhāva*), it carries the meaning of substantial reality (*dravya*).
If the characteristics of conditioned phenomena possess four distinct entities, why does the *sūtra* speak of only three?
The sūtra does not mention "abiding" (sthiti) because its purpose is to reveal the distinction between the virtues and faults of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Alternatively, if a characteristic were to express only the conditioned, the sūtra would have specifically mentioned it; however, the essence of the characteristic of abiding expresses both the conditioned and the unconditioned, as it also exists in the permanent. Therefore, the fact that it is not mentioned here is not due to the absence of a cause for abiding.
Other sūtras state that conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess the nature of arising and ceasing, and are not devoid of distinct characteristics; this [case] should be understood in the same way.
Although there are four characteristics, they are taught as three by concealing one according to what is appropriate for those to be trained, yet there is no error in doing so.
Alternatively, dwelling (*sthiti*) has already been implicitly taught in this sūtra, as there is no word "only" (*mātra*).

Or else, dwelling and change (*anyathātva*) are taught together in this sūtra; for if it were not so, one would have simply said "change," in order to show that the dwelling of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) necessarily entails change, unlike unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which possess dwelling but lack change.

The statement in this sutra regarding "abiding and change" (sthity-anyathātva) does not indicate that abiding is itself change; rather, it indicates that conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) possess arising, ceasing, abiding, and change, whereas unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) possess abiding but lack the other three. Therefore, all conditioned phenomena are distinct from the unconditioned.
For this reason, the Abhidharma states that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) necessarily possess four characteristics; this principle is unshakeable.
Since these characteristics of arising and so forth are themselves conditioned, they must in turn possess their own distinct set of four characteristics, such as arising and the rest.
If there were further characteristics, it would lead to an infinite regress, because those [characteristics] would themselves possess further characteristics such as birth and so forth.
While we indeed admit that there are further [characteristics], they do not constitute an infinite regress. Why is this?
The verse says:
These [conditioned phenomena] possess "arising-of-arising" and so forth, which have efficacy with respect to eight and one.
The commentary says:
In this context, some say that the mention [of "existence"] also serves to clarify its definition, intending to show that existence consists only of these four and nothing else.
This refers to the four primary characteristics previously mentioned.
As for "arising-of-arising" and so forth, these refer to the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇas*), namely: the arising-of-arising up to the cessation-of-cessation.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are conditioned by the four primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and these primary characteristics are themselves conditioned by the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).
Where did the Blessed One speak of these secondary characteristics?
There is a sūtra that says:
Because old age and death arise.
This sutra also states:
"There definitely exist secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas), namely the characteristics of birth and so forth."
Furthermore, because they are also conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the characteristics such as "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*) also possess the nature of "arising" and so forth.

Since the Sūtra states that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned—namely, that the arising of the conditioned can be known, as can its cessation (*vyaya*) and its alteration while abiding (*sthity-anyathātva*)—it is understood that these secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are also included herein.
Furthermore, since the word "also" (*api*) is applied to all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this sūtra also speaks of the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).

When it says that the arising of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) can also be known, "arising" refers to the primary characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); it also implies the full meaning of the secondary characteristic of birth (*jāti-jāti*), as well as the fact that duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*) can likewise be known.
Regarding the phrase "likewise arises" (*api utpadyate*), it should also be explained according to reason.
Otherwise, what purpose would the word "likewise" (*api*) serve?

Therefore, it should be understood that the Sūtra’s statement that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) "do not even exist" implies that [characteristics] such as arising and so forth are likewise absent.
The meaning of this statement is as follows:

since even the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa), such as arising, cannot be perceived in unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), how much less could the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa), such as "arising-of-arising," be found?
If it were not so, one should have simply stated that "arising and so forth cannot be known," rather than using the word "even" (api).
Furthermore, the Bhagavat stated in a sūtra that conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa) themselves possess further characteristics.
The sūtra says: "Form has arising and ceasing; one should know that this [arising and ceasing] also has arising and ceasing," and so forth, as explained at length.
From this, it is known that characteristics (lakṣaṇa) themselves possess further characteristics.

If this were so, then just as the primary characteristics correspond to the phenomena they characterize, each of these primary characteristics would likewise have four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa), and those in turn would each have four more, resulting in an infinite regress. [However,] there is no such fault.

The four primary characteristics and the four secondary characteristics have distinct functional capacities regarding eight factors and one factor, respectively; thus, their activity as direct conditions is termed "functional capacity" (*kāritra*).
That is to say, each of the four primary characteristics has a function with respect to eight factors, while each of the four secondary characteristics has a function with respect to one factor.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that when a dharma arises, nine dharmas arise together with its own self-nature (*svabhāva*).

The self-nature constitutes one; the eight characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) constitute the other eight. Among these, excluding their own intrinsic nature, they act as immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to produce the remaining eight dharmas, because no dharma possesses the function of arising and so forth with respect to its own self-nature.
The "arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) functions as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for its own primary arising; within the nine factors, it gives rise solely to that primary arising.
This single arising produces many [factors] due to the distinction in their functional capacities (*śakti*).
[Objection: Since the nature of arising is without difference, how can there be a distinction in functional capacity?
Just as with sensation (*vedanā*), although their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is no different, there are functional distinctions between benefit and harm.

Furthermore, there are differences in the extent of the primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) regarding their objects (*viṣaya*). For example, the objects of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) differ in magnitude. That which serves as a direct condition (*pratyaya*) enables the activity that draws forth its own fruit to arise; this is the generative function (*janana-śakti*). Within the primary characteristic of "abiding" (*sthiti*), excluding its own self-nature, it can also serve as a direct condition for the remaining eight dharmas.

The "subsistence of subsistence" (sthiti-sthiti) acts as the immediate condition for the nine dharmas; among these, it serves specifically as the immediate condition for the "subsistence of the fundamental" (mūla-sthiti), causing that dharma to abide momentarily and enabling it to draw forth its own fruit.

This [subsidiary characteristic] is distinct within the primary characteristics of the functional capacity (*kāritra*) of abiding; excluding its own nature, it acts as a direct condition (*pratyaya*), being distinct from the other eight dharmas.

Each subsidiary characteristic is distinct and acts as a direct condition; among the nine dharmas, it is distinct only from the primary characteristic of abiding itself. That is to say, acting as a direct condition, it causes the activity that draws forth its own fruit to undergo decay.

This distinct functional capacity perishes within its own primary characteristic (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*). Excluding its own nature, which serves as a direct condition (*pratyaya*), it causes the other eight dharmas to perish.

The secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of perishing perish within their own primary characteristic of perishing; among these nine dharmas, they cause only the primary characteristic of perishing to perish. Acting as a direct condition, this functional capacity of perishing causes the activity that draws forth its own fruit to perish and disintegrate. This is the function of perishing.

Therefore, the characteristics such as arising (jāti) also have further characteristics; however, since there are only four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa), there is no fault of infinite regress.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Exposition of the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Volume Seven.

Chapter Three: Distinguishing the Differences, Part Four. Although arising and the other [characteristics] exist separately from the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya*) and arise simultaneously with it, there is no fault of a single phenomenon being simultaneously produced, abiding, changing, and ceasing, because their essences are distinct and their functions differ.

If one maintains that there are no characteristics such as arising distinct from the characterized object itself, and that each moment possesses these four characteristics, such a fault is incurable; for the principle of functional differentiation within a single phenomenon at a single time is logically untenable.

If one allows that there exists something distinct from the characterized (lakṣya), such as arising (utpāda) and so forth, there is no such fault, because the nature of the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) differs, the auxiliary conditions (sahakāri-pratyaya) are distinct, and the principles regarding temporal divisions and functional capacities differ.

However, conditioned phenomena differ in their states; briefly, there are three types, distinguished by the activity of projecting a fruit: whether it has not yet been attained, is currently being attained, or has already ceased.
These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are further of two kinds: those possessing activity (*kāritra*) and those possessing only substance (*svabhāva*).
The former are the present; the latter are the past and future. Each of these, in turn, is of two kinds: namely, their functional capacities (*śakti*) may be either superior or inferior.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), that which can act as a cause to draw forth and encompass its own effect is termed "activity" (*kāritra*);
that which can act as a condition to assist other categories is called "efficacy" (*śakti*).

If there is a distinct dharma which, at the time when the function of projecting a fruit has not yet been acquired, encounters the conditions of "not yet acquired," "presently being acquired," and "already ceased"; and at the time when the function of projecting the fruit is assisted by external conditions, it initiates the functional capacity of internal conditions to assist in accomplishing its own task—this is called the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, there may be a phenomenon which, at the time it exerts its activity of projecting a fruit upon its actual acquisition, encounters that which has not yet been acquired; and when the actual acquisition has already ceased, while the external conditions assist during the time of projecting the fruit, it initiates the functional capacity of internal conditions to assist in accomplishing its own task.

Regarding these other three characteristics: in the state of "presently arising," arising acts as the internal condition for the produced phenomenon; once that produced phenomenon reaches the state of "already arisen," it is termed "having originated. In the state of "presently ceasing," duration acts as the internal condition for the abiding phenomenon, causing it to draw forth its own fruit until it reaches the state of "already ceased"; at this point, the abiding phenomenon is termed "having already been able to draw forth its own fruit," which is precisely the state of "presently ceasing."

Cessation acts as the internal condition that brings about the destruction of the phenomena to be ceased, reaching the state where they have already been ceased; these phenomena to be ceased are then termed "already destroyed.
The same should be understood to apply to the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*).
Other masters say:
Because a cause must depend upon place, time, stage, and companions in order to be able to yield its fruit.

There is a distinction in the operation [of causes] at the moment they arise and when they have already arisen; that is to say, some causes yield their fruit by depending on a place, such as rain, which only arises in a place where there are clouds.
One must be at the Vajrāsana in Jambudvīpa to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Alternatively, there are causes that depend upon time to yield their fruit; for example, a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) can only yield its fruit when it is in the past.

Furthermore, there are causes that yield their fruit by depending on time; for example, the karma of a wheel-turning monarch can only result in the attainment of the rank of a wheel-turning monarch when the aeon is in its period of increase (*vivartakalpa*).
Furthermore, there are causes that yield their fruit by depending on a particular stage; for example, seeds can only produce sprouts once they have reached the stage of transformation (*vikāra*).

Although the essence of the initial untainted mind, the light, and so forth exists previously, they must perform their function during the stage of being currently produced in the future; alternatively, there may be causes that depend on companions to yield their fruit.

Just as the four great elements, the mind, and mental factors must function in conjunction with their associates to perform their respective activities, so too, according to the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) exercise their functions at different stages.

Specifically, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) exercises its function at the moment of actual birth; once the state of having already arisen is reached, the three characteristics of duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*) each exercise their distinct functions simultaneously.
Since these four characteristics function at distinct times, there is no fault of a single dharma being simultaneously produced, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

Furthermore, at the very moment of cessation, this characterized dharma—by virtue of the characteristic of abiding acting as the predominant cause—temporarily remains stable and is able to project its own fruit; yet at that same time, by virtue of the characteristic of change acting as the predominant cause, it is made to decay, and at that same time, by virtue of the characteristic of cessation acting as the predominant cause, it is made to perish. Thus, there is no contradiction in their simultaneous occurrence.

At that time, as for the characterized phenomena (lakṣya), are they termed "abiding," "changing" (anyathātva), or "disintegrating"? Due to the power of the characterizers (lakṣaṇa), these three meanings are all present within the single moment of the characterized phenomenon, depending on the different perspectives from which they are viewed.
What is the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*)?

It is the process by which, during the very moment of abiding, the capacity to induce its own result undergoes decay; this impairment of that capacity causes the subsequent result to arise as inferior to its preceding cause—this is the power of the characteristic of change.
The subsequent result gradually becomes inferior due to differences in its causes.
Furthermore, this result is impaired by the conditions of co-arising dissimilar characteristics, which cause the subsequent result to become even more inferior than the preceding one.

In this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) undergo a moment-to-moment transformation such that each subsequent moment is different from the preceding one; thus, the principle that each preceding moment possesses distinctness is established.
This point being established, it should be formulated as an inference (*anumāna*).
This means that because a difference is observed in the final moment of existence, there must necessarily be differences in the preceding moments.
If this were so, then when a continuum gradually increases, there would be no difference between the preceding and succeeding moments, as no effect would be perceived.
There is no such fault, because at that time, the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is strengthened by the auxiliary power of external conditions and thus subdues the others.
If birth (*jāti*) arises in the future and gives rise to the phenomena it is meant to produce, why do all future phenomena not arise simultaneously?
Because their respective productive causes are eternally conjoined;
this has already been argued previously.
What was argued previously?

It refers to a distinct dharma which, while the capacity to project its fruit has not yet been acquired, encounters external conditions—whether unobtained, currently being obtained, or already ceased—to assist in projecting that fruit; it then initiates an internal conditioning function to accomplish its own task. This is called the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is said that causes must depend upon place, time, state, and companions in order to yield their fruit.
It is precisely based on this principle that the following verse is spoken: [Verse:]
Birth can produce that which is to be produced, but not apart from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
The commentary says:

It is not the case that, apart from the conjunction of all other causes and conditions, the power of the characteristic of birth alone can produce that which is to be produced; therefore, all future phenomena do not arise simultaneously.

Although the characteristic of arising acts as the immediate cause that arises simultaneously with it, the various conditioned phenomena that are produced must necessarily depend upon their own preceding causes of the same kind, as well as the assistance provided by the convergence of other external conditions.
Just as various causal conditions such as seeds and soil assist in the production of sprouts and cause them to arise, so it is in this case:
