we perceive only that causal conditions possess the functional capacity for production; there is no separate characteristic of "production" apart from them.
If phenomena arise only when causes and conditions conjoin, and do not arise when they are absent, what need is there for a "characteristic of arising"?
Therefore, it should be that phenomena arise solely through the power of causes and conditions.
This objection is not valid; for if one asserts that phenomena arise solely from a multitude of conditions, this same objection applies equally.
That is to say, if one were to admit that future dharmas arise solely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, this objection would likewise apply:
since there is no distinction among the causes and conditions for all future dharmas, why do they not all arise simultaneously?
Furthermore, within a causal complex, if even one factor is missing, the effect should still arise because the remaining factors are complete.
For instance, the visual faculty, which is projected by prior karma, should likewise arise even when separated from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Alternatively, the eye-organ should arise solely through the power of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and not through prior karma;

or, since the primary elements that produce the various eye-organs are drawn forth by karma, there would never be a time when they do not coincide, and thus when one arises, the others should also arise.

Alternatively, the primary elements (mahābhūta) would have no efficacy regarding the eye, because we do not observe them arising independently apart from the preceding ocular primary elements; rather, the subsequent eye must arise based on the preceding one, and thus it would follow that the capacity of the primary elements to produce [the eye] is rendered useless.
Furthermore, just as with the conditions of seeds, soil, water, and so forth, if even one of these is lacking, the sprout will certainly not arise.
Therefore, it is known that the causal efficacy of the seed and other factors is fully established in the production of the eye and other faculties.
The capacity of the great elements, such as earth, to produce [sensory faculties] is not directly perceived.
Since the causal power of the great elements is not directly perceived, they should not serve as causes for the production of the eyes and other faculties.
Furthermore, regarding the continuity and transformation of the seeds of karma that you maintain: what acts as an obstacle such that all karmic fruits cannot be produced instantaneously?
If it is only through the assistance of conditions that the seeds of karma can produce [fruits], then it should be the conditions alone that produce them; why labor with the seeds of karma?
Because the fruit of karma arises only when assisted by various conditions, and because the fruit does not arise if those conditions are absent;
since the seed of karma exists in reliance upon such assistance, how could one deny the characteristic of arising, even while acknowledging the necessity of various conditions?
Furthermore, regarding the arising of the various consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness, various sūtras state:
"Even though the eye and visible forms exist, if attention (manasikāra) is absent, eye-consciousness does not arise.
Nevertheless, it is also said that the conditions for the arising of consciousness are the eye and visible forms; therefore, one should not raise this objection: [that there is a contradiction].
Since it arises through the power of causes and conditions, what need is there for a "characteristic of arising"?

Furthermore, when observing the initial moment of the arising of the untainted (anāsrava), this arising can serve as the cause for the production of the attainment (prāpti) of the untainted; that this attainment possesses its own intrinsic characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) has already been fully established.
One should explain what distinct dharma, other than birth (*jāti*), can act as the simultaneous cause for the arising of this acquisition (*prāpti*).
If there were no cause at all, the acquisition would not arise; consequently, the initial untainted state (*anāsrava*) could not be said to be accomplished.

When the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa) arises, does it also have a separate co-arising cause? One should not say that it does; for, apart from the essence of arising itself, what other single dharma of the same fruit could serve as such?
How could a distinct cessation (nirodha) act as an auxiliary cause for arising?
The masters of old all offered this explanation:
dharmas that share the same fruit act as causes for one another, just as the great elements (mahābhūtas) are mutually concordant.
Furthermore, there is another explanation which states:

Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess the nature of arising and so forth, when each of the four characteristics—arising and the rest—functions, it serves as the primary gateway while the others provide auxiliary support.
Therefore, the statement that the "arising of arising" and the "arising of what is arisen" do not exist apart from causes and conditions is well-established by reason.
For a detailed determination of the other characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), one should consult the *Nyāyānusāra* and the commentary on the *Pañcavastuka*.
Having briefly analyzed the characteristics of conditioned phenomena,
what is the meaning of the categories such as "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth?
The verse says:
"Name-bodies and so forth" refers to the collective designations for concepts (*saṃjñā*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*).
The commentary states:
"And so forth" includes the inclusion of phrase-bodies (*padakāya*) and phoneme-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*)."
Regarding the groups of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), they are so designated because they are explained in the *Mūla-śāstra*:

the collective designation for all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) is the group of names; the collective designation for all chapters (*vākya*) is the group of phrases; and the collective designation for all phonemes (*akṣara*) is the group of syllables.
"General statement" (saṃkṣepa) means the sense of a collective synthesis; it is so called because within the sense of collective synthesis, the *uṣman* and *anta* elements are taught.

"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to perceptions such as "eye," "ear," "bottle," or "garment"—that is, the conceptualization and grasping of various phenomena, and the perception produced by the words conventionally established for them. Such a collection of perceptions (*saṃjñākāya*) is precisely the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), namely: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Chapter" (*pariccheda*) refers to "discriminative exposition.

The worldly scholars explain it as a chapter that possesses inexhaustible discrimination and differentiation; it is capable of definitively explaining the intended meaning, such as how merit brings about the ripening of pleasant results and so forth.
In this way, the body of phrases (*vyañjana-kāya*) is itself the body of sentences (*pada-kāya*), as it is said:
“Merit brings about pleasant ripening; Whatever one desires is fulfilled as wished;
And together with the swift realization of the foremost, There is the eternal peace of *nirvāṇa*.”
Regarding such phrases as these:

"syllables" refers to syllables such as *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and so forth; such bodies of syllables (*akṣara-kāya*) are themselves bodies of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), such as *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and so forth.
Other masters say that the *Mūla-śāstra* states:
"What is a manifold designation (*nāmakāya*)?
It refers to names, names of things, and so forth."
It is not that those masters intended to debate whether names and so forth possess the characteristic of being substantially real while relying on a provisional combination to initiate their inquiry.
Therefore, when they ask about "name-bodies" and so forth, they must certainly be asking about the substantial reality of the essence of names and so forth.
In investigating the actual nature of names and so forth, what is the use of further scrutinizing their conventional conjunction?

Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among the three characteristics of names and so forth: that which is manifested by sound, which reveals meaning, and which is collectively established as the definitive means of expression (*vācaka-pramāṇa*); which displays the intrinsic nature of the objects of knowledge produced from the intended mental disposition of the speaker; and which, like a shadow or an echo, represents that nature—this characteristic is "name" (*nāman*).
If one can analytically distinguish the broad and concise categories of meaning within the objects of knowledge, this characteristic is a "phrase" (*pada*).

When the sound of the speaker has already ceased, that which still causes one to maintain mindfulness and retain the meaning without confusion, transmitting it to others, this characteristic is a "syllable" (*vyañjana*).
In this context, "name" refers to that which follows and accords with the sounds of speech as they conform to suchness (*tathatā*).
In this manner and in that manner, names follow after and invoke their respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
A "phrase" (*pada*) is that which can differentiate the meaning of what is spoken; that is, it can analyze and distinguish the various categories of meaning.
A "syllable" (*vyañjana*) is that which is capable of manifesting; for it is by depending upon and through this that those [meanings] are manifested.

This is precisely what constitutes a "syllable" (*akṣara*): it means that which causes mindfulness to be bound [to the object] so as to prevent forgetfulness; or alternatively, that which is sustained by this [mindfulness] so as to eliminate doubt; or that which can maintain those [mental factors] and transmit them to others.

Some say that, just as for one in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the characteristics of the objects of the preparatory means (*prayoga*) serve as a ladder to the objects realized within the absorption itself, so too is it with respect to the words, phrases, and meanings.

In principle, the sets of names (nāma-kāya), phrases (pada-kāya), and syllables (vyañjana-kāya) are all formations dissociated from thought (viprayukta-saṃskāra). However, when the sūtras and śāstras state that all non-material phenomena (arūpa-dharma) are termed "names" (nāman), this is because names are established based on the manifestation of their own essential nature through material characteristics; whereas for non-material phenomena, their designations are established based on their expressive function, as their material characteristics are not manifest.
Is meaning expressible or inexpressible?
In reality, one should say that meaning is inexpressible.
Nevertheless, it is conventionally established that upon hearing words one understands the meaning, for names are produced based on speech, and names manifest the meaning.
The phenomena of the three times each have three names, namely past, future, and present, because they are spoken of in terms of these three periods.
Furthermore, there is no phenomenon that lacks a name; if it were so, it would follow that it could not be an object of knowledge.
Therefore, the Bhagavān spoke these words:
"Name can overshadow all things; there is nothing that surpasses name.
For this reason, name is called the one dharma, which follows and acts with sovereign mastery over all."
Other masters say: "The referent is few while the names are many, because there are many names for a single referent. Still others say:
Names are few while meanings are many; names are comprised by only a small portion of a single realm (*dhātu*), whereas meanings encompass all eighteen realms.

Furthermore, some say that there is a mutual relation of fewness and manyness: with respect to the inclusion of meanings within the realms, meanings are many and names are few; however, according to the establishment of the teachings, meanings are few and names are many, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, establishes boundless names for each and every phenomenon in accordance with its meaning.

Just as greed is called craving, fire, a serpent, a creeper, thirst, a net, poison, a spring, a river, long, broad, a needle-thread, and so forth—everything of this kind is what the Sūtra-master has stated here.

Since these three types of speech have words as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and thus take sound as their substance (dravya), being subsumed under the self-nature of form (rūpa), how can they be said to be formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra)?
This criticism is unreasonable.
Why is this so? Because both principle and scripture clearly establish that [the ālayavijñāna] exists as something distinct.
"Teaching" refers to the power of the words and the power of the phrasing of the sūtras.
If the phrasing were identical to the words, what would be the purpose of mentioning them separately?
Furthermore, it is said that one "should uphold the phrasing and sentences of the True Dharma."
Furthermore, it is said that one should rely on the meaning and not on the literal expression.
Moreover, it is stated that the cause for a *gāthā* is called *chanda*, while the *chanda* of the syllables refers to the composition of verses, having the measured length of words as its essence.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One knows the phenomena (dharma) and knows their meaning (artha). Here, "phenomena" refers to names and so forth, while "meaning" refers to that which is expressed.
Another sutra states:
The phrasing and meaning are skillful.
It further states:
"One should recite the True Dharma using well-spoken phrases; if one recites the True Dharma using poorly spoken phrases, its meaning will be difficult to understand."
Furthermore, it is said:
"The Tathāgata has attained rare names, phrases, and phonemes.
It is also said:
The various phrases and expressions of that [teaching] are truly rare and marvelous.

Based on these scriptural authorities, it is established that there exist distinct sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) capable of denoting various meanings; their essence is like sound, being real rather than merely conventional.

The principle is that they are perceived as distinct: sometimes one perceives the sound but not the syllable, and sometimes one perceives the syllable but not the sound; thus we know their essences are different.
"Sometimes perceiving the sound but not the syllable" means that although one hears the sound, one does not comprehend its meaning.
It is observed that some people, upon merely hearing the words of another, further inquire:
"What did you say? This failure to comprehend the meaning of the sounds heard is entirely due to not having mastered the phonemes (*vyañjana*) from which they are produced.
How can you maintain that the written word is no different from the sound?
There are times when one obtains the word but not the sound; this refers to cases where one understands the meaning without hearing the sound.
We observe people who, without hearing another's speech, perceive what is being said by observing the movement of the lips and so forth.
That one attains the definitive meaning without hearing the sound is entirely due to having already mastered the articulated syllables (*vyañjana*).
Based on this logical proof, the syllable must necessarily differ from the sound.
Furthermore, we observe in the world that people recite mantras while suppressing their voices; thus, we know that the mantra-syllables are distinct from the mantra-sound.
Furthermore, one observes that among worldly debaters whose speech sounds similar, one is defeated and the other victorious; this cause of victory and defeat must therefore exist apart from sound.
Moreover, because the spheres of the two unimpeded analytical knowledges—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of expression (*nirukti*)—are distinct, one knows that syllables are separate from sound.
Therefore, sound is merely vocal expression; its characteristics possess no differentiation. Its internal inflections necessarily depend on [the phonemes] ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and so forth.

It is through the vocal sounds that various syllables (*akṣara*) are initiated; the combination of these syllables in sequence produces a name (*nāman*), and once this name has arisen, it is able to manifest the meaning.
From this, it follows through a series of steps that they say:
speech can produce names, and names can manifest meanings.
Therefore, the distinction between sound and name is established as an ultimate principle.

It should be understood that herein, sound (*śabda*) is the speaker, while names (*nāman*) and so forth are what is spoken; the meaning (*artha*), however, is neither of the two. This constitutes an unerring establishment [of the categories].
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) further states:
"Not all vocal sounds are designated as 'speech' (*vāk*)."
It is because meaning can be understood through this that such sounds are properly designated as "speech.
That is to say, among all meanings, these have been established by common consensus as the definitive means of expression for the speaker.
If the meaning of this sentence is manifested by means of names (*nāman*), then sound itself would be the expressive agent; why then would names and so forth be required?
What is designated as the definitive standard for the expressive agent?

Is it not the case that when a conventional designation (*saṃjñā*) and name are established together with respect to an object, this very thing is called the definitive standard for the expressive agent?
This means that when a speaker first establishes these various syllables in common for various meanings, they are definitely able to express those meanings through successive articulation.
Because such syllables are established in common, names are produced from these syllables; these names are the definitive means of expression.

Whenever those who are capable of speaking are about to utter words, they must first reflect upon such established conventions; it is by means of this that, whether through their own speech or the speech of others, they are able to comprehend the meaning revealed therein.

Therefore, it is not that sound alone can manifest meaning; rather, speech produces syllables (*vyañjana*), syllables in turn produce names (*nāman*), and only then can a name express the intended meaning.
Just as speech produces syllables and syllables produce names, one should likewise consider the principle by which phrases (*pada*) are produced.
In this regard, the Sūtra-master further states:
"Moreover, it is not yet understood how this name is produced by speech—
is it manifested by speech, or is it generated by speech?"
If [names] were produced by speech, then because speech is of the nature of sound, all sounds should be able to produce names.
If it is argued that there is a distinction among the sounds that produce names, this [distinction] alone would suffice to manifest the meaning; why then wait for a separate name?
If it is manifested by speech, then since speech is of the nature of sound, all sounds should be able to manifest names.
If you claim that there is a distinction among sounds that manifests names, then this alone would suffice to manifest meaning; why wait for a separate "name"?
If one maintains that sound is capable of signifying meaning, this objection applies equally.
That is to say, if the very essence of sound were itself able to manifest meaning, then all sounds whatsoever would necessarily be capable of manifestation.
If it is argued that there is a distinction among those sounds capable of manifestation, then such a distinction must be the name itself.
Therefore, the objections raised by the opponent are ultimately groundless.
However, the speaker first holds the names they intend to use within their mind; only then do they reflect:
"I shall produce such and such words to proclaim such and such meanings for others."
Consequently, at a later time, speech is produced following thought; based on speech, syllables are produced, and syllables in turn produce names, whereby the meaning is finally manifested.
It is by means of this sequential process that it is said that speech produces names, and names are able to manifest meaning.
Established in this manner, the principle is necessarily so.

If one does not first direct the mind toward the name within the aggregates, then even if one were to utter speech in its entirety, it would lack definitive expression and would not cause another to generate understanding of the meaning.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Master says:

"Alternatively, one should maintain that there exists only a distinct textual substance (*vyañjana-rāśi*), which, when collected as a whole, constitutes the 'bodies' of names and so forth; to further maintain that there exist other [entities] would be useless."
This is also unreasonable, because there are no texts stating that these [elements] function simultaneously.
Since they do not function simultaneously, how could they be aggregated as a whole?

Alternatively, it is like trees and other things which are composed of the great primary elements; it is not that shadows are not produced in dependence upon them, yet while the shadow arises through a conventional designation, its substance is not itself conventional.
In this way, these various phonemes should also be collectively assembled to produce distinct names and phrases.
Although those names and phrases are manifested by means of the provisional (prajñapti), their essence is not provisional.
If that were so, then all provisional phenomena could be established as having a truly existent nature.
There is no such fault, because even within a single syllable there exists a name.
Since no provisional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*) is established by grasping a single real entity, the provisional and the name are not similar in meaning.
Since a name can also be established for a single syllable, how is it known that this name exists apart from the syllable?

Just as a single syllable—like a meaningless syllable—has nothing to be expressed (*vācya*), yet based on this [syllable] as a condition, a distinct name arises which alone is able to express meaning; however, because they are so extremely close, their distinct characteristics are difficult to discern.
Just as the light on a wall makes two colors difficult to distinguish,

if one grants that sound itself [is the name], then it is said that by means of the distinctions in vocal utterance established through prior convention, it is able to signify meaning and is thus designated as "name" and so forth.
What fault is there in this?
This too is not the case, because it is logically untenable that the convention of a signifier is merely a particularity of sound.

If the convention of a signifier established by common consensus were merely a particularity of sound, then—just like a particularity of form—it would be cognizable even without a convention being established by common consensus.
The distinction between the two colors blue and yellow does not exist inherently; it can only be known after a convention has been mutually established.

Although no such conventional designation for their distinction was previously established among the two colors, because blue and yellow are not different types of color, once they have been apprehended by the visual consciousness, the mental consciousness is then able to discern their respective distinctions through subsequent conceptualization.

Furthermore, it is logically untenable to apply a linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) to that which is itself a linguistic convention; therefore, one should not say that [the word] can express the convention. Although it is not distinct from sound, it was previously not shared [with the convention].

Although one who establishes a convention may perceive a sound, because they must further depend on other instances of establishing conventions, they are unable to discern the specific characteristic that differentiates this sound from others.

Furthermore, if the convention established for a term were merely a particularity of sound, then one should also be able to cognize the distinction between meaningful sounds and meaningless sounds even before a convention for that distinction has been collectively established; that is, one should recognize that this particularity exists in one sound and does not exist in other sounds.

Previously, when no conventional agreement (*saṃketa*) regarding distinctions had been established, although the meaning was not understood upon hearing two sounds, one should nevertheless be able to discern the distinction between sounds that possess a convention and those that do not, just as one discerns the distinction between two colors.

Therefore, we know that there exist distinct entities called the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), which arise based on sound and are capable of manifesting and clarifying meaning.
Furthermore, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) states: "Momentary sounds cannot be accumulated, nor does any single dharma arise gradually in parts."
How can it be said that the arising [of unmanifest action] is triggered by speech?
Furthermore, he himself explains:
"How is it that, depending upon the past moments of manifest action, the final moment of manifest action is able to produce the unmanifest?"
Furthermore, he raises an objection himself:
"If that were so, since a name (*nāman*) is produced by the sound at the final stage, one should be able to comprehend the meaning upon hearing only the final sound.
If one holds such a position—that speech produces the phoneme (*vyañjana*), the phoneme in turn produces the name, and only then does the name manifest the meaning—[the following objection applies].
The critique regarding this point should be stated as before, because the phonemes (*vyañjana*) cannot be accumulated.
As for the fault that speech manifests names (*nāman*), it should be illustrated by analogy with [the case of] production.
Furthermore, whether phonemes manifest or produce [names], based on the same logic applied to speech, both [possibilities] are unreasonable when applied to names.
This objection contradicts the tenets you yourself have accepted.

Since you assert that the past and future lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and that sounds cannot arise instantaneously across preceding and succeeding moments, how can there be the formation of phonemes (*vyañjana*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*)?
If preceding moments successively assist one another so that the final moment constitutes the phoneme, word, or sentence, then one should understand the meaning upon hearing only the final moment.
Furthermore, there is no mutual assistance, because past and future moments do not exist [simultaneously].
Since each moment is constantly a single thought-instant, how can they assist one another?

If there is no mutual assistance, then the preceding and succeeding moments would be identical; consequently, a subsequent moment should be unable to signify its object just as the initial moment was, and hearing the subsequent moment should likewise fail to comprehend the meaning, just as with the initial moment.
Therefore, the position held by those [opponents]—that name and so forth mutually support one another across time such that sound itself is the signifier—is logically untenable.
In our own school, all three times exist and are not non-existent; thus, the subsequent [moment] depends on the preceding [moment] to produce names and the like.

Although names and so forth arise only at the final moment, one cannot comprehend their meaning by hearing them alone; this is because the conditions for hearing are incomplete, unlike the case where a previously established convention regarding names and so forth can produce the sound.
However, there are those who attain realization upon hearing a single sound; this is due to the power of habitual cultivation (*abhyāsa*).
Based on this, one may infer the case of others; thus, the Sūtra Master says:
"That [realization] refutes them, but it is not this [case]."
The *Vibhāṣā* states that name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and phoneme (*vyañjana*) each have three types.
As for the three types of name, they are: the name, the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), and the large collection of names; the same applies to phrases and phonemes.
Names have several levels: namely, those produced by a single syllable, those produced by two syllables, or those produced by many syllables.
When a single syllable is uttered, it can only be called a "name" (*nāman*); when two syllables are uttered, it is termed a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
Some say: when three syllables are uttered, that is called a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*). Others say:
It is only when four syllables are spoken that one speaks of a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
Regarding those produced from two syllables: when two syllables are spoken, there can only be a "name," but when four syllables are spoken, it is then called a name-group.
Some say: when six syllables are uttered, that is called a "multifarious name-group" (nāmakāya). Others say:
It is only when eight syllables are spoken that one refers to them as a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).

Regarding the production of multiple syllables, when three syllables are produced—that is, when three syllables are spoken—there may simply be a "name," but when six syllables are spoken, it is then called a "name-group."
Some say that when nine syllables are uttered, it is called a "multitude of names" (nāmakāya). Others say:
When the twelve syllables are spoken, it is then called a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
Because this serves as the gateway, other multi-syllabic [names] arise.
One should explain the name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and phrase-groups (*padakāya*) according to the principle.
Phrases (*pada*) also have multiple varieties, namely: intermediate phrases, initial phrases, final phrases, short phrases, and long phrases.
If eight syllables form a name, it is called an intermediate phrase; it is termed "intermediate" because it is neither long nor short.
The thirty-two syllables arise from four lines; such four lines constitute a *śloka*, and the compositions of sutras and treatises mostly rely upon this number.
If six syllables or more arise, it is called the first line; if twenty-six syllables or fewer arise, it is called the subsequent line.
If fewer than six syllables are produced, it is called a short phrase; if more than twenty-six syllables are produced, it is called a long phrase.

For now, based on the intermediate length of a phrase, three types will be distinguished: when eight syllables are spoken, there is merely a phrase; when sixteen syllables are spoken, it is called a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*).
Some say that when twenty-four syllables are spoken, it is called a "multitude of phrases" (*padakāya*). Others say:
When thirty-two syllables (*akṣara*) are spoken, they are then called a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*).
Since a phoneme (*vyañjana*) is identical to a syllable, it possesses only a single position.
When one syllable is spoken, there can only be a phoneme; when two syllables are spoken, it is then called a "phoneme-body" (*vyañjanakāya*).
Some say that when three syllables are uttered, it is called a "multitude of phonemes" (vyañjana-kāya). Others say:
It is only when four syllables are spoken that one speaks of a "multitude of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*).

For this reason, it should be stated as follows: when a single syllable is spoken, there is a name (*nāman*), but no "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*) and no "multitude of name-bodies"; there is no phrase (*pada*), no "phrase-body" (*pada-kāya*), and no "multitude of phrase-bodies"; there is a phoneme (*vyañjana*), but no "phoneme-body" (*vyañjana-kāya*) and no "multitude of phoneme-bodies."

When two syllables are spoken, there is a name and a name-body, but no multi-name-body; there are no sentences or the other two [categories]; there is a phoneme (vyañjana) and a phoneme-body, but no multi-phoneme-body.

When four syllables are spoken, there are the three categories beginning with name (nāman), the absence of the three categories beginning with phrase (pada), and the presence of the three categories beginning with phoneme (vyañjana).

When eight syllables are spoken, there are the three categories beginning with name; there is the category of phrase (pada), the absence of the category of phrase-body (padakāya), and the absence of the category of multiple-phrase-body (anekapadakāya); and there are the three categories beginning with phoneme.

When sixteen syllables are spoken, there are the three categories of name (*nāman*) and so forth; there are phrases (*pada*), but no phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), and no multiple phrase-bodies; there are the three categories of phoneme (*vyañjana*) and so forth.
When thirty-two syllables are spoken, each of the three—name, phrase, and phoneme—possesses its own three varieties.
Taking this as the gateway, the rest should be explained according to reason.
Furthermore, one should reflect: to which realm are these names and so forth bound?
Are they included within the category of sentient beings, or are they not?
Is this of the nature of maturation (*vipākaja*), or of growth (*aupacayika*), or of outflow (*naiṣyandika*)?
Is it wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral? All of these points should be analyzed.
The verse says:
They are comprised within the sentient beings of the desire and form realms; they are of the nature of outflow and are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The commentary says:
These three, beginning with name (nāman), are bound exclusively to the two realms of desire and form.
Regarding the realm of form, some say they exist only in the stage of the first dhyāna;
others say they also extend through the upper three dhyānas, because their binding varies according to whether it follows speech or the body.

If one speaks of these three as being bound according to the speech, then when one is born in the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm, the name-body and so forth of that speech are all bound to the desire realm.
The meaning expressed by that speech may be bound to any of the three realms, or it may be unbound.

When that same person utters speech belonging to the first dhyāna, the speech and the names (*nāman*) and so forth are bound to the level of the first dhyāna, while the body is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The meaning is as previously explained.
Likewise, if one born in the level of the first dhyāna utters speech belonging to two levels, it should be understood accordingly.
If one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages and utters speech belonging to two stages, it should also be understood according to reason.

If it is said that these three [name, phrase, and syllable] are bound to the same stage as the body, this means that for one born in the desire realm or in the four dhyānas, name and so forth and the body are each bound to their own respective stages, while speech may be bound to its own stage or to another stage; the meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding these two explanations, some say that although the higher stages also possess names and so forth, they cannot be articulated; yet, despite these two views, the first is superior.

Furthermore, the triad of name, word, and phrase is subsumed under the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), because non-sentient conditioned phenomena do not achieve [these]; rather, they are achieved by the speaker.
They do not manifest their meaning; they exist only in the present and are not established in the past or future.
Furthermore, the three—names and so forth—are exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*); they are neither nurtured (*aupacayika*) nor born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
As for the statement that names and so forth arise from karma, this is because they are the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) produced by that karma.
Furthermore, these three—name, phrase, and syllable—are comprised exclusively within the category of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.

Therefore, when one who has severed the roots of goodness speaks of wholesome dharmas, although they establish the names and so forth of the wholesome, they do not establish the wholesome dharmas themselves.

One who is free from sensual desire does not establish unwholesome [dharmas], and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not establish defiled [dharmas]; this is because they establish the names and so forth that express [these things], rather than the dharmas that are expressed.
As has been explained above,
the remaining meanings concerning the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) that have not yet been discussed shall now be briefly analyzed.
The verse says:
The same applies to the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), as well as the formless [attainments] and maturation (*vipāka*).
Possession (*prāpti*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain to all three categories; non-possession (*aprāpti*) is definitely outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The treatise says:

The phrase "likewise" is used to indicate that this is similar to the *nāmakāya* (sets of names) and so forth, which pertain to both the desire and form realms, are the outflow of sentient beings, and are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The inclusion of the term "formless" indicates that these are not restricted solely to the desire and form realms.

The mention of "both" and "maturation" (vipāka) indicates that these are not merely outflowing (niṣyanda) results; this refers to the meaning that they pertain to all three realms and both types [of beings].
What is meant by "maturation"?
It refers to the generic similarity (nikāya-sabhāga) of rebirth in destinies such as the hells and modes of birth such as the egg-born.
What is meant by "homogeneity" (nikāyasabhāga)?
It refers to the commonality found among various realms, stages, locations, lineages, castes, śramaṇas, brahmins, those in training (śaikṣa), and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Other masters say:
That which is produced by the projection of prior karma is the *vipāka-sabhāgatā* (homogeneity of maturation).
That which arises from present application is the *niṣyanda-sabhāgatā* (homogeneity of outflow).

Both acquisition (*prāpti*) and the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) pertain to all three types—namely, they possess the momentary (*kṣaṇika*), the outflowing (*niṣyanda*), and the maturational (*vipāka*). Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are exclusively outflowing.
The word "only" (kevala) is used to clarify that [these] are not non-maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth.

As for the remaining [factors] that ought to be mentioned but are not, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) have already been explained as before, and the other meanings can be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Because it is stated that "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth pertain exclusively to possession (*samanvāgama*), the meaning that they are subsumed under the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*) can be inferred accordingly.

Because it is stated that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess "arising" (*utpāda*) and so forth, it can be inferred accordingly that the [four] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) apply to both sentient and non-sentient things.
The meanings of the remaining factors have already been clarified as appropriate; therefore, there is no need for further elaboration here.
Thus has the analysis of the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) been completed.

As previously stated regarding the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), when that which is to arise comes into being, it does not occur apart from the conjunction of other causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*).
Among these, what dharma is designated as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)?
Briefly, there are six kinds of causes. What are the six?
The verse says: The efficient cause, the co-existent cause, the similar-type cause, the associated cause, the universal cause,
and the maturation cause— these six alone are accepted as causes.
The treatise states:
This treatise maintains that causes are exclusively of six kinds, neither more nor less.

First, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); second, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); third, the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); fourth, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*); fifth, the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*); and sixth, the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The essence of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) pervades all phenomena; therefore, it was explained first.
The essence of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, it is placed second.

As for the remaining causes, such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and others, each includes a small portion within the category of the conditioned according to its respective application; they are explained in their sequence so that the phrasing remains smooth and convenient.
Because they are that upon which the arising of dharmas relies, they are called "causes" (*hetu*); this means they are factors that directly and favorably assist the production of their effects.
Since these six causes were not taught by the Buddha, how does the root treatise establish these names on its own authority?
There is certainly no meaning not taught by the Great Teacher that the Abhidharma would venture to expound.
Since it is not currently present in the Sūtras, it must necessarily exist as something whose specific characteristics can be apprehended, even if it has become obscured.

Furthermore, because of the capacity of those to be trained, the Blessed One employed skillful means to teach through various methods; yet, by observing even a few signs, the masters of the Abhidharma knew that [the Dharma] definitely existed and compiled it with clarity.
Therefore, some have said:
"The meaning of these six causes was taught in the *Ekottarika-āgama* and the *Ṣaḍvarga-āgama*, but as much time has passed, their texts have been lost."

The Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others sought the characteristics of all phenomena through uninterrupted reflection; thus, they moved the celestial beings by their profound resonance, who appeared and bestowed [the teachings] upon them.
This is as certain as the principle of the *Vatsasūtra* being bestowed by the gods.

Although the meaning of the four conditions is fully set forth in this sūtra of our own school, there are those in other schools who do not recite it, because much has been lost over the long passage of time.
Since we observe that other sūtras contain some omissions, we know that this passage as well is not complete.
Furthermore, because the meaning of the six causes is explained scattered throughout various parts of the sūtras, it must certainly exist in reality.
That is to say, as it is stated in the Sūtra:
"With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
And again, as it is stated in the Sūtra:
Two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view.
Such factors as these constitute the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
All phenomena possess the sense of being an efficient cause for others, and this cause is established because it functions by not obstructing their arising.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are three path-factors that proceed in accordance with right view.
And as it is further said in the Sūtra:
Contact arising from the conjunction of the three, together with feeling, perception, and volition—
such factors as these are the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise simultaneously and perform a single function by way of mutual concomitance, this cause is established.
As it is said:
"Such a person is endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

It should be understood that for such a person, although wholesome dharmas have disappeared and unwholesome dharmas have appeared, there remain accompanying roots of goodness that have not been severed."
Because it has not been severed, there remains the possibility for further roots of goodness to arise from these roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it is said: "O Bhikṣus!"

If one frequently engages in discursive thought and investigation regarding various objects, the mind will frequently enter into those very objects; with ignorance as the cause, various defilements and attachments arise, whereas with clarity as the cause, one becomes free from all defilements and attachments.
All such factors as these are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Past and present homogeneous dharmas are established as this cause because they draw forth their own effects.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Seeing is the root of faith, which is conjoined with realized wisdom.
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"If there is discernment, there is comprehension; comprehension while in meditative concentration is according to reality, whereas that which is not in concentration is not."
All such factors as these constitute the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Mind and mental factors are associated because they perform a single function together; this cause is established on the basis of their collectively apprehending a single object.
As the Sūtra says:

For those with wrong views, whatever physical, verbal, and mental actions they perform, and whatever aspirations they harbor, all accord with their views; all their conduct is of that same nature, and thus all such phenomena can only bring about results that are not desirable, unpleasant, and disagreeable.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
When any of the various views arise, they all take the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root.
If this view arises, one cannot tolerate anything; this view can give rise to both craving and aversion.
All such factors as these constitute the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Doubt, views, and ignorance—along with their associated and co-existent factors—that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the past and present, are established as this cause because they are able to give rise to all defiled phenomena of both similar and dissimilar types.
Because one category can serve as the cause for producing fruits of five categories, the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is established in addition to the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As the Sūtra states:

"If the karma performed is wholesome yet contaminated (*sāsrava*) and is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), one will experience its various maturations (*vipāka*) upon being born in that realm."
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"All intentional karmas that have been performed and accumulated will certainly bring about maturation (vipāka).
Such instances as these are precisely the causes of maturation (vipāka-hetu).
All unwholesome and wholesome-outflowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena are established as this cause because they produce dissimilar results.

Thus, the Buddha has taught these six causes in various places; those who harbor aversion and turn their backs on the Dharma fail to see them due to delusion, whereas those possessed of wisdom should strive to discern them clearly.

Furthermore, in various sūtras, the Blessed One has taught the meaning of simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and antecedent causes (*pūrvaja-hetu*), stating: "Depending on this, that exists; because this arises, that arises."
One should understand that, in sequence, there are two meanings of "cause.
Furthermore, the Blessed One clearly and explicitly taught these two meanings of cause within the sūtras.
As the sūtra states:
Those who are dull-witted and abide in ignorance also perform meritorious formations due to that very ignorance.
This sūtra thus demonstrates the existence of causes from previous lives.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
With the eye and visible forms as conditions—and so on, in detail, up to the mind and mental phenomena as conditions—there arises a defiled attention born of delusion.
Herein, "mind" refers to delusion, which is ignorance; "seeking" refers to craving; and the "manifestation of craving" refers to karma.
This sūtra clearly demonstrates the existence of co-arising causes (*sahaja-hetu*), because it states that within a single moment of mind there are [dharmas] that serve as causes for one another.
It cannot be claimed that this sūtra speaks in terms of a continuous stream (*saṃtāna*), for such an interpretation is logically untenable.
To maintain that things arising from the same cause do not co-arise is a profound delusion.
This point is extensively analyzed in the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, and should be understood as it truly is.
Having briefly presented the causes, they shall now be explained in detail.
First, what are the characteristics of the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause)?
The verse says:
Excluding itself, all other factors are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The treatise says:
This efficient cause is briefly of two kinds: first, that which possesses the power to produce; second, that which merely does not obstruct.

When any phenomena arise, with the exception of their own self-nature, all phenomena serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because at the time of their arising they do not act as obstructions; among these, some possess the power to produce [the effect].

Furthermore, for instance, when a single visual consciousness arises, it takes the eye as its basis as the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*); it takes the perceived form as the establishing cause (*pratisthā-hetu*); it takes the visual consciousness and so forth, acting like seeds, as the non-interruption cause (*anuccheda-hetu*); it takes associated phenomena as the sustaining cause (*parigraha-hetu*); it takes co-existent phenomena as the auxiliary companion cause (*sahāya-hetu*); and it takes the ear faculty and so forth as the causal basis for its abiding (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*).
These are collectively designated as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Among them, one portion is called the "powerful cause" because it possesses the superior capacity to produce [the result];
the remaining portions are called "powerless causes" because they merely abide without constituting an obstacle.
The cause that is itself the producer is called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because this cause possesses the power to produce the effect.

Although the natures of other causes are also efficient causes, the term "efficient cause" has no further distinct designation, just as the general term for the sense-bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth serves as their specific name.
Alternatively, this cause can fulfill two functions: it may be called a "cause" because it does not obstruct;
it may be called a "non-cause" because it does not produce [the result] itself.
Furthermore, as for that which acts as a "capable agent," it refers to other direct causes; this [condition], by assisting them, is termed the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Alternatively, this [cause] enables another to perform an action, and that other is the result.
The cause that performs this enabling is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
For what reason is a thing's own self not its own efficient cause?
Because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) does not exist with respect to its own self-nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, the meaning of non-obstruction is the efficient cause; yet, a thing itself is always an obstruction to itself.
Furthermore, all phenomena do not depend upon their own self-nature, for otherwise there would be the consequence that they would constantly undergo production, destruction, and so forth.
If it were so, it would contradict the nature of manifest phenomena.
When one dharma arises, other dharmas that are contrary to it remain unimpeded; therefore, they can serve as causes.

It is not the case that these [dharmas] act as causes for this [dharma] at some times and not at others; rather, it should accord with correct reasoning that all dharmas are capable of acting as causes.
All phenomena possess the power of obstruction when compared to one another, yet they do not actually obstruct; thus, they can function as causes.
This is because if one is present in a given location, the others must necessarily be absent.
Even formless phenomena possess this power of obstruction, for their timing, bases, and so forth are fixed; therefore, they too possess the power of obstruction when compared to one another.
Furthermore, when one dharma arises among all dharmas—as in the case of a dharma associated with desire—none of the others present any obstruction.
A dharma cannot arise due to two conditions: first, the absence of favorable causes; second, the presence of adverse conditions.
When all phenomena arise, they necessarily depend on specific dominant causes and conditions, as well as the presence of other non-obstructing factors.

Because phenomena arise only when the dominant conditions exist—meaning the productive causes are present and obstructive causes are absent—it is said that all phenomena are "efficient causes" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) solely by virtue of their non-obstruction; it does not mean that they possess an obstructive power yet fail to obstruct.

Regarding that which possesses the power of non-obstruction yet does not act as an obstruction: there is a slight distinction in its state of non-obstruction; however, it is identical in possessing the power of non-obstruction, as it lacks any superior functional efficacy.

By this principle, phenomena do not arise instantaneously; they are not like an agent who simultaneously incurs all karmic actions such as killing, because [actions] arise dependent on superior functions, conditions, causes, and so forth.

It is precisely by this principle that past phenomena serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the other two time periods, while those phenomena of the two periods in turn become the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of the past.

Future dharmas serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the other two time periods; however, because those dharmas of the two periods are neither simultaneous with nor subsequent to them, they do not constitute the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of future dharmas.

Since a fruit must be apprehended by means of a cause, there are only two types of causes; however, because they are permitted to function as non-obstructing conditions (*anantarāya-hetu*) in all three time periods, they are said to extend across all three.
Present phenomena act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for phenomena of the other two periods, while among those two periods, only future phenomena serve as the fruit of present phenomena.
When conditioned phenomena are considered in relation to other conditioned phenomena, they stand to one another as cause and effect.
When conditioned phenomena are considered in relation to the unconditioned, the former is not the cause of the latter, nor is the latter the effect of the former.
When unconditioned phenomena are considered in relation to other unconditioned phenomena, they do not stand to one another as cause and effect.
When comparing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the former is the cause and the latter is not the fruit.

For this reason, it is said that the fruit is few while the causes are many; because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) pervades all phenomena, whereas its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is exclusively conditioned.
*Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Three: Distinguishing the Differences, Part Five. Having already explained the characteristics of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), what are the characteristics of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)?
The verse says:
Those dharmas that exist together and share a single fruit, such as the great characteristics and the characterized,
the mind and its mental concomitants, and so forth.
The treatise states:
If conditioned phenomena attain the same single fruit, they may be said to be co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), because by virtue of assisting one another’s power, they attain that single fruit.
What is their characteristic?
It is like the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which, when considered in relation to one another, act as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Although there may be cases where the substance increases or does not increase, they all function as mutual causes in groups of three or one; for a self-substance should not depend upon itself, nor should it depend upon a substance of its own kind.

Each individual great element depends solely upon the other three; it is only when the four great elements aggregate as different types that they possess the capacity to produce derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

Likewise, regarding the relationship between these characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized phenomena (*lakṣya*), as well as between the mind (*citta*) and its concomitants (*cittānuparivartin*), the phrase "also mutually acting as causes" and so forth is intended to clarify that both the mental concomitants and the various characteristics also act as mutual causes for one another.
This would mean that the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), by virtue of producing a single fruit, universally encompasses all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) as appropriate.
However, in the root treatise, it has never been stated that matter which follows the mind (cittānuvartin-rūpa) serves as a cause for the mind.
One should now discern the intention of the author of this treatise.

As I perceive the intention of that treatise: if a phenomenon necessarily arises simultaneously with the mind, pervades all states of mind, and functions in dependence upon the mind, then that phenomenon and its supporting mind are said to be mutually simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to one another.
The various mental factors (caitta-dharma) do not necessarily arise together, for they are observed to appear either in fewer or more numbers.
Furthermore, bodily and vocal actions are not present in all states of mind, because they are entirely absent in states of non-concentrated mind.

The characteristics such as arising and so forth all evolve in dependence upon the mind; they do not depend upon one another. With the dharma as the primary factor, arising, abiding, change, and cessation mutually support one another.
For this reason, it is not said that they serve as causes for one another.

Furthermore, within this context, it is intended to demonstrate that only those of different categories are stated to be simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), whereas it is established by implication that those of the same category are mutual causes without being explicitly mentioned.

Moreover, it is to show that there are bodily and vocal actions which depend solely upon the mind and not upon manifest action (*vijñapti*), and for this reason, it is not stated that they serve as causes for the mind.
Furthermore, the intention of that Great Virtuous One is difficult to discern; those who possess wisdom should investigate it further.
However, within this context, some hold the following view:

"Mind alone is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) of matter, but matter is not [the cause] of mind, because it evolves in dependence upon the mind. This is according to the principle of a king and his minister: the superior does not depend on the inferior."
This analogy is not tenable, because they also support one another.
What is the nature of the dharmas that follow the mind?
The verse says:
The two types of discipline that are mental concomitants, as well as their [respective] characteristics and those of the mind itself—
these are the dharmas that follow the mind.
The commentary says:

All mental factors, the two types of restraint—meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*)—as well as the characteristics such as arising and so forth of those phenomena and the mind itself, are all called "phenomena that follow the mind" (*cittānuvartin*).
For what reason are the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) of the mind not dharmas that follow the mind?
Because the secondary characteristics are not simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu) with respect to the mind.
For what reason are the secondary characteristics of the mind not simultaneous causes of the mind?

Because the mind cannot arise by the power of those [factors], because they possess efficacy with respect to a single dharma, because they do not share the same fruit as the mind-king (*cittarāja*), and because the majority within the aggregate is not their fruit.
If that is so, how can the mind serve as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for those [mental factors]?
It is because, by following the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), they—such as arising (*jāti*) and the rest—come into operation.

Should it not be the case that, just as with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their arising, the mind also takes them as its co-existent causes? That is to say, just as derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is not the effect of arising and the rest, yet arising and the rest are not non-co-existent causes for the primary elements, this [case] should be understood in the same way.
The reasoning in these examples is not uniform; for [the elements] produce both single and multiple results, yet [the derived matter] is not among those results.
Since derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is not subsumed under any single result within the mutual results produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), how could it be contained therein?
Because they are not produced as effects such as arising from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), citing this as an analogy constitutes a fallacy.
Furthermore, it is as previously stated.
What was stated previously?
Because the mind does not arise by the power of those [great elements],
yet the great elements and the characteristics such as arising produce one another through mutual force, there is no such fault.
For what reason is this dharma called "conforming to the mind" (*cittānuvartin*)?
The verse says:
"By way of time, fruit, virtue, and so forth.
The commentary says:
Briefly stated, it is called "conforming to the mind" (*cittānuvartin*) due to ten conditions, such as time and fruit, and so forth.
First, regarding time: this means that it arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the mind, and belongs to the same temporal period.
"By way of result, etc. means that this [mental factor] shares the same result, outflow, and maturation as the mind.
"By way of being wholesome, etc. means that this shares the same nature—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—as the mind.
Is it not the case that by merely stating that a single lifetime abides and ceases, one already knows it likewise falls within a single world-age (*kalpa*)?
Although one thus knows it falls within a single world-age, one has still not yet fully understood that this phenomenon and the mind are likewise inseparable throughout the past and the future.
Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that all dharmas are non-arising that it further states they "fall within a single time period.
If this were so, one need only say they "fall within a single time period"; otherwise, one would not cause it to be known that they definitely fall within a single time period.

Is it not the case that both the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) are also subsumed under the category of "one fruit"? How then can one speak of an outflowing or ripening fruit as being outside of "one fruit"?
Indeed, this is so; however, the term "one fruit" used here refers exclusively to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Is it not the case that because this statement is general, it also includes results of equal outflow (*niṣyanda*) and results of maturation (*vipāka*)?
Although they are said to be included, they are not what is being elucidated here.
Nevertheless, there are generally four kinds of results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*):
There are four types: (1) co-nascent, (2) immediate, (3) separated, and (4) non-arising.

This demonstrates that there are fruits that do not coexist with their causes, in order to refute the exclusive adherence to the view that the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) exists only within a composite aggregate that arises simultaneously with its cause, for in such an aggregate, the members mutually serve as each other's fruits.
Since it is not its own substantial fruit (*svabhāva-phala*) or its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), this demonstrates that it is not co-arising or conjoined with it.
Within the fruit of human effort, there is the sense of being a single fruit; therefore, the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) are mentioned separately.
It should be understood that within this context, although "one time" and "one fruit" are mentioned, their meanings differ from those of "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*) and "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).

Herein, the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), at its very minimum, acts as a simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for fifty-eight factors. These are: the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), their forty primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*), and the eight primary and secondary characteristics of the mind itself; these are termed the fifty-eight factors.
Among the fifty-eight [factors], excluding the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of mind, the remaining fifty-four serve as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind.
Other masters say:

"Within the fifty-eight, only fourteen factors can act as causes for the mind—namely, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) together with the four primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*) of the mind. It is not the case that the characteristics such as 'arising' (*jāti*) of the mental concomitants have the power to act as causes for the mind in the same way that the primary characteristics of the mind do."
If that were so, it would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
As that treatise states:

"There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but does not act as a cause for the view of a self-identity—excluding the future view of a self-identity and the factors associated with it, namely their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence."

Regarding other defiled truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are those that have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause and also serve as the cause for the view of a self-identity; these are the factors excluded [from the aforementioned categories].
They say this: "We do not recite [the scriptures], for one must first analyze the treatises according to their underlying principles and meanings before they can be properly recited and upheld."
Otherwise, the definition of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) would be undermined;
or else, one would have to admit that even the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are co-existent causes of the mind.
Furthermore, some say:

All members of a simultaneous assemblage are mutually *sahabhū-hetu* (coexistent causes) for one another, because within such an assemblage, if even one element is missing, the remaining phenomena will not arise.
Among these various explanations, the first is the best, because the primary characteristic (mūla-lakṣaṇa) and its associated phenomenon possess equal power.

Furthermore, within this co-arising assemblage of harmonious factors, there is that which is the "active agent" (pravartaka) rather than the "concomitant" (anuvartaka), namely, the mind-king (citta-rāja) itself.
Some are merely concomitants, namely matter (*rūpa*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Some are both movers and concomitants; namely, the mental factors (*caitta*), because they turn according to the mind and because they move the formations dissociated from mind.
There are two cases where neither applies, namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Having already explained the characteristics of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
what are the characteristics of the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) consists of those that are similar; they belong to their own category (nikāya) and level (bhūmi), and are previously arisen.
The Path (mārga) operates across the nine levels, taking only its equals or superiors as its fruit.
The same applies to those produced through application (*prayoga*), such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*).
The treatise states:
"That which can nourish and produce various outflowing fruits (*niṣyandaphala*), whether distant or proximate, is called a similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*)."
It should be understood that this cause consists solely of similar dharmas, and not of dissimilar types.
For example, the five wholesome aggregates act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) in relation to one another; it should be known that the same applies to defiled and neutral [aggregates].
Other masters say:
"The five pure-neutral aggregates are the fruits of form, but four are not the causes of form, because their nature is inferior.
Other masters say:
The five [aggregates] are the four fruits, while matter is not a cause for the four, because its power is inferior.
Other masters say:
matter and the four aggregates do not act as causes for one another in mutual relation, because they are inferior and belong to different categories.
If explained according to their stages, other masters say:

the *kalala* stage can act as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for ten stages; each of the nine stages beginning with the *arbuda* acts as a cause for the subsequent stages while excluding its own preceding stage; thus, for the later stages in relation to the earlier ones, there exists only the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If that were so, the blue color of the *kalala* at its initial stage would have no cause, and the color of old age at the final stage would have no effect; therefore, this reasoning is incorrect.
Furthermore, other masters say:
each of the ten stages of the preceding birth serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the corresponding color of each of the ten stages of the subsequent birth.
Following this principle, all external factors should be explained accordingly within their own respective categories.
Are all similar things capable of being designated as "homogeneous causes" (*sabhāga-hetu*) with respect to similar phenomena?

Not so. Why? Because [a dharma] of its own category and its own stage acts as a cause only for those of its own category and its own stage; therefore, it is said to be "of its own category and its own stage."
"Category" refers to the five categories, namely: those to be abandoned by seeing suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.
"Level" refers to the nine levels, namely: the desire realm as one, and the eight consisting of the dhyānas and the formless realms.

Among these, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.

This continues in the same manner until that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm serves as a cause for that which is abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
As it was stated regarding the five categories of afflictions to be abandoned in the desire realm, so it should be stated accordingly for each of the four stages of the form and formless realms.
Does this apply to all [stages]?

Not so; "arising earlier" means that only those dharmas that have already arisen and are similar to subsequent dharmas—whether those subsequent ones have already arisen or are yet to arise—act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*). This is called the complete definition of a homogeneous cause.

To claim that only the preceding birth is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the subsequent birth is deficient in meaning, as it fails to state that it is also the homogeneous cause of what has not yet arisen.
Likewise, to claim only that the past is the homogeneous cause of the future and present is also deficient in meaning, because it does not state that the past possesses both cause and effect.
Why is there no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future?
Because it lacks the sense of sequential priority and posteriority.

Is it not the case that when dharmas are in the process of arising, they have already been able to eliminate all obstacles; thus, in relation to those yet to arise, could they not be said to be prior?

Furthermore, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) should also not exist in the future, because the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) cannot be simultaneous with or prior to its retributive cause; it is only by depending on a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established.
It is not at the time of its actual arising, for it has already transcended the subsequent stage and lacks functional activity, just like other future dharmas.

The past exists only prior [to the present], the future only posterior [to the present], and the present extends across both prior and posterior, because these are fixed according to the [three] time periods.

Although all past dharmas are prior, their sequence is already established at the time they take up their fruit; however, for future dharmas, there is no distinct functional activity at the moment of their actual arising that would allow one to establish a sequence of priority and posteriority.
It is only upon reaching the present stage of having already arisen that the future is excluded so as to constitute the subsequent state, because its own activity takes that [future] as its fruit.
If this is so, then let it be that the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) likewise does not exist in the future; otherwise, these two would not be of the same category.

Why is this so? Because this homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) and its resultant flow (niṣyanda-phala) are indistinguishable in terms of being wholesome and so forth; if there were no sequence of priority and posteriority, they would have to serve as causes for one another, and since they would be mutual causes, they would likewise have to be mutual results.
For two things to be mutually cause and effect contradicts reason.

Since there is no principle that can preclude their being mutually effects, one would have to admit that an effect exists prior to its cause, and furthermore, that two minds could stand in a relationship of mutual causality; this would then contradict and undermine the texts of the *Jñānaprasthāna* and other such works.
Because that retributive cause differs in character from its fruit, there is no fault of it existing before or after [the fruit], even though they are separated in time.
Therefore, the homogeneous cause is established according to its stage; it does not exist in the future.
If the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is established according to its characteristics, it does not fail to exist in the future.

As for the statement that the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) belongs only to its own level (*svabhūmi*), on what basis is this definitively stated? It is definitively stated based on the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [dharmas].

If the untainted paths are considered in relation to one another, each serves as a cause for all nine stages; that is to say, the four dhyānas, the three formless attainments, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara) are called the nine stages.
The remaining states lacking meditative absorption (asamāhita) cannot give rise to the untainted noble path because they are not intense.
As for the nine untainted stages being mutual causes for one another, it is because they are not bound to specific levels (aniyata-bhūmi).
The craving for each respective stage does not grasp the Noble Path as its own, because it is not of the same category [as the Path].
Although stages that differ from one another may serve as causes for each other, this is not the case for all of them.
Why is this? Because they arise from application (*prayoga*) and serve as causes only for those that are equal or superior.

The noble path of the first dhyāna may have its basis in the first dhyāna, up to and including having its basis in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); it should be understood that the same applies to the paths of the second dhyāna and so forth.
Regarding those based on their own level or higher levels, there is [causality]; regarding those based on lower levels, there is none.
That is to say, the noble path based on the first dhyāna serves as a homogeneous cause for the noble paths based on all nine dhyānas and nine stages.

That is to say, this [noble path] based on the first dhyāna functions solely as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for paths based on the first dhyāna, but does not function as a cause for paths based on higher [dhyānas], because its nature is inferior.
A noble path based on the second dhyāna—or the first dhyāna—functions as a homogeneous cause for noble paths based on the remaining nine stages, excluding those based on the first dhyāna itself.

That is to say, this [noble path] based on the first two dhyānas acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) only for the noble paths of the nine stages; it does not act as such for those based on higher stages.

A noble path based on the third dhyāna or the first dhyāna acts as a homogeneous cause for the noble paths of the nine stages, excluding those based on the first two [dhyānas], and including those based on the other dhyānas.
That is to say, this [path] takes only the noble paths based on the first, second, third, and ninth stages as its homogeneous cause, not those based on higher stages.

Furthermore, if it is based on the noble path of the first dhyāna within the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), it serves as a homogeneous cause only for the noble paths based on the nine stages within that same sphere of nothingness.
Thus, these universal [paths] take the noble paths of the nine stages as their homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) based on the concentrations of the nine stages.
