For example, just as the noble path of the first concentration takes the noble paths of the other concentrations as its basis, so too should one extensively analyze each case accordingly for the noble paths based on the remaining eight concentrations throughout the nine stages.

Furthermore, while the various paths of no-outflow (anāsrava-mārga) subsumed within a single stage (*bhūmi*) do not all serve as causes for one another, they do so as causes that are equal or superior, rather than inferior.

For example, a previously arisen receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for a future receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering; this is what is meant by "equal."

Furthermore, this very patience (*kṣānti*) can also serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for subsequent states, from the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);

thus it is called "superior. To speak more extensively, up to the already-arisen various knowledges of non-arising, they serve only as homogeneous causes for their own equal class, as there is nothing superior to them.

Furthermore, the various paths that have already arisen—the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning—act as homogeneous causes for three, two, and one [subsequent paths] respectively; it is also not contrary to reason that they serve as causes for one another in succession.

It is not the case that a superior path and an inferior one serve as causes for each other; rather, a previously arisen path of cultivation belonging to the dull-facultied lineage within one's own continuum serves as the homogeneous cause for a future path of seeing belonging to the sharp-facultied lineage that will certainly not arise.
What principle constitutes an obstacle?
It is because all sentient beings have distinct continuums, and by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), six types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*) are established.
One should know that the same applies when considering those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) in relation to those preceding them.

However, there is a distinction: namely, that a previously arisen path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) within one's own continuum can serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for a subsequently arisen path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because it is possible for one who has fallen away from the state of no-more-learning to subsequently develop sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) within the path of cultivation.

However, this does not contradict what is taught in the *Indriya-skandha*, for it is spoken with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of referring to faculties that belong to the same category.
Furthermore, it is spoken in reference to faculties that are currently manifest and functional, just as when one speaks of the "presently manifest" state of the *agradharma*.

If that were so, then since the mental continuums of all sentient beings are naturally established for the enlightenment of the three vehicles, an inferior [vehicle] would also have to serve as the causal nature for a superior vehicle.

This is not the case, because the past nature is extremely remote; because an inferior vehicle cannot be transformed into a superior one; because the two types of noble paths—those of the follower by faith and the follower by dharma—are proximate in their essential characteristics; because their basis is one; and because even if one emerges from contemplation during the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), transformation is still possible.
The noble paths of the three vehicles do not possess such a characteristic.
For this reason it is said that the path of those with dull faculties serves as a homogeneous cause for both the dull and the sharp.

However, the path of those with sharp faculties is a cause only for the sharp. For example, the paths of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), and those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) serve, respectively, as homogeneous causes for six, four, and two types of paths in their respective order.

If one follows the path of practice according to the Dharma (dharmānusārin), the path of attainment through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or the path of untimely liberation (asamayavimukta), they serve as similar causes (sabhāgahetu) for three, two, and one [subsequent paths] respectively, in that order.
This should also be understood, as before, to be non-universal.
If the paths of higher stages serve as causes for lower stages, how can they be described as being "equal" or "superior"?
This is due to the increase of the cause and due to the faculties (*indriya*).
Is it the case that only the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for what is equal or superior?
It is not so. Why? Other mundane dharmas produced through application (*prayoga*) likewise serve as causes for those that are equal or superior, but not for those that are inferior.
What is the nature of the dharmas produced by application (*prayoga*)?
It refers to those produced through hearing (*śruta-maya*), reflection (*cintā-maya*), and so forth.

The term "and so forth" includes those produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). These are called "produced from those" because they are qualities generated by hearing, reflection, and cultivation; since they are produced through application, they serve as causes only for that which is equal or superior, not for that which is inferior.

For example, dharmas consisting of hearing-accomplished wisdom (śrutamaya) bound to the desire realm can serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) for dharmas consisting of hearing-accomplished and reflection-accomplished wisdom (cintāmaya) within their own realm, but they cannot serve as causes for those consisting of cultivation-accomplished wisdom (bhāvanāmaya), because such [cultivation-accomplished wisdom] does not exist in the desire realm.

Dharmas produced through reflection (*cintā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those produced through reflection, but not for those produced through hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior.

If dharmas produced through hearing belonging to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are able to serve as homogeneous causes for those produced through hearing and cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) within their own realm, they do not serve as causes for those produced through reflection, because such [dharmas] do not exist in the realm of form.

Dharmas produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) only for dharmas produced by cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior.

Dharmas produced by cultivation pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) serve as homogeneous causes only for dharmas produced by cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced by hearing or reflection (*cintā-maya*), because such [dharmas] do not exist there and because [those produced by hearing and reflection] are inferior.
These dharmas produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation each have nine grades, namely the lowest-of-the-low and so forth.

If the lowest-of-the-low grade serves as the cause for all nine grades, the lowest-middle grade serves as the cause for eight, and so on, until the highest-of-the-high grade serves as the cause for only the highest-of-the-high grade, because the preceding inferior grades are excluded.

Wholesome dharmas acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for wholesome dharmas produced through effort (*prāyogika*), but wholesome dharmas produced through effort do not serve as causes for those acquired at birth, because the latter are inferior.

Furthermore, wholesome dharmas acquired at birth are also of nine grades; they all stand in a reciprocal relationship as causes for one another, because it is possible for each of them to manifest subsequently, and because all of them can be attained within a single moment of mind.
However, because there are nine grades of manifesting maturation (*vipāka*), one may establish nine distinct grades; the nine grades of affliction (*kliṣṭa*) should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, this is due to the existence of nine grades of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

The unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are of four types: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those associated with the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika*). These, respectively, can serve as causes for four, three, two, and one [subsequent states].
Some say: "All [factors] are mutually causes for one another because they share the same bondage.
This statement is unreasonable, lest it follow that factors such as *ūṣman* (heat) and so forth would also be mutual causes for one another.

Furthermore, the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the desire realm has four dhyānas as its fruits; it does not have a higher dhyāna as its fruit nor a lower dhyāna as its cause. Nor is it obtained through the cause of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), lest one’s exertion be rendered fruitless.
The characteristics and categories of the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) are indeed numerous; they should be determined according to one's capacity as in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Having already explained the characteristics of the similar cause, what are the characteristics of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The associated cause is determined by the fact that minds and mental factors share the same basis.
The commentary says:

Only mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). One might object: "Since there is no qualification here, would it not follow that even those differing in time, object, or aspect are associated?

Furthermore, if one were to add the qualification that these three [time, object, and aspect] must be identical, then individuals of different bodies looking at the same thing simultaneously should be said to be associated. Therefore, it is stated that they must have a common basis (*sāśraya*); this universally refutes such objections. That is to say, only those mental factors and minds that share a common basis can mutually serve as associated causes for one another.

In this context, the term "same" indicates that the basis is one. That is to say, if a visual consciousness takes the eye-faculty of this particular moment as its basis, the associated factors such as sensation (vedanā) likewise take that same eye-faculty as their basis. It should be understood that this applies similarly up to the mental consciousness and its associated factors, which share the same basis in the mind-faculty (manas).

Now, one should reflect upon this: since the nature of the bases for the faculties such as the eye and ear is the same, for what reason is it said that the consciousnesses which depend upon them have distinct bases?
Why trouble yourself with this question? Although the nature of the bases for the various consciousnesses is the same, they are categorized as distinct types.

If that is so, why do we know that the expression "sharing a common basis" refers only to the sense of a simultaneous momentary basis—stating that visual consciousness and the like share a single basis—and does not refer to the sense of a long-term generic basis—stating that all instances of visual consciousness share a single basis?
Furthermore, because they are of the same kind and share an immediate basis, the visual consciousness and others should also be considered associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Therefore, the verse should be qualified as follows: "mind and mental factors that are simultaneous and share the same basis."
Therefore, that commentary itself subsumes two meanings, stating: "If visual consciousness takes this momentary eye-faculty as its support," and so forth at length.
Since the verse lacks the term "simultaneous," how can it be known that these "shared supports" do not refer to a single type [of faculty] existing in a single moment?

If you argue that there is no fault because it is subsumed within the commentary, then the composed verse should not have mentioned "same basis" (*sāśraya*), but should instead have stated only that the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) consists definitively of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Furthermore, the term "associated" (*samprayukta*) is sufficient to exclude all such objections; for association cannot exist between things that differ in time or basis.
What is the distinction between the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)?

Briefly stated, while all phenomena that are associated causes are also co-existent causes, there are co-existent causes that are not associated causes; these refer to the derivative matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*) and the various formations (*saṃskāra*) such as arising (*jāti*).
If the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) were identical to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), what would be the distinction between the meanings of these two causes?
It is not the case that the associated cause is identical to the co-existent cause, because the meanings of these two causes differ from one another.

However, a single dharma is both an associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). As for the distinction in their meanings: the sense of being inseparable is the associated cause, while the sense of having a common fruit is the co-existent cause.

Furthermore, those factors that arise and abide simultaneously through mutual power constitute the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); if they mutually take a single object through mutual power, they constitute the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
The co-existent cause is established by virtue of being mutual effects, while the associated cause is established by virtue of the fivefold equality.
Since one of these must be absent while the others cannot, it is therefore fully established that they function as mutual causes.
Having already explained the characteristics of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), what are the characteristics of the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)?
The verse says:
"Universal [factors] refer to those previously mentioned as universal; they are the causes for defilement within their own stage.
The commentary says:

Regarding the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu): it refers to previously arisen universal proclivities (anuśaya) and their associated factors, which serve as the universal cause for all subsequent defiled phenomena within the same stage, whether belonging to their own category or other categories.
What are the factors termed "pervasive" (sarvatraga)?
These shall be analyzed in detail in the Chapter on Latent Dispositions (anuśaya).
They are established separately because their causal power operates beyond the scope of the power of homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu).
It is also the cause for the defiled dharmas of other categories, because by its power, the afflictions and their attendants of other categories are likewise produced and grow.
Among the afflictions comprised within its own category, what is the distinction between the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)?
From the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), various forms of craving arise; likewise, various forms of craving can also give rise to the view of a self-identity.
How are the distinct characteristics of these two to be known?

There is also a distinction between their two respective causes: because of the grasping at a self, it causes various forms of craving to arise, become firm, expand, and intensify, since the view of a self universally takes the objects of craving as its domain.

Attachment causes the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) to arise with firmness, yet it cannot cause it to increase, intensify, or become pervasive, because attachment does not take the object of the view of self as its universal objective range.

Since all pervasive afflictions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) are mutually capable of taking each other’s objects as their universal objective ranges, each individual pervasive affliction can cause the others to arise with firmness, increase, and intensity. Therefore, these two causes are not without distinction.
What is the difference between the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), both of which can produce results of the same category at one time?

Although they simultaneously take two types of outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*), the results of their own category are more abundant than those of others; because they are nurtured through the gateway of these two causes, they produce only their own category.
What is the distinction between these two causes?

The universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) produces only its own category; that is to say, when a universal dharma is present, it simultaneously possesses the power to take on results from all five categories. Within the results of its own category, there is also a distinction: their arising is firm due to the power of the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), while their expansion and intensification are due to the power of the universal cause.

It should be understood that the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the past and present act as causes for the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), can take the five categories as their objects, and are also augmented by the five categories.

Regarding their associated dharmas, with the exception of those factors that increase through augmentation and further excluding those that take the five categories as their objects, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those various dharmas do not have pervasive causes.

Due to temporal sequence, the remoteness of their nature, or the fact that they do not share a single fruit, there are pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are not pervasive causes (*sarvatragahetu*), and so forth; the detailed determination of these matters is as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The characteristics of the universal cause have already been explained.
What are the characteristics of the ripening cause?
The verse says:
The ripening cause consists of the unwholesome and the wholesome that is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The treatise says:
Only those dharmas that are unwholesome and those wholesome dharmas that are with outflows are ripening causes, because they are dharmas subject to maturation (*vipāka-dharma*).
Because this cause can, according to its respective nature, produce a ripened result (*vipāka-phala*), it is called the "ripened cause" (*vipāka-hetu*).
In the verse, the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that although this cause and its result differ in their essential nature and characteristics, they are not confused in their categories.
The word "only" (eva) serves to exclude the nature of the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) while including the meaning of all other causes. Some say:
"If all fruits were called 'ripening' (vipāka), then their ripening causes would also have to be included universally."
Fearing that [others] might hold such a view, he therefore uses the word "only" (*kevala*).
For what reason is it definitively known that only unwholesome dharmas and wholesome *sāsrava* (contaminated) dharmas are causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*)?
Because it is so stated in the Sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"There is karma that is black with black ripening; there is karma that is white with white ripening; there is karma that is black-and-white with black-and-white ripening; and there is karma that is neither black nor white, which has no ripening and can exhaust all karmas."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"We clearly perceive that one experiences agreeable maturation or experiences wailing and lamentation as maturation, due to wholesome or unwholesome [actions].
It further says:
I encounter harm to my bodily karma and so forth; that is to say, when painful feelings arise, one experiences the ripening of suffering.
Again, it is said:
I encounter benefit to my bodily karma and so forth; that is to say, when pleasant feelings arise, one experiences the ripening of pleasure.
There are many such proofs of this kind.
For what reason do untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas not produce maturation (*vipāka*)?
Because they lack the moisture of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), just as a genuine seed does not germinate without the nourishment of water.
Furthermore, since uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not bound to any level (*bhūmi*), how can they produce a retributive result (*vipāka*) that is bound to a level?
For what reason do neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas not produce a retributive result?
Because their power is weak, like a rotten seed.
Other wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] are capable of summoning maturation (*vipāka*), just as water moistens various firm and genuine seeds.
This cause of maturation is generally said to be twofold:
first, that which can project (*ākṣepaka*); second, that which can fulfill (*paripūraka*).
Furthermore, the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) cannot be projected by the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) alone.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Karma is the cause of birth."
Birth consists of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), because other factors such as matter and mind are not necessarily universal.

Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states that all life-faculties are the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma; since they are not themselves karma, the two types of karma—body and speech—which follow the mind, cannot also project the life-faculty and the homogeneous character.
The Sūtra states:
"The inferior realm is induced by volitional karma.

One should understand that the "inferior realm" refers to the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*); this explains that the life-force and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the existence of desire are induced solely by mental karma, and not by bodily or vocal karma.

The informative acts of body and speech consist of many atoms; however, that which is produced by a single moment of mind can alone project the life-force and the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga), for it is illogical to suppose that others possess this capacity.
If it were admitted that they simultaneously produce a single fruit together, they would necessarily be mutual simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.
However, that resistant derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is a simultaneous cause is not what is accepted in our school, because this [matter] is not produced by the power of mutual interaction.
Nor do individual atoms sequentially project the life-faculty and the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga), because they arise from a single mind.
Since they do not arise from a single mind, there is no fault in their having distinct functional capacities to separately project and produce subsequent states.
This fault applies equally to the case of completing karma (*paripūri-karman*), because within a single lifetime, each [moment] is individually capable of bringing about a complete result.

This same explanation applies to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) as well; since the substance of multiple abstentions (*virati*) arises from a single mind, they are not admitted to be simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.
The Sūtra states:
"If one cultivates, practices, or frequently practices the taking of life, one will be reborn in hell.
The Śāstra states:

The statement that "the evil karma of lying to cause a schism in the Sangha results in a lifespan of one kalpa in the Avīci Hell" cites the result in order to reveal the motivating volition (*cetanā*); this is because the nature of volitional karma is non-material and its characteristics are difficult to perceive.

In the desire realm, there are times when a single aggregate serves as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to the acquisition of memory (*prāpti*) together with its arising and so forth.

There are also times when two aggregates serve as the ripening cause to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to wholesome or unwholesome form (*rūpa*) together with its arising and so forth.

Sometimes four aggregates function as a maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; that is to say, wholesome or unwholesome mental states and mental factors, along with their [characteristics] such as arising.
Because there is no matter (*rūpa*) that follows the mind in the desire realm, there are no five aggregates that function as a maturation cause to collectively produce a single fruit.

In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are times when a single aggregate (skandha) acts as a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) to collectively produce a single fruit; that is, the acquisition of the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and its arising, etc.

Sometimes two aggregates act as a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers, for example, to the wholesome informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) of the first dhyāna together with its birth-characteristic (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
There are no informative actions in the second dhyāna and above, because there is no capacity to initiate them.

Sometimes four aggregates act as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to wholesome mind and mental factors that lack concomitant matter, along with their [characteristics] such as arising.

Sometimes five aggregates act as the ripening cause to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to various minds and mental factors accompanied by concomitant matter, along with their [characteristics] such as arising.

In the formless realm, there are times when a single aggregate acts as a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers, for example, to the acquisition of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), that attainment itself, and its arising and so forth.
Sometimes four aggregates function as retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to all wholesome mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Thus, there are nine types of retributive causes in total, categorized according to their respective numbers in the three realms: three, four, and two kinds, respectively.
There is karma that produces maturation in only one sphere; this refers to that which produces the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
If it produces maturation in the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), it necessarily produces maturation in two spheres, namely mind and mental objects.
If one experiences the sense-field of tangibles, it should be known that there are also two [factors involved], namely tangibles and mental objects (*dharma*).
If one experiences the sense-field of forms, one necessarily experiences three sense-fields, namely form, tangibles, and mental objects.
If one experiences odors or tastes, it should be known that there are likewise three [objects]: namely, the self, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*).
If one experiences the body-base (*kāyāyatana*), one necessarily experiences four bases: namely, the body, visible forms, tangibles, and mental objects.
If one experiences the sense base of the eye, one necessarily experiences five bases, namely: the eye, the body, visible forms, tangibles, and mental objects.
It should be understood that for the ear, nose, and tongue, there are likewise five; namely, each respective organ as the first, along with the body, visible forms, tangibles, and mental objects.
There are karmas capable of producing six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven bases (*āyatana*).

Since sound is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it is not discussed here; furthermore, karma may have either few or many fruits, just as external seeds produce fruits that are either few or many.

There is karma of a single moment that has maturation over many moments, but there is no karma of many moments that has maturation in a single moment, lest the fruit be diminished relative to the effort of the cause.

There is karma of one lifetime that has maturation across three lifetimes, but there is no karma of two lifetimes that has maturation in a single lifetime; for it is the natural law of the power that induces maturation that wholesome or unwholesome causes produce neutral results.
However, the maturation fruit does not coexist with the karma, because the fruit is not experienced at the very moment the karma is created.
Furthermore, when karma is present, its fruit does not yet mature, for the principle governing the gateway of experiencing karma must necessarily be determinate.

Nor is it without interval, because it is induced by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in the subsequent moment, and because the force of a moment’s actual arising is difficult to restrain.
Furthermore, since a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) produces a fruit of a different category, it must depend upon a continuum (*saṃtati*) to be able to accomplish its effect.
The remaining details of this determination are as set forth in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Having thus explained the distinctions between the characteristics of the six causes,
what is the definition of the three time periods (*adhvan*) as stated here?
The verse says:
Universal [causes] and similar-type [causes] belong to two time periods; [the remaining three causes] belong to three time periods.
The commentary says:
The universal (sarvatraga) and similar-type (sabhāga) causes exist only in the past and present; they do not exist in the future, for the reasoning is as previously explained.
The three causes—associated (samprayukta), co-existent (sahabhū), and retributive (vipāka)—are entirely present throughout all three time periods.

Since the verse does not specify the temporal locus of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it should be understood by implication that it extends across the three time periods as well as the non-temporal; for its specific temporal division cannot be definitively stated.
Having already distinguished the characteristics and temporal determinations of the six causes, one must now establish their names in relation to their respective effects.
What is called the fruit that corresponds to a cause?
The verse says:
Fruits are conditioned phenomena and disjunction; The unconditioned has neither cause nor fruit.
The treatise says:

There are briefly five kinds of fruits, which shall be explained in detail later; for now, we shall first present them collectively as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and disconnection (*visamyoga*).
Thus, the root treatise states:
What are the phenomena that are results? They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
But surely analytical cessation must have a cause, since it is admitted to be a result; for it has never been observed that something can be called a result without having a cause.
I also grant that the Path is the cause for realization,
for the Sūtra states:
"This is the fruit of the śramaṇa."
From among these six causes, by which cause is this [attainment] obtained?
I say that this fruit is not obtained from the six causes, because the six causes previously mentioned are what depend upon for its arising.
If that is so, one must admit that this cause of attainment (*prāpti-hetu*) exists apart from the previous six causes as a seventh distinct cause.
What my school accepts is exactly as you have stated.
Is it not the case that our own tradition recites:
"Nirvāṇa is a fruit, yet it has no cause"?

Although this recitation exists, there is no loss of meaning; for it is commonly established in the world that the name "result" (*phala*) is applied to the accomplishment of a desired object through the exertion of effort.
Since death is an extreme state of decay and affliction for a person, the state of non-death is what is most desired.
Because that which is thus desired is realized through the functional power of the Path, it is called a "fruit.
To say it is "without cause" means that the Path is not any of the six causes with respect to the unconditioned state of cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) that has been attained.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not a fruit produced by the Path, but rather a fruit realized through it; the Path is not a cause that produces cessation, but rather a cause that realizes it. Therefore, as the Path and cessation stand in mutual relation, one must not dogmatically adhere to fixed notions of cause and effect or identity and difference between them.

If the Path is the cause for the attainment (*prāpti*) of cessation, then it should follow that [the attainment] alone constitutes the fruit of the Path; who says that the fruit of the Path is necessarily not the attainment of cessation?
For the Path serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the attainment of cessation, or is also said to be its co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

However, this is not the fruit sought by the noble ones, for the noble ones do not cultivate the noble path while seeking conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*). With respect to cessation (*nirodha*), the path serves as the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) for its attainment; with respect to the essence of cessation, the path serves as the realizing cause (*sākṣātkāra-hetu*).
Since it is granted that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), one must grant that they possess dominant results (*adhipati-phala*).

Because they are established as acting causes by virtue of non-obstruction, rather than by virtue of being productive, they lack dominant results. By this principle, while causes and results are established for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is not so for the unconditioned. Therefore, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is a cause without a result, and a result without a cause; the other two unconditioned phenomena are causes but not results.
The principle that there is no cause without an effect is thoroughly established.

Regarding the five effects to be discussed—namely, the matured effect (*vipākaphala*), the outflowing effect (*niṣyandaphala*), the disjunction effect (*visamyogaphala*), the virile effect (*puruṣakāraphala*), and the sovereign effect (*adhipatiphala*)—it should be stated which effect is obtained from which of the six causes.
The verse says:
The final cause has the ripening fruit; The prior cause has the dominant fruit;
The similar and pervasive causes have the outflowing fruit; The simultaneous and associated causes have the virile fruit.
The treatise states:

Among the five fruits, the third—the fruit of disjunction—is not obtained through a productive cause; therefore, it is not discussed here. For now, we shall analyze how the six causes obtain the remaining four fruits.

Regarding the "subsequent cause," this refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it is mentioned last among the verses on causes; the first ripening fruit is obtained from this cause. Some say:
since ripening arises from ripening, this [cause] should not be called "without ripening" (*avipāka*).

That statement is unreasonable, because the meanings of being produced by the two causes—homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—are distinct. That is to say, the preceding retribution acts as a homogeneous cause to produce a subsequent retribution as its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*); thus, the subsequent retribution is established by prior karma.
That which is capable of producing various karmas is called the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); that which is produced as the ripening is the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Since the two causes differ in essence and the two fruits are distinguished in meaning, there is no fault of confusion between them, as the categories of cause and effect are distinct.

However, the essence of maturation (vipāka) is like cooked food; it lacks any superior capacity for producing further maturation. Therefore, only unwholesome states and wholesome states associated with outflows (sāsrava) are called "maturation causes" (vipākahetu), and they alone are said to "possess maturation."

Regarding the "prior cause," this refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because it is mentioned first among the verses on causes; the subsequent dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is that which is obtained from this cause.
As for the term "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*): if it is merely abiding without obstruction, what kind of dominance (*adhipatya*) is there?
That which dwells without obstruction is designated as "predominant" (*adhipati*).
Furthermore, within the process of the arising and ceasing of all phenomena, there is also a mutually reinforcing predominant power.

Those of the same class (*sabhāga*) and those that are universal (*sarvatraga*), as well as acquisitions (*prāpti*), produce "concordant results" (*niṣyanda-phala*); because the result resembles its cause, it is called "concordant."
In this way, because the two causes are similar in their characteristics, although there are two causes, their result is one.

The simultaneous (sahabhū) and associated (samprayukta) causes obtain the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala). There is no separate human effort apart from the substance of the person; that which is obtained by this very [substance] is called the fruit of human effort.
What phenomenon does this term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) designate?
It designates the functional capacity inherent in all phenomena. This accords with what is stated in a subsequent verse:
"If something arises through the power of another, that fruit is called 'human effort'."
In this context, "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), "human power," "human capacity," and "human domain" are all synonymous.
Because the functional efficacy of all phenomena is like that of human effort, it is termed "human effort"; just as a brave and strong man is called a "lion" because he resembles one.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is necessarily present and superior; therefore, it is said to be "associated.

As for the fruit obtained through the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it may or may not be present without interval, and even if it were present, it would not be superior; furthermore, it would overlap with other fruits. For these reasons, it is not stated that this fruit is obtained by the other causes.
*Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine [continued] / *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

Chapter Three, Part Six: "Discrimination of Distinctions. Having already established the determination of causes and effects in their mutual relation, we shall now properly discuss the distinctions among the characteristics of the results.
What are the characteristics of the results, such as the maturation result (*vipākaphala*)?
The verse says:
The maturation result consists of neutral dharmas, which belong to sentient beings and arise from determinate karma.
The outflowing fruit resembles its own cause; disjunction results from the exhaustion [of defilements] through wisdom.
If a result arises by the power of that [cause], it is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Excluding the aforementioned [results], all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
The Treatise says:
Only within the category of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena is there a fruition result (*vipākaphala*).
If that were so, then even those things not included among sentient beings would have to be fruition results.
In order to exclude those [factors], the term "sentient beings" (sattva) is employed, because only within sentient beings does maturation (vipāka) exist.
If that were so, then among those things counted as sentient beings, nurtured (aupacayika) and outflowing (naiṣyandika) factors would also have to be considered maturation.

Furthermore, in order to distinguish this from the claim that "arising from the determinate" (*vijñapti-ja*) refers to all unwholesome states and wholesome tainted states (*sāsrava-kuśala*)—which are called "determinate" because they can determine a maturation (*vipāka*)—the term "arising from the determinate" means that the maturation arises at a later time following those [actions], rather than simultaneously or immediately thereafter. Thus it is called "arising from the determinate."
Such is what is called the characteristic of the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).

Is it not the case that maturation itself also takes the substance of a prior maturation fruit as its homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), since it is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of that prior maturation? If so, one should also say that it arises from the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is of the nature of an outflow; why then do you say that it arises from the determinate (*vyākṛta*) and is not of the nature of an outflow?

There is no such fault; for while the substance of the maturation fruit is confused by the characteristics of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is not confused by the characteristics of the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*). Therefore, it is said that [the maturation fruit] arises only from the determinate (*vyākṛta*).
From this, it should be understood by analogy that [unconditioned phenomena] are not of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), because an outflow fruit resembles its cause and thus involves confusion;
whereas a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is distinct from its cause and thus free from confusion. Why, then, are non-sentient things not ripening fruits?
Because it is obtained through collective karma and is collectively enjoyed;
the abode of Mahābrahmā is produced by the collective karma of all the Mahābrahmās, as there is the principle that others may also enjoy it within that realm.
How can the karma of many sentient beings collectively produce a single non-sentient result?
There is no fault in there being a single cause of the same class (*sabhāga-hetu*) while there are many karmic conditions (*karma-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, we observe that a small amount of karma can produce many fruits; how then could a small fruit not be produced by much karma?
Regarding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it causes no obstruction whether the result is few or many.
The power of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is not like this, because its results are not shared.
Since a shared result would not constitute the meaning of "ripening" (*vipāka*), non-sentient things are not included within the ripening [cause].

A phenomenon that resembles its own cause is called a "result of outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*); this refers to those resembling the two causes of similar type (*sabhāgahetu*) and universal pervasion (*sarvatragahetu*).
Just as with the similar-type cause, the nature of the result of outflow—whether wholesome, defiled, or neutral—is such that its characteristics are likewise identical.
Just as the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is exclusively of the nature of a defiled outflow-result (niṣyanda-phala), its characteristics are likewise so.
Is it not the case that the activity-result (puruṣakāra-phala), which arises simultaneously [with its cause], also resembles its own cause?
How can it be said that a phenomenon resembling its own cause is called a "result of outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*)?

There is no result of outflow that does not resemble its own cause, whereas there are results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) that differ from their own causes; therefore, by naming that which resembles its own cause a "result of outflow," there is certainly no error of confusing it with that result of human effort.

Is it not also the case that there are outflow-homogeneous causes (niṣyanda-hetu) that have different [types of] results, such as the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) in relation to its results in a different category? Because they share the same defiled nature, they are called "similar to their own cause.
However, the nature of the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) differs from its cause.
Furthermore, regarding the cause, it means that the fruit and the cause possess two kinds of similarity:

similarity in essence (*ātman*) and similarity in nature (*svabhāva*). Essence refers to [mental factors] such as sensation (*vedanā*), while nature refers to [their moral quality] such as being wholesome (*kuśala*).

Within the case of the simultaneously arising *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort), although their natures are identical, their essences must necessarily be distinct, because two instances of sensation or the like cannot arise at the same time.

Regarding the virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) that arises subsequently, both its nature (*svabhāva*) and its substance (*dravya*) may differ [from the cause]; therefore, it cannot be said that the fruit necessarily resembles the cause.
As for the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), its nature must resemble the cause, and its substance may also resemble it; thus, it is only this fruit that is said to resemble its own cause.

However, because these two causes differ in their respective scope—one being broader and the other narrower—they are established separately; yet, since the result must necessarily resemble its own cause, they are combined into one.

Because the exhaustion of phenomena occurs through wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*); it is "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) because of cessation, and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) because of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*). Thus, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is itself designated as the fruit of dissociation.
Because one realizes this cessation by means of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) as its cause, thereby becoming free from all fetters, it is called the "fruit.
If a phenomenon is produced through the power of another, that phenomenon is said to be the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
These are of four kinds, as previously explained.
"Simultaneous" refers to phenomena that arise at the same time through the power of being mutual causes for one another.

"Immediate" refers to that which arises immediately thereafter, such as the arising of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) following the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
"Separated by an interval" refers to arising after a lapse of time, such as when farmers [reap] grain, wheat, and so forth.
"Non-arising" refers to *nirvāṇa*, because it arises through the power of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Since this [result] does not arise, how can it be spoken of? It is called the "fruit of human effort" (puruṣakāra-phala) because it arises through the power of that [effort].
We observe that the term "arising" is also applied to acquisition (*prāpti*); for example, when one says, "My wealth has arisen," the meaning is "I have acquired wealth."

If the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized by the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) involves the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it is termed both the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If the uninterrupted path does not abandon the latent dispositions, the analytical cessation realized thereby is solely the fruit of human effort and not the fruit of disjunction.

As explained throughout the various stages in the *Nyāyānusāra*, all conditioned phenomena—excluding those that have already arisen—are the dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) of other conditioned phenomena; however, there is never even the slightest fruit that arises prior to its cause.
If the fruit were to arise prior to its cause, the subsequent cause would be useless, and future phenomena would never arise at all.
What is the distinction between the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*)?
The designation "fruit of human effort" applies exclusively to the agent, whereas the designation "sovereign fruit" applies both to the agent and the recipient.
Among the six types of causes explained above, at which stage and by which cause is the fruit grasped, and at which stage is it given?
The verse says:
Five grasp the fruit only in the present; Two give the fruit in the same way.
The past and present [causes] give two causes; one gives only the past.
The Commentary says:
The five causes take their fruit only in the present; they certainly do not do so in the past, because that [fruit] has already been taken by them.
Nor is it future, because it lacks functional activity.
To say that it "takes the fruit" (phala-grahaṇa) means it has the sense of "drawing forth" (ākṣepa), namely, drawing forth the future so as to cause its arising and so on.

It acts as a seed for things of the same category; for things of different categories, by virtue of having the same result; for non-unitary results, by virtue of being of the same nature; and for things of different natures, by virtue of possessing this continuity of its own aggregate. Therefore, all such [causes] are called "drawers-forth," and this capacity to draw forth is termed "taking the fruit."
This function of grasping the fruit exists only in the present, not in the past or future; only this may be called the activity (*kāritra*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding the three causes—associated, co-existent, and retributive—it is taught that their functional capacity is termed "activity," because the fruit differs from the cause and because both [cause and fruit] exist simultaneously.
The mention of "five" serves to exclude the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
However, regarding the efficient cause that can actually produce a fruit, it must necessarily be present; whereas [the other causes] may belong to the past or the present.
This should be understood as being similar to the two causes—the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*)—yet it does not apply to all [of them].
There is also a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) that may be grasped or bestowed; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
How is it that this cause grasps its fruit only in the present?
As stated in the treatise:

Past dharmas serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) capable of producing two types of minds: namely, the mind emerging from the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). If these [past] minds were to grasp [the present] at the moment the minds entering the two attainments are present, then the two attainments would never manifest again, because the equal-and-immediate condition would be grasped simultaneously with its object.

Such a thing does not exist; rather, the mind entering the two meditative absorptions (dhyāna) can only take as its object the absorption itself and the fruit of the emerging mind at the very moment it is present.

However, because the absorption is what is being sought, it must necessarily arise first; due to this obstruction, the mind emerging from absorption does not arise immediately after the mind entering it.
According to the meaning of "yielding a fruit," it is said that two minds arise in the past; this point shall be further analyzed later.

Therefore, like the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) takes all future phenomena collectively as its own sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
However, some may say:
"This efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) takes up its fruit and gives it forth across all three time periods—past, present, and future.
This is logically untenable, because the activity of taking up the fruit exists only in the present.

The same applies to the simultaneous (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayukta*) causes regarding the giving of results; these two causes give results only in the present, because for these two causes, the taking of the result and the giving of the result must necessarily occur at the same time.
The similar-type (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) causes, however, give results throughout both the past and the present.
Regarding those factors that produce results within the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), they should be explained in the same manner.
However, since not all [causes] are capable of having a result, this is not discussed here.

As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), when their outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*) arise immediately, at the present moment, they both grasp and give forth the immediately succeeding result.
When this fruit has already arisen and the two causes have already ceased, it is called "already taken and given.

If these two causes cease and reach the past, and their resultant flow (niṣyanda-phala) only reaches the time of its arising, then these two causes first take [the fruit] at the stage of arising and now give it.
Regarding "giving fruit": this refers to these various causes directly providing the power for that [effect] to arise and so forth;

it is when the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is currently present that its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) has already arisen in the present, such as the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) giving rise to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

There is immediate succession, such as when the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) and so forth give rise to the "Receptivity to the Dharma-knowledge of Suffering" (duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti) and so forth.

There is successive succession with an interval, such as when the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla) and so forth give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and so forth within the enlightenment of the three vehicles.

Regarding the various homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*)—whether with or without conditions, wholesome or unwholesome, and so forth—there are similarities and differences in their taking and giving of fruits, categorized into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). This should be understood as explained in detail in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) exist only in the past, because a ripening fruit neither co-exists with its cause nor occurs immediately after it.

The masters of the West (the Westerners) maintain that in addition to the five fruits, there are four other fruits: first, the fruit of application (*prayogaphala*); second, the fruit of establishment (*vyavasthānaphala*); third, the fruit of conjunction (*saṃnipāta-phala*); and fourth, the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*).
All of these are subsumed under the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*); for this reason, it is said that there are only five fruits.
Having already analyzed cause and effect, one should further investigate: among these, which dharmas are produced by how many causes?
It should be understood that, in brief, there are four types of phenomena herein: namely, defiled phenomena, phenomena born of maturation, the first untainted phenomena, and the remaining phenomena.
What are these remaining phenomena?
This refers to all neutral dharmas (*avyākṛta*) excluding those that are maturation (*vipāka*),
and all other wholesome dharmas (*kuśala*) excluding the first moment of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding these four types of dharmas, the verse says:
Defiled and born-of-maturation states, The remaining [states] and the first noble [state], respectively;
Excluding the maturation and pervasive [causes], And the two types of similar-origination causes, These are said to be the mind and mental factors; For the others, the associated cause is excluded.
The treatise says:
All defiled dharmas arise from five causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because the dharmas produced by the ripening cause are not defiled.

Dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*) arise from five causes, excluding the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), because all dharmas produced by the omnipresent cause are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

The remaining three types of dharmas arise from four causes, excluding both the maturation cause and the omnipresent cause, because these remaining dharmas are neither of the nature of maturation nor are they defiled.

The first untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas arise from the remaining three causes, excluding the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the two causes—maturation (*vipāka*) and universal (*sarvatraga*)—are also excluded. This is because the first untainted dharmas have no previously arisen similar-type dharmas, and because they are wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding these four dharmas, what is being explained?
It should be understood that only the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are being discussed.
If that is so, how many causes give rise to the remaining four dharmas—the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and matter (*rūpa*)?

Just as with the mind and mental factors—excluding the causal condition and excluding the associated condition—it should be understood that other phenomena arise from four, three, or two remaining conditions.

Specifically, defiled matter and non-associated formations, like the mind and mental factors, arise from the remaining four conditions, excluding the ripening cause and excluding the associated condition.

Matter born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and formations dissociated from mind arise from four causes, excluding the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), just as the mind and mental factors do.

The remaining three types of matter and formations dissociated from mind arise from three causes, excluding both the maturation and pervasive causes as well as the associated cause, just as the mind and mental factors do.
Initial untainted matter and formations dissociated from mind arise from two causes, excluding the first three causes and excluding the cause of association, just as with minds and mental factors.
There is no dharma whatsoever that arises from only a single cause.
Now it should be examined: among all phenomena (*dharma*), which phenomena can serve as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of how many causes?
That is to say, there may be some phenomena that fully possess the intrinsic nature of all six causes, and so on in succession down to those that possess the intrinsic nature of only one cause.
Among these, there are dharmas that fully possess the nature of all six causes; namely, all past and present unwholesome universal (*sarvatraga*) minds and mental factors.

There are dharmas that possess the nature of five causes; namely, all past and present unwholesome non-universal minds and mental factors, or neutral universal minds and mental factors, or wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors, or unwholesome non-universal dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

There are dharmas that can function as the nature of four causes: namely, all past and present unwholesome material dharmas; or wholesome, out-flowing (sāsrava) material dharmas and mental non-associated formations; or unwholesome non-pervasive mental non-associated formations; or neutral pervasive mental non-associated formations; or neutral non-pervasive minds and mental factors; or all uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors; or all future unwholesome, wholesome, and out-flowing minds and mental factors.

There are dharmas that can function as the nature of three causes: namely, all past and present indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) material dharmas; or indeterminate non-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*); or untainted (*anāsrava*) material and formations dissociated from mind; or future unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome-tainted (*sāsrava-kuśala*) material and mental formations dissociated from mind; or indeterminate and untainted minds and mental factors (*caitta*).

There are dharmas that can function as two types of causes; these are all future indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, namely matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).

There are dharmas that can function as only one type of cause; these are unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). There are no dharmas that are not causes, yet there are dharmas that are not effects, namely space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

Furthermore, one should reflect upon how these six causes relate to one another in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), whether they are homogeneous or heterogeneous. First, regarding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) in relation to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it follows the latter clause: that is, a co-existent cause is necessarily heterogeneous with respect to the efficient cause.
There are cases where the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) alone exists and is not a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu); this refers to unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).

Furthermore, when the efficient cause is contrasted with the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), it follows the latter part of the logical formula: that is, a homogeneous cause is necessarily accompanied by the efficient cause.

There are cases where the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) functions purely as such and does not function as a cause of similar kind (*sabhāga-hetu*); these are future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, when the efficient cause is contrasted with the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it follows the latter clause: that is, an associated cause is necessarily a mixed efficient cause.

There are purely efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) that are not associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), namely all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, regarding the relationship between the efficient cause and the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it follows the latter clause: the omnipresent cause is necessarily mixed with the efficient cause.

There are cases where the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*); these include future dharmas, past and present non-pervasive dharmas, and unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Furthermore, when the efficient cause is compared with the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it likewise conforms to the latter category; that is, a retributive cause is necessarily a mixed efficient cause.
There are purely efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) that are not retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*), namely, neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.

If the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is contrasted with the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it conforms to the latter clause: that is, a similar-type cause is necessarily accompanied by a co-existent cause.
There are cases where there is only co-existent causality (*sahabhū-hetu*) and not causality of the same kind (*sabhāga-hetu*), namely, future dharmas.

Furthermore, regarding co-existent causality in relation to associated causality (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it also conforms to the latter part of the verse: that is, associated causes are necessarily mixed with co-existent ones.
There are cases where factors are co-existent causes but not associated causes; namely, all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, regarding the co-existent cause in relation to the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it also conforms to the latter part of the verse: that is, a pervasive cause is necessarily mixed with the co-existent cause.
There is that which is exclusively co-existent but not a pervasive cause; namely, future dharmas and past or present non-pervasive dharmas.

Furthermore, regarding the co-existent cause in contrast to the retributive cause, it also conforms to the latter part of the statement: a retributive cause must necessarily be mixed with the co-existent.
There are cases where factors are co-existent but not homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), namely: all neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena.
Regarding the homogeneous cause in relation to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first phrase refers to past and present form and formations dissociated from mind.
The second phrase refers to future minds and mental factors.
The third phrase refers to the mind and mental factors of the past and present.
The fourth phrase refers to future matter, non-associated formations, and unconditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in relation to the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it follows the latter clause: that is, the pervasive cause is necessarily mixed with the homogeneous cause.
However, there are purely homogeneous causes that are not pervasive causes, namely: those dharmas of the past and present that are not pervasive.
Furthermore, regarding the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) in relation to the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu), one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
The first permutation refers to past and present indeterminate (avyākṛta) and untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
The second permutation refers to future unwholesome (akuśala) and wholesome tainted (sāsrava) dharmas.
The third phrase refers to unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of the past and present.
The fourth phrase refers to indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, as well as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, of the future.
Regarding the association cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu) in relation to the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu), four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
The first alternative consists of future mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), as well as past and present mental states and mental factors that are not universal.
The second phrase refers to all past and present non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The third phrase refers to all past and present minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

The fourth clause refers to all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), all future non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), past and present non-pervasive non-associated formations, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu) and the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) also form four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
The first permutation refers to all neutral (avyākṛta) and untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma).
The second permutation refers to unwholesome (akuśala), wholesome-tainted (kuśala-sāsrava) matter (rūpa), and non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
The third phrase refers to all unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

The fourth phrase refers to indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) matter (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If one were to establish four propositions regarding the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) in relation to the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu), they would be as follows:
The first proposition refers to past and present indeterminate (avyākṛta) universal dharmas.
The second proposition refers to future unwholesome (akuśala) and wholesome contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas, as well as past and present wholesome contaminated and unwholesome non-universal dharmas.
The third phrase refers to past and present unwholesome pervasive dharmas.
The fourth phrase refers to future indeterminate and untainted dharmas, as well as past and present untainted, indeterminate non-pervasive dharmas, and unconditioned dharmas.

Furthermore, one should reflect upon the distinctions among these six causes according to various categories such as material and non-material. That is to say, among the six causes, the two causes of association (*samprayuktaka*) and pervasive concomitance (*sarvatraga*) are non-material; the remaining four causes pertain to both the material and the non-material.
The same should be understood for visible and invisible, and resistant and non-resistant.
Furthermore, among the six causes, only the associated cause consists exclusively of associated dharmas; the remaining causes pertain to both associated and non-associated dharmas.

One should know that it is likewise with having a basis or being without a basis, having an awakening or being without an awakening, having a mode of activity or being without a mode of activity, and having an object of cognition or being without an object of cognition.

Furthermore, among the six causes, two—the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); the remaining four causes pertain to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Moreover, among the six causes, the single "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) pertains to both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while the remaining five causes are invariably conditioned.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single cause of pervasive activity (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), while the remaining five causes pertain to both the defiled and the non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).

It should be understood that the same applies to what is with fault (*sāvadya*) and without fault (*anavadya*), black and white, obscured (*nivṛta*) and unobscured (*anivṛta*), and conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) and not conducive to decline (*vighāta-bhāgīya*).
Furthermore, among the six causes, the single cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) possesses only maturation; the remaining five causes admit both maturation and non-maturation.

Moreover, among the six causes, the single cause of efficiency (*kāraṇa-hetu*) extends across the three time periods and the non-temporal; the three causes of coexistence (*sahabhū*), association (*samprayukta*), and maturation extend across the three time periods; while the two causes of similar type (*sabhāga*) and universal operation (*sarvatraga*) extend only across the past and present.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is both unwholesome and neutral; the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) pertains to both wholesome and unwholesome; and the remaining four causes pertain to all three natures.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) pertain to all three realms of existence; the remaining four causes pertain both to the three realms and to that which is non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Moreover, among the six causes, the two causes—the pervasive and the retributive—are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); the remaining four causes all pertain to all three types.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*); the single ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is abandoned by both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); and the remaining four causes are abandoned by both insight and cultivation, as well as being non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).

Furthermore, among the six causes, the single cause of efficient operation (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is subsumed under all four truths as well as that which is not a truth; the two causes of pervasive association (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) are subsumed exclusively under the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origination (*samudaya-satya*); and the remaining three causes are subsumed under the three truths of suffering, origination, and the path (*mārga-satya*).

Furthermore, among the six causes, the associated and pervasive causes are comprised solely within the four aggregates; the co-existent, similar-type, and retributive causes are comprised within all five aggregates; and the enabling cause is comprised within both the five aggregates and that which is not comprised within the aggregates.

Furthermore, among the six causes, the associated and pervasive causes are subsumed within the sense bases of mind and mental objects; the retributive cause is subsumed within four sense bases—visible form, sound, mind, and mental objects; and the remaining three causes are subsumed within the twelve sense bases.

Furthermore, among the six causes: the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is subsumed within the three realms of mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness; the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is subsumed within the seven mind-elements and the mental-object element; the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is subsumed within the elements of form and sound, as well as the seven mind-elements and the mental-object element; and the remaining three causes are subsumed within all eighteen elements.
These various differentiated characteristics of cause and effect cannot be fully known by anyone other than an omniscient one.

Having followed the scope of our own cognitive faculties, I have briefly explained these characteristics within the context of the meaning of cause and effect, in order to further clarify and discern the various conditions (*pratyaya*).
What are the various conditions?
The verse says:
It is taught that there are four kinds of conditions; the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) consists of the nature of the five causes.
The equal-and-immediate [condition] is not subsequent; it consists of mind and mental factors that have already arisen.
The object-condition consists of all phenomena; the dominant condition is simply the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The commentary says:
Where is this taught? It is taught in the sūtras.

As it is said in the sūtras regarding the nature of the four conditions: namely, the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

In this context, "conditionality" (*pratyayatā*) refers to the four conditions. Just as the term "abode" implies the nature of being an abode, the word "nature" (*tā*) is used here to indicate the category; its intended meaning is to demonstrate that, according to the distinctions among various phenomena, these conditions possess an infinite number of entities.
However, to summarize their meaning, they are all subsumed within four categories; that is to say, there is no condition whatsoever that transcends these natures.
Among the six causes, with the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As stated in the treatise:
"What is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)."
Since the treatise does not state that it also subsumes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the five causes are established as the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Why is the unconditioned not established as a causal condition?
This is explained as before: only by abiding without obstruction is it established as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); it is not subsumed under any other cause.
Although the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is primordially present and not non-existent, the accomplishment of their activity necessarily depends on causal power.
For example, although the substance of derived matter is primordially not non-existent, the accomplishment of its function necessarily depends upon the primary elements.
Among causes, those that are predominant are only five; for example, there are no more than five predominant causes for derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

As for the subsequent mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that have already arisen, they are all collectively termed "equal-and-immediate conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*); that is to say, with the exception of the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat, all other previously arisen minds and mental factors are, without exception, equal-and-immediate conditions.
The term "already arisen" is stated in order to exclude future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The terms "mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitta*) are stated in order to exclude all material phenomena (*rūpa*) and formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Why is it that only mind and mental factors constitute the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
This corresponds to the meaning of the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Because these produced phenomena are equal and arise without interval, this term "equal and immediate" is established based on this meaning.
That is to say, within a single continuum, two phenomena of the same kind never arise simultaneously; therefore, it is called "equal."
This condition, in relation to its fruit, is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) because no similar dharma intervenes between them.

If one were to define it as "uninterrupted" simply because the fruit arises immediately in succession, then the mind and mental factors emerging from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and so forth would not be considered "uninterrupted" in relation to their preceding states.
Alternatively, "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) refers to the arising of equal dharmas in the interval; there is no possibility for other equal dharmas to arise between these two.
Alternatively, the preceding collection of simultaneously arisen mind and mental factors serves as the condition for the subsequent collection that is both equal and immediate.
It is not only those of the same category that are called "equal and immediate" (samanantara). Why?

Because within a single body, there are no two entities of the same category—whether mind or mental factors—that arise simultaneously; for the equal and immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) admits no second [simultaneous] occurrence.
For what reason is there no second immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Because the mind of each and every sentient being arises one at a time.
