For what reason does each [sentient being] have only a single mind arise at once?
For when the mind is actively distracted toward other objects, it lacks cognition of those other objects;
furthermore, when the mind is in meditative concentration focused on a single object, a distracted mind directed toward other objects necessarily does not arise.
Furthermore, if a single continuum possessed multiple minds, there would be no one capable of subduing the mind.
Moreover, if multiple minds were to arise simultaneously within a single body, would they each have distinct objects, or would they correspond to a common object?
If they were associated with one another, then because they would share a single object and a single aspect without distinction, their simultaneous arising would be redundant.
If their objects were distinct, then defilement and purity, or good and evil, would arise together, and there would consequently be no liberation.
Furthermore, there is authoritative scripture that proves that for a single sentient being, only a single mental continuum evolves.
As the Sūtra states:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time, two feelings have both ceased."
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"The mind travels alone.
How can it be known with certainty that when the mind and mental factors arise, they necessarily rely upon the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

As stated in the sūtras, that which gives rise to it—the mental attention (*manasikāra*)—arises when correct, present, and manifest cognitive wisdom (*buddhi*) is fully engaged; it arises preceded by such cognitive wisdom.
If this were not the case, what reasoning could prevent the sudden emergence at this time of sentient beings who previously did not exist?
For what reason are the final mind and mental factors of the various Arhats said not to be equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
It is because they cannot draw forth subsequent fruits.
Furthermore, for what reason do these lack the capacity to draw forth a fruit?

Since other conditions were lacking at that time, it is accepted that the subsequent consciousness does not arise due to the absence of those conditions; what fault is there in admitting that [the preceding consciousness] possesses the capacity to draw forth a subsequent fruit?
If it can project [a result] in the subsequent stage, then the mind and mental factors of the preceding stage should likewise be able to yield their results.
If the meaning of yielding a result is absent because the conditions are deficient, then it must be that the deficiency of conditions prevents the projection of a result.

When mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*) are in the process of ceasing, they are able to draw forth and provide a locus for those states that are in the process of arising; thus, they are called the "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

However, because the final minds and so forth of Arhats in the state of ceasing have no subsequent states in the process of arising to serve as their equal-and-immediate [successors], it cannot be said that they function as an equal-and-immediate condition.

If that were so, then regarding the mental states and mental factors preceding the state of non-conception and the two meditative attainments, since there are no mental states or mental factors in their positions of immediate cessation or immediate arising, they should not be described as having the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Because it is certain to arise, it is also called "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*).
Since that which is dissociated (*viprayukta*) cannot arise immediately due to being separated [by other factors], there is no fault in speaking of its "arising" once it is determined to arise.
The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and others do not have a fixed determination regarding the taking up of results; therefore, one should not use them as an analogy for this case.
For what reason is it that future mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are entirely not permitted to be established as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
The equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is manifested by what precedes and follows; in the future, there is as yet no determination of what precedes and follows.
If that [future state] already possessed a determination of precedence and succession, then the cultivation of correct preparatory application (prayoga) would be in vain.

Although the cause and effect of maturation (*vipāka*) are fixed in terms of temporal sequence, they are established based on their characteristics rather than their chronological order; therefore, this does not apply to the future and cannot be used as an analogy.
If there were no fixed sequence in the future, how could the Blessed One have prophesied specific times?
The meritorious functions of all Buddhas are inconceivable; they are able to directly perceive all causes and effects, whether past, present, or future. Some say:
within the bodies of sentient beings in the present, each possesses the prior signs of their future causes and effects; it is by observing these that a Buddha knows the future.

This clear realization through direct perception is not the wisdom of divination; regarding these dense forests of *jñeya* (the objects of knowledge), the Buddha is able to realize and perceive them only because there is a logical basis for doing so—it is not the case that his omniscience functions without such a basis.

While they are capable of exercising a function toward objects such as visible form (*rūpa*), for what reason are neither the various forms nor the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) established as having the condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Because within a single body, those of the same class arise simultaneously, whether more or fewer than one another, and thus do not constitute an equal and immediate succession.

If that were so, since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) does not arise simultaneously with two [other factors], why do you not allow it to rely upon an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
It arises through the power of past karma and is not projected by a preceding life-faculty.
Although the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are produced by prior karma, the case of relying on objects and faculties cannot be used as an analogy.
Furthermore, it is not determined that [the mind] arises as a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
However, the *Vibhāṣā* states:

"The mind and mental factors have constraints regarding their basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), and mode of activity (*ākāra*); for this reason, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is established."
In the case of form (*rūpa*), such a thing does not exist.

This condition (*pratyaya*) is established not merely by way of making room, but also based on its capacity to draw forth [the effect]; therefore, although atoms and the like may arise only after preceding ones have vacated space, they do not constitute this specific condition.

The arising of mental states and the like is both determinate and indeterminate; therefore, we know that this also refers to being drawn forth by a potent force. This determinacy and indeterminacy are as explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Since all minds and mental factors arise through the power of their own causes, what function does the immediately preceding ceased [moment] perform?

This means that although the sense faculties and their objects are currently in conjunction, there is no simultaneous arising of consciousnesses and their corresponding mental factors; therefore, we know that at the moment the preceding mind ceases without interval, it possesses the power to draw forth and cause the subsequent mind and its associates to arise.
There is no such thing as a non-associated [dharma] with respect to form (*rūpa*), as it is said:
"What are the dharmas that arise immediately after the mind?

They are the other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that have already arisen or are currently arising immediately after the mind, as well as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)," and so forth, at length.
The term "already arisen" includes the past and present; the term "arising" includes the future moment of birth.

If that were so, then the minds of the second moment and subsequent moments—whether in meditative absorption or emerging from it—would not be "immediately preceding" (samanantara) states, because at the time immediately following the mind of entry into absorption, those [subsequent minds] have not yet arisen. It is only when they subsequently reach the stage of "arising" that they are designated as "immediately preceding" states of mind.
Because there is no intervening immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) between them, the latter is also called "immediate" in relation to the former.
Furthermore, that which is destined to arise is also termed "the time of arising," because once the fruit has been grasped, it is certain to be produced.
If that were so, it would contradict the text of the *Dṛṣṭiskandha-śāstra*. As that work asks:
"If a dharma serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for another dharma, could there ever be a time when this dharma does not serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for that one?"
He replied: "If this dharma has not yet arrived but has already arisen,
what contradiction or harm is there?"
The immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) must necessarily reach that which has already arisen;
however, there are two interpretations regarding this matter, neither of which is contradictory.
This applies when this dharma has not yet arisen.
What is this dharma? Is it prior or posterior?

For example, when the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) gives rise to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), does the supreme mundane dharma not serve as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering while it has not yet arisen, or does it serve as the immediate antecedent condition once it has reached the state of having already arisen?

When the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has not yet arisen, it does not serve as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*). Is it, however, when it reaches the state of having already arisen that it serves as the immediate antecedent?
If one adheres to the former [position], it may be so in the state of having a mind; however, how could it be so in the state of being without mind?

That is to say, in the case of a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*), once the entering mind has already arisen, it cannot serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the second moment of that absorption or for the emerging mind.

If the mind entering meditative absorption, upon reaching the stage of having already arisen, were to serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for those various dharmas, then since the dharmas that are the fruits of the equal-and-immediate condition would be grasped and nothing could possibly obstruct their arising, all of them should arise simultaneously.
If the subsequent mind were to arise immediately after the mind that enters [the meditative absorption], then these two absorptions would never be able to arise again.

If one maintains the latter position, then as long as the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* has not yet arisen, it should not serve as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for that *laukikāgra-dharma*.

Nevertheless, one must certainly admit that when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is in the process of arising, it is designated as being the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for that Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Regarding this point, one class [of scholars] accepts the previous position; however, since the text of the *Dṛṣṭi-skandha* explains the immediately preceding condition with reference to states possessing mind, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Alternatively, it may be argued that this fault does not apply if one explains this based on the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).

That is to say, the mind entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) abides in the present moment, and simultaneously grasps all the factors of the absorption as well as the fruit of the emerging mind; furthermore, the cessation of the fruit of the absorption from the very first moment enters the past.

Subsequently, as each of the minds of the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the minds emerging from them arises, it gives its fruit but does not grasp it, because it has already been grasped previously.
Is it not the case that all equivalent immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) give their fruit and grasp their fruit at different times?
This criticism is unreasonable; for while the grasping of the fruit is necessarily instantaneous, its yielding of the fruit occurs gradually, and thus there is no fault.

One should instead question why various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the mind emerging from absorption arise sequentially rather than simultaneously, given that they share the same mental continuum as their fruit.

That which is being sought must necessarily arise first as a matter of principle; that is to say, because the mind entering meditative absorption seeks absorption accordingly, absorption must necessarily arise prior to the mind without any interval.
If this is so, for what reason do the various moments of absorption arise sequentially?
Since it would be useless for multiple moments of concentration to arise simultaneously, they do not arise together.

Because they are projected by the force of prior preparatory effort, many moments of concentration continue to arise over a long duration; it is not that multiple moments of concentration arise at once, because what cannot be accomplished by a single moment of concentration does not occur instantaneously, just as in the case of consciousness and other mental factors.
However, although various moments of concentration (*samādhi*) are immediate antecedents (*samanantara*), they cannot be called "immediate conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*).

If a phenomenon is induced by a preceding mind or similar state, belongs to the same category, necessarily does not arise simultaneously [with its cause], and once arisen, is further able to induce a subsequent [moment] to arise, it may be termed both "immediately antecedent" and "immediate condition."

Although various meditative absorptions are induced by preceding minds of the same category, they necessarily do not arise simultaneously; however, once they have arisen, they cannot induce what follows them. Thus, while they may be termed "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*), they are not "equal and immediate conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Therefore, there is no fault in establishing this by means of a summary that does not analyze the state of mindlessness.
Regarding those who maintain this view—

that the mind entering the two meditative attainments ceases and enters the past before it can gradually grasp the second moment and so forth of the attainment, as well as the mind of emergence— it follows that their mind of entry into concentration would not be of the past.

Now, that which grasps a fruit is the capacity to grasp a fruit; these capacities to grasp fruits are the functional activities (*kāritra*) of formations (*saṃskāra*). It is based on these functional activities that the distinctions of the three time periods are established.
If there were functional activity that was not present, would this not then subvert the very basis for the distinction between the time periods?
Some commentators explain:
"The past eye and so forth do not possess the distinct functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, or touching with regard to objects such as visible forms; therefore, they are not present."

That explanation by the Śākyas is not correct; we must together examine and decide whether the functions of the eye and so forth consist in the capacity for seeing and other such activities with respect to an object, or in the capacity for producing a result?
If they consisted in the capacity for seeing and other such activities with respect to an object, then the eye and so forth would have to exist even in the darkness.
What distinguishes the eye and other faculties when they have not yet arisen or have already ceased from those that are future or past, such that they are not designated as such?

Although the eye and other faculties lack the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, or tasting in the dark, they all currently possess the capacity to project their effects, and thus may be termed "functional activity."
Whatever possesses this specific activity is termed "present.
All other activities, such as grasping an object or yielding a fruit, are not actual activities (kāritra) but are merely potencies (śakti).
Such potencies may exist across the three time periods; this shall be fully examined and analyzed in the section discussing the three times.

Furthermore, the various minds and mental factors of past lives cannot act as obstacles regarding their objects of perception and so forth; therefore, they cannot function as this condition to grasp a result.

Moreover, there is another class who permit the subsequent apprehension [of the result]: would it not be the case that when the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* is in the state of arising, it immediately serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the *laukikāgra-dharma*?

In principle, it should indeed be so; however, since this context explains that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is established only when [the subsequent state] has already arisen, there is no fault.
Thus, regarding the two explanations of the term "not yet arisen," neither contradicts my own doctrinal position.

The nature of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyayatā*) consists of all phenomena; apart from the objects apprehended by mind and mental factors, no other phenomenon can be found. Since all phenomena are that which the mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon and cling to, they are called "objects" (*ālambana*).
Because this very object of focus serves as the condition for the arising of the mind and mental factors, it is called the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya).

"All phenomena" refers to the twelve bases (āyatana): namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousnesses, along with their associated mental factors; these take, respectively, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects as their respective objects of focus.
The six sense faculties are exclusively objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
For what reason is this known?
The Sūtra says:
Because mental consciousness arises from many factors;
because the sense organs, such as the eye, are not subsumed within the objects of the five consciousnesses; and because that which is cognized and known pervades all phenomena.

The objects of the five consciousnesses are exclusively real and not provisional, whereas the objects of mental consciousness pertain to both the provisional and the real; the objects of all minds and mental factors exist and are not non-existent.
The refutation of other schools is as presented in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

However, the objects of perception for the mind and mental factors are fixed; that is to say, visual consciousness and its associates have form as their object, and so on, up to mental consciousness and its associates having all phenomena (*dharmas*) as their objects.

Regarding this certainty of mind and mental factors with respect to their objects: is it by way of location (*sthāna*), by way of category (*jāti*), or by way of moment (*kṣaṇa*)? Some say it is by way of location;

that is, visual consciousness and the like take only the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) as their object, and the others are each described according to their respective domains. This is so that many minds and mental factors do not abide simultaneously upon a single object and fail to arise; therefore, the others are not fixed.
Furthermore, among the various forms, visual consciousness and the others arise by taking as their object whichever form it encounters.
If this is so, how is it that the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth do not become confused in their essential nature?
To avoid this error, some say that [the distinction] is based on location (*deśa*) and category (*jāti*), not on the moment (*kṣaṇa*).

If that were so, how could the essences of cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth not be confused? In such a case, one must state that all three—location, category, and moment—are determinate. Would it not then follow that many minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) could abide in a single object without arising?
There is no fault here; for how could the vastness of future time not accommodate it?
Furthermore, regarding their respective objects, the mind and mental factors are able to recollect subsequently what was previously cognized.

Furthermore, regarding the objects of the five consciousnesses and so forth, the mental consciousness and others can recollect them accordingly, whereas the five consciousnesses and others cannot; this is because the former perceive their objects in a single momentary cognition and are devoid of conceptual discrimination.
The mind is of two kinds, namely, defiled and non-defiled; it cognizes one or the other and can subsequently recollect both.
Furthermore, there are three kinds: wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate; it cognizes one or the other and can subsequently recollect all three.

Furthermore, there are four kinds—namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-neutral, and the unobscured-neutral—which are respectively cognized and recollected by the four [consciousnesses].

Furthermore, there are five kinds, namely: those abandoned through the vision of suffering up to those abandoned through cultivation; those abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and cultivation; and the single realization thereof, which allows for the five types of recollection.
The cognitions abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path can each recollect four [objects], excluding one object in each case.
To speak in detail, there are twelve types: namely, four in the desire realm, three in each of the upper realms, and those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
If one wishes to correctly cognize the twelve types of recollection (*anusmaraṇa*),
it is likewise for the incorrect cognition of form and the correct cognition [of others].

If one wishes to cognize the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), eight are capable of recollecting them, excluding the obscured form and the three of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the obscured cognition of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), ten [types of cognition] can subsequently recollect it, excluding the desire realm’s obscured and unobscured-neutral cognitions.
The same applies to the wholesome cognition of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the unobscured-neutral cognition of the form realm, ten [types of cognition] can subsequently recollect it, excluding the formless realm’s obscured and unobscured-neutral cognitions.

Regarding the awarenesses of the formless realm—both obscured and unobscured—nine can be recollected, excluding the obscured [awareness] of the desire realm and the unobscured [awareness] of the desire and form realms.
Regarding the awareness of one in training (śaikṣa), eleven can be recollected, excluding the obscured [awareness] of the desire realm and the awareness of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

The *parihāṇadharman* (one subject to falling away) is as described for the *śaikṣa*. If one is an *aparihāṇadharman* (one not subject to falling away), seven [mental states] are capable of being recollected (*anusmaraṇa*), excluding those of the *śaikṣa* and excluding four from each of the three realms.

Regarding the various distinctions among the twenty defiled minds (*kliṣṭacitta*) and so forth, one should reflect upon them according to principle, such as through awakening (*saṃprajanya*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa*).

The nature of the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyayatā*) is precisely the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*). Because the meaning of the efficient cause is subtle and boundless, it encompasses all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
If this [factor] does not obstruct that [other factor] and allows it to arise, it is an efficient cause.

Regarding the meaning of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is called "dominant" because its categories are the most numerous and its functions are truly manifold compared to the other three conditions. One might object:
"Since the phenomena subsumed under the dominant condition are all-inclusive, why should it be contrasted with the other three?"
When it is said that this [condition] is "predominant" (*adhipati*), the name "predominant" is not established in relation to the three [other] entities.
In relation to what three meanings or functions is it established?
The meanings and functions of the various conditions do not overlap with one another, whereas the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the various conditions are mutually intermingled.

Just as the categories of the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) are immeasurable and its functions are manifold and extensive, the other three conditions are not so; therefore, this one alone is designated by the term "predominant condition.

To include the nature of the five causes (*kāraṇahetu*) and those meanings not subsumed under the other three conditions, the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) and the predominant condition are established.

Because these two categories of meaning are the most extensive, they are established as general designations, just as in the cases of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), the sphere of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*), the jewel of the Dharma (*dharma-ratna*), refuge in the Dharma (*dharma-śaraṇa*), and the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Other masters say:
This dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is called "dominant" because its nature and categories are most numerous.

Although the nature of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) pervades all phenomena, it does not function as an object for co-existent factors; thus, because its scope is narrow, the name "dominant" is set aside for it.
Others further explain:
it is called the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) because that which is produced is extensive.
That is to say, all phenomena—excluding their own selves—are universally capable of giving rise to all conditioned things.
For example, at the moment an eye-consciousness arises, with the exception of its own nature, it takes all phenomena as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It is the same for all other [consciousnesses] arising.
The extent of the substance and function of this condition is boundless.

As stated in the sūtras, regarding the three types of predominance—of the world, of phenomena, and of oneself—one ceases evil and practices good by taking one of these as the object of observation, because they serve as the causes for such observation. That is to say, when an object is present before one and afflictions are about to arise, by observing any one of these three, one ceases evil and practices good; thus, within this process of cessation and practice, they attain the status of "predominance."
The Sūtra states that there are only three types of predominance (*adhipatya*) and no others, for in other cases the sense of predominance does not apply.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle Ten; *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā-samuccaya*, Fascicle Eleven.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three, Part Seven: On the Distinction Between the Meanings of Condition (*pratyaya*) and Cause (*hetu*). What is the distinction between their meanings?

Some say: There is a distinction between conditions that are pervasive and those that are non-pervasive; for the first four [conditions] subsume the six causes, whereas the second and third [conditions] do not subsume the causes.

Although the substance of the six causes and four conditions is not different, their meanings differ. Since the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are not included among the causes, we know that the other two [conditions] also differ in meaning. This is because they share the general sense of "condition" while both being distinct from "causes."

There is a general explanation of the distinction between causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*): "cause" refers to that which can produce, while "condition" refers to that which can nurture, just as there is a distinction between the two mothers—the one who gives birth and the one who nurtures.
Furthermore, it is only when a cause is assisted by conditions that it can produce; once produced, it continues in succession because of the power of the conditions to nurture it.
Some say: The cause is singular while conditions are manifold, just as a seed differs from manure, soil, and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is unique is the cause, whereas that which is common is the condition, such as the eye and its object.
Furthermore, that which performs its own function is called a cause (*hetu*), while that which performs the function of another is called a condition (*pratyaya*), such as seed and fertilizer.
Moreover, that which can induce [an effect] is called a cause, while that which can sustain it is called a condition, such as a flower and a garland.
Furthermore, that which is proximate is called a cause (*hetu*), while that which is remote is called a condition (*pratyaya*), such as a gem or the sun.

Moreover, the cause is able to produce, whereas the condition is able to bring about completion; it is like the production of butter from curds, where the person and the churning vessel serve as the means of accomplishment.

Furthermore, that which possesses the actual meaning is called the cause (*hetu*), while that which can assist in its manifestation is called the condition (*pratyaya*), just as, for example, the phoneme (*akṣara*) is the cause and the letter (*vyañjana*) is the condition.
There are distinctions regarding the meaning; such categories of distinctions are numerous, and for this reason, the designations "cause" and "condition" are established separately.
This general intent reveals that because causes are proximate while conditions are remote, the number and extent of causes are greater than those of conditions.
Having briefly analyzed the various conditions according to both reason and scripture, one may ask:
do these various conditions function by manifesting the arising and ceasing of phenomena?
One should explain: by what conditions and at what stage do dharmas exercise their activity?
The verse says:
Two causes [exercise their activity] when [the dharma] is in the process of ceasing; three causes [exercise their activity] when [the dharma] is in the process of arising.
The other two conditions function in opposition [to the cause].
The treatise says:

The five causes previously mentioned constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Two of these causes exert their activity at the moment of "presently ceasing. The phrase "at the moment of presently ceasing" indicates that the phenomenon is in the present; it is called the moment of presently ceasing because its cessation is imminent.
The two causes—the co-existent (*sahabhū*) and the associated (*samprayukta*)—exert their functional efficacy at the stage when a phenomenon is present and ceasing.

Regarding these two causes exerting efficacy at this stage, it refers to the category of co-arising factors: if even one moment of their activity is lacking, they all become non-existent and are unable to apprehend an object while in the present state.
Although these two causes both take up and give their fruit simultaneously, here we are considering only the functional capacity to give the fruit.
As for the statement that "three causes [operate] at the stage of arising," this means that future dharmas are called "at the stage of arising" because they are about to arise into the present state.
The three types of dharmas—homogeneous, pervasive, and retributive—exert their functional efficacy at the stage of actual arising;
therefore, some say that the two fruits of outflow and maturation are drawn forth and brought into existence by the power of the cause.

In the case of homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) causes, it is possible for their outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) to arise immediately; thus, one may say that the cause exerts its activity at the very moment the fruit is arising.

However, in the case of retributive (*vipāka*) cause and effect, there must necessarily be a long interval of time; the cause has long since ceased when the fruit is finally arising. How, then, could the activity of the cause exist at the time the fruit arises?

It is not the case that an action can exist at a past time; this statement regarding "action" intends to signify "functional capacity," as has already been examined in the section on the distinction between the two characteristics.
Although the cause may have ceased after an immeasurable period of time, it possesses the functional capacity to bring about its own effect, because it is unique (asādhāraṇa).

Although there is no actual activity at the time its own fruit arises, the term "activity" is applied to its capacity with respect to that fruit; only that which takes up the capacity for the fruit is called true activity, while all other instances of "activity" are merely figurative designations.
The functional activity of the two causes has already been explained as occurring at two distinct times; the activity of the two conditions is the opposite of this.

The equal-and-immediate condition exerts its activity at the moment a dharma arises, because at the time that [dharma] arises, the preceding mind and mental factors have induced and cleared the way for it.

If the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) exerts its function at the moment when the subjective cognition (ālambaka) is ceasing, this is because the mind and mental factors must be in the present moment to apprehend an object; as for the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), since it remains unobstructed throughout both the arising and ceasing phases of phenomena, its function is entirely unimpeded.

Now it should be considered: since the co-existent, associated, and object conditions only exercise their functions once a dharma has already arisen, why is it necessary to establish these two causes and one condition?

If one maintains that a cause and condition must possess an actual activity (*kāritra*) in order to be established as having the nature of a cause and condition, then there would be no causes and conditions in the future.
However, this should not be raised as an objection against what is accepted by our own school.
If that is so, how can one speak of "activity"?

If these two causes and one condition were absent, then the various phenomena being projected during the state of actual cessation would lack the activity and functional capacity to apprehend objects.

If that which lacks functional activity were also called a condition, then the final moments of consciousness of Arhats and so forth would also have to be established as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This objection is unreasonable, for it has already been refuted previously.

It is not necessary for an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) to be established solely by virtue of having an active function; what relevance, then, is there in using those [conditions] as an analogy for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

That condition must be established through the opening up [of the way] and the drawing forth [of the effect]; therefore, it can only be properly established in the present. It certainly does not exist in the future. Since it once had an active function at the time of the present, it can also be established as existing in the past.

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is not limited to the present; rather, anything that possesses substantial existence (*svabhāva*) can function as a condition, and it does not necessarily depend upon its activity (*kāritra*) for its establishment.
It is only with respect to a small portion of conditions that they receive the name "activity," and this applies to all conditions.
How is it known that an entity must exist for a condition to be established?
If the entity of the object-condition (*ālambana*) were non-existent, cognition would not arise.
If the object-condition necessarily requires functional activity, then subsequent unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) would have to possess prior effects.

Alternatively, this "activity" (kāritra) is not established on the basis of directly producing various effects; rather, it is designated as "activity" based on what serves as the support for the arising of the functions of various phenomena. Therefore, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) that follows does not incur the fault of lacking a preceding effect.
One should state: by how many conditions do which phenomena arise?
The verse says:
Mind and mental factors arise from four; The two meditative attainments arise from only three.
The others arise from two conditions, because they are not [produced] by a creator god (*īśvara*) or by succession, and so forth.
The treatise says:
Here, the word "by" (*yena*) serves to clarify the meaning of "because," namely that mind and mental factors arise by way of four conditions.

As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it has no function other than that of producing the mind and its concomitants; that is to say, the six groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors take the five objects, such as form, and all phenomena as their object-conditions, according to their respective requirements.

The mind and its associates possess five types of causal nature as their conditions: they open the way for and induce subsequent moments of their own kind that have already arisen; this is called the mind-and-mental-state equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
As for this dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it consists of all phenomena, each excluding its own self-nature, according to what is appropriate.
Is it not the case that the functions of the two causes operate upon a single object?
Yet these functions do not exist at the very moment that phenomenon arises.
How, then, can mental states and the like arise by virtue of the four conditions?
How do the causal conditions possess the nature of the five causes?

Although their function is established only at the stage when a phenomenon ceases, they are not devoid of efficacy at the time the phenomenon arises; for without them, that phenomenon would necessarily not arise, since mind and mental factors must rely upon an object-condition and depend upon two causes in order to arise.
If a phenomenon serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for another phenomenon, it cannot do so even for a moment, because this is not stated in the fundamental treatise.
Furthermore, the two mindless attainments arise by way of three conditions, excluding the object-condition, because they are not capable of taking an object.
These causal conditions consist of only two causes:
first, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), which refers to the various characteristics such as arising and so forth associated with the two meditative attainments;
second, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which refers to the previously arisen wholesome dharmas of one's own stage.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the mind entering meditative absorption and its associated mental factors.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously described.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) is also produced by three conditions? Since it is the immediately preceding condition for minds and mental factors, it should also be called the "immediately preceding condition" of the mind.
However, because it is not produced by the application of mind and so forth, it is omitted and not discussed here.
Alternatively, this "non-conception" (āsaṃjñika) is indicated merely by its name, as it is not established in contrast to the two meditative absorptions (samāpatti).
For what reason are the two meditative attainments (samāpatti) considered "immediately antecedent" to mind, yet not called "immediately antecedent conditions" (samanantarapratyaya) for mind?

Because they are produced by the power of the mind and its mental factors; because their arising is necessarily bound to the cessation of the preceding mind; because, unlike material phenomena (rūpadharma), they cannot coexist with other minds at the same time; because, unlike acquisitions (prāpti) and so forth, they do not appear in a disordered or simultaneous manner; and because, unlike birth (jāti) and so forth, they are not merely companions to other factors.

However, because it is produced by the application of mental skillful means (*upāya*), it may be said to be the equal-and-immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) of the mind; yet, because it is diametrically opposed to and destructive of that which arises simultaneously with the mind, it is not the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind and its concomitants.

Furthermore, this would contradict the logical principle that [the mind] acts as a condition for it; for a practitioner enters a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*) out of aversion toward the manifest mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). If, in that mindless absorption, the mind and mental factors were again induced by this very condition, then the practitioner would have no reason to take pleasure in entering such an absorption.

Because one enters a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*) in order to abandon the currently active mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), it would be contrary to correct principle for this [absorption] to subsequently induce those mental states and mental factors; therefore, it is not a homogeneous immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Regarding the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), why is the relationship of "equal and immediate antecedent condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) not established between a preceding moment and a subsequent one?
It is because all moments are induced by the mind and its mental factors; it is not the case that a preceding moment induces the arising of the subsequent one.
If what precedes can induce what follows, then the very last [moment] should have no fruit.
Nor can it be said that this induces the mind that arises subsequently, for it has already been stated that a contrary mind is not a condition for the mind.
Furthermore, because the mind emerging from meditative absorption is the fruit of the mind entering it,
how can that [emerging mind] be said to be the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) when the emerging mind has not yet arisen immediately after the mind entering?
This is because there is an interval between them, and thus no equal-and-immediate condition exists.

There is a distinction between the two meanings of "immediate" (*ānantarya*) and "equal-immediate" (*samanantara*). When a preceding mind, through its equalizing power, induces the arising of a subsequent dharma, that subsequent dharma is termed the "equal-immediate" of the preceding one. Because there is no interval between moments, it is designated as "immediate. Therefore, the two terms have distinct meanings; for this reason, the statement was made.
If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for the mind, is that phenomenon also immediately preceded by the mind? This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first permutation refers to the mind and mental factors emerging from the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), as well as the second and subsequent moments of various meditative attainments.

The second phrase refers to the initial moments of the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), as well as the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) during states of consciousness.
The third phrase refers to the initial moments of the various meditative absorptions, as well as the mind and mental factors during states of consciousness.

The fourth phrase refers to the moments of the second and subsequent meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), as well as the arising, abiding, alteration, and cessation of the mind and mental factors upon emerging from a mindless absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
If a dharma serves as the equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind, does it also serve as the immediate antecedent for the mindless absorption?

One should formulate four propositions: that is, the former third and fourth propositions become the present first and second propositions, while the former first and second propositions become the present third and fourth propositions.

The remaining dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) and all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are produced by two conditions: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, how is it known that all worldly phenomena arise solely from the causes and conditions as described above, and not from a single cause such as Īśvara, the Self (*ātman*), or Pradhāna?

By virtue of their sequential occurrence: if all worldly phenomena were produced by a single cause, such as Īśvara, they would have to arise simultaneously rather than sequentially, because that cause would be constantly present.
What factor acts as an obstruction so that [dharmas] do not arise simultaneously?
We observe that all dharmas arise in succession; therefore, we know they are not produced by a single cause alone.
If one maintains that the world follows the will of Īśvara, then because there are distinctions between earlier and later moments, things cannot arise instantaneously.
In that case, one must admit that things do not arise from a single cause, since you also admit that desire (*chanda*) is the cause for the arising of phenomena.
Furthermore, the distinction between the prior and subsequent arising and ceasing of this desire is logically untenable, because there is no difference in its cause.
It is not the case that there can be a distinction among effects without a distinction among their causes, for an effect becomes distinct only by depending on a distinct cause.

Alternatively, because they are distinct [from one another], one must admit that they arise simultaneously, since there would be no distinction between the preceding and succeeding moments of their cause.
In that case, all phenomena should also arise simultaneously; who could act as an obstacle to prevent them from arising all at once?

If the Lord’s will must further depend on other causes to produce things in a sequential order of distinction, then those causal factors themselves would have to depend on further causes, resulting in an infinite regress of dependencies.

Because causes are infinite, the principle of beginninglessness is established; this does not deviate from the correct reasoning of dependent origination within the Buddhist tradition. To claim that Īśvara is the cause under a different name is merely a hollow distinction; furthermore, since he would have no purpose [in creating], one should not falsely cling to the view that the various phenomena of the world have Īśvara as their cause.

It is not the case that the Lord (Īśvara), through the exertion of great power, has even the slightest utility in producing worldly phenomena; therefore, one should not claim that the Lord is the cause.
If his purpose were to produce joy for himself, he should simply produce joy; why would he need to produce anything else?
If joy does not arise without other auxiliary conditions, then that joy must be produced by those other conditions; it would therefore not be autonomous in this regard.
As it is with joy, so it should be with the others as well, for no distinct causes and conditions can be found.
If other means should arise from other means, what is the use of postulating that they originate from Īśvara?
If joy arises from other means independently of other means, it likewise should not be produced by Īśvara.
Or they are born as instruments of suffering that oppress and harm sentient beings, doing so out of self-satisfaction. Alas!
What is the use of serving such a cruel and malevolent Īśvara?

Furthermore, if one believes that the world arises solely from the single cause of Īśvara, one then negates the visible fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)—namely, merit and demerit—as they are perceived in the world.

If it is argued that Īśvara requires the assistance of other factors, such as merit and demerit, to activate his causal capacity, this is merely a statement out of partiality toward the god Īśvara; for apart from other causes and conditions, no distinct function [of Īśvara] is observed.

At that time, various causes and conditions such as earth and water possess manifest efficacy in the production of sprouts and the like, because the existence or non-existence of the sprouts follows them.

Since no function other than their efficacy is observed in the production of sprouts and the like, one should not postulate that a creator god (*īśvara*) is the cause for the arising of worldly phenomena.

Since this is the case regarding the Lord (Īśvara), the same principle should be applied accordingly to the nature of the Self (ātman) and so forth; thus, it should be understood that there is no phenomenon produced by a single cause alone, but rather all arise from the various causes and conditions previously described. This reasoning is thoroughly established.

Since it has already been stated that material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are produced by the two conditions of cause and dominance, and that what is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is collectively termed "matter," how is it that among these, some are derived from the primary elements?
Self and other are mutually related as causes and conditions.
The verse says:
The primary elements are the two causes of the primary elements; they are the five kinds of causes for the derived elements.
The derived [elements] have three kinds of causes; the primary [elements] have only one cause.
The commentary states:

Regarding the initial statement that "the primary [elements] act as two causes for the primary [elements]," this means that when these various primary elements are considered in relation to one another, they function solely as simultaneous (sahabhū) and homogeneous (sabhāga) causes. This is because there is a distinction between those that arise simultaneously and those that serve as causes by having arisen previously.
This means that because the remainder does not arise if even one [of these factors] is missing, they possess the *sahabhū-hetu* (simultaneous cause) in relation to one another.
Although their natures and categories differ, they constitute a single entity and accord with one another; therefore, they possess the *sabhāga-hetu* (homogeneous cause).
That which is greater than what is produced can serve as five causes. What are these five?
They are distinguished as the causes of arising, dependence, establishment, maintenance, and nourishment.

Although they arise simultaneously, because they function in accordance [with one another], they are like the mutual production of shadows, lamps, flames, and light; thus, the "great" (mahābhūta) elements possess the status of being causes for their "derived" (upādāya-rūpa) effects.

In this way, the five causes are merely specific distinctions of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). It is logically untenable for the great elements to be the other five causes in relation to their derived effects, because they do not share a single result.
It is not a co-existent cause nor an associated cause, because it is dissociated and because it is non-defiled.
It is not a pervasive cause nor a maturation cause, because it is of an indeterminate nature.
Because they are not of the same class (*asabhāga*), they do not constitute a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The questions and answers for this definitive analysis are as presented in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Furthermore, there is textual evidence within the root treatise itself: from a broad perspective, derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) lacks five types of causes. As it is said: "There is a sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that is neither caused by the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor is itself indeterminate; namely, wholesome spheres of form."
If that were so, it would contradict the sūtras and treatises.
As a sūtra states: "The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is designated based upon the four great elements (mahābhūta)."
This treatise also states:

"The [relationships of] being produced from the four great elements, being their cause, being predominant, and so forth, are all mutually non-contradictory, as they are explained according to the five causes, such as the producing cause (*janana-hetu*).
That the great elements act as the producing cause for what is derived from them is because the latter arises from the former, just as a mother gives birth to a child."
As the cause of dependence (*āśraya-hetu*), it functions because [the dependent] follows along with it, just as a minister depends upon a king.
As the cause of establishment (*pratisthā-hetu*), it functions because it is able to sustain [it], just as the earth supports things.
It is the sustaining cause because its power maintains [the continuum] so that it does not cease, just as food sustains life.
It is the nourishing cause because it can cause growth, like the roots of a tree being moistened and saturated by water.
In this way, it is shown that the primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as the causes for the arising, transformation, maintenance, persistence, and growth of derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Alternatively, they are "causes of production" because all primary elements produce derived matter; for derived matter does not arise apart from the primary elements.
Once derived matter has arisen, during the stage of its continuous succession of similar types, fire acts as the supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*), for it can cause drying and prevent decay;
water acts as the establishing cause (*pratisthā-hetu*), for it can provide moisture and prevent dispersal;
earth acts as the sustaining cause (*dhṛti-hetu*), for it can support that matter and prevent it from falling.
Wind serves as a supporting cause (*puṣṭi-hetu*), for it can induce those derived elements to arise and increase.

Thus, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not possess the five types of causes—such as coexistent cause and so forth—in relation to their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), they do possess five distinct causes such as the cause of production (*janana-hetu*) and so on; therefore, there is no contradiction with the sūtras or śāstras.

When all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is mutually compared with one another, there are only three causes: namely, co-existent (*sahabhū*), homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and retributive (*vipāka*). Based on the category of derived matter, these three causes may potentially exist, though they do not necessarily exist in every instance.
The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) refers to the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—which follow the mind; these seven branches serve as causes for one another in mutual relation.
The similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) refers to all preceding moments being causes for subsequent moments of their own similar type.

Regarding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*): it refers to all unwholesome actions and wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) actions of body and speech, which can bring about the ripening of the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as visible form and so forth.

Derived matter has only one cause with respect to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), namely the ripening cause; this is because the two types of action—body and speech—are able to bring about the ripening of the four primary elements.

Having already explained how all phenomena arise from their respective objects, we shall now thoroughly analyze the meaning of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) according to our school’s tenets.

Although it was previously stated in general that all previously arisen minds and mental factors—excluding the very last one—serve as equal-and-immediate conditions, it has not yet been definitively established which mind is immediately followed by how many types of minds arising.
Furthermore, from how many minds does it arise, and by what mind is it produced?
Now, it must be definitively stated that the mind is of many kinds.
How can it be definitively stated based on those [kinds]?
Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are twelve kinds of mind.
What are these twelve?
The verse says:
In the desire realm there are four types of mind: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral;
in the form and formless realms, the unwholesome is excluded; and in the untainted realm, there are two types of mind.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, within the desire realm there are four types of mind: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
Within the form and formless realms, there are respectively three types of mind; that is, excluding the unwholesome, the rest are as described above.
These ten types are said to be with outflows (sāsrava).
As for the mind without outflows (anāsrava), there are only two types, namely, that of the learner (śaikṣa) and that of the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
Together, they constitute twelve.
Regarding the mutual production of these twelve minds, the verse says:
The wholesome mind of the desire realm produces nine; It, in turn, arises from eight.
The defiled arises from ten and produces four; The remaining [neutral] arises from five and produces seven.
Wholesome form-born [consciousness] gives rise to eleven; it, in turn, arises from nine.
Obscured [neutral] arises from eight; it, in turn, gives rise to six.
Unobscured-neutral arises from three; it, in turn, can give rise to six.
The wholesome mind of the formless realm gives rise to nine; this, in turn, arises from six.
The defiled mind arises from seven, while the non-obscured-unspecified is explained as being like that of the form realm.
The mind of training arises from four and gives rise to five; the remaining minds arise from five and give rise to four.
The Treatise says:

Nine minds arise immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm; namely, four of its own realm and two minds of the form realm—the wholesome and the defiled minds—which arise respectively at the time of entering meditative absorption and at the stage of rebirth-linking.
What kind of virtuous mind arises?
Furthermore, by which stage is it subsumed?
This arises as a preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) at the initial stage.

If, at a later time, one attains the state of being free from desire (*vairāgya-lābha*), because one dwells in accordance with that [attainment], there is no possibility for those [defiled states] to arise; for a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) arising in this realm cannot cause them to manifest.
Some say: "That mind is subsumed under the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold). Others say:
It is also included within the first dhyāna;
some say it is also present in the intermediate dhyāna.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"It even occurs in the second dhyāna, just as when one arises from a leap-concentration (vyutkrāntakasamāpatti) by skipping over stages. Others say:
A non-concentrated mind lacks the power to draw forth a mind of a different level; therefore, that argument is certainly illogical.

Furthermore, in the case of the formless realm, at the moment of rebirth-linking, a wholesome desire-realm mind immediately gives rise to a defiled mind of that [formless] realm, as well as minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), because they are conducive to abiding therein.

Desire-realm wholesome [states] will certainly not give rise to the unobscured-neutral states associated with the form and formless realms, because those are all bound to the minds of their own respective realms; nor will they certainly give rise to the wholesome states of the formless realm, because the latter are distant from these four types of distance: first, distance of the basis (*āśraya-viprakarṣa*); second, distance of the mode of activity (*ākāra-viprakarṣa*); third, distance of the object (*ālambana-viprakarṣa*); and fourth, distance of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viprakarṣa*).

This [desire-realm wholesome mind] in turn arises immediately after eight [minds]: namely, the four minds of its own realm and two minds of the form realm. It arises from those wholesome [minds of the form realm] at the time of emerging from meditative absorption; and when one is afflicted by a defiled samādhi of the first dhyāna, it arises from that defiled mind as a wholesome mind of the desire realm, seeking to rely on the lower wholesome state to prevent falling back.
As for the learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), this refers to the time when they emerge from meditative absorption.

Regarding the defiled—namely, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—each arises immediately after ten [minds], namely: the four of its own realm and the six of the form and formless realms.
Regarding the stage of rebirth, all six types of minds from the upper realms can serve as the final moment of life to produce two types of defiled minds in the desire realm.
Since it is impossible for an uncontaminated mind to give rise to a defiled mind, this [rebirth] does not arise from the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Immediately following this, four minds can arise: namely, the four of its own realm; there is no possibility for others to arise. It is absolutely impossible for a defiled mind of a lower stage to arise immediately after [a mind of] a higher stage or an uncontaminated (anāsrava) mind.

The remainder refers to the unobscured-neutral states bound to the desire realm; this mind arises immediately after five [minds], namely the four of its own realm and the wholesome mind of the form realm, because the transformative mind of the desire realm arises from those.

Immediately following this, it can produce seven types of minds: namely, the four of its own realm; two from the form realm—the wholesome and the defiled (the wholesome being produced when entering meditative absorption, as the desire-realm transformation-mind gives rise to that wholesome mind, and the non-obscured [neutral] mind of the desire realm producing that defiled mind at the moment of rebirth); and one from the formless realm (this non-obscured mind being able to produce that defiled mind at the moment of rebirth).
Thus, having already established the determination regarding the four minds of the desire realm that arise immediately after one another and their respective capacities to produce others:

eleven minds may arise immediately after a wholesome mind of the form realm; that is to say, excluding the non-obscured neutral mind of the formless realm, because the mind born of maturation belongs to its own [respective] realm.
This same [state] arises immediately after nine [states]: namely, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and excluding the unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm.
The obscured-neutral mind arises immediately after eight [states], excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Immediately following this, six types of mind can arise: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-unspecified minds of the desire realm.
The non-obscured-unspecified arises immediately after three types of mind, namely only those of its own realm; there is no possibility for it to arise from any others.
Immediately following this, six minds can arise: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the defiled minds of the desire and formless realms.
Having already explained the mutual arising of the three minds of the form realm, [we shall now discuss the formless realm:

the wholesome mind of the formless realm immediately gives rise to nine minds—namely, excluding the wholesome mind of the desire realm and the unobscured-neutral minds of the desire and form realms. This same mind arises immediately from six minds: namely, the three of its own realm, the wholesome mind of the form realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The obscured-uninterrupted [mind] can immediately give rise to seven minds: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the wholesome mind of the form realm, and the defiled minds of the desire and form realms.

This same mind also arises immediately after seven [minds], namely, excluding the defiled minds of the desire and form realms, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The unobscured [neutral mind] arises immediately after three [minds], as explained for the case of form; that is, the three of its own realm. Any other [possibilities] are irrational.
This very [unobscured neutral mind] can immediately give rise to six minds: the three of its own realm, as well as the defiled [minds] of the desire and form realms.

Having already explained the mutual arising of the three types of mind in the formless realm, we now consider the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*). From four [minds] does the mind of one in training arise without interval: namely, that very mind of one in training and the wholesome minds of the three realms.

Immediately following this, it can give rise to five minds: the aforementioned four minds and the single mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It does not arise from the defiled minds of the three realms, because they are mutually contradictory.
It is not the non-obscured [neutral states], because they are not sharp and clear.

"The rest" refers to those of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); they arise immediately after five [types of minds]: namely, the wholesome [minds] of the three realms, as well as both the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Immediately following this, four types of minds can arise: namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the one mind of the Aśaikṣa (the Unlearner). It does not give rise to the mind of a Śaikṣa (the Learner), because that is not its fruit;
nor does it give rise to defiled or non-obscured-neutral minds, as previously explained.
Having explained how the twelve minds arise from one another,
how are these divided into twenty minds?
The verse says:

The twelve become twenty: namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms are divided into those acquired through application and those acquired by birth; the non-obscured-unspecified minds of the desire realm are divided into four:
those of maturation, those of deportment, those of craftsmanship, and those of supernormal powers.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the mind of craftsmanship, the remaining numbers are as previously stated.
The treatise says:
The wholesome minds of the three realms are each divided into two types, namely, those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the non-obscured (*anivṛta*) [mind] is divided into four types: first, that born of maturation (*vipākaja*); second, the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); and fourth, the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñāphala*).

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the non-obscured mind is divided into three types, excluding the sphere of craftsmanship, because in the higher realms there are no such activities as the various crafts;
and in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no path of deportment because of the absence of activities such as walking and so forth.
Because there is no samādhi that possesses the factors of absorption (*anuparigṛhīta*), there is likewise no supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*).

According to this principle, there are eight [minds] in the desire realm, six in the form realm, and four in the formless realm; including the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they total twenty.

Regarding these twenty [minds] that arise mutually: first, concerning the eight types of minds in the desire realm, it is said that from the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*), ten [minds] arise immediately thereafter. These are the seven minds of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) because a mind of its own kind in a meditative absorption arises without interval—as well as one mind of the form realm, which is the wholesome mind of application, along with the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This, in turn, arises immediately after eight [minds]: namely, four from its own realm—two wholesome and two defiled—as well as two from the form realm—the preparatory and the obscured—and those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).

The innate wholesome mind arises immediately after nine minds: namely, seven of its own realm—excluding the fruition-of-superknowledge mind—and the obscured-neutral minds of the form and formless realms.
This same mind, in turn, arises from eleven minds: namely, seven of its own realm—excluding the fruition-of-superknowledge mind—and two of the form realm—the preparatory and the obscured-neutral.

Both the *śaikṣa* (learner) and *aśaikṣa* (non-learner) minds are included. Two defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*) arise immediately after seven [minds], namely the seven of their own realm, excluding the mind of fruition (*abhiñā-phala-citta*).

These, in turn, arise from fourteen minds: the seven of their own realm, excluding the mind of fruition; the four of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), excluding the preparatory wholesome (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of fruition; and the three of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), excluding the preparatory wholesome.

The *vipāka* and *airyāpathika* minds give rise to eight immediately after them: namely, the six minds of their own realm—excluding the *prāyogika-kuśala* and the *abhijñā-phala-citta*—as well as the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the form and formless realms.
This same [artistic mind] arises immediately after seven minds of its own realm, namely the seven excluding the result-of-communication mind.
Immediately after the artistic mind, six minds arise, namely the six of its own realm excluding the preparatory wholesome mind and the result-of-communication mind.
Furthermore, this [resultant mind] arises immediately after seven [minds], excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

Immediately after the mind of supernormal fruition, two [minds] arise: one from its own realm, namely the mind of supernormal fruition itself, and one from the form realm, namely the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
This [resultant mind] also arises immediately after two [minds]: namely, the two minds previously mentioned that take their own form as their object.

Having explained how the minds of the desire realm arise from one another, we now explain that among the six types of minds in the form realm, twelve arise immediately after the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*): namely, the six minds of its own realm, the three minds of the desire realm—namely, those of application, those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), and the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*)—as well as the single wholesome mind of application of the formless realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This [mind] in turn arises immediately after ten [minds]: namely, the four minds of its own realm—excluding those of the *airyāpathika* and *vipākaja* types—as well as two from the desire realm—the *prāyogika* and *abhijñā-phala*—and the two from the formless realm—the *prāyogika* and the *nivṛta-avyākṛta*—along with the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* minds.

Immediately after a wholesome mind acquired at birth, eight minds arise: namely, five of its own realm (excluding the mind of supernormal fruition), two from the desire realm (the unwholesome and the obscured-neutral), and one from the form realm (the obscured-neutral).
This [state] in turn arises immediately after five [minds], namely the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

Immediately after the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind, nine minds arise: the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition; and the four of the desire realm—two wholesome and two defiled.

This [mind] in turn arises from eleven minds: namely, the five of its own realm—excluding the mind of fruition; the three of the desire realm—namely, the wholesome mind acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*), the functional mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), and the mind of maturation (*vipākaja*); and the three of the formless realm—excluding the wholesome mind produced through application (*prāyogika*).

The resultant (*vipāka*) and the deportment (*airyāpathika*) minds arise immediately after seven types of mind: namely, four from their own realm—excluding the preparatory wholesome (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*); two from the desire realm—the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); and one from the formless realm—the obscured-neutral.
This [resultant mind] in turn arises immediately after five minds, namely the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
Immediately after the mind of supernormal fruition, two minds arise: the two of its own realm, namely the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the supernormal fruition minds.
This [unobscured-neutral mind] also arises immediately after two [minds]: namely, the two minds of its own realm previously mentioned.

Having explained how the minds of the form realm arise from one another, we shall next explain that among the four types of minds in the formless realm, the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala*) gives rise to seven immediately after it: namely, the four of its own realm, the one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) and non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) minds.

This, in turn, arises immediately after six [minds]: namely, three from its own realm—excluding only the *vipāka* [mind]—one preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala*) of the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Immediately after a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), seven minds arise: namely, the four of its own realm, one obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the form realm, and two minds of the desire realm—the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified.
This [state] in turn arises immediately after four states, namely the four of its own realm.

Immediately after the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), eight states arise: the four of its own realm, the two of the form realm—the preparatory (prayoga) and the obscured—and the two of the desire realm—the unwholesome (akuśala) and the obscured.

This, in turn, arises immediately after ten [minds]: namely, the four of its own realm, the three of the form realm—namely, those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), the ripening (*vipāka*), and the deportment (*airyāpathika*)—and the three of the desire realm; these are named as explained in the case of the form realm.

From a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*), six minds arise in immediate succession: namely, three of its own realm—excluding the wholesome produced by application (*prāyogika-kuśala*)—one obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the form realm, and two minds of the desire realm, namely the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified.
This same [uncontaminated mind] further arises immediately after four [minds], namely, the four of its own realm.

Having explained how the formless minds arise from one another, next we shall explain that from the two types of uncontaminated minds, six arise immediately after the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*): namely, the applied wholesome minds of all three realms, the innate wholesome mind of the desire realm, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This [unshakable mind] in turn arises immediately after four types of minds: namely, the three preparatory minds and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

Immediately after the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), five minds arise; that is, among the six previously mentioned as arising from the mind of one in training, one excludes the single mind of one in training itself.
Furthermore, these [minds] arise immediately after five types of minds: namely, the three preparatory minds, as well as those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
For what reason, then, can a mind of maturation (*vipāka*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), or deportment (*airyāpathika*) arise immediately after a preparatory mind?

The preparatory wholesome state does not arise immediately after that [wholesome mind], because the mind born of maturation is weak in its power—having been induced by the force of prior karma—and because it is not induced by deliberate effort; thus, it cannot give rise to a preparatory wholesome mind, as the emergence of such a mind does not proceed without the application of effort.
There is no contradiction in the preparatory (*prayoga*) mind arising immediately before that [wholesome mind].
