Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"There is karma and there is its maturation, but an agent cannot be found."

This refers to that which is able to relinquish these aggregates and is able to continue other aggregates, and so forth, as explained at length in the *Nyāyānusāra* regarding the refutation of the four types of self-grasping.
If this is so, upon what object do the non-Buddhists give rise to their grasping for a self?
Although there is no self-nature distinct from the aggregates that serves as the objective referent for grasping, it is only upon the aggregates themselves as objects that grasping arises.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whatever grasping of a self there is, whatever one perceives accordingly, all arises only with respect to the five aggregates of clinging."
Although there is no such real nature of a self as that asserted by the non-Buddhists, there is the provisional self spoken of in accordance with worldly convention within the holy teachings.
Since there is no real self, upon what basis is this provisional self designated?
Although there is no real self, one conventionally designates a "self" in accordance with worldly usage with respect to the aggregates (*skandha*).
For what reason is it known that this designation of a "self" relies solely upon the aggregates and nothing else?
Because both defiled and purified phenomena are established only in dependence upon the aggregates; thus, the self is truly non-existent.

Furthermore, the defiled phenomena depend solely upon the momentary continuity of the aggregates; driven by the power of afflictions and karma, this continuity of the intermediate state enters the mother’s womb.
Just as the flame of a lamp, through a momentary succession, moves to another location, so too it is with the aggregates (*skandha*).

Furthermore, in the desire realm, if one has not yet abandoned craving, improper mental attention arises conditioned by the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*); from this, afflictions such as craving arise. Inferior, middling, or superior volitions (*cetanā*) and consciousness arise simultaneously; once arisen, they are able to draw forth future undesirable fruits and also serve as the conditions for the immediate arising of subsequent consciousnesses and so forth.

When the immediately preceding consciousness and its associates arise by observing homogeneous or heterogeneous conditions that co-arose with them, they may be wholesome, defiled, or indeterminate in nature; once arisen, they are further able to project their own future results and serve as the generative condition for the immediately succeeding consciousness and its associates.
With this as a condition, one should understand that each subsequent stage in succession can draw forth two fruits as appropriate.

This continuity of the aggregates experiences the factors such as the lifespan drawn forth by the afflictions and karma of previous lives; when the power of that maturation (*vipāka*) reaches its exhaustion, the death-consciousness, together with its basis, arrives at the state of cessation and serves as the condition for the arising of the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and so forth.

Among these, the various aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava), through the power of prior afflictions and karma, proceed like a magical illusion toward the place of birth; upon reaching the mother’s womb, when the intermediate state ceases, it again acts as the condition for the arising of the aggregates of the birth-existence (upapattibhava).
For example, although the flame of a lamp perishes moment by moment, it is able to proceed to another location through a continuous succession of causes and effects without interruption.
Therefore, even though there is no self (*ātman*), the principle that the aggregates (*skandha*) perish momentarily yet are able to migrate to future lives is established.

These very aggregates, drawn forth by the power of prior afflictions and karma, gradually increase in succession; throughout a single lifetime, they continue in a revolving stream, and further, through afflictions and karma, they proceed toward another world.

It is observed that because causes differ, their effects must necessarily be distinct; therefore, the magnitude of the fruits of various projecting karmas (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is not equal. The length or brevity of the life-span as its fruit results from the differences in karma.

Depending on whether the karma projected is increased or diminished, the life-span—mutually dependent with the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) and so forth—gradually increases through each successive stage, such as the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so on.
What are those called the *kalala* and so forth?
They refer to the transformation and differentiation within the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*), increasing gradually until the stage where the sense faculties mature.

Through the conjunction of conditions such as attention directed toward internal and external bases (*āyatana*), afflictions such as craving arise; one thereby performs and accumulates various types of karma. Due to these afflictions and karma, there occurs once again—as before—the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as it proceeds toward another world.

One should know that this wheel of existence has no beginning. That is to say, with afflictions as the cause, one is able to create various karmas; with karma as the cause, one is able to project and bring forth birth; and with birth again as the cause, afflictions and karma arise. From these afflictions and karma, there is yet further birth. Thus, it is known that the wheel of existence revolves in a cycle without a starting point.
If one maintains that there is a beginning, then that beginning must be without a cause.
Since the beginning would be causeless, all other things would likewise arise spontaneously, as there would be no distinct cause for them.
This contradicts what is observed in experience; therefore, it is certain that there is no phenomenon that arises without a cause.

There is not a single permanent phenomenon that can even slightly function as a cause; this has already been extensively refuted in the critique of Īśvara. Therefore, saṃsāra definitely has no beginning.
Just as with grains and the like, which continue in a successive succession, it nevertheless has an end because its causes are exhausted.
Just as when seeds and the like are exhausted, sprouts and the like do not arise, so too, since birth and death no longer exist, there is ultimate purity.
Therefore, defilement and purification are established solely in dependence upon the aggregates; thus, the clinging to a real self is rendered useless.
*Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Fourteen.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four, Part Three: An Analysis of Dependent Origination. Having already explained the principles of the internal and external *kalala* and so forth, as well as the continuity of cause and effect, one should know that this is precisely what is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
What are the characteristics of such dependent origination?
The verse says:
Such dependent origination consists of twelve factors across three time periods.
Two each for the prior and subsequent limits, and eight for the middle based on completeness.
The treatise says:
It is not that dependent origination consists of only twelve factors.
How is this known to be so?
As the root treatise states:
"What is dependent origination?"
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

However, in the sūtras where dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained, the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are sometimes fully set forth, as stated in the *Paramārthaśūnyatāsūtra* and other such texts.
Some say there are eleven, as in the *Jñānavastu-sūtra* and other scriptures;
some say there are only ten, as in the *Upamāna-siddhi-sūtra* and others;
and some say there are nine, as taught in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*.
Some say there are eight, as the sūtra states:
"There are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not know the nature of all phenomena as it truly is," and so forth.
For what reason do these various distinctions stated [in the treatise] differ from those in the sūtras?

Treatises follow the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), while sūtras conform to what is appropriate for conversion; therefore, within the *sūtras*, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is analyzed and explained differently according to the specific capacities of those to be converted.
Thus, a treatise may clarify the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), whereas the meaning of a sūtra may not be definitive.

While the treatises explain this in general terms for both sentient and insentient beings, the sūtras speak only in reference to those categorized as sentient. It is by relying upon sentient beings that defilement and purification can be established.

The Buddha revealed these two for the sake of sentient beings; it was solely for this purpose that the Buddha appeared in the world. Therefore, within the sūtras, he speaks in reference to sentient beings, desiring to establish this great benefit.

Within the analysis of the various links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are infinite categories of meaning and distinctions; for now, I shall briefly explain the twelve links that constitute the uninterrupted succession of the three lifetimes:

first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); third, consciousness (*vijñāna*); fourth, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); fifth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); sixth, contact (*sparśa*); seventh, sensation (*vedanā*); eighth, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); ninth, grasping (*upādāna*); tenth, becoming (*bhava*); eleventh, birth (*jāti*); and twelfth, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Regarding the "three periods": first, the past period; second, the future period; and third, the middle period—these are the three lifetimes of the past, future, and present.
How are the twelve links established across these three periods?
This means that two members are established for each of the prior and posterior limits, with eight members in the middle limit, thus totaling twelve.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the prior limit, which refers to past existence.
Birth and old age and death belong to the posterior limit, which refers to future birth.
The remaining eight factors belong to the middle limit, which refers to the present birth.

Five fruits are drawn forth by two causes of the anterior limit, and three causes are required for the two fruits of the posterior limit. It is not the case that every single lifetime possesses all eight of these; rather, it is said that there are eight branches based on the complete case.
What is meant by "complete"?
It refers to being without deficiency in its constituent parts, or being summoned by fully developed afflictions and karma—meaning it is induced by previously predominant afflictions and karma.

Here, the intended meaning is that a *pudgala* who passes through all stages is called "complete"; this does not apply to those who die prematurely, nor to those in the form or formless realms, nor to the *kalala* stage and so forth, because these lack various stages.

World-Honored One, you have spoken of the twelve [links] as being complete only with respect to a limited portion of individuals within the desire realm, as stated in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, where the Buddha told Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to enter the womb, would it be able to increase and expand?"
"No, World-Honored One! ...
[and so on, as extensively explained]."

Therefore, if there is a person (pudgala) who, in the immediately preceding life, produced ignorance (avidyā) and formations (saṃskāra), they fully bring about the five links beginning with consciousness (vijñāna) in the present life.
Furthermore, by producing craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and existence (bhava) in the present life, they bring about the two links beginning with birth (jāti) in the subsequent life.

It should be understood that this sutra speaks in reliance upon that [system]. If one were to establish the various links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) based on all *pudgalas* indiscriminately, it would result in confusion.

That is to say, for some, the five present links might not be the results of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) from the immediately preceding life, nor might the links of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in a subsequent life be the results of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) in the present life.

None of those [other views] clarify the intended meaning of this sūtra. Do not, upon seeing that the fruit and cause are separated by a vast interval, suspect that there is no capacity for cause and effect to interact and respond.

One should know that the members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are, in brief, only two; they are divided into the prior and posterior limits as seven members and five members respectively, because the fruit and the cause are subsumed under the categories of "effect" and "cause."
Alternatively, there are five members for the cause and seven members for the fruit, because the cause subsumes the cause and the fruit subsumes the fruit.

That is to say: present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are identical to past ignorance (*avidyā*); the present member of existence (*bhava*) is identical to past formations (*saṃskāra*); present consciousness (*vijñāna*) is identical to future birth (*jāti*); and the remaining four present members are identical to future aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This is called the distinction between the two divisions of cause and fruit.
Since it has been stated that the twelve links are established across the three time periods— namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*),
and so forth up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)— what phenomenon here is designated as "ignorance"? And what phenomenon is designated as "old age and death"?
The verse says:
Ignorance is the state of past afflictions; the various past karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*);
consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the aggregates at the moment of linking birth; and prior to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

From the arising of the sense organs such as the eye, prior to the three [conditions] and before the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), there is contact (sparśa) which is the cause of the three types of feeling (vedanā); it is called "contact" because it has not yet been fully understood.
Prior to sensual craving (kāmatṛṣṇā) is feeling; craving for the necessities of life is sensual craving.
To obtain various objects, one universally pursues them; this is called "grasping.
That which is said to be capable of actualizing, namely karma that draws forth the fruit of future existence, is "becoming.
The linking to future existence is "birth," leading to old age and death, which are to be experienced.
The Treatise says:
From the state of the various afflictions throughout past lives until the present ripening of the fruit, this is collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
For what reason is the term "ignorance" used to speak of the afflictions in general?
Because it is the definitive cause for drawing forth future existence (*punarbhava*).

Karma, being incited by afflictions (*kleśa*), is able to draw forth future existence; since there is no future existence when there is karma without afflictions, such karma cannot draw forth future existence.

When the various conditioned formations arise, craving and the other afflictions all possess functional activity within them; since those formations necessarily depend upon ignorance at the stage of their origination, the term "ignorance" is used here as a general designation for the afflictions.
If that is so, why is it that only the afflictions of the preceding life are collectively termed "ignorance" (avidyā), while those of this life are not?
It is because only the afflictions of the preceding life resemble ignorance.
When afflictions such as greed have not yet yielded their fruit, their power remains unimpaired and they are said to be "clear and sharp."
If, after attaining the fruit, its acquisition, bestowal, and utilization are deficient, it is not called "clear and sharp.
Even if its power of ignorance has not yet been diminished, it is still not clear and sharp, because when it manifests, it is likewise difficult to discern.

The various afflictions (kleśa) from previous lives that reach the present life have their power diminished because they have already produced their fruits; thus, their characteristics are not distinct and resemble the category of ignorance (avidyā). Therefore, it is only the afflictions of previous lives that can be designated by the term "ignorance."
It should not be said that the designation of names and concepts applies equally to the *saṃskāras* (formative forces) as well; it applies only to those of the same class.
From the stage of karma—such as merit—in a previous life until the maturation of the present fruit, this entire continuum is collectively termed *saṃskāra*.
The phrase "the stage of the first link" extends through to old age and death.
The characteristics of various karmas, such as merit and so forth, shall be discussed extensively in the *Karma-pāda*.
For what reason is this past karma alone designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*)?
The name is established in accordance with its meaning. What is that meaning?
It refers to that which has arisen based on the convergence of various conditions, and which has been produced through the mutual conjunction of the forces of delusion.

Furthermore, it can act as a condition that brings about the convergence of its effects, or, once this convergence has occurred, it can serve as the condition for the effect; this is what is meant by the "actual meaning" (vastu-artha) that follows the designation "formations" (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding those karmic fruits from previous lives that are now ripening: when their characteristics are fully perfected, they independently receive the name "formations. By this, the karma for fruits in future lives is already excluded, because the fruits of that karma have not yet ripened.

If a factor is not established as "karma" (saṃskāra) because its characteristics are not yet complete, then since all [factors] that serve as the substantial cause for their own resultant maturation possess these very characteristics, should they not all be established as "karma"?
What is the nature of this?
It refers to all that is non-karma, as well as karma that has arisen previously and has already produced its fruit.
Although this principle holds true, it is taught preeminently that karma is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it is most excellent in drawing forth its fruit.

Since the karmic fruits of the present life are coarse, manifest, and easy to know, one can thereby believe in and know the karma that produces the fruits of past lives; for this reason, only this [present karma] is established as bearing the name "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*).

Although all causes that have already produced their results should collectively be termed *saṃskāra*, this term here refers specifically to those ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*) capable of summoning a future existence. Therefore, there is no fault of the definition being too narrow to include everything called *saṃskāra*. Consequently, it is established that only those karmas performed in a previous life that induce this present life are uniquely designated as *saṃskāra*.

At the very moment of linking rebirth within the mother’s womb and so forth, the five aggregates existing for that single kṣaṇa are termed "consciousness" (vijñāna), because consciousness is predominant during that kṣaṇa.
This is exclusively mental consciousness (manovijñāna), as the conditions for the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses have not yet been fully assembled at this stage.
What is the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)?

It refers to that which is capable of cognizing; for the Buddha has stated that that which is capable of cognizing is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). As it is said in the *Phalguna-sūtra*:
I never say that there is one who can cognize.

This statement of "not saying" expresses the sense of non-manifestation; its intent is to preclude the existence of a self-sufficient, unconditioned, and non-dependent self as a cognizer, but it does not preclude that consciousness has the nature of being a cognizer.
The *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra* negates a separate agent because it is accepted that the essence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is itself the agent.
From the moment after the consciousness that links rebirth until before the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise, the intermediate stages are collectively termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Is it not the case that since the two bases of body and mind have already arisen, one should say that these [six] exist prior to the arising of the six bases?
This objection is not valid, because they are not yet fully developed and superior.
That is to say, in the preceding two stages the bases are still deficient and inferior; it is only within the stage of the six bases that the bases become fully developed and superior.
Furthermore, it is only at the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that the two faculties of body and mind are fully attained, because they are present in their actual functioning.

That is to say, it is only upon reaching the stage of the differentiation of limbs that the male and female faculties are obtained; it is at that time that all the groups of consciousnesses (*vijñānakāya*) are permitted to arise simultaneously.

Therefore, it is only within the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that the body and mind bases (*kāya- and mana-āyatana*) are fully attained and manifest in their entirety. For this reason, it is well said that the stage prior to the arising of the six sense bases is the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This explanation is correct.
From the arising of the four faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue, prior to the conjunction of the three, it is designated as the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

That is to say, after *nāmarūpa* and once the six sense bases have arisen, up until the stage where the faculty, object, and consciousness have not yet fully conjoined, there is a gradual increase through the stages of inferior, medium, and superior; this entire period is collectively termed the "six sense bases."
How could it be said that the three [factors] have not yet attained union when consciousnesses do not arise in this stage?

Furthermore, there is no single stage in which mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise; even in the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises. How much more so in the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), where it would be incorrect to say there is no union of the three. While other groups of consciousness may also arise, they are neither constant nor predominant; therefore, the designation "union of the three" has not been established for them.
Within this stage, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) alone are predominant; therefore, the distinction of this stage is designated by means of the six sense bases.
The Blessed One said:
"The coming together of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—is called contact (*sparśa*)."
This means that when one has not yet understood the distinct causes of the three types of feeling, but merely possesses the conjunction of the three [bases], that stage is called contact (*sparśa*).
The specific meanings of the various types of contact shall be discussed extensively later.
Once one has understood the distinct characteristics of the causes of the three types of feeling, [the next stage follows].

When sexual desire has not yet arisen, this stage is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). This means that while one is already able to discern conditions such as pleasure and pain, sexual craving has not yet come into operation; thus, it is designated as the stage of feeling.
The specific distinctions of feeling shall be discussed extensively later.
When one experiences craving for excellent material requisites and sexual desire, yet has not yet extensively pursued them, this stage is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving).
"Excellent material requisites" refers to excellent wealth; craving for these as well as sexual desire are collectively termed *tṛṣṇā*.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of *tṛṣṇā* (craving) is as [set forth] in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
The stage in which one universally runs about in pursuit of various desirable objects in order to obtain them is called *upādāna* (clinging).

There are four kinds of clinging, namely: clinging to sensual desires (*kāma*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi*), clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*), according to their distinctions.
Because they are capable of grasping, they are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).

These are the afflictions that perform the functions of forming signs, conceptualizing, and karmic activity; specifically, the afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the desire realm—excluding views—are called "desire-grasping" (*kāma-upādāna*), just as one speaks of a "horse-cart" and so forth.
The four views within the three realms are called the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Those [clinging to] precepts and observances are called the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the form and formless realms, excluding the five views, are called the clinging to the discourse of self (*ātma-vāda-parāmarśa*).
These various types of grasping will be analyzed in detail in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Latent Dispositions).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not established as a separate form of grasping because independent ignorance is not intense and is not of a nature that seeks liberation; furthermore, associated ignorance is able to grasp only through the power of other afflictions.
The view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established separately from the other views because it possesses the most predominant power for accumulating karmic force.

In the process of accumulating karma, its power is equal to that of the [other] four views; yet, by means of this single view, karma is made to blaze intensely, causing one to deviate from the Noble Path and remain far removed from liberation. Therefore, the view of precepts and observances is established as a distinct category of "clinging" (*parāmarśa*).

The term "grasping" (*upādāna*) is used here to signify the sense of "clinging. Although all categories of afflictions are capable of clinging, these two types of grasping possess a superior sense of clinging; therefore, only these two are designated as "grasping," because they are the most stubborn forms of attachment toward others.

However, among these two, the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is particularly strong; because it functions with such intense attachment as to obscure [the truth], it is established as a separate "grasping" apart from the others.

Since all four views have discernment (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, they possess a stronger sense of "grasping" than other afflictions; thus, by including these four and excluding the rest, they are established as "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

The other two types of grasping are established because there are distinctions between the various afflictions regarding their fixed or unfixed states, and because there are distinctions between their causes—whether they are unwholesome or neutral.
The remaining detailed analysis is as set forth in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Precisely because grasping (*upādāna*) functions as a condition in this way, when one runs about in pursuit of various desirable objects, it inevitably induces karma that draws forth future existence (*punarbhava*).

That is to say, when grasping becomes intensified through the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one pursues various wholesome and unwholesome objects; in order to obtain them, one accumulates numerous pure and impure karmas capable of drawing forth a future existence. At the stage when this karma arises, it is collectively termed the "existence" link (*bhavāṅga*).
It should be understood that herein, because existence (*bhava*) by means of this and based upon this is capable of producing future results, it is established as "existence.
There are two kinds of existence: namely, karmic existence (*karma-bhava*) and resultant existence (*vipāka-bhava*).
In this context, only karmic existence is taken up to explain the production of future results, because it possesses the nature of being the proximate cause.
Because the Sūtra states that "existence has grasping as its condition," it is only through the condition of grasping that karmic existence arises;
just as, in the past limit, formations have ignorance as their condition, so too does karmic existence in the future limit arise with grasping as its condition.
The very moment of linking rebirth is established as the "link of birth" (*jāti-aṅga*), because within this life, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as its condition.
The initial stage of linking rebirth is called the "link of consciousness" (*vijñāna-aṅga*), because it serves as the condition for the existence (*bhava*) in the future life.
The stage of initial rebirth-linking is called the "birth" (*jāti*) member, because this name is precisely required for this stage.

That is to say, while the function of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is distinct in the present life, the function of birth is most prominent in the future life; thus, the name of the member is established according to its own predominant function.

Alternatively, because other sūtras speak of birth as suffering, it is called "birth" so that those who perform karma leading to future existence in the heavenly realms may develop revulsion and renounce it.
Or, it is called "birth" to demonstrate that all karma for future existence is capable of summoning bitter fruits, thereby causing one not to create such karma.

Therefore, other sūtras state that the ultimate cessation of suffering, such as birth and so forth, is called *parinirvāṇa*. For this reason, the term "birth" (*jāti*) refers to the manifest presence of the future fruit.
All stages from after this branch of "birth" until the intermediate stage prior to the branch of "feeling" (*vedanā*) in the future are collectively termed "aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Just as the four factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling exist in the present, these same four stages in a future birth are termed "aging and death.
In order to cause one to weary of and abandon the desire for a future existence, the faults of that future life are manifested through the designation "aging and death"; thus the Sūtra says:
"One should know that the arising of the five aggregates of clinging is the meaning of the occurrence of aging and death."
The remaining determinations are as explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Furthermore, the various classifications of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are taught as fourfold:
first, the momentary (*kṣaṇika*); second, the prolonged (*prākarṣika*); third, the continuous (*sāmbandhika*); and fourth, the situational (*āvasthika*).
Others further state that this reveals the functional capacity of phenomena (*dharma*).
Herein, "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the simultaneous occurrence of cause and effect.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness and so forth arise.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, delusion arises, as well as the defiled attention produced thereby."

In this context, whatever delusion exists is ignorance (*avidyā*); the seeking that arises from delusion is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*); and what is manifested by craving is called karma (*karma*). Thus, within a single moment, there is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Other masters say: Within a single moment, all twelve links exist substantially and arise simultaneously. For example, in a mind that initiates karma accompanied by craving, delusion is called ignorance (*avidyā*); volition (*cetanā*) is itself formative action (*saṃskāra*); the discernment of objects is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); the three aggregates co-arising with consciousness are collectively termed name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the material sense faculties are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); contact associated with consciousness is called contact (*sparśa*); feeling associated with consciousness is called feeling (*vedanā*); craving itself is called thirst (*tṛṣṇā*); the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) associated with it are called grasping (*upādāna*); the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—initiated by these are called existence (*bhava*); the arising of these various factors is called birth (*jāti*); their maturation and transformation is called aging (*jarā*); and their disintegration is called death (*maraṇa*).
This detailed analysis is as presented in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Regarding the distant continuity of dependent origination—that is, the past and future limits—there are [karmas] to be experienced in subsequent lives and those of indefinite timing.
Due to karma and afflictions, one revolves through beginningless saṃsāra; as it is said, regarding craving and so forth, their original limit is unknowable.
Furthermore, a verse should state:
"In the past, I and you all, regarding the four noble truths..."
"Because they do not see things as they truly are, they have long wandered through birth and death.

This refers to "continuous dependent origination" (*saṃbandha-pratītyasamutpāda*), meaning that causes and effects of both similar and dissimilar types arise in uninterrupted succession and mutual connection.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Ignorance (*avidyā*) as cause gives rise to defiled attachment; because clarity (*vidyā*) is the cause, defiled attachment does not arise.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
From the wholesome, there arise the immediate [result], the defiled, and the neutral;

or conversely, this may be reversed. This refers to the dependent origination of states (*avasthā-pratītyasamutpāda*), which demonstrates the functional capacity of phenomena through the uninterrupted succession of the twelve factors among the three lifetimes. As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Karma is the cause of birth; craving is the cause of arising."
Regarding such distinctions in functional capacity among these five types of dependent origination, what did the Blessed One teach?
The verse says:
The Buddha spoke according to the various stages, establishing the names of the members based on their predominance.
The treatise says:
The Buddha spoke of the various dependent originations (pratītyasamutpāda) by relying upon their respective stages.
If each of these factors contains all five aggregates, for what reason are they designated specifically by names such as "ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth?
Because ignorance and the others are predominant within their respective stages, they are designated by those specific names based on their predominance.

This means that in whichever state ignorance is predominant, the five aggregates of that state are collectively termed "ignorance"; likewise, up to the state in which old age and death are predominant, the five aggregates of that state are collectively termed "old age and death. Therefore, although their substance is the same, there is no fault in assigning these distinct names.

In this way, the five aggregates of the preceding stage serve as conditions that collectively induce the five aggregates of the subsequent stage; this should be stated for all such cases, one and all.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) falsely claims that the above interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this so? Because the sūtras present different explanations.
As it is said in a sūtra:
What is ignorance? It refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the past, and so forth, as explained at length.
This is a definitive teaching; it cannot be suppressed or forced into being of non-definitive meaning.

Therefore, what was previously stated does not contradict the meaning of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, for there is no contradiction here, as it is presented according to its heading and explanation.

That is to say, although craving and other factors also serve as conditions for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), only ignorance (*avidyā*) is mentioned as the heading, because it is viewed as the specific cause.
Furthermore, although all twelve bases (*āyatana*) serve as conditions for contact (*sparśa*), it is by observing specific causes that only the six bases are designated.

Moreover, although perception (*saṃjñā*) and other factors also take contact as their condition, by observing specific causes, only the sensation conditioned by contact (*sparśapratyayā vedanā*) is specified.
There are indeed many such instances of this kind.

Just as when observing specific causes one cites only a small portion, so too here, one has merely explained what was indicated [by the text]. How, then, can you insist that this constitutes a definitive (nītārtha) teaching?
This detailed analysis is as presented in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
For what reason are the members of dependent origination established across the three time periods?
The verse says:
Regarding the past, future, and middle limits, [the teaching] is for the purpose of dispelling the delusions of others.
The Commentary says:
The twelve links are established based on the category of sentient beings, in order to dispel their delusions regarding the three time periods.
What is meant by "delusion regarding the three periods"?
As the Sūtra says:
"Did I exist, or did I not exist, in past lives?"
"What was I in the past? In what way was I in the past?
Shall I exist or not exist in future lives?"
"What shall I become? How shall I become? What is this self in the present world?"
What is this "I"? To whom does this "I" belong? Who will this "I" become?
In order to eliminate such delusions regarding the three time periods, the Sūtra speaks only of the dependent origination of sentient beings.

The dependent origination of the three time periods has already been explained above; that is to say: ignorance, formations, and birth-and-old-age-and-death, together with consciousness through feeling.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the phenomena of dependent origination and dependently arisen, is able to perceive them with correct wisdom as they truly are, he will certainly not be deluded regarding the three periods of time, such as [thinking], 'Did I exist or not exist in the past?'"
Therefore, in order to eliminate delusion regarding the three time periods (*traiyadhvika*), dependent origination is established solely in relation to sentient beings.
Although there are twelve links, they are characterized by three or two natures: the "three" refer to afflictions, karma, and the basis; the "two" refer to result and cause.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
Three are afflictions, two are karmas; seven things are also called fruits.
The fruit is abbreviated and the cause is abbreviated; by means of the middle [link], the two may be inferred.
The treatise says:
Ignorance is the cause for the past limit, while craving and grasping are the causes for the future limit; these three types have affliction as their nature.
The causal formations of the past limit and the existence that is the cause of the future limit—these two types have karma as their nature.

The five factors beginning with consciousness in the past limit and birth and old age and death in the future limit—these seven are called "factual bases" (*vastu*), because they are either karma itself or the substratum for karma.
These seven matters are also termed "fruits," while by extension the remaining five are also termed "causes," because their intrinsic nature consists of afflictions and karma.
For what reason is cause and fruit explained in detail regarding the middle period [of existence]?
The future limit briefly summarizes the fruit, and the past limit briefly summarizes the cause; the middle limit is easy to understand and should be explained in detail.
Since the two [extremes] are fully established by inferring from the middle, they are not explained separately; to do so would be redundant.
How are the two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) established separately?
The initial moment of craving is designated by the term "craving.
When this very continuity increases, expands, and becomes intense, it is established as "grasping," because the continuity of grasping at objects becomes increasingly firm and violent.
Within each individual object, there is a primary craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which, when combined, constitutes multiple moments; therefore, only two moments are mentioned.
For what reason, among all the states of present afflictions (*kleśa*), is craving alone specifically mentioned and not the other afflictions?
Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is easy to understand its gratification (*āsvāda*) and its danger (*ādīnava*); among the other afflictions (*kleśa*), these characteristics are difficult to discern.

Craving is the predominant cause for the production of future existence (*punarbhava*); thus, the Blessed One specifically taught [its characteristics] so that its danger might be known. How, then, can one be made to diligently seek the path of remedy? For this reason, he spoke only of the distinctions between the two states of craving—momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and continuous (*prabandhika*)—and not of the other afflictions.

However, the term "grasping" (upādāna) is used here as a general designation that subsumes all afflictions; if this dependent origination consisted of only twelve links, then old age and death would have no fruit, and apart from the cultivation of the path of antidotes, birth and death would necessarily have an end.
If ignorance were without a cause, then because ignorance is the beginning [of the cycle], birth and death would have a starting point.

Alternatively, one would have to establish further factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and those further factors would require yet others, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s holy teaching would consequently be incomplete;
yet this must not be admitted. This objection is invalid because you have not understood the principle of dependent origination as it has been explained.
How, then, should this principle of dependent origination be understood?
The verse says:
From afflictions arise further afflictions and karma; from karma arises the basis of existence;
from the basis of existence arise further afflictions. Such is the principle of the links of dependent origination.
The Commentary states:

The word "only" (*kevala*) precisely indicates that the number of links is fixed; it also indicates that karma and afflictions may arise together, or that what arises after an affliction is itself an affliction. This clarifies the meaning that when an affliction arises, karma may be simultaneous with it or may follow it. By means of this principle, the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are comprehensively subsumed, thereby effectively resolving the objections previously raised.
From affliction arises affliction, meaning that craving gives rise to grasping.
From affliction arises karma, meaning that grasping gives rise to becoming, and ignorance gives rise to volitional formations.
From karma arises the actualized entity, meaning that volitional formations give rise to consciousness, and becoming gives rise to birth.

Regarding the arising of phenomena from phenomena: this refers to how name-and-form arises from the link of consciousness, up to and including how the link of feeling arises from contact, and how aging and death arise from the link of birth.
The arising of afflictions from active engagement refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arising from feeling (*vedanā*).

Since this alone constitutes the logical basis for establishing the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), it is already established that old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the causes of both objective entities and afflictions, as they correspond to the four present members; and it is established that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the result of both objective entities and afflictions, as it corresponds to the present craving and grasping (*upādāna*). Why, then, would it be necessary to postulate further members of dependent origination?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"In this way, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

This expresses the meaning of the mutual elucidation between the two limits—the past and the future. Consequently, there is no fault of there being old age and death without ignorance, or of there being results without causes, nor of having a beginning or an end.
Within this meditative absorption, the meaning of cause and effect is fully encompassed; thus, there is no fault of establishing further factors that would lead to an infinite regress.
Because the Buddha has exhaustively taught cause and effect without omission, there is no deficiency or loss in the sacred teaching.
As the Blessed One said:
"I shall teach you the dharma of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and the dharmas arisen from conditions (pratītyasamutpanna).
What is the difference between these two?
The various masters have offered diverse interpretations of these two lines, as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Regarding their definitive meaning, the verse states:
"The intended meaning here is correctly explained: The cause arises; the fruit has already been produced."
The Treatise says:
The causal portions of the various members are called dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Why is this so?
Because it serves as a condition capable of producing an effect, and because dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained in terms of the mutual connection between cause and effect;
this meaning of dependent origination is established solely by means of the term "condition" (*pratyaya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is dependent origination?

It means that because this exists, that exists; and because this arises, that arises—namely, with ignorance as condition there is volitional formations, and so on, up to birth as condition there is old age and death."
Having spoken thus, he further said:
"In this context, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), up to and including its ultimate non-erroneousness, is called dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
What is meant by 'the nature of phenomena' in this context?"
This means that within the mutual dependence of cause and effect, the causal capacity is termed "dharmatā.
Because there must be a cause, the cause and effect can exist; they are mutually dependent and do not occur without a cause.
In this way, the term "nature" (*dhātu*) signifies the sense of being able to produce; thus, only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) receive the name "nature.

Although this sutra does not explicitly show that the causal nature within the mutual connection of cause and effect is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it nonetheless reveals the meaning of dependent origination through the word "condition" (*pratyaya*). Therefore, one should know that the causal nature receives the name "dependent origination," because the word "condition" functions solely to indicate the sense of being able to produce.

Because they are able to manifest a fruit, they are called conditions; therefore, the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat are not equivalent and immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), as there is no fruit to be manifested by them.
It is precisely by this reasoning that it is proven the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is established as necessarily referring to the relationship between cause and effect.

Therefore, in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*, the Buddha taught that the phenomena herein are conventional designations (*prajñapti*), stating: "ignorance conditions formative forces," and so on, up to "birth conditions aging and death."

Because it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is established by means of conventional terminology (*prajñapti-śabda*), which refers to the meaning of cause and effect being mutually related.
The resultant portions of the various members are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Why is this so?
Because all these arise from conditions, and because "result" (*phala*) is a designation for the accomplishment of phenomena, this meaning is established only for phenomena that have already arisen.
Since the accomplishment of *nirvāṇa* occurs through its attainment once it has arisen, it too is called a "result" by virtue of having arisen.
Alternatively, if this is explained by way of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no room for the objection that *nirvāṇa* is included therein.

If the meaning of "result" (*phala*) is restricted to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), then that is what is being clarified here, as in the case of the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).

The meaning of the result of dharmas in the past and present is determinate, and thus they are called "dependently arisen"; since the meaning of the result of dharmas in the future is not determinate, it is set aside and not mentioned.
This brief definition is that the nature of the arising of dharmas is termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
All phenomena of the past and present are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because their status as results is certain.

That is to say, within the mutual dependence of cause and effect, that which serves as the causal factor is designated as "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), while that which is determined to be the result is called "dependently arisen."
Furthermore, that which is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) among these is so named because it is able to act as the condition for the arising of various effects.
Among these, those phenomena that are effects are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because they do not arise apart from conditions in the past or present.
In this way, both meanings are established together, because all the members possess the nature of cause and effect.

Although there is no difference in the substantial entity of the causal and resultant natures, the establishment of their meanings is by no means unproven, for there are differences in what they depend upon, just as with designations such as "cause and effect" or "father and son."
However, this sūtra was spoken with an underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*), whereas the Abhidharma was not spoken with an underlying intention.
What is the underlying intention of this sūtra?
It is that the Bhagavat, intending to reveal that saṃsāra is beginningless but has an end, spoke these two phrases.

Regarding the term "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it reveals that the stream of birth and death has circulated without interruption since beginningless time; thus, the mutual arising of the various members in both forward and reverse order is taught.

The term "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) is used to reveal that if birth and death encounter their antidote, they have a limit and an end. That is to say, if there are conditions, they continue to arise subsequently; if those conditions are absent, they do not continue to arise. For this reason, the Sūtra states that one brings an end to suffering.
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras:
"Dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is conventional (prajñapti), because its causes and effects are mutually dependent and lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
That which has arisen dependently (pratītyasamutpanna) is real in its essence, for it is the basis upon which that [convention] depends, just as a jar is the basis for its designation."
The Abhidharma states that both are real, because the two entities of cause and effect both substantially exist.
Setting this matter aside for now, one should further provide an extensive explanation of the four links: ignorance, name-and-form, contact, and feeling.
Why is this so? Because *saṃskāra*, *bhava*, *tṛṣṇā*, and *upādāna* will be explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Analysis of Karma and Afflictions" (*Karmakleśavibhāga*).
Furthermore, because *vijñāna* and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have already been explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Fundamental Subjects" (*Mūlavastuvibhāga*).
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*), what are its characteristics?
Is it the absence of knowledge, or is it something subsumed under that which is not knowledge?
If one adopts the former sense, then ignorance would necessarily be non-existent.
If one adopts the latter interpretation, then the eyes and so forth would constitute its essence.
Since neither of these two logical positions is tenable and both are unaccepted, there is no fault.
Since both [positions] are not accepted, what is it that you do accept?
We accept that there is a distinct entity.
What is this distinct entity?
The verse says:
Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge, just as "non-friend" and "untruth" are the opposites of "friend" and "truth.
The commentary says:

Just as those who stand in opposition to one's friends are called "non-friends" because they are contrary to the nature of a friend, there is no such thing as a "non-friend" among all other neutral persons who are distinct from friends.

Truthful speech is called "real," while its opposite, deceptive discourse, is called "unreal. This does not mean that everything other than the real—such as all categories of form, fragrance, and so forth—is unreal or non-existent.
The word "etc. (ādi) is used to indicate that they are not gods (*asura*), not white, not *dharma*, not beloved, not meaningful, and so forth.
Asuras and others receive names such as "non-gods" (*asura*) because they are the opposites of gods and the like; it does not mean they are something other than the absence of gods and so forth.
Thus, ignorance has a distinct, real essence; it is that which is counteracted by knowledge (*vidyā*), being neither different from it nor non-existent.
How is this known? It is because, like consciousness (*vijñāna*) and other phenomena, it is said to exist dependent on conditions and serves as a condition for others.
Furthermore, there is corroborating evidence.
The verse says:
Because it is described as a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, And because it is not [simply] a view of poor wisdom (*dauṣprajña*).
Because it is associated with views, and because it is said to defile wisdom.
The treatise states:

The Sūtra explains ignorance (*avidyā*) as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), an outflow (*āsrava*), a yoke (*yoga*), and a flood (*ogha*). It cannot be said that these functions of being a fetter and so forth belong to other types of sleepiness (*middha*) or to a total absence of anything; therefore, there exists a distinct dharma called ignorance, just as a bad wife or son is termed "no wife" or "no son."
In this way, such corrupted wisdom (*kuprajñā*) ought to be called ignorance (*avidyā*); yet it is not ignorance, because it contains [wrong] view (*dṛṣṭi*).
All defiled wisdom is termed corrupted wisdom; since view exists within it, it is therefore not ignorance.
Since this [ignorance] is observed to involve investigation, vigor, wisdom, and decisive judgment, it cannot be called "delusion.
If that were so, then ignorance would have to be a defiled wisdom that is not a form of view (*dṛṣṭi*).
This is also unreasonable, because it is admitted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*).
If ignorance were wisdom (*prajñā*), it would have to be dissociated from views;

for two entities of wisdom cannot be associated together. It cannot be said that views are not accompanied by ignorance, because a view does not constitute a perversion unless it is characterized by delusion. Furthermore, it is stated that ignorance is able to defile wisdom.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Lust defiles the mind, preventing liberation; ignorance defiles wisdom, preventing purity.

It is not the case that wisdom can defile the essence of wisdom itself; rather, just as lust—which is of a different category—can defile the mind, so too should ignorance be something distinct from wisdom that can defile it.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that ignorance (avidyā) and wisdom (prajñā), though dissociated, can yet constitute defilement; for while greed, as a defilement, must necessarily coexist with the mind, among the mental states and their concomitants (citta-caitta-dharma), there is no defilement that initiates [the mind], but only defilement through association by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-saṃprayoga).
A self-essence cannot be associated with itself; therefore, ignorance is certainly not unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) offers a hypothetical defense:
"Why do you not allow that defiled wisdom, by being interspersed with wholesome wisdom, causes it to be impure, and thus [ignorance] is said to be that which defiles?"
This defense is untenable, for it would follow that all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) should be subject to defilement.

Furthermore, if untainted wisdom were mixed with tainted wisdom, it would imply that the tainted must transform into the untainted; however, the power of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is stronger, not that which is to be countered (*vipakṣa*).
Furthermore, when that wholesome wisdom is actively functioning, defiled concentration does not exist;
and when various defiled wisdoms are actively functioning, wholesome concentration does not exist. Of what, then, can one say it is capable of being defiled?
Furthermore, with whom could there be defilement?
If it were granted that existence and non-existence could mutually defile one another, then there would ultimately be no possibility of attaining liberation.
If liberation occurs when the perfuming (vāsanā) is extinguished, yet perfuming is logically non-existent, what then is there to be extinguished?
Therefore, it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) defiles wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus its nature is not wisdom; this principle remains unshakable.
If there were a distinct dharma called ignorance, one should state what constitutes the nature of that distinct dharma.
Furthermore, there is a distinct dharma called "non-comprehension" (*anabhijñā*), which is itself ignorance (*avidyā*); why then labor over such investigations?
One must first determine which specific dharma is designated as "non-comprehension" before it can be said to be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance.

Only the Bhagavat possesses correct knowledge and correct teaching regarding all phenomena, whether in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); others merely have a general understanding. Why, then, do you laboriously subject this to such scrutiny?

However, I perceive in this regard the following characteristic: there exists a distinct dharma capable of impairing the power of wisdom; it is the cause of inverted views and an obstacle to the discernment of virtues and faults; it does not desire to engage with objects of knowledge and obscures the mind and mental factors—this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
How can it be definitively known that there exists a distinct dharma?
Because it is spoken of as "permanent separation" just as with sensual desire; as the Sūtra says:
"Through the departure from sensual desire, the mind is liberated; through the departure from ignorance, wisdom attains liberation."
Furthermore, this is because ignorance is stated to be the cause, as the sūtra says:
"With ignorance as cause, all defilements arise; with clarity as cause, one is free from all defilements."
Furthermore, it is said that because there is a direct antidote to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), as stated in the Sūtra:
"The abandonment of all wrong views occurs through the arising of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); the separation from all ignorance (*avidyā*) occurs through the emergence of clear wisdom (*vidyā*)."
Furthermore, it is because a sūtra speaks of "one dharma. As the sūtra says:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is able to abandon one dharma, I truly declare that he has accomplished what was to be done; that [dharma] is precisely ignorance."
Furthermore, it is said that because darkness has an antidote,
as a gāthā states: “Those who are able to sever ignorance, And are no longer deluded regarding what is delusive,
They turn away from and extinguish ignorance and delusion, Just as the rising sun dispels the darkness.”
Therefore, ignorance (avidyā) definitely exists as a distinct dharma whose essence is non-cognition; it is not merely the absence of knowledge.
Furthermore, this non-cognition is briefly of two kinds: namely, afflicted and non-afflicted.
What is the distinction between these two? Some say:
that which can obstruct knowledge is defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*), whereas non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is merely the absence of knowledge.

Now, let us examine in detail the distinction between the characteristics of these two types of ignorance (*ajñāna*). That by which the difference between the ignorant and the wise is established is called the characteristic of afflicted ignorance (*kliṣṭa-ajñāna*).
If, due to this [other factor], there is a case where wisdom does not reach its full extent regarding a certain object while ignorance does, this is the second characteristic.
Furthermore, if after [defilements] have been severed, there is no distinction between the Buddha and those of the two vehicles, this is the first characteristic.

If after they have been severed, there is a difference between the Buddha and those of the two vehicles regarding whether [certain practices] are performed or not performed, this is the second characteristic.

Furthermore, if one is deluded regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, this is called the first characteristic of defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*).

If one is unable to realize, as they truly are, the characteristics of various phenomena—such as their flavor (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), maturation (*vipāka*), qualities (*guṇa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), location (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), and similarities or differences (*sārūpya-vairūpya*)—this is non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
This non-afflicted ignorance is precisely what is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
An ancient master says:

"The term 'habitual tendency' refers to a distinct category of non-afflicted mental factors (*caitta*) that are induced by the repeated practice of both afflicted and non-afflicted phenomena. It is not the manifestation of the continuum of omniscience; rather, it causes the mind and its mental factors to function without mastery, and this is termed 'habitual tendency.'"
It is not merely that wisdom is absent, for there is no phenomenon capable of serving as a cause [for it].

Nor should one say that there exists a certain kind of mind and mental factors collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), because non-afflicted ignorance has already been discussed previously. That is to say, does this ignorance have the mind abiding in its own nature (*svabhāvavihāra-citta*) and so forth as its essence, or is it something distinct?
If the essence consists of the mind abiding in its own nature and so forth, then even a Buddha would possess non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
If there is a distinction [between them], it is the differentiator that could be ignorance, not that which is differentiated.

We observe the differentiation of categories such as the wholesome and so forth; therefore, among the mind and mental factors, there must necessarily be distinct dharmas that act as the differentiators, rather than everything being identical.

For instance, within the category of the wholesome, there must be faith and so on; within the unwholesome category, there are shamelessness and so on; and within the defiled category, there are negligence and so on.
Within such categories of mind and mental factors, there must necessarily be a distinct dharma capable of producing differentiation.
Therefore, we know that among these, the distinct dharma capable of producing differentiation is non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
Now, upon careful examination, that statement contains excessive errors.

For the minds and mental factors of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not all perceive the characteristics of taste, potency, and ripening as they truly are; yet, one does not observe the arising of other mental factors [in such cases].

Furthermore, since those minds and mental factors arise with distinct characteristics in each and every moment of thought, there should be a separate instance of "non-cognition" arising within each such moment.

If you claim that a distinct characteristic renders the non-cognition differentiated, then this alone is sufficient to differentiate the categories of mind; why then must one separately postulate "undefiled non-cognition"?

Therefore, regarding taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and so forth, one does not exert effort in seeking them; rather, the wisdom of understanding and the factors of distinct characteristics together act as causes to induce a subsequent wisdom of the same kind.
This wisdom, in turn, does not exert effort in seeking further understanding, and again acts as a cause to induce a wisdom of understanding that does not involve effortful seeking.
Thus, through this continuous succession from beginningless time, cause and effect have followed one another until these tendencies have become ingrained as one's nature.

Consequently, by repeatedly habituating oneself to objects such as flavors and so forth, there arises an intellect incapable of comprehension; this inferior intellect thus induced is termed "non-afflicted ignorance."
Thus, these co-emergent mind and mental factors are collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*); this is logically certain.

Alternatively, during the state of affliction, all the non-defiled minds and their continuities of sentient beings, having been perfumed by the intermingling of various afflictions, possess a functional portion capable of conforming to the production of further afflictions.

Therefore, all non-defiled minds and their associated mental factors arise with appearances that resemble those [defiled] modes of activity; because they arise in succession through the power of repeated habituation, the body free from faults is still said to possess "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). However, the Omniscient One has eternally severed these so that they no longer function.

However, within the continuum of both afflicted and non-afflicted minds at the stage where what is to be abandoned by insight has already been severed, there remains a certain habit-energy conducive to the arising of afflictions, which is a residual portion of the afflictions to be abandoned by insight. Among these, that which is afflicted is termed "homogeneous nature" (*nikāya-sabhāga*); it is all eliminated by the vajra-path and never manifests again.

If it is non-defiled, it is called the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of afflictions abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*); it is also severed by that same path, though its activity or non-activity depends on the distinctions among the faculties (*indriya*).

If, at the stage where those [afflictions] abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have already been severed, there remains within the continuum of a non-defiled mind a residual habitual tendency conducive to the arising of afflictions—a portion of the nature of afflictions abandoned by cultivation—this is termed "abandoned by cultivation."

Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions (*kleśa*) are tainted (*sāsrava*), they have been severed by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); whether they manifest or not depends on the superior or inferior nature of their faculties.

Since the World-Honored One has attained mastery over all phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), these tendencies never manifest at all, just like the afflictions; therefore, the Buddha alone is called "one whose mental continuum is perfectly pure."
Precisely because of this, his conduct is free from error, and he attains the uncommon dharmas such as the three applications of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*).
Furthermore, it is for this reason that, with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), it is said that only the Buddha alone is called one who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vyākhyā-śāstra* (Treatise Elucidating the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Fascicle Fourteen.

Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
