Chapter Four: Discerning Dependent Origination, Part Four. Having already discerned ignorance, one should now discern name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Form has already been extensively discerned; what are the characteristics of name?
The verse says:
It is called the four formless aggregates.
The commentary says:
The Buddha taught that the four formless aggregates are called "name" (nāman).
Why are they called "name"?
Because they are able to denote and summon [objects].
This means that it is able to designate various objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
If this were so, it would not fully encompass the formless (*ārūpya*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*) phenomena, because they lack an object of cognition.
This is not the case; designation occurs even in the formless realm, just as there is no fault in the explanation given for the etymology of "form" (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, because it is subtle, a name is established according to reason among various meanings and designated by that name; however, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and the like cannot be called "names," because their bases are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, because it is able to universally seek out all realms, stages, destinies, and births, the designation "name" (nāma) is established; it is not that the untainted (*anāsrava*) and formless (*ārūpya*) states cannot be so named. Although "name" is not explicitly explained here [in this context], it is similar to what is being discussed.
Furthermore, regarding the formless realm, following the intention of those who speak of it, we shall generally refer to it as "name" (nāma); there is no need for further inquiry or refutation.
The detailed determination of the remaining points is as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The definitions of the [mental factors] have already been explained. What is the characteristic of contact (*sparśa*)?
The verse says:
Contact arises from the conjunction of the three.
The treatise says:
There are six kinds of contact, namely, visual contact through to mental contact.

What, then, is this? It is that which arises from the conjunction of three; that is to say, because of the coming together of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—a distinct contact arises.
Although the sixth [consciousness] and its three [factors] belong to different time periods, their causal relationship is interconnected; thus, the meaning of "conjunction" is established.

Alternatively, "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) has the meaning of having a single result; although the sense faculty, object, and consciousness do not necessarily arise simultaneously, they are called "conjoined" because their resultant contact is identical.
That the substance of contact exists separately has already been established within the section on the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).

Although consciousness arises from the conjunction of the three, it necessarily arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is taught that both arise from two conditions, just as in the case of [mental] consciousness.
As the Sūtra says:
"The internal body of consciousness and external name-and-form—these two pairs serve as conditions for the arising of all contacts," and so forth, at length.

The phrase "conscious body" (*vijñānakāya*) indicates the six internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), while the term "external name-and-form" (*bāhya nāmarūpa*) indicates the six external bases; this meaning is certain, for it is stated in a verse of the *Gāthā*:
"The eye and forms," and so forth.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Consciousness and contact both have name-and-form as their condition.
Since the conditions for their arising are identical, how could they occur at different times?
When conditions are complete, [the effect] necessarily arises, as there is nothing capable of obstructing it.

From this, it is proven that the various phenomena such as sensation produced by contact with the eye and so forth arise simultaneously with the visual consciousness and other cognitions, because they share the same causes of production as the visual consciousness and the rest.
As this sutra states:
"This is feeling;
this is perception."
This is volition;
this is consciousness.
Since these various phenomena are thus intermingled and inseparable, it is logically established that consciousness and contact coexist.
These aforementioned six contacts are further combined into two. What are these two?
The verse says:
The first five are associated with resistance; the sixth is associated with the designation (adhivacana).
The treatise says:

The five contacts, beginning with that of the eye, are called "associated with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because they have resistant sense-faculties as their basis and take only resistant phenomena as their objects.

The sixth, mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), is termed "designation-contact" (*adhivacana*). "Designation" refers to names (*nāman*); since names are the predominant objects of mental contact, this alone is specifically called designation-contact.

The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes both general names and meanings as its objects; because the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not take names as their objects, it is said that the mental consciousness is "longer" [in its range].

As it is said: the visual consciousness can only cognize blue, but cannot cognize that "it is blue"; the mental consciousness cognizes blue and also cognizes that "it is blue," and so on, as explained at length.

Therefore, the name "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is derived from its objective basis; the name "contact with designation" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is established in reference to its predominant object.
Some say that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "designation" because it exercises sovereignty over the production of speech.

Some say that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) alone is called "designation" (adhivacana) because it engages with its objects by taking speech as its predominant condition, whereas the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not; therefore, the mental consciousness alone is termed "designation," and the contact associated with it is termed "designation-contact" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa).

Therefore, the name "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-sparśa*) is established based on its objective support (*ālambana*), while the name "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-sparśa*) is established with respect to its primary associated [mental factor].
These aforementioned six types of contact further constitute eight kinds according to their specific associations.
The verse says:
Knowledge, ignorance, and that which is neither; The untainted, the defiled, and the remainder;
Associated with the two—craving and aversion; Conducive to the three feelings, such as pleasure and so forth.
The treatise says:

Contact associated with knowledge (*vidyā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth, constitutes three types: first, contact associated with knowledge; second, contact associated with ignorance; and third, contact associated with neither knowledge nor ignorance. These three should be understood, respectively, as contact associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*), the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and the remaining [neither-tainted-nor-defiled] states.

The "remainder" refers to that which is other than the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), namely, the tainted wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Within the category of defiled contact, there is a portion that arises frequently; based on this, two further types of contact—namely, attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*)—are established, because they are associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of attachment and aversion.

In summary, all [contacts] further constitute three types of contact: first, contact conducive to pleasant feeling; second, contact conducive to painful feeling; and third, contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is contact conducive to feeling (*vedanīya-sparśa*)?
It is so called because it is experienced by pleasant and other feelings, or because it serves as the basis for the activity of feeling; thus, it is termed "conducive to feeling."
In what sense is contact the basis for the activity that is experienced by feeling?
It is because its mode of activity (ākāra) closely resembles that of feeling, as it arises dependent upon contact;
furthermore, because it is associated with pleasant and other feelings, or because it can induce pleasant and other feelings, it is termed "conducive to feeling" (vedanīya).
Thus, these combine to form sixteen kinds of contact (*sparśa*).
Having already analyzed the characteristics of contact,
what are the characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*)?
The verse says:
From this arise six types of feeling; five belong to the body, the rest to the mind.
These further become eighteen through the distinctions of mental application (*manopavicāra*).
The Treatise says:
From the six types of contact, six types of feeling arise—namely, from the feeling born of eye-contact up to the feeling born of mind-contact.
These together constitute two categories: first, bodily feeling; second, mental feeling.
Among these six, the first five are described as bodily feelings (*kāyikī vedanā*) because they depend upon the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
That which is produced by mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja*) is described as mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*), as it depends solely upon the mind.
Within these aforementioned mental feelings, eighteen types are further distinguished based on the differences among the mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
What are the eighteen mental applications (*manopavicāra*)?
They are the six applications each of sorrow, joy, and equanimity.
For what reason are these further established as eighteen?
Because these three types of feeling are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they become eighteen due to the differences among the six objects.
It is not that a single entity of feeling associated with the mental consciousness becomes six because of different objects; rather, it is because the modes of experiencing them differ.
What is the meaning of the term *manopavicāra* (mental application)?
It is so called because joy and the other [feelings] possess the power to act as proximate conditions, causing the mind to range repeatedly over its objects.

If it were said that joy and the others are called *manopavicāra* because they cause the mind to range repeatedly over objects by acting as its proximate conditions, then mental formations (*saṃjñā*) and the rest would also deserve this name, since they are associated with the mind and proceed by means of the mind.
If mental applications (*manopavicāra*) existed only on the level of the mind (*manobhūmi*), would this not contradict the sūtra? As the sūtra says:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to a mental application of joy toward a form that is conducive to joy," and so forth, as explained at length.

This is not contradictory; it is like how, based on visual consciousness, one induces the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), yet this contemplation of impurity is comprised solely within the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
Nevertheless, the Sūtra states:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one dwells fully established by contemplating its impurity accordingly."

This case is also like that; it is spoken of in this way because the mental applications (*manopavicāra*), such as joy and so forth, are induced by the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).
As that sutra states:
"Having seen forms with the eye," and so forth, at length.
It should not be objected that the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) associated with the consciousness induced by the five sensory consciousnesses are intentional (*saṃcetanika*).
For what reason are bodily sensations (*kāyikī vedanā*) not mental applications?
Because they do not share the same nature as mental applications.
Because mental applications (manopavicāra) rely exclusively upon the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), they are termed "applications" (upavicāra).

Because they differentiate objects—both their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)—across the three periods of time, they are termed "applications" (vicāra).
All bodily sensations are the opposite of this; therefore, they are not "mental proximity" (*manopavicāra*), nor are they called "mental applications" (*saṃskāra*).
Is it not the case that bodily sensations also possess these characteristics?

After bodily sensation has experienced objects such as form, the mental consciousness follows along; because it proceeds repeatedly toward its objects by the power of the bodily sensation, [it too possesses these characteristics].
This is also not the case, because the characteristics have already been explained: namely, that various bodily sensations do not depend on the mental consciousness, as it is non-conceptual.
Since it cannot differentiate between the merits and faults of its objects, it is not by the power of that [mental consciousness] that the mind repeatedly ranges over objects.

Furthermore, because it is not fixed: following a bodily feeling, there is no certainty that a mental consciousness will arise in succession; however, at the same time as a mental feeling, a mental consciousness necessarily exists. Therefore, only mental feelings are called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
Furthermore, since those such as the congenitally blind possess mental applications (*manopavicāra*) despite lacking [visual] seeing up to [tactile] touching,
the pleasure belonging to the mental level in the third dhyāna should likewise be included among the mental applications.
This criticism is not valid, because it does not exist in the first realm (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, it is because [the other realms] are stagnant; that is to say, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there is no pleasure of the mental level (*manobhūmi*), and although it exists in the third dhyāna, it is not established [as such].

Furthermore, the pleasure of that stage is stagnant with respect to its object; it is called "mental application" (*manopavicāra*) only because it approaches the object and frequently shifts through several objects rather than remaining fixed on a single one.
Moreover, there is no mental application associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), as such a faculty does not exist there.
If that were so, there would be no mental application of equanimity (*upekṣā-manopavicāra*), because there would be nothing for it to counteract.
This is not the case, because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*) are themselves the counteracts to equanimity.
Furthermore, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) belonging to the mental level of the third dhyāna has no faculty of equanimity belonging to its own fundamental level to serve as its counteract.

However, there is no fault of lacking preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) or the lack of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth as mental applications (*manopavicāra*), because within the first realm (*kāmadhātu*) there exist counter-objects belonging to the same level.

Alternatively, it is because some [mental applications] can have such counterparts while others cannot; that is to say, mental equanimity and the like may have counter-factors belonging to the same level, whereas mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) certainly has no counter-factor belonging to the same level. Therefore, there is no fault.
Among the various mental applications (*manopavicāra*), how many are bound to the desire realm?
How many objects of focus do the mental applications of the desire realm have?
The same questions apply to those of the form and formless realms.
The verse says:
In the desire realm, eighteen [minds] take the desire realm as their object; In the form realm, twelve; and in the higher realms, three. Twelve [minds] take the desire realm as their object;
Eight take their own [realm] as their object; and two take the formless realm as their object.
The latter two take the six desire-realm [factors] as their objects; four take their own realm, one takes the higher realm;
the preliminary stage of the first formless realm takes the four form-realm [factors], its own realm, and one from above;
the four fundamental [formless stages] and three of the limit-taking [formless stages] take only their own sphere as their object.
The treatise states:
Those bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) number eighteen, and those that take the objects of the desire realm as their domain are likewise eighteen in number.
Those that take the objects of the form realm (rūpadhātu) as their domain number only twelve, excluding the six [consciousnesses] of smell and taste, because those [objects] do not exist there.
There are only three [types of acquisition] when taking formless objects as their domain, because those [formless realms] lack the five types of objects such as form and so forth.
There are likewise only three when taking unconditioned (unbound) objects as their domain.
Having explained those bound to the desire realm, one should now explain those bound to the form realm.

In the first and second dhyānas, there are only twelve [mental factors], namely, with the six types of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) excluded. If it is said that those [factors] which have a fixed object (*ālambana*) are necessarily non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) and cannot take a lower realm as their object, then even when wholesome states take objects of the desire realm, they likewise possess twelve;
excluding the four [objects] of odor and taste, the remaining eight take themselves as objects.
Two take the formless as their object, namely the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) regarding phenomena (*dharmas*).
Those taking unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) phenomena as their object are likewise only of two kinds.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only six, namely those of equanimity (*upekṣā*) taking the objects of the desire realm as their domain.
Wholesome [mental applications] also possess six, excluding the two—those associated with odor and flavor; the remaining four take their own objects as conditions.
One takes the formless realm as its object, namely the mental application to dharmas (*dharmopavicāra*).
Taking unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) dharmas as objects likewise consists of only this one kind.
Having explained those bound to the form realm, one should now explain those bound to the formless realm.
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space has only four types, namely: equanimity that takes as its objects only visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Taking the fourth dhyāna as an object also possesses four types; this is said from the perspective of those who maintain that there are distinct objects.
If one holds that that stage takes only the lower levels as its object in a collective manner, then there would be only the mental application of the mixed-object dharma-mental-application.

Taking the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as an object, there is only one, namely the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*). Taking the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) dharmas as objects, there is likewise only one kind.

In the four fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) and the three upper levels, there is only one, namely the mental-object element; furthermore, these take their own stage as an object. This is because the fundamental formless realm does not take lower stages as objects, and those three upper levels do not take the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as objects.
That they do not take lower objects will be explained later.
This [type of] object, being unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*), is likewise only one.
Do all mental applications (*manopavicāra*) also include the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
"The eighteen [bases] are exclusively with outflows.
The commentary says:
There is no proximate application-attainment (upapatti-pratilambhika) that is untainted (anāsrava). Why is this?
Because it causes the increase of existence (bhava).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are the opposite of this.
Some say that while all sentient beings possess the "near-operations" (*upavicāra*), the untainted are not so; therefore, they are not near-operations.

Others say that because the Noble Path proceeds spontaneously, it accords with the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*); thus, it is not the substance of a near-operation, for the substance of a near-operation is contrary to this.
Who accomplishes how many mental applications (*manopavicāra*)? It is said:

one born in the desire realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm accomplishes all [six]; one in the first or second dhyāna accomplishes eight; one in the third or fourth dhyāna accomplishes four; and one in the formless realm accomplishes one.
Those [minds] accomplished in the higher realms do not take lower realms as their objects, because they are exclusively defiled.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned desire-greed, one accomplishes all [minds] of the desire realm and ten [minds] of the first dhyāna.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) possesses six types, because the wholesome mind within the *anāgamya* stage takes odors and tastes as its objects.
Joy (*prīti*), however, possesses only four types, because it is exclusively defiled and does not take lower stages as its objects.
Is it not the case that mental applications (*manopavicāra*) are induced by visual consciousness and the others?
Since those [beings] lack the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue, they should likewise lack the applications directed toward odors and tastes.

This objection is not valid; for if it were so, then self-natured recollections (*svabhāva-smṛti*) in those born blind or deaf, as well as those occurring within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), would all lack the applications directed toward visible forms and so forth. Therefore, [mental applications] are not induced by all five consciousnesses.
They accomplish eight [minds] in the second dhyāna; the third and fourth dhyānas and the formless attainments are as previously described.

Having already abandoned desire and greed, if one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna, they accomplish twelve minds of the desire realm and the first dhyāna—namely, excluding the six [types of] mental grief (*daurmanasya*).
The two dhyānas and so forth are all as previously explained.

If one has already attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna but has not yet attained detachment from craving for the first dhyāna, one possesses ten [mental factors] of the second dhyāna: specifically, joy (*prīti*) consists of only four types because it is exclusively defiled;
equanimity (*upekṣā*) possesses all six types, because one has already attained the wholesome state of its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).
The rest is as previously explained; by this principle, the remainder should be understood accordingly.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one accomplishes only one neutral mental application (*upekṣā-dharmopavicāra*) of the desire realm, namely that which is concomitant with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-citta*).
How are the various mental applications (manopavicāra) obtained?

It is said: having abandoned sensual desire, through the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (anantarya-mārga) and the eight paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), one obtains the six applications of equanimity within the preparatory stage (sāmantaka-bhūmi) of the first dhyāna; then, within the ninth path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation, one obtains the application of equanimity associated with the mind of supernormal fruition (abhijñā-phala-citta) belonging to the desire realm.
Upon attaining the first dhyāna, there are twelve applications (*upavicāra*); here, the term "first dhyāna" includes its associated factors (*parivāra*).
By this same principle, one should understand the abandonment of the defilements of the higher stages as appropriate.

However, there is a distinction: at the time of abandoning attachment to the fourth dhyāna, during the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one necessarily does not acquire the mental applications of equanimity associated with the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) belonging to one's own level or a lower level.

When one becomes detached from the desire for the various stages beginning with the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), during all the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one acquires only a single equanimity-application (*upekṣopavicāra*).

Upon attaining the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one acquires twelve applications of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas, as well as six applications of equanimity of the third and fourth dhyānas.

There are four equanimity-approaches (*upekṣā-upavicāra*) in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). In each of the higher stages, there is one approach to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) characterized by equanimity.

At the moment of rebirth—when passing away from a higher stage and being born into a lower stage—one acquires all the approaches belonging to that [new] stage. When giving rise to the various dhyānas, one also simultaneously possesses the approach to phenomena through equanimity belonging to the lower stages; these are precisely the eighteen mental activities (*manopavicāra*), such as joy and the rest.

Because they serve as distinct bases for the emergence from attachment, the Blessed One has spoken of them as the thirty-six "Teacher's Words" (*śāstṛpada*). These differentiated words can represent the Great Teacher; because they are the insignia of the Teacher, they are called "Teacher's Words."
These various phrases can only be known and expounded by the Great Teacher, the Buddha, for others lack such capacity.
That which is based on attachment refers to all defiled feelings (*vedanā*).
That which is based on renunciation refers to all wholesome and non-obscured neutral feelings, because they accord with what is wholesome and defiled respectively.
These are subsumed within two categories as appropriate, and are not explained separately.
Regarding the determination of the realms and stages for these thirty-six factors: within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all thirty-six are present.
In the first and second dhyānas, there are only twenty; namely, eight based on worldly attachment (*gardhāśrita*) and twelve based on renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita*).
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only ten types: namely, four based on attachment (*gardhāśrita*) and six based on renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita*).

Regarding the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), if one allows for distinct objects of focus, there are five types: namely, one based on attachment and four based on renunciation;
if one maintains that it focuses only on the aggregate as a whole, there are only two types: namely, one based on attachment and one based on renunciation.
The fundamental dhyānas of the formless realm (*ārūpya-maula*) and the three higher categories each possess only two [aspects], as should be understood from what precedes.
Regarding those fixed by their object according to realm and stage: when the desire realm takes objects of the desire realm as its focus, it possesses thirty-six [aspects].
The objects of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consist of only twenty-four, excluding the six based on each of the two supports [nose and tongue] that take fragrance and taste as their objects.
The objects of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consist of only six types, namely the six mental applications (*dharmopavicāra*), with three based on each of the two supports.
The objects not bound [to a realm] that serve as conditions are likewise only these six.
By this principle, the distinctions among the objects conditioned by the form and formless realms should be understood accordingly.
For what reason are the remaining members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) not mentioned?
The verse says:
"The remainder has been explained and will be explained.
The commentary says:
As for the remaining members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), some have already been explained and some will be explained, as has been previously demonstrated.
If this is so, for what reason is this verse further propounded?
The subsequent verse is intended to preclude doubts regarding the detailed explanation.
Since that later verse mentions "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth, one should not harbor such a doubt as this:
"The meaning of the four factors has already been extensively clarified; next, the remaining factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) should be explained in detail."

To clarify that the subsequent text relies upon afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and entities (*vastu*) to metaphorically illustrate the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as a whole, the Master (Ācārya) further offers this verse.
As previously stated, the twelve links of existence are briefly subsumed into three categories—namely, affliction, karma, and entity—and these three have distinct functions.
What is the analogy?
The verse says:
Herein, the afflictions are said to be like seeds and also like dragons.
Like the roots of grass and the trunks of trees, and like rice encased in husks;
karma is like rice with its husk, like medicinal herbs and like flowers;
the various matters of ripened results (*vipāka*) are like cooked food and drink.
The Treatise says:

How are these three types similar? Just as sprouts, leaves, and so forth arise from seeds, so too do afflictions, karma, and the objective basis arise from afflictions; it is like a dragon guarding a pond, whereby the water never runs dry.
In this way, the afflictions obtain a continuous succession that settles within the pool of birth, causing the flow of deluded karma and its effects to be inexhaustible.

Just as the sprouts will grow back again and again if the roots of a plant have not been pulled out, so too, if the roots of the afflictions have not been uprooted by the Noble Path, the crops of rebirth will arise again and again even after they have been severed.
Just as from the trunk of a tree branches, flowers, and fruits repeatedly arise, so too do afflictions, karma, and their effects repeatedly arise from afflictions.
Just as rice enveloped in husks can produce sprouts and the like, but not by itself, so too karma enveloped by afflictions can bring about future existence, but not by itself.
Just as rice with its husk can produce sprouts and the like, so too karma accompanied by afflictions can summon a ripened result (*vipāka*).
Just as various medicinal herbs have the ripening of their fruit as their final limit, once the fruit of karma has ripened, it no longer summons further ripened results.
Just as a flower is the proximate cause for the production of fruit, so too is karma the proximate cause capable of producing maturation (*vipāka*).

Just as cooked food is merely to be consumed and cannot be transformed back into other food, once the matter of a matured fruit of maturation has reached completion, it cannot further summon another birth-maturation.
If these various maturations (vipāka) were to further induce another birth, and that [birth] were to further induce yet another, there would be no liberation.

Having already explained dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), we shall now divide it into four types of existence (bhava) based on their positional distinctions: intermediate existence (antarābhava), birth-existence (upapattibhava), fundamental existence (mūlabhava), and death-existence (maraṇabhava), as previously explained.
The distinctions regarding the existence or non-existence of wholesome states and so forth within the three realms shall now be briefly explained.
The verse says:
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively defiled.
By the afflictions of its own level; the other three [existences] and the three formless [existences] are likewise.
The treatise says:
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively defiled; it is definitely neither wholesome nor non-obscured neutral.
By which affliction do all afflictions, the defilements of the various existences (*janma-bhava*), and the various states of existence arise? It is not so. How then?
It occurs only by means of its own level; that is, when one is born in a particular level, it is only through all the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that level that birth becomes defiled.

Among the various afflictions, there is not a single one that lacks the capacity to moisten at the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi*). However, this linking of existence occurs solely through the power of the afflictions, and not through the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) or the outflows (*upakleśa*).

Why is this so? Because the latent tendencies of regret (*kaukṛtya*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and so forth, arise through the force of one's own application (*svabalavāhana*) only after being brought forth by deliberate discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*).
However, within this state, the body and mind are dull and weak; thus, only those afflictions that operate spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) can manifest.

Only the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) possess a superior force through repeated cultivation; therefore, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to manifest repeatedly and arise spontaneously at the time of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*).

The various outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and stains (*mala*), however, have a weaker force of repeated cultivation and do not manifest without deliberate reflection; for this reason, the various outbursts and stains do not link rebirth.
Therefore, it is logically established that only the afflictions of one's own level defile the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*).

As for the others, such as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and so forth, each is common to all three [moral qualities]; that is to say, they are all common to the wholesome, the defiled, and the neutral.
One should know that the very first moment of the linking of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is necessarily defiled, just like the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
Regarding which realms these four existences belong to:
the desire and form realms possess all four, while the formless realm possesses only three; for the karma of the formless realm does not produce the fruit of an intermediate state.
As has already been fully analyzed in the *Nyāyānusāra*,
by what means do sentient beings abide within these four kinds of existence (*bhava*)?
The verse says:
Sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment; In the realm of desire, the substance of edible food consists of only three [realms];
Matter cannot benefit itself, because it is its own sense organ and because it is liberated [from craving].
The three nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness Are with-outflows and pervade all three realms.
The mind-made (*manomaya*) and the seeking rebirth (*abhinirvṛtti*), the fragrance-eating (*gandharva*), and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The former two benefit this life as the support and the supported;
the latter two, regarding future existence, function as the projecting and the actualizing, respectively.
The treatise says:

The Sūtra states that the Blessed One, having personally realized it, attained perfect enlightenment and correctly taught this one dharma: namely, that all sentient beings, without exception, subsist by means of nutriment.
What is this nutriment?
There are four kinds of nutriment:
first, morsel food; second, contact; third, volition; and fourth, consciousness.
Morsel food is of two types, namely, subtle and coarse.
"Subtle" refers to the food of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because its nutriment is fragrance;
it also refers to the food of the gods and at the beginning of a kalpa, because it does not undergo transformation or impurity.
Just as oil poured onto sand disperses and enters the grains, or like the food of minute insects, infants, and the like, it is called "subtle"; the opposite of this is called "gross."
Thus, edible food exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because one who is free from craving for edible food is born in the higher realms.

The bodies in the higher realms do not depend on external conditions for their subsistence; although the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that provide benefit exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are not edible food, just as the objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are not [considered such] when they are not exquisite.
Just as within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), although there exist subtle objects of form, sound, and touch, they are not called "sublime desires" because they do not induce superior craving;

likewise, although there exists a most excellent, subtle, and beneficial tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*), it is not "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) because it is ultimately devoid of being divided into portions and swallowed.
Although it is not included among the types of material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it does not lack the meaning of "food.
For example, although joy (*prīti*) is not included among the four kinds of sustenance, the Sūtra describes it as food because it possesses the functional meaning of food.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"I feed on the food of joy;
by feeding on joy, I abide for a long time, just like the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven."

However, although the substance of edible food consists of thirteen factors, when categorized by their location, they are subsumed into only three types: namely, only the odors, tastes, and tangibles of the desire realm.
All of these constitute the essential nature of edible food, as they can be formed into distinct morsels and swallowed.
This means that it is received part by part through the mouth and nose; because the small is included within the great, this statement is made.

Although it is not swallowed or chewed, if it can benefit the body and cause it to endure for a long time, it is also subsumed under "subtle food" (*sūkṣmāhāra*), just like shadows, light, heat, cold, ointments, or washes.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the kalpa, foods such as the "essence of the earth" (*pṛthivīrasa*) are also called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because they are consumed in distinct morsels.
Moreover, various drinks and the like are also termed edible food, because they can all be enjoyed by dividing them into separate portions.
The sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is termed a "morsel" (*kavaḍa*), yet it is not called "nutriment," because it cannot sustain and benefit its own corresponding sense-faculty.
That which is called "nutriment" must sustain and benefit both the sense-faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The sense-sphere of visible form lacks the power to benefit its own faculty and the primary elements, because it is not an object of apprehension reached by the faculties.

As the Sūtra states regarding edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*): it does not constitute the act of eating merely by being in the hand or in a vessel; rather, it must enter the nose and mouth, be chewed by the teeth, moistened by saliva, pass through the throat, descend into the stomach, be gradually digested, and have its flavor, potency, and ripening qualities flow into the various channels to benefit the internal worms—only at that time is it called "food," for only then does it accomplish the function of food.

If the name is applied based on the vessel that holds it—just as Devadatta is named after Naraka—even though the entire portion [of food] collectively receives the name "food," at the time it is actually consumed, it consists only of odor, flavor, and tangibility, because at that moment these alone serve as the sense bases (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya).
Furthermore, how is it known that the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not nutriment?

Because its function of internally sustaining the faculties and the primary elements is not perceived separately, as is the case with odor, flavor, and tangibles; at that time, consciousness of those objects does not arise.

When they first arise from consciousness, they do not even benefit or harm their own sense organs or primary elements; how much less, once they have entered the body, could they produce their own consciousness and function as food?
We observe that the disks of the sun and moon can benefit or harm the eye organ; this is the function of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), not the power of shape or color (*saṃsthāna* and *varṇa*).

Is it not the case that suffering and pleasure arise simultaneously with consciousness, and because these two can cause harm or benefit, the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) likewise causes harm or benefit to the eye?

This is logically untenable, for it would follow that the eye, light, and so forth would constitute nutriment (*āhāra*). However, while those [objects] serve as conditions for contact (*sparśa*) that accords with suffering or pleasure and thereby function as nutriment, the sense-base of form does not do so.

When one sees various forms such as añjana or counting sticks, the eye neither increases nor decreases; it is only when [the substance] reaches the eye that the eye then undergoes increase or decrease. Therefore, edible food is certainly not the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
If that is so, why does the Sūtra praise edible food as possessing color, fragrance, and taste?
It is to inspire delight by praising its auxiliary conditions; it is like praising respectful giving—does "respectful" itself then become "edible food"?

However, for a substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) to be established, it must possess both primary and auxiliary conditions; furthermore, by citing its visible form (*rūpa*), it is implied that its odor, taste, and tangibility are also excellent and desirable. Therefore, this statement was made.
Consequently, the substance of food consists only of odor, taste, and tangibility, for visible form cannot benefit its own sense organ or liberation.
Generally, that which is called "nutritious food" must first benefit one's own roots and primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and only thereafter reach others.

When consuming edible forms (*rūpa*), it does not even benefit one's own roots and primary elements, let alone reach others, because those sense faculties and their respective objects are distinct from one another.
When one sometimes experiences joy and pleasure upon seeing forms, it is conditioned by contact with form that this nutriment arises; it is not the form itself.
Furthermore, those who are non-returners and arhats are liberated from craving for nutriment; thus, although they may see exquisite food, no joy arises in them, as it provides no benefit.
The realm-affiliation and essential nature of edible food have already been explained; the three—contact, volition, and consciousness—shall now be demonstrated.

Contact refers to that which is produced by the conjunction of the three: the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness; this has already been extensively analyzed within the *Pratītyasamutpāda* [chapter].
Volition refers to mental action (*manas-karman*), and consciousness refers to the cognition of objects.
These three are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and exist throughout all three realms.

Thus, the substance of these four nutriments (*āhāra*) consists of sixteen items in total; the term "contaminated" is applied only to the latter three nutriments to demonstrate that the three beginning with odor (*gandha*) do not overlap with the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
For what reason are untainted (*anāsrava*) contacts and so forth not considered nutriment (*āhāra*)?
Nutriment is that which can draw forth and sustain the various states of existence (*bhava*)—those places where loathsome craving, which is to be abandoned, grows.

Although the untainted sustains the existence drawn forth by others, it lacks itself the functional capacity to draw forth existence; nor is it a place where loathsome craving, which is to be abandoned, grows. Therefore, it is not established among the four nutriments.

Precisely for this reason, when compared to other realms and stages, even though tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) may serve as causes that support what is presently existing, they do not constitute the essence of nutriment (*āhāra*).

Although phenomena of other realms and stages can also act as causes that sustain the present, they cannot function as the cause that draws forth future existence (*punarbhava*); therefore, they are not called nutriment.

When various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas manifest, although they can act as causes to support the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), they cannot function as causes that draw forth a future existence (*punarbhava*).

Although they temporarily serve as causes to support the sense faculties and the primary elements, they do so solely to establish a superior basis for themselves, so as to swiftly proceed toward *nirvāṇa* and eternally extinguish all forms of existence.
When the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) states of one's own level manifest, they sustain the present and cause it to increase, thereby being able to summon a future existence (*punarbhava*).

By this, the meaning of how edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) acts as a cause to summon a future existence has already been explained. That is to say, when the foods of contact (*sparśa*) and so forth draw forth a future existence, they also draw forth the internal dharmas such as odors (*gandha*) of the future. The present internal odors and so forth sustain the causes—contact and the rest—that draw forth that future existence; furthermore, they themselves can take the future odors and so forth as their concordant results (*niṣyanda-phala*). Therefore, because edible food shares the same result as the cause of future existence, it is also able to draw forth existence and is thus called "food."
However, the substances of odor, taste, and tangibility are of three types: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), and those produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*).

Because external odors and so forth awaken the internal odors, tastes, and tangibilities within the body, causing them to function as food, the principle of what has been described as "food" is established as certain.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are four kinds of food that enable beings who have already been born (*bhūta*) to remain stable, and that provide sustenance for those seeking birth.
The term *bhūta* indicates the sense of having already come into existence.
Once beings have been born into the various realms of existence (*gati*), they all consider themselves already born.
Yet it is further said that they "seek birth" (*upapatti-icchā*); what does this refer to?
It refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because the Blessed One has described the intermediate state by means of five names.
What are the five? First is the mind-made (*manomaya*), so called because it arises from the mind; this refers to the meaning of the fruit projected by the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
If that were the case, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It is not so, because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not take external conditions such as semen and blood to form its body.
Second, it seeks birth, for it generally delights in searching for and examining the place where it is to be reborn.
First is birth, which refers to the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*). Second is seeking, wherein one frequently seeks out the place of birth-existence.
Third is the eater of fragrance, because the body subsists on fragrant food as it proceeds toward the place of birth.
Fourth is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because it exists without interval between the two existences of death and birth.
The fifth is called "arising" (*utpāda*), because immediately after the existence at death (*cyuti-bhava*), the body arises instantaneously with all its limbs intact;
or alternatively, because it arises for a brief moment, being directed toward the certainty of rebirth.
For what reason is it said that there are only four kinds of nutriment?
For all conditioned phenomena possess the function of nutriment, since the Sūtra states that even Nirvāṇa has nutriment.
As the Sūtra says:
Nirvāṇa has nutriment, namely the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) possess the function of nutriment, this is stated with reference to what is preeminent.

That is to say, for the sake of those to be converted, the Great Sage taught that there are specifically four nutriments based on their superior capacity as sustenance: the first two nutriments benefit this body—the basis and that which depends upon it—while the latter two nutriments draw forth future existence and give rise to future existence.
The four nutriments are established because they respectively sustain and give rise to the two types of existence-bodies: name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The "basis" refers to form, which is the body endowed with sense faculties;
the "based upon" refers to name, which consists of the mind and mental factors.
Among these, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) benefits the basis (*āśraya*), because the body endowed with sense faculties (*sendriya-kāya*) subsists by means of it;
contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*) benefits that which depends on the basis (*āśrita*), because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) are sustained by means of it.
These two types of nutriment possess the most preeminent capacity for sustaining and benefiting existence that has already arisen.

Volition acts as the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), while consciousness acts as the seed; together they bring about future existence. That is to say, by means of karma, one is able to project the two forms of existence—name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—in the future.
Once karma has performed its projection, craving moistens the seed of consciousness, enabling the arising of the body of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in a future existence.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause of birth; craving is the cause of origination."
These two types of nutriment possess the most preeminent capacity for inducing the arising of existence; therefore, only these four are designated as nutriments.
Among these four, the latter two are like a birth-mother, because they give rise to what has not yet arisen;
the former two are like a foster-mother, because they nourish that which has already arisen.
The detailed determination of these points is as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Now, one should further consider the previous explanation of the four modes of existence (*bhava*): since the two existences of death and birth each last for only a single moment, which consciousness manifests during that time?
With which sensation (*vedanā*) is this consciousness associated?
Can death and rebirth occur in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*) or a mindless state (*acittaka*)?
In what kind of nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness does one abide to enter *nirvāṇa*?
At the time of death, where does consciousness cease?
What is the nature of the "vital points" (marman) that are severed?
The verse says:
The severing and reconnecting of the roots of virtue, the loss of detachment, death, and birth are held to occur only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Death and birth occur only in the state of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), not in meditative absorption or the two mindless states. These two neutral states lead to nirvana.
In the process of gradual death, [the consciousness] passes through the feet, the navel, and the heart; finally, the mental consciousness ceases.
For those not reborn in the lower realms or the heavens, the vital points (*marmaccheda*)—such as water and so forth—are severed.
The treatise says:

In the six stages—severing the roots of goodness, reconnecting the roots of goodness, becoming detached from the defilements of a realm or level, falling away from such detachment, death, and rebirth—it is held that only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is present; for these are all unique functions of the mental consciousness, and the five sensory consciousnesses lack the capacity for them.
The statement regarding "birth" also encompasses the first moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is associated with all three types of feeling, at the time of death and birth there is only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and not the feelings of suffering or pleasure. This is because the nature of the feelings of suffering and pleasure is not clear or sharp, which makes them conducive to the time of death and birth; whereas the nature of equanimity is extremely clear and sharp, making it unsuitable for the time of death and birth.
A consciousness that is not clear and sharp does not possess the nature of death and rebirth, because at the time of death and rebirth, it is necessarily dull and inferior.

For this reason, it is said that in the lower three dhyānas, only the minds of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) possess the principle of death and rebirth, because the fundamental stages lack the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā).

Although it is said that death and birth occur in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), this does not mean that the principle of death and birth applies to the mind in meditative absorption (*samāhita-citta*). This is because death and birth do not occur across different realms (*dhātu*) or levels (*bhūmi*).
Even if the realm and level were the same, [the mind in absorption] is extremely clear and sharp, having been induced by superior preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, because a mind in meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*) is capable of providing benefit and support, death can only occur through harm;
and because all minds in meditative concentration are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*), rebirth can only be attained through defilement (*kliṣṭa*).

Because a defiled mind of a different stage also provides sustenance, there is no principle for death [to occur therein]; because it is an active preparatory state (*prayoga*), there is no principle for taking birth [therein].
A defiled mind of a different stage must be subsumed under a superior stage; it is impossible that one would desire to go to a lower stage to take birth.

The neutral states of other stages arise from non-defiled preparatory effort; furthermore, they are neither states of birth-and-death nor states without mind, as such would contradict the logical principle of the occurrence of death and rebirth.
There are two kinds of death: either being killed by another or dying through natural course.
One in a state of mindlessness cannot be killed by another, because there is a superior dharma that sustains the body;
yet one in a state of mindlessness does not die through natural course, because entering a meditative absorption of the mind is capable of inducing the emergence of the mind.

This means that when the mind of entry acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it grasps the resultant phenomena such as the body and mind based upon this [previous state]. There is certainly no other distinct phenomenon capable of obstructing them so as to prevent their arising.

If the supporting body is about to undergo transformation and decay, one must necessarily give rise again to a body and mind belonging to this [state] before death can occur; there is no other principle.
Furthermore, there is scriptural evidence proving that death does not occur in a state of mindlessness; thus, a sutra states:

"Sentient beings in the realm of non-conception pass away from that place once consciousness has arisen. Birth cannot be attained in a state of mindlessness, because birth must be induced by the manifestation of a superior mind, because one enters birth while abiding in a state of dull and inferior [consciousness], and because birth cannot occur apart from the arising of afflictions.
Furthermore, there is a sūtra that proves one is not born without consciousness; thus the sūtra says:
"If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, would name-and-form (nāmarūpa) be able to form the kalala?"
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Now, although the mind at the moment of death can be of any of the three natures, an Arhat necessarily lacks a defiled mind.
Although they may possess a virtuous mind or one of the two types of neutral minds, because these are too powerful, they do not enter nirvana [at that time].
The mind that enters *nirvāṇa* is exclusively of two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states: namely, either the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or that born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
If one asserts that there is a mind entering *nirvāṇa* that is a neutral state of equanimity born of maturation in the desire realm, it would pertain to both types of neutral states;

however, if one asserts that there is no such mind of equanimity born of maturation in the desire realm, then it must be only the path of deportment, for there is certainly no mind existing independently apart from feeling (*vedanā*).
Why do inferior wholesome states not enter nirvāṇa?
Because those wholesome minds possess maturation (*vipāka*).
All Arhats, being weary of and turning away from all future fruits of maturation, enter nirvāṇa.
If that were so, one abiding in maturation (vipāka) would not enter nirvāṇa. It is not so;
for it has already been specified that this refers to aversion toward the future.
Why, then, would one not feel aversion toward present maturation?
Because one knows that by depending on the present matured fruit (*vipāka*), all forms of existence (*bhava*) are permanently severed;
and because one realizes the fruit of Arhatship by depending on the present matured fruit, one recognizes its great benefit and does not feel profound revulsion toward it.

All Arhats, however, feel deep revulsion toward future rebirth; therefore, at the time of death, they avoid those wholesome states that serve as causes for such rebirth. Since only the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states possess weak power, they accord with the faint and inferior mind that severs the continuum; thus, they enter *nirvāṇa* through these two types of neutral states alone.

Although the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, rely upon the physical sense organs (*rūpindriya*) and yet possess no spatial location, this is even more so for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Nevertheless, if one speaks in terms of the place where the body organ ceases: in the case of sudden death, the mental consciousness and the body organ cease abruptly and simultaneously, without a specific location;
in the case of gradual death, for those destined for the lower realms, the human realm, or the heavenly realms, the consciousness ceases respectively at the feet, the navel, or the heart.
That is to say, falling into the miserable realms is called "going downward," and in those cases, consciousness ceases last at the soles of the feet.
If one is going to the human realm, consciousness ceases at the navel.
If one is being born in the heavens, consciousness ceases at the heart.
The Arhats are called "unborn" (*ajāta*); their final mind also ceases in the heart-base (*hadaya-vatthu*).
Other teachers say that its cessation occurs at the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*).

At the time of death, because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) ceases in the feet and other parts of the body, consciousness (*vijñāna*) follows and ceases accordingly. As one approaches the end of life, the body-faculty gradually diminishes until it suddenly and completely ceases in the feet and other locations; this is like placing a small amount of water on a heated stone, which gradually decreases and evaporates until it is entirely gone in one spot.
There is certainly no continuity of the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) that can act as a cause to produce the subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) of the destination immediately thereafter;
rather, it is only for those who die gradually that, at the moment of death, they are oppressed by the painful sensations of the "fatal organs" (*marmaccheda*).

There is no separate entity called a *marmman*; rather, there are specific locations within the body which, when assailed by the intense heat of the wind-element, give rise to extreme painful sensations that immediately cause death, thereby receiving the designation of *marmman*.
As a verse says:
"There is a specific place within the body where contact causes the end of life,
just as when the filaments of a blue lotus are touched by even a single mote of dust."

If the elements of water, fire, wind, and earth combine in an unbalanced manner—whether individually or collectively—and their respective potencies become excessively intense, they will injure the *marmans* (vital points).

This is like having one's limbs and joints severed by a sharp blade; because of this, extremely painful sensations are induced, and from that moment on, one will certainly lose one's life within a brief instant.
For this reason, they are called "vital points" (*marmaccheda*).
They are not called "severed" in the same sense as when one speaks of cutting wood; rather, they receive the name "severed" because, once severed, they are devoid of sensation.

One who delights in uttering speech that mocks and ridicules others—whether true or false—and who inflicts such piercing wounds upon the human heart, shall thereby incur the suffering of the severance of the vital points.
For what reason is the earth element not a terminal faculty (*marmaccheda*)?
Because there are no internal calamities corresponding to it as a fourth.
There are three internal calamities—namely, wind, heat, and phlegm—which arise respectively when water, fire, or wind increases.
Some say that this resembles the three calamities of the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
This severing of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) does not occur among the gods;
however, when the sons of the gods are about to die, five kinds of minor signs of decay first appear:
First, the sounds of his clothing and ornaments became utterly unpleasant;
second, the radiance of his own body suddenly grew dim and inferior;
third, while in the state of bathing, drops of water adhered to his body.
Fourth, one’s nature was originally restless and wandering, yet now it is stilled within a single object;
fifth, the eyes were originally fixed and tranquil, yet now they blink repeatedly.
These five signs appearing do not mean that death is imminent, for even these may still be turned back if one encounters superior and virtuous conditions.
Furthermore, five signs of great decline appear:
first, the robes become stained with dust;
second, the flower garlands wither and fade.
Third, sweat breaks out from both armpits;
fourth, a foul odor enters the body;
fifth, one finds no pleasure in one's own seat.
When these five signs appear, death is certain, for even if one encounters powerful external conditions, they cannot be averted.
Regarding this world of sentient beings—its birth, abiding, and passing away—the Blessed One established three categories.
What are the three categories?
The verse says:
The categories of the right, the wrong, and the indeterminate; the noble ones, those who commit the immediate transgressions, and the rest.
The treatise says:
First, the group of those fixed in the right nature; second, the group of those fixed in the wrong nature; third, the group of those of indeterminate nature.
What is meant by "the right nature"?
That is to say, the Blessed One said:

"The complete and total abandonment of greed, the complete and total abandonment of hatred, and the complete and total abandonment of delusion—the complete and total abandonment of all afflictions—is called the 'Right State' (samyaktva)."
Why is it that only the abandonment [of defilements] is designated as "right nature" (*samyaktva*)?
Because this brings about the eternal exhaustion of all false and deceptive phenomena.
Furthermore, its essence is virtuous and permanent, and thus it is certainly cherished by the wise.
The World-Honored One has also said:
"The Noble Path is called Right Nature (samyaktva).
As the Sūtra states:
Because one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
What is called "wrong nature" (mithyātva)?
It is said to be of three kinds:

The first is the perversity of destination, the second is the perversity of karma, and the third is the perversity of view; these are, respectively, the essence of the evil destinies, the five deeds of immediate retribution, and the five types of incorrect views.

Regarding the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) within the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), because they lead respectively and with certainty to the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyoga*) and hell,
one who accomplishes these acquires the designation of that collection and is thus called a noble one (*ārya*).

Those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*) because they are currently being liberated from or have already been liberated from the bonds of affliction (*kleśa*).
"Noble" (*ārya*) carries the meaning of being autonomous and free from fetters.
Alternatively, they are called "Noble" because they have distanced themselves from all evils, having attained the ultimate acquisition of liberation from fetters.
Because they proceed toward what is wholesome, they are called "noble" (ārya).
Because there is no interval between them, they are called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
Because they take pleasure in acting as the cause for these [retributions], they are called "committed" (kṛta).
Those that remain beyond the states of right and wrong determination are called the indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*), because they can become either depending on two conditions;
since they do not belong definitively to one side, they receive the name "indeterminate.

Chapter Four: On the Exposition of Dependent Origination, Part Five. Having thus already explained the world of sentient beings, the receptacle world shall now be explained.
The verse says:
The establishment of the receptacle world: The wind-circle dwells at the very bottom.
Its extent is immeasurable in width, and its thickness is sixteen lakṣas;
next above, the water wheel is eleven hundred million and twenty thousand [yojanas] deep,
with eight lakṣas of water below, the remainder solidifying into gold.
The diameter of this water wheel (*jala-cakra*) is twelve lakṣas and three thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas]; its circumference is three times this.
The Commentary says:
These hundred koṭis of four-continent world systems are thus established, perishing and forming together.

This is because sentient beings, by the very nature of things, cultivate and attain the various dhyānas; having passed away from the lower realms, they are reborn in the second or higher dhyāna stages.

When the receptacle world below has been destroyed by the three calamities and a vast period of time has passed, there arises from the power of the predominant karma of sentient beings a subtle wind within the lower space; this wind subsequently increases in strength and coils together to form a wheel, whose substance is firm and dense.
Suppose there were a mahānagna who, brandishing a vajra-wheel with great force, struck it suspended in the air; the vajra might shatter, but the wind-circle would remain undamaged.
Such is the wind-circle: its breadth is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen hundred million yojanas.

Furthermore, through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds and rains arise and pour upon the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*); the drops, as large as axle-trees, accumulate to form the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*).
Thus, while this water-circle has not yet congealed, it is eleven billion two hundred million *yojanas* deep and, in breadth, is said to be equal to the wind-circle.

Some say that the karmic power of sentient beings of limited scope maintains [the body] so that it does not disperse; just as when food and drink have not yet been digested and transformed, they never shift or flow down into the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*).
Other masters say:
It is held by wind so that it does not flow sideways, just as a grain basket holds grain.

Through the power of the karma of sentient beings, a distinct wind is drawn forth which strikes this water, causing it to solidify into gold, just as when boiled milk cools, a film forms on the surface; thus, the water wheel diminishes until its thickness is only eight hundred thousand *lakṣas*.
The remainder transforms into gold, three hundred and twenty million *yojanas* thick.

There are one billion distinct circular layers (*cakravāḍa*), each pair of layers being equal in extent; that is, their diameter is twelve hundred and thirty-four and a half million *yojanas*. The circumference is three times that amount, totaling three hundred and sixty-one million, one thousand, three hundred and fifty *yojanas*.
Having already explained the three wheels, the mountains shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Sumeru stands in the center; next is Yugandhara.
Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Kakudaka, Sudarśana, Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka Mountain, and Mount Nimindhara.
Outside the great continents and so forth, there is the Iron Rim Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
The first seven are composed of gold; Sumeru is made of four jewels.
They all enter the water to a depth of eighty thousand [yojanas]; the height of Mount Meru above the water is likewise.
"The other eight decrease by half and half; their widths are all equal to their heights.
The commentary says:
Upon the Golden Wheel there are nine great mountains; Mount Meru, the king of mountains, dwells in the center, while the other eight surround Mount Meru on all sides.
Among the eight mountains, the first seven are called the inner mountains; outside the seventh mountain lie the great continents and other regions.
Beyond these is the Iron Rim Mountain (Cakravāḍa), which encircles the four continents like a wheel.

The seven mountain ranges, beginning with Yugandhara, are composed solely of gold; Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, has four precious substances as its substance, namely, from north, east, south, and west respectively: gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal.
Because the colors of the precious jewels manifest in space according to their majestic power, the sky over Jambudvīpa appears to have the color of lapis lazuli.
From what do such jewels arise? They arise from the predominant force of the karma of sentient beings.

Again, great clouds arise and rain upon the golden wheel, with drops as large as chariot axles; after a long time has passed, the accumulated water surges in waves to a depth exceeding eighty thousand [yojanas], and through the piercing impact of fierce winds, the jewels and other elements are transformed and produced.

Once these have thus transformed into gold, jewels, and so forth, further winds are induced by the power of karma to distinguish the jewels and other materials, gathering them together to form mountains and continents; they also separate the waters into sweet and salt, establishing the inner seas and the outer oceans respectively.
How can water of one kind give rise to various kinds of jewels and other substances?

Rainwater can serve as the supporting matrix for the seeds of heterogeneous jewels and the like; furthermore, when it is struck by winds of various powers and intensities, these many jewels and other things are produced. Therefore, there is no logical fault.

Thus, these nine mountains rest upon the golden wheel (*kāñcanacakra*), and the depth of their submersion in water is equal to eighty thousand *yojana*s; the height of Mount Sumeru above the water is likewise.
Thus, it is said that from the golden wheel below to its summit, the King of Mountains, Meru, measures one hundred and sixty thousand *yojana*s in total.

Regarding the height of the water emerging from the remaining eight mountains, from the innermost to the outermost, they gradually decrease by half each time: that is, the first, Yugandhara, emerges forty thousand [yojanas], and so on, until the final Cakravāḍa mountain, which emerges three hundred and twelve and a half [yojanas].
Thus, the individual breadth of each of these nine mountains is equal to the height of the water it emerges from.
Having explained the nine mountains, the oceans shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Within the mountain ranges there are eight seas; the first seven are called the inner seas.
The first is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide, with each side being three times that length.
Each of the remaining six is half as wide as the one preceding it. The eighth is called the outer sea.
Three hundred and twenty-two thousand, three hundred and two more.
The treatise says:

Starting with Mount Sumeru and ending with the Cakravāḍa mountains, there are eight seas in between; the first seven are called the inner seas, and within each of these seven, there are the waters possessing the eight meritorious qualities:
First, sweet; second, cool; third, soft; fourth, light; fifth, pure; sixth, odorless; seventh, not harming the throat when drinking; eighth, not injuring the stomach after drinking.

Regarding these seven seas, the first is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide; measured by the circumference of the inner edge of Mount Yugandhara, its four sides each number three times that amount, meaning each side measures twenty-four million four hundred thousand yojanas.

The remaining six oceans decrease by half and half respectively; that is, the second ocean is forty thousand [yojanas] in breadth, continuing down to the seventh, which is one thousand two hundred and fifty [yojanas] in breadth.
The circumference of these is not stated because it would be too cumbersome and because it can be understood by analogy with what precedes.

The eighth is called the Outer [Ocean], filled with salt water; its extent is three hundred and twenty-three thousand two hundred and eighty-seven and a half *yojanas*, as indicated by the remainder of the number "eighty-seven and a half."
Having already explained the eight seas, we shall now explain the differences in the shapes and dimensions of the various continents.
The verse says:
Regarding the characteristics of the great continents therein: Jambudvīpa in the south is like a chariot;
Each of its three sides is two thousand [yojanas], while the southern side is three and a half.
Pūrvavideha Island has the shape of a half-moon;
its three sides are like those of Jambudvīpa, and its eastern side is three hundred and a half [yojanas].
The continent of Aparagoyānī is shaped like the full moon;
its diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas], and its circumference is three times this.
The northern continent is like a square seat, with each side measuring two thousand [yojanas].
There are eight intermediate continents, two on each side of the four great continents.
The treatise says:
Within the outer ocean there are four great continents, situated on the four sides facing Mount Sumeru.
Jambudvīpa is broad in the north and narrow in the south; its three sides are equal in measure, and its shape is like that of a chariot.
Its southern side is only three and a half yojanas wide, while each of the other three sides is two thousand yojanas long.

Only on this continent is there the Vajrāsana, which reaches the surface of the earth above and rests upon the golden wheel below; all Bodhisattvas in their final existence who are about to ascend to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment sit upon this seat and give rise to the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), for no other place possesses the firm strength capable of sustaining this concentration, nor does any other basis of existence (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The continent of Pūrvavideha is narrow in the east and broad in the west; its three sides are equal in measure, and its shape is like a half-moon.
It is three hundred and fifty [yojanas] wide in the east, and each of its three sides is two thousand [yojanas].
Because this eastern continent is broad at its eastern edge and the southern continent is wide at its southern limit, Pūrvavideha is like a half-moon, while Jambudvīpa is like a chariot.
Aparagoyānīya is shaped like a full moon; its diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas], and its circumference is seven thousand five hundred.
The continent of Uttarakuru is shaped like a square seat; its four sides are equal in measure, each measuring two thousand yojanas, with a total circumference of eight thousand yojanas.
The faces of the people there correspond to the shape of their own continent.
Furthermore, there are eight intermediate continents that are dependencies of the great continents; that is, there are two intermediate continents on each side of the four great continents.
Regarding the two intermediate continents at the edge of Jambudvīpa: the first is Cāmara Island, and the second is Avara-cāmara Island.
The two intermediate continents bordering Videha are: first, Deha; second, Videha.
The two intermediate continents bordering Godānīya are: first, Śāṭhā; second, Uttaramantriṇa.
Regarding the two intermediate continents bordering Kurūdvīpa: the first is Kaurava and the second is Kauravāvatī.
All these continents are inhabited by humans; because they are produced through the predominance of inferior karma, the physical forms of those people dwelling there are base and ugly.
Other masters say:
"The island of Yamadvīpa is inhabited by rākṣasas; all other islands are inhabited by humans.
Having thus explained the various continents.
In which direction and of what dimensions is the Lake Anavatapta?
The verse says:
To the north of this [Mount Sumeru] are nine Black Mountains; Within the Snowy Mountains and the Fragrant Intoxication Mountain, [lies the lake].
The Lake Anavatapta is fifty yojanas in length and breadth. The Commentary states:

According to the authoritative scriptures, within this Jambudvīpa, proceeding gradually northward from Central India, there are three locations each possessing three layers of Black Mountains (Kṛṣṇagiri). To the north of these Black Mountains lies the Great Snowy Mountain (Himavat); to the north of the Great Snowy Mountain is Mount Gandhamādana. Between the north of the Snowy Mountains and the south of Mount Gandhamādana lies a great lake named Anavatapta, from which four great rivers flow toward the four oceans on their four sides: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Sindhu; third, the Sītā; and fourth, the Vakṣu.
