they are welcomed by others, or they go themselves to subdue them. They prevail through debate or battle, yet without causing harm.
Their marks are not perfectly bright and complete; therefore, they are not equal to the Buddha.
The treatise says:
From the time when the lifespan of the people of this continent is immeasurable years down to eighty thousand years, there are the births of Cakravartin kings.
When [the lifespan] decreases to eighty thousand years, the wealth, happiness, and life-span of sentient beings diminish because they are no longer suitable vessels [for such excellence].
Because the king leads and guides all by means of the revolving wheel-treasure (cakraratna) to subdue them through his majesty, he is called a Wheel-turning King (cakravartin).

The *Prajñapti-pāda* states that there are four types, because the wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron must be distinguished; these correspond respectively to superior, middle, inferior, and lowest.

In reverse order, the wheel-turning kings rule over one, two, three, or four continents: that is, an iron-wheel-turning king rules over one continent; a copper-wheel-turning king, over two; a silver-wheel-turning king, over three; and a gold-wheel-turning king, over the four continents.
The sūtra speaks only of the gold wheel because it emphasizes the most excellent case; thus the sūtra says:

"If a king is born into the Kṣatriya caste and has received the consecration of the crown, when he observes the fast on the fifteenth day, having bathed his head and body and undertaken the superior fast and precepts, and while he is seated upon a high hall with his ministers surrounding him like spokes, suddenly a precious gold wheel appears in the east."

Its wheel is complete with a thousand spokes, a hub, and a rim; its various features are perfectly pure and not the work of a craftsman. It radiates wondrous light and has come to attend upon the king; this king is certainly a Wheel-Turning King of Gold.
It should be understood that the same applies to other wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*).
Just as with the Buddha, two wheel-turning kings do not arise simultaneously; therefore, the Sūtra states:
"There is no place and no occasion where two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world, neither before nor after; there is only one Tathāgata at a time."
As it is said regarding the Tathāgata, so it is with the Wheel-turning King (cakravartin).
One should carefully examine this singular statement: does it refer to a single trichiliocosm, or is it intended for all world-systems?
One should state that all realms (*dhātu*) are without distinction; thus, it is said they do not exist.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks only of "this world," and there is no sūtra stating that there is only one world.
How can one definitively know that [the teaching] refers only to a single trichiliocosm and not to all realms, simply because it was not explicitly stated?
If that is so, why does the *Brahmā-rāja-sūtra* state:
"I now exercise sovereign mastery over these worlds of the trichiliocosm"?
This statement has an underlying intention (*saṃdhi*): it means that if the Blessed One does not apply effort (*prayoga*), he can perceive only this trichiliocosm.

If at times the Blessed One exerts his application of effort (*prayoga*), infinite worlds all become the range of his divine eye; the same should be understood for his supernormal power of the divine ear and so forth.

If this were not admitted, by what cause would the Buddha lack the capacity for mastery in transformation within other realms? Would it be due to a deficiency in great compassion, or because his wisdom is obstructed?
If [the Buddha] lacked great compassion, the Sūtra should not have stated:
"The Tathāgata’s heart of compassion universally covers all.
If his wisdom were obstructed, the Sūtra should not have stated:
There is not a single object of knowledge (*jñeya*) upon which the Buddha’s wisdom does not operate.

If the Buddha’s wisdom and compassion pervade all things without obstruction or deficiency, then he ought to preach the Dharma so as to universally deliver all sentient beings; for within boundless realms, the Tathāgata possesses inconceivable power capable of transforming all universally.
The detailed analysis of the remaining points is as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Regarding these four types of wheel-turning kings thus described, there are also differences in how they establish authority over the various regions.
Specifically, as for the one with a golden wheel, the minor kings each come to welcome him and make this request:
"Our lands are vast and abundant, peaceful, prosperous, and filled with many people.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will personally bestow his instructions upon us; we are all your followers and attendants."
If it is a silver-wheel-turning king, he goes to that land himself, and by the majesty of his presence, the people of that region submit.
If it is a copper-wheel-turning king, having arrived in that country, he proclaims his majesty and vies in virtue, whereupon the people of that region acknowledge his superiority.
If it is an Iron Wheel-Turning King, he likewise proceeds to that country, manifests his majesty, and arrays his troops; once he has achieved victory, he stops.

None of the Wheel-Turning Kings inflict injury; having subdued them and secured victory, they allow each to remain peacefully in their own dwellings and exhort them to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action. Therefore, when a Wheel-Turning King dies, he most often attains rebirth in the heavens.
The Sūtra states:
"When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, seven treasures likewise appear in the world.
Thus, such a Wheel-Turning King is distinguished from other kings not only by these seven treasures, but also by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
If that is so, what is the difference between a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and a Buddha?
The marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*) on a Buddha are correctly positioned, distinct, and perfectly complete, whereas those of a king are not; thus, there is a distinction.
"Correctly positioned" means that among the various marks on the Buddha’s body, none are biased, as each occupies its proper place.
"Clarity" means that the physical marks of the Buddha's body are extremely distinct, such that they captivate the mind.
"Perfection" means that the various marks of the Buddha's body are complete and all-encompassing, without any deficiency or omission.
At the beginning of the eon, did the multitude of beings have a king?
The verse says:
At the beginning of the eon they were like the gods of the Form Realm; later, their craving for flavors gradually increased.
"Due to laziness, hoarding, and the arising of thieves, / To prevent [theft], they were hired to guard the fields.
The Commentary says:
At the beginning of the eon, all people were like those who had passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Form Realm to be born among humans; after a long period of time, kings gradually appeared.
Therefore, a sutra states:

At the beginning of the kalpa, humans were corporeal yet mind-made (*manomaya*), with limbs fully developed and sense faculties complete; their forms were upright and dignified, their bodies radiated light, they moved freely through the air, and they took joy as their food and drink.
After they had dwelt for a long time, a kind of essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) gradually emerged, its taste sweet and delicious and its fragrance rich and pervasive.

At that time, there was a man whose nature was to crave flavors; upon smelling the fragrance, he conceived a desire, took some to taste it, and then ate it. Others followed his example, vying with one another to take and eat it.
At that time, it was first called "receiving solid food.

Because they were sustained by solid food, their bodies gradually became firm and heavy; their radiance vanished and darkness arose, whereupon the sun, moon, and various stars appeared from that point on.
Due to their gradual addiction to its flavor, the *pṛthivī-rasa* (earth-essence) vanished; from this, there subsequently arose the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-crust cakes).
As they vied with one another to consume them, the earth-crust cakes also vanished.
At that time, forest creepers (*vanalatā*) appeared, but because they vied with one another in consuming them, the forest creepers also vanished.
There grew wild fragrant rice that required no cultivation; the multitude gathered it together to serve as their food.
Because this food was coarse, waste and impurities remained in their bodies; to eliminate these, two passages naturally formed, and from this, the male and female organs subsequently arose.

Due to the difference between the two organs, their physical forms also became distinct; through the power of past habitual tendencies, they looked at one another and gave rise to improper mental attention, engaging in unchaste conduct. It was at this time that the "lust-demons" among human beings first emerged.
At that time, people would gather fragrant rice as needed according to the timing of their meals, without storing any away.
Later, there was a person of a lazy disposition who took a large quantity of fragrant rice to store for future consumption; others followed his example, gradually accumulating larger stores.

Consequently, they conceived the notion of "mine" regarding the rice; each, following their greedy impulses, harvested as much as possible without satiety. Thus, where it was harvested, it no longer grew again. Thereupon, they divided the fields among themselves, fearing that the supply would eventually be exhausted.

Regarding their own plots of land, they developed a sense of stinginess and attachment, while toward the plots of others, they harbored thoughts of seizure and plunder; thus, the transgression of robbery first arose at this time.

Desiring to prevent such occurrences, they gathered together for detailed deliberation and, having weighed the merits of those within the community, they hired one virtuous man with a sixth portion of each person’s harvest to protect them and appointed him as the Lord of the Fields (*kṣetrapati*). For this reason, the name *Kṣatriya* was established.
The great assembly reverently received his grace, which flowed throughout the land; thus, he was again named King Mahāsammata.
From that time forth, all subsequent kings have taken this king as their progenitor.

At that time, some among the people grew weary of domestic life and took pleasure in seclusion to cultivate the practice of the precepts with diligence; for this reason, they obtained the name "Brahmins."
Later, there was a king who was greedy and stingy with wealth; he could not distribute it equitably among the people of his realm, and thus many impoverished individuals engaged in acts of theft.
To prohibit such behavior, the king imposed light and heavy punishments, and it was at this time that the karma of killing first began.
At that time, there were those with guilty minds who, fearing punishment, concealed their transgressions and spoke with deceptive intent; thus, false speech first arose at this juncture.
During the period of the kalpa’s decline, there are the three minor calamities.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
As the paths of unwholesome action increase, the lifespan decreases until it reaches thirteen years, at which point the calamities appear.
Sword, plague, and famine occur in sequence, lasting for seven days, seven months, and seven years respectively.
The commentary states:

From the time sentient beings began to utter false speech, the various paths of unwholesome karma increased progressively; consequently, the lifespan of the people of this continent gradually diminished until it reached a minimum of ten years, at which point the three minor calamities manifest.
Therefore, all calamities and afflictions are rooted in two factors: first, the craving for fine food; second, a nature of indolence and negligence.
These minor three calamities arise before the intermediate kalpa has begun.
As for the three great calamities, they are: first, weapons; second, pestilence; and third, famine.

This refers to the time at the end of an intermediate kalpa when the lifespan is ten years; at that time, people have their mental continuums defiled by unrighteous greed, their minds are shrouded by partiality and attachment, they are entangled by false teachings, and their hatred increases to such an extent that as soon as they see one another, they give rise to fierce and harmful intentions.
Now, when hunters see wild birds and beasts, whatever they grasp in their hands becomes a sharp blade, and each gives rein to their ferocity and madness to slaughter one another.

Furthermore, at the end of the intermediate kalpa, during the time of humans with a ten-year lifespan, because they possess all the aforementioned faults, non-human spirits emit poison and epidemics spread; those who encounter them die immediately, and it is difficult to provide medical treatment or salvation.

Furthermore, at the end of the intermediate kalpa, when the human lifespan is ten years, because people likewise possess all the aforementioned faults, the devas and nāgas reprove them in anger and do not send down sweet rain. Consequently, the world suffers from famine for a long time; as there is no means of relief, the majority of people perish.

If there is anyone who can observe the precept against killing for one day and one night, and with a mind of profound purity offers a medicinal herb to the Sangha, or offers a single morsel of food to the assembly of monks, they will certainly not encounter the arising of these three calamities.
How long does each of these three calamities last?

The calamity of weapons lasts for at most seven days; the calamity of pestilence lasts for seven months and seven days; and the calamity of famine lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days. Once these have passed, they cease, and the lifespan of human beings gradually increases.

In the two continents of the East and West, there arise calamities resembling those [of the three great disasters]: namely, the intensification of hatred, the weakening of physical strength, and the frequent occurrence of hunger and thirst.
In the Northern Continent, none of these exist at all.
What are called the characteristics of the three great disasters?
The verse says:

The three calamities are fire, water, and wind; the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas) serve as their limits, corresponding respectively to internal calamities and so forth; in the fourth [absorption], there is no movement.
However, those receptacles are not permanent, for they arise and perish simultaneously with sentient beings;
thus, there must be seven fires and one water, followed by wind after seven cycles of fire and water.
The treatise says:
These three great calamities oppress sentient beings, causing them to abandon the lower realms and gather in the higher heavens.
First, the calamity of fire arises through the appearance of seven suns.
Some say that these seven solar discs travel like a flight of geese, moving in separate paths and circling about.
Some say that as these seven suns move, they travel in ascending and descending paths, revolving with each being five thousand *yojanas* apart from the others.
Subsequently, the calamity of water arises due to the falling of torrential rain.
Some say that from the space at the edge of the third dhyāna, hot ash-water suddenly rains down.
Others further say:
From the water wheel below, boiling surges arise as the water ascends, flooding and submerging everything.
According to the true meaning, this occurs when the subsequent wind-disaster arises at that edge, caused by the mutual impact of the winds.
Some say that a wind suddenly surges forth from the space at the edge of the fourth dhyāna.
Others further say:
From the lower wind-circle, the striking winds rise upward, surging and tossing [the world].
This true meaning should be understood according to what was previously explained.
If these three calamities destroy the receptacle world until not even a subtle particle remains, what serves as the seed for the subsequent arising of coarse matter?
Is it not the case that the wind at the summit of the previous calamity serves as the condition, while the drawn-forth wind serves as the seed?
Or, as previously stated, the wind produced by the karma of sentient beings is able to serve as the seed.
Within the wind there exist various subtle entities that, acting as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), draw forth the arising of coarse entities.

Alternatively, the destruction of various world-systems does not occur simultaneously; thus, it would involve no logical fault if winds from other regions, endowed with various qualities, were to come here to serve as the seeds.
Therefore, a sūtra of the Mahīśāsaka school states:
"The wind carries seeds from other regions and brings them here.
Regarding the wind at the summit of the previous calamity as previously described, what calamity is this one, and what constitutes its summit?
Fire, water, and wind are, in order, the upper limits of the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"There are three limits of calamity; when the world is consumed by the calamity of fire, the Ābhāsvara Heaven serves as the limit of that calamity."
When at times the world is submerged and rotted by the calamity of water, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven serves as the upper limit of this calamity.
When at times the world is blown apart by the calamity of wind, the Bṛhatphala Heaven serves as the upper limit of this calamity.
Any place that is not reached by the power of a particular calamity is designated as the "summit" of that calamity.
For what reason do the lower three dhyānas encounter the calamities of fire, water, and wind?
Because within the first, second, and third dhyānas, there are internal calamities that correspond to those external ones.
This means that in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra serve as internal calamities, capable of burning and distressing the mind and its associates, just like external fires.

Therefore, in the second dhyāna, the feeling of joy (*prīti*) serves as the internal calamity; because it is moistening like water when accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), all the grossness (*dausthulya*) throughout the body is thereby eliminated.
The Sūtra states that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) ceases in the second dhyāna because it is taught that internal joy (*prīti*) attains physical pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Since this joy is predominant in this stage and absent in other stages, the external calamity of water reaches its limit here.
In the third dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation constitute the internal calamity; since these breaths are also wind, they are equivalent to the external calamity of wind.
Therefore, if one enters this dhyāna, such an internal calamity arises, and within this dhyāna, one encounters destruction by this external calamity.
Therefore, the first dhyāna possesses three calamities internally and is likewise externally subject to destruction by those three calamities.
The second dhyāna possesses two calamities internally, and thus is externally subject to destruction by those two calamities.
Because the third dhyāna has only one internal calamity, it is destroyed externally by only one external disaster.
In the fourth dhyāna, there are no external disasters, because that realm is entirely devoid of internal calamities.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"That realm is called 'Immovable' (Acalā), because it is not reached by the three internal and external calamities.
If that were so, then the physical environment (*bhājana*) of that stage would have to be eternal.
Not so; for they arise and perish simultaneously with sentient beings.
That is to say, that celestial realm has no collective physical terrain, but rather consists of individual abodes, like those of the various stars.
When sentient beings are born or die there, the celestial palaces in which they reside arise and perish accordingly; therefore, the substance of that receptacle world is also impermanent.
What is the sequence of the three calamities mentioned?

First, seven calamities of fire must arise in immediate succession; next, one calamity of water must necessarily arise; thereafter, another seven calamities of fire arise in immediate succession. After these seven calamities of fire, there is again one calamity of water. In this manner, until seven calamities of water have been completed, followed by seven more calamities of fire, a calamity of wind then arises.
Thus, in total there are seven cycles of seven fire calamities, one cycle of seven water calamities, and one wind calamity.

The arising of the water and wind calamities both follows from the fire calamities; since the wind calamity necessarily arises after the water calamity, which in turn follows the fire calamity, this sequence of calamities is logically inevitable.
For what reason do seven fires occur before a single water disaster?
It is due to the power of the lifespan of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
That is to say, their lifespan extends for eight great kalpas; therefore, it is only upon reaching the eighth [kalpa] that a single water disaster occurs.

From this it should be understood that one wind-disaster occurs only after seven water-disasters and eight cycles of seven fire-disasters have passed, due to the power of the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
That is to say, since their lifespan lasts sixty-four kalpas, it is only at the end of the eighth fire-disaster that a single wind-disaster occurs.

Just as when sentient beings cultivate meditative concentration increasingly superiorly, the resultant body and lifespan they experience gradually lengthen, and by this means their dwelling place also remains for a longer duration; it must necessarily be so by the principle that the external is induced by the internal.
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen.
*Abhidharma-piṭaka-samuccaya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eighteen.

Chapter Five: An Analysis of Karma (Karmavibhāga). Part One. In this regard, a certain class of people who follow after the commission of evil and are timid in debate speak as follows:

"As has been stated above, the various distinctions among internal and external phenomena do not have karma as their cause; for we observe in the world that numerous differences among objects such as fruits and stones exist without any other [karmic] cause."
This refers to the arising of many fruits from a single seed, whereas things such as stones exist without being preceded by seeds.
To counter that position, the thesis is established.
The verse says:
The differentiation of the world arises from karma; it consists of volition (*cetanā*) and that which is produced by volition.
Volition itself is mental action (*manas-karman*); that which is produced refers to bodily and vocal actions.
The treatise says:
It is certain that the various differences among internal and external phenomena arise from the pure and impure karma of sentient beings.
How is this known? Because we observe the functional efficacy of karma.
That is to say, it is observed in the world that when the distinction between desirable and undesirable fruits arises, it is invariably due to the operation of karma.
For instance, among those such as farmers, through diligent and correct labor, there arise desirable fruits such as crops;
whereas when certain fools perform acts such as theft, they immediately encounter undesirable fruits such as execution and imprisonment.
Furthermore, one observes that there are also cases where, from the very moment of entering the womb, pleasure and pain arise not due to present causes;

having seen that in the present, it is only when preceded by karma that one can draw forth desirable or undesirable fruits, one knows that prior pleasure and pain must likewise have been preceded by karma.
Therefore, it is not without cause that internal and external phenomena possess their various distinctions.
What is the nature of the karma by which these distinctions arise?
It is volition (*cetanā*) and what is produced by volition (*cetayitvā*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There are two kinds of karma: first, the karma of volition (cetanā-karma); second, the karma after having willed (cetayitvā-karma).
Karma after having willed refers to that which is performed by volition; that is to say, it has the meaning of being originated by volition.
It should be understood that volition (*cetanā*) is itself mental action (*manas-karman*), while that which is produced by volition consists of bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*).
These two types of action are taught by the Blessed One in the sūtras as three, namely: bodily, vocal, and mental action.
Thus, these three types of action are established according to their sequence based on their respective bases, intrinsic natures, and origins.
Among these, the intrinsic nature of mental action has already been explained; it is volition (*cetanā*).
Volition has been explained as before.
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the two types of action—bodily and vocal?
The verse says:
These two types of action—bodily and vocal—are both of the nature of informative and non-informative.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that among all these aforementioned actions, both bodily and vocal actions possess the nature of both the informative (*vijñapti*) and the non-informative (*avijñapti*).
Therefore, the root treatise states:
"What is bodily action?
It refers to all that is manifest and unmanifest belonging to the body."
What is vocal action? It refers to all that is manifest and unmanifest belonging to speech.
Furthermore, for what reason do only bodily and vocal actions possess the nature of the manifest and the unmanifest, while mental action does not?
Because that characteristic does not exist within mental action (*manas-karman*).

That which can manifest is called "informative" (*vijñapti*), because it manifests one's own mind so that others may know it; since volition (*cetanā*) lacks this function, it is not termed "informative."

For this reason, it is said that only the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are capable of manifesting [intention], whereas mental action is not; because there is no unmanifested form (*avijñapti*) in the mind, there is likewise no unmanifested form there, as the term "unmanifested" is intended to exclude that which resembles it.
This refers to the category of informative [action] (*vijñapti*), yet it cannot establish the name "non-informative" (*avijñapti*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* provides a distinct explanation for this lack of logic, stating that there is no underlying mind (*citta*) for its continuity.
Is bodily and vocal movement itself informative action (*vijñapti-karma*)? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:

We maintain that bodily intimation is a distinct shape; It is not a conditioned phenomenon consisting of motion, Because [conditioned things] perish moment by moment, And because there would otherwise be no cause for its cessation.
Because the cause of arising must cease; because there is no fixed cause;
because earth and the other elements are not distinct [in substance]; because their defining characteristics are differentiated;
because grasping does not depend on anything else; and because contradictory causes are distinct.
Because there is cessation and non-cessation, because it is admitted that atoms exist separately,
because they are not apprehended by two sense-faculties, and because they are necessarily objects of the mental consciousness.
Only after having conceptually distinguished solidity and so forth does the cognition of length and so on arise.
On one hand, because many [atoms] are touched, one knows by inference that there is length and so forth;
for within a collection of many touches, length and so forth must necessarily exist.
Since they are identical and the fault is the same, verbal intimation is admitted to be vocal sound.
The treatise states:

The collection of hair, body hair, and so forth is collectively termed the "body. Within this body, there exists a differentiation of shape and color that is the fruit of the four great elements produced by the mind; because it is capable of manifesting the mind, it is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyavijñapti*).

Just as the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), though momentary in its cessation, is established as mental action (*manas-karman*) without contradicting reason, so too is the physical form (*rūpa-śarīra*) established as bodily action (*kāya-karman*).

It is not established that visible color (*varṇa*) or the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth constitute the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), because intimation can pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), whereas these [visible colors and elements] are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, because visible forms and so forth do not arise in accordance with the desires of an agent, and because they can arise even when separated from the mind, whereas informative action (*vijñapti*) necessarily depends upon the mind to arise.

If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth were produced by a single mind, then just as there is a distinction in their substance, there would likewise have to be a distinction in their dharmic nature; however, one cannot claim that things produced by a single mind possess distinct substances that constitute a distinct nature.
Furthermore, how is it known that the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are both wholesome and unwholesome?
Because it is stated in the sūtras. As a sūtra says:

Whatever phenomena are cognized by the defiled eyes and ears, for that venerable one they are not cognized by the pure eyes and ears; the same applies to what he says regarding those [phenomena] as well.
Furthermore, how is it known that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
This is also established by what is taught in the sūtras. As a sūtra states:
Or there is a certain class [of beings] whose bodies remain for ten years, and so forth, as explained at length.

Since it is taught that mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise and perish differently, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Although the dharmas of conditioned formations arise in different locations without an interval between cause and effect, they are conventionally designated as "action" (*gati*) and also termed "informative action" (*vijñapti-karman*).

However, bodily informative action is necessarily ultimate (*paramārtha*); it is not the case that all formations possess real movement, because conditioned phenomena exist only for a single moment (*kṣaṇika*).

It is not that the substance of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) moves to another location before its cessation occurs; rather, as conditioned phenomena arise in a particular place, they immediately pass away and cease right there.
What, then, is meant by "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)?
This refers to the shortest possible duration, which cannot be further analyzed into prior or subsequent parts.
What, then, is meant by "time"?
It refers to the differing states of the past, future, and present; it is by means of these that one numerically cognizes the distinctions among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Among these, the most minimal state of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called a *kṣaṇa*.
Therefore, it is said that because time is extremely brief, it is named a *kṣaṇa*.

Here, a *kṣaṇa* refers only to the state in which phenomena possess functional activity; that is, only the present. Thus, the measure of duration during which a present phenomenon exists is called "possessing a *kṣaṇa*," just as one speaks of a "moon-child" (*candramas*).

Alternatively, it is called "momentary" (kṣaṇika) because it is capable of destroying; this means that it functions as the cause for the destruction of all phenomena. That is to say, the characteristic of impermanence (anityatā-lakṣaṇa) is able to destroy all phenomena, and the factors that coexist with it are termed "possessing moments" (sakṣaṇika).
Furthermore, how is it known that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish moment by moment and do not endure for long?
Because all conditioned phenomena must eventually cease, and because the currently existing phenomenon of cessation depends upon adventitious causes.
Since it does not depend on external conditions, it ceases as soon as it arises.
If it did not cease at the beginning, it would likewise not cease later, because the primary cause remains identical from the beginning to the end.
Since one perceives that there is an end to what follows, one knows that preceding moments perish moment by moment.

If one were to say this is not so, it is because it is directly perceived in the world; for we see in the world that fuel and the like first exist, and when they subsequently encounter adventitious causes such as fire, they reach a state of cessation and non-existence, no longer being seen.

Since there is certainly no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that surpasses direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not the case that all phenomena cease without depending on adventitious causes.

Should it not be like the sound of a bell or the flame of a lamp? Just as those sounds and flames, although separated from the hand or the wind, perish moment by moment through their primary causes, yet when the hand or the wind ceases to contact them, they do not arise again; consequently, the subsequent sounds and flames can no longer be perceived.

In this way, fuel and other such things are made to perish moment by moment by a primary cause of destruction; subsequently, when they come into contact with fire, they do not act as further causes for their own destruction at that point of cessation, because they no longer arise and can no longer be perceived.
Therefore, this meaning is established by inference (*anumāna*), not by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
What is meant by inference?
It means that [the world] must have arisen [from causes], because there is nothing without a cause.

Regarding conditioned phenomena that do not arise without seeing or depending upon the two causes of guest and host—namely, the kalala, sprouts, walls, consciousness, and so forth—they necessarily depend on external conditions such as semen and blood, water and soil, and roots for assistance before they can arise.
If conditioned phenomena were to perish only by depending on external causes such as firewood, then they would have to be like their arising, requiring external causes before they could perish.
However, we observe in the world that cognitions, flames, and sounds perish through their primary causes alone, without depending on external causes.

Therefore, the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) does not depend on any adventitious cause; because the cause of their cessation is ever-present, these conditioned things perish as soon as they have arisen. Thus, the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*) is established.

Furthermore, if the conjunction with fire were the cause for the extinction of fuel and so forth, then since there are inferior, middling, and superior degrees within the process of transformation through heating (*pākaja*), the very entity that serves as the cause of production would necessarily become the cause of extinction. Why is this so?

That is to say, through contact with fire, fuel and other substances undergo transformation through heating; as the middle and superior degrees of heating arise, the lower and middle degrees of heating perish. Thus, the very entity that serves as the cause of arising would have to become the cause of destruction.
However, this is logically untenable: that which exists due to something else would, by virtue of that same thing, become non-existent.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the flame arises without remaining, this is also illogical; for since their essential natures are not distinct, there is no definitive principle whereby one thing can serve as the cause for both arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, while it may be plausible to calculate that there are distinct causes for the arising and ceasing within the production of various flames,
how can one calculate that there are distinct causes for the arising and ceasing when firewood and the like undergo transformation through contact with earth, water, vinegar, ash, snow, or the sun?
Therefore, the cessation of all phenomena does not depend on external causes; rather, it is caused solely by their primary cause.
By virtue of this reasoning, the principle of momentary destruction is established; consequently, all conditioned phenomena are devoid of movement.
Because there is no such thing as "action," the principle that what is called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is merely a particularity of shape (*saṃsthāna*) is thoroughly established.
How is it known that shape exists externally, distinct from color (*varṇa*)?
It is because the characteristics of shape and color are clearly distinct.
If shape were identical in substance to manifest color, there would be no distinction between the cognitions of them.
Since there is a difference between the two cognitions of "long" and "white," shape must exist separately from manifest color.

It is observed that there are tangible objects apprehended by the same sense organ which, because their perceived characteristics differ, must differ in substance—just as hardness differs from coldness, or warmth differs from hardness.

Likewise, although white color and length are apprehended by the same sense organ, they must be distinct in substance because their perceived characteristics differ; therefore, the substances of manifest color and shape are each different.

Furthermore, the substance of various shapes and forms is necessarily not identical to manifest color, because shape can be apprehended independently of manifest color; just as the cognition of one manifest color arises independently of other manifest colors, these two manifest colors possess distinct substances relative to one another.
Since the cognition of shape arises without depending on the manifestation [of color], we know that manifestation and shape must certainly have distinct substantial entities.

Furthermore, because there are differences among contradictory causes, their entities cannot be non-distinct; otherwise, there could not be the distinction between two contradictory causes, such as "this" and "that."

If it is necessarily the case that they do not coexist, this is termed "contradiction. Since contradiction exists between two dharmas due to a difference in their causes, their substantial entities (*svabhāva*) must be distinct.

We observe in the world that when contradictory causes differ, their substantial entities are necessarily distinct; for example, mental states such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, being of the same category, necessarily do not coexist.

Although manifest color and shape coexist within a single aggregate, we observe that while the shape may perish, the manifest color persists; therefore, we know that their contradictory causes must differ, and it is not the case that their substance is identical.

It may be argued that because there are distinct causes for their divergence, one exists while the other perishes; therefore, the meaning that shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color (*varṇa*) are separate entities is established.

However, although mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) possess distinct characteristics and the sense of having divergent causes, they must arise by acting as mutual causes for one another; thus, their existence and destruction must necessarily be equal.
Furthermore, since it is evident that color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna) undergo cessation while others do not, it is established by reason that the two dharmas have distinct essences.

In the world, we observe cases where names differ but the essence is one, yet there is certainly no principle whereby one part ceases while another does not; for example, the fire element itself is also called "heat."

Since it is observed that although manifest color and shape appear together in a single aggregate, there are instances where one ceases while the other does not, we know that manifest color and shape must certainly possess distinct substantial entities.

If it is argued that shape lacks distinct atoms because its atoms are like those of manifest color and thus not real, this is also unreasonable, for you admit that the atoms of shape exist just as those of manifest color do.

It is not that they do not exist substantially; for instance, just as there is no principle for individual atoms of manifest color (*varṇa*) to arise in isolation, even if they were to arise in isolation, they would be imperceptible by the eye due to their extreme subtlety. However, since they are perceived by the eye when accumulated, it is proven that atoms of manifest color certainly exist.
The same should apply to the atoms of shape and color; why then do you alone refuse to admit that there are real atoms?
In all places where resistant matter is accumulated, atoms are invariably present and can be apprehended.

Since, within the arising of the differentiation of aggregated matter, there arises a cognition of shape just as there is a cognition of color, it must necessarily be the case that there exist distinct atoms of shape, such as length and so forth, which are capable of growing and developing.

It does not mean that the manifest atoms themselves constitute the long and so forth; for when the basis of a designation perishes, the designation must necessarily perish, since a designation takes a real entity as its own essence.

If it were the case that manifest atoms constitute coarse manifest color and shape, then when the manifest color within a single aggregate perishes, the shape would also have to perish, because they share the same basis, just like the various manifest colors.
Since it is observed that when the manifest color (*varṇa*) is destroyed, the shape (*saṃsthāna*) still persists, we know that the bases for manifest color and shape are distinct.
Since their bases are distinct, the principle that their substances (*dravya*) are distinct is established.
Regarding this point, the Master of the Sūtra (Sthiramati) raises the following objection:

If one were to claim that there exists a distinct category of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), then a single color-form would have to be apprehended by two sense-faculties; that is, regarding the distinctions such as length within a collection of color-forms, both the eye and the body could perceive them simultaneously. Consequently, this would entail the fallacy of being apprehended by two faculties, for it is logically impossible for a single objective sphere of form to be apprehended by two sense-faculties.

However, as one grasps characteristics such as length based on tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), so too one can grasp shape (*saṃsthāna*) based on color (*varṇa*); this objection is not valid, because it is not admitted that the various conventional shapes, such as length and so forth, are apprehended by two sense organs.
Because those conventionally existent phenomena such as length and so forth are definitely the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

As previously argued, all conventionally existent things are exclusively the objective spheres of the mental consciousness. Just as seeds and atoms are capable of producing length and so forth, it is their specific arrangement that is designated as "length" and the like; this is apprehended by non-conceptual visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and not by tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Such visible forms are understood—such as hardness, moisture, and so forth, or length, shortness, and so forth—just as they are understood by relying on the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

It is not the case that because one does not perceive hardness, moisture, and so forth in the dark, one is therefore able to perceive characteristics such as length and shortness at that very moment or immediately thereafter.

Only after one has first distinguished the characteristics of hardness and so forth can inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*) regarding length and so forth subsequently arise; therefore, shape such as length is not an object of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

That is to say, when many instances of contact arise on one side, once contact has been distinguished by means of the body-faculty door, one is then able to inferentially know that the specific differentiation of form-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*)—which is experienced by the mental consciousness drawn by the visual consciousness co-arising with that contact—is such as it is. This is like seeing the color of fire and smelling the fragrance of a flower, whereby one is able to recollect the fire-touch and flower-color that co-occur with them.
The Master of the Sūtras further states here:
"When two dharmas are invariably inseparable, one may apprehend the other by apprehending one of them;
but since tangibility and shape are not invariably inseparable, how can one apprehend tangibility and thereby definitely recollect shape?"
This too is irrational, for it is observed in the world that within various aggregates of tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya-skandha*), shape (*saṃsthāna*) is invariably present.

That is to say, although shape is not invariably present within every single tangible object, when many tangibles arise on one side, there is invariably the color of length; when tangibles arise pervasively across all sides, there is invariably the color of circularity. Such categories should be understood accordingly. Therefore, the concordant example cited is established.

Furthermore, this [argument] must share the same logical implication as that [previous one]. That is to say, just as the sensation of heat is not determinately related to color or white color, nor to fragrance—unlike shape is to tactile sensation—one should not be able to recollect and know the tactile sensation of fire or the color and fragrance of flowers simply because of those [objects]. Therefore, it is not by means of this [argument] that one can refute the position that shape has a distinct substantial entity separate from manifest color.

Furthermore, it is shown that there would be logical faults regarding the possession of identical forms. That is to say, one may also perceive the tactile sensation of smoke within the throat, or sometimes smell its fragrance with the nose; based on this, one cognizes the manifest color (varṇa) within the smoke. Thus, manifest color should also be apprehended by two sense-faculties. It is not a case of a real entity existing such that, like the body-faculty cognizing various tactile sensations, one subsequently knows characteristics such as length and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is a distinct shape (*saṃsthāna*), existing as a real entity (*dravyasat*).
What is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñaptikarman*)?
It has the sound of speech as its essence (*śabdātmaka*), because apart from sound there is no separate speech capable of intimating [intention].
It is not as with the body and mind, which exist separately from karma; for verbal karma is established by name based upon its substance (*dravya*).
Thus has the characteristic of the two types of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) been explained.
The characteristic of unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*) was already explained in the first chapter; one must necessarily admit that this is of a substantially existent nature (*dravyasat*).
Why is this so? The verse states:
"Because it speaks of the three types of untainted form, and because of the increase [of merit], the non-created nature, and so forth."
The treatise states:

Because the sūtras teach that there are three kinds of form (*rūpa*), these three serve as the bases (*āyatana*) that encompass all forms: first, form that is visible and resistant; second, form that is invisible and resistant; and third, form that is invisible and non-resistant.
Apart from non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), what else is further taught here as the third kind of invisible and non-obstructive matter?
By this, the actual existence of non-informative matter is established through reasoning.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of untainted matter (*anāsrava-rūpa*), as the Sūtra says:
What are the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?
They are said to be the non-arising of craving or aversion toward any form whatsoever—past, future, or present—and so on up to consciousness; these are called untainted phenomena.
Excluding unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), what phenomena are designated as "all untainted forms" (*anāsrava-rūpa*) in this sūtra?

Since the Buddha has consistently taught that the ten material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) are exclusively of a tainted nature (*sāsrava-svabhāva*), it is established by reason that unmanifest form truly exists.
Furthermore, a sūtra speaks of the increase of merit, as it says:

"Whosoever possesses pure faith—whether they be a virtuous son or a virtuous daughter—who accomplishes the seven bases of meritorious action with a physical basis, whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, their meritorious actions constantly and continuously increase and their meritorious actions arise in succession; the same applies to those without a physical basis."

Excluding non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*), when one gives rise to another state of mind or is without mind, in dependence upon what dharma can it be said that meritorious action increases?
Since there is no informative action within merit that is independent of a basis (*anupādhi-puṇya*), how could there possibly be non-informative action?
Who says that there is no manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) in this case?
It must logically exist.

For it is said that when one hears that the Tathāgata or his disciples are currently residing in a certain place or region, and through the arising of joy their merit constantly increases, that person must necessarily possess superior faith; they would then reverently offer salutations and praise toward that direction from afar, generating both meritorious manifest karma and meritorious non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*), thereby adorning themselves with the hope of personally attending upon them. Thus, it is based on the non-manifest [karma] that the increase of merit is taught.
Furthermore, when one does not act oneself but merely dispatches another, if there were no unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*), it could not constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*).
This is because the manifest action (*vijñapti*) of dispatching another is not included within that person's own course of action, as this action has not yet directly performed what was to be done.
Once the motivating impulse (*anuśaya*) has performed its function, this nature remains without change.

However, because the preceding manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the volition (*cetanā*) that gave rise to it served as the preliminary application (*prayoga*), even if the teacher subsequently gives rise to a wholesome mind, there remains an unwholesome state persisting through a long succession of moments; thus, the motivating impulse continues to arise and its function is accomplished.

At that time, there is a capacity capable of drawing forth the production of such primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); the production of this derived matter constitutes the fundamental course of action (*karmapatha*).

That very prior manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the volition (*cetanā*) capable of initiating it, when present, act as the cause to take up the presently produced derived matter as its outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
At the present moment when non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) arises, that [past action] existing in the past is able to yield its present fruit.
It is solely that volitional karma (*cetanā-karman*) previously arisen which serves as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) for the undesirable fruit.
That which arises from the paths of action acts as an auxiliary to fulfillment, ensuring that the projected fruit will necessarily arise.
If non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) did not exist, this would not be possible.

Furthermore, if there were no non-informative matter, there would be no eight branches of the path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*), because speech and the other members are absent during meditative absorption; thus, the reality of non-informative matter is established by reason.
What is the essential nature designated by the term "unmanifest" (avijñapti)?
It refers to the nature of detachment; detachment is neither an act nor a creation.
Unmanifest karma is a single entity with different names; it is not merely the negation of an act that is called unmanifest.

Just as when people in the world say "non-Brahmin," it is commonly understood to refer to a specific class of persons distinct from Brahmins because of their actions (karma), such as the act of painting;
so too this non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) is given the name "action" (karman), because it arises based on informative action (vijñapti) and volition (cetanā).
Are all non-informative [karmas] produced by these two powers? No. How so?

Only those unmanifest actions (*avijñapti*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) can be produced by two powerful causes; for the volition (*cetanā*) of the desire realm is not in a state of meditative equipoise (*asamāhita*), and thus lacks the capacity to produce unmanifest karma without bodily or vocal manifest action (*vijñapti*).

However, because the volition associated with dhyāna is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it possesses a superior capacity to produce unmanifest karma without depending on manifest action.
Because this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti), although it lacks the characteristic of action, is caused by action, it also receives the name "karma.
Are the primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as the basis for both the informative (vijñapti) and the non-informative matter different or the same?
The verse says:
These primary elements that constitute it are distinct from those upon which the manifest [action] relies.
The commentary says:

Although the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and the manifest (*vijñapti*) arise simultaneously, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as their generative causes are distinct; for the causes of two effects—one coarse and one subtle—must necessarily differ, and there is a distinction in the combination of the generative causes.
All derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) mostly arises simultaneously with its generative primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, there are also some instances in the present and future that have past [elements] as their cause.
What are these few instances?
The verse says:
The non-informative [action] of the desire realm in subsequent moments arises based on past primary elements.
The commentary says:
It is exclusively bound to the desire realm; all non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) subsequent to the first moment arises from past primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That is to say, the non-informative matter of the first instant, which is bound to the desire realm, arises simultaneously with its constituting primary elements.
Once these primary elements (*mahābhūta*) have arisen, they serve as the cause for the arising of all subsequent unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) within one's own continuum.

When these [elements] perish together with the unmanifest form of the first moment, and the unmanifest form of the second moment and thereafter arises, all of it is produced by the preceding past primary elements.

These primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as the basis for subsequent moments of non-informative matter (avijñapti), because they are capable of inducing it; thus, they arise simultaneously with each subsequent moment of non-informative matter.
Within the body, the primary elements can only function as a basis, for if these primary elements were absent, the non-informative matter would not proceed.

Thus, the two sets of four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that arise simultaneously with the preceding [action] serve as the primary cause (*pravartaka-hetu*) and the secondary cause (*anuvartaka-hetu*) for all subsequent non-informative actions (*avijñapti*).
This is, for example, like the causes for the movement of a wheel: it depends on the hand and the ground; the hand is able to initiate the motion, while the ground merely serves as its support.
It should be understood that the same applies to the primary elements (mahābhūta) that coexist with them.
The primary elements pertain to all five levels; bodily and vocal actions are likewise so.
To which levels do bodily and vocal actions belong?
By what primary elements (mahābhūta) are they produced?
The verse says:
Those with outflows (sāsrava) depend on the primary elements of their own level; those without outflows (anāsrava) follow the place where they arise.
The treatise states:
The two types of action—bodily and vocal—are briefly of two kinds: first, those with outflows (sāsrava), and second, those without outflows (anāsrava).
If they are with outflows, they are bound to the five stages.
The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—bound to the desire realm are produced solely from the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm.
In this manner, up to the bodily and vocal karma of the fourth dhyāna, they are produced solely from the primary elements of that respective stage.

If it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it arises in dependence upon the body of one of the five stages; as it should manifest according to whichever stage it is born into, it is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that very stage. This is because untainted phenomena do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*), because there are certainly no primary elements that are untainted, and because the untainted arises through the power of its support (*āśraya*).
What is the nature of informative and non-informative karma?
Furthermore, by what kind of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are they produced?
The verse says:
The unmanifest (avijñapti) is non-appropriated (anupātta), and it is also a derivative (naiṣyandika) belonging to the category of sentient beings.
That which arises from a state of distraction (vikṣipta) depends on derivative primary elements (mahābhūta) that are with-appropriation (sopādāna) and distinct;
that which arises from meditative concentration (samāhita) depends on nurtured (aupacayika) primary elements that are without-appropriation (anupādāna) and not distinct.
The [unmanifest] is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), and it belongs to the body as something appropriated (*upātta*).
The treatise says:
In this verse, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is first explained.
Non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karman*) is briefly of two kinds, distinguished by whether it belongs to the meditative state (*samāhita-bhūmi*) or the non-meditative state (*asamāhita-bhūmi*).

However, in its general characteristics, it is all without appropriation (*anupātta*), because it is the opposite of that which is appropriated (*upātta*) and because it is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.
It is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*), because it lacks an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
It is not nurtured (*aupacayika*), because it possesses a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
It is a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).

This is also said to demonstrate the presence of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*); that is, the initial untainted (*anāsrava*) co-arisen non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is included within the category of sentient beings because it arises dependent upon consciousness.

If one distinguishes its basis according to its specific characteristics, all non-informative matter in the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) arises from great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are outflowing (*naiṣyandika*), homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and possessed of sensation (*sāvedana*).

The statement that "unlike [the material derived from] the primary elements" means that each of the seven types of bodily and vocal [karma] is produced by its own distinct set of primary elements. Regarding the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are two distinctions:

namely, the restraint of the dhyānas and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*). Both of these are nurtured by concentration; they lack sensation and are not produced by a set of primary elements distinct [from those of the body].
The statement that they are "not different" indicates that these seven branches of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) are all equally derived from the same set of four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

It should be understood that informative matter (*vijñapti*) is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*); if it belongs to the body, it is appropriated (*upātta*), while its other characteristics are all the same as those of non-informative matter in the state of distraction (*vyagrā avijñapti*).

This refers to those belonging to the category of sentient beings and those arising from outflows (*niṣyanda*), which are produced by distinct sets of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) accompanied by feeling.
For what reason can the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) belonging to the realm of non-concentration (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) be produced by the great elements?

The unmanifest (avijñapti) of the meditative state is exclusively of the nature of a result of uniform outflow (niṣyanda), because it is produced by being nurtured; for when a particularly distinguished mind is present, it is necessarily able to nurture the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the sense faculties. Therefore, that which co-exists with the concentrated mind must possess particularly distinguished, nurtured primary elements that can act as the generative cause (janakahetu) for the production of that which co-exists with the concentrated mind.

All unmanifest [form] (*avijñapti*) and unmanifest [form] belonging to the non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) have great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are solely of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), because their causal motivating mind (*hetu-samutthāna-citta*) does not exist simultaneously with them, and because they arise even during states of non-consciousness (*acittaka-avasthā*); this is because the causal motivating mind cannot nourish the great elements that produce the unmanifest form.
If that is so, what is the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the non-manifest (*avijñapti*) of the distracted stage (*vikṣiptabhūmi*) depends? Some say:

it is the outflow of the primary elements that have ceased immediately prior; these are the non-obstructive (*apratigha*) primary elements capable of producing [the non-manifest], not the outflow of the obstructive (*sapratigha*) primary elements, because there is a distinction between the categories of subtle and coarse for the fruits they produce.

According to this explanation, there has been from time immemorial a determinate, non-obstructive derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) capable of acting as a creator; having ceased, it serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the production of the present great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are its outflow (*niṣyanda*).

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) should likewise be the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of similar primary elements from beginningless time, rather than arising from dissimilar ones.

As for the non-appropriated primary elements upon which the uninformative action (*avijñapti*) produced by meditative concentration depends, because they are the result of a concentrated mind, there is necessarily no affectionate mind that appropriates these primary elements as its own present internal self.
Furthermore, because these primary elements (mahābhūta) lack any other characteristic of being appropriated (upātta), they are termed "unappropriated" (anupātta).

As for the primary elements upon which the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the non-concentrated stage depends, they are "appropriated" because they are the fruit of a distracted mind; that is, because they are grasped with a mind of attachment as one's own internal present self.

Just as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for visible color and so forth are subject to destruction because they arise in dependence upon the body, so too can suffering and pleasure arise when external objects come into contact with them.

For what reason is the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by a concentrated mind generated from non-distinct primary elements (mahābhūta), whereas the unmanifest produced in a distracted state arises depending on distinct primary elements?
Because the seven branches of the unmanifest produced by concentration arise through mutual power as a single fruit, they are generated solely from one set of the four primary elements.
Because these [two types] are mutually exclusive, they rely on different primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If the dispersed *avijñapti* shared the same cause of arising, then upon the transgression of even one [limb], one would have to transgress them all.

This is because, since the seven limbs of the *avijñapti* born of meditative concentration share the same cause of arising in relation to one another, they must necessarily be abandoned simultaneously.

Is it not like the precept of abstaining from killing, which arises in relation to the mental continua of all sentient beings? Although it is produced by the same set of great elements, one does not transcend [the precept] toward all beings simultaneously by transcending it toward even one.
The principle should likewise apply to the seven limbs in their mutual relationship.

This analogy does not hold; for although those [seven limbs] are each produced from a single set of primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the individual continuums (*saṃtāna*) of the sentient beings they relate to are distinct.

If the sevenfold precepts were not distinct from the great [vows], and since the mental continuum of the sentient beings toward whom they are directed is one and the same, for what reason would violating one not constitute violating all?
Therefore, this and that do not serve as comparable examples.
If that is so, this should follow the same principle as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Just as the essence of the life-faculty serves as the support for the possession of the body, it also serves as the support even when the body is incomplete; therefore, although the body may be deficient, as long as other faculties remain, the life-faculty is still able to sustain them, preventing their interruption or destruction.

In this way, a single set of great elements serves as the cause that can produce seven branches, whether complete or incomplete; therefore, even if some branches are missing, as long as the remaining branches exist, the great elements are still able to sustain them so that they do not cease or perish.

This is not a valid analogy, because that life-faculty (jīvitendriya) first arises simultaneously with a deficient body, subsequently arises together with a complete body during the intermediate period, and later arises again simultaneously with a deficient body when it is reduced; therefore, it sustains each state—whether complete or deficient—individually.

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not like this; a single set of primary elements constitutes a single continuum. If the cause for the arising of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) were to serve as the cause for the arising of the seven branches [of the path], it would never, even for a moment, arise together with a deficient branch.
How can one maintain the remaining [precepts] without interruption when one is lacking for a single moment?

It is precisely by this principle that the precepts of abstaining from killing and so forth—which arise with non-greed and other [wholesome roots] as their cause—may, although directed toward the continuum of a single sentient being, lapse for a single moment without lapsing for all [moments], because they are the results of distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the distinction of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*):

because the categories of their results differ, although many non-informative (*avijñapti*) forms produced by non-attachment arise in relation to the diverse continuities of various sentient beings, they nonetheless have only a single set of primary elements as their cause, since there is no difference in the category of the results produced.
Therefore, if for a single sentient being’s body the causes for the production of each of the seven limbs are identical, then by transgressing one, one must necessarily transgress all.
The objection previously raised is thus well-established in principle.

Therefore, the seven branches [of the bodily posture] are based on distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Just as when the divine eye arises it does not destroy its original form, the same principle should apply to the arising of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).

Thus, although bodily informative matter arises within the body, there is no fault of a maturation-form (*vipāka-rūpa*) being interrupted and then resumed; nor is there the fault of two distinct shapes arising simultaneously within a single aggregate of primary elements, because each instance of bodily informative matter has newly arisen, similar-flowing (*naiṣyandika*) primary elements as its basis.

When the manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) arises in dependence upon a particular part of the body, that specific part of the body ought to become larger than before, because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of both magnitude and shape have increased.
Yet, this is not perceived; how can this be logically explained?
Some explain this as follows:

because the informative matter (*vijñapti*) and the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are subtle and thin, they are like dyeing a limb; thus, although the great primary elements are present, they cannot be perceived.
Others say that because there are interstices within the body, even though [the new matter] can be accommodated therein, it does not become larger than its original state.
Having already explained that, in brief, there are two types of karma— namely, the distinction between volition (*cetanā*) and karma after having willed (*cetayitvā*)—
there are furthermore three types, namely, the distinction between bodily, vocal, and mental karma.

Furthermore, there are five types, namely: the two of body and speech, each consisting of informative and non-informative [action], as well as volition (*cetanā*), which is a single category of action.
How are these five types of action established in terms of their nature (*svabhāva*) and their realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*)?
The verse says:
Non-informative [action] exists in three [realms], while the others do not; The unwholesome exists only in the desire realm;
Non-informative [action] pervades both the desire and form realms; Informative [action] exists only where there is sustained thought (vicāra), in two [realms].
Desire lacks unobscured manifest action, because it lacks a motivating cause.
The treatise says:
Non-manifest action (avijñapti) pertains exclusively to the nature of the wholesome and the unwholesome; it does not exist as indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Why is this? Because it is originated by a mind of powerful force.

A neutral (avyākṛta) mind is weak and lacks the functional capacity to act as a causal origination (hetu-samutthāna) that draws forth a karma of powerful force, causing it to continue arising constantly throughout subsequent moments of other minds and even during states of non-consciousness.
As for what is referred to as "the rest," it refers to the two types of manifest action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*), which are threefold—namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

Among these, the unwholesome exists only in the desire realm and not elsewhere, because the unwholesome roots, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are absent [in the higher realms].
Wholesome and neutral [unmanifest karma] exist in all three realms as appropriate, since there is no specific prohibition against them.

Both desire and form realms possess unmanifest [karma], but it certainly does not exist in the formless realm. This is because within the formless realm, the perception of form has been suppressed; having become averse to all forms, one enters the formless attainments, and thus form cannot arise within those meditative states.
Wherever there is the activity of body or speech, only there is the restraint of body and speech.
Since there is no activity of body or speech within the formless realm, there is no restraint of body or speech there.
The Vaibhāṣika masters state as follows:
Śīla arises as an antidote to immoral conduct (duḥśīla), and it is only within the desire realm that various forms of immoral conduct exist.

The formless realm is distant from the desire realm in four ways: first, distance of the basis (āśraya); second, distance of the aspect (ākāra); third, distance of the object (ālambana); and fourth, distance of the antidote (pratipakṣa).

Regarding "remoteness of basis": this means that during the states of entering and emerging from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), there is no possibility for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) to serve as its basis.

Regarding "remoteness of aspect" (*ākāra*): this means that a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is ultimately incapable of forming aspects such as suffering or coarseness toward phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The meaning of "distance through object" (*ālambana-dūratā*) should be understood in this same way: because the mind of the formless realm can take only the impure phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the fourth dhyāna as its objects through the aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering, coarseness, and so forth.

Regarding "remoteness by way of antidote": this means that as long as one has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, it is absolutely impossible to give rise to the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), because these [formless attainments] can serve as the two types of antidotes—namely, the antidote of revulsion and the antidote of abandonment—for unwholesome conduct and other such phenomena of the desire realm.

Because it is not impossible to take [form] as an object of cognition and to cause its destruction through aversion, there is no unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

Manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) exists only in the two levels where discursive thought (*vitarka*) is present—namely, throughout the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna—but manifest form cannot be said to exist in the higher stages.

The mention of "possessing investigation" (*savicāra*) is intended to show that informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) exists throughout the entire first dhyāna; if there were no informative action at all in the stages above, and since vocal informative action is absent, how could there be the sense-sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*)?
There are sounds produced with external primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause; since this does not preclude external sound, there is no fault.
Other masters say:
"The three higher dhyānas also possess unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action (*vijñapti-karman*); logically, this must necessarily be so."

Since there is no fault in the arising of the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) within the three higher stages, why do they not give rise to the mind that expresses manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*)?

However, a wholesome or defiled mind of a higher stage does not arise from a lower one, because the wholesome and defiled minds of the lower stages are inferior and have been severed; therefore, there is no wholesome or defiled manifest action produced in the higher stages.
The previous explanation is correct.
Why is this so? Because although that [object] is present before one, one is not bound by it.
Overt action that is obscured-unspecified is certainly non-existent in the Desire Realm; it can only be said to exist within the First Dhyāna.
It has been heard that Mahābrahmā spoke words of deception and flattery—namely, he falsely praised himself and so forth among his own assembly in order to avoid being questioned by Aśvajit.
Furthermore, for what reason are there no informative actions (*vijñapti-karman*) at all from the second dhyāna upward?
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action, because there is no motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) that initiates such action.
A mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra is capable of manifesting informative action (vijñapti-karman); in the two higher meditative attainments (dhyāna) and above, such a mind is entirely absent.

Although one may give rise to a mind of a lower stage to manifest bodily or vocal informative action, it is not bound to those higher stages, just as in the case of the *Vijñānakāya* and other [treatises].

Furthermore, manifest karma (*vijñapti*) is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) operate within the internal domain (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*).
Since there are no afflicted-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) afflictions abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), manifest karma is entirely absent in the three higher realms.

In the desire realm, there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest action (*vijñapti*). Is it only by virtue of the motivating cause (*samutthāna*) that dharmas become wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth?
No. Why is this so?

The nature of wholesomeness and so forth is established by four causes: first, by way of ultimate reality; second, by way of intrinsic nature; third, by way of association; and fourth, by way of origination.
What dharma possesses what nature?
By what causes is it established?
The verse says:
Ultimate goodness is liberation; intrinsic goodness consists of shame, dread, and the [wholesome] faculties.
Associated with that, associated therewith, Arising together with form and karma, etc.;
The opposite of these is called unwholesome; Superiority, the two types of indeterminate, and the two constants.
The Commentary says:
Ultimate goodness refers to true liberation; it is designated as "good" in the sense of being secure and peaceful.
