That is to say, within nirvāṇa all sufferings are eternally stilled, and its supreme security is like being free from illness. Because this is established as "good" by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), nirvāṇa is called ultimately good.
Alternatively, true liberation is "supreme" (*parama*) and "object" (*artha*); thus it receives the name "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*).

"Supreme" means most venerable and peerless; "object" means that there exists a distinct, true ontological nature. This indicates that *nirvāṇa* is a peerless, truly existent entity, and is therefore called "ultimate reality."
"Serenity" (*kṣema*) is termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*), because this wholesomeness is permanent.
Regarding "wholesomeness by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-kuśala*):

this refers to moral shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and the [three] wholesome roots. Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), only moral shame, dread of blame, and the three wholesome roots—namely, non-attachment (*alobha*) and so forth—are wholesome by their very essence, independent of association (*samprayoga*) or other co-arising factors (*samutthāna*), just like efficacious medicine.

Regarding "wholesomeness by association" (*saṃprayoga-kuśala*): this refers to that which is associated with them; for the mind and mental factors must be associated with wholesome roots such as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) in order to constitute a wholesome nature.
If they are not associated with those qualities such as shame, their wholesome nature is not established, just like water mixed with medicinal herbs.

Regarding "wholesome by origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*): this refers to bodily and vocal actions, as well as the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), because they are originated by that which is wholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*) and by association (*samprayoga-kuśala*). Thus, the designation "origination" is established, just as milk is produced from the essence of medicinal herbs.

Acquisitions (*prāpti*) also arise due to minds of a different category; for example, when a mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) is attained through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one acquires all defiled dharmas because a superior neutral mind has become manifest, and one acquires all wholesome dharmas because a superior defiled mind has become manifest.
How do these [mental factors] constitute the nature of being wholesome and so forth?

This statement is made cryptically because they arise simultaneously with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those dharmas; there is no fault, for it is not the case that a mind of a different category does not function as a causal condition (*pratyaya*).
Although minds of different categories also arise as conditioned phenomena (*pratyaya*) to become wholesome and so forth, they do not depend on those [other] minds.

Alternatively, because these acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth arise due to those [minds], they attain the nature of being wholesome and so forth by depending upon them; thus, the nature of being wholesome and so forth of an acquisition differs based on its origination (*samutthāna*).
Just as it was explained that there are four distinctions of the nature of virtue (*kuśala*), the four types of non-virtue (*akuśala*) are the opposite of these.
How are they the opposite?
Ultimate non-virtue refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra; because all phenomena within saṃsāra have suffering as their intrinsic nature, they are utterly unstable, like a chronic illness.

Intrinsic unwholesomeness refers to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*). Among the outflowing states (*sāsrava*), it is precisely shamelessness, lack of dread, and the three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and so forth—that are unwholesome by their very nature, independent of association (*samprayoga*) or other co-arising factors (*samutthāna*), just like a poisonous drug.

"Associated with the unwholesome" means that which is associated with them; for it is only when the mind and mental factors are associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and the unwholesome roots that they constitute an unwholesome nature, whereas otherwise this is not the case, just as water mixed with poison.

That which is unwholesome by way of origination refers to bodily and vocal actions, as well as their arising, etc., and their acquisitions; this is because they are originated by that which is unwholesome by nature and by association, like milk produced from a poisonous decoction.

If that were so, there would be no single contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon that is either neutral (*avyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*), because all such phenomena are subsumed within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Consequently, everything would have to be subsumed under the unwholesome (*akuśala*); although this would indeed be the case according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), here the explanation is given in terms of maturation (*vipāka*).

Among all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), those that cannot be designated as having a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) are established under the name "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*); among these, those that can be designated as having a desirable ripened fruit are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
If both the wholesome and the unwholesome possess ultimate reality, does the indeterminate (avyākṛta) also possess ultimate reality? It does. How so?
This refers to two eternal phenomena:

non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and infinite space (*ākāśa*). Since they have no other categories and possess only an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are established as the ultimate indeterminate (*paramārthāvyākṛta*).

There is no separate self-nature (svabhāva), concomitance (samprayoga), or origination (samutthāna), nor is there any single mental factor (caitta), because only those of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta) are universally associated with an indeterminate mind.
Even if one were to establish the three categories of self-nature and so forth through expedient means, they would still not encompass all cases, as indeterminate states are numerous.
Thus, the indeterminate (avyākṛta) consists of only two types: first, the ultimate (paramārtha), and second, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Conditioned indeterminate phenomena are subsumed under the category of intrinsic nature, because they are established as indeterminate without depending on any other distinct cause.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are included within the ultimate (*paramārtha*), because their nature is eternal and lacks any alternative modes.

If the power of motivation (*samutthāna*) causes bodily and vocal actions to become wholesome or unwholesome, then the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which these bodily and vocal actions depend should likewise be so; for both arise from the same single mind.
This objection is unreasonable, because the agent’s mind originally intends to initiate action, not the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

That is to say, the agent does not generate a desire within the primary elements, thinking, "I shall bring forth such a kind of primary element into manifestation"; rather, it is with these [elements] as a gateway that wholesome or unwholesome minds arise.
Furthermore, it is observed in the world that the two types of action—bodily and vocal—arise dependent upon the mind; never has it been seen that bodily or vocal action arises apart from the mind.
However, the four great elements arise even apart from the mind; therefore, one knows that those phenomena do not arise dependent upon the mind.
Furthermore, just as the eye and other faculties do not depend on the mind for their arising, and thus their nature lacks distinctions such as being wholesome and so forth;
likewise, since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not depend on the mind for their arising, it follows logically that they too lack distinctions such as being wholesome and so forth.

If that were so, then acquisitions (*prāpti*) and the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth would lack distinctions such as being "wholesome by origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*), because they are not what the primary mind intends to produce, and because they manifest even during states of non-consciousness (*acittaka*).
This objection is irrational, because the distinctions such as "wholesome" and so forth are established through the power of the dharmas themselves.

That is to say, the acquisition (prāpti) and the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are established in dependence upon the dharma; they do not exist independently of anything else like the primary elements (mahābhūta).

Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is not a single dharma that does not depend upon the power of the mind to become wholesome or unwholesome. Therefore, it is well established by reason that the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) must, like the dharmas to which they belong, attain their nature as wholesome and so forth through the power of the mind.
Once it has arisen, it is dissociated from the mind; thus, even as it continues in a stream, there is no fault, because it is induced to proceed by the force of the preceding moment of mind.
It should likewise be established by reason that the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) associated with meditative concentration arises through the power of that concentration and so forth.

If it were the case that the nature of being wholesome is defined by its origination (*samutthāna*), then the divine eye and divine ear should be categorized as wholesome, because they are originated by a wholesome mind.

This objection is unreasonable, because those two supernormal powers are associated with the mind of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which is neutral (*avyākṛta*), and because those two arise simultaneously with that path.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti*, Fascicle 18;
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, Fascicle 19, composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: On the Analysis of Karma, Part Two. As stated above, it is through the power of motivation (*samutthāna*) that the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—become wholesome or unwholesome.
How many types of motivation (*samutthāna*) are there?
What kind of motivating force causes bodily and vocal actions to become wholesome or unwholesome?
What are the distinctions between these motivations when they are compared with one another?
The verse says:
There are two kinds of motivation—causal and simultaneous;
they should be understood according to their sequence as "impelling" and "concomitant."
The consciousnesses abandoned through seeing are exclusively *pravartaka* (initiators); the five sensory consciousnesses are exclusively *anuvartaka* (concomitants).
The mental consciousness abandoned through cultivation pertains to both; those not abandoned by either cultivation are neither.
Regarding the nature of being wholesome and so forth in the initiator, each of the concomitants may correspond to all three.
The Sage’s [actions] are necessarily wholesome; the indeterminate [actions] follow [the motivation] or are wholesome.
The commentary states:

There are two types of origination for the two karmas of body and speech, namely, causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*) and momentary origination (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*), because the former acts as the cause and the latter exists at that very moment.
Respectively, the first is called the "originating" (*pravartaka*) and the second is called the "conforming" (*anuvartaka*).
This means that when the causal motivation is about to perform an action, one thinks:
"I shall now perform such and such an action that ought to be done."
Because it is capable of initiating [action], it is called "primary" (*pravartaka*).

At the moment when the action is actually performed through its instantaneous arising, because it proceeds simultaneously with the karma initiated by the previously mentioned primary mind, it is called "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*).

If there were no *anuvartaka* (concomitant), then even though a prior cause exists as the initiator, the manifest (*vijñapti*) would fail to proceed—just as in a state of mindlessness or like a corpse.

The *anuvartaka* possesses the functional capacity to sustain the manifest; however, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) does not depend on a concomitant to proceed, because the unmanifest continues to proceed even in states of mindlessness.
As stated above, because the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) operate internally (*antar-mukha*), they cannot manifest external action.
If this is so, for what reason did the Blessed One say:
"Due to wrong view, one gives rise to wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, and so forth"?
This is not contradictory.

A consciousness abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) can only act as the *pravartaka* (the initiator) regarding the manifestation of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*); it does not act as the *anuvartaka* (the follower) because it serves merely as a provision for the arising of vitarka and vicāra that give rise to the informative action. This is because such a consciousness does not exist at the time when the mind directed toward external objects (*bahir-mukha-citta*) is actually performing the action.

For this reason, it is said that the mind abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) serves as the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) for bodily and vocal actions, but it can certainly not serve as the momentary motivation (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
Although consciousness abandoned through seeing is capable of deliberation, it lacks the functional capacity to move the body or produce speech.

However, within a single manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) that is set in motion, there may be many moments of thought deliberating and initiating it; yet, only the final moment of thought proceeds simultaneously with the manifestation. Otherwise, this manifestation would not possess the nature of being momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Although the consciousness abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) can act as the motivating force for the production of manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), manifest action does not arise immediately after this consciousness without an interval; for a mind that functions internally (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*) cannot induce it, as it is not a consciousness that operates simultaneously with bodily or vocal manifestation.

If it were otherwise, the mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) would also have to serve as the momentary co-arising cause (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*) for manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*). This is because the applied mental consciousness (*prāyogika-manovijñāna*) abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can immediately induce the mind that accompanies manifest action, and thus also serves as its momentary co-arising cause in being concomitant with that manifestation.

Therefore, although that which is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) can serve as a cause to project various manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*), apart from the motivating mind abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), a mind concurrent with the manifest action cannot possibly arise; for this reason, there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest action in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, the sūtras merely state, based on the principle of successive causation and motivation,
that "due to wrong view, wrong speech and so forth arise. The Abhidharma, however,

maintains that because such [wrong view] cannot immediately induce the consciousness concomitant with manifest action (*vijñapti*), it speaks with intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) that the mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya-citta*)— which operates only internally— cannot produce manifest action.
Therefore, the sūtras and śāstras do not contradict each other in principle.
Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) were to manifest as material form (rūpa), then this form would also have to be abandoned by insight.
However, it has already been established previously that form is not abandoned by insight.
If the five groups of consciousness function solely as concomitants, it is because they lack discrimination and operate toward external objects.
The mental consciousness that is abandoned through cultivation pertains to both types, because it possesses discrimination and operates toward external objects.
From this, a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:
there is that which is a primary movement (*pravartaka*) but not a concomitant movement (*anuvartaka*, namely, the mind abandoned through seeing);
and there is that which is a concomitant movement but not a primary movement (namely, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness).
There are those that are both the primary mover and the concomitant mover, namely, one portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
There are those that are neither the primary mover nor the concomitant mover, namely, all other forms of consciousness produced through cultivation.

Because it is non-conceptual as produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), the consciousness born of maturation (*vipākaja-vijñāna*) also functions as its concomitant (*anuvartaka*). This point is established in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Must the nature of the primary evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and its concomitant necessarily be identical?

Not so. Why? It means that if the preceding evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is of a wholesome nature, the subsequent conforming evolving consciousness (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*) may be any of the three—wholesome and so forth; the same applies when the evolving consciousness is unwholesome or neutral.

Only in the case of the Muni does the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the concomitant consciousness (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*) mostly share the same nature and rarely differ; that is to say, if the evolving mind is wholesome, the concomitant is also wholesome, and if the evolving mind is neutral (*avyākṛta*), the concomitant is likewise so, because there is certainly no delusion within the continuous moments [of his stream of being].

There may be occasions when the wholesome mind follows the indeterminate, but there is never a time when the indeterminate follows the wholesome; for the mind of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whether in preaching the Dharma or other activities, either increases or remains steady, never declining or ceasing.

Since it has already been stated that the primary (pravṛtti) and secondary (anuvartaka) [minds] of the wholesome and so forth each consist of three types, this very heading and explanation serve as sufficient clear evidence: the various karmas produced thereby become wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, according to their *samutthāna* (origination) and not according to their *kṣaṇika* (momentary) state.
Apart from this, since karma induced by a wholesome mental state coexists with unwholesome or neutral states of mind, by what principle could it be prevented from becoming unwholesome or neutral?
It would then follow that there must be karma of a distinct nature produced as a result of a distinct volition serving as its cause.
Thus, for one who exerts diligent effort with the desire to perform wholesome deeds, unwholesome or neutral karma may instead arise; conversely, if this occurs, it contradicts correct principle.

Therefore, it is established that the establishment of karma as wholesome and so forth is determined by the power of the primary motivation (*maulakarma*), not by the power of the concomitant motivation (*anuvartaka*); this principle is well-founded.
However, the various non-informative actions (*avijñapti-karman*) arise simultaneously with the concentrated mind, because they share a single result with that mind.
Their virtuous nature is established through the power of conformity (*anuvartana*), since they arise as being necessarily bound to this mind.

The discussion on the secondary treatise concerning the stages of the *vijñapti* (informative) realm is now complete; one should now further discuss the characteristics of the aforementioned *vijñapti* and *avijñapti* (non-informative).
The verse says:
Non-informative [action] is of three types: restraint, non-restraint, and that which is neither.
The Treatise says:
It should be known that, briefly stated, there are three types of non-informative action (*avijñapti*): first, restraint (*saṃvara*); second, non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
[and third, intermediate non-restraint].
Third is that which is neither of the two, namely, neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
It is called restraint because it can obstruct and extinguish the continuity of immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*).
How many varieties of such restraint are there?
The verse says:
Restraint is of three types: that of the Prātimokṣa, that born of dhyāna, and that born of the Path.
The commentary says:
Briefly, there are three types of discipline (*saṃvara*): first, the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*), which refers to the precepts of the desire realm;
second, the discipline born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja-saṃvara*), which refers to the precepts of the form realm;
and third, the discipline born of the path (*mārga-ja-saṃvara*), which refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts.
What are the distinctions regarding the characteristics of the initial vows?
The verse says:
The initial vows are of eight kinds, but in terms of their actual substance, there are only four.
Because their forms shift and their names differ, they are each distinct and not mutually contradictory.
The treatise says:
There are eight distinctions in the characteristics of the prātimokṣa vows.

1. The discipline of a bhikṣu; 2. the discipline of a bhikṣuṇī; 3. the discipline of a śikṣamāṇā; 4. the discipline of a śrāmaṇera; 5. the discipline of a śrāmaṇerī; 6. the discipline of an upāsaka; 7. the discipline of an upāsikā; 8. the discipline of an upavāsastha.
These eight types of distinctions in the characteristics of restraint are collectively termed the first, the Prātimokṣa restraint.

Among these, the first five distinctions in restraint are established based on those individuals (*pudgala*) who are able to cultivate the abandonment of unwholesome conduct and the abandonment of sensual conduct; for such individuals are able to abstain from various unwholesome conducts, such as killing, and are able to remain far removed from non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*) until the end of their lives.

Next, based on the individual (*pudgala*) who is capable of practicing the avoidance of unwholesome conduct but not the avoidance of sensual desire, the distinctions between the two lay ordination vows (*vrata*) that last for as long as life endures are established; this is because such an individual is able to avoid unwholesome acts such as killing until the end of their life, yet is unable to distance themselves from unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*).
For this reason, the sūtra states only this:
"One abstains from sexual misconduct, not from non-celibacy.

Subsequently, based on the *pudgala* who is able to practice [restraint] but cannot entirely abandon evil conduct and sensual desires, the specific distinction of the one-day, one-night (*rātri-divasa*) lay vow (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) is established. This is because such a *pudgala* is unable to completely abandon evil conduct and various sensual desires; it is for the sake of enabling them to gradually habituate themselves to the skillful means for abiding in the complete abandonment of evil conduct and sensual desires.
Although there are eight names, the actual entities are only four:
first, the bhikṣu vow; second, the śrāmaṇera vow; third, the upāsaka vow; and fourth, the upavāsa vow.
Only these four types of distinct vows of individual liberation possess substantial reality, as their characteristics are each distinct.

Why is this so? Because there is no separate bhikṣuṇī vow apart from the bhikṣu vow; there is no separate śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerikā vow apart from the śrāmaṇera vow; and there is no separate upāsikā vow apart from the upāsaka vow.
How is this known to be so?
Because while the substance itself undergoes no loss or acquisition, its designation changes due to the transformation of its form.
"Form" refers to the physical appearance, namely the male and female organs; it is by means of these two organs that the forms of male and female are distinguished.
It is solely due to the transformation of gender that the various vows of restraint are designated as "bhikṣu" or "bhikṣuṇī" and so forth.

That is to say, at the stage of changing one's faculties, the original bhikṣu vow of restraint is termed a bhikṣuṇī vow of restraint, or the bhikṣuṇī vow of restraint is termed a bhikṣu vow of restraint.
It causes the śrāmaṇera vow to be called the śrāmaṇerī vow, or it causes the śrāmaṇerī vow and the śikṣamāṇā vow to be called the śrāmaṇera vow.
The original upāsaka restraint may be termed the upāsikā restraint, or the upāsikā restraint may be termed the upāsaka restraint.

This is because at the stage of changing one's gender (indriya-parāvṛtti), there is no cause for abandoning a restraint previously obtained or obtaining a restraint not previously obtained; therefore, the four types of restraint do not differ in substance from the three.

If one receives the *śrāmaṇera* vows from the *upāsaka* vows, and subsequently receives the *bhikṣu* vows from the *śrāmaṇera* vows, these three sets of vows are established with distinct names based on the increasing degrees of the means of abstention (*virati-upāya*). Just as single and double gold coins, or the numbers fifty and twenty, are distinct in substance yet arise simultaneously in their fullness, the substances of the three types of vows do not intermingle; their characteristics are distinct, yet they arise simultaneously in their fullness.

Within the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*), there are three distinct instances of abstaining from killing; each instance of abstaining from killing has a separate ontological essence (*svabhāva*). It should be understood that the same applies to the remaining [precepts] as appropriate.

Because their causes and conditions differ, their essences are not the same; just as one seeks to receive various training rules (*śikṣāpada*) in increasing numbers, so too is one able to abstain from various [unwholesome actions] in increasing numbers.

When one is in situations conducive to negligence, such as high and wide beds or seats and the drinking of various liquors, one immediately abandons numerous conditions that give rise to killing and other misdeeds.
Because these abstentions arise based upon causes and conditions, there are distinct differences among the abstentions according to their respective causes and conditions.
If this were not the case, then upon relinquishing the bhikṣu vows, one would have to relinquish all three sets of vows simultaneously, because the former two would be subsumed within the latter one.
Since this is not permitted, the three must be distinct.
However, these three types [of vows] do not contradict one another; they function simultaneously within a single body, rather than the former restraint being relinquished upon receiving the latter.
Otherwise, one would cease to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth as soon as one relinquishes the bhikṣu precepts, because those two previous restraints would have already been abandoned.
Regarding the four types of restraint—the lay follower (*upāsaka*), the one observing the fast-day vows (*upavāsa*), the novice (*śrāmaṇera*), and the monk (*bhikṣu*)—how are they established?
The verse says:
"By undertaking the abstention from five, eight, ten, and all things that ought to be abandoned," [the four restraints are established].
The lay devotee (upāsaka), the one observing the fast (upavāsa), the novice (śrāmaṇera), and the bhikṣu.
The commentary states:

It should be understood that herein, according to their numerical order, four types of discipline (saṃvara) are established based on the four kinds of abstention (virati). That is to say, by undertaking the abstention from the five things to be abandoned, the first, the lay devotee’s discipline, is established.
What are the five things that should be abandoned?
First, killing; second, taking what is not given; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, drinking various intoxicants.
If one undertakes the renunciation of the eight things that ought to be abandoned, one establishes the second restraint, the *upavāsa* discipline.
What are these eight things that ought to be abandoned?

First, killing; second, taking what is not given; third, unchaste conduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, drinking various intoxicants; sixth, anointing with perfumes and wearing garlands, and watching or listening to dancing and singing; seventh, sitting or lying on high, broad, or luxurious beds and seats; eighth, eating at improper times.
If one undertakes the renunciation of the ten dharmas that ought to be abandoned, the third *śrāmaṇera* restraint is established.
What are these ten dharmas that ought to be abandoned?

They consist of the first eight [prohibitions], with the application of perfumes, ointments, garlands, dancing, singing, and watching performances divided into two separate items, and further adding the acceptance and possession of gold, silver, and other precious objects as the tenth.

To inspire those who are fearful and timid regarding the numerous rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), and to show that they are easy to undertake for lay sentient beings, the eight precepts combine two into one; this is just as when the *Kṛṣṇa* clan son was given a brief explanation of the rules of training consisting of only three.
If one undertakes the abstention from all bodily and vocal actions that ought to be abandoned, the fourth bhikṣu restraint is established.
Regarding the various synonymous designations for the prātimokṣa restraint, the verse says:
It is called by the names *śīla*, Excellent conduct (*sucarita*), and restraint (*saṃvara*).
Only the initial manifest and unmanifest [karma] are termed *prātimokṣa* and the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
The treatise says:
it is called *śīla* because it is cooling.
In this context, *śīla* has the meaning of "leveling" or "smoothing. Because ethical discipline (*śīla*) can level out rugged karma, it receives the name *śīla*.
It is called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*) because the wise praise it.
Alternatively, it is called "karma" because by practicing this, one obtains desirable results, and because it constitutes the very nature of what is performed.
It is also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*); as has already been explained previously, it should be understood in this way.

The Prātimokṣa vows share the same name throughout both their initial and subsequent stages without distinction; however, it is only at the first moment that the manifest (vijñapti) and unmanifest (avijñapti) actions receive the names "Prātimokṣa" and "karmapatha."

This means that at the time of receiving the precepts, because one individually abandons various evils through both the manifest and unmanifest [karmas], the name "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) is established based on the sense of this initial, individual abandonment.
Alternatively, it is called *prātimokṣa* because it is what should be cultivated at the very beginning;
or, it is called *prātimokṣa* because its initial arising is most capable of transcending the perilous and evil destinies that are like a prison.

The manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions of the very first moment may also be termed the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*), because they initially restrain body and speech and give full expression to the karma of volition.

From the second moment until the vow is relinquished, these are not called "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), but are termed "individual liberation restraint" (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*); they are not called paths of action, but are merely termed "subsequent occurrences" (*pṛṣṭha*).
Having already explained the establishment of the distinctions among the restraints, we shall now explain the distinctions regarding the attainment of those restraints.
Which person attains which restraint?
The verse says:
Eight types of prātimokṣa, those attained by noble ones who have acquired dhyāna,
and those born of the path of dhyāna— these latter two follow the mind.
The commentary says:
The eight classes of persons all achieve the prātimokṣa restraint, ranging from the bhikṣu down to the upavāsastha.
That which arises from dhyāna refers to this restraint because it arises from or relies upon dhyāna.
If one attains dhyāna, one will certainly accomplish this restraint (saṃvara).
That which belongs to the retinue of dhyāna is also called "born of the path of dhyāna"; noble ones (ārya) all accomplish this restraint.
Furthermore, there are two types: those of training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Among the three types of restraint previously mentioned, that born of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and that born of the path (mārgaja) follow the mind in their operation; the prātimokṣa does not.
Why is this? Because even when the mind is different or when there is no mind, [the non-informative matter] continues to evolve.
The two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)—are also called the "restraint of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
On what basis are these established?
The verse says:
In the nine uninterrupted paths of the *anāgamya*, the two that arise together are termed "abandonment."
The treatise states:

Within the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) are accompanied by both the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*). Because they can permanently sever the evil conduct of the desire realm as well as the afflictions that give rise to it, they are called the "restraint of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
Because the antidote that abandons exists only in the *anāgamya* (preliminary concentration), this [category] includes only the nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*).

In this context, since ethical discipline (*śīla*) eliminates immoral conduct, it may be the case that a certain restraint of dhyāna (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) is not a restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
This should be formulated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first proposition consists of the remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyāna-restraints, excluding those of the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).
The second proposition consists of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) restraints based on the nine paths of immediate succession of the threshold concentration.

The third phrase refers to the contaminated restraint (*sāsrava-saṃvara*) associated with the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).
The fourth phrase refers to all remaining uncontaminated restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), excluding those associated with the nine paths of uninterrupted transition of the threshold concentration.
In this way, there may be cases where there is untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) that is not the restraint of abandonment (prahāṇa-saṃvara).
One should formulate four permutations;
that is, one should understand them as the reverse order of the preceding four permutations.
If that is so, then regarding the brief precepts spoken by the Blessed One:
“Excellent is restraint of the body; Excellent is restraint of speech;
Excellent is restraint of the mind; Excellent is universal restraint.”
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One should well-guard and well-abide in the restraint of the eye faculty.
Of what is this restraint of the mind faculty (manas-saṃvara) the intrinsic nature?
These two intrinsic natures are not unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). If so, what are they?
The verse says:
The conjunction of correct knowledge and correct mindfulness is called the restraint of the mental faculty (*manaindriya-saṃvara*).
The treatise says:
Since the restraint of the mental faculty has, for each instance, the conjunction of correct knowledge and correct mindfulness as its essential nature, the Sūtra states:

Having seen forms with the eye, one is neither glad nor sad, but dwells constantly in equanimity, with clear comprehension and mindfulness; and so it continues up to the mind having cognized mental phenomena.
Having listed the individual names, he now states them collectively.
"Restraint" refers to the two types of discipline; as stated, their respective natures are these two.
Now, one should investigate: who accomplishes which—manifest action (*vijñapti*) or non-manifest action (*avijñapti*)—and for what duration?
Furthermore, to distinguish the accomplishment of non-informative discipline (*avijñapti-śīla*) and non-discipline (*aśīla*),
the verse says:
Abiding in the non-informative [state] of the Pratimokṣa, One always accomplishes the present [non-informative] as long as it has not been relinquished.
After the first moment, they become past; the same applies to non-restraint.
Those who have attained dhyāna restraint mostly always possess the past and future;
the noble ones, at the very beginning, exclude the past; those entering meditative absorption or the Path possess the present.
The treatise states:
For a person abiding in the pratimokṣa, from the first moment until they encounter conditions for relinquishing the precepts—such as abandoning the training—they always possess the present [precept].
This unmanifest (avijñapti) of the prātimokṣa restraint also becomes past after the first moment; the preceding statement "as long as it has not been abandoned" applies universally to what follows.
Just as it is said for one abiding in the prātimokṣa restraint, it should be understood that the same applies to one abiding in non-restraint (asaṃvara).
This means that from the first moment until one encounters the conditions for abandoning the unwholesome restraint—such as receiving the formal vows—one constantly possesses it in the present.
Furthermore, after the initial moment, one also possesses the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the unwholesome restraint in the past.
For those who have attained the dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara), as long as they have not yet relinquished it, they generally and constantly possess it in both the past and the future.
This is because one necessarily reacquires that very same past restraint at the first moment of its present existence, even if it was lost in a previous life.
The discipline (saṃvara) comprised within the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) does not become past during its first moment.
That which is obtained in other lives is relinquished at the time of death; it is impossible for that dharma to be acquired again in this life.
To distinguish these from those [other] dharmas, the word "many" is used.

Regarding the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), all noble ones (*ārya*) generally possess it in both the past and future; however, in the very first moment, they do not possess the past [restraint], because this category of the Noble Path has not yet arisen previously.
That which was never previously obtained is now obtained for the first time; this is called "the beginning.
When that which was previously obtained has been lost and is now obtained for the first time, it is also obtained as something past.
Regarding that which has already arisen: from the moment after the first instant until it is relinquished, it constitutes the past; it is also accomplished as future.

Until one attains parinirvāṇa without remainder, if one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one successively establishes the present restraint of absorption and the restraint of the path.

It is not the case that these are established as present at the time of emerging from contemplation, because the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of absorption and the path follows the mind; since such [non-informative matter] necessarily does not exist when a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) is manifest.
Having already explained those who abide in the discipline of good or evil, how does one abide in the intermediate state?
The verse says:
Abiding in the intermediate state possesses non-informative [action]; At the first moment it is established as the intermediate; thereafter, it consists of both.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the term "abiding in the intermediate," this refers to actions initiated by those who are neither in a state of discipline (*saṃvara*) nor in a state of non-discipline (*asaṃvara*); it is not necessarily the case that all such actions possess unmanifest form (*avijñapti*).
If there is an unmanifest [action] (avijñapti), it is comprised within the category of either virtuous discipline or non-virtuous discipline, or it belongs to neither of these two categories.
Its first moment constitutes only the intermediate period; that is, it constitutes the present, because this [present] is the middle between the past and the future.
From the moment after the first instant until it is relinquished, one always possesses the non-informative (avijñapti) karma of both the past and present periods.
If one abides in either restraint (saṃvara) or non-restraint (asaṃvara), does one also possess unwholesome or wholesome non-informative karma?
If such a thing exists, for how long does it endure?
The verse says:
Abiding in discipline or non-discipline, One gives rise to defiled or pure non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
The first is established at the beginning, while the latter two persist until the force of defilement or purity is exhausted.
The treatise says:

If one who abides in restraint (*saṃvara*) commits various unwholesome deeds such as killing or binding due to predominant afflictions (*kleśa*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of an unwholesome nature is thereby produced, and one comes to abide in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
By means of pure faith, one performs various supreme virtuous deeds such as prostrating to the Buddha; through these, one also generates various virtuous non-informative (avijñapti) factors.

As long as these two types of mind have not been severed, the non-informative factors they generate continue in a constant succession. However, the first moment constitutes only the present, while from the second moment onward, they constitute both the past and the present.
Having already explained the establishment of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), how is informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) established?
The verse says:
The manifest [karma] is being accomplished in the present; it is not accomplished in the past or the future.
Both the obscured and the unobscured [neutral karmas] are accomplished only in the present.
The treatise says:

All those who abide in restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), or the intermediate state (*madhyama*), as long as they are currently performing various manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*), constantly possess present manifest action. After the first moment until it is relinquished, they constantly possess past [manifest action]. There is absolutely no one who possesses future manifest action, because it is not concomitant with the mind and its force is too weak.
The same explanation applies to all non-informative (avijñapti) actions that are non-restrained.

Furthermore, regarding informative (vijñapti) actions that are obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) or unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta), it is certain that there can be no possession (prāpti) of those in the past or future, because the power of such dharmas is weak.
It can only induce the acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises simultaneously with the dharma, because the power of the acquisition is weak.

It cannot induce the acquisition of its own kind in a continuous succession; thus, once the dharma has ceased, one cannot speak of "attaining it in retrospect," nor does it have the capacity to attain a future dharma in advance.
Is it not the case that, just as this informative [action] can give rise to a mind, it should also possess existence in the past and future?

This objection is unreasonable because the power of this informative action is weak; it is due to its weakness that such a charge does not apply, for that which is produced is weaker than the mind that produces it.

The reason for this is that while an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) can manifest a manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*), the manifest action it manifests does not give rise to an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*). Therefore, we know that the mind which initiates [the action] is inferior to the mind that gives rise to the unmanifest.
Just as there are distinctions among the names for restraint (*saṃvara*), are there also distinctions among the designations for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? There are indeed. How so?
The verse says:
Misconduct, bad discipline, and karma—these are the paths of action and non-restraint.
The commentary says:
These five synonyms, such as "misconduct" (*duścarita*) and so forth, are variations of the term "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*), for they are censured and loathed by the wise.
Because their fruit is undesirable, they are designated by the name "misconduct."
It is called "bad discipline" because it obstructs pure ethical conduct (*śīla*).
It is called "action" (*karman*) because it is produced by body and speech.

It is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*) because it is comprised within the fundamental [actions], because it can fully manifest the volition of action, and because it is the path along which action travels.
The lack of tranquility in body and speech is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
However, the term "path of action" (*karmapatha*) refers exclusively to the first moment, whereas the remaining four names are established by encompassing both the initial and subsequent stages.
Now, one should investigate: if one possesses the manifest (*vijñapti*), does one also possess the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)?
One should formulate four propositions.
The verse says:
One accomplishes informative action but not non-informative action, When one performs an act with weak volition while abiding in the intermediate state.
Having abandoned the non-manifest karma of the meditative state that has not yet arisen, one achieves the unmanifest but not the manifest.
The treatise says:

Those who achieve the manifest but not the unmanifest refer to those dwelling in neither-discipline-nor-non-discipline who, through inferior wholesome or unwholesome volitions, perform good or evil deeds. Their bodily and vocal actions are capable of producing only manifest karma; they cannot even produce unmanifest karma, let alone the manifest karma produced by neutral (avyākṛta) volitions.

Excluding meritorious action based on material things (*aupadhika-puṇya*) and the completion of a course of action (*karmapatha*), because even those arising from inferior volition (*cetanā*) can produce non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

Only that which constitutes non-informative action and not informative action refers to a person who has attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), whose current informative action has not yet arisen, or whose previously arisen [informative action] has already been abandoned.
Both [positions] result in untenable propositions; this should be reflected upon according to reason.

Having thus established the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), as well as their possession (*prāpti*), how are the three distinctions of restraint (*saṃvara*) therein to be understood?
The verse says:
That which arises from meditative concentration is obtained through dhyāna; that which arises from the Path is obtained by the Noble Ones.
The prātimokṣa restraint is obtained through the instruction of others and so forth.
The treatise says:
The dhyāna restraint is acquired simultaneously with the mind.

If one acquires the dhyāna restraint associated with the outflow-tainted minds of the preparatory or fundamental stages of dhyāna, it is because at that time one has acquired that which is concomitant with those minds.

When one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm, one acquires the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) obtained by birth in that stage; one simultaneously also acquires the restraint (saṃvara) that accompanies them, because the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) likewise arises together with the mind.
If one attains the mind belonging to the stages of the preparatory (sāmantaka) or fundamental (maula) dhyānas that are untainted (anāsrava), at that time one attains them.
The word "those" (teṣām) serves to indicate the aforementioned dhyāna-minds; furthermore, the term "noble" (ārya) is stated to specifically select the untainted [minds] of the six dhyāna stages.

There is untainted mind, namely that of the *anāgamya*, the intermediate (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas, but not the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), as will be explained later.
The prātimokṣa restraint is acquired through the instruction of another and so forth.
One who is capable of instructing others is called "another.
Since the precept arises from the power of such instruction by another, it is said that this precept is obtained through the instruction of another.
This, moreover, is of two kinds, distinguished by whether it is received from the Saṃgha or from an individual (pudgala).
Those obtained from the Saṃgha refer to the precepts of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and śikṣamāṇās.
Those obtained from a *pudgala* (individual) refer to the remaining five types of precepts.
The masters of the Vinaya and the Vibhāṣā teach that there are ten ways of obtaining full ordination; in order to include these, the word "etc.
is further stated. What are these ten?
First, by means of spontaneity, namely the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"Spontaneity" refers to wisdom;
when they realize this wisdom without relying on a teacher, they obtain full ordination.
Second, by the Buddha’s command “Come, Bhikṣu,” as in the case of Yaśas and others, due to the power of their original vows and the Buddha’s majestic empowerment.

Third, by entering the state of right nature and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), as in the case of the five bhikṣus, who obtained full ordination through the realization of the Path of Seeing.
Fourth, by accepting the Buddha as the Great Teacher, namely Mahākāśyapa;
fifth, by skillfully answering questions, namely Sudāyin;
sixth, by respectfully receiving the eight rules of respect, namely Mahāprajāpatī.
Seventh, by means of a messenger, as in the case of the nun Dharmadinnā.
Eighth, by having a Vinaya-holder serve as the fifth member, as in the case of border regions.
Ninth, by means of a group of ten, as in the case of central regions.

Tenth, by means of the threefold recitation of refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha: this refers to the sixty virtuous groups (bhadra-varga) gathering together to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

In this context, they obtain the complete precepts according to their respective needs—whether through the power of their original vows, through the extreme perfection of their *āśaya* (resolute intention), or through the empowerment bestowed by the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).
Regarding the prātimokṣa discipline thus described, for how long should it be undertaken as a formal commitment?
The verse says:
The prātimokṣa discipline Is for the duration of one's life, or for a day and night.
The treatise says:
The prātimokṣa precepts upon which the seven classes of followers rely should be undertaken with a commitment for as long as life lasts.
The prātimokṣa precepts upon which the upavāsa (fasting) discipline relies should be undertaken with a commitment for only one day and night.
This is certainly so at this time.
For what reason is it thus?
Because it is not a principle consistent with the Vinaya, its true nature cannot be measured even by an Omniscient One.
Other masters say:
When the Blessed One realized the limits of the precepts, there were only two kinds: first, the limit of one's lifespan; second, the limit of a day and night.
Since the day and night are further explained as constituting the half-month and so forth, the Buddha spoke of only two times for receiving the precepts.
Because the Buddha’s sūtras mention only the day and night, the Abhidharmikas likewise state this.

Since the *upavāsa* restraint is received for only a single day and night, there must necessarily be a factor capable of acting as an obstacle that prevents that precept from arising once the day and night have passed.
Therefore, the Buddha’s sūtras mention only the period of a day and night, and do not mention periods such as five or ten days.
However, some say:

"The Buddha, observing that those to be converted have faculties difficult to discipline, provisionally bestowed upon them the precepts for one day and night; it is not that there is nothing beyond this.
On what principle or scriptural authority is such a statement made?
Beyond this, the arising of the precepts does not contradict reason.
Furthermore, what contradiction in reason would there be in reducing it further?
It is said that for those to be trained whose faculties are difficult to subdue, it was already permitted to teach them the day-and-night discipline (*rātri-divasa-saṃvara*).
Why not, for the sake of those who are difficult to discipline and gradually become even more so, explain that it lasts for only one night and day, or even a mere moment?
This is because there are many grades among those with faculties that are difficult to discipline.
However, it has never been stated that by this one knows there is a fixed duration for the *upavāsa* (fasting vow); if it were shorter or longer than that, the precepts would not be generated.
The World-Honored One, having observed this, spoke only this.
Based on what limit does one obtain non-restraint?
The verse says:
The unwholesome precepts have no duration of a day and night, because they are not received in the same manner as the wholesome ones.
The commentary states:
One acquires non-restraint by vowing to commit various evil deeds for the duration of one's life; it does not last for a single day and night like the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts.
Why is this so? Because it is not received in the same manner as the precepts of virtuous discipline (*śīla*).
That is to say, there is certainly no such thing as establishing a time limit before a teacher to receive non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) in the way one receives the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts.
I definitely incur non-restraint for one day and night.
This is because it is an action censured and loathed by the wise.

Although there is no formal limitation set before a teacher—such as a vow that "I shall commit various evil deeds for as long as I live"—one nevertheless incurs non-restraint by initiating a corrupted intention and desiring to engage in evil forever; it is not incurred by merely initiating an intention to commit evil for a limited time. Since non-restraint can be incurred even without a teacher, non-restraint does not last for only one day and night.

Nevertheless, the merit of the one-day precepts (upavāsa-śīla) is worthy of admiration; because it is received through the power of making a formal commitment in the presence of a teacher, one obtains the discipline of the one-day fast for a single day and night even without having completely eliminated the underlying intention to commit evil. Therefore, the acquisition of non-discipline differs from the acquisition of discipline.
Regarding the one-day-and-night *upavāsa* restraint (*samvara*), how should it be received when one wishes to formally undertake it?
The verse says:
The *upavāsa* is observed at dawn; Sitting on a lower seat, one receives it from a teacher.
"According to the instruction, it is said to possess the full branches; it is free from adornments and lasts for a day and night.
The commentary states:
The *upavāsa* restraint is received at dawn; that is to say, one must receive this precept at the time of sunrise, because this precept must last for a full day and night.
If there are those who have previously made such a commitment as this:
"I shall always, on the eighth day of the month and so forth, definitely receive this Upavāsa restraint," then even if there are obstructing conditions in the morning,
they may still receive it at the conclusion of the fast.
Regarding "descending from one's seat," this refers to occupying a lowly and inferior seat before the teacher with physical and mental humility and respect.
As for physical humility, one should either squat or kneel with the body bent and palms joined, except in cases of illness.
One who possesses a humble and respectful mind does not treat the preceptor of giving and morality with contempt, but gives rise to a most reverent, earnest, and pure faith toward the Triple Gem.
Since all forms of restraint (saṃvara) arise from respectful faith, if one lacks humility and respect, restraint will not be generated.
This must be received from a teacher; it cannot be accepted on one's own.
Hereafter, if one encounters conditions that lead to the violation of precepts, one will be able to avoid such violations through shame toward the precept-teacher.
That is to say, although one may lack the influence of the Dharma within oneself, one can still remain free from transgressions through the influence of the world.
Upon receiving this discipline, one should follow the teacher’s instructions; the recipient should speak after [the teacher], not before, nor simultaneously.
Only in this way is it properly accomplished as being received according to the teacher’s instruction; otherwise, neither the bestowing nor the receiving is accomplished.

One becomes established in the *upavāsa* (fasting) vow only when all eight branches are fully received; if any are lacking, the *upavāsa* is not accomplished, because the various branches of abstinence are mutually dependent.

Thus, the four branches—abstaining from killing and so forth—can be designated as occurring simultaneously within a single body, because among these interconnected abstentions there are distinctions of being either few or many.
One who receives these precepts should have a mind free from adornment, because such things are the basis for arrogance and indulgence.

However, one need not necessarily discard the usual articles for adorning the body, provided that they do not give rise to arrogance and indulgence due to them, as would be the case with something new or unusual.

When receiving this restraint, the mind must be directed toward it for a full day and night; that is, until the sun rises at dawn. When time has passed in this manner, the precept remains continuously connected.
If one receives it otherwise, although one may give rise to excellent conduct (*sucarita*), one does not obtain the restraint (*saṃvara*).
Nevertheless, because it causes one to attract desirable fruits, it should also be accepted.
As for the term "near-dweller" (*upavāsa*), it means that this discipline dwells near the Arhat, because one trains in accordance with them.
Some say that this abides in proximity to the precepts for as long as life lasts;
others say that these precepts abide in proximity to time.
Such restraint is also called "nurturing" (*poṣadha*), because it nurtures sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager, causing their roots of goodness to gradually increase.
For what reason must this Upavāsa (near-dwelling) vow be observed with exactly eight branches, neither more nor less?
The verse says:
The branches of morality, non-negligence, and abstinence, Are four, one, and three respectively.
To prevent the commission of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), as well as loss of mindfulness and arrogance/heedlessness.
The treatise says:

Among the eight [limbs], the first four are the branches of ethical discipline (*śīla-aṅga*), namely, abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from false speech; this is because these four abandon natural transgressions.
Next, there is one factor that constitutes the limb of non-negligence: namely, abstaining from drinking various intoxicants, which are the source of negligence.

Although one may have received the precepts (*śīla*), if one drinks intoxicants, the mind becomes negligent and the precepts are violated; for when intoxicated, one will certainly be unable to guard the remaining limbs.

Thereafter, there are three types that constitute the branches of restraint: namely, abstaining from the application of perfumes and garlands up to abstaining from eating at improper times, because these accord with the mind of renunciation, and renunciation is capable of realizing the fruit of discipline.
For what reason are these three branches fully observed?
If the branches were not complete, one would be unable to avoid the faults of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), loss of mindfulness, and negligence.

That is to say, the first [branch], from abstaining from killing up to abstaining from false speech, can prevent natural transgressions, because it avoids the various evil karmas such as killing that arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.

Next, abstaining from intoxicants prevents the loss of mindfulness; for when one drinks intoxicants, it causes one to forget what actions should and should not be performed, whereby one is unable to protect the remaining factors of abstinence.

Subsequently, the remaining three [vows] prevent arrogance and negligence; for if one enjoys various perfumes, garlands, high and broad beds and seats, or indulges in song and dance, the mind becomes arrogant and elated, and one will soon violate the precepts. By abstaining from those things, the mind becomes free from arrogance.

This means that if one constantly uses things such as perfumes and garlands, they still conform to arrogance and serve as conditions for violating the precepts; how much more so when receiving new and unprecedented items? Therefore, one should abandon them in every respect.

If there is one who can observe eating at the proper time, because they are able to refrain from eating at all times, they will remember their own undertaking of the *upavāsa* vows and be able to develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward the world.
If one does not eat at improper times, both [purposes] are absent, for eating frequently causes the mind to become lax and unrestrained.
For this great reason, one fully undertakes all three.

Among these eight, abstaining from food at improper times is both the fast (*upoṣadha*) and a limb of the fast; the remaining seven limbs are limbs of the fast but are not the fast itself. This is just as right view is both the path and a limb of the path, while the other seven limbs are limbs of the path but are not the path.
Is it only a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who can receive the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), or can others also receive them?
The verse says:
The one-day precepts may also be received by others; there is no receiving them without having taken the three refuges.
The treatise says:

For those who have not yet received the lay devotee’s discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), if they take refuge in the Three Jewels for the duration of one day and night, and having recited the three refuges, receive the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*), they also obtain the discipline of the one-day fast (*upavāsa-saṃvara*).
Apart from this, there is none—except for those who are ignorant.
Since the power of one's intention (*āśaya*) can also give rise to restraint (*saṃvara*), would it not follow that merely taking the Three Refuges constitutes becoming a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
As stated in the Sūtra, the Buddha told Mahānāman:

Any layman, a white-robed householder, who possesses the male organ, takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and with a heart of profound purity utters these truthful words, declaring: "I am an upāsaka; may the Venerable One remember me and protect me with compassion."
One who is thus [designated] is called an upāsaka.
This does not contradict the fact that one who has received the three refuges but has not yet completed the status of a lay devotee [is not yet an upāsaka]. Why is this so?
Because it is necessary to generate the restraint (*saṃvara*) in order to accomplish the state of being near [to the goal].
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle 19; *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, Fascicle 20.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five on the Analysis of Karma, Part Three: At what time is the upāsaka (lay follower) discipline generated?
The verse says:
"Upon declaring oneself an upāsaka, the precepts arise; this is explained as being like that of a bhikṣu and others.
The commentary says:
Arousing a fervent and pure mind and uttering words of sincerity, one declares: "I am an upāsaka; may the Venerable One remember me and protect me with compassion.

At that moment, the upāsaka discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) is generated, for it is only by uttering such words as "upāsaka" that the discipline is produced; this is because the Sūtra further states: "From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking life."
If one were to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) merely by receiving the three refuges without being addressed by a title, then such statements as "I am a lay follower" would be rendered useless.
For what purpose, then, is the expression "vowing to protect living beings" taught?

Because the protection of the vows of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) is obtained through the safeguarding of living beings, or for the sake of protecting one's own life, one does not transgress the prohibitory precepts of the Tathāgata.

Even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are about to receive the vows possess such a firm intention that, even for the sake of saving their own lives, they ultimately never violate the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) they have undertaken.
Such a vow as this can be found in the extant world.
However, there is an alternative recension that speaks of "renouncing life" (*jīva*).
The intended meaning of this statement is that one renounces killing and so forth; it omits "killing" and the like, referring only to "renouncing life."

Although he has already obtained the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) discipline, in order to cause him to understand the training rules he should observe, [the teacher] further explains for him the characteristics of the five precepts, such as abstaining from taking life, so that he may recognize and firmly maintain them.

Just as after a bhikṣu has received full ordination, he is instructed in the heavy rules of training so that he may recognize and maintain them with diligence, the same applies to a śrāmaṇera; it should be likewise here.
Therefore, an upāsaka must necessarily possess the discipline (saṃvara); one does not become an upāsaka merely by receiving the three refuges.
The verse says:
If all were fully endowed with the restraint, why speak of "one part" and so forth?
It is said in reference to their capacity to maintain it.
The treatise says:
Herein, those who harbor resentment and jealousy toward the meaning of the Abhidharma do not give rise to joy in their hearts and further raise this objection:

"If all lay followers (upāsaka) possess the full restraint (saṃvara), for what reason did the Blessed One state that there are four types: first, one who trains in a single part; second, one who trains in a small part; third, one who trains in a large part; and fourth, one who trains in the complete part?"
Is it not already established by this very point that one does not become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) merely through the three refuges?

For if there were another kind of person who, by receiving only the three refuges, became a lay follower, then such a lay follower would not be included within the four types previously mentioned; consequently, one would have to state that there is a fifth type of lay follower.
Since this [lay follower] has nothing at all to train in regarding the training rules (śikṣāpada), they should also be described as having only one duty;
for the Buddha observed that a lay follower is not separate from the code of discipline (vinaya), and thus in the Sūtras he spoke of only four types.
Although all lay followers (*upāsaka*) possess the discipline (*vinaya*), they are categorized into four types based on their capacity to maintain it.

That is to say, although one may have fully received the fivefold discipline (*pañcāṅga-vinaya*), one might later encounter circumstances that cause it to be impaired or deficient; among them, some may be able to maintain only a portion of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), while others may maintain all five branches. Therefore, it is said:
"Because they are able to maintain what was previously received, they are called 'those who train' (*śikṣamāṇa*)."

This is not so; rather, one should say that [the restraint] consists of a portion of the precepts and so forth. Therefore, these four types are established solely on the basis of their capacity to uphold [the precepts].
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states:
"The categories such as 'a portion' and so forth are explained in relation to the upholding or violating of the precepts."
One should not even ask such a question, much less provide an answer to it.

For who, having already understood that the lay devotee’s vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) necessarily comprises five branches, would be unable to understand that one may observe only a single precept among those to be learned and not the rest, up to the point of observing all of them, which is termed "one part" (*ekadeśa*) and so forth?
Since they have not yet understood the extent—whether small or great—of the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) vows they receive, one should ask:
"How many kinds of upāsakas are there who are able to train in the precepts?"
He replied:
"There are four types of upāsakas, namely those who train in one part and so forth, yet have not yet fully mastered them.
He asked again:
What is meant by "able to train in one part," and so forth, as explained at length?
This [position] is entirely without reason; it is only within the reasoning set forth by the Abhidharma school that such questions and answers should be made.

Although one knows that the status of a lay follower necessarily entails the possession of the discipline (*vinaya*), one has not yet fully understood whether the transgression of even a single type of offense constitutes a violation of all [the precepts], or whether it is only that specific one and not the others.
Because of this doubt, one should inquire.
If there are members of various schools who have not yet seen this text, they continue to debate this point even to this day.
Otherwise, the Buddha’s sūtras repeatedly state:
"An upāsaka is endowed with the five precepts."
Who, having already thoroughly understood this, would further harbor doubt and ask how many [precepts] are received?
If one were to grant such a thing, it would contradict the nature of the doubt.
That is to say, while the person originally doubted the quantity of what was received, they now ask how many training rules (*śikṣāpada*) can be learned.
The response, "It is a portion of what is to be cultivated," etc., does not resolve the original doubt;
therefore, such a question and answer should not have been posed within that context.

The Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrāntika) failed to reflect correctly on this matter, harboring partisan bias regarding the principles of debate, and conversely claimed that within the meaning explained by the Abhidharma, even a question should not be permitted, let alone an answer.

If one were to lack the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*) yet still be called a lay follower (*upāsaka*), then it would follow that a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) could likewise be established [as such] even if they lacked those vows.
Yet the Master of the Sūtras asks:
"For what reason is this not permitted?"

Due to differences in the conventions established by the power of the Buddha's teachings, one may become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) even if lacking formal vows (*saṃvara*), whereas a bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera must necessarily possess them.
This [assertion] follows personal sentiment, for it is not stated in the sūtras.
Where did the Blessed One say that one becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*) even while being separated from the vows?
It has never been heard that the Sautrāntikas hold such a position as that monks and others do.

Furthermore, there are *śrāmaṇeras* and *bhikṣus* who lack the precepts; their adherence would then be identical to the views of the heretics such as Pūraṇa and others. This is not the tenet of the Buddha’s Dharma, for all categories of vows are neither equal nor unequal, as they consist of three distinct grades.
By what cause are the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior established?
The verse says:
"Inferior, middling, and superior follow the mind."
The treatise states:
The Prātimokṣa restraint received by the eight classes of practitioners is categorized as superior, middling, or inferior according to the strength of the mind at the time of reception.
By this principle, some Arhats may possess only an inferior grade of restraint, whereas some ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) may possess a superior grade.
Regarding those who take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, in what do they actually take refuge?
The verse says:
They take refuge in the qualities of the Arhat and the two types of non-learner (aśaikṣa) dharmas that constitute the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
And with nirvāṇa as analytical cessation—this is said to be the complete threefold refuge.
The treatise says:
As stated in the original treatise:
In taking refuge in the Buddha, in what phenomena is one taking refuge?

It refers to those phenomena that exist as sublime realities, which—by way of conceptualization, designation, and verbal expression—are termed "Buddha"; one takes refuge in these unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) dharmas that constitute the capacity for buddhahood.
The phrase "it is said that 'if'" serves as a general heading for the meaning to be explained.
The term "all phenomena" (*dharmas*) indicates the augmentative expression of selflessness.
The term "sublime existence" (*sadbhāva*) reveals its union with the nature of sublime existence; "manifest existence" clarifies the sense of being currently obtainable.
Alternatively, it is called "wondrous existence" (*sadbhāva*) because it is conjoined with wondrous virtue; its actual existence reveals that it is of the nature of the knowable.
"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "conceptualization" (*saṃjñāna*) are distinctions of name.
Because he awakens to all phenomena and all their modes without relying on the instruction of others, he is called a Buddha.
Alternatively, because the various virtues such as the wisdom of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) are spontaneously awakened within him, he is named Buddha.
Alternatively, the name "Buddha" manifests that he possesses awakening, just as a material object is called "possessing material obstruction."
Alternatively, the name "Buddha" reveals his capacity as a teacher: having realized awakening himself, he awakens others.
This is explained in detail in the *Brāhmaṇaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
The phrase "one who can become a Buddha" reveals that those dharmas serve as the establishing causes for the designation "Buddha."
How is it that, within this context, a single name of a Buddha is established as a general designation for immeasurable dharmas?

It is without fault, just as a single *saṃgha-ratna* (the Jewel of the Sangha) is established based upon a multitude of harmoniously combined persons as a supreme refuge, and a single *mārga-skandha* (aggregate of the path) is established based upon a multitude of untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Or perhaps it has already been explained.
What was explained previously?

It refers to the designation and conventional expression of "conception" (*saṃjñā*) and "ideation" (*saṃjñā-saṃketa*). That is to say, within the unlearned qualities (*aśaikṣa-dharma*) of the Buddha’s own continuum, the single name "Buddha" is established; there is no separate, individual Buddha who can establish the Buddha-qualities.

What is this? It refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, along with their retinue; by attaining these dharmas, one is able to awaken to all things. Because these are preeminent, the body receives the name "Buddha," and not because the body of form and so forth undergoes any change before or after [attainment].
Is this taking refuge in a single Buddha or in all Buddhas?
In principle, one should say that it is taking refuge in all Buddhas, because the characteristics of the path of all Buddhas are without distinction.
There are briefly five types of Saṃgha: first, the shameless Saṃgha; second, the sheep-like mute Saṃgha; third, the factional Saṃgha; fourth, the conventional Saṃgha; and fifth, the ultimate Saṃgha.
A "shameless monk" refers to a person (pudgala) who violates the prohibitive precepts while wearing the dharma robes.
A "dumb-sheep monk" refers to a person who has no comprehension of the Tripitaka, being like a dumb sheep that lacks the capacity for speech and debate.
To say they are "mute" reveals their lack of the capacity to preach the Dharma;

further, to describe them as "like sheep" reveals their lack of the faculty to hear the Dharma. This thus demonstrates that such types of *pudgalas* possess neither the capacity to hear nor the capacity to speak within the Three Piṭakas.
Regarding "faction-forming monks," this refers to individuals who, through skillful means, organize factions among those who are dissipated, preoccupied with worldly affairs, or engaged in strife.
These three types of persons mostly commit unrighteous deeds.
The conventional Saṃgha refers to virtuous ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); these are capable of performing both legal and illegal acts.

The ultimate Saṃgha refers to the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the individuals (*pudgala*) who serve as the substratum for those dharmas; it is absolutely impossible for them to commit illegal acts.
The most excellent among the five, it is that to which one should take refuge.
As it is said in the verse praising refuge:
"This refuge is the most excellent; this refuge is the most venerable."
"By taking refuge in this, one is able to be liberated from all suffering.
