Chapter Five, Part Four: “Discrimination of Karma. Having thus explained the acquisition of the vows (*saṃvara*) and so forth, the relinquishment of the vows and so forth shall now be discussed.
Furthermore, how is the Prātimokṣa restraint abandoned?
The verse says:
The Prātimokṣa discipline is abandoned Through formal renunciation or through death.
And when both sexual organs arise together, when the roots of virtue are severed, and at the end of the night;
some say it is through committing a grave offense, while others say it is through the disappearance of the Dharma;
the Kashmiris say that committing two [grave offenses] is like being burdened by debt.
The Commentary states:
The term "subduing" (*damana*) is a synonym for "restraint" (*vinaya*), because by means of it, the faculties are brought under control.
One abandons the prātimokṣa restraint due to five conditions:

First, by intentional relinquishment: this refers to the lack of aspiration for the restraint due to one's underlying intention (*āśaya*), whereby, for the purpose of abandoning the training rules, one initiates a specific contrary manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) before a person capable of understanding.
It is not merely by the arising of the intention to abandon the precepts, for the mind [in such a state] lacks the capacity to obtain restraint;
furthermore, abandonment is not accomplished while in a dream.
Nor is it merely by the arising of a specific manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), for abandonment is not accomplished in cases of anger, insanity, and so forth.
It is not merely because the vow is not relinquished when one gives rise to a thought or performs an action toward animals and so forth;
secondly, it is due to death, because the restraint is acquired through the predominant power of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class).

Third, it is due to the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs; that is to say, because when the body undergoes transformation, the mind follows suit, and furthermore, because one possessing both organs lacks predominance.
Fourth, it is due to the severance of the roots of goodness that serve as its cause; that is to say, because the motivating mind for manifest and unmanifest karma is severed.

This refers to the meaning of the severance of the causes and conditions of this restraint (*saṃvara*). The lifelong precepts (*yāvajjīvika-śīla*) are relinquished through the aforementioned four conditions.

The one-day precepts (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) are also relinquished by the end of the night; that is, the one-day precepts are relinquished through the aforementioned four conditions as well as by the exhaustion of the night, because their time limit has expired.
The "end of night" refers to the time when the dawn light appears; this is the view generally accepted by most masters of discipline (*ācārya*).

Regarding these five conditions for the relinquishment of the vows, other masters of the various schools maintain that one relinquishes the monastic precepts upon committing any single offense entailing a grave downfall (*pārājika*).

Other schools maintain that at the time when the True Dharma perishes, the discipline of individual liberation (*pratimokṣa-saṃvara*) is entirely abandoned, because all the sacred teachings—including the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the ritual boundaries (*sīmābandha*), and the formal acts (*karmavācanā*)—come to an end.
The masters of the Abhidharma state as follows:
"At that time, although there is neither the acquisition nor the non-acquisition of a new restraint, there is no possibility of abandoning the restraint previously acquired.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra, who have internalized the principles and teachings within their hearts, state as follows:
It is not the case that when one commits any single root offense, there is the sense of abandoning all vows of discipline.
However, for one who commits a grave offense, there are two designations: first, "one endowed with ethical discipline" (śīlavat), and second, "an offender" (duḥśīla).
If one has committed an offense that ought to be confessed and eliminated, it is only when one confesses and eliminates it that one is said to possess the precepts.
It is like a wealthy person who, when owing a debt to another, is called both "a wealthy man" and "one in debt"; once the debt has been repaid, he is called only "a wealthy man."
This should also be the case here; therefore, it does not constitute the relinquishment of the precepts.
How, then, are the two types of restraint—the dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava)—relinquished?
The verse says:
One abandons the wholesome states born of meditative concentration through changing levels or through falling away;
one abandons all untainted wholesome states through attaining a fruit or through falling away.
The commentary says:
The wholesome dharmas associated with the various dhyāna stages are relinquished through two conditions:
first, by changing the stage, namely, being reborn in a higher or lower realm;
and second, by falling away, namely, regressing from a superior meditative concentration.

When one abandons the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) or becomes free from passion (*vairāgya*), one also abandons the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, as well as the concentration of the "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*).
To include these cases, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is stated again.

Just as wholesome states of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are abandoned by changing levels or through falling away, the same applies to the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) when one becomes free from passion.
The abandonment of untainted wholesome states occurs through two conditions:
first, by attaining a fruit, whereby one generally abandons the preceding path; second, by falling away, whereby one abandons the various superior paths.
These [abandoned paths] are either the fruit itself or are subsumed under the superior fruits.
I shall provide a brief analysis of this point.

If one relinquishes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it should be understood that this occurs solely through the attainment of a fruit (*phalaprāpti*) and not through falling away (*parihāṇi*); for that which is subsumed under the fruit of the subsequent knowledge of the path is necessarily free from falling away.
There is also the sense of "retrogression" regarding the faculties that have been cultivated;
for one of unshakable dharma (*akopyadharman*), neither exists, whereas for the remaining [types of] untainted [faculties], both may be present.
Thus has the relinquishing of the various vows been explained.
How is non-restraint abandoned?
The verse says:
Non-restraint is abandoned by death, By the acquisition of restraint, or by the emergence of both sexual organs.
The treatise says:
All forms of non-restraint are abandoned through three conditions:
first, by death, because the basis [of the body] is abandoned and the power of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) acquires restraint.

Second, by the acquisition of restraint: that is to say, if one receives and obtains the prātimokṣa restraint, or by obtaining the dhyāna restraint, one then abandons immoral conduct; because the power of the antidote is superior, one abandons non-restraint.
Third, it is because both sexual organs arise simultaneously within the continuum, as the basis [of the body] undergoes transformation at that time.

When one who possesses non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) receives the *upavāsa* precepts and relinquishes the restraint upon the completion of the night, does he acquire non-restraint again, or is he designated as one who abides in the intermediate state?
Other masters say:
"One acquires non-restraint because the evil intention (*āśaya*) has not been permanently abandoned; it is like when hot iron is set aside: the red color vanishes and the blue color arises.
Other masters say:
If one does not act again, there is no basis for causing that person to obtain non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because non-restraint is acquired based on informative action (*vijñapti*).

What was stated previously is logical: since the negative intention (*āśaya*) at the time of first receiving the precepts was not permanently abandoned, the evil precepts arise again based on the previous informative action.
How is the intermediate non-manifest (avijñapti) abandoned?
The verse says:
The abandonment of the intermediate [non-manifest] arises from the cessation of the undertaking, the force, the activity, the life-span, or the faculties.
The treatise states:
The abandonment of the intermediate non-manifest (avijñapti) occurs through six conditions.

First, it is abandoned due to the interruption or destruction of the volition of undertaking; that is to say, when one has previously vowed to always perform acts such as prostrating before a caitya and offering hymns of praise at a certain time.
Now he forms this thought:
"I shall not do it again hereafter.
From that moment, his underlying disposition (*āśaya*) ceases, because he has abandoned his original intention.

Alternatively, when one performs a distinct action with intensified force that contradicts a previously manifest activity, the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)—which was originally intended to cease—is then severed.

Second, it is abandoned due to the cessation of its sustaining power; that is, the non-informative matter induced by the power of pure faith or afflictions is abandoned when the limited force of those two is severed, just like a released arrow or a potter’s wheel.
Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] has stated:

because it is projected by the power of the motivating impulse (*samutthāna*), even if one abandons the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the intention (*āśaya*), the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) may continue to persist for the duration of one's life; this should be understood to apply likewise even when one strikes birds and beasts out of the arousal of extremely intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Alternatively, if a time limit was previously established for such a duration, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is severed when that period has elapsed.

Third, it is relinquished due to the cessation or destruction of the performed action; that is to say, although one has not relinquished the fundamental volition of the vow, one no longer performs the actions undertaken, except in cases where they were not performed due to forgetfulness.
Because this non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) arises contingent upon preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it is abandoned when that preparatory effort ceases.

Fourth, it is abandoned due to the destruction or cessation of the object (*vastu*); that is to say, regarding the shrines, gardens, and groves given as offerings, or the nets and other such items provided as gifts—the non-informative action originally induced by those objects is abandoned when those objects are destroyed.
Fifth, it is relinquished through the destruction of the life-span, meaning that the basis [of the body] undergoes transformation.

Sixth, it is relinquished through the destruction of the sense-faculties upon which it depends; this means that when one initiates the application of effort to sever either wholesome or unwholesome roots, one respectively relinquishes the non-informative matter (avijñapti) induced by those respective faculties.

One does not abandon intermediate wholesome or unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) only upon reaching the abandonment of the roots of goodness or the attainment of dhyāna; rather, because it is weak and inferior, one abandons the intermediate wholesome or unwholesome non-informative matter at the very moment the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) arises.
What is called a "root" (indriya) here refers to both wholesome and unwholesome roots.
The term "abandonment" (prahāṇa) mentioned refers to the abandonment through preparatory effort (prayoga).
But how does one abandon non-material wholesome states of desire and all other non-material defiled states?
The verse says:
One abandons the wholesome states that are non-material through the severance of the faculties and through rebirth in a higher realm;
one abandons all defiled states that are non-material through the arising of the path of counteraction.
The treatise states:
All non-material wholesome dharmas of the desire realm are abandoned through two conditions:
first, the severing of the roots of goodness; second, rebirth in a higher realm.

It should be said that a portion [of these factors] is also relinquished through detachment from defilement (*vairāgya-prahāṇa*), such as the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and other non-material wholesome dharmas.
All non-material defiled dharmas of the three realms are relinquished by a single condition: namely, the arising of the path of remedy (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
When the path capable of abandoning a particular category of defilements arises, one abandons the afflictions of that category along with their attendants.
Which sentient beings possess wholesome or unwholesome restraints?
The verse says:
Those with immoral discipline exclude those of the North, the two types of eunuchs, and hermaphrodites;
Discipline of restraint also exists among the gods, yet only humans possess all three types.
Those born in the desire realm, the heavens, and the form realm possess the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
The untainted [karma] and that which belongs to the formless realm, excluding the intermediate dhyāna and the state of non-conception.
The treatise says:
Non-discipline exists only within the human realm; however, excluding the Northern Continent, it exists only in the other three directions.
Within the three continents, one further excludes the *śaṇḍha* and the *pandaka*.
The same applies to those possessing both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
That is to say, among humans, one excludes those previously mentioned, and since it also exists among the gods, the restraint (*saṃvara*) can exist within these two realms of rebirth (*gati*).
However, only among human beings are all three types present—namely, the prātimokṣa, dhyāna, and anāsrava [vows].

If one is born in the desire realm heavens or the form realm, it is possible for them to possess the dhyāna restraint; yet, while it is possible for those in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva) to accomplish it, it does not exist at all for those born in the formless realm.
The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) also exists in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).

That is to say, if one is born among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—one may possess the untainted restraint.

However, for those born in the formless realm, it can only be accomplished (*samanvāgata*); because there is no form, it necessarily does not manifest, yet since one who is born in a higher realm can still accomplish that which belongs to a lower realm, it remains present as an attainment.
Having already distinguished the different natures and characteristics of various karmas, we shall now explain the various types of karma designated in the sūtras.
First, the sūtras state that there are three kinds of karma: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Actions that are peaceful, unpeaceful, or neither are termed wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The Commentary states:

All actions that bring about security are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*), because they can attain desirable maturation (*vipāka*) and nirvāṇa, thereby rescuing beings from suffering both temporarily and eternally.
Insecure karma is termed "unwholesome" (*akuśala*), because it can bring about undesirable maturation (*vipāka*) and is most effective at obstructing progress toward *nirvāṇa*.

The other two types of karma are not designated as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because they cannot be defined as either wholesome or unwholesome; this is the meaning of being neither secure nor insecure.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"Karma is of three kinds: merit, non-merit, and so forth.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Merit, non-merit, and the imperturbable; wholesome karma of the desire realm is called merit, unwholesome is called non-merit, and the wholesome of the higher realms is the imperturbable.
"Because karma and its fruit are immovable within their own respective spheres.
The treatise says:
Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "merit" (*puṇya*); it is the opposite of non-merit (*apuṇya*), because it brings about desirable fruits.
All unwholesome karmas are called "non-merit" (*apuṇya*), because they bring about undesirable results and are contrary to meritorious karma.
The wholesome [karma] of the two upper realms is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*).
But did not the Blessed One state that the first three dhyānas are all "subject to movement"?
The Noble One has stated that this [attainment] is characterized by movement because it involves vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and vedanā.
Since the calamities such as vitarka and vicāra have not yet subsided in the three lower dhyānas, they are designated by the term "movement."
Regarding "immovable" (*āniñjya*), it is so named because the sūtras state that it can induce immovable maturation (*vipāka*).
How, then, can a meditative absorption involving movement (*iñjana*) bring about immovable maturation?

Although there is movement caused by calamities within these meditative attainments, they are designated as "unshakable" because karma does not undergo such fluctuation with respect to its fruit as it does in the desire realm.

This means that in the desire realm, the ripening karma (*niyata-vipāka-karma*) for other destinies or locations may be experienced in a different destiny or location due to the power of specific conditions.

Because there may be karma capable of producing external or internal wealth, status, physical dimensions, complexion, strength, pleasure, and so forth, which is destined to ripen among gods and other such realms, yet due to the influence of other conditions that redirect it, this same karma instead ripens among humans and others.

Karma belonging to other stages or locations within the form and formless realms cannot be redirected to produce results in a different stage or location, because the locus of karmic fruition is immutable and because such karma is comprised within the states of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi) and is thus free from distraction.
Based on this meaning, the name "immovable" (*āniñjya*) is established.
It should be understood that herein, due to ignorance regarding the interconnectedness of cause and effect, one performs non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*).
Because non-meritorious karma is purely defiled, it necessarily depends upon the continuity of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Due to this ignorance being present, one is unable to understand or believe in the causal connection between actions and their results; therefore, one initiates non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*).
Because of delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*), one performs meritorious (*puṇya*) and immovable (*āniñjya*) karmas.
The ultimate reality refers to the Four Noble Truths.

If one is deluded regarding them, ordinary worldlings may occasionally give rise to wholesome states of mind; by the power of this, they fail to know the nature of the three realms as it truly is—that all is suffering—and thus they generate meritorious and immovable formations that serve as causes for future existence.

For one who has already seen the truths, such a thing does not occur; rather, as they gradually distance themselves from defilements through the power of prior practice, they are born successively in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"Karma is of three kinds: that which leads to pleasant feeling, and so forth."
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Those conducive to pleasure, pain, and neither, The wholesome [roots] up to the third dhyāna are conducive to pleasure.
All unwholesome [karma] conforms to suffering; the superior wholesome conforms to neither.
Others say that the inferior [wholesome] also conforms to both, because it brings about maturation from the intermediate state.
Furthermore, these three types of karma are so designated because they do not mature sequentially.
There are five types of feeling in total: namely, those by way of intrinsic nature, association, object, maturation, and manifestation.
The treatise says:
Among all wholesome karmas, those from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna are called "karmas conducive to pleasant feeling," because pleasant feelings exist only up to that point.
All unwholesome karmas are called "conducive to painful feeling.

The wholesome karmas of the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms are said to be "conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling," because from this point upward, there are no longer feelings of pain or pleasure.
It should be understood that these various karmas do not only produce the fruit of feeling (*vedanā*); they also produce the provisions for that feeling.
Here, both the feeling and its provisions are termed "feeling," as the name "feeling" is established in general according to the inclinations of those to be converted.
Regarding whether karma that is neither [conducive to pleasure nor pain] is admitted in the lower stages, or whether it is definitively absent:

some other masters state that such karma exists even in the lower stages, because since there is neither suffering nor pleasure in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there should likewise be no such karma there.
Furthermore, there is additional proof; namely, the *Mūla-śāstra* asks:
"Is it possible for the three types of karma to experience their maturation neither before nor after one another?
It replies: [Yes.]

There is: namely, the matter of karma conducive to pleasant feeling; the mind and mental factors of karma conducive to painful feeling; and the formations dissociated from mind of karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and so forth, as explained at length.
From this it is proven that the lower stages also possess karma that is neither [wholesome nor unwholesome].

It is not the case that these three types of karma exist apart from the desire realm, because they ripen simultaneously; thus, this [argument] regarding simultaneous ripening is not a definitive proof.

Nevertheless, within the lower stages, it stands to reason that there must certainly exist karma that is neither [wholesome nor unwholesome], as should be understood from the extensive discussion in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Is this karma wholesome or unwholesome?
Some say: This is wholesome yet inferior;
furthermore, it cannot be specified individually but can only be stated collectively.

Among all wholesome karmas, there is one class that can induce pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and the requisites for feeling, and another class that can induce neither. It should be understood that this karma which benefits pleasant feeling is called "conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya*), just as [one speaks of] a place conducive to horses (*aśva-bhūmi*).
Alternatively, this karma that can experience pleasure is called "conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya*), just as there are bath-powders that are "conducive to bathing.
It should be understood that the same applies to karma conducive to other feelings.
Since this karma does not merely result in the maturation (*vipāka*) of feeling, how is it given the general designation of "karma conducive to feeling"?
The various maturations (*vipāka*) induced by karma as their cause all resemble feeling (*vedanā*), and thus they receive the name "feeling. Why is this so?

Because they all, like feeling itself, bring about benefit, harm, or neutrality for the body; just as water, fire, and so forth are established as being beneficial, harmful, or neutral in relation to tree branches and the like.
Furthermore, there are many ways in which [feelings] are experienced; briefly stated, there are five:
first, experience by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anubhava*), which refers to the essence of feeling itself. As the Sūtra says:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling," and so on at length.
Second, association with what is conducive to feeling (*anulomika-vedanīya*), which refers to all contacts (*sparśa*); as the Sūtra says:
"contacts conducive to pleasant feeling," and so forth, at length.
Third, the object of focus that is conducive to feeling (*ālambana-anulomika-vedanīya*), which refers to all objects (*viṣaya*); as the Sūtra says: [and so forth].

Having seen a form with the eye, one experiences only the form itself and does not experience craving for the form; this is explained at length because forms and so forth are the objects (*ālambana*) of feeling (*vedanā*).
Fourth are the four types of feelings concordant with maturation (*vipāka-anukūla-vedanīya*), which refer to karma that brings about maturation, as stated in the Sūtra:
"karma conducive to pleasant feeling," and so forth, explained at length.
Fifth is "presently manifest experience," which refers to currently active feeling (*vedanā*). As the Sūtra says:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, the other two feelings cease," and so forth, as explained at length.
It is not that when this pleasant feeling is present, there is another feeling capable of experiencing it;

rather, it is simply on the basis of the manifestation of the pleasant feeling itself that one says "one experiences a pleasant feeling," because there are many types of what is experienced accordingly.

Although the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma is not entirely identical to feeling (*vedanā*), it may nonetheless be designated collectively by the term "karma conducive to feeling" (*vedanīya-karman*).

This is because all wholesome karmas, as causes, produce matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that can give rise to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) by serving as its objects; because these are what are experienced by pleasant feelings; and because their desirable maturation is conducive to pleasant feeling, they are also termed "pleasant feeling."

Although the various fruits summoned by this wholesome karma are not themselves pleasant sensations (*sukhavedanā*), because they are conducive to pleasant sensation, the karma that summons them is designated as "karma conducive to pleasant sensation" (*sukhavedanīya-karman*).
The same principle should apply to "karma conducive to painful sensation" (*duḥkhavedanīya-karman*) and "karma conducive to neither [pleasant nor painful sensation]" (*aduhkhāsukhavedanīya-karman*).
Thus, these three types of karma are either determinate or indeterminate; what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
"These are determinate or indeterminate; the determinate are the three [types] such as those to be experienced in the present life."
Some say that karma is of five types; other masters speak of four categories.
The treatise says:

Regarding the "conducive to pleasant feeling" and so forth mentioned above, one should know that each has the distinction of being determinate or indeterminate. Because it is not necessarily experienced, it is designated as "indeterminate."

This refers to karma conducive to pleasure that is not necessarily destined to ripen; yet if it were to ripen, one would certainly have to experience its pleasant maturation. The same applies to the descriptions of the other two types of karma. Furthermore, there are three determinate types:

first, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*); second, karma to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*); and third, karma to be experienced in subsequent births (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
These three types of determinate karma necessarily produce maturation (*vipāka*); together with the previously mentioned indeterminate karma, they constitute four kinds in total.

Some maintain that indeterminate karma to be experienced further has two types—namely, determinate and indeterminate regarding its maturation—and thus, when added to the three types of determinate karma, they form five kinds.
The Dārṣṭāntikas state that there are four permutations regarding karma:

first, there is karma for which the timing is fixed but the maturation is not fixed; this refers to the three types of karma—such as karma to be experienced in the present life—that are not certain to obtain maturation.
Second, there is karma for which the maturation is certain but the timing is uncertain; that is, indeterminate karma that is certain to yield maturation.
Third, there is karma for which both are certain; that is, karma such as the "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (niyata-dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) that is certain to yield maturation.
Fourth, there is karma that is indeterminate with respect to both [time and ripening], meaning that indeterminate karma does not necessarily result in the attainment of maturation (*vipāka*).

They explain that all such karmas collectively constitute eight types: namely, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is either determinate or indeterminate, and so on, up to indeterminate karma, which also has two types.
Regarding these explained distinctions of karma, the verse says:
Four wholesome [karmas] may be performed simultaneously; three alone can project a homogeneous existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
In all realms, four types [of karma] are created; in the hells, wholesome [karma] excludes the present.
In the stage of detachment from passion, ordinary beings do not produce [karma] that leads to rebirth;
noble ones do not produce karma for rebirth or subsequent existence, nor do they fall away from the desire realm or the Peak of Existence.
The commentary says:

In this context, it is solely to clarify that karma conducive to pleasure and so forth may be determinate or indeterminate with respect to its timing—such as the present life—and to explain the distinct characteristics of the four types of karma taught in the sūtras, such as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Therefore, determinate karma is divided into three types, which, when combined with indeterminate karma, constitute the four; this explanation is considered correct.

In principle, there can be no such thing as karma that is indefinite regarding its maturation (*vipāka*) yet definite regarding its timing, because a definite time is merely a specific stage within what is already definite regarding its maturation.
Since there is no temporal essence distinct from maturation itself, how could that which is definite in time not be definite in its maturation?

In this context, the categories of "conducive to the present life" and so forth are established solely based on the distinctions in the timing of the attainment of results from determinate karma of maturation (*vipāka-niyata-karma*).
Is it possible for four types of karma to be performed simultaneously?
It is indeed possible.
How so? After dispatching the three messengers, one personally engages in sexual misconduct; these are all brought to completion simultaneously.
Among the four types of karma—karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth—how many types of karma have the power to project a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?

Only three [types of karma] are capable of projecting [rebirth], excluding karma conducive to the present life; for karma conducive to the present life necessarily arises depending on the homogeneous status (nikāya-sabhāga) projected by prior karma, and thus it must yield its fruit within the very same lifetime.
In which realms and destinies can how many types of karma be created?
In all realms and destinies—whether wholesome or unwholesome—all four types of karma may be created as appropriate; this is the general explanation.

If we consider specific prohibitions, within the *naraka* (hells), wholesome [karma] excludes that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because there is no pleasant fruit there;
all other types may be produced.

Those called "steadfast" (*sthira*)—referring to those who do not fall back from their state—if they are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) in a stage free from passion (*vairāgyabhūmi*), may produce the other three types of karma, excluding that which is to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*).
The Noble Ones eliminate both types of karma to be experienced in the next life and in subsequent lives; they may, however, perform the other two types.

As for ordinary beings who do not fall back, if they have become detached from those realms, there is no possibility of being reborn in them immediately thereafter; therefore, such beings must also eliminate karma to be experienced in the next life.

Since one who passes away from the upper realms must necessarily be reborn in the lower realms, it is possible for them to create karma there that is to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).

However, if an *ārya* who is non-retrogressive (*avinivartanīya*) becomes detached from those realms, they will certainly never be reborn there again; therefore, such a person excludes both karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives. In accordance with the realm where they are born, they may create karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), as well as indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*), which is not prohibited in any location.

However, when noble beings have attained freedom from passion regarding the desire realm and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), even though they may undergo retrogression, they do not create karma conducive to rebirth in those realms or subsequent lives; for one who retrogresses from those states necessarily retrogresses from the fruit itself.
Once one has fallen away from the fruits [of the path], one will certainly not die until the original fruit is regained.
Does one also create karma while abiding in the state of *antarābhava*?
One does indeed create it.
How so? The verse says:
In the intermediate state of the desire realm, one can create twenty-two kinds of karma.
All are comprised within karma to be experienced in the present life, because their type and homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are one.
The treatise says:
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one may be capable of creating twenty-two types of karma.
This refers to five stages each for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the period within the womb, and the period after birth from the womb.
Regarding the five stages within the womb: first, the *kalala*; second, the *arbuda*; third, the *peśī*; fourth, the *ghana*; and fifth, the *praśākhā*.
The five stages outside the womb are: first, infancy; second, childhood; third, youth; fourth, middle age; and fifth, old age.
These eleven positions are comprised within a single lifetime.

One dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) can create intermediate-state karma that is both determinate and indeterminate, and so on, up to creating the two types of karma for the time of old age;
it should be understood that this is likewise the case.

It should be known that the eleven kinds of determinate karma created during such an intermediate existence are all subsumed under "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because there is no distinction in the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).

This means that the state of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and its ten corresponding states belong to the same homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) because they are projected by a single karma; therefore, karma to be experienced in the intermediate state is not mentioned separately, as it is already subsumed under the karma to be experienced in the next birth and so forth.

Regarding "homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*): this refers to categories such as humans and so forth, which are neither destinies (*gati*) nor births (*upapatti*), because within the destinies and births there exist distinct homogeneous classes for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of existence (*bhava*).
What are the characteristics of those karmas that are definitely experienced?
The verse says:
Due to intense afflictions or a pure mind, And that which is habitually performed,
Arising toward a field of merit, Or karma involving the harming of one's parents— these are determinate.
The treatise says:
If an action performed arises from heavy afflictions, or from a mind of pure sincerity, or is performed habitually, or is directed toward a field of superior merit.
The field of merit refers to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or to superior individuals (pudgala) who have realized mundane or supramundane excellence.

Although one may lack intense afflictions, a pure mind, or even a habitual disposition toward such a field, any karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—arising therein, or even if one commits an act of harm toward one’s parents while motivated by only a minor degree of entanglement (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), all such cases are subsumed under the category of determinate karma (*niyata-karma*).
Other masters say:

If an action is performed with an intense intention, or if after performing it one gives rise to a joyful mind, or if it is repeatedly practiced at all times, or if it is an action initiated by the power of a superior vow or the power of circumstances, such actions are all determined to have their results in the present life.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Because of the excellence of the field and the intention, And because it necessarily brings about a specific maturation.
One attains the state of being forever free from the karma of the ground, which certainly brings about results in the present life.
The Commentary says:

Regarding the excellence of the field, there is the report that a certain bhikṣu spoke to the Saṃgha using feminine language, and in an instant he was transformed into a woman; such accounts of this kind are not unique.

Regarding the superiority of intention (*āśaya*): it is heard that there was a *śaṇḍha* who rescued and liberated several oxen from being castrated; as a result, he was transformed into a man in an instant. Such legendary accounts are not few.

There may also be other karma that yields results in the present life; that is to say, when one is born in a certain stage and has permanently abandoned the defilements of that stage, all wholesome and unwholesome karma belonging to that stage must necessarily be experienced in the present life, as it will not be reborn again.

Regarding Arhats and Non-returners, they had already performed those karmas prior to being free from defilement; now that they are free from defilement, these become karma to be experienced in the present life. What kind of karma is this?
This refers to karma with fixed maturation (*vipāka-niyata*). It should be understood that the karma described here is karma fixed in its maturation but not fixed in its timing (*akāla-niyata*).

If there were karma destined to be experienced in another state that was fixed in its maturation, it would necessarily lack the possibility of permanent freedom from defilement; such karma would inevitably have its maturation fruit experienced in that other state.
If it were also indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*), then because they have permanently abandoned defilement, they would not undergo maturation.

This is because Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arhats, even if they were to fall back and give rise to defilements within the desire realm or the three realms, would certainly not be reborn in the lower states, as they are destined for *nirvāṇa*.

Karmas that are determinate with regard to maturation (*vipāka-niyata-karma*) all become karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). The others should be explained accordingly as appropriate.
By what kind of field (*kṣetra*) does one produce karma that is fixed to be experienced immediately?
The verse says:
Toward the Buddha and the foremost of the Saṃgha, as well as those in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), those free from contention (araṇā),
and those emerging from the meditations of loving-kindness (maitrī) or the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)— karma that causes benefit or harm toward these is experienced immediately.
The Commentary says:
Regarding such fields of merit, wholesome or unwholesome karma performed therein will certainly yield its fruit immediately.
A "field of merit" refers primarily to the Saṃgha headed by the Buddha.
In terms of the distinctions among individuals (*pudgala*), there are five types:

First, emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): this refers to attaining tranquility of mind within this absorption, for the tranquility of this absorption resembles *nirvāṇa*.

When the mind first arises from this absorption, it is as if one who has entered *nirvāṇa* returns once more; adorned with the merit of supreme tranquility, it serves as the basis for the growth of a profoundly pure mind.

Second, emerging from the *araṇā* (the state free from conflict): this refers to the fact that within this meditative absorption, one has already been able to permanently uproot the continuity of all afflictions and calamities; having taken all sentient beings as its object, it gives rise to boundless superior intentions (*adhyāśaya*) and the accumulated perfuming of the merit of *araṇā*, which saturates the body. Upon emerging from this state, that mental continuum cannot be overcome by any worldly concentrated or non-concentrated minds; it is a field of supreme excellence for the immediate fruits of both merit and demerit.

Third, emerging from the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*): this means that within this concentration, there is the accumulation and perfuming of the body by a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) directed toward immeasurable sentient beings as its object, for their benefit and happiness.
Upon emerging from this meditative absorption, the body is perfumed by immeasurable and most excellent conditioned virtues; it proceeds in a continuous succession capable of producing superior karma.

Fourth, [emerging] from the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): that is to say, within this path, one is able to transcend a portion of the root of birth-and-death within the saṃsāra of the three realms—a root which has persisted since beginningless time and could not otherwise be transcended. Upon emerging from this path, there is a superior, pure body that arises in a continuous succession and is capable of producing superior karma.

The fifth [type of field of merit] consists of those who have emerged from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This refers to those within this path who are able to transcend a portion of the root of birth and death; the rest is as previously explained.

From each such initial stage of emergence, by virtue of the momentum of the superior merits previously cultivated, their minds continue to look back with focused mindfulness without abandoning it. Their faculties are exceptionally tranquil, differing from the ordinary, such that no mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned merit can surpass, subdue, or eclipse them. Therefore, these five are called fields of merit.
If one performs an action that brings about either harm or benefit toward such a person, this karma will certainly bring about its immediate fruit.

When emerging from other meditative absorptions or other fruits [of the path], because the previously cultivated absorption was not particularly sublime and the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have not been completely exhausted, their mental continuum is not a supreme field of merit; among the various types of ripening fruits, the experience [of sensation] is the most prominent.

Now, one should investigate whether, among the various types of karma, there is any that brings about only the maturation of mental sensation (*citta-vedanā*), or perhaps brings about bodily sensation (*kāya-vedanā*) but not mental sensation.
There is indeed such karma.
How so? The verse says:
It is maintained that all wholesome karma devoid of vitarka produces only mental sensation.
"Evil [karma] produces only bodily sensation; this is the distinction among karmas that produce sensation.
The treatise says:
"Wholesome karma without vitarka refers to all wholesome karma from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)."
Among these, that which attracts the maturation of feeling should be understood as inducing only mental feeling, not bodily feeling, because there is no bodily feeling in those stages.
Bodily feeling is necessarily associated with vitarka; an action without vitarka does not induce a result associated with vitarka.

Regarding those unwholesome karmas that can be experienced, it should be understood that they produce only bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*) and not mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*), because the fruit of an unwholesome cause is a painful sensation.

Painful sensation on the level of the mind is definitively termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*); since sorrowful sensation is necessarily not included within the category of *vipāka*-fruit (maturation), unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation.

If one maintains that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is definitely not a maturation (*vipāka*), then in which consciousness does the mental derangement produced by sentient beings reside, by what cause is it induced, and upon what basis does it arise—given that it is not a maturation?
The verse says:
Mental derangement occurs only in the mental consciousness;
it arises from karmic maturation, as well as from fear, injury, adverse conditions, or grief; excluding the Northern Continent, it exists within the desire realm.
The treatise states:

The mental derangement of sentient beings occurs only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); if it were present in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*), there could be no mental derangement at all, because the five bodies of consciousness are devoid of conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*).
For what reason do sentient beings become deranged in mind?
It arises from the karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of sentient beings.
From what kind of karmic maturation does it arise?

That is to say, by means of medicinal substances or incantations, one causes another’s mind to go mad; or again, one makes another drink what they do not desire, whether it be poison or alcohol; or one displays a majestic and terrifying presence to frighten birds, beasts, and the like; or one releases fierce fires to burn mountains and marshes; or one constructs pits and traps to cause sentient beings to fall into them; or through other such activities, one causes others to lose their mindfulness.
Due to this karmic cause, one obtains in a future life a maturation (*vipāka*) consisting of heterogeneous primary elements (*mahābhūta*); by their power, the mind is driven to madness.

Since the substance of this mental madness is not itself a maturation—because both wholesome and unwholesome minds can be subject to madness—it is therefore said to arise solely from the maturation of karma.

This means that due to the cause of unwholesome karma, one experiences the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of an uneven maturation (*vipāka*); based on these great elements, the mind loses mindfulness, and is therefore said to be "deranged.
Regarding this mental derangement in contrast to mental distraction (*vikṣepa*), one should formulate four logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Those who are deranged but not disordered refer to those who are deranged with an undefiled mind.
Those who are disordered but not deranged refer to those who are not deranged with various defiled minds.
Those who are both deranged and disordered refer to those who are deranged with various defiled minds.
"Non-deranged" refers to those who are not insane and whose minds are undefiled.
When the minds of sentient beings become deranged, is it solely due to this [cause], or are there four other causes as well? What are these four?

First, due to terror: this refers to when non-humans and the like appear in terrifying forms and come to oppress one; upon seeing them, sentient beings consequently fall into madness. Second, due to injury:
this refers to when, because of one's actions, one vexes non-humans and the like; due to their anger, they injure one's limbs and so forth, whereby one consequently falls into madness.
Within the bodies of sentient beings there are distinct joints and members; if these are struck or touched, the mind immediately becomes deranged.

Third, it is due to disharmony, meaning that because the internal elements of wind, heat, and phlegm mutually oppose one another, the primary elements (mahābhūtas) become unsuitable, thereby causing the mind to go mad.

Fourth, due to grief (*śoka*): that is to say, because of events such as the loss of loved ones, one is bound by the poison of sorrow until the mind subsequently becomes deranged, as in the case of Vāsiṣṭha and others.
Which classes of sentient beings possess this mental derangement?
With the exception of those in Uttarakuru, all other sentient beings within the desire realm may experience derangement of mind.

If even among the gods of the desire realm there are those whose minds are deranged, how much more so for humans and those in the miserable destinies? How could they possibly be free from mental derangement?
Those in the hells are perpetually deranged because they are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Among the noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with the exception of the Buddhas, mental derangement may occur when the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) become disharmonious.

All Tathāgatas are free from mental derangement; they do not die gradually, nor do they break their voice, nor do they experience such things as graying hair or wrinkled faces, for they are born of extremely pure and sublime karma.
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
"There are three kinds of karma, namely: crookedness (*vaṅka*), corruption (*doṣa*), and turbidity (*kaṣāya*).
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
It is taught that crooked, corrupt, and turbid karma arises based on deceit, hatred, and greed.
The commentary says:

The three of body, speech, and mind each have three types—namely, crookedness (*vaṅka*), corruption (*doṣa*), and turbidity (*kaṣāya*)—which should be understood as arising respectively from deceit (*māyā*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and greed (*lobha*).

This refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind that arise based on guile (*śāṭhya*); these are called "crooked karma" (*kuṭilakarma*) because they belong to the category of crookedness. True crookedness, however, refers to [wrong] views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, a sutra asks:
"What is true crookedness?"
This refers to various wrong views; flattery (*śāṭhya*) belongs to that same category, and thus it receives the name "crooked" (*vaṅka*).

Because the bodily, vocal, and mental actions arising from flattery have crookedness as their cause, the effect takes on the name of the cause; for this reason, the Blessed One described them as crooked.
If the bodily, verbal, and mental actions arising from that anger are called "defiled actions" (*kaṣāya-karman*), it is because they belong to the category of the defilement of anger.

Anger is termed "defilement" because when it manifests, it is like a red-hot iron ball; wherever it is cast, it is able to burn and harm the bodies and minds of both oneself and others. Among all afflictions, it is the most grievous fault; therefore, the Bhagavān specifically established the name "defilement" for it, as it is the most extreme defilement among all defilements.
Bodily, vocal, and mental actions arising from hatred are called "corrupt" (*daurmanasya*) because they have corruption as their cause; thus, the Blessed One designated them as "corrupt.
If bodily, vocal, and mental actions arise based on greed, they are called "turbid" (*kaṣāya*) actions, because they belong to the category of turbid greed.
Greed is called "turbidity" because greed, when manifesting, is an afflicted nature that clings to its object.
The arising [of karma] from that [greed] and so forth should be explained according to the previous [analogy].
Furthermore, the truly straight path refers to the Eightfold Noble Path; the three types of karma that can obstruct its arising are called "crookedness."
True health is the pursuit of *nirvāṇa*; the three types of karma that obstruct the realization of its cause are called "impurities.
According to the views of non-Buddhists, within the Buddha’s teaching, that which obstructs pure faith—namely, lack of faith—is called "impurity," because it can disturb and turbidify pure faith.
The three types of karma arising from those [afflictions] are called "turbid.

Furthermore, because they fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism and thus deviate from the Middle Way, the physical, vocal, and mental actions arising therefrom deviate from the meaning of the straight path; therefore, they are designated as "crooked."

The various karmas arising from the view of negation (apavāda-dṛṣṭi) are termed "corrupting" (*kaṣāya*) because they defile pure dharmas; this designation of "corruption" necessarily relies upon the sense of being extremely defiled.

The various karmas arising from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) are termed "turbid" (*āvilaka*) because they obstruct the truly pure vision of non-self; this designation of "turbidity" relies upon the sense of obstructing purity.

Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras: "There are four kinds of karma: namely, there is karma that is black with black ripening; or again, there is karma that is white with white ripening; or again, there is karma that is black-and-white with black-and-white ripening; or again, there is karma that is neither black nor white, which has no ripening and is capable of exhausting all karmas."
Although the Sūtra briefly indicates this but does not explain it extensively, it should now be explained.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Based on the distinctions of "black-black" and so forth, four types of karma are taught:
evil karma, wholesome karma of the form and desire realms, that which can exhaust those [former karmas], and the outflow-free (anāsrava) [karma].
One should know that these are designated as black, white, both, and neither, respectively.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha, based on the different natures and categories of karmic fruits and the distinction between that which is to be remedied and its remedy, taught the four types beginning with "black-black.
All unwholesome karma is designated as "black" because it possesses both the blackness of defilement and the blackness of being disagreeable.
The maturation is also black because it is disagreeable.
Wholesome karma of the form realm is exclusively called white, because it is not intermingled with any unwholesome afflictions or unwholesome karma;
its maturation is also white because it is agreeable. This is not the case for the formless realm, as it is largely deficient in these qualities.
Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "black-and-white" because it is interspersed with evil;
its maturation is also black-and-white because it is interspersed with undesirable fruits.

This designation "black-and-white" is established based on the continuity [of the individual], not according to the intrinsic nature [of the actions themselves], for these two are mutually contradictory.
In the desire realm, evil is powerful and not interspersed with the wholesome; therefore, the fruit of evil karma receives the name "pure black.
All untainted (anāsrava) karma that can eternally sever and exhaust the three preceding types of karma is called the fourth type of karma.
This untainted karma (anāsrava-karma) is called "non-black" because it is not defiled; it is so named because it does not accord with craving.
Furthermore, because it cannot induce a white karmic maturation (vipāka), it is said to be "non-white."

However, the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* states that the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) are purely white because these dharmas can be attained within a body that has transcended all defilements, unlike the dharmas of one in training (*śaikṣadharma*), which cannot be so attained.
Do all untainted (anāsrava) karmas have the power to exhaust the three preceding types of karma? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
The four dharmakṣāntis and the detachment from desire, Accompanied by the first eight uninterrupted paths,
These twelve untainted volitions Exhaust only the purely black karma.
The ninth thought-moment of abandonment (*ānantarya-cetanā*) in the four dhyānas that are free from desire:
one [thought] exhausts the mixed and purely black [karma], while four cause the purely white [karma] to be exhausted.
The commentary says:

In the path of seeing, there are four moments of dharma-knowledge-acceptance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*); and in the path of cultivation, during the stage of abandoning the defilements of desire, there are eight preceding moments of uninterrupted noble paths (*anantaryamārga*). The twelve volitions (*cetanā*) associated with these are exclusively for the exhaustion of purely black karma.

Accompanying the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the defilements of the desire realm, a single untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*) simultaneously causes both the black-and-white and the purely black [karmas] to be exhausted; for at this time, it completely severs the wholesome karma of the desire realm and also severs the ninth category of unwholesome karma.

The volition (cetanā) associated with the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) that abandons the defilements of each stage of the four dhyānas is exclusively what causes pure white karma to be exhausted, because all other remaining karmas lack ripening (avipāka).

Since it is not the subject under discussion here, it is not analyzed; therefore, within this context, it is stated that only the noble volition (ārya-cetanā) associated with the seventeen [moments] and the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) can eternally exhaust the three types of contaminated karma (*āsrava-karman*).
Although the exhaustion of all karma constitutes the liberation of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*), within this context we speak of its proximate antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Although bodily and vocal actions also serve as proximate antidotes for the three [poisons], they are not associated with wisdom; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
For what reason can only the final path abandon the contaminated wholesome karma of the various stages, and not other paths?
This is because wholesome dharmas are not abandoned by their own nature; even when they have been abandoned, there is the possibility for them to manifest again.

However, it is only when the afflictions that take those [wholesome factors] as their object are exhausted that one speaks of having severed those wholesome factors, because at that time the wholesome factors attain dissociation (*visamyoga*).

For this reason, as long as even a single grade of the afflictions taking them as objects remains, the sense of "severance" is not established, because the wholesome factors are still bound at that time.
The verse says:
Some say that [karma] experienced in hell is black; others say that other karma of the desire realm is black or mixed.
Some say that [karma] to be abandoned by seeing in the desire realm is black; others say that other karma of the desire realm is both black and mixed.
The treatise states:
Regarding the first and third [categories], there are differing explanations. Other masters say:
Karma that leads to experience in the hells and karma that leads to other experiences within the desire realm are, respectively, called "purely black" and "mixed" karma.
This means that since the maturation in the hells is induced solely by unwholesome karma, the karma leading to such experience is termed "purely black."

With the exception of the hells, all other maturations (*vipāka*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are produced by both wholesome and unwholesome karma; therefore, karma that leads to such experiences is called "black-and-white" karma.
This assertion has already been refuted previously, because it is impossible for a wholesome state to be mixed with an unwholesome one.
Other masters say:
"The karma to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm, and all other karma within the desire realm, are respectively called 'pure black' and 'mixed' karma.

That is to say, because the karma to be abandoned by insight is not interspersed with the wholesome, it is called pure black karma; because the karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm includes both the wholesome and the unwholesome, it is called mixed karma."
This is also unreasonable, because among the two types of karma to be abandoned, co-existent karma cannot produce a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

If it is argued that the three types of karma mentioned here are stated according to those with ripening and not those without ripening, then one should not have specified them as "to be abandoned by desire and by vision."

Furthermore, it is logically impossible for a karma of superior power to be overwhelmed by one of inferior power; therefore, one should not say that unwholesome karmas abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) also receive the designation "detached" (vītarāga), nor should one claim that within the desire realm there exists wholesome karma so powerful as to overcome unwholesome karma, for such a position is not accepted.
Why is this? Because wholesome states of the desire realm are not frequently practiced, they lack the power to induce a fruit that lasts for an entire kalpa.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-prakaraṇapāda* (Exposition of the Abhidharma), Fascicle 21.

In the fifth section of the fifth chapter, "Exposition on Karma," it is stated in the Sūtras that there are three types of *muni*, and it is further stated in the Sūtras that there are three types of purification, both pertaining to body, speech, and mind.
What are their respective characteristics?
The verse says:
The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training, Together with the mind, are the three forms of *mauna*.
The three purities should be known as the three sublime conducts (*tri-sucarita*).
The commentary states:

The bodily action of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called the *muni* of body; the vocal action of one beyond training is called the *muni* of speech; and the mental action of one beyond training is called the *muni* of mind.
The sagehood (*muni*) is not essentially the mental action (*manas-karman*) of the mind;
for what reason is it said that this sagehood exists only within the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), and not in the other aggregates?
Other masters say:
By mentioning the end and the beginning, it is implied by analogy that the middle also possesses this same meaning.
According to the true sense, the ultimate Muni has mind alone as its essence; therefore, a sūtra states:
"Because the mind is tranquil, sentient beings are tranquil."
This mind of the Muni can be inferred from his bodily and vocal actions because they are free from all evils;
however, mental action has no such capacity for inference therein. It is only through the conjunction of the object of inference and the means of inference that "Muni" is established.
Why is it that only the Muni is considered one who has attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Because the Arhat is a true Muni, for his verbal expressions and all afflictions have been eternally stilled.
The three types of excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind are termed the three purities of body, speech, and mind.
Untainted sublime conduct can be called pure because it is forever free from the defilements of misconduct and afflictions;
however, how can tainted sublime conduct be pure when it is still defiled by the stains of misconduct and afflictions?
This is also given the name "purification" because it is able to temporarily distance one from the defilements of misconduct;
alternatively, it is established as "pure" because its power can induce the supreme, ultimate purification that is untainted (*anāsrava*).

If it is argued that this [uncontaminated state] should not be called "pure" because it can also induce the stains of affliction—specifically by acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for afflictions—this too is unreasonable.

When a wholesome mind arises, it does not do so by initiating preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for the sake of an afflicted mind; therefore, the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind does not arise immediately after an afflicted mind.
Because a tainted wholesome mind can induce the untainted, this tainted wholesome mind receives the name "pure," as it accords with the untainted mind and is capable of removing defilement.
These two are taught in order to quell sentient beings' adherence to false sages and false purifications.

Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras that there are three types of unwholesome conduct, and it is also stated in the sūtras that there are three types of sublime conduct; both pertain to body, speech, and mind.
What are their respective characteristics?
The verse says:
"Evil actions of body, speech, and mind Are called the three types of unwholesome conduct."
As well as greed, hatred, and wrong view; the three sublime conducts are the opposites of these.
The treatise says:

All unwholesome actions of body and speech—including their preliminary applications (*prayoga*), subsequent activities (*pṛṣṭha*), and their fundamental states (*maula*), as well as unwholesome volition (*cetanā*)—are called, respectively, the misdeeds of body, speech, and mind.
However, there are three types of mental misconduct, namely: non-mental action consisting of greed, hatred, and wrong view.
Is it not the case that the Sūtras also state that greed and so forth are called "mental action"? How can it be said now that greed, hatred, and wrong view are not mental action?
Because these are the provisions for karma, they are also called "karma," just as the provisions for the outflows (*āsrava*) are also called "outflows" and so forth.

Because they are censured and loathed by the noble ones (*ārya*) and because they can bring about undesirable results, these courses of action are evil; therefore, they are called "evil conduct" (*duścarita*).
The three types of sublime conduct (*sucarita*) should be understood as the opposite of these;

that is, all wholesome bodily and vocal karma—including the preliminary (*prayoga*), the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*), and the fundamental (*maula*)—as well as all wholesome volitions (*cetanā*), are respectively termed sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, there are three types of mental wholesome conduct (*manas-kusala-karman*): non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
Because they are praised by the wise, because they bring about desirable fruits, and because this conduct is itself sublime, it is called "wholesome conduct."
Although right view and wrong view do not directly benefit or harm others, they serve as the basis for such actions; therefore, they too constitute good and evil.
Furthermore, the Sūtras state:
"There are ten courses of action (karmapatha), which are either wholesome or unwholesome."
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The ten courses of action that have been explained are subsumed within the categories of unwholesome and wholesome conduct.
Those that are coarse in nature constitute [the karmic paths], becoming wholesome or unwholesome as appropriate.
The commentary states:
Among the previously mentioned unwholesome and excellent courses of action, those that are coarse, manifest, and easily understood are subsumed under the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*).
As appropriate, wholesome courses of action subsume the previously mentioned excellent conduct, while unwholesome courses of action subsume the previously mentioned evil conduct.
What kinds of excellent or evil conduct are not so subsumed?
Preparatory and consecutive actions, and so forth; for these are not coarse or manifest.

Furthermore, among the ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*), those bodily misdeeds that cause other sentient beings to lose their lives, their wealth, or their wives and concubines are designated as "courses of action" (*karmapatha*) for the purpose of causing them to abstain from such acts.
If verbal misconduct is particularly grave in its faults, it is designated as a path of action (*karmapatha*) so that one may abstain from it.
If mental misconduct, such as intense greed or hatred, is particularly grave, it is designated as a path of action so that one may abstain from it.

The preliminary application (*prayoga*), the subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*), and other factors that are minor transgressions, as well as unwholesome reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), are all not paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Within the wholesome paths of action, the wholesome bodily path of action does not encompass one portion of the excellent bodily conduct (*kāyasucarita*); namely, the preliminary application, the subsequent action, and other wholesome bodily actions, such as abstaining from intoxicants and the practice of giving grass.
The path of wholesome verbal action does not encompass one portion of verbal excellent conduct, namely, kind speech (*priyavāda*) and so forth.
The path of wholesome mental action does not encompass one portion of mental excellent conduct, namely, all wholesome volitions (*cetanā*).
Among the ten courses of action (*karmapatha*), do all seven of the first ones necessarily possess both manifest (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest (*avijñapti*) forms? Not so. How is this?
The verse says:
The six unwholesome [karmas] are necessarily non-informative; Those performed by oneself include sexual misconduct as two [types];
The seven wholesome [karmas] arise from undertaking as two [types]; Those arising from meditative concentration are exclusively non-informative.
The treatise says:
Among the seven paths of unwholesome action, six definitely possess non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), namely killing and the others, with the exception of sexual misconduct.
This is because, in the case of these six, if one commissions another to perform them, informative matter (*vijñapti*) arises at the moment the fundamental act is completed.

If one personally commits those six courses of action, then all six possess both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). This refers to cases such as when the victim dies at the very moment the manifest action is initiated, or when death occurs later; in these instances, it is the same as sending an agent, because at the moment the fundamental path of action is completed, there is only the unmanifest.

Only sexual misconduct necessarily possesses both [types of action], because it must be personally completed by oneself; one does not experience joy as if it were produced in oneself by sending another to act.

As for the seven wholesome courses of action, if they arise from formal undertaking (*samādāna*), they necessarily possess both—the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)—because the morality (*śīla*) arising from an undertaking must depend upon the manifest.

The restraint comprised by dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) is called "born of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-ja*); this consists solely of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), because it arises depending exclusively on the power of the mind.
Are the preparatory (*prayoga*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages like the fundamental (*maula*) stage?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
The preparatory stage (prayoga) necessarily possesses informative action (vijñapti); non-informative action (avijñapti) may or may not be present.
The subsequent stage (pṛṣṭha) is the opposite of this.
The treatise says:

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of a course of action (*karmapatha*) necessarily possesses informative action (*vijñapti*). As for non-informative action (*avijñapti*) at this stage, it may or may not exist: if it arises from intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*) or a mind of pure faith (*prasādacetana*), then non-informative action exists; otherwise, it does not.

The subsequent [action] (pṛṣṭha) is the opposite of the preceding; it necessarily possesses non-informative action (avijñapti). In this stage, the manifest action (vijñapti-karman) may or may not exist. Since the second moment, beginning with the non-informative action, is designated as "subsequent," it necessarily exists.
If at that time one initiates an action following the preceding karma, then there is also manifest action (*vijñapti*); otherwise, there is none.

Regarding this matter, the distinctions between the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the fundamental stage (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) of the paths of action (*karmapatha*) should be understood as they are extensively explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are three kinds of killing: first, that arising from greed; second, that arising from hatred; and third, that arising from delusion."
This applies likewise even up to the three types of wrong view.
How could it be that all courses of action (karmapatha) at the time of completion arise from all three roots?

The Buddha made this statement, but it is not the case that all courses of action at the time of completion arise from all three roots; rather, there are differences in their preliminary applications (prayoga).
How is there a distinction?
The verse says:
It arises from the three roots of preparatory effort, because it is produced immediately thereafter.
They arise from the three roots, such as greed.
The Treatise says:

When the preliminary stages (*prayoga*) of unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*) arise, each one originates from the three unwholesome roots; this statement is made because it refers to their initial origination (*samutthāna*).

The preparatory action (*prayoga*) of killing arising from greed is as follows: for instance, when one has a craving for another's teeth, hair, or limbs; or when acting to obtain wealth, for the sake of amusement, or to rescue a friend or oneself—one initiates the preparatory action of killing out of greed.
That which arises from hatred (*dveṣa*) is, for example, when one gives rise to the preparatory action of killing out of a mind of fierce resentment in order to eliminate an enemy.
That which arises from delusion (*moha*) is, for example, as the Persians (*Pārasīka*) say:

"If one causes one's parents to die when they are old and sick, one generates superior merit, because it liberates them from their present sufferings and enables them to newly obtain a superior body with sharp faculties."
Furthermore, it is claimed that killing occurs within the context of dharma-sacrifices;
moreover, kings and others, relying on worldly laws, execute enemies and eliminate malevolent elements, asserting that they generate great merit by initiating the karmic application of killing.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhists say that since snakes, scorpions, bees, and the like inflict harm upon humans, one obtains merit by killing them.
They also claim that sheep, deer, water buffaloes, and other birds and beasts are intended for food; therefore, there is no sin in killing them.
Furthermore, killing sentient beings due to wrong views—these preparatory acts all arise from delusion (*moha*).
The remaining six preparatory acts arise from the three roots; their characteristics are explained in detail in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
How do the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of greed and the other [unwholesome roots] arise from the three?
Because they arise immediately after the three roots.
That is to say, from each of the three unwholesome roots—greed and the rest—it is possible for three courses of action (*karmapatha*) to arise immediately thereafter.

By this, it has already been shown that three types of preparatory actions arise immediately and in association with greed, hatred, and delusion; furthermore, based on the sense of "immediacy," the courses of action themselves also arise.
It has thus been explained how unwholesome [actions] arise from the three roots.
What further is meant by "wholesome"?
The verse says:
The wholesome, throughout its three stages, Arises from all three wholesome roots.
The treatise says:

All preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages of the various wholesome courses of action arise from the wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for all three stages of the wholesome are originated by wholesome mental factors, and a wholesome mind must necessarily be associated with these three types of wholesome roots.
What are the characteristics of these three stages of the wholesome?
It should be understood that all three stages which are the opposite of the aforementioned three stages of the unwholesome are wholesome.

For example, when a śrāmaṇera receives full ordination, from the time he enters the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) and pays homage to the community of bhikṣus, through his sincere utterance of words to request a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), up until the one motion and two formal acts (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), all are termed the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of the wholesome path of action (*karmapatha*).
When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, the manifest and unmanifest karma within that single moment is called the "fundamental course of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).

From this point onward, until the proclamation of the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), as well as whatever continues to follow based on those preceding conditions, both manifest and unmanifest karma are termed "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*).

As previously stated, it is not the case that all courses of action (karmapatha) reach their culmination through all three roots. One should explain which root brings each course of action to its conclusion.
The verse says:
Killing, harsh speech, and malice—these are all brought to completion by hatred alone.
Stealing, sexual misconduct, and covetousness are all brought to completion by greed;
false view is brought to completion by delusion; it is held that the remaining [non-virtuous paths] are brought to completion by all three.
The treatise says:
