Among the unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), the courses of killing, harsh speech, and malice are brought to completion by hatred (*dveṣa*); for these three are accomplished only when a mind that is utterly reckless and extremely coarse and evil is present.

These three courses of action—taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and covetousness—are brought to completion by greed; for these three are accomplished only when a mind that is intensely defiled and characterized by attachment is present.
The culmination of wrong view must necessarily arise from delusion (*moha*), because it is accomplished through the manifestation of superior-grade delusion.

As for the three—false speech, divisive speech, and frivolous speech—it is accepted that each can be brought to completion by all three [roots], since when greed, hatred, and so forth manifest, each is capable of bringing these three to completion.
In what locations do the various paths of unwholesome karma arise?
The verse says:
They arise in relation to sentient beings, the possession of name-and-form, And in relation to names, bodies, and so forth.
The treatise says:
Regarding the four categories of paths of action previously mentioned, three, one, three, and one arise respectively in relation to the four bases, beginning with sentient beings.

This means that the three [unwholesome paths of action], such as killing, arise in relation to the sphere of sentient beings; they must depend upon sentient beings for these courses of action to arise. Therefore, they do not arise depending solely on external objects.
One might ask: "Are these three not also said to arise in relation to the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*)?"
A single aggregate (skandha) and a single moment may also be designated as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa), because these three factors depend upon the totality of the aggregates.

The three [karmic paths] beginning with stealing arise in relation to the requisites; they constitute a full course of action (karmapatha) only when one intends to appropriate for oneself the objects of enjoyment belonging to another sentient being.
Although they depend upon sentient beings, because their objective bases (ālambana) are superior, it is said that these three types are established by relying on objective bases.
Only false view arises in relation to the sphere of name-and-form (nāmarūpāyatana), because it denies the existence of dharmas consisting of name-and-form.

Although this also negates *nirvāṇa* as being non-existent, it does so through the gateway of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), negating its eternal cessation; for [the proponent] says that since even suffering does not exist, how much less could there be *nirvāṇa*, which is the cessation of suffering. Therefore, it is stated that [this negation] arises only in relation to the sphere of name-and-form.
Is it not the case that wrong view also negates sentient beings? Why, then, is it said [only] that [wrong view] arises in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?

Because from this condition, distinct name-and-form also arise; however, since one who negates the name-and-form that is the basis for sentient beings necessarily negates the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) that depends upon it, the latter is established by implication and need not be stated separately.

Furthermore, within the Noble Teachings, there are cases where sentient beings do not exist; logically, it must be that where there is no name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is likewise no one who is a sentient being.

Denying what is real as non-existent constitutes a full course of action (*karmapatha*) because it is grave; denying a conventional designation (*prajñaptidharma*) as non-existent is light and thus is not a full course of action. Therefore, it is not said that [the path of action] arises in the locus of a sentient being.

The three [vices], such as false speech and so forth, arise from the bases of name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) and so on, because the substance of speech necessarily arises in dependence upon names and so forth.
Although speech also arises by depending upon sentient beings and other factors, it directly and primarily arises in dependence upon name-bodies and so forth.
Furthermore, frivolous speech does not depend upon sentient beings; there is nothing that does not rely upon the group of names (nāmakāya) and so forth.
Alternatively, there is no fault in establishing the courses of action (karmapatha) based on their uncommon locus.

Although harsh speech arises based on name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, there is a concern that this path of action might be thought to be accomplished even by relying solely on external objects; therefore, it is stated that it arises only with respect to sentient beings.
Furthermore, since the utterance of harsh speech does not require the use of ornate phrasing, it is not said to arise based on name-groups and so forth.
By what is the completion of the path of action of killing established?

It is established by means of both the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the fulfillment of the result (*phala-paripūri*); if either of these two factors is lacking, one does not incur the fundamental offense of taking life.
Is there a case where one who initiates the preparatory effort for killing and brings it to completion is nevertheless not touched by the offense of killing?
He said: "There is. How so?
The verse says:
"If they die together, or if one dies first, there is no root [of the offense], because the basis is different.
The commentary says:

If one who intends to kill initiates the preparatory action with the definite intent to kill another, yet dies at the same time as the victim or dies prior to them, the path of action (karmapatha) is not established for that killer.
Why is this so? It is because the life of the one being killed has not yet been severed,
whereas the life of the one who kills has already ended, as they have already taken rebirth in another basis.

This means that the body which served as the basis for the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of killing has now been severed and extinguished; although a different type of body belonging to the same homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) has arisen, it is not the basis for the transgression. Since this [new body] never previously initiated the preparatory effort for killing, the principle that it could complete the karmic action of killing would be untenable.

If a large number of people assemble as an army with the intent to kill enemies or to hunt wild animals, and among them any one person commits the act of killing, who becomes established in the path of action (karmapatha) of killing?
The verse says:
If an army and so forth act with a common purpose, all are as culpable as the actual perpetrator.
The commentary says:

If any one among a group, such as an army, commits the act of killing, all of them become established in the karmic path of killing, because they have collectively consented to that single undertaking.
Just as when several people instruct one another in turn to accomplish a single task, so that if one commits killing, the others all incur the offense;

likewise, if one is coerced by external force into joining them, one also incurs the sin of killing because of the shared intent. However, this excludes those who have made a solemn vow or pledge not to kill even for the sake of saving their own lives; since they lack the murderous intent, they do not incur the sin of killing.

Now, the characteristics of the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*) should be explained individually. That is to say, to what extent is one said to have committed "killing," and so on, up to what extent is one said to have "wrong view"?
First, let us distinguish the characteristic of killing; the verse says:
Killing arises from intentional thought, [directed] toward another being, without error.

The commentary says: It requires first generating the intentional thought of a desire to kill; regarding another sentient being, one perceives them as such another being; one performs the preparatory action of killing; and one kills without error—meaning one kills only that specific individual and does not kill others indiscriminately. Up to this point, it is designated as the karmic path of killing.
One harbors hesitation, wondering whether it is a tree stump or a human being;
even if it is indeed a human, one wonders whether it is that specific person or not.

Having formed a resolute intention, thinking, "Whether it is he or not, I shall certainly kill him," because the mind has no regard for the consequences, if one kills a sentient being, it constitutes a full course of action (*karmapatha*).
Whether these courses of action are certain or doubtful, as long as the conditions for killing are fully present, there is a logical basis for their completion.
How can the offense be established when one performs the act of killing within a momentary cessation?

When one initiates the preparatory action of killing with an evil mind, at the moment the life of the victim ceases, that [moment] cannot serve as a cause to project a subsequent life of the same kind; rather, it obstructs the life that ought to arise, causing it never to arise again. This is therefore called "killing," and by this means one incurs guilt.
Having already analyzed killing, one should now distinguish taking what is not given.
The verse says:
Taking another's property without it being given, by force or by stealth, and making it one's own.
The Commentary states:
The preceding terms, such as "without error" and so forth, should be understood as applying accordingly to what follows.

That is to say, one must first generate the volitional intent (*cetanā*) to steal; then, regarding another's property, one forms the perception that it is another's property; subsequently, through either force or stealth, one initiates the preliminary action (*prayoga*) of stealing and takes it without error, thereby making it belong to oneself. Up to this point, it is termed the offense of taking what is not given (*adattādāna*).
If one steals property belonging to a stūpa, one incurs an offense against the Buddha, because the Buddha, prior to his parinirvāṇa, accepted all offerings made by the world as a whole.

If one steals the property of deceased monks who have already undergone the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one incurs the offense of theft against the Saṃgha within that boundary; if the ritual has not yet been completed, one incurs it against the entire Saṃgha.
If one steals the property of others, such as elephants or horses, the path of action is only completed once they have been removed from their place of residence.
Having already analyzed taking what is not given, one should now analyze sexual misconduct.
The verse says:
Sexual misconduct is of four kinds; it consists of engaging in what ought not to be engaged in.
The commentary says:
In total, there are four types of sexual conduct that should not be practiced; all are termed the offense of sexual misconduct.
First, engaging with an improper object (*agocara*), meaning one who is protected by another—such as a mother, a father, a relative of one's parents, or even one whose protection has been lost.
Second, regarding improper ways (*amārga*): this refers to even one's own wife, [approaching her] through the mouth or other orifices.
Third, regarding improper places (*adeśa*): this refers to sacred shrines (*caitya*), monasteries, or secluded locations.
Fourth, regarding improper times (*akāla*): this refers to when she is pregnant, when she is nursing, or when she is observing the fast (*upoṣadha*).
Some say that if one has undertaken the observance of the fast (upavāsa) and yet violates it, only then is it termed "untimely" (*akāla*).
Since this was not said in error, the same principle applies here as well.

If one regards another’s wife as one’s own, or regards one’s own wife as another’s, or regarding the path as non-path and so forth—provided there is merely a mistaken mind (*bhrānti-citta*), although an act is performed, it does not constitute a full course of action (*karmapatha*).

If one engages in unchaste conduct with another's wife while perceiving her as someone other than that wife, some say the offense is nonetheless established, because both the preparatory effort and the actual enjoyment are directed toward the object belonging to another.
Some say that, as in the case of the path of action of killing, the preparatory effort is not established because the objects are distinct prior to its completion;
however, if a bhikṣuṇī or similar person has a wife who observes the precepts, if one violates her, the path of action is likewise established.
Having already analyzed sexual misconduct, one should now analyze false speech.
The verse says:
To utter words with a defiled mind while having a different perception, and for the meaning to be understood, is false speech.
The treatise says:
False speech is established through the power of both the speaker and the listener.

That is to say, one speaks with a perception different from that which corresponds to what is being said, and the person being deceived understands the meaning of what was spoken; it constitutes a full course of action (*karmapatha*) only when there is no error and the mind is defiled.
If the person being deceived has not yet understood, it is subsumed under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).

Since speech is composed of multiple syllables, the path of action is only completed when the final moment of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*) manifests both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) karma.
Alternatively, it is established as soon as the meaning is understood by the person being deceived.
The preceding characters are all preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for this.

Regarding the meaning of "understanding" (*vijñāna*) herein: it is called "understanding" based on the fact that the person being deceived is capable of understanding; it does not refer to the actual comprehension of the meaning itself.
To what extent is one said to be "capable of understanding" or "possessing correct understanding"?
The former refers to the time when the understander abides in auditory consciousness;
the latter refers to being able to correctly discern its meaning.

If one correctly understands the meaning, it is known by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) has already ceased simultaneously with the auditory consciousness; therefore, this course of action (*karmapatha*) should consist solely of the non-intimated (*avijñapti*).

Therefore, it is logically correct that for one who speaks words with a malicious intent, the path of action (karmapatha) is established as soon as they abide in the consciousness of hearing; this is because they are capable of deceiving others through the full possession of both manifest (vijñapti) and unmanifest (avijñapti) karma.
Some say that regardless of whether the deceived person understands the meaning or not, the path of action is established simply by speaking with a contrary intention.
Not so; because this is identical to divisive speech (*paiśunya*), it must be understood that the act is only completed when the listener either accepts or rejects the statement.

The Sūtra states that there are briefly sixteen types of speech: namely, to say one has actually seen, heard, sensed, or known regarding matters not seen, heard, sensed, or known; and to say one has not seen, etc., regarding matters that were seen, etc. These eight kinds are called non-noble speech (*anārya-vāk*).
Regarding that which is not seen, one says "not seen," and regarding that which is seen, one says "truly seen. These eight types are called noble speech (*āryavāk*).
What are the characteristics of "that which is seen" and so forth?
The verse says:
That which is realized by the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and mind, together with the other three,
is termed, in their respective order, "the seen," "the heard," "the known," and "the cognized."
The treatise states:
If an object is realized by the eye, ear, mind, or the other consciousnesses, it is respectively termed "seen" and so forth.

Because the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile faculties apprehend objects that have reached them, they are collectively termed "cognized" (*vijñāta*), for other sūtras definitively state that what is apprehended by these three faculties is "cognized."
The Sūtra says:
"O Great Mother!
What do you think?"

Regarding all forms whatsoever that you do not see with your eyes, have never seen, will not see, nor desire to see—do you, on account of them, give rise to desire, give rise to lust, give rise to attachment, give rise to affection, give rise to a store-consciousness (*ālaya*), give rise to a settling-point (*niyanti*), or give rise to clinging?
"No, Venerable Sir!
None of the sounds whatsoever are heard by your ear; [to speak at length] up to: none of the phenomena whatsoever are known by your mind; [to speak at length] up to: no, they are not."
"Venerable One!
He further addressed the Great Mother:

'In this regard, you should know that what is seen is merely what is seen; you should know that what is heard, what is sensed, and what is cognized are merely what is heard, what is sensed, and what is cognized.'"
Since this sūtra describes visible forms, sounds, and mental objects as being "seen," "heard," and "cognized," it follows by analogy that other objects must be established as "sensed.
If this were not admitted, what would "the sensed" be?
Furthermore, regarding the three [objects] beginning with fragrance, one should not utter words concerning them as being external to what is seen and so forth.
Having already analyzed false speech, we shall now analyze the remaining three types of speech.
The verse says:
Speech that harms others with a defiled mind is called divisive speech;
unkind and harsh words are abusive speech; all other defiled utterances are frivolous speech.
Others say that it differs from the three [types of] defilement, such as sycophantic song, heterodox treatises, and so forth.
The Treatise says:
If one utters speech intended to cause division with a defiled mind, whether the other party is actually divided or not, it constitutes divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
The conditions of "understanding the meaning" and "not erring" also apply here.
If one utters unpleasant speech with a defiled mind to disparage another, it is called harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
Since the preceding defiled mind and speech carry over into this case, "understanding the meaning" and "not erring" are likewise the same as before.
All speech uttered by a defiled mind is termed frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), because it is entirely defiled.
Only the term "speech" (*vāk*) from the preceding [category] carries over into this context.

Some say that frivolous speech includes only those things other than the previous three [kinds of unwholesome speech], such as flattery, song, and false doctrines, which are uttered by a defiled mind.
*Naṭana* (flattery) refers to a bhikṣu seeking fame and profit through crooked means, uttering words of affectionate flattery.
*Gīta* (song) refers to performers who, with defiled minds, delight others by performing various crooked acts, as well as those with defiled minds who chant and flirt with one another.
"Heterodox doctrines" refers to the teachings of the Sāṃkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, and others; "utterances of evil views" refers to lamentations and frivolous discourse produced by a defiled mind.

When a Wheel-Turning King appears, his songs and other such utterances accord with renunciation and are contrary to defilement; therefore, they are not subsumed under frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).

Some say that expressions such as those concerning marriage and so forth are subsumed under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), but are not included among the courses of action (*karmapatha*). Because they belong to the category of weak defilements (*tanu-rajas*), they do not induce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); yet it is not the case that there is no non-informative matter that can be subsumed within the courses of action.
Having already explained the three [unwholesome paths] of speech, we shall now explain the three of the mind.
The verse says:
Covetousness is the desire for another's wealth; Ill will is hatred toward sentient beings.
To reject [the existence of] good and evil and so forth is called the path of action of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-karmapatha*).
The treatise says:
To unrighteously crave another's property with the desire to make it one's own—whether by force or by theft—such evil desire is called the path of action of greed (*abhidhyā-karmapatha*).
To give rise to a mind of hatred and resentment toward sentient beings, desiring to oppress them, is called the path of action of anger (*vyāpāda*).
To deny the existence of good, evil, and so forth through wrong views is called the path of action of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The word "etc. (*ādi*) is used to indicate that the subsequent items are included by citing the first;

it should be understood in full as described in the Sūtra. There are eleven distinct categories of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), such as the denial of cause and the denial of effect, concerning the two [lives] and so forth, as summarized by the Blessed One. These range from "there is no giving" up to the full exposition.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the ten courses of action (*karmapatha*),
by what meaning are these courses of action defined?
The verse says:
Among these, three are exclusively paths, and seven are both karma and paths.
The treatise says:
Among the ten courses of action (*karmapatha*), the latter three are exclusively paths; because they are the paths of karma, they are designated by the name "courses of action."

The volition associated with that [mind] is called "action" (*karman*), because it moves as that [mind] moves and it proceeds as that proceeds, performing its activity according to that [mind's] power.
The first seven are action, because they are bodily and vocal actions;
they are also the paths of action, because they are the domains in which volition (*cetanā*) operates.

Because the volition that initiates bodily and vocal actions functions by taking those very actions as its object, they are termed "paths of action" (*karmapatha*), meaning "the path (*patha*) for the action (*karman*).

Thus, when the term "path of action" is used here, it fully expresses both the sense of "path of action" and "action that is a path of action. Although these are not of the same category, one serves as a designation for the other, as both are universally established in the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*.
Alternatively, they are called "paths of action" (karmapatha) because they are the paths of karma; they are also called "paths of action" because they are both karma and paths.
In full, one should say "paths of action and karma," but by taking one as representative of the other, it is simply called "paths of action."
The meaning of the wholesome paths of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) should be understood in the same manner.
The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) should also be termed "paths of action," because volition (*cetanā*) also operates by taking them as its objects.

Although it would be logical to state this, it is not stated because they proceed in dependence upon and based upon the fundamental [action]; because the coarse aspects are first designated as the paths of action; and because internal and external increases or decreases follow the fundamental [action].
All paths of unwholesome action manifest as contrary to what is wholesome and sever all roots of goodness.
By which path of action are the roots of goodness severed?
What are their distinctions?
The verse says:
Only wrong view severs the roots of goodness; that which is severed consists of those acquired at birth within the desire realm.
It severs all [wholesome states] by denying cause and effect; they are severed gradually, and both [roots and states] are abandoned together.

Humans of the three continents, both male and female, [attain it]; through vision and practice, there is non-possession; the restoration of roots of goodness occurs through doubt or the presence of views; it is sudden and manifest, excluding those who have committed the heinous crimes. The treatise says: The roots of goodness are restored by humans belonging to the three continents, whether male or female. This restoration occurs through two paths: by means of vision (*darśana-mārga*) or by means of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). It is characterized by "non-possession" (*aprāpti*). The restoration of the roots of goodness occurs either through the arising of doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding the truth, or through the arising of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) that subsequently lead to right view. This restoration is instantaneous and manifests immediately, with the sole exception of those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karman*). The treatise says: [The roots of goodness] are restored by humans of the three continents, both male and female, through vision and practice, as a state of non-possession; the restoration of the roots of goodness occurs through doubt or the presence of views, being sudden and manifest, except for those who have committed the heinous crimes. The treatise says:
Among the unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), only a superior and complete wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) can sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
If this is so, for what reason does the fundamental treatise ask:
"What are the superior unwholesome roots?"?
This refers to those unwholesome roots that are capable of severing the wholesome roots, or which are the first to be eliminated at the stage of detachment from desire.

Because unwholesome roots can induce wrong view, the actual function of wrong view is attributed to those roots; just as when a fire burns a village, the fire was started by bandits, so the world says "the village was burned by the bandits."
Which roots of goodness are severed by this?
It refers exclusively to the roots of goodness acquired at birth within the desire realm, because wholesome states of the form and formless realms have not yet been attained.
The *Prajñaptipāda-śāstra* states:

Regarding the severance of the wholesome roots of the three realms: based on the superior wholesome roots, it is explained that these [roots] become even more remote within this continuity, for [this continuity] is not a vessel for them.
For what reason is it only the innate wholesome roots (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala-mūla*) that are severed?
Because the roots of goodness of the preparatory stage have already been lost, by what cause and at what stage does this severance of the roots of goodness occur?

It is said that there is a certain class of persons who possess extremely violent and evil latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); later, supported by the power of external conditions such as evil friends, these dispositions become further intensified, whereby the roots of goodness diminish and the unwholesome roots increase.
The subsequent wrong view that denies causes and denies effects causes all wholesome states to become completely obscured; by means of this, the mental continuum remains devoid of virtue.

Regarding the wrong views that sever the roots of goodness at this causal stage, there are two types: those with objects within one's own realm and those with objects in other realms, as well as those with contaminated objects and those with uncontaminated objects.
Who is capable of severing the roots of goodness?
One should say that all [such persons] are capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Can the nine grades of the roots of goodness be severed instantaneously, as the roots of evil to be abandoned through seeing are severed by the Path of Seeing?

It is not so. Why? Because the nine grades of false views are abandoned gradually; as the nine grades of wholesome roots are abandoned through mutual correspondence in both forward and reverse order, it is like the abandonment of afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Just as with the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation, it is logically possible for [the fruit] to arise or not arise during the intermediate stage.

Among the fruits of the various restraints (*saṃvara*), some are produced from the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and some are produced from the innate wholesome mind (*upapattilābhika-citta*); one abandons them immediately upon abandoning their respective causes.
In what location can the roots of goodness be severed?
It occurs within the three continents of the human realm, not in the miserable destinies, because the wisdom—whether defiled or undefiled—is not firm there.
Nor does it occur in the celestial realms, because one directly perceives the fruits of both wholesome and unwholesome karmas therein.
Regarding the "three continents," this excludes Uttarakuru, because there is no such extremely evil *āśaya* (intent) there.
Upon what kind of body does such a severance of the roots of goodness depend?
It depends only on the bodies of males and females, because their mental dispositions are fixed.
Why is it that practitioners are able to sever the roots of goodness?
It is only those who follow views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), not those who follow craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*).
This is because the negative mental disposition (*āśaya*) of those who follow views is extremely firm and deep.
Because those who act out of desire possess an extremely restless and unstable mental disposition (*āśaya*).
By this reasoning, eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and others are excluded.
Furthermore, such persons are like those in the miserable realms (*apāya*).
What is the nature of this severance of the roots of goodness?

It should be understood that the essence of their thorough severance is non-possession (*aprāpti*). This is because when a powerful false view manifests, it causes the possession (*prāpti*) of the roots of goodness to cease and brings about the continuous arising of the non-possession of them; therefore, the essence of the severed roots of goodness is precisely non-possession.
It has already been established that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is not a real entity. Once the roots of goodness have been severed, by what means are they resumed?
It is through doubt regarding existence and views; that is to say, at the stage of resuming the roots of goodness.

Alternatively, it may be due to the power of causes, or by relying on a virtuous friend, that one suddenly develops doubt regarding cause and effect: "Is there or is there not a future world resulting from [one's actions]?"

When one suddenly develops right view regarding cause and effect, becoming certain that there is a future life, the prior adherence to wrong views is abandoned; at that moment, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the roots of goodness is attained, and the acquisition of their non-attainment is extinguished—this is called the "reconnection of the roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhi*).

The nine grades of wholesome roots are suddenly reconnected and then arise gradually, just as when a chronic illness is suddenly cured, one's strength increases gradually. Can one reconnect with the wholesome roots in this present life?
Yes, there are those who can, with the exception of those who have committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Other masters say:
"Those for whom the view of nihilism has increased are likewise unable to reconnect their roots of goodness in the present life; this refers to those two types of persons.
Thus the Sūtra says:
It is certain that he cannot reconnect the roots of goodness in the present life; that person will certainly be about to pass away from hell.
It is only at the very moment of being about to take rebirth there that he can reconnect the roots of goodness, and not at any other stage.
The phrase "the stage of being about to be born" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The phrase "at the time of being about to pass away" means when one is on the verge of death.
If, by the power of causes, one has severed the roots of virtue, they are reconnected at the time of death.
If one severs the roots of goodness through the power of conditions, they will be reconnected at the time of rebirth.
It should be understood that the same applies when it occurs through the power of oneself or others.
Furthermore, it is a corruption of intention (*āśaya*), not a corruption of application (*prayoga*).
One who has severed the roots of goodness can reconnect them in the present life.
However, if both [the view and the precepts] are destroyed and the roots of goodness are severed, one must wait until after the destruction of the body for the roots of goodness to reconnect.

This should be understood to apply similarly to the relationship between views and precepts; it is not the case that the severing or reconnecting of the roots of goodness occurs during the period when a kalpa is about to end or at the beginning of a kalpa’s formation, because there is no moisture for the roots to reconnect.
Regarding the fourfold classification of the wrong view that severs the roots of goodness:
one should know that the wrong view which severs the roots of goodness and the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha will certainly bring about the retribution of the Avīci hell.
Having taken this opportunity to discuss the severing of the roots of goodness, we shall now clarify the meaning of the fundamental paths of action.
Among the two paths of action—wholesome and unwholesome—that have been explained, how many arise simultaneously and function together with volition (*cetanā*)?
The verse says:
The paths of action that function together with volition, In the unwholesome, range from one to eight.
"Good [paths] generally open up to ten, while specifically excluding one, eight, and five.
The Commentary says:
Among the various courses of action that co-occur with volition (*cetanā*), regarding those that are unwholesome, they range from one up to only eight.
"Simultaneous occurrence with one" refers to the manifestation of any one among the three [roots], such as greed and so forth, while being separated from the others;
or when an evil karma previously committed through preparatory effort reaches its completion upon the presence of any one of the remaining defiled minds, such as greed, or non-defiled minds.
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of both: this refers to practicing unwholesome conduct.

If one personally commits killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, or dispatches another to do so, one establishes a state based on any one of these; at that time, any one of greed, hatred, or wrong view manifests.

If an evil karma previously committed through preliminary effort (*prayoga*) is brought to completion by two [factors] when other defilements such as greed (*lobha*), or a non-defiled mind, are present;

or if three [factors] operate together, meaning that an evil karma previously committed through preliminary effort is brought to completion by three [factors] at the time when greed and so forth arise.

If one dispatches a messenger to commit one act, such as killing, while simultaneously completing another act, such as sexual misconduct, through one's own action, both are brought to completion at the same time.
If one performs two acts oneself, this should be considered according to the same principle.
Regarding the evil karma created through prior preparation, when other defiled states such as greed or non-defiled minds manifest, the matter is completed in accordance with these three factors.
When one gives rise to other defiled states of mind such as greed and so forth, they are subsumed under the category of autonomous karma (*svayamkṛta-karma*).
One should reflect accordingly on how [the karmas of] divisive speech, false speech, and so forth are likewise categorized when incited by others (*pṛṣṭhataḥ-kṛta*).

Regarding the four simultaneous occurrences: this refers to when one intends to subvert another by speaking false speech or harsh words; there is one path of action for the mental karma and three paths of action for the vocal karma.

This also applies if one sends two messengers while personally engaging in sexual misconduct and so forth, or if, at the moment greed and other afflictions arise, the evil karma previously initiated through preliminary effort reaches its culmination according to these three [vocal paths].
Examples of this kind should be considered by analogy.
One should explain the cases of five, six, or seven [paths of action] occurring together according to reason.

Regarding those that occur simultaneously in eight: this refers to when one first performs the preliminary application for six unwholesome actions and, at the same time, personally carries out sexual misconduct, such that they all reach completion simultaneously.
Other cases should be considered accordingly.
Since the last three [paths of action] do not occur simultaneously, there are no instances of nine or ten paths.
Thus, the unwholesome paths of action have been explained.

Regarding the number [of paths of action] that arise simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*), there are differences: when considering the wholesome paths of action in general, they may reach a total of ten; however, when specifically accounting for their manifest characteristics, one, eight, or five are excluded.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of both: this refers to when the five wholesome consciousnesses and the *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) and *anutpādajñāna* (knowledge of non-arising)—based on the formless realm—are present. At that time, there are no seven types of non-dispersed wholesome [paths of action], because the wisdom associated with them is not of the nature of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), and because there is no discipline (*saṃvara*) concomitant with the formless absorptions.
Three [factors] arise together when the mental consciousness associated with right view is present, provided there are no seven types of material wholesome factors.
Four [factors] arise together when an unwholesome or neutral mind is present, and one attains the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a lay devotee (*upavāsa*), or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).
Six factors occurring together refers to when the five wholesome sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) manifest while one has attained the three higher types of restraint (*saṃvara*).

Seven factors occurring together refers to when the wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) manifests in association with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and without accompanying form (*rūpa*), while one has attained the three higher types of restraint.
Alternatively, one may obtain the bhikṣu precepts when an unwholesome or neutral state of mind is manifest.

As for the ninefold simultaneous occurrence: this refers to obtaining the bhikṣu precepts when wholesome five-fold sensory consciousnesses, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising based on the formless realm, are manifest.
Alternatively, when a consciousness associated with the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), which is subsumed under meditative absorption (dhyāna), manifests, ten [factors] operate together;
that is to say, when a wholesome mental consciousness associated with right view, which lacks accompanying matter (rūpa-anuvartin), manifests while one receives the bhikṣu precepts.
Those who maintain that one also receives the *saṃvara* of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) through a preparatory wholesome mind provide this general explanation.

Alternatively, at the moment when any other mind associated with right view arises together with the concomitant matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*), such [restraints] are excluded based on their manifest characteristics; however, if one considers both the manifest and the latent, there is nothing that is excluded.
That is to say, apart from the formal restraint (saṃvara), there are one, eight, and five [types of abstention].
Regarding the single simultaneous occurrence: this refers to when an unwholesome or neutral state of mind is present, one attains the abstention from a single branch [of misconduct].

Regarding the fivefold simultaneous occurrence (*pañca-sahavartin*): this refers to when a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), associated with right view and lacking accompanying formative factors (*anuparivartin-rūpa*), manifests, one obtains two branches [of the path], and so forth.

Regarding the eightfold simultaneous occurrence (*aṣṭa-sahavartin*): this refers to when this same mental consciousness manifests, one obtains the five branches, etc., of wholesome or unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*).
In which realms, destinies, and locations are how many [mental factors] exclusively accomplished (*samanvāgata*), and how many also manifest (*samudācāra*)?
The verse says:
In the unwholesome states within the hells, Coarseness, harshness, and malice pertain to both.
Greed and wrong view are accomplished [only] through possession; in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), the latter three are accomplished;
idle chatter is both manifest and accomplished; the remaining ten in the desire realm are both;
as for the wholesome, they exist in all places; the latter three are both manifest and accomplished.
In the formless and non-percipient heavens, the first seven are exclusively accomplished;
in other places, they are both accomplished and manifest, with the exception of the hells and the northern continent.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, among the ten unwholesome paths of action, three are present in two ways within the hells: namely, harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) and frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Malice (*vyāpāda*) is present in all three ways; it is both manifest and possessed, because beings there are oppressed by suffering and revile one another.
There is harsh speech;

because of resentful lamentation and wailing, there is frivolous speech. Because the body and mind are coarse, rigid, perverse, and unrefined, and because of mutual hatred, there is ill will, greed, and wrong view.
They exist but do not engage in action because they lack desirable objects and because they directly perceive the fruits of karma.
Since there are no phenomena that cause mutual harm, there is no killing;
that is to say, they all die solely through the exhaustion of their own karma.
Because there are no women who possess property, there is neither theft nor sexual misconduct, as these would serve no purpose.
There is no false speech, for false speech causes others to have distorted perceptions, yet their perceptions are already constantly distorted.
There is no false speech, because they are constantly free from it or because it serves no purpose.

There is no divisive speech; in Uttarakuru, greed, hatred, and wrong view are all invariably present but do not manifest, because they do not grasp at "mine," because their bodies and minds are supple, because there are no causes for affliction or harm, and because they lack malicious intentions.
Only frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) is present there as an actual manifestation, because at times they sing with defiled minds.
Since their lifespan is fixed, there is no killing.
Because they possess neither property nor women, there is no taking what is not given and no sexual misconduct.
Because he has no deceitful mind, he has no false speech that deceives; or [he refrains from it] because it would be useless.
Because he is always harmonious and conciliatory, he has no divisive speech.
Because his words are pure and beautiful, he has no harsh or evil speech.
Excluding the aforementioned hells and the continent of Uttarakuru, the remaining ten [paths of action] within the desire realm all pertain to both [types:

manifest and acquired]. That is to say, among the gods, hungry ghosts, animals, and humans of the three continents within the desire realm, all ten unwholesome paths of action pertain to both being accomplished and being manifest; however, there are distinctions. Specifically, for gods, hungry ghosts, and animals, the first seven paths of action are comprised only of the intermediate category and lack non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
whereas among humans in the three continents, both types exist.
The unwholesome [paths of action] have already been explained.

Regarding the wholesome paths of action, the three beginning with non-greed are present in both ways—namely, as possession (*samanvāgama*) and as actual manifestation (*samudācāra*)—throughout the three realms and five destinies.
Regarding the seven branches of body and speech, although they may be accomplished in the formless realm where there is no form or perception, they certainly do not manifest there.
This refers to noble beings born in the formless realm who accomplish past and future untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
Non-percipient beings necessarily possess the past and future dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) of the fourth dhyāna;

however, as for the noble ones, regardless of which dhyāna stage they rely upon, when they are born in the formless realms (ārūpya), they possess that past untainted (anāsrava) morality (śīla) that they have previously arisen and ceased, while in the future, they possess it across all six stages.
Regarding the fact that there is no sense of manifest arising in either of these two locations: in the formless realm, there exists only the nature of the four aggregates;

and for sentient beings in the state of non-conception, there is no concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*). Since ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) must rely upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and a concentrated mind, it does not manifest in these two locations because they mutually lack these conditions.

In other realms and destinies—excluding the hells and the northern continent—all seven types of wholesome karma are both currently active (*samudācāra*) and possessed (*samanvāgata*). Nevertheless, there are distinctions: among hungry ghosts and animals, there are intermediate courses of action (*madhyama-karmapatha*) apart from the formal vows (*saṃvara*); in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are only those arising from vows; and in the three continents and the desire-realm heavens, both types are present.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Twenty-two [and] Fascicle Twenty-three,
composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five, Part Six: On the Paths of Wholesome and Unwholesome Action—How Are Their Fruits Attained?
The Verse says:
All [of these] can produce the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
This causes others to undergo suffering, because it severs life and destroys their majesty.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, let us first distinguish how each of the ten paths of unwholesome action brings about three types of results.
What are these three? They are distinguished as the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*), the result concordant with the cause (*niṣyanda-phala*), and the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
This refers to the ten [unwholesome paths of action]: if one habituates, cultivates, or frequently practices them, by the power of this, one is born in the hells as a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).

Having emerged from there and come to be born here among the human class (*manuṣyasabhāga*), one experiences a concordant fruit (*niḥṣyandaphala*): namely, for the killer, the lifespan is short; for the thief, resources and wealth are meager; for the one who engages in sexual misconduct, the wife is unchaste; for the liar, one frequently encounters slander; for the one who speaks divisively, friends and kin fall into discord; for the one who uses harsh speech, one constantly hears unpleasant sounds; and for the one who uses frivolous speech, one’s words lack authority and gravity.

In those who are greedy, greed increases; in those who are hateful, hatred increases; and in those with wrong views, delusion increases. These are also called "outflowing results" (*niṣyanda-phala*) because they approximate the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
As for the dominant results brought about by these ten [non-virtues], regarding all external means of subsistence: due to killing, they lack luster;
due to taking what is not given, they frequently suffer from frost and hail, and crops are meager with fruits being scarce.
Because of sexual misconduct, there is much dust and grime;
because of false speech, there is much foul stench and impurity;
because of divisive speech, one's dwelling place is rugged and crooked.
Due to harsh speech, there are many unpleasant tactile sensations; the fields abound with thorns and are stony and saline.
Due to frivolous speech, the seasons are altered.

Because of greed, the fruit is meager; because of anger, the fruit is bitter; and due to wrong view, the fruit is either scant or non-existent. These are called the specific dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) of the paths of action.
Once a single act of killing has already brought about retribution in hell, does it further bring about the external evil fruit of a short lifespan?
Other masters say:
"That same single act of killing first undergoes its ripening (*vipāka*), then its immediate dominant condition (*adhipati*), and finally its remote dominant condition; thus there are three fruits."

In reality, at the time of killing, one causes the victim to experience suffering, their life to be severed, and their majestic radiance to be lost; because one inflicts suffering upon another, one is born in hell, and because one has taken another's life, one’s lifespan is shortened among human beings.

The former is the fruit of the preliminary application (*prayoga*), and the latter is the fruit of the fundamental act (*maula*); both the fundamental and the preparatory stages are termed "killing. Because it destroys majestic splendor and brings about adverse external conditions, the karma of killing thus obtains three kinds of fruits.
The remaining unwholesome paths of action should be reflected upon according to the same principle.
From this, one should infer the three fruits of the wholesome paths of action.

For instance, regarding the abstention from killing: if one practices it, cultivates it, or frequently performs it, by the power of that, one is born among the gods and experiences the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).

Having passed away from that state and been reborn among humans, they experience an extremely long lifespan as a proximate dominant fruit; furthermore, by means of this very same [karma], they bring about external objects of great majestic radiance as a remote dominant fruit.
The three fruits of other wholesome [actions] should be explained by reversing the case of the unwholesome.
Furthermore, a sutra states that among the eight branches of the wrong path (*mithyā-aṣṭāṅga*), bodily action is divided into three: namely, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
Having abandoned wrong speech and action, what is wrong livelihood?
Although it is not distinct from those [two], it is explained separately; as the verse says:
Bodily and vocal actions born of greed are wrong livelihood, because they are difficult to eliminate.
The claim that [wrong livelihood] arises from greed for the necessities of life is irrational, as it contradicts the Sūtras.
The Treatise says:
The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising from hatred and delusion are, respectively, designated only as wrong speech and wrong action.

The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising from greed are termed wrong speech and wrong action; they are also called wrong livelihood because it is difficult to eliminate, and thus it is established separately from the other two.

Greed for fine things can steal the hearts of all sentient beings; even those of supreme wisdom find it difficult to restrain and guard against it. Therefore, among these two, it is the most difficult to eliminate.
For householders, wrong views are difficult to sever, because they frequently cling to such things as [false notions of] auspiciousness.
For those who have left the household life, wrong livelihood is difficult to eliminate, as all the conditions for their sustenance depend upon others.
Therefore, so that they may diligently cultivate right livelihood, the Buddha set it apart from the preceding items and taught it as a separate category.

Other masters maintain that only those bodily and vocal actions arising from greed directed toward the requisites for life are termed "wrong livelihood," and not those arising from other forms of greed. Why is this so?
To engage in singing, dancing, and the like for one's own amusement rather than as a means of livelihood contradicts the Sūtras; therefore, it is certainly not reasonable.

In the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, the Blessed One also classifies activities such as watching elephant fights under "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*), because such things involve the improper reception of external objects and merely protract life in vain.
Therefore, it is not the case that only bodily and vocal actions arising from craving for the requisites of life are termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood should be understood as the opposite of this.

Among the paths of action (*karmapatha*), body is mentioned before speech according to their relative coarseness or subtlety; however, within the eight branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*), speech is placed before body because they arise in accordance with their natural sequence. Thus, the Sūtra states that after vitarka and vicāra have arisen, speech is uttered.
As previously stated, there are five kinds of results.
Which karma has how many results?
The verse says:
The path of abandonment consists of impure karma, which possesses all five results;
pure karma has four, namely, excluding the ripening result.
Other impure wholesome and unwholesome karma likewise have four, excluding the result of dissociation.
The remaining untainted (*anāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) [dharmas]—three [categories], excluding those previously excluded.
The treatise says:

The Path (*mārga*) is able to realize abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus it receives the name "path of abandonment" (*prahāṇamārga*), which is precisely the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
This path is of two kinds, namely, with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The karma of the path with outflows possesses five fruits.
Regarding the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*): it refers to subsequent states that are equal to or superior to [the preceding], which are similar dharmas within their own stage (*svabhūmi*).
The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) refers to the desirable ripening result summoned by the path of abandonment within its own level.
The fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*) refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) realized through the power of this path in severing the afflictions.

The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) refers to that which is drawn forth by the Path, namely: the coexistent factors, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), that which is cultivated, and that which is abandoned.
"Coexistent" refers to factors that arise simultaneously.
"Path of liberation" refers to the path of deliverance that arises immediately [after the path of uninterrupted continuity].

Regarding what is called "that which is cultivated," this refers to the abandonment through future cultivation, namely analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which arises only by the power of the Path.
As for the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), there is this explanation:
it consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) other than its own nature, with the sole exception of those that have already arisen previously.

Some say: Cessation (*prahāṇa*) should also be the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of the Path, because it is through the dominant power of the Path that one realizes it; thus, within the path of cessation, the untainted karma of the Path possesses only four fruits, namely, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Other contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karmas also have four fruits, namely, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
They are termed "other" because they differ from the aforementioned path of abandonment; the subsequent term "other" should be interpreted by analogy with this.

This means that other untainted (*anāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) karmas have only three fruits; excluding those previously excluded, namely, excluding the previously excluded fruition (*vipāka*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga*).

Having thus generally distinguished which karmas possess fruits, we shall next explain the characteristics of the fruits of karma through various categories, beginning first with the three types of karma—wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The verse says:
Regarding wholesome and so forth in relation to wholesome and so forth, the first has four, two, and three;
the middle has two, three, and four; and the last has two, three, and three results.
The Commentary states:
All that was said at the end regarding "in respective order" (yathākrama) indicates that the meaning applies universally to the preceding categories as appropriate.

To begin with, for each of the three types of karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—one should distinguish the number of fruits they produce when taken individually as causes, in relation to the three dharmas of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral, respectively; the subsequent cases should be understood by analogy.
That is to say, a wholesome karma of the first category has four results consisting of wholesome dharmas, excluding the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*).
It has two results consisting of unwholesome dharmas, namely the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
It has three results consisting of neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, excluding the outflowing result (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the result of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Unwholesome karma of the intermediate level has two fruits by way of wholesome phenomena, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
It has three fruits by way of unwholesome phenomena, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).

Taking the indeterminate as four fruits—excluding the fruit of disconnection—the outflowing fruit refers to all unwholesome karma abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as the pervasive unwholesome karma abandoned through the vision of origination; this is because, within the desire realm, the various indeterminate factors belonging to the category of the view of self-identity and extreme views serve as their outflowing fruits.
Subsequently, neutral karma has wholesome dharmas as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
It has unwholesome dharmas as three fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).

Regarding the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): this refers to the various neutral (*avyākṛta*) karmas belonging to the category of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), because these take the five classes of unwholesome states as their outflow.
Neutral states function as three fruits, just as unwholesome states do.
Having already analyzed the three natures, one should now analyze the three time periods.
The verse says:
In the past, there are four for each of the three; in the present, it is likewise for the future.
The present [karma] has two results in the present; the future [karma] has three results in the future.
The treatise says:

Regarding the past, present, and future three types of karma, each acting as a cause, their respective fruits—past and so forth—are distinguished as follows: namely, past karma takes the dharmas of the three time periods as its four fruits respectively, excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga*).
Present karma takes future [dharmas] as four fruits, as previously explained.
It takes present [dharmas] as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the predominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Karma of the future world takes future [dharmas] as three fruits, excluding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
It is not said that a subsequent karma has a preceding fruit, because a preceding dharma is certainly not the fruit of a subsequent karma.
Having already analyzed the three time periods, we shall now analyze the various stages (*bhūmi*).
The verse says:
In the same stage there are four fruits; in different stages, two or three.
The treatise says:
Among the various stages, for the karma of any given stage, the dharmas of that same stage constitute four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
If it is impure (*sāsrava*), it takes dharmas of a different stage as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the predominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

If it is pure (*anāsrava*), it takes dharmas of a different stage as three fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*); because it does not fall within the realms (*dhātu*), its outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) is not excluded.
Having already analyzed the various stages (*bhūmi*), one should now analyze those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
The verse says:
Those in training have three [types] for each of the three [stages]; those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have one, three, and two.
Neither-learner-nor-non-learner [karma] has two, two, and five fruits.
The treatise says:

when each of the three types of karma—learner and so forth—is taken as a cause, they each take three dharmas as their respective fruits in that order. Specifically, learner-karma takes learner-dharmas as its three fruits, excluding the ripened fruit and the fruit of disconnection.
The same applies to the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as the three [results].
Taking non-dual [dharmas] as the three results, excluding the ripened (*vipāka*) and the outflowing (*niṣyanda*).
An action of one beyond training takes the dharmas of one in training (*śaikṣa*) as one result, namely, the dominant (*adhipati*).
Taking the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as three fruits—excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*).
Taking that which is neither [training nor beyond training] as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Regarding non-dual karma, taking the factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*) as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit.
The same applies to taking the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as two [results].

Taking those that are neither [of the three categories] as five results has already been explained. Having distinguished [the results] according to the categories of those in training and so forth, one should now distinguish them according to those to be abandoned by vision and so forth.
The verse says:
Regarding karma to be abandoned by seeing and so forth, each one has three [results];
for the first, there are three, four, and one; for the middle, two, four, and three results.
"Subsequently, there are one, two, and four; all should be understood according to their respective order.
The treatise says:
Regarding the three types of karma—those to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and so forth—each serves as a cause in its respective order, with each having three dharmas as its result.

As for the distinctions: karma to be abandoned by seeing has dharmas to be abandoned by seeing as its three fruits—excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*).
It has dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation as its four fruits—excluding the fruit of disjunction.
Taking non-abandonable dharmas as its single fruit, namely the sovereign (adhipati) fruit;
middle karma to be abandoned by cultivation, taking dharmas to be abandoned by seeing as its two fruits, namely the virile (puruṣakāra) and the sovereign fruits.
Taking the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) as the four fruits— excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*)—
and taking the dharmas not to be abandoned (*aheya*) as three fruits— excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Regarding the final category, the karma not to be abandoned, it has the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) as one fruit, namely, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation constitute two fruits—namely, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Dharmas not to be abandoned constitute four fruits, excluding the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The phrase "all according to their respective order" means that, as appropriate, this brief method should be applied throughout all the preceding categories.
In the course of discussing various types of karma, one should further ask:

regarding the three kinds of karma mentioned in the treatise—namely, karma that ought to be performed, karma that ought not to be performed, and karma that is neither to be performed nor not to be performed—what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Defiled actions are those that should not be performed; some say these also include those that violate proper decorum.
Actions that ought to be performed are the opposite of these; the third category consists of those that differ from both.
The treatise says:
Some maintain that defiled actions of body, speech, and mind are called "unfit to be done" because they arise from improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Other masters say:

All bodily, verbal, and mental actions that violate conventional norms (*ācāra*) should not be performed even if they are undefiled (*akliṣṭa*), because they are inconsistent with worldly conventions.

That is to say, regarding all unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily actions—whether standing, walking, eating, drinking, or otherwise—whatever is inconsistent with the social etiquette of the world is termed "bodily action violating convention."

All unobscured-neutral vocal actions that, at the time of uttering words or performing gestures, involve the agent and so forth acting contrary to worldly etiquette, are all termed "vocal actions that violate proper conduct."

The two preceding types of volition (*cetanā*) that give rise [to misconduct] are called "intentional karma that violates proper conduct. This, along with defiled karma, is termed "that which should not be done" (*akaraṇīya*).
That which "should be done" (*karaṇīya*) is the opposite of this.
That which contradicts both of the preceding two is the third type of karma.
If one relies on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the latter may also be so; however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the former is said to be wholesome (*kuśala*).

That is to say, only wholesome karma is called "to be performed" (*kārya*); only all defiled karma is called "not to be performed" (*akārya*); and unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) karma of body, speech, and mind is called "neither to be performed nor not to be performed."

However, not all actions that should not be performed are subsumed under "misconduct" (*duścarita*); only those that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) receive the name "misconduct" because they possess a wicked nature.
Those that bring about desirable fruits are called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*), while those that bring about undesirable fruits are called "misconduct."

Although that which is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) is something that should not be done, it is not included among unwholesome courses of action (akuśalakarmapatha), because what is performed by means of it cannot, as a matter of certainty, bring about either desirable or undesirable fruits.
Now, within this context, one should further investigate: does a single karma project only a single birth, or does it project many births?
Furthermore, regarding a single birth, is it projected by a single karma, or is it projected by multiple karmas?
The verse says:
One karma draws forth one birth; many karmas can bring it to completion.
The commentary says:
If one follows correct reasoning, it should be definitively stated that a single karma alone projects only a single birth.
This term "one birth" indicates the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class), for it is only upon acquiring such a homogeneous class that one is said to have "born."
If it is said that a single lifetime is projected by multiple karmas, or if it is said that a single karma can project multiple lifetimes—what logical faults are there in these two statements?

First, the former position is faulty: since within a single lifetime the fruit of a prior karma ends while the fruit of a subsequent karma arises, and because these karmic fruits are distinct, there would necessarily be repeated deaths and births, or else there would have to be multiple lifetimes [within what is considered one].
If there were no intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), the process of death and birth would ultimately fail to arise, just as it does not in a single lifetime; thus, both positions entail faults.
Furthermore, within a single existence, there would have to be numerous instances of death and birth, or else there would never be any death or birth at all until reaching *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

For what reason is it that when there is birth from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) into a single realm of existence due to the ripening of distinct karmic fruits, there is both death and birth;

whereas when distinct karmic fruits arise without death and birth—where one karmic fruit ends and another karmic fruit begins—it is logically certain that one must establish the existence of both death and birth?

Furthermore, if it is admitted that a single lifetime is fixed as being of many types because it is projected by karma that has been both performed and accumulated, then there should certainly be no such thing as dying prematurely; or else, one would have to abandon those karmas forever without ever experiencing their results.
However, this has already been stated.
What was stated previously?
It means that it is logically impossible for the maturation (vipāka) induced by karma with fixed timing to manifest and be experienced at a different time.

Furthermore, it is logically impossible for karma with fixed timing (*kāla-niyata-karma*) not to be both performed and accumulated (*kṛta-upacita*), because its maturation (*vipāka*) must necessarily be experienced.

If one were to argue that there are births induced by various types of karma—both fixed and unfixed—or that some births are induced solely by various types of fixed karma, and thus there are those who die prematurely as well as those who live their full lifespan; [this would be untenable].
This is also not the case, because there is no fixed determination regarding whether the karma of a specific period is to be experienced as certain or uncertain.

If there is a class of beings who, during middle age or old age, have the karma of that period determined to be experienced, while the karma of infancy, childhood, or youth is not determined to be experienced—how then would that be?

In principle, it is impossible for a subsequent [moment] to exist apart from a preceding one; otherwise, it would follow that all karmic actions belonging to the preceding stage must necessarily result in their fruit being experienced.

However, within this context, there is no definitive principle that causes the karma of the preceding stage to necessarily experience its fruit while causing the karma of the subsequent stage to experience its fruit indeterminately. Therefore, a single birth cannot be projected by multiple karmas.
There is also a further fault: if a single karma were to project multiple births, then those karmas with fixed timing would become confused.
This confusion does not occur, as has already been explained; therefore, a single karma cannot project multiple births.
If that is so, for what reason did the Venerable Aniruddha himself say:

"I recall that once, as the maturation of a single gift of food given to an exceptionally meritorious field of merit, from that time onward I was reborn seven times in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, seven times among humans as a Wheel-turning Sage King, and finally I was born into the great Śākya clan, possessing abundant wealth and enjoying much happiness"?

The *Vibhāṣā* has already explained this statement: because a single act of giving food serves as the basis for generating many superior volitions (*cetanā*), which aspire to bring about the arising of many distinct maturations (*vipāka*) across various states, it was spoken in this way.

Regarding the maturation of a single gift of food: it is not that the maturation itself can again induce rebirth; rather, this statement is made to clarify the distinctions in the states of maturation summoned by many volitions and aspirations arising from the object of a single gift of food, or to indicate its foundational basis.

By means of that single karma, he experiences a life of great nobility and abundant wealth, as well as the knowledge of his past lives; riding upon this, he further creates merit that brings about other future births, continuing in this succession until, in his final body, he is born into a wealthy and noble family and attains the ultimate fruit.

Suppose there is someone who, having obtained a single *kārsāpaṇa*, diligently seeks profit through skillful means until it becomes a thousandfold, saying: "It was originally from this one *kārsāpaṇa* that I have now come to possess great wealth and status."
Therefore, a single karma induces only a single birth.

Although it is said that one birth is induced by a single karma, it is admitted that its completion is achieved by many karmas; this is like a painter who first outlines the shape with a single color and subsequently fills it in with various hues.
Now, regarding the single "form" used as an analogy here: does it represent a single category of karma or a single moment?

If it were to represent a single category, it would contradict the principles of this school’s doctrine; for the statement that "a single [karmic] action projects a single birth" cannot be applied to a single category, since a category necessarily comprises many [moments].
It is unreasonable to cite many [moments] as constituting a single lifetime.
If one were to say that a single color represents a single moment, then since a single moment cannot form a shape, the proposed analogy would be incapable of proving the point.
Now, observing that this [text] uses an analogy for a single type of karma (*nikāya-sabhāga-karman*), how can it be established that projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is categorized by type?
This is because there are many karmas that project a single realm of existence (*gati*).

The intent of this statement is to clarify that within a single type of karma, only one moment projects the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), whereas multiple moments of karma—both of the same and different types—are able to bring it to completion; therefore, they are said to be "many."
Therefore, it is as when one first sketches the outline of a form with a single color and subsequently fills it in with various hues; this statement accords with reason.

Consequently, although all beings equally receive a human body, among them there are those who possess the full complement of limbs, sense faculties, proportions, complexion, strength, and adornments.
If there are cases where [the causes] previously mentioned are deficient, does birth arise through the power of karma alone for both projection (*ākṣepa*) and completion (*paripūraṇa*)?

No; because all karma that possesses the nature of a single fruit has strong efficacy, it can also project and complete birth. Conversely, that which is contrary to this can complete [birth] but not project it.
What is the nature of these two types?
The verse says:
The two mindless attainments and acquisitions Cannot induce other supernormal powers.
The treatise says:
Although the two mindless attainments possess maturation (*vipāka*), they lack the power to project a common destiny (*nikāyasabhāga*), because they do not coexist with [projecting] karmas.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of all unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas likewise lacks the power to project a common destiny (*nikāyasabhāga*), because it does not share the same fruit as the various karmas.
All other unwholesome and wholesome contaminated dharmas may pertain to both [functions], namely projecting and completing.
The Sūtra states:
"There are three heavy obstructions, namely: the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of afflictions, and the obstruction of maturation.
What is the essential nature of these three obstructions?
The verse says:
The three obstructions consist of the deeds of immediate retribution, the afflictions that are frequently practiced,
all the evil destinies, the northern continent, and the heaven of non-perception.
The treatise says:

The essence of karmic obstructions refers to the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*): first, killing one’s mother; second, killing one’s father; third, killing an arhat; fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and fifth, shedding the blood of a Buddha with a malicious mind.
The essence of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to those afflictions that frequently manifest.

Even if afflictions of a weak grade (*mṛdu-prakāra*) frequently manifest, one finds it difficult to suppress or eliminate them; because they lead successively to the arising of those of a superior grade (*adhimātra-prakāra*), which are likewise difficult to suppress or eliminate, they are also termed "hindrances."

If superior-grade afflictions do not manifest frequently, it is easy for the path of antidotes to find its opportunity; thus, although they may be extremely intense, they are not subsumed under the category of "obstructions.

Although all sentient beings dwelling in the desire realm who are bound by fetters equally possess all afflictions, their actual manifestation differs, and thus the obstructions they constitute are not the same.
Therefore, among the afflictions, those that are practiced frequently according to their varying degrees of intensity are termed the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
