The roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) refer to establishing a wholesome intention (*āśaya*) for liberation such that it cannot be shaken; by means of this, one is certain to attain parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the nature, stage, and other characteristics of these roots of goodness, they should be understood as explained in the section on the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

The wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) refer to the four [stages] beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*); these shall also be explained as they are discussed later in the section on the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
Regarding what is spoken of in the world—writing, sealing, calculation, composition, and arithmetic—how should the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these five be understood?
The verse says:
Those things that accord with reason, the three types of action together with their motivating impulses,
are respectively the intrinsic natures of writing, seals, calculation, letters, and numbers.
The treatise says:
That which arises in accordance with reality is produced through correct application.
It should be understood that the three types of action consist of body, speech, and mind.
That which is capable of producing is precisely that which gives rise to these three [actions], namely the dharmas such as sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), as appropriate to each case.
Among these, writing and seals have as their essence the prior bodily action and the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) that produce it.
It is not that the mere forms of letters are called "writing," nor that the carved or printed marks are called "seals.
Rather, because the forms of letters and the patterns of seals are produced by karma, one should know that these are what are meant here by "writing" and "seals."
Next, calculation (*gaṇanā*) and letters (*vyañjana*) have as their essence the previous vocal karma and the five aggregates that can produce it.

It should be understood that subsequent counting (*saṃkhyā*) has as its essence the previous mental karma and the four aggregates that can produce it, because it is by means of mental volition (*manas-karman*) alone that one is able to count phenomena.
One should distinguish the various partial synonyms among the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma*) in the Noble Teachings so as not to fall into confusion.
The verse says:
The wholesome and untainted are called "sublime" (*praṇīta*); The defiled, the blameworthy, the concealed, and the inferior [are called "unsublime"].
One should practice wholesome conditioned phenomena; liberation is called supreme.
The Commentary says:
Wholesome untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are also termed "sublime" (*praṇīta*), because they surpass the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and defiled (*kliṣṭa*) tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas.
All defiled phenomena are also termed "blameworthy" (*sāvadya*), because they are censured and loathed by the wise;
they are also termed "obscured" (*nivṛta*), because they can obstruct the path to liberation.
It is also termed "inferior" because it is extremely base and defiled, and because it ought to be abandoned.

Based on this distinction between the sublime and the inferior, the intermediate category is already established; therefore, the verse does not analyze it separately—this refers to contaminated wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*).
The unobscured-neutral states are collectively termed "intermediate.
All conditioned wholesome states are also termed "to be cultivated.
It is established by implication that all others are not to be cultivated.
Liberation and nirvāṇa are also called "unsurpassed," because there is not a single dharma that can surpass nirvāṇa, as it is wholesome, permanent, and transcends all dharmas.
Nirvāṇa is wholesome because it is the ultimate peace and security.
The fact that other dharmas are "surpassable" (sottara) is already established by implication; this refers to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
Space (ākāśa) and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) do not possess the previously mentioned characteristics of being wholesome and eternal.
*Abhidharmasamayasāstra* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Abhidharma-piṭaka),
Fascicle Twenty-Four, composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra. Fascicle Twenty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Six: Analysis of the Latent Defilements (Anuśaya), Part One. Having already analyzed all karmas.

The sūtras state in various places that karma brings about existence (bhava); yet, one observes in the world that those who have already abandoned defilement, even though they perform virtuous deeds, lack the capacity to attract the fruit of future existence.
Therefore, regarding the production of existence (*bhava*), karma would not be the cause.
It is not my position that karma alone acts as the cause;
rather, it must be assisted by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be able to produce existence. For this reason, the teaching on dependent origination first mentions the latent dispositions.
What is the reason for this?
How many latent dispositions (anuśaya) are there?
The verse says:
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are the root of all existence; they are differentiated into six types:
namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
The treatise says:
Since the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are the root of all existence, it is only through the karma generated by them that there is the capacity to produce existence.
Herein, the term "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the fruit of the three realms of existence.
Therefore, although one who is free from defilement may perform wholesome karma, it lacks the power to bring about the fruit of future existence.
Thus, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) are briefly of six kinds: namely, greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.

The word "also" (*api*) in the verse indicates the sense of similarity; that is to say, although hatred (*dveṣa*), like attachment (*rāga*), has many varieties, it may be collectively designated as a single underlying tendency (*anuśaya*).
The same applies to pride (*māna*) and the others; therefore, the word "also" is used again.
Alternatively, this is to show that just as greed and hatred are established separately because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ,
so too are pride and the others established separately, even though their modes of activity are similar, because they differ in other respects.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used to clarify that the basis for the explanation is contradictory, or to indicate the complete inclusion of all categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
If the number of latent dispositions were only six, for what reason does the Sūtra speak of seven latent dispositions?
The verse says:

The seven [types of craving] arise from the differentiation of craving into six; "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*) pertains to the two upper realms, because it operates toward internal objects, and is thus established to exclude the notion that those realms constitute liberation.
The treatise says:

Within the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) previously mentioned, craving (*rāga*) is divided into two; therefore, the Sūtra speaks of seven. This is because there is a distinction between the characteristic of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*) and the characteristic of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*). The Buddha spoke of "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*) as referring to attachment to the realms of form (*rūpa*) and formlessness (*ārūpya*), because that craving mostly functions by relying on the internal door [of the mind].

Furthermore, because there arises the notion of liberation regarding the two higher realms, the term "existence" (*bhava*) is established to refute that attachment; by this word "existence," the meaning of "arising in a body" is indicated.

Since it has already been stated that craving for existence pertains to the two higher realms, it follows by implication that craving in the desire realm is termed "craving for sensual pleasure" (*kāmarāga*); therefore, it is not mentioned separately in the verse.

It is shown that because [the afflictions] mostly operate toward external objects through the five sense-desires, the six types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) previously mentioned are further established as ten by way of another classification.
The verse says:
The six become ten due to the differentiation of views; The "difference" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The view of extremes, false view, the grasping at views, and the grasping at precepts and observances.
The commentary states:
Among the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those that function as views are differentiated into five; the remaining five, which are not views, are added to these to form a total of ten.
These same six types further become ninety-eight when categorized according to different perspectives.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Due to differences in aspect, category, and realm, there are ninety-eight [afflictions].
Those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth in the desire realm are seventeen, seven, seven, and four respectively;
that is to say, they possess [the afflictions] in order, excluding three, two views, view, and doubt.
In the realms of form and formlessness, hatred is excluded; the rest are explained as in the case of the desire realm.
The commentary states:
The six types of underlying tendencies (anuśaya), through the distinctions of their modes of activity, categories, and realms, become ninety-eight.
That is to say, among these six, ten are established based on differences in their modes of operation (*ākāra*) and their objects (*ālambana*), as has already been explained above.
These very ten types of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), when differentiated by category (*nikāya*) and realm (*dhātu*), constitute ninety-eight.
The "families" (*nikāya*) refer to the five families: those abandoned through the vision of the four truths and those abandoned through cultivation.
The "realms" (*dhātu*) refer to the three realms: the desire, form, and formless realms.
Now, regarding the five distinct families within the desire realm, when combined with the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they constitute thirty-six.
That is to say, from the vision of the Truth of Suffering up to those abandoned through cultivation, there are respectively seventeen, eight, and four [categories].
These five classes [of afflictions] correspond to the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) as follows: one, two, one, one, and one, respectively; they fully possess or are devoid of three views:
the two views, the view of [wrong] doctrine, and doubt.
This means that those abandoned by the vision of the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) consist of ten [factors], as all of them are in opposition to the vision of the truth of suffering.

Those abandoned by the vision of the truths of origin (samudaya-satya) and cessation (nirodha-satya) each consist of seven, excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi), and the attachment to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Those abandoned by the Truth of the Path number eight; to the previous seven, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is added.
Those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) number four, excluding views and doubt.
Thus, they total thirty-six types.
The first thirty-two are called "to be abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-heya*), because they are abandoned as soon as the truths are seen.

The final four are called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they are abandoned only after one has seen the four truths and subsequently practices the path repeatedly over time.

By this it has already been shown that among the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) belongs to only one category, namely, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The same applies to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The grasping at rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) pertains to two categories, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) and those abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya).
False view (mithyādṛṣṭi) pertains to four categories, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The same applies to the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

The remaining four, beginning with craving (*rāga*), each pertain to all five categories (*pañca nikāyāḥ*); that is, they are abandoned through the vision of the four truths as well as through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Thus, the view-portion is said to consist of twelve [factors] in total.
Doubt is divided into four types, while each of the other four [afflictions] is divided into five; thus, there are thirty-six [afflictions] in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Among these, if a view takes suffering as its object, it is called "viewing suffering" (*duḥkhadarśana*); this is abandoned by the two—namely, the receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* and *anvayajñānakṣānti*)—and is collectively termed "abandoned through viewing suffering."
The same applies up to what is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

"Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to repeated practice; that is to say, for one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*), in order to attain the higher goal, the repeated perfuming of the knowledge of suffering and so forth is called cultivation.
That which is eliminated by this path is called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).
In the realms of form and formlessness, five categories [of afflictions] each eliminate hatred; the remainder is the same as in the desire realm, and thus there are thirty-one [afflictions] in each.

Thus, all masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* establish ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) by classifying the six latent dispositions according to their modes (*prakāra*), categories (*nikāya*), and realms (*dhātu*).
Of these ninety-eight that have been explained, eighty-eight are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), because they are destroyed by the patiences (*kṣānti*);
ten latent dispositions are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), because they are destroyed by the knowledges (*jñāna*).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are established according to the realms (*dhātu*), not the stages (*bhūmi*), because the knowledge of exhaustion (*parijñā*) is established by means of abandoning craving for a realm.

That is to say, the four dhyānas possess a certain degree of similarity in the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of their afflictions; thus, although they consist of four stages, they are spoken of collectively as one.
The same applies to the combined explanation regarding the four formless realms (*ārūpya*), as the Sūtra only mentions "greed for form" (*rūparāga*) and "greed for the formless" (*ārūpyarāga*).
For what reason is there no latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) in the higher realms?
Because the objective basis (*vastu*) for that latent tendency of aversion does not exist there.
This means that hatred increases in accordance with painful feelings (*duḥkhavedanā*), whereas those [beings] lack painful feelings; therefore, hatred does not exist [in them].
Furthermore, their mental continuity is moistened by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and moreover, because hatred is not a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) for them.

Some say: Because it is free from the occurrence of affliction and harm, because it is the abode of wholesome roots such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and because all forms of grasping are far removed from it.
Regarding the statement that "eighty-eight [defilements] are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*)," is it certain that these are abandoned by insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) destroyed by patience (*kṣānti*)—those at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*);
the others are abandoned by both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Those destroyed by knowledge (*jñāna*) are abandoned only by cultivation.
The Commentary says:

Among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) eliminated by the patiences (*kṣānti*), those comprised within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned exclusively by the vision-path (*darśana-mārga*), because they can only be severed by the patiences of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).

Those comprised within the remaining eight stages are abandoned through both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*); that is to say, for noble ones (*ārya*), they are abandoned through vision alone and not through cultivation, because they are severed by the patiences of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge as appropriate.

If they are abandoned by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and not through insight (*darśana*), because they are abandoned by the repeated practice of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are destroyed by knowledge, regardless of which stage (*bhūmi*) they belong to, are abandoned solely through cultivation; for both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings abandon them as appropriate through the repeated practice of either untainted (*anāsrava*) or conventional knowledge.
Among the six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) as previously analyzed, the view (dṛṣṭi) is divided into five based on differences in their modes of activity (ākāra).
Their names have already been listed; what, then, is their essential nature?
The verse says:
The self and what belongs to the self, annihilationism and eternalism, Denial [of reality], regarding the inferior as superior,
and falsely claiming what is not the cause or the path— These are the essential natures of the five views.
The treatise says:

Due to the power of causes and teachings, there are certain deluded persons who, within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), grasp at them as "self" or "belonging to self. This view is called the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
It is called "sa" because it exists; "kāya" refers to the "collection" (*gaṇa*); this indicates that the object of this view exists but is not a single entity.

Regarding the objects grasped as "self" and "what belongs to self," to grasp them as either annihilated or eternal is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), because one falsely clings to the extremes of annihilation or eternity.
To give rise to a view that denies the existence of the truly real entities—the Truths such as suffering—is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

These five kinds of false views all function in a perverted manner and should all be termed "wrong"; however, only that which denies [existence] is called "wrong view" because its fault is so extreme, just as one speaks of "stinking ghee."

Regarding "evil attachment," "evil views," and so forth: because these involve only the deprecation of what remains while exaggerating it, the act of regarding the inferior as superior is termed *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views).
That which is *sāsrava* (tainted) is called "inferior" because it is to be abandoned by the Noble Ones; thus, clinging to the inferior as superior is collectively termed *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*.

In reality, it should be established as "grasping at views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭy-ādi-parāmarśa*); however, by omitting the word "and so forth," it is simply called "grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*). Alternatively, because views are preeminent, only the name "view" is mentioned, since one grasps other dharmas with views as the primary factor.
To regard what is not a cause or a path as a cause or a path—this is collectively termed the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
That is to say, to falsely conceive an attachment to causes regarding Maheśvara, Time, Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*), or other such entities, which in reality are not the causes of suffering.
There are two kinds of paths: first, the path of higher rebirth; second, the path of definitive excellence.

Engaging in various forms of wrongful conduct, such as throwing oneself into fire or water, is not a cause for rebirth in heaven; yet to falsely cling to such acts as being the cause is called the first path.

Only the nature of observing vows and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), as well as the human intellect (*puruṣajñāna*) and so forth, are not causes for liberation; yet to falsely grasp them as such is called the second path.
Because these are like the aforementioned "removal" (*apavarga*) or are considered superior through vows and prohibitions, they are designated solely by the name "vows and prohibitions."
One should understand that the intrinsic nature of the five views is thus.
If one regards Īśvara and so forth—which are not causes—as causes, such adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is a delusion regarding the meaning of cause.
For what reason is this view not abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*)?
The verse says:
Regarding Maheśvara and others, falsely clinging to what is not a cause as a cause arises from the inversions of permanence and self; therefore, it is abandoned only by the vision of suffering.
The Treatise says:

To regard Īśvara and others as causes when they are not causes means that such persons are necessarily unable to investigate profound principles; rather, regarding the coarse, resultant phenomena of the aggregates such as Īśvara and so forth, they falsely claim these to be permanent, unitary, self, and agent. Taking these as primary, they then cling to them as the cause. Therefore, this clinging is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).

That is to say, the grasping at a self is the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); because one falsely clings to the meaning of the fruit of suffering as being a self, when suffering is directly realized (*abhisamaya*), this clinging to a self is immediately eliminated, and the knowledge of non-self arises—not at a subsequent stage.

If there were a view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it would persist even when the view of arising and so forth is abandoned; because the view of self would still follow within the continuum, the knowledge of non-self (*anātma-jñāna*) should not arise. This is because the view of self is extinguished precisely when one perceives only phenomena (*dharma-mātra*); thus, when the knowledge of non-self arises, the view of self has already been eliminated.

Nevertheless, possessing the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one conceives a singular self within the phenomena of a continuum such as that of Īśvara; subsequently, one gives rise to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) regarding those very phenomena of the continuum, reckoning them to be eternal.

From this it should be understood that the two types of grasping—the grasping at permanence and the grasping at self regarding phenomena such as Īśvara and the like—are abandoned only through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). This is because when the various untainted modes of practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) such as impermanence are seen during the vision of the Truth of Suffering, these two views are extinguished; consequently, the false attribution of causality to non-causes such as Īśvara, which arises in accordance with those two views, is also extinguished simultaneously. Therefore, it is said that the grasping at causality is abandoned only through the vision of suffering.

However, regarding that which is not the path, when it is conceived as the path, if the strength of this [false] view opposes the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is then abandoned by the Path of Seeing.

Is this not just like when one conceives Īśvara and so forth as the cause and clings to suffering as the cause; one allows only its abandonment through the seeing of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) and not through the seeing of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*). Likewise, in this case too, when one conceives what is not the path as the path and clings to suffering as the path, one should allow only its abandonment through the seeing of suffering and not through the seeing of the path.
This objection is not valid, because viewing the Truth of Suffering as impermanent and so forth does not serve as its antidote.

That is to say, if one holds that Īśvara and other such entities are the cause, one must first conceive of them as being without beginning or end; therefore, this adherence to a [false] cause is abandoned only through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), since the perception of impermanence and so forth serves as the antidote to the perception of permanence and so forth.

When one perceives the Truth of Suffering as impermanent and so forth, it cannot counteract the attachment that conceives what is not the Path to be the Path; therefore, that attachment to the Path is not abandoned by the vision of the Truth of Suffering.
By this, its abandonment through the vision of the Truth of Origination is also precluded, because the vision of causes and so forth is not the antidote to it.
That is to say, when one perceives the origin [of suffering] as its cause and so forth, this does not yet counteract the attachment that conceives what is not the path to be the path.

It is only when one perceives the Truth of the Path as the path and so forth that one can counteract that attachment to what is not the path as being the path; therefore, that attachment to the path should be abandoned through the vision of the path.

If that is so, then this kind of attachment to what is not the path as being the path must logically be understood as being abandoned through the vision of the origin and the cessation [of suffering] as well.

That is to say, just as wrong view denies the existence of the true path, one subsequently reckons that this very [denial] can lead to purification; such clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is admitted to be abandoned through the vision of the path.

If such wrong views deny the existence of origination and cessation, yet later reckon them as capable of attaining purification, then those two forms of clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) should be abandoned through the vision of origination and cessation.
This objection is not valid, because their essential nature is not established.

Regarding the essence of the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it has two aspects: first, regarding what is not a cause as a cause; second, regarding what is not the path as the path.

If one were to hold the view that those [precepts] which slander the truth of origination can bring about purification, would this view not fail to arise? For it would lack the cause for abandoning origination, since there is no mental conviction whatsoever that such a cause exists.
Furthermore, since suffering and its origin are not distinct entities, the aggregates such as the "sovereign" (īśvara) and so forth should also be negated.

If one were to maintain that this false view which slanders cessation can lead to purification, would it not be the case that such a view could not arise unless there were a basis for proving the existence of cessation?
How can one deny its existence?

After the vision of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), one considers that the means for cessation are not in vain; thus, the essence of the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not established.
To say, however, that it "should exist" does not constitute a valid objection.

How is it criticized? It would also follow that the essence of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) would not be established.
This is because, immediately after the view that denies the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), one would have to reckon that there is a path, which would be untenable.

This refers to wrong view or doubt directed toward the Truth of the Path—either denying it or doubting it by thinking that there is no path to liberation. How could one then cling to this [denial] as being able to attain eternal purification?

This clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not non-existent in its essence, for it is admitted that there exists a wrong view that denies the Path, which is then clung to as the means to realize eternal purification, because that [view] is conceived as being understood according to reality.
This means that one first retains another path of liberation within the mind, and subsequently clings to it rather than repudiating it.
One regards this false view as a correct realization of the true path.

Regarding what is called "correctly" (yoniśas), they claim that their denial of the true path of liberation is non-erroneous; because they consider it "correct," they cling to it as a cause of purification, thereby establishing the essence of the grasping at rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Those mental factors belonging to the remaining paths of liberation are not abandoned by the path of seeing, nor are they the objects of the grasping at rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), because they take only the dharmas of their own category as their objects.
The paths are of many types; thus, there is no logical flaw.

If that were so, then the substance of the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) would also necessarily be established, because it is identical in nature to the path.

That is to say, one might first harbor within their mind another mode of liberation, and subsequently, while regarding a false view that slanders true liberation as a correct realization—taking it to be "correct" because it conforms to reason—they cling to it as a cause of purity; in this way, the substance of clinging to precepts and observances would be established as before.
There is no such principle; for it is universally accepted that liberation is permanent and quiescent.
To hold that a mind characterized by slander is the cause of purification is logically untenable.
Just as one may assert whether the essence of nirvāṇa is real or unreal, if one seeks the means to attain liberation, they must necessarily admit that liberation exists.
Those who assert that liberation definitely exists must necessarily admit that its essence is eternal and quiescent.
If one does not admit this, one should not seek it.

Just as within the True Dharma, although there are differing views regarding the essence of nirvāṇa—some claiming it is real and others claiming it is unreal—all nonetheless agree that it is eternal and quiescent; therefore, both [the denial and the affirmation] are seen as faults when it comes to repudiating it.
Thus, if one holds any other aggregate of liberation in mind, they must necessarily concede that nirvāṇa is eternally quiescent.

Because of this, one does not grasp the view that slanders liberation as being a correct understanding; therefore, attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is certainly absent within the vision of cessation.

Furthermore, just as Devadatta, while generally accepting the existence of the eternal and quiescent *nirvāṇa*, nevertheless reckons five separate factors—apart from the Eightfold Path—as the path to liberation, so too should it be understood that the reasoning of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) is likewise fallacious.

Therefore, there may be a wrong view that slanders the Noble Eightfold Path yet claims to be a "realization according to reality" (*yathārtha-bodha*), but there can be no such thing as a "realization according to understanding" (*yathā-artha-avabodha*) regarding the slander of cessation (*nirodha*).

Since the intrinsic nature and phenomenal characteristics of ascetic observances (*śīla-vrata*) and the like differ from those of the Noble Path, there is no basis for asserting that the essential nature of Nirvāṇa as eternal quiescence possesses any distinction [from them]; therefore, cessation (*nirodha*) does not share the same meaning as the Path (*mārga*).

Now it should be examined: regarding the misapprehension of what is not the path as the path—namely, clinging to precepts and observances as the cause of liberation, or clinging to the view of self as being able to realize liberation—is this abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), or is it abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*)?

If one maintains that both [types of views] are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), then those to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) would necessarily be non-existent;

or else, one must state a distinct cause for why these two are abandoned through the vision of suffering while the remainder are abandoned through the path of vision. For what reason are these two abandoned by the vision of suffering, whereas the rest are abandoned by the path of vision?
If one maintains that both are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one must explain why they are so abandoned:

it is not because at the time of the path of seeing one can cognize their object, or cognize their intrinsic nature, or abandon their objective support (*ālambana*); otherwise, the principle for establishing thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) would be undermined.

That is to say, if the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) can take as their object those things to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), who could prevent the loss of the establishment of "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*)?

For example, during the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering remains bound by the objects of that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin; thus, although it is permanently severed, complete knowledge is not yet established.

In this way, even until the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering remains bound by the fetters of what is to be abandoned by seeing the path; thus, although it has been abandoned, "universal knowledge" (parijñā) should likewise not yet be established.
However, this is not what is accepted; therefore, the underlying principle must be explained.

Our school asserts that both are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), because they are abandoned solely by the vision of suffering, as they take such things as the "cow-vow" (*go-vrata*) as their objects.

However, because one calculates coarse fruits as being the cause for those [higher realms], it is not admitted that both [types of views] are abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). If they were abandoned by seeing the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), then [the view of self as a real person] would be utterly non-existent. This is because there are two types of the "view of what is not the path as the path" (*amārga-mārga-dṛṣṭi*): first, that which takes upholding of precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata*) as its object; and second, that which takes direct delusion regarding the path as its object.

Because taking up ascetic observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the like contradicts the faith that awakens to the Path, and because its power is inferior to that of one who takes up what is directly delusive regarding the Path—since those who take up ascetic observances have extremely coarse modes of activity, do not pursue [the goal] with sustained effort, and lack firm resolve—their practice is extinguished even with little exertion.
The delusion regarding the path due to attachment to kin is the opposite of this.
From this, it should be understood that there are two categories of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which misapprehend what is not the path as being the path:
first, those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*); second, those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).
As previously stated, the view of permanence arises from the inversion of self;
however, are there only these two types of inversion? No, there are four inversions in total:

first, the inversion of grasping at the impermanent as permanent; second, the inversion of grasping at suffering as pleasure; third, the inversion of grasping at the impure as pure; and fourth, the inversion of grasping at the non-self as self.
What is the essential nature of these four inversions?
The verse states:
The essential nature of the four inversions Is said to arise from three views.
"Only because they are inverted and increase [in intensity], perception and mind follow the power of views.
The commentary states:

The four inversions are established based on three of the [five] views; specifically, from among the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), only the eternalist view (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is taken as the inversion of permanence (*nityaviparyāsa*).
Among the various types of views grasped as supreme (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), grasping that which is not pleasant or pure as being pleasant and pure constitutes the inversion of pleasure and purity.
Within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), grasping only the view of a self constitutes the inversion of self.
Such is the doctrine of one master.
However, according to the definitive meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*, when the twelve views are analyzed according to their categories, only two and a half views constitute the essence of inversion.

These are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) in their entirety; and from among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the portion that clings to permanence. Since the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the views of eternalism and nihilism are mutually contradictory, it can be said that these two entities are distinct.
Those who propound theories of a self grasp at a self that possesses sovereign power over those [aggregates], viewing them as "mine"; thus, this view of self functions through two doors.
Is it not the case that since all afflictions arise through perversion (*viparyāsa*), they should all be considered perversions, rather than only four types?
This is not so, because the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) established for these perversions are distinct.
What is meant by "perverted characteristics"?
It refers to being endowed with three causes. What are these three causes?
Because it is consistently inverted, because it is of a nature that conjectures, and because it falsely superimposes [attributes].
The inclusion of the term "increased" (*adhi*) also indicates that its essence is particularly preeminent; other afflictions do not possess these three causes.

That is to say, the grasping at rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively erroneous, because that which is clung to may potentially be free from the defilement of desire and so forth, and because one may attain a degree of purity for a short time.
The view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) do not involve false superimposition, as these two operate by way of the negation of existing things.

Because the *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) of other schools is not predominant, and because the remaining afflictions do not involve inferential deliberation (*ūhana*), there are only four inversions and no others.
Is it not said in the Sūtras that inversions total twelve? As the Sūtra states:

"To conceive of the impermanent as permanent constitutes an inversion of perception, mind, and view; the same applies to [conceiving] suffering, the impure, and non-self as [permanent, pure, and self]."
It is not so, because perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) do not involve inferential deliberation (*tarka*).

They are designated as "perversions" (*viparyāsa") by the power of association with the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa"), since their mental factors (*caitasika-dharma") are identical to those of the view.
However, sensation (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] cannot be designated as perversions in the same way as perception and mind, because there is a distinct reason for this.

This means that when one gives rise to views such as permanence regarding what is impermanent and so forth, one must necessarily grasp the characteristic of permanence and so forth within the object; since it is perception (*saṃjñā*)—and nothing else—that is capable of grasping these characteristics, the name "perversion" is established for it, and not for feeling (*vedanā*) or the other aggregates.

Furthermore, the term "perception" (saṃjñā) is also established for the corrective wisdom (prajñā); that is to say, within the context of the mental applications such as impermanence, it is referred to as the "perception of impermanence" and so forth. This is because wisdom and perception closely support one another, and thus the name is applied by following their mutual association. This is not the case for sensation (vedanā) and the other [mental factors].

Because the power of the basis (āśraya) causes the increase of erroneous inference and the accomplishment of the aspect of grasping objects, the mind is called "erroneous" (viparyāsa). As a sūtra says:
"The mind leads the world, causing it to drift and drown everywhere in the torrential flow of afflictions."
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
Only perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) can be designated as "perversions" (*viparyāsa*), because this is universally established in the world.

That is to say, the perversion of perception and mind is universally established in the world, whereas feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] are not; therefore, the Sūtra does not mention them.

Based on this mental perception, the designation "perversion" (*viparyāsa*) is established according to the power of the perversion of view, and not with respect to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates.

Thus, these perversions are abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), because the perversion of permanence (*nitya-viparyāsa*) and so forth operate only with respect to suffering, and because the realization that [things] are impermanent and so on arises only by taking suffering as its object. Furthermore, one should not abandon the views of permanence, bliss, self, and purity only at a later time when viewing the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Having already explained the distinctions among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of views, one might ask: do others also possess such distinctions?
They indeed do.
How so? The verse says:
"The seven types of pride and the nine [afflictions] arise from three; all are subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation."
The Noble Ones, such as those who have eliminated the fetters of killing and so forth, possess [the defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation but do not manifest them.
The treatise says:
There are those who, being deluded, first compare themselves with others regarding things that exist and things that do not exist; the resulting elevation of the mind is called pride (*māna*).
Due to the variations in their modes of operation, they are divided into seven types:
first, pride; second, excessive pride; third, pride beyond pride; fourth, the pride of "I am"; fifth, overweening pride; sixth, inferiority pride; and seventh, false pride.
To consider oneself superior or equal among others who are inferior or equal in terms of lineage, social circle, and so forth, and to thus become puffed up with pride, is called *māna* (pride).
To consider oneself superior or equal among others who are equal or superior in terms of lineage, social circle, and so forth, is called *atimāna* (excessive pride).
To claim superiority over others who belong to superior lineages, social circles, and so forth, is called *mānātimāna* (excessive pride).
To grasp at the five aggregates of clinging as "I" and "mine," whereby the mind becomes uplifted, is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
To claim for oneself that one has attained the distinguished qualities of the stages, the paths, the abandonments, and so forth, when they have not yet been attained, is called *adhimāna* (conceit).

When those who are either householders or renunciants, regarding others who are largely superior in qualities such as craftsmanship or ethical discipline (*śīla*), consider themselves slightly inferior yet give rise to a sense of mental loftiness, this is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority conceit).
To claim for oneself virtues that one does not possess is called *mithyāmāna* (false pride).

That which is called "lack of virtue" refers to various unwholesome actions; it is designated by the name "lack of virtue" because they contradict virtuous qualities, just as the term "unwholesome" (*akuśala*) is used.
However, the root treatise states:
"There are nine types of pride.
The term "type" (prakāra) has the meaning of "category," referring specifically to the distinctions within pride.

What are the nine types? First, the type of pride thinking "I am superior"; second, the type of pride thinking "I am equal"; third, the type of pride thinking "I am inferior"; fourth, the type of pride thinking "There is someone superior to me"; fifth, the type of pride thinking "There is someone equal to me"; sixth, the type of pride thinking "There is someone inferior to me"; seventh, the type of pride thinking "There is no one superior to me"; eighth, the type of pride thinking "There is no one equal to me"; ninth, the type of pride thinking "There is no one inferior to me."

These nine all arise based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "I am superior" is a type of excessive conceit (*atimāna*); "I am equal" is a type of conceit (*māna*); "I am inferior" is a type of inferiority-conceit (*ūnamāna*). "There is one superior to me" is a type of inferiority-conceit; "there is one equal to me" is a type of conceit; "there is one inferior to me" is a type of excessive conceit. "There is no one superior to me" is a type of conceit; "there is no one equal to me" is a type of excessive conceit; "there is no one inferior to me" is a type of inferiority-conceit.

Therefore, these nine [types of pride] arise from three: namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*). Due to differences in their modes of operation, they form three groups of three.
How can the class of "I-am-not-inferior" pride (*asmimāna*) be established as a form of loftiness?

This refers to those who, within a superior assembly of sentient beings whom they themselves desire to join, recognize their own person as being extremely inferior, yet nevertheless hold themselves in high esteem—like a soothsayer or a *caṇḍāla*.
Although he knows for himself that this is universally despised by the world, when manifesting auspicious signs or performing his duties, he becomes arrogant because he holds himself in high esteem.
By what means are these seven types of pride abandoned?
Other masters say:

"The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and false conceit (*mithyāmāna*) are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), while the others pertain to both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
In truth, however, one should say that all seven pertain to both; therefore, [the Master] was able to speak with such confidence."
I do not adhere to a self within form and the other aggregates.
Nevertheless, among these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of self-conceit (*asmimāna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) have not yet been abandoned.
When those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have not yet been abandoned by an noble one (*ārya*), must they necessarily manifest?

This [distinction] is not fixed; that is to say, there are cases where [a defilement] has already been abandoned yet can still manifest, such as the latent tendency toward the view of suffering (*duḥkha-anuśaya*) in one who has already become detached from sensual desire.

Conversely, there are cases where [a defilement] has not yet been abandoned but certainly does not manifest, such as the fetter of killing (*vadhaparyavasthāna*) in a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet become detached from sensual desire.
Regarding the "fetter of killing" (*vadhaparyavasthāna*), it refers to the intentional thought (*saṃcetanā*) initiated by this fetter that results in the taking of a living being's life.

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the fetters of stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception, as well as the entirety of craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) and a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*).
What dharma is called "non-existence"?
It refers to the impermanence of the three realms; craving for this is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
By this, the impermanence of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is already excluded, because that is certainly not a basis for the satisfaction of craving.
There is a portion of craving, namely the aspiration to become a great nāga king such as Elāpattra;
although this is stated to illustrate [the case of] the asura kings, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, the non-conceptualizing gods (asaṃjñisattva), and so forth.

Although these fetters of killing and so forth are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they certainly do not manifest in noble ones (*ārya*). The reasons for their non-manifestation shall be explained later.
The same principle should apply to the conceit of self-existence (*asmimāna*) and others.

Within the craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), there is also that which is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*); however, because it is stated in accordance with the Sūtras, it is said to be abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As a Sūtra says: "A certain class of people, oppressed by suffering, thinks thus:
'O, may I, after death, be annihilated and cease to exist; how wonderful would it be to be free from illness!'"
This craving arises only by taking the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) as its object.
For what reason do noble ones (*ārya*) possess various types of conceit, such as the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), yet these states do not manifest?
The verse says:
The types of conceit, such as the conceit "I am," and the unwholesome [mental factor] of regret do not arise in noble ones,
even though they possess them, because they are increased by views and doubt.
The commentary says:

The word "etc. is used to indicate that the various outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) such as killing, as well as the entirety of craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) and a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), are absent [in noble ones], because the noble ones have well-cultivated emptiness and correctly understand the principle of the causal connection between karma and its results.
Regarding these types of conceit, such as the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) and evil regret (kaukṛtya), although the noble ones have not yet abandoned them, they certainly do not manifest.
Furthermore, because these are closely increased by views and doubt, and because views and doubt have already been abandoned, they no longer manifest.

That is to say, the types of pride and the *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") are increased by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the entanglements such as killing are increased by false views; various forms of craving for non-existence are increased by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); one portion of craving for existence is increased by the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*); and unwholesome remorse is increased by doubt. Therefore, although these may not yet have been abandoned within the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*), they certainly do not manifest because they have been discarded and analyzed away.
Because the others are not increased by views or doubt and are associated with what is proximate, they may manifest even when one has attained the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and how many are non-universal?
The verse says:
Those associated with the views and doubt abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
as well as the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), are pervasive within their own realm and stage.
Among these, excluding two views, the remaining nine can take the higher realms as their object;
excluding acquisition (*prāpti*), the remaining concomitants (*anuvartaka*) are likewise subsumed under the universal [mental factors].
The treatise says:

Only the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin have the power to function as pervasive; however, this applies not to all of them. Specifically, it refers only to the various views, doubt, and their associated or independent ignorance (*avidyā*), but not to others such as craving (*rāga*).
There are seven views (*dṛṣṭi*) and two doubts (*vicikitsā*); the ignorance associated (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*) with them is subsumed under those very categories.
There are two types of non-associated (*asāmānya*) ignorance; thus, there are eleven [unwholesome universal mental factors].

These eleven are each able to function as universals (*sarvatraga*) within their own realm (*dhātu*) and stage (*bhūmi*), operating across all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) of those respective realms and stages.

This means that among the five categories of dharmas within one's own realm and level, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which universally take [all] as their object and arise as defiled causes are designated as "universal" (*sarvatraga*). Thus, with reference to the realms, it is said that thirty-three are universal bases.
In what sense is the term "unshared ignorance" (āveṇika-avidyā) established?
According to this explanation, that which is mixed is called "shared" (sādhāraṇa); because this is not shared, it is given the name "unshared," which means it is distinct from others.
As stated in the sūtra:
"Not shared by the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
This reveals that the two jewels of the Buddha and the Saṅgha are distinct; they are called "not shared" because their practices are not shared.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not [called "universal"] because it does not operate in association with other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Alternatively, the term "universal" (*sāmānya*) may mean "common";
since this [ignorance] is not common [to all], it is designated as "unshared" (*asāmānya*), because it is not associated with the various latent dispositions.
Why is it that among the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, only these are universal?

It is because these alone universally take all contaminated phenomena as their object; they are uniform in their underlying intention and possess firm power, and are thus able to act as causes to produce [defilements] throughout all five categories.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) have only the capacity to take a portion of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object; because their objects are distinct and their force is not firm, they cannot serve as causes to produce [defilements] universally across the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*). Therefore, only the first two categories possess universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

This pervasive latent tendency (*anuśaya*) possesses three meanings of "pervasiveness": namely, it pervasively conditions the five categories [of defilements] as its object, and it can serve as a cause to universally produce defiled phenomena.
This associated dharma possesses two meanings of "pervasiveness," meaning that it lacks only one of these three meanings, namely the latent tendency.
These co-existent dharmas possess the characteristic of being universal, meaning that as causes, they universally produce defiled dharmas.

If the universal afflictions can take the five categories [of dharmas] as their objects, then the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises taking those dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path as its object.
By seeing what are they abandoned?

If greed and so forth are abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), then because they would also take the five categories as their objects, they too should be abandoned solely by seeing suffering.

Furthermore, for example, the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) takes as its object that which is abandoned by seeing cessation and the path; since those [afflictions] directly delude one regarding the uncontaminated objects—deluding one regarding cessation and the path—they are likewise abandoned by seeing cessation and seeing the path.
Thus, this view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is also a direct delusion, for it is deluded regarding cessation and the path; therefore, it should be seen as abandoned [by those insights].
Alternatively, one should distinguish the specific causes and conditions for this.

Furthermore, just as the views abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path are abandoned primarily through the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of their respective objects of focus (*ālambana*), so too should it be understood by analogy for the view of a self.

Alternatively, just as the object of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned, so too should it be for the case of the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Since neither of these two alternatives is accepted by our own school, the position established is therefore not tenable from a logical standpoint.
The principle must necessarily be so, for the meanings are distinct.

Furthermore, regarding the initial example, since greed and other afflictions would likewise have to take the five categories as their objects, they would [absurdly] be abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Alternatively, taking this as a counter-example to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the principle should logically also apply to those [afflictions] subsumed within all five categories.
This example is unreasonable, for it would follow that greed and other afflictions should likewise simultaneously apprehend the five categories of phenomena within a single moment.
That is to say, within a single instant, the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) would simultaneously apprehend the five categories—ranging from sensation to consciousness—as "I" and "mine."

It is logically untenable to claim that the substance of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within a single moment of thought consists of five categories, for greed and the like are all afflictions characterized by their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*). Since there is not even a single moment of thought that can simultaneously take two categories as its object, how much less could it take five? Therefore, the analogy does not hold.

As stated in the subsequent analogy regarding the views of cessation and the path, the same applies to the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); since both are direct delusions—deluded with respect to cessation and the path—they should likewise be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.
This is also illogical, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) cannot praise that which it slanders;
furthermore, its objective referent (*ālambana*) has no limits whatsoever.

It is not the case that the view of a self-identity must first praise [the aggregates] and then, upon slandering the views of cessation and the path, conceive of them as "self," nor does it take its object by establishing limited boundaries.
The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) necessarily involves praising [one's own view] and only then conceiving it as supreme through the false view that slanders the Path and Cessation;
since the meaning of its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as a limited condition (*pariccheda-pratyaya*) is thus distinct, it cannot be used as an analogy.

However, regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), at the time of seeing the Truth of Suffering, its object is fully and eternally abandoned through thorough knowledge; this is not the case for the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
There is a distinct reason for this: because their objects, modes of activity, and modes of comprehension are dissimilar.

This means that just as the aggregates (*skandha*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the three realms are not-self, up to and including the aggregates abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), their characteristics are likewise so.
Therefore, at the time of seeing suffering, the view of non-self arises; by taking the seen suffering as its object, all views of self are eliminated.
The notion that [the view of superiority] is not so is because there are cases where one contemplates a certain minor phenomenon and conceives another minor phenomenon as superior.

For this reason, although the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that accompanies the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) takes as its object phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, it arises as something coarse; thus, like the view of a self-identity, it is abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), just as when it arises taking phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as its object.

The view of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that accompanies the view of denying the Path (*mārga-nāstika-dṛṣṭi*), although it also arises by taking as its object those phenomena abandoned by that [view], is nonetheless more subtle than the former; it is not subsumed under the modes of conduct regarding pleasure or purity; and because it is directly grasped by the ignorance that leads to the false view of not desiring the cessation of the Path, it is considered the most preeminent. Thus, while it may fully cognize its objects during the stage of the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), it is only severed when those objects are permanently abandoned.

Therefore, the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is not like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is completely and eternally severed at the very moment one perceives suffering; thus, the principle regarding the distinctions in their abandonment as previously stated is established, or [it is established] because it takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.

The clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists of three types each, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), and cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*), because they are abandoned one by one accordingly.
If one clings to [the views] abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path as being superior in their aspect of being results, this is abandoned through the vision of origin.
If one clings primarily to the causal aspect [of a view], it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

If one clings only to that as being truly realized, without specifically clinging to either its causal or resultant aspects, then whichever conditions arise, it is abandoned simultaneously with them; therefore, the abandonment of the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is not like that of the "view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

If the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) were to take all five categories [of afflictions] as their object simultaneously, they would be termed "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*). However, pervasive factors would not be limited to only those;

for wherever the view of a self operates, there must necessarily arise self-love and self-pride. Wherever the views of purity and superiority operate, there must necessarily arise longing and haughtiness. Thus, love and pride should also be considered pervasive.
This objection is not valid.
Although they arise through the power of seeing (*darśana*), because these two types [of afflictions] have limited objects (*pradeśālambana*), there are only eleven universal [afflictions].

Regarding the eleven previously mentioned, do they each universally pervade the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) of their own realm and level (*sva-dhātu-bhūmi*) within all realms and levels, or do they also universally pervade other realms and other levels?
To exclude those [factors], it is said they pertain to "one's own realm and one's own stage," yet there are also universal factors belonging to other realms and other stages.

That is to say, among the eleven [types of universal factors], excluding the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the remaining nine kinds are also capable of taking higher objects as their cognitive range.

The preceding statement clearly elucidates the higher realms and higher stages, while simultaneously demonstrating that there are no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take lower levels as their objects.

If they were to take lower levels as objects, the spheres of existence (*dhātu*) would have to be understood as being destroyed; however, because the upper objects are superior, this fault does not apply to those [tendencies] that take them as objects.

Furthermore, one wishes to see that the false view abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya-mithyādṛṣṭi) slanders the fruits of suffering in the realms of form and formlessness as being non-existent; the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) clings to these [denials] as being supreme; the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) reckons what is not a cause to be a cause; and doubt harbors hesitation while ignorance lacks understanding.
Those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) should be explained accordingly.
The case of form being the condition for the formless should be understood by analogy with this.
One should reflect upon the distinctions according to the levels (*bhūmi*) based on the realms (*dhātu*).

However, as for the definite distinctions between the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*): from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna, there are universal [defilements] that take the higher realms and higher stages as their objects.

Among the three formless realms, those taking the higher realms as objects are absent; in the single stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), both types are entirely absent. Although these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do extend to take their own and higher stages as objects, [the specific categories mentioned above are excluded].

However, it is logically impossible for [a defilement] to suddenly take as its object that which is both above and itself; for within its own stage, all objective phenomena are both the objects of perception (*ālambana*) and the objects where the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) reside.

If the objective phenomena of a higher stage were only the objects of perception and not the objects where the latent tendencies reside, it would be impossible for a single moment of affliction to have an object where some latent tendencies reside while others do not.
Since this is also the case for associated [factors], must those in the higher realms and stages necessarily take [their objects] all at once?
It is not necessary that they take them all at once; they may do so either individually or collectively.
Observing what is present before one, for what reason would one not take the higher realms as an object, nor take other realms as an object?
This is because the logical grounds for grasping at "self" and "mine," as well as for calculating [the extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism, are untenable.

This means that it is not the case that one who is born in a particular realm or stage perceives the aggregates belonging to another realm or stage as "self," for the logical position that there are two selves is untenable.
Because the grasping at a self is not established, the grasping at "mine" is also not established, since whatever is grasped as "mine" necessarily arises based on the grasping at a self.
Since the view of extremes follows from the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it likewise has no possibility of taking other realms or stages as its object.
For these reasons, it is established by logic that only nine [afflictions] take the higher realms as their objects. Other masters say:

Because the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as craving (*tṛṣṇā*), arise through the power of grasping; because they grasp at what is appropriated as being "mine"; and because they take presently perceived phenomena as their objective domain, they certainly do not take the higher realms as their objects.

If one born within the desire realm, taking Mahābrahmā as their object, gives rise to the view of a self among sentient beings (*sattvadrṣṭi*) and the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), by which [of the two] views are they subsumed?
In truth, it should be said that these two are not views; they are false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*) induced by the view of a self and the view of extremes (*satkāyāntagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Having perceived the self as permanent within the manifest aggregates, one infers it to be so regarding what is not manifest; that is, regarding birth in the desire realm, one does not conceive "I am Mahābrahmā," nor does one conceive "Brahmā is mine. Therefore, this is not the view of a self in the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not exist, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) also does not exist, for the view of extremes necessarily arises dependent upon the view of a self-identity.
Since no other view produces this mode of activity, it is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) induced by the views of a self-identity and extremes.
Is the substance of the universal [defilements] exclusively the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)? No. Why is this so?

Furthermore, regarding the concomitant factors (*anucara-dharma*): the aforementioned universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), along with their concomitants such as feeling (*vedanā*) and arising (*jāti*), are all subsumed under the category of the universal, because they share the same fruit.
However, among the concomitants (*anucara*), only the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) are excluded, because the acquisition and that which is acquired do not share a single fruit.
Consequently, when the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is contrasted with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), four distinct permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are fully established.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), how many take contaminated objects (*sāsrava*) as their object, and how many take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava*) as their object?
The verse says:
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, which are associated with false view and doubt—
Including the unique ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), six [of these] can take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Among those, that which takes cessation (*nirodha*) as its object takes only the cessation of its own level as its object;
that which takes the path (*mārga*) as its object takes [the paths of] the six and nine levels as its objects, because they serve as specific remedies for one another.
Greed, hatred, pride, and the two types of grasping do not have uncontaminated objects as their focal points;
they should be abandoned because their objects are not hostile and because they possess a nature of purity and excellence.
The commentary states:

Only the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubts (*vicikitsā*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), along with their associated and unshared ignorance (*avidyā*), constitute six [factors]—three for each—capable of taking the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.

That is to say, the three false views and two doubts abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, together with the associated ignorance which is subsumed under them, and because there are two types of unshared [ignorance], they form six.
Thus, among these six kinds of realms and stages, those that can take cessation and the path as their objects are called "taking the uncontaminated (anāsrava) as an object.
The remainder, which take the contaminated (sāsrava) as an object, need not be mentioned as they are established by implication.
Regarding this taking of the uncontaminated as an object: within each respective stage, how many stages of cessation and the path does it take as its objective sphere?

Regarding those [latent dispositions] whose objects are cessation, they take as their object the cessation belonging to their own level; that is to say, the latent dispositions whose objects are cessation bound to the desire realm take as their object only the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the formations belonging to the desire realm, and so on, up to the latent dispositions whose objects are cessation at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which take as their object only the analytical cessation of the formations belonging to the Peak of Existence.
Regarding those that take the Path as their object, they take the six and nine stages as their objects.

Specifically, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the Desire Realm that take the Path as their object take only the Path belonging to the category of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) in the six stages as their object; this is because all categories of Dharma-knowledge are capable of taking as their object whichever [Path] counteracts the Desire Realm or whichever is capable of counteracting the others.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the path as their object within the eight stages of the form and formless realms, each one is able to universally take as its object the category of the knowledge of classes (*anvaya-jñāna*) across all nine stages—whether it be the path that counteracts its own stage or the path that counteracts other stages—because all categories of the knowledge of classes are capable of being taken as objects.
For what reason can the wrong views that deny suffering and deny the origin, when bound to the desire realm, take nine stages as their objects?

And why can the wrong view that denies cessation, when belonging to the first dhyāna, take eight stages as its object, up to the point where it belongs only to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and takes only that stage as its object?
Within each of the nine stages, one can only take the cessation (*nirodha*) of its own stage as an object;
there is a reason for this. Why is that?

It is because whatever phenomena are moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) belonging to a particular stage, and are grasped as "self" or "mine" by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of that same stage, the cessation of those phenomena becomes the object of the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation within that very stage.

The meaning of this statement is as follows: if there are various formations (*saṃskāra*) of a particular level that serve as the objects of self-love (*ātmasneha*) and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), then because one is attached to those formations of that level, upon hearing it said that the formations of that level are subject to cessation, one gives rise to wrong views regarding that level and denies their existence.

One does not have a lower attachment within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a higher realm; how much less would one hold the false view of negation (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) that denies the cessation [of suffering] in those realms?

Although the causes and effects of different realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) are mutually isolated, the suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) of the nine stages nevertheless draw one another together; furthermore, because causes are established based on arising, they function as mutual causes for one another.

While it is possible for wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) of a single stage (*bhūmi*) to have multiple objects, this does not apply to the cessation [of suffering], because the principles of mutual attraction and causal dependence do not extend to it; therefore, wrong views that slander cessation take only the cessation of their own stage as their object.

However, since wholesome cognition (*kuśalajñāna*) realizes its objects through universal principles, it is possible for it to suddenly take the formations and cessations of multiple stages as its object.
All false views arise from delusion regarding their objects; because they are obstructed by their own stubborn adherence, they cannot take [all four truths] as a collective object.
For what reason do false views that take suffering, origin, and cessation as objects sometimes have both general and specific modes, whereas those taking the path as an object do not?
Because their antidotes differ and they serve as mutual causes for one another:

although the paths taken as objects of focus (*ālambana*) differ according to the various stages (*bhūmi*), they are successively connected and function as mutual causes and effects. Therefore, by virtue of this, these false views take six or nine stages collectively as their object; however, the cessation (*nirodha*) of suffering does not act as a cause for others and thus takes only its own stage as its object.

Is it not the case that the paths of the two categories of knowledge—dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge—are likewise mutually dependent? If so, then false views of the lower and upper stages should both be able to take the paths of these two categories as their objects, just as there is no obstruction when taking the truths of suffering and origin as objects across all stages.
This criticism is not valid, because [the path] is not an antidote.
