If that were so, then the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) in the six stages would not pertain to the desire realm; for when false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) take all five upper stages as their object, the path of the category of dharma-knowledge is not an antidote to the phenomena of the desire realm.
The stage of the Not-yet-arrived (anāgamya) does not belong entirely to the higher stages either, because it is not intended to counteract [the afflictions of] the desire realm.
Furthermore, that which counteracts the desire realm is also not complete, because false views are likewise countered by this patience (kṣānti).

The wrong view that slanders the path in the form and formless realms should likewise be able to take the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge as its object, because the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge serves as the antidote to the form and formless realms.

If it is argued that dharma-knowledge does not entirely counteract those [realms], because the categories of dharma-knowledge regarding suffering and origin are not their antidotes; [we reply: [this is not so].
Nor can it universally cure the afflictions of the form and formless realms, because it cannot cure those [afflictions] abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).

The first category of Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) cannot cure the afflictions of that first category, because they are not what is cured by this; thus, the category of Dharma-knowledge is not the object-condition (*ālambana*) of those [afflictions].

In that case, one must admit that false views regarding the form and formless realms cannot collectively take as their object both the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the category other than subsequent knowledge across the nine stages, because [such a collective object] would be able to counteract all afflictions within the two higher realms simultaneously.

This means that the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) on the level of the second dhyāna and above cannot serve as an antidote to the afflictions of the first dhyāna level and below;
nor can the first dhyāna and its levels themselves [serve as such an antidote]. The logical deduction for both cases is as previously explained.

Furthermore, because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that take the Truth of the Path as their object are not counteracted by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) toward suffering, origin, or cessation, it stands to reason that the view of denial regarding the Path cannot take the six or nine stages of the lower and upper paths collectively as its object.

Thus, in reality, there are no such logical fallacies, because the categories of phenomena (*dharmas*) and their types are distinct when compared to one another; because the classes of knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and their subsequent types (*anvaya-jñāna*) share the same antidotes; and because they serve as mutual causes and mutual objects of cognition.

This refers to the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*), which is of the same type as the antidote to the afflictions that take the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) within the desire realm as their object.

Because these paths of the same type act as mutual causes and mutual objects for one another, even if they are not direct antidotes, they are still the objects of the afflictions in the desire realm that take the path as their object. Although the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*) and the category of dharma-knowledge act as mutual causes, because they differ in type by way of being antidotes and do not serve as mutual objects, they are not the objects of the afflictions in the desire realm that take the path as their object.

By this same principle, the objection that afflictions taking the Path as their object in the Form and Formless Realms should likewise be able to take the categories of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)—which counteract those realms—as their objects is also refuted.

This is because, although within these [afflictions] there may be a small portion of the category of Dharma-knowledge that can counteract a small portion of the afflictions of the higher realms and which acts as a mutual cause, they do not take the category of Subsequent Knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as their object; rather, due to the distinction between types based on the gate of counteraction, they are not the objects of the afflictions that take the Path of the higher realms as their object.

Within the nine stages, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) functions as a single type through mutual causality and reciprocal objectification; because their antidotes and categories are identical, although it is not a direct antidote [to those specific stages], it may collectively serve as the objective sphere for the path-conditioned states within the upper eight stages.
Therefore, the principle as stated in the verse is established.
Why is it that greed, hatred, pride, and the two types of grasping—which are abandoned through the path of seeing—are not directed toward the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
Because those who joyfully seek true liberation must certainly abandon the affliction of greed.
If they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, then—just as one who desires wholesome dharmas seeks after nirvāṇa and the noble path—one who seeks liberation would not be free from craving.
Furthermore, the truths of cessation and the path would have to be abandoned, because the Buddha stated that the objects of detachment are called "abandoned."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If you can sever craving toward form, that form is also called 'severed.
Furthermore, it is only by perceiving the faults within the objects of craving that one is able to become free from craving."
If it were admitted that craving can take the untainted as its object, then craving could only be abandoned when one perceives faults in cessation and the path.
Since such a perception is not pure, how could it ever exhaust the afflictions?
Furthermore, greed arises only when one perceives merit within its object.

If you grant that greed can take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, then when one contemplates the untainted through the aspects of cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), and so forth, greed should increase; how then could this lead to the exhaustion of all afflictions?
Since both [greed and hatred] would fail to exhaust delusions, birth and death would be endless; therefore, we know that greed does not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.

Hatred arises only by taking objects of enmity and harm as its basis; since the untainted state is free from the characteristics of enmity and harm, hatred will certainly not arise when taking the untainted as its object.

Furthermore, the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*) is coarse and harsh in its nature, whereas all untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are supremely subtle; therefore, there is no possibility for hatred to operate with respect to them.

Because the latent tendencies of pride (*mānānuśaya*) have the characteristic of loftiness, their nature is not tranquil; since untainted phenomena are utterly tranquil, they do not give rise to loftiness.
Furthermore, regarding one who gives rise to conceit, they think:
"I have attained this Dharma.
It is not the power of the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas that serves as the condition for such conceit to arise, because untainted dharmas are capable of counteracting conceit.

If the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) could take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they would necessarily be identical to right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), because the untainted is the truly pure and supreme nature.
Since the two types of grasping are not erroneous, they should not be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*); therefore, the two types of grasping do not have the untainted as their object.
If that were so, when one gives rise to the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*) toward wrong views and the like that deny *nirvāṇa*, there would be no fault since it conforms to its object.

To give rise to a mind of revulsion toward things that are faulty is precisely appropriate, as they ought to be abandoned; thus, hatred would not be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*darśana-heya*), yet such an error does not follow.
Regarding the characteristic of the extinction of folly: it is because anger arises only toward those who slander.
That is to say, having first grasped at liberation elsewhere, one subsequently gives rise to an intolerant mind toward those who slander true liberation.

Therefore, it is only those who truly understand the characteristic of cessation who give rise to extreme aversion toward the false view that slanders cessation; by seeing cessation, they eliminate hatred.

As for those who do not truly understand the characteristic of cessation, if they develop a sense of weary detachment toward the false views that slander cessation, this is not the latent tendency of hatred, but is rather subsumed under the wholesome root of non-attachment.

Furthermore, it is like one who has accumulated many ailments within the stomach; for the sake of sustaining life, although they consume fine food, because it is mixed with illness, it all results in deterioration.
One whose stomach is free of disease finds that whatever they eat is entirely beneficial to the body and causes no harm.

Thus, if one falsely claims that what is not cessation is cessation and thereby gives rise to craving, because their mental continuity is defiled, the hatred and aversion they direct toward wrong views and the like are all said to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the hatred arising from such factors as wrong views: if one understands, in accordance with reality, that true cessation is indeed cessation and is free from craving, then because the mental continuum is purified, there is no fault whatsoever in feeling revulsion toward those wrong views and the like that slander such cessation.
If one gives rise to hatred toward the right view that recognizes the existence of nirvāṇa, by what [type of abandonment] is this view severed?

This need not be questioned; for it is logically impossible for a hatred severed by insight (*darśana-heya*) to take a wholesome phenomenon as its object. Therefore, this [hatred] which takes right view as its object is certainly severed by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
However, for one who has already seen the Truths, this [hatred] no longer functions as a condition, because the craving associated with the view of nihilism has been permanently severed.
How can you not believe that there is hatred directed toward the untainted (*anāsrava*)? For is it not the case that such hatred is known to exist in the world?
It refers to certain non-Buddhists who say, "In nirvana, all faculties are eternally extinguished; this is a great loss.
Therefore, I certainly do not seek it with joy.
This is fundamentally not hatred, but rather a false view.

Therefore, the root treatise states that regarding pleasure as suffering is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*); this must necessarily be so, because all suffering is only eternally extinguished upon reaching the state of ultimate bliss.
The "Land of Ultimate Bliss" is none other than true *nirvāṇa*.
This term "Ultimate Bliss" reveals the bliss of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

Because they cannot comprehend the characteristics of this bliss, nor can they understand the faults of saṃsāra, they remain attached to the various realms of existence (*bhava*) and take no pleasure in renunciation; thus, they give rise to false views and do not attain *parinirvāṇa*.
Would you rather grasp this as the condition for the cessation of hatred?
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Exegesis on the Treasury of Abhidharma), Fascicle 25;
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (Exegesis on the Compendium of Abhidharma), Fascicle 26.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Six, Part Two: An Analysis of the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya). Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions, how many increase by way of their object (*ālambana*)?
How many [latent dispositions] increase by way of association?
The verse says:
The unabandoned pervasive latent dispositions increase with respect to everything within their own stage.
They do not increase universally within their own category, because they increase only with respect to their objects (*ālambana*).
They do not take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states or higher realms as objects, because such objects are not grasped and would be contradictory [to defilement].
They increase with respect to their associated factors (*saṃprayukta*), because they increase through association (*saṃprayoga*).
The treatise says:

There are two distinctions of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), namely, those that are universal within one's own realm and stage (*svadhātu-bhūmi*) and those that are universal across other realms and stages (*paradhātu-bhūmi*).
There are also two distinctions of the non-universal latent dispositions, namely, those with outflow objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and those with outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).

Furthermore, among the universal [defilements], those that pertain to their own realm and level increase in accordance with their objects across all five categories of phenomena within that same realm and level.
Among the non-universal [defilements], those that take contaminated phenomena as their object increase in accordance with their objects only within their own category and their own realm and level.

Regarding those [afflictions] among the non-universal that take the untainted as their object, as well as those among the universal that take objects belonging to other realms, they lack the sense of "increasing" (anuśaya) with respect to their objective spheres. Why is this so?
Because that object of focus is neither grasped nor compatible [with those defilements].

That is to say, if a phenomenon were grasped as "mine" by the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) belonging to a particular stage, it would be possible for the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) existing within that stage of self-view and craving to increase by taking that phenomenon as their object.

"Anuśaya" (proclivity) means that the various proclivities dwell within and increase in this dharma; that is to say, it signifies the sense of being bound by them and becoming increasingly obscured and stagnant.
It is like dust settling upon moist clothing, or like seeds growing in a moist field.
This is because the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas and those of the higher stages are not grasped as "mine" by the views and craving of the lower stages;
thus, the afflictions of those lower stages do not increase through the object (*ālambana-anuśaya*), since they do not increase through being bound by or becoming stagnant within that object.

If one born in a lower stage seeks a higher stage and so forth, this is a desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) and is not considered defiled (*kliṣṭa*), because such a desire arises in order to seek liberation from defilement.

Since the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), Nirvāṇa, and the dharmas of the higher stages are incompatible with the lower afflictions that take them as objects, it follows that these two [Nirvāṇa and the Noble Path] likewise lack the principle of being increased by the objects of those [afflictions].
Just as one's feet do not remain upon a heated stone, and just as a goose does not grow within a flame,
so too these latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise directly from their basis;
yet at the very moment they arise, they also depend upon their respective objects.
Thus, having already explained how [defilements] increase with respect to their objects (*ālambana*),
as for which latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase with respect to associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) by virtue of association (*saṃprayoga*),
it is said that such "increase" occurs until they have been abandoned; therefore, the word "unabandoned" (*aprahīṇa*) is placed at the beginning of the first verse.

From this it should be understood that for those [afflictions] conditioned by uncontaminated phenomena or by phenomena of another realm or level, only associated increase (*saṃprayoga-anuśaya*) occurs; whereas for those conditioned by contaminated phenomena of their own realm and level, both objective-sphere increase (*ālambana-anuśaya*) and associated increase are fully present.
Do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the past and future increase [in their influence]?
One must say that they certainly do, because they are capable of producing acquisitions (*prāpti*).
If it were otherwise, then individuals who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) would be free from latent dispositions during states of mind that are undefiled.
However, the World-Honored One stated:
"In infants, children, and those suffering from illness, although there is no manifest defilement (*rāga*), the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of desire still increases.

Therefore, it is said that [the latent tendency] increases until it is abandoned; once it has been abandoned, there is no longer an object of perception (*ālambana*). How could there be an increase through association (*samprayoga*)? For even then, the latent tendency does not lose its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

This means that because their power has been destroyed by the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), they do not increase further; however, since the essential nature and characteristics of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have not been lost, it is said that they "still exist.
Alternatively, based on the fact that they have had or will have this function, they are still designated as "latent dispositions" even though they currently lack such a function.
Just as one who has lost his kingdom still retains the title of "king," or as a craftsman who has ceased working still retains his name;
among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and how many are neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the two higher realms, as well as the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm, together with their associated ignorance (*moha*), are neutral (*avyākṛta*); all the remainder are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The treatise states:

Because all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms are suppressed by the fourfold and fivefold meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), they lack the power to project a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*); therefore, they are all subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

If it is argued that those [defiled states] can induce a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), then there would have to be undesirable sensation (*aniṣṭavedanā*) in the two higher realms; for it is not established that defilement induces desirable sensation.
However, there is no fault of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) becoming indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because only tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) possess ripening fruits.
Within this category, only that which lacks any ripening result (*vipāka*) can be designated as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Therefore, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), along with their associated delusion (*moha*), when bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are also indeterminate; for they function as distortions (*viparyāsa*), so how could they not be unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
Furthermore, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is certainly not unwholesome, as it accords with wholesome conduct and opposes the severing of roots of goodness.

Although craving and pride may accord with the performance of meritorious deeds, they are induced to arise by the power of [wrong] views; moreover, because they serve as powerful causes at the time of severing roots of goodness and because they turn one away from virtuous friends, those associated with desire are unwholesome.

Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), that which clings to the extreme of annihilation (*ucchedānta*) is not unwholesome because it conceives of the cessation of rebirth; thus, it does not contradict *nirvāṇa* and accords with the gateway of revulsion and detachment (*vidūṣaṇa-nairyāṇika-mukha*).
As the Blessed One said:
"If such a view arises, I do not tolerate it in any respect."
One should know that this view does not accord with greed, but accords with non-greed, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"Among all the various views of the non-Buddhists, this view is the most excellent: namely, 'I do not exist, and what belongs to me does not exist.'"

"I shall not exist" and "what belongs to me shall not exist"—the adherence to the extreme view of eternalism arises in accordance with the view of self; this is of indeterminate moral quality (*avyākṛta*), as explained in the discussion on the view of self.
All other latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm that are contrary to those mentioned above are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Among these unwholesome latent dispositions, how many function as the substantial entity of the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*)?
The verse says:
The unwholesome roots in the desire realm are greed, hatred, and unwholesome delusion.
The commentary says:
Only all greed, hatred, and unwholesome delusion bound to the desire realm are subsumed under the unwholesome roots;
in their respective order, the Blessed One has declared them to be the essence of the three unwholesome roots: greed, hatred, and delusion.
Only unwholesome afflictions that serve as roots for unwholesome phenomena are designated as "unwholesome roots" (akuśalamūla); such is the tenet.

Is it not the case that all evil phenomena already arisen serve as causes for subsequent ones? It is not merely these three types [of afflictions] that do so, nor does this contradict the principle of non-excess, because the unwholesome roots are established in contrast to the wholesome roots.
For what reason are non-conceit (*amāna*) and other such wholesome roots not established [as roots]?
Because within the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), there are no unwholesome forms of conceit or the like to serve as their opposites.

Furthermore, the designation of "unwholesome root" (*akuśala-mūla*) requires the possession of five criteria: it must pertain to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), be universal across the six consciousnesses, be of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), incite unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, and serve as the predominant preliminary application (*prayoga*) at the time of severing the wholesome roots.
Pride and the other [defilements] are not like this.
Just as unwholesome phenomena have unwholesome roots, do indeterminate phenomena possess such roots? They do.
How so? The verse says:
There are three neutral roots: neutral craving, delusion, and wisdom.
Because the other two are not "lofty," the masters of the Western Regions establish four types:
craving, views, pride, and delusion for the middle [realm]; in the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas), all are delusion alone.
The treatise says:

The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr state that there are also three kinds of neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*): namely, the three—neutral craving (*tṛṣṇā*), delusion (*moha*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—which should all be understood as being subsumed under the category of neutral roots.
The faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) comprehensively includes both the obscured-unwholesome and the unobscured-neutral.
Since "faculty" (indriya) carries the meaning of "cause" (hetu), and unobscured-neutral wisdom can also function as a cause, it is therefore subsumed under the neutral faculties.
These three possess the power to give rise to various neutral states (*avyākṛta*).
For what reason are doubt (*vicikitsā*) and pride (*māna*) not considered neutral roots?
Because doubt functions by oscillating between two courses, whereas pride functions by being loftily elevated.

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and indecision (*vimati*) involve wavering and shifting between two courses; therefore, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*), because faculties are firmly established.
Pride (*māna*) has the characteristic of loftiness and turns upward; therefore, it is not established as a faculty, because faculties tend toward the downward direction.

The characteristics of roots as commonly perceived in the world are such that they are called "roots" because they are hidden beneath the soil; this signifies a substance that extends downward while producing sprouts above.
These three [faculties] are like those [worldly roots], and therefore they are also called "roots."
Other states that are not *anuśaya* (latent dispositions), or those that lack superior functional efficacy, are therefore not established as neutral roots (*avyākṛtamūla*).

Teachers from outside [this school] establish four such roots, namely: neutral craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*). The term "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) is used here to exclude both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
For what reason are these four established as the indeterminate roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*)?

Because when foolish persons cultivate higher meditative concentrations, they do not go beyond relying upon craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*); and since these three all function by depending on the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), these four are established as the indeterminate roots.

He says this: "The wisdom that is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is not a root of the neutral because its power is weak; for the meaning of a 'root' must be established upon what is firm and stable.

Because of the power of pride (*māna*), practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) fall away from hundreds of thousands of excellent qualities; therefore, the power of pride is superior, and it is established as a root of the neutral."
These four can give rise to neutral (*avyākṛta*) defiled phenomena.
Among the various sūtras, it is said that there are fourteen "unanswered" (*avyākṛta*) matters; do these correspond to what is called "neutral" because they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome?
It is not so. Why? Because it should be set aside.
Regarding the exposition of questions and answers, there are four types in total. What are these four?
The verse says:
One should provide categorical, analytical, counter-interrogative, or setting-aside answers,
as in the cases of death and rebirth, excellence, and whether the self and the aggregates are identical or distinct.
The commentary states:
The word "etc. (ādi) also includes other alternative classifications.

To briefly explain the four types of questions: first, those to be answered categorically; second, those to be answered analytically; third, those to be answered with a counter-question; and fourth, those to be set aside.
These four correspond respectively to cases where an inquirer asks about death and rebirth, superiority, identity, or difference.
There are four types of responses because there are four ways of answering these questions.
For example, if one were to ask as follows:
"Will all who are born necessarily die?
One should answer categorically:
"All who are born will certainly die."
If one were to ask:
"Do all who die necessarily come to be born? one should answer by means of analytical distinction (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*):
Those with afflictions will be reborn after death; those without afflictions will not be reborn after death.
If one were to ask: "Are humans superior or inferior? [the answer is as follows].
One should answer with a counter-question:
"To what does 'direction' refer?
Does it refer to the various heavens, or does it refer to the evil realms?"
If one says [the gods] are superior, one should record humans as inferior;
if one says [humans] are superior, one should record those in the evil destinies as inferior.
If one were to ask this question:
Are the aggregates and the sentient being one or different?

This should be set aside as an answer that is to be rejected (*sthāpanīya-avyākṛta*), because since the sentient being lacks substantial reality, the nature of being either identical or distinct cannot be established—
just as, for example, the properties of sharpness or dullness cannot be predicated of a horse's horn.
Having already analyzed the unwholesome and indeterminate latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), we should now investigate: to which objects (*vastu*) are which latent dispositions bound?
What is meant by an "object"?

Although the matters are not singular, herein we shall distinguish the objects to which [the latent dispositions] are bound. This further consists of two parts: distinguishing them by way of their bases and objects, and by way of their categories. Regarding the bases and objects:

the latent dispositions associated with visual consciousness are bound to the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) solely as objects; they are bound to the sense-bases of mind (*manāyatana*) and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)—namely, the various minds and mental factors associated with themselves—as concomitants.

In this manner, up to and including those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that coexist with body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna), they are bound to the sense base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) solely as objects of perception; they are bound to their own associated minds and mental factors within the sense bases of mind (manāyatana) and phenomena (dharmāyatana) through association.

If there are any latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the mental consciousness, they constitute a bond by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) with respect to the twelve bases (āyatana); they constitute a bond by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana) with respect to the mind-base (manāyatana) and the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana), which are the various minds and mental factors associated with themselves.

Regarding their categories: the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) constitute a bond by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to the phenomena of the five categories, and a bond by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*) with respect to the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are associated with them.

The non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) function as objects of attachment (*ālambana-bandhana*) only within their own category, and as associated attachments (*samprayoga-bandhana*) toward the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are associated with them.

All such cases should be explained accordingly. To analyze this in terms of the three time periods, one must determine: what kind of sentient being possesses which latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and to what object they can bind.
The verse says:
"If, within this particular object, greed, hatred, and pride have not yet been abandoned..."

If past and present [factors] have already arisen, and future mental factors are universal, then five [types of factors] that are subject to arising bind their own time; those not subject to arising are also universal.
The remainder, whether past or future, are universal; those in the present bind when they are currently being taken as objects.
The Treatise says:
If a class of sentient beings has latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in accordance with a particular object, they are said to be "bound" to that object.
Since that which acts as the binder must necessarily be unabandoned, it flows pervasively according to its respective application at the very outset, prior to abandonment.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are generally of two kinds:
first, those with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely greed, hatred, and pride;
second, those with common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), namely views, doubt, and delusion.
The three—greed, hatred, and pride—are afflictions of specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa-kleśa), as is clearly stated repeatedly within the various holy teachings.
For instance, as a sutra says, addressing the mother of Kāṣāyadhārī:
"When your eye does not see a form, does that form serve as a condition for the arising of desire-greed?"
"Not so, Venerable Sir! and so forth,
as explained at length.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that the Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī:
"What do you think?

Regarding all forms whatsoever—those not seen by your eye, those not previously seen by you, those not yet to be seen by you, and those for which you have no desire to see them—do you, on account of these, give rise to desire, give rise to greed, give rise to intimacy, give rise to affection, give rise to *ālaya*, give rise to *nyanti*, or give rise to attachment?"
"Not so, Venerable Sir! and so forth,
as explained at length.

Therefore, among these objects, greed, hatred, and pride—which have already arisen in the past and have not yet been abandoned—can bind one to these objects in the present once they have arisen, because greed, hatred, and pride are specific-characteristic afflictions (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*) that do not necessarily arise universally in all sentient beings.

Is it not the case that if the meaning of "being bound" (*baddha*) were already severed, then the term "bound" would no longer apply? Since the word "bound" has already been spoken, it clearly indicates that [the defilement] is not yet severed.
For what reason, then, do you say that this is "bound by the future," and further state that it is "past, having arisen, and not yet severed"?
The statement "this is not yet abandoned" would be rendered useless.

There is no fault of uselessness, for this statement "not yet abandoned" indicates that there is a gradual abandonment according to specific categories; thus, it is within this very treatise [that this is shown].
In the subsequent passage, it is also stated that the future mental universal [factors] and so forth exist;
that is to say, since those [defilements] such as greed differ according to nine grades, they are abandoned individually by grade when the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) eliminates them.

Regarding this object, although the superior-grade latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already arisen and ceased and have been permanently abandoned, there still remain other future grades of latent dispositions for that person regarding this same object; since these have not yet arisen, have not yet ceased, and have not yet been permanently abandoned, they are still capable of acting as a fetter.

Therefore, although this treatise states in this context that [the mind] is bound by future craving and so forth, it employs the expression "not yet abandoned" with respect to the past; thus, the term "not yet abandoned" is profoundly purposeful.

However, when the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of this category belonging to the past are permanently severed, those of the future are also severed. Yet it is possible that there remain other categories of future latent dispositions capable of binding this object which have not yet been permanently severed; for the three—greed, hatred, and pride—associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the future world universally take the three time periods as their objects. Although they may or may not arise in relation to this specific object, as long as they are not severed, they are all termed "capable of binding."
Regarding future greed and hatred associated with the five consciousnesses, if they have not been abandoned and are capable of arising, they bind only the future life.
By this, it has already been demonstrated that the proclivities (anuśaya) associated with the five consciousnesses which are capable of arising are [bound] in the future.
If [the latent disposition] pertains to the past, it is bound only to the past; the same applies when it pertains to the present.

By extension of this principle, if a latent disposition capable of arising is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and if it has not been abandoned in the past, present, or future, it may be bound to dharmas that do not belong to its own time period.

It is not only the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the mental consciousness that can bind the three time periods if they exist in the future; those latent dispositions associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, if they are definitely not to arise, likewise bind the three time periods.

That is to say, regarding those objects—whether they exist in the future, the present, or the past—even though they have already attained ultimate non-arising, their temporal nature remains unsevered and continues to bind.

All remaining views, arisings [of affliction], and ignorance that have not been abandoned bind one universally across the three times, both past and future; because these three types are universal delusions (*sāmānyalakṣaṇakleśa*), they universally bind all sentient beings alike.
If, in the present life, when correctly taking an object as its condition, [the affliction] is able to bind one to that very thing as appropriate,

what proof is there to know that the afflictions such as greed arise by taking objects of the three times— past and so forth— as their conditions, and that they are able to act as a bond within those very objects?
This is established by scriptural authority; for a sutra states:

"There are, in total, three kinds of phenomena that are objects of sensual desire: first, phenomena that are objects of sensual desire in the past; second, phenomena that are objects of sensual desire in the future; and third, phenomena that are objects of sensual desire in the present."

If desire-and-lust arises with respect to phenomena that were objects of desire-and-lust in the past, this arising desire-and-lust should be said to be bound to those past phenomena and not dissociated from them; and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"If one gives rise to craving or aversion toward forms seen in the past, future, or present, it should be known that in this case the eye is not bound by the form, nor is the form bound by the eye; rather, it is desire and greed (*kāmarāga*) that truly act as the bond."
There are many such scriptural authorities of this kind.
Is it said that there is bondage for those who possess past and future [dharmas]?
One should say that they do possess them.
What of those with characteristics?
They differ from the ultimate non-existence.
Furthermore, are present conditioned phenomena real or provisional?
It should be said that this is real.
How should one understand the existence of a real entity through its provisional characteristics?
That which serves as the object for the arising of cognition is the characteristic of "existence-in-general."

If a cognition arises with respect to something without depending on anything else, that is the characteristic of substantial existence (*dravyasat*), such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth.

If a cognition arises with respect to something while depending on other things, that is the characteristic of conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*), such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), an army (*senā*), and so forth.

One must not dogmatically maintain that the past and future exist only as conceptual designations (*prajñapti-sat*), because they lack a basis for such designation and because there are no objects upon which cognition could depend to arise [regarding them].

That is to say, when one takes the three objects of the past, future, and present as conditions, cognitions arise respectively without dependence on others: the recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsa-anusmṛti*) regarding the past, the aspiration for the future (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) regarding the present.
Since the past and future have been explained as having real characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are definitively real entities.
Furthermore, these real dharmas are of two kinds: first, those possessing functional activity (*kāritra*); second, those possessing only substantial essence (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, phenomena that possess functional activity are of two kinds: first, those possessing efficacy; second, those lacking efficacy.
By this, it has already been explained that there are only those which have substantial existence (*dravya*).
Phenomena that exist as designations (*prajñapti*) are also of two kinds: first, those based on the real; second, those based on the designated.
These two are, respectively, like a jar and an army.

However, that which possesses capacity (*śakti*) is not termed "activity" (*kāritra*), while all activity is also termed "capacity. Based on a specific type of capacity, the previous statement was incomplete.
Keeping such reasoning in mind, one should firmly establish the thesis that the past and future definitely exist.

Because there are the matters of cause and effect, as well as defilement and the state of being free from defilement, their intrinsic nature is not non-existent and is thus said to be substantially existent; however, this does not mean they possess the status of "substantial existence" in the same way as the present does.

We observe in the world phenomena that exist simultaneously; though their essential natures and characteristics are one, their specific qualities differ, such as the internal and external natures of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) being distinct, or the natures of pleasure and so forth experienced by oneself and others being different.
This nature and existence are logically inseparable; since their natures differ, their existences must necessarily be distinct.
Consequently, although the essential characteristics of earth and the other elements are identical, they may be described as having the distinction of internal and external natures.

Although sensation (*vedanā*) and the like share the same essential nature (*svabhāva*) in their characteristics of experiencing and so forth, they can nonetheless be described as having distinct natures such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest.

This is just as with the eyes and other faculties: although within a single continuum the essential nature of the pure derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is the same, there are distinctions of nature among them because their functions—such as seeing and hearing—are distinct.
It is not that within this [system] there exists a functional capacity distinct from existence; rather, it is possible for distinctions such as the capacity of "existence" and so forth to exist.
However, since functions such as seeing and so forth are themselves the eye-faculty and others, the specific determination of their existence follows from the distinction between these functions.

Therefore, we know that among all phenomena (*dharma*), there are those that exist at the same time, whose essential nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are without difference, yet whose categorical natures (*dharmatā*) are distinct.

Since we currently perceive that there are phenomena whose bodies exist simultaneously, whose essential natures and characteristics are without difference, yet whose categorical natures are distinct, we know that when all phenomena pass through the three periods of time, their essential natures and characteristics remain without difference while their categorical natures are distinct. Thus, the past and future are different from the present; how then could one claim that all three periods of time are substantially existent?
The verse says:

The existence of the three times is established by scripture, by the existence of objects and results, and because of the teaching that the three times exist; thus, they are accepted as the Sarvāstivādins.
The treatise states:
The past, future, and present truly exist, for this is established both by scriptural authority and by correct reasoning.
While the real existence of present phenomena is universally established, what scriptural authority and reasoning prove the real existence of the past and future?
Furthermore, it is because the Blessed One has so stated in the sūtras.
That is to say, the Blessed One said:
"If even past and future form (*rūpa*) are impermanent, how much more so the present?"

If one can contemplate form in this way as impermanent, then the many learned noble disciples will diligently cultivate disenchantment and relinquishment toward past form, diligently sever longing and seeking toward future form, and diligently cultivate disenchantment, detachment, and cessation regarding present form.
If past form did not exist, the community of learned noble disciples would not diligently cultivate disenchantment and relinquishment toward past form;
because past form does exist, the community of learned noble disciples diligently cultivates disenchantment and relinquishment toward past form.
If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciples would not strive to sever their longing for future form;
because future form does exist, the learned noble disciples must strive to sever their longing for future form.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Although karma, though past, exhausted, ceased, and transformed, still exists.
On what basis is this known?

The sūtras cited which speak of the existence of the past and the future are definitely of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), for there is no other passage that definitively negates them, as is the case with [the denial of] the person (*pudgala*) and so forth.
This means that although a *pudgala* is spoken of in various places, it can be said to lack any real substantiality;
furthermore, because the sūtras and other scriptures explicitly negate its existence, all those sūtras that speak of a *pudgala* are of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
Furthermore, as the sūtra states:
"One should kill one's father and mother.

This principle must also be of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), because other sūtras state that these constitute immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), and through such immediate transgressions, one inevitably falls into hell (*naraka*).
Furthermore, as a sūtra states:
"There is no evil karma that those who indulge in sensual desires cannot commit.
This [sūtra] must also be of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), because other sūtras prohibit noble ones (*ārya*) from intentionally (*saṃcintya*) committing any evil karma.
Such categories should be understood accordingly.

Since it has not been clearly and definitively stated here that past and future worlds exist, yet in other places it is clearly and definitively denied that past and future exist, one may infer by analogy that this [present passage] is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
However, this definitive [teaching] is an exposition of the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*), because it transcends the non-explicit characteristics found in other sūtras.
Is it not the case that there are also sūtras that negate the past and future? For example, as stated in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*:

"At the moment the eye-faculty arises, it comes from nowhere; at the moment the eye-faculty ceases, it accumulates nowhere; what was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, it returns to non-existence."
If the eye-faculty already existed in the future, one should not say that it "was originally non-existent and now exists.

This intent refutes the notion that the eye comes from a fire-wheel, or from primordial nature (*svabhāva*), or from the Lord (*īśvara*), such that when the eye-faculty ceases, it would again create and accumulate those [causes].
To clarify the correct principle, it is further stated:
"That which was originally non-existent now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence.
Because the effect is not present within the cause, it is said to be "originally non-existent"; alternatively, it is said to "now exist" with reference to its functional activity.
Furthermore, consciousness arises only when two conditions are present; as it is said in the Sūtra:
"Consciousness arises dependent on two conditions.
As the Sūtra states:
Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms; likewise, up to mental consciousness arising conditioned by the mind and mental phenomena.
If future things did not truly exist, the consciousness that takes them as its object would lack two of its necessary conditions.

Since it has been stated that two conditions can produce consciousness, this means that only the real and the provisional bases function as the faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) respectively in order to produce consciousness; for these two take those very [bases] as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and there is nothing that cannot be subsumed under these two conditions.
From this it is known that the Buddha has already skillfully refuted [the view] that consciousness cannot arise even when taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.
Since consciousness can also arise by taking the past and future as its objects, we know that the substance of the past and future is truly existent.
Furthermore, because all consciousnesses must necessarily have an object— meaning that consciousness can only arise when there is an object to be perceived—
as the Blessed One said:
"The distinct discernment of various respective objective characteristics is called the aggregate of consciousness."
What is it that is cognized? It refers to everything from form (*rūpa*) up to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
That sūtra does not state that consciousness exists without an object.
From this it should be understood that because consciousnesses taking past and future objects as their conditions must necessarily have an object, the past and future exist substantially.
Furthermore, because past karma has future results; that is to say, wholesome and unwholesome karma previously performed awaits conditions to summon its future desirable or undesirable fruits.

Having already established at length in the investigation of karma that the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) does not arise immediately after the action, nor is the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) present at the time the future fruit arises;
if past phenomena were non-existent in their essence, it would follow that a fruit could arise without a cause, or else that such a fruit would never arise at all.
From this, one should know that the past and future truly exist.

Only those among both householders and renunciants who believe in the three time periods as previously explained, as well as in the three kinds of real unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), may rightfully call themselves Sarvāstivādins (Proponents of the Existence of All).
Because they teach that only such phenomena as these exist, they are accepted as the Sarvāstivāda school.
Others are not so, because they involve additions or subtractions.
Specifically, those who propound accretion claim that there exists a real *pudgala* (person) as well as the aforementioned phenomena.
The Vibhajyavādins maintain that only present phenomena and past karma that has not yet yielded its fruit exist.
The Kṣaṇikavādins maintain that only the substance of the twelve bases (āyatana) exists within a single present moment.
Proponents of the theory of provisional existence (prajñapti-sat) maintain that all phenomena existing in the present world are also merely provisionally existent.
Proponents of the theory of universal non-existence maintain that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and are entirely like flowers in the sky.
None of these [schools] assert that "all exists" (sarvāstivāda) in the sense intended by the Sūtra.
When the Sūtra speaks generally of "all that exists," it refers to the twelve bases (āyatana); it never specifically states that only the present exists and that the past and future do not.
Since various sūtras state that the past and future exist, they are called "Sarvāstivāda" (Proponents of All Existence).

This term applies to all three time periods as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, those who maintain that only a small portion of the present exists should not call themselves Sarvāstivādins.

Just as those who propound that the present exists only nominally or that it is entirely non-existent cannot rightly call themselves Sarvāstivādins (Proponents of the Existence of All), so too should it be with them [the proponents of the three time periods], for their assertions contradict both the sacred teachings and correct reasoning.
In order to refute the real existence of a *pudgala* and to generally open up the scope of all knowable phenomena (*jñeya-dharma*), the Buddha spoke these words to a brahmin:
"All that exists consists solely of the twelve bases (*āyatana*)."
Therefore, the past and the future definitely exist as real entities.
Regarding this accepted Sarvāstivāda school, how many different lineages of masters have there been from antiquity?
And whose formulation of time (adhvan) is the most excellent and reliable?
The verse says:
Within this, there are four types: differences of category, characteristic, phase, and relative dependence;
the third, based on activity, establishes the "time periods" most excellently.
The treatise says:
The Venerable Dharmatrāta spoke thus:
"The distinctions between the three time periods arise from differences in their modes of existence."
He maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods (*adhvan*), they differ by way of their mode (*bhāva*) but not by way of their substance (*dravya*).
It is like when a golden vessel is broken to be fashioned into another object; although the shape differs, the substance remains unchanged.
Furthermore, just as when milk transforms into curd, it relinquishes its taste, potency, and so forth, but does not relinquish its color;

likewise, when these phenomena proceed through the time periods—moving from the future to the present and from the present into the past—they relinquish and acquire their categories (*jāti*), but do not relinquish or acquire their substance (*dravya*).
The Venerable Ghosaka stated as follows:
"The three time periods are distinct due to differences in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

He [asserts that] when dharmas proceed through the time periods, a past dharma is currently conjoined with its past characteristic, yet it is not said to be separated from its present and future characteristics."
The future is currently conjoined with the future aspect, yet it is not said to be separated from the aspects of the past and present.
The present is currently conjoined with the present aspect, yet it is not said to be separated from the aspects of the past and future.
Just as when a man is currently attached to one wife, he is not said to be detached from his other concubines,
so too did the Venerable Vasumitra state:
"The three time periods differ because their states are distinct."

He maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods (*adhvan*), they receive different designations at each successive stage; these differences arise from the distinction between stages, not from a difference in their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
It is like moving a single counting-stick: placed in the units place it is called "one," in the hundreds place it is called "hundred," and in the thousands place it is called "thousand."
The Venerable Buddhadeva asserts the following:
The distinctions among the three time periods arise from their mutual dependence.

He maintains that when dharmas proceed through the time periods, they are designated with different names based on their mutual relation as preceding or succeeding; it is not that there is any difference in their substance, category, or characteristics.
Just as a single woman is called a "daughter" when she is in relation to her predecessor and a "mother" when she is in relation to her successor, according to their respective order;

so too, when these dharmas proceed through time, they are called "past" in relation to the present and future, "future" in relation to the past and present, and "present" in relation to the past and future.

Regarding these four types of Sarvāstivādins, Paramārtha states that the first maintains that phenomena undergo transformation; therefore, he should be classified among the followers of the Sāṃkhya school.

Now, I say this is not so, for that Venerable One does not assert that the essence of conditioned phenomena is eternal, nor that when they traverse the three periods of time, the phenomenon itself becomes hidden or manifest.
It is merely stated that when various phenomena proceed through time, although their substantial forms (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) are identical, their essential natures (*svabhāva-jāti*) differ.
This is consistent with the position of the Venerable Vasumitra; how could it be judged to be the same as the Sāṃkhya heretics?

The second and fourth [theories] establish the characteristics of the time periods as being intermingled; therefore, among these four, the third is the most excellent, because it establishes distinctions among the time periods based on differences in the states of functional activity, and the differences in the time periods are established by virtue of these differing states.
As I have argued, the actual existence of the past and future does not contradict the nature of reality (dharmatā) and is permitted by the sacred teachings (āgama).
To deny the past and future would contradict the nature of reality and constitute a repudiation of the sacred teachings, resulting in many faults.

From this, it should be understood that the Venerable Vasumitra’s establishment of the real existence of the past and future accords with reason and conforms to the sūtras, such that no one can shake it.
For that Venerable One spoke thus:
"The Buddha stated in the sūtras that there are three time periods; how are these three times differentiated and established?"
The distinctions among the three time periods are established based on activity.

That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have not yet manifested their activity are called "future"; when they possess activity, they are called "present"; and when their activity has already ceased, they are called "past. There is no difference in their substantial essence.
What is the referent of this term "activity" (*kāritra*)?
It refers to the capacity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) to project an effect;
that is, it has the sense of being able to function as a causal nature at the time another entity arises.

If one can establish distinctions among the time periods based on this, or can provide other faultless arguments for their differentiation, the wise should recognize such a person as one who discerns the principles of reality.

Conversely, if there are those who, due to delusion regarding the principles for establishing the distinctions between time periods, abandon the sacred word out of fear of others' objections; or who misrepresent definitive sūtras as being of interpretable meaning; or who assert that while the present exists, the past and future do not; or who maintain that even the present is merely conventionally existent; or who altogether deny the existence of all three time periods—these all contradict the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, and the wise should reject them as people deluded about the principles.

Nevertheless, for my part, I shall follow the Venerable Vasumitra in establishing the distinctions of the three time periods based on functional activity (*kāritra*), and I shall refute various objections according to my own capacity.
Thus, the doctrine that the three time periods truly exist is established; all wise persons should follow this with faith and study it.

Having already explained how the latent dispositions (anuśaya) bind such objects at such stages, one should further investigate: when an object has not yet been abandoned, is it necessarily bound by them?
Conversely, if an object is bound by them, is it necessarily un-abandoned?

If a thing has not been abandoned, one is necessarily bound by it; however, there are things by which one is bound without them being unabandoned. What are the characteristics of such binding that is not non-abandonment?
The verse says:
Regarding those [defilements] already abandoned upon seeing suffering, The remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take this as their object [are what bind].
"And although what was previously abandoned in the preceding chapter has been cut off, one is still bound to it by remaining conditions.
The treatise says:

For instance, during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, the various entities (*vastu*) to be abandoned through the seeing of suffering have already been cut off; however, if the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatragānuśaya*) to be eliminated through the seeing of origin have not yet been permanently severed, those [dispositions] that can take these [entities] as objects remain bound to them.

Furthermore, at whichever stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) a particular path arises, among the nine grades of objects, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet been abandoned—which can take as their object those things already abandoned by the preceding grade—remain bound to them.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to clarify that while the preceding [factors] have already been abandoned, the succeeding ones have not yet been abandoned, yet all are capable of binding.

Regarding which objects are increased by how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), one need only analyze the characteristics of the objects of cognition here; that is, by analyzing which phenomena are the objects of which consciousnesses, it will be easily understood that these bound objects definitely possess such-and-such a number of latent dispositions increasing therein.
Furthermore, how many categories of phenomena (*dharma*) and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are there?

Although phenomena are numerous, they are briefly categorized as sixteen: the five classes of the three realms (*dhātu*) along with the untainted (*anāsrava*). The number and names of the consciousnesses that can take these as objects are likewise the same.
Among these, which dharmas serve as the objects of how many consciousnesses?
The verse says:
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, if they are bound to the desire realm—
The three [realms] of one's own sphere and one [realm] of the formless are the objects of untainted consciousness.
The three [realms] of one's own sphere and those below are the objects of each of the three [types of] form-sphere consciousness; the one [realm] above is the object of pure consciousness.
The formless realm is common to all three spheres, and each of its three [levels] is the object of pure consciousness.
Those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path all increase the objects of their own respective consciousnesses.
Within the three realms, the latter three pure consciousnesses are the objects of the untainted [consciousness].
The Treatise says:

If one considers the factors bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation, each is the object of five consciousnesses. These are: the three belonging to its own realm (as previously described), one from the form realm—namely that which is abandoned through cultivation—and the fifth, the untainted [consciousness], because all of these are capable of taking them as objects.

Furthermore, regarding the phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are three types of consciousness within their own realm that take them as objects: namely, all [consciousness] abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm; the universal [consciousness] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; and the wholesome and neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm. As for the wholesome consciousness abandoned through cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is not the others.

Within untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), it should be understood accordingly that only those factors belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna-pakṣa*)—which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin and through cultivation—are so characterized.

Regarding those bound to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), each of the three aforementioned groups of factors is the object of eight consciousnesses; that is to say, the three [groups] of its own and lower realms are as previously stated, and the one [group] of the higher realm—which is abandoned through cultivation—and the eighth, the untainted, are all capable of taking them as objects.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) bound by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are the objects of three consciousnesses of their own realm and one consciousness of the higher realms, this should be understood according to the previous explanation.

As for their being the objects of three consciousnesses of the lower realm, these refer to the wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin (*samudaya*), which take the upper realms as their object, as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and, if untainted (*anāsrava*), only those belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The abandonment through cultivation by seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) should be understood accordingly.

If they are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpya-pratisaṃyukta*), then each of the three groups of dharmas previously mentioned is the object of ten consciousnesses; that is to say, the three [groups] of each of the three realms are as previously explained, and the tenth, the untainted (*anāsrava*), is included because all are capable of taking them as objects.

Following the analogy of those factors bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), one should understand that for all factors abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), each should be understood to increase by one additional consciousness as its object.
Furthermore, how is this so?

That is to say, those factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) serve as objects for six consciousnesses. The five [sensory] consciousnesses are as previously described; to these are added the consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and by the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).

By extension of this principle, it should be understood that those factors bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path serve as objects for ninety-one or eighty-one consciousnesses respectively; the eighty are as previously described, with each adding its own corresponding consciousness.

If uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas serve as objects for ten consciousnesses—namely, the three final categories within each of the three realms (i.e., those consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation), plus the tenth, which is uncontaminated—they are all capable of taking them as objects.
That which has not been explained in detail should be contemplated as appropriate.

One should keep the sixteen factors briefly established above in mind and investigate the objects (*vastu*) upon which the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase; fearing that the text would become too prolix, I shall provide only a brief indication of the general direction.
Furthermore, it may be asked:
within the objects to which they are bound, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in association with the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?

One should observe that the eye-faculty, in its entirety, possesses only two [types of] underlying tendencies; namely, those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) respectively. These increase in association with the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire and form realms, as well as their universal (*sarvatraga*) underlying tendencies, according to what is applicable.
If someone were to ask:
"Regarding the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object, how many kinds of latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with it?

One should observe that this consciousness consists of eight types in total: namely, three types each in the desire realm and the form realm—specifically, those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, those abandoned through the universal concomitants, and those abandoned through cultivation—which together constitute six types.

One [consciousness] belongs to the formless realm: namely, the wholesome consciousness included within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The eighth, the untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness, both take the eye faculty as their object.
Furthermore, it should be understood that all untainted consciousnesses are definitely not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Regarding the first seven [categories], they correspondingly increase through the three classes of each of the desire and form realms, as well as by the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.

Specifically, for a consciousness associated with the pervasive [defilements] to be abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that is bound to the desire realm, the pervasive latent dispositions to be abandoned through seeing suffering and the pervasive latent dispositions to be abandoned through seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase. One should understand that this is reversed for consciousnesses to be abandoned through seeing the origin and consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The manner in which the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation and those that are universal increase in association should be understood accordingly.

As for the three consciousnesses of the form realm and the wholesome consciousness of the formless realm, they can take the eye-faculty of the fourth dhyāna as their object; therein, the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm and those that are universal increase in association.
Furthermore, if it is asked:
"With respect to the eye-faculty as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), how many kinds of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with that consciousness?

One should observe that there are thirteen kinds of such consciousness: namely, four consciousnesses for each of the three realms—excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*)—which together constitute twelve, plus the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) that can take the eye-faculty as its object-condition.

This applies as appropriate to the four categories within the three realms, excluding the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).

That is to say, a consciousness associated with the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm can take the eye faculty as its object; such a consciousness may be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.

The wholesome and neutral consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) and through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-heyā*), as well as the wholesome consciousnesses of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) abandoned through cultivation, together with the untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*), take these as their objects. Regarding these various consciousnesses that take the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) as their object, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—namely, those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin, those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm, and those to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm, along with their universal [tendencies]—increase accordingly.
The remaining cases should be explained accordingly as appropriate.
Even an untainted consciousness that takes the eye faculty as its object may be bound by the three realms.

Regarding these various consciousnesses that take the eye faculty as their object—namely, the untainted consciousnesses abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the wholesome untainted consciousnesses abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)—the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation within the three realms increase in accordance with their respective objects.

If one were to separately enumerate the twelve aforementioned types [of consciousness], each would have a corresponding number of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in association with them.

It should be stated that for the consciousnesses that take all objects and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the increase of all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions.

The reverse of this should be understood: for consciousness abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and consciousness abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation and all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) ones increase.
For consciousness abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the path and all pervasive ones increase.

However, regarding the untainted (anāsrava) objects, there is only binding through association (saṃprayoga-bandhana); for the remainder, they merely increase [affliction] by way of being objects (ālambana-anuśaya).

Based on this, one should understand the distinctions between the form (rūpa) and formless (ārūpya) realms. Regarding the consciousnesses to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya), those of the desire realm and the higher realms should be understood respectively as having the categories of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) as their objects. As for the consciousness perceiving the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), other instances of what is bound should be considered analogously to the example of the eye.
Now, within this context, one should further investigate: if a mind is said to be "with latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because of them, do those dispositions necessarily increase within that mind?
This is not certain; for while those latent dispositions increase as long as they have not been abandoned, they do not so increase once they have been abandoned.
As stated in the treatise:
"In relation to this mind, those [defilements] may either increase or not increase.
How do they increase?"
This means that those latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with this mind and take it as their object, yet have not been abandoned.
How is it that they do not increase?
This means that those latent dispositions are associated with this mind, but have already been permanently severed.
What is called "a mind with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya-citta*)?
On what basis is the term "with latent dispositions" established?
Furthermore, by virtue of what is it designated as "with latent dispositions"?

Furthermore, regarding what was previously stated—that there are fifteen types of consciousness, five for each of the three realms, termed "minds accompanied by latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*)—each of these minds is of two kinds.

This is because there are distinctions between those that are universal and non-universal, and those that have outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) objects, as well as between defiled and non-defiled minds.

The designation "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) is established based on two meanings: first, because [the mind] is increased by the latent dispositions that follow it; second, because the latent dispositions serve as its companions.
It is called "possessing latent dispositions" by virtue of these latent dispositions.

The associated latent dispositions (anuśaya) are both abandoned and unabandoned; however, only those whose objects (ālambana) are unabandoned are said to have a mind "possessed of latent dispositions" (sānuśaya).
How is it that the afflictions associated with the mind continue to increase within the mind until they are abandoned?

That is to say, those latent dispositions (anuśaya) are able to give rise to acquisition (prāpti), which acts as an obstruction within the mental continuum; furthermore, they serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) for future lives, because they induce the arising of the mind and its concomitants as a continuous stream of similar effect (niṣyanda).

Up until they have been abandoned, it is said that [the afflictions] increase in accordance with the mind; once abandoned, this is not the case, as there is no longer the sense of "increasing in accordance.

It is not by virtue of being abandoned that they cause [the mind] to be separated from them; therefore, although they have already been abandoned, they are still said to exist [in relation to the mind], because their nature as auxiliary companions cannot be destroyed.
