This means that the power of the antidote is able to obstruct the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) within the mental continuum so that they do not manifest, and it is also able to obstruct the acquisition (*prāpti*) induced by them so that it does not act as a constraint upon the mental continuum; therefore, it is said that they have been "abandoned."

There is no principle by which the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated [with a mind] would fail to increase; for the power of the antidote cannot obstruct the nature of the latent dispositions as concomitants. Therefore, even though they have been abandoned, that mind is said to possess latent dispositions.

If the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the mind as their object have not been abandoned, they increase in accordance with the abandonment or non-abandonment of those dispositions toward the mind; therefore, the mind is always designated as "possessing latent dispositions.

However, if those latent dispositions taking the mind as their object have already been abandoned, the mind is no longer called "possessing latent dispositions" on account of them, because the power of the Path has caused the mind to become free from those latent dispositions.

Although they serve as associates (*sahāya*) and as objects (*ālambana*), neither can be separated from them by the power of the Path; however, because they are more remote than their respective associates and objects, this designation [of "defiled"] is applied solely with respect to what has not yet been abandoned.
The nature of being an associate (*sahāya*) is also called "existence" (*bhava*).

In this context, the mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is said to be "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) because the ignorance and the view of a self-identity that are associated with it increase as its associates.

Because those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the remaining [truths] (i.e., the origin and cessation) are exclusively of the nature of pervasive increase within their own category, they are termed "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*). The remainder are neither, and therefore do not possess them.
The other minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin—whether pervasive or non-pervasive—should be considered accordingly.

The mind associated with wrong view that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because of the nature of its accompanying factors—namely, the ignorance and wrong view that increase along with it through association.

It is also called "possessing latent dispositions" because of the nature of those factors belonging to its own category which take tainted objects as their focus and increase exclusively through universal increase.
The remainder are neither; therefore, they do not exist [as such].

As for the other [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, whether they take uncontaminated objects or contaminated objects as their focus, they should be analyzed accordingly, following the same principle.

A mind associated with craving that is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation is called "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) due to the nature of its concomitants—namely, the ignorance and craving that increase along with it.
It is also called "possessing latent dispositions" by virtue of the nature of increase alone, through other factors of its own category and all universal factors.
The remaining cases are neither, and therefore do not possess them.
One should likewise analyze, as appropriate, the minds associated with the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those non-defiled minds abandoned through cultivation are said to "possess latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) by virtue of the nature of being increased by the latent dispositions belonging to their own category and those that are universal.
All that has been discussed thus far refers to the state where [the defilements] have not yet been abandoned.
If they have been abandoned and yet possess a concomitant nature (*sahāya-bhāva*), then they are said to be "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) solely by virtue of that concomitant nature.
Based on this method of exposition, a brief explanation should be provided.
The verse says:
There are two types of minds with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), namely those that are defiled and those that are undefiled.
A defiled mind is associated with both [types of *anuśaya*], whereas an undefiled mind is restricted to those that increase (*anuśerate*).
The treatise states:
There are two general types of minds accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), distinguished as defiled and non-defiled.

Among these, when the latent dispositions associated with a defiled mind have not yet been abandoned, they possess both [types of] concomitance (*samprayoga*) and object-condition (*ālambana*). However, in the case of the object-condition, it is only one.
When [the defilements] have already been abandoned, there is one [defilement] associated with the mind, but none at all as objects.
Regarding those afflictions belonging to an undefiled mind, they are said to possess "latent dispositions" (anuśaya) only during the state in which they have not yet been abandoned.
Once abandoned, they are entirely non-existent, as they are not associated [with the mind].

These latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take non-defiled objects are abandoned either prior to the mind or simultaneously with it; those that take defiled objects are abandoned either before, after, or simultaneously with the mind. Those that are associated with the mind are necessarily abandoned simultaneously with it.
Therefore, those that are defiled pertain to both [categories] and are termed "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).
Those that are undefiled pertain exclusively to one [category], possessing the nature of being subject to increase (*anuśayana*). *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle 26.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra, Fascicle Twenty-Seven.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The Sixth Chapter on the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya), Part Three: Regarding the ten types of latent dispositions explained above, in what order do they arise—what comes before and what comes after?
There is no fixed sequence for the arising of the various latent dispositions, as it is possible for all of them to arise after any other.
Nevertheless, there is a class of afflictions that manifest in a sequence where preceding and succeeding states draw one another along;
regarding this class, the verse explaining their order says:
Ignorance, doubt, wrong view, the view of a self, the view of extremes, attachment to precepts and rituals, and the grasping at views.
Greed, pride, and hatred arise sequentially, with each preceding one inducing the subsequent.
The commentary states:
Regarding the sequential arising of those afflictions, first, due to ignorance, one lacks understanding of the truths and has no desire to contemplate suffering, up to the truth of the path.
Because they lack understanding, they possess no capacity for discernment; having heard both sides, they harbor doubt as to whether it is suffering or not suffering—and so on, in detail.
If they encounter false doctrines, they give rise to wrong views and deny the existence of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
To speak at length: having already denied the existence of suffering within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), one consequently gives rise to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

From this, one further clings to the notions of the self as being either annihilated or eternal; adhering to one extreme or the other, one reckons it to be the means to purification, regarding such a conception as supreme.

Having seen [another's] views, one gives rise to greed based on their perceived virtues; one gives rise to pride by thinking "this is superior" and relying upon it; and one gives rise to hatred toward others based on conflicting views—just as those who cling to the view of a self-soul harbor animosity toward the view of non-self. Alternatively, within the process of adopting or abandoning one's own views, one must necessarily give rise to hatred and resentment toward what is being abandoned.
This explanation of the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as they arise in succession is based on one particular school;
in reality, the sequence in which the afflictions (*kleśa*) operate is boundless, because the conditions upon which they depend differ.
By how many causes and conditions do the various afflictions arise?
There are many such causes and conditions for their arising; however, according to their coarseness and preeminence, there are essentially only three.
The verse says:
Because the latent dispositions have not been abandoned, because the corresponding objects appear,
and because improper mental attention arises, it is said that the afflictions possess their full causes and conditions.
The treatise says:
The various afflictions arise due to three causes and conditions.

For example, when a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire is about to arise: because the latent tendency of sensual desire has not been abandoned and has not been fully understood; because an object conducive to sensual desire has appeared before one; and because improper mental attention directed toward that object arises—thereby other latent tendencies arise as well.
One should understand that it is analogous to this.

Regarding those who have not yet abandoned or fully understood the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), they are said to have not abandoned or fully understood it due to three conditions: namely, because they have not attained its abandonment, because its antidote has not yet arisen, and because the object has not been fully understood.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abandonment: first, abandonment with remainder; second, abandonment without remainder.
Therefore, the expressions "not yet abandoned" and "not yet fully known" are used.

This explains that latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise through the power of their causes: when an object conducive to sensual desire manifests before one, that is, when a real object favorable to the fetters of sensual desire is present, sensual desire arises accordingly.
This explains that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise through the power of their objects.

Regarding those that arise by taking improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) as their condition: it is like a piece of wood as an object appearing before one, and like a fire-drill; when improper mental attention acts as the drill upon the wood of the object, the fire of sensual desire arises.
In this context, what is called "unwise attention" (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*)?

It refers to the perception of a woman manifested through exquisite clothing, flower garlands, ornaments, scented unguents, painted decorations, and graceful postures; and the perception of a sentient being arising toward a heap of excrement. The perverted arousal of the mind that sustains these perceptions is termed unwise attention.
This explains that latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise through the power of application (*prayoga*).
If the arising of latent dispositions requires three causes and conditions, how can one admit the falling away (*parihāṇi*) of an Arhat?

It is not the case that an Arhat’s latent dispositions have not been abandoned; furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that the manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*) must occur for one to be designated as having fallen away from Arhatship.
However, this is merely based on the fact that [the subsequent mind] is immediately induced by preceding afflictions; therefore, there is no fault in the statement.
Generally, there are two ways in which afflictions arise: first, they are immediately induced by afflictions; second, they arise from other factors that are not afflictions.
If it were otherwise, afflictions would not arise immediately after a wholesome or neutral state of mind.
This argument does not concern the arising of subsequent states; therefore, one should not raise the objection based on retrogression.

Alternatively, this is stated provisionally based on the presence of all causal conditions; in reality, there are those that arise solely by relying on the power of the object (*ālambana-bala*) and lack the power of a cause.

As for the power of application (*prayoga-bala*), it refers to the aforementioned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) together with their attendants, which the Buddha described as the outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*).
The outflows (āsrava) refer to the three outflows: first, the outflow of desire (kāmāsrava); second, the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava); and third, the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava).
There are four floods (ogha): first, the flood of desire; second, the flood of existence; third, the flood of views (dṛṣṭyogha); and fourth, the flood of ignorance.
The yokes (yoga) refer to the four yokes, as explained in the section on the floods (ogha).

Appropriations (upādāna) refer to the four appropriations: first, the appropriation of sensual desire; second, the appropriation of views; third, the appropriation of precepts and observances; and fourth, the appropriation of the theory of self.
What is the nature of these outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth?
The verse says:
The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, together with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), excluding ignorance (*moha*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The outflows (*āsrava*) of the two upper realms consist solely of afflictions (*kleśa*), excluding ignorance (*moha*).
Because they share the same neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature, their antidotes, and their status as meditative stages (*samāhitabhūmi*), they are combined into one.
Since ignorance is the root of all existence (*bhava*), it is established separately as a distinct outflow.

The floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga) are likewise; they are established separately because views are particularly sharp and because views do not accord with abiding. They are not established as independent outflows (āsrava).
The yokes of desire and existence, together with delusion, are divided into two categories called "grasping" (upādāna).
Ignorance is not established separately because it is not a grasper.
The treatise says:

The forty-one entities consisting of the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm, excluding delusion (*moha*), are collectively termed the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*); that is, the thirty-one fundamental afflictions bound to the desire realm together with the ten envelopments.

The fifty-two entities consisting of the afflictions of the form and formless realms, excluding ignorance, are collectively termed "outflows" (*āsrava*). That is to say, there are twenty-six fundamental afflictions in each of the two upper realms. Although torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) also exist in the form and formless realms, these enveloping afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) should not be categorized according to the realms, as the enveloping afflictions of the upper realms are few and lack autonomy.

For this reason, the *āsravas* (outflows) are spoken of solely as afflictions (*kleśa*). If the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) were also categorized according to the realms (*dhātu*), the substance of the *āsravas* would then consist of fifty-six [factors].
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states: "What are the *āsravas*?"

This refers to the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to the two realms—the form and formless realms—excluding ignorance (*avidyā*).
For what reason are the afflictions of these two realms combined and designated as a single "tainted" (*sāsrava*) category?
Because they share the same neutral nature (*avyākṛta*), the same antidote (*pratipakṣa*), and the same stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*),
and because they also take visible form, sound, and tangibles as their objects, it should not be said that they function solely within the internal door.
By implication, the fifteen types of ignorance within the three realms constitute the essence of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*); therefore, they are not mentioned separately in the verse.
For what reason is this alone established as a distinct "outflow"?
It is to manifest that the affliction of ignorance possesses a particularly grave fault.
This means that ignorance alone is capable of acting as the root of birth and death, as stated in the Sūtra:
"With ignorance as the cause, craving and defilement arise," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"All evil destinies, both in this world and in other worlds, have ignorance as their root and are originated by craving.

Herein, it is based on their predominance that one hundred and eight afflictions are specifically designated as "outflows" (*āsrava*). This means that non-defiled volitions, resentment, and so forth are not included among the outflows; rather, it is these afflictions alone that cause sentient beings to linger long in *saṃsāra*, or cause them to circulate within *saṃsāra* from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci Hell. Because they possess such powerful efficacy and are easily understood, they are explained here exclusively.

The nature of the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) is identical to that of the outflows (*āsrava*); however, among them, the views (*dṛṣṭi*) are established separately. That is to say, the aforementioned outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is itself the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*); likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is itself the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) and the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*).
The reason for extracting the various views (*dṛṣṭi*) to establish them as the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) and the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*) is that they are particularly violent.

That is to say, the meanings of "flooding," "yoking," and "grasping" are established for the floods, yokes, and graspings; like other afflictions, with the exception of ignorance (*avidyā*), they all mutually assist one another to be able to flood, yoke, and grasp.

The various views (*dṛṣṭi*) are likewise; because they are so intense, they can, even without the assistance of other factors, cause one to drift away from what is correct and adhere to what is false. Therefore, they are established separately as floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, all afflictions cause sentient beings to drift and sink into defiled phenomena and depart from all wholesome qualities. Ignorance (*avidyā*) and views produce surging waves of non-understanding and false understanding, violently tossing sentient beings further and further away from the wholesome; for this reason, ignorance and views are established separately in this context.
If that is so, why not establish "outflow of views" (dṛṣṭy-āsrava) as a separate category?
That which causes one to abide [in saṃsāra] is called an "outflow," as will be explained later.
Views do not conform to this definition, because their meaning is distinct.

That is to say, they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they cause both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) alike to remain within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Since various views (*dṛṣṭi*) lack this capacity to cause the noble ones to remain [in *saṃsāra*], their meaning as "outflows" is incomplete; therefore, they are not established separately.

Regarding the meaning of "drifting" (*plava*), there is a distinction between noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); therefore, in the latter three categories, "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is established separately.

This is because these afflictions can cause ordinary beings to drift away from all wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*), potentially leading them to abandon them entirely; however, this cannot be said of noble ones.
Having caused them to drift, it brings all ordinary beings into union with various undesirable realms, destinies, and births, though it cannot do so for noble ones.
Having brought them into union, it causes all ordinary beings to lack anything they do not rely upon or cling to, whereas it does not do so for noble ones.
Because ordinary beings and noble ones perceive superiority within these three gates, they are established separately.
Other masters say:

because their vision is restless and sharp, they alone cannot accomplish the purpose of causing [the mind] to abide; therefore, they are established in conjunction with the other [gates] within the gateway of the outflows (*āsrava*).
If combined with others, they possess the capacity for persistence, just as when a young elephant is born from the binding of an elephant king.

Thus, twenty-nine factors have been shown to be called the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*): namely, five types each of greed, hatred, and pride; four types of doubt; and ten types of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
Twenty-eight factors are called the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*): namely, ten each for attachment and pride, and eight for doubt.
If torpor and restlessness are added, they become thirty-two, because there are two of each in both the form and formless realms.
The thirty-six factors are called the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*); that is, twelve views in each of the three realms.
The fifteen factors are called the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*); that is, five types of ignorance in each of the three realms.
One should know that the four yokes (*yoga*) are identical to the floods (*ogha*). One should know that the four graspings (*upādāna*) are identical in substance to the four yokes.

However, desire (*kāma*) and the discourse on self (*ātman-vāda*) each include ignorance (*avidyā*), while views (*dṛṣṭi*) are divided into two; these differ from the preceding yokes. Specifically, the former yoke of desire, together with the ignorance of desire, consists of thirty-four factors collectively termed the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*): namely, greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance—five of each—and doubt (four), along with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

That is to say, the previously mentioned yokes (*yoga*), together with the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the two realms, constitute thirty-eight entities collectively termed "clinging to the discourse of self" (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*): namely, ten each for craving (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance, and eight for doubt (*vicikitsā*).
If torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are added, they become forty-two.

Within the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*), excluding the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the remaining thirty entities are collectively termed the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The six excluded entities are termed the clinging to precepts and observances; this is because it alone acts as an enemy to the Noble Path and deceives both the laity and the ordained alike.
Why is ignorance (*avidyā*) not established separately as "clinging" (*upādāna*)?
The term "clinging" is established based on the sense of being an active grasper; however, various forms of ignorance are not active graspers.
That which is defined as the non-comprehension of characteristics is called ignorance, and it is not an active grasper because it lacks intensity.
However, they may be combined with others and established as "grasping" (*upādāna*).

Having already explained the ten kinds of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) along with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the Sūtra speaks of them as outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*).
What is the meaning of these designations, such as "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
Subtle, twofold increase, pursuing, and binding;
"Dwelling, flowing, drifting, uniting, and grasping—these are the meanings of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth.
The treatise says:
When the fundamental afflictions manifest, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are difficult to discern; therefore, they are called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
Therefore, the noble Ānanda said:
"I do not know now whether I have given rise to pride toward my fellow practitioners of the holy life.

He did not say that it was entirely absent, for since the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*) is subtle, he himself could not yet discern whether such pride existed or not, let alone ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Other examples should be understood accordingly.
One explanation holds that even within a single moment, the atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses "increase" (*anuśaya*), and is therefore called "subtle.
As for the two types of increase, they refer to the fact that [the defilements] increase both with respect to their objects (*ālambana*) and their associated factors (*saṃprayukta*).
How do afflictions increase through association with and adherence to their objects?
This has already been explained previously; alternatively, it is like an enemy seeking out a vulnerability or like the poison of a glance.
One should understand that afflictions have the sense of "increasing" (*anuśaya*) with respect to their own objects, just as a red-hot iron ball can heat water or like the touch of poison.
One should understand that afflictions have the sense of "increasing" with respect to their own associated factors; both cases are like a nurse who causes an infant to grow.

Just as a wet nurse can cause an infant to grow and gradually accumulate skills, so too do the objects of perception (*ālambana*) and mental associations (*samprayoga*) cause the various afflictions (*kleśa*) to continue increasing and to be accumulated.
"Following along" (*anubandha*) means that from beginningless time, it has arisen within the continuum and persists as an acquisition (*prāpti*).
"Binding along" (*anubaddha*) refers to its extreme difficulty to abandon, like a quartan fever or the venom of a rat.
Some say that "concomitant bondage" refers to the constant following [of the afflictions], just as the movement of seawater follows the movement of its reflection in the sky.
For these aforementioned reasons, the ten types of afflictions are established under the name of *anuśaya* (latent dispositions).

To explain this term by way of its etymological derivation (*nirukti*): it is called an "underlying tendency" (*anuśaya*) because it lies dormant within the continuum of one who follows the stream; that is, it signifies the state of dwelling within the body of one who flows along, increasing dullness and stagnation.

Alternatively, they are called *anuśaya* because they lie dormant within the continuum of the Victorious One; that is, they have the sense of being a state of delusion regarding the stage of entering into reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
Or, they are called *anuśaya* because they pursue sentient beings for a long time within the prison [of cyclic existence] and conceal them.

Why are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) only the ten beginning with greed and not others such as anger? It is because only these ten types of habitual tendencies are firm and stable, whereas those such as anger are not;

they cause sentient beings to linger long in *saṃsāra*, or cause them to wander within *saṃsāra* from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci Hell. Because their continuity leaks faults inexhaustibly through the six wounds [the sense organs], they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*). Because they violently sweep away wholesome qualities, they are called "floods" (*ogha*). Because they bind one to the realms, destinies, and births, they are called "yokes" (*yoga*). Because they grasp at various individual existences (*ātman*), they are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
The ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) along with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) have already been explained.
The Blessed One has also spoken of them as outflows (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*). Are they only these many, or are there others?
The verse says:
Due to the distinctions among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, they are further said to be of five kinds.
The treatise states:

"Because there are differences in meaning among these various afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely, the fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*)—they are further said to be of five kinds."
Furthermore, what are the fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
The verse says:
The fetters are nine; because their objects, nature, and so forth are equal, the two fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and grasping (*parāmarśa*) are established.
Because these two are exclusively unwholesome and arise independently, among the *paryavasthānas*,
only envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are established as two separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, it is because they frequently occur together, and because they are the causes of low birth and poverty.
Because they fully manifest the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and because they disturb both groups [of practitioners].

The treatise says: There are nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*): first, the fetter of craving; second, the fetter of hostility; third, the fetter of pride; fourth, the fetter of ignorance; fifth, the fetter of views; sixth, the fetter of grasping; seventh, the fetter of doubt; eighth, the fetter of envy; and ninth, the fetter of avarice.
Because these nine possess the power to bind one to objects and to rebirth, they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
As the Sūtra says:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that it is not the eye that binds to forms, nor are forms that bind to the eye."
"Attachment" (saṃyojana) refers to the desire and greed present therein.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"All classes of foolish worldlings, those ordinary persons who have not heard [the Dharma], are born because of fetters and die because of fetters."
Because of these fetters (*saṃyojana*), one goes from this world to that world.
Because their presence causes sentient beings to encounter manifold sufferings, they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*); for they serve as the foundation upon which all these afflictions rest.
Among these, the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) refers to greed within the three realms; this is categorized according to its basis (*āśraya*) and its object (*ālambana*).
If it causes the mind to feel aversion toward formations (*saṃskāra*) comprised of disagreeable perceptions or the desire for separation, it is called the fetter of hostility (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
Pride refers to the seven types of pride, as previously explained.
As for the "fetter of ignorance," it refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the three realms; this is defined in terms of its basis (*āśraya*), not its object (*ālambana*).
Because all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*), ignorance (*avidyā*) likewise takes them as its object.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) refers to the three views;
the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) refers to the two graspings.

For what reason are the three views established separately as the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), while the two graspings are established separately as the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
It is because the three views and the two graspings are equal in terms of their substance and their grasping.
That is to say, those three views consist of eighteen substances, and the two graspings are likewise; therefore, they are called "equal in substance."
What is the benefit of stating that these things are equivalent in meaning?
It is because they are seen to be beneficial within the context of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The intent of this statement is as follows: just as greed, hatred, and so forth can each individually constitute the function of a single fetter, so too do the three views and the two graspings—each consisting of eighteen entities—combine to collectively constitute the function of a single fetter.
If it were otherwise, one would have to state that each of the five views constitutes a separate fetter, just as greed, hatred, and so forth do.
Therefore, since views and grasping each consist of eighteen entities, they must be established together as a single fetter in order to correspond with greed and the other [fetters].

If that is so, then the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) each consist of eighteen entities; since the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) likewise consist of eighteen, are they not equal in terms of their constituent entities?
Not so; the original explanation establishes the principle with certainty.
Why is this? Because they are equal in terms of grasping and so forth.

The three views and so forth are the grasped objects (*grāhya*), while the two graspings and so forth are the grasper (*grāhaka*), because there is a distinction between the grasped object and the grasper.

That is to say, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one clings to them as having a self, as being eternal or annihilated, or denies their existence; subsequently, one gives rise to the two graspings, clinging to the view as supreme or as pure, because it is not confused with others.
This explanation is excellent.
Some say it is because of objects, sounds, and so forth;
others say that for those who are attached to existence and wealth, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) has a predominant binding function toward them.
If there is one who is greedily attached to the bliss of nirvāṇa, the fetter of attachment exerts a predominant influence of binding upon them.
As for the fetter of doubt, it refers to hesitation regarding the Four Noble Truths; this is distinct from wisdom and possesses a separate ontological essence.

That which causes the mind to lack joy is termed *īrṣyā* (envy); this is distinct from *dveṣa* (hatred) because it possesses a separate ontological essence (*dharmasvabhāva*). Thus, some explain envy as an intolerance of another's prosperity.
That which causes the mind to be stingily attached is termed *mātsarya* (avarice); that is to say, "May this not depart from me"—because it causes the mind to hold fast, it is called avarice.
For what reason are envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) alone established as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) among the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), and not the other envelopments?
If one posits eight envelopments, this explanation should be given:
these two are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) because they arise independently (*svatantra*).
This means that only these two possess both meanings, whereas among the remaining six, not a single one possesses both.
Although lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), they do not arise independently;
whereas regret (*kaukṛtya*) arises independently, it is not exclusively unwholesome.
The other two [categories] are entirely absent.
If one establishes ten *paryavasthānas*, the explanation should be as follows:

only the two faults of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are particularly grave; therefore, among the ten *paryavasthānas*, these two are established as *saṃyojanas* because these two types manifest with great frequency.
This refers to those born among the human and celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), in whom this envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) frequently manifest.

Furthermore, these two serve as causes for low status and poverty; that is, those born among the human and celestial realms of the desire realm are mostly oppressed by the heavy suffering of low status and poverty.
It is observed that those who are lowly and destitute of wealth are not even respected or loved by their closest relatives.

Furthermore, because envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) universally manifest the two types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), it should be understood that there are generally two kinds of secondary afflictions: first, those associated with dejection (*daurmanasya*), and second, those associated with joy (*saumanasya*); envy and avarice universally manifest these two characteristics.
Furthermore, these two [afflictions] are able to disturb both groups: namely, among the laity, they are extremely disturbing within the context of wealth and status due to envy and avarice;
whereas among those who have left the household life, they are extremely disturbing within the context of the teachings and practice due to envy and avarice.
Some are able to afflict the hosts of devas and asuras, meaning they cause extreme mutual disturbance due to the flavor of form (*rūpa-rasa*).
Others are able to afflict both the human and deva hosts, as the Blessed One told Kauśika:
"By the fetters of envy and stinginess, humans and devas are troubled and disturbed."
Alternatively, these two are able to afflict both oneself and others: through envy, one disturbs the circle of others, and through internal stinginess, one disturbs one's own companions.
Therefore, among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), these two are established as fetters (*saṃyojana*).
In other places, the Buddha, relying on the method of differentiation, spoke of five kinds using the term "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are five lower-tier fetters; By two of them, one does not transcend the desire realm.
Due to three [factors], one returns to the lower realms; because they encompass the gates and the faculties, there are three.

Alternatively, those who lack the aspiration for departure, those who are deluded regarding the path, and those who doubt the path—since these can obstruct progress toward liberation, only the abandonment of these three is taught.
The treatise says:

What are these five? They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*). These five kinds are conducive to the factors of the lower realm; therefore, they are called "lower-fettering" (*avarabhāgīya*).
However, the factors of the lower realm (avarabhāgīya-dharma) are briefly of two kinds:
first, the lower world, namely the desire realm (kāmadhātu);
second, lower sentient beings, namely all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Although one may have attained the noble Dharma, one cannot transcend the lower realms because of being bound by the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will.

Although one may be free from sensual desire, one cannot transcend the lower states of sentient existence because of being bound by the fetters of the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt.
All sentient beings dwell within the prison of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); desire-attachment and aversion are like the wardens, for by their restraint, one does not escape the prison.

The three views, beginning with the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), are like the patrol guards; even if one employs skillful means to transcend the prison of the desire realm, those three graspings place one back within the prison.
The fetters conducive to the lower realm (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana) consist of these five alone.

For one who has already seen the truths, it is logically consistent that they do not transcend the lower realm due to sensual desire (kāmarāga) and ill-will (pratigha), because these two are exclusively bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

Regarding those who have abandoned sensual desire: since one sees that all [fetters] to be abandoned through vision prevent sentient beings from transcending the lower realms, why did the Blessed One speak of only three?
Although this objection may be raised, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, briefly summarized the gates and faculties and spoke of only three.

Regarding the "comprehension by way of categories" (*saṃgraha-mukha*): there are three general types of afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*). Because one type pertains to two categories and another pertains to four categories, these three types are said to comprehend those three gates, as they manifest their respective classes.

Regarding the statement that [the latter] subsumes the [former] faculties: the three [views], beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), are the remaining three faculties. This is because the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) function respectively in accordance with the three superior faculties of the view of a self-identity, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*); therefore, it is said that these three [latter views] subsume those three faculties.
Therefore, there are only these five factors that accord with the lower realm.
Although those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) have abandoned six afflictions, for what reason are only the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) mentioned?
This is also because, as previously explained, they are subsumed under the gates of the faculties (*indriya*).

Although there is but one single penetration that applies to both categories, it cites their characteristics to reveal their essential nature; for this reason, it is said that these encompass those three gates.
Alternatively, other masters offer this explanation:
there are three kinds of obstacles for those traveling to a different region:
First, the lack of desire to set out: this refers to refraining from going because one perceives the faults and the excellence of other regions.
Second, being deluded regarding the right path: this refers to setting out despite one's intent, yet failing to reach that region due to following a deviant route.

Third is doubt regarding the right path; that is, being unacquainted with it, one sees two routes both frequented by many travelers and thus harbors hesitation toward the right path, wondering: "Is this the way to reach that destination, or is it not?"
It should be understood that those who aspire to liberation likewise encounter three similar obstacles.

Namely, due to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one perceives both the aggregates and nirvāṇa through the lens of grasping at self and annihilation, as well as clinging to virtues and faults; consequently, one lacks the desire to set out toward liberation.

Due to the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), although one seeks liberation, one becomes confused regarding the correct path; relying on worldly paths, one undergoes toil in vain and fails to reach *nirvāṇa*.

Due to doubt (*vicikitsā*), one is unable to observe correctly for oneself; seeing that many people practice various false paths, one harbors hesitation toward the true path, wondering whether this is the way to liberation or not.
The Buddha revealed that the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has eternally severed such obstacles to the path toward liberation; therefore, he spoke of "severing three.

Although those who hold the view of permanence do not proceed toward liberation, and those who view worldly paths as superior likewise lose the correct path, those who deny the existence of the noble path do not even believe in the correct path.

The first three [fetters] are the latter three faculties, because the latter three necessarily function in accordance with the former three; thus, by citing the root to encompass the branches, only the first three are mentioned.
As the Buddha taught five types of "lower-tier fetters" (*avarabhāgīya*) in other sūtras, he likewise taught five types of "upper-tier fetters" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
The verse says:

The fetters conducive to the higher realms are also five: attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, pride, and ignorance; for they prevent one from transcending the higher realms.
The Treatise says:
These five types consist of eight entities, as the three factors beginning with restlessness (auddhatya) also differ according to their realms.

Only those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are called "factors conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhvaṃbhāgīya), because they facilitate the higher realms; thus, they are termed "fetters conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhvaṃbhāgīya-saṃyojana).
They must be abandoned by the path of seeing, because they manifest only at that stage.

Since the afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing can also assist them in making one conform to the lower fetters as long as those afflictions have not been permanently severed, those that manifest only after the afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing have been permanently severed are called "conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).

Since it is stated here that there is greed for the form and formless realms and mention of "conducive to the higher," one knows that restlessness (*auddhatya*) and the others also pertain to the form and formless realms, and are not bound to the desire realm.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states exactly this:
"What are the dharmas of fetters (*saṃyojana*)?"
That is to say, the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*). What are the phenomena that are not fetters?
They are all phenomena other than those nine fetters.
By this it is established that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is partially a fetter (*saṃyojana*), namely that which is bound to the two upper realms;
and partially not a fetter, namely that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
That which is a fetter in one case is not a fetter in another: namely, for a noble one (ārya).
That which is not a fetter in one case is a fetter in another: namely, for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
That which is a fetter at one time is not a fetter at another: namely, for one who has already abandoned sensual desire (kāmarāga).
There are certain non-fetters, namely those who have not yet abandoned desire and greed.
Because such distinctions are indefinite, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* does not classify them as fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Because restlessness disturbs and agitates samādhi, it is established as a fetter among the higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
It is for this reason that torpor (*styāna*) is not mentioned among the higher-tier fetters, as it is conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fetters (*saṃyojana*) have already been explained; what then are the bonds (*bandhana*)?
The verse says:
"There are three bonds, arising from the three feelings."
The treatise states:
Because they are able to bind, they are designated by the name "bonds" (*bandhana*); this signifies their capacity to obstruct the progress toward the state of freedom from defilement.
Although there is no difference between the two characteristics of "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) and "bonds," three types of bonds are taught according to the *Mātṛkā*.
First is the bond of greed, second is the bond of hatred, and third is the bond of delusion.
Because the remaining categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*) are similar in nature, they are subsumed within these three:

namely, the five views and doubt are of the same category as delusion; the two fetters of pride and stinginess are of the same category as greed; and the fetter of envy is of the same category as hatred; therefore, they are all included within the three.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate what remains to be done by those who have already seen the Truths, the three bonds are taught; they bind the six groups of consciousness and place them within the prison of saṃsāra.
Moreover, because the Buddha specifically reveals coarse manifestations of affliction for those of inferior wisdom, he speaks only of the three bonds.
Other masters say:
Because they are induced by the power of the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), it is said that there are three bonds (*bandhana*).

That is to say, craving (*rāga*) for the most part increases in two ways—both as an object-condition (*ālambana*) and as an associated-condition (*samprayukta*)—with respect to one's own pleasant feeling.
To a small extent, it also increases in relation to the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling];

regarding one's own suffering and the happiness of others, it increases through both the object and the associated [factors], while only the single type of increase through the object occurs in relation to equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Hatred (*dveṣa*) also largely increases through both the object and the associated [factors] in relation to the object of one's own painful feeling; [in other cases, it increases] only through the object.
To a small extent, ignorance also increases with respect to neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling];
regarding one's own pleasure, others' pleasure, and others' pain, it increases with respect to only one type of object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Ignorance also largely increases with respect to two types—object-condition and association-condition (*samprayoga-pratyaya*)—in relation to one's own neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
To a small extent, one also experiences feelings of suffering within pleasant feelings;
as for all other feelings, they merely increase [affliction] by way of being objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Therefore, the Blessed One, relying on the principle of the majority of cases, taught that the three bonds (*bandhana*) are established in accordance with the three feelings.
What kind of craving and so forth are designated as "bonds" (*bandhana*) because they obstruct the progress toward freedom from passion?

It refers exclusively to those that are currently active (*samudācāra*). If it were otherwise, since all [defilements] would constitute the three types [of bonds], then progress toward freedom from passion would be absolutely obstructed.
The fetters have already been analyzed.
What, then, are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been explained previously.
The treatise says:
There are six, or seven, or ten, or ninety-eight latent dispositions, as has already been explained above.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been explained; what, then, are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
The verse says:
"The secondary afflictions are these others, the defiled mental factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)."
The treatise says:
They are called *kleśas* (afflictions) because they are capable of causing disturbance.
Those that function in accordance with the various *kleśas* receive the name *upakleśas* (secondary afflictions).
An ancient master said:

"If a phenomenon does not possess the full characteristics of a primary affliction (*kleśa*), it is called a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*), just as the moon, when not yet full, receives the name 'following the moon.
However, since the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are termed 'afflictions,' they also receive the name 'secondary afflictions,' because they belong to the category of complete afflictions."

For this reason, it is said that the various afflictions (*kleśa*) possess the meanings of fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and obsessions (*paryavasthāna*). As for the other defiled mental factors arising within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), they are called "secondary afflictions" because they afflict the mind; however, they are not called "afflictions" because they lack the complete characteristics of an affliction.
How many dharmas are designated by the term "secondary afflictions" (upakleśa)?
Since they are described in various ways in the sūtras, they are numerous; that is to say, they include outbursts of anger, intolerance, the utterance of harsh words, and so forth.
As the Blessed One told the brahmin:
"There are twenty-one secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that can disturb the mind," and so forth, as explained at length.
This shall be briefly analyzed later.
Regarding those included within the stains of the enveloping afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa-mala*), they should first be analyzed.
What are the characteristics of these envelopments?
The verse says:

The eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), along with regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*styāna*); or ten, when anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are added.
Shamelessness, avarice, and restlessness all arise from greed (*lobha*).
Lack of shame, sleep, and torpor arise from ignorance;
envy and anger arise from hatred; regret arises from doubt; and concealment and contention arise from greed.
The commentary says:
The root afflictions are also called "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*), because the Sūtra states that they take the envelopment of sensual desire as a condition.
If it were otherwise, how could greed and the other afflictions be designated as "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) afflictions?
However, various commentators, setting aside the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), speak of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) as being either eight or ten in number according to their prominence.

That is to say, the *Prakaraṇapāda* speaks of eight outbursts, while the Vaibhāṣika school asserts that there are ten outbursts, adding anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) to the previous eight.
These ten types bind sentient beings and place them within the prison of birth and death; therefore, they are called *paryavasthāna* (entanglements).
Alternatively, these ten serve as causes that give rise to various evil deeds, causing one to be confined in the miserable realms; therefore, they are called *paryavasthāna*.

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), along with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*styāna*), have already been explained as before.
That which causes the mind to become dull and withdrawn, associated with lethargy, and renders one unable to sustain the body—this is the characteristic of sleep (*middha*).
Although sleep (*middha*) is also dissociated from torpor (*styāna*), this [text] speaks only of the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), and thus makes this statement.
The reason these three are mentioned here all at once as characteristics of sleep is that these three accord with the meaning of sleep.
It arises from reflecting upon one's own harm and the benefit received by an enemy; preceded by malice, the mind’s indignation is called *krodha* (anger).
Other masters say:

it arises from encountering what is improper or contrary; its power enables the mind to turn away without regard, even to the point of causing the mind to flare up in indignation toward one's own children—this is termed *krodha*.
Concealing one's own transgressions is termed *mrakṣa* (concealment).

"Transgression" refers to that which is censurable, namely the violation of the *śīla*, the rules of conduct, and the pure livelihood (*ājīva*). "Concealing" means hiding these transgressions out of a desire for their cause.
Another commentator explains:
"To wipe away" (*praticchādana*) means to conceal; that is, harboring evil within while wiping away the exterior, with the intent that others may not perceive it.
It was previously stated that only those phenomena arising from the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) can be established as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Among these, which phenomena arise from which afflictions?
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are outflows of greed (*lobha*); for they can only arise when greed serves as their proximate cause.

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), torpor (*middha*), and lethargy (*styāna*) are the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā-niṣyanda*), because they are extremely closely related to the characteristics of ignorance.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) and anger (*krodha*) are the outflows of hatred (*dveṣa-niṣyanda*), because their characteristics are identical to those of hatred.
Regret is an outflow of doubt, because it arises from hesitation.

Regarding concealment, some say it is an outflow of greed, some say it is an outflow of ignorance, and some say it is an outflow of both; for those with knowledge, it arises from craving, while for those without knowledge, it arises from delusion.
Precisely because of these characteristics, it is said:

when the mind is attached to praise, gain, and honor, and fails to understand that misconduct brings about its future retribution, this is the cause for the desire to conceal one's own faults. It is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of craving and ignorance; the mental factor that arises in accordance with such affliction is called *mrakṣa* (concealment).
These ten types arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*) and are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of those afflictions; therefore, they are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
What are the characteristics of the remaining stains of affliction (*kleśamala*)?
The verse says:
The afflictions and stains consist of the six vexations—harmfulness, resentment, flattery, deception, and arrogance.
Deception and arrogance arise from greed; harmfulness and resentment arise from hatred.
"Vexation arises from the grasping at views; flattery arises from all [wrong] views.
The treatise says:
That which is a cause for stubbornly adhering to a blameworthy matter and being difficult to cause to relinquish it is called vexation (*pradāśa*).
Because this exists, the world says one is "unleadable.

Clinging to what is wrongly grasped, one shows no regard whatsoever for other sentient beings; intending to take them under one's influence as a cause for harm and affliction, with compassion obstructed and the mind afflicted—this is called "harmfulness" (*vihiṃsā*).
To repeatedly engage in conceptualization regarding disagreeable signs, giving rise to a continuous state of anger and subsequently harboring a grudge, is called *upanāha* (enmity).

To skillfully conceal one's own affairs and employ deceptive stratagems to manipulate the feelings of others, being contrary to actual knowledge and characterized by mental crookedness, is called *śāṭhya* (deceit).

Because greed for fame and profit precedes it, the intention to cause others to be deluded by false demonstrations is called *śāṭhya* (deceit); it is a state of mind that contradicts right concentration and is characterized by treachery.

As for the distinction between the characteristics of a treacherous mind (*śāṭhya*) and a crooked mind (*māyā*), they differ in terms of being like a path versus a staff, in relation to others versus oneself, and in being caused by greed versus views.
The characteristics of *mada* have already been analyzed in detail above.
Other masters say:
that which arises from greed, consisting of a haughty state of mind based on one’s own youth, health, longevity, and other flourishing prosperities, is called *mada*.
Other masters say:

Pride (*mada*) is defined as the mind’s self-exaltation and reliance upon itself, preceded by attachment and indulgence toward one's own flourishing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), while disregarding others and considering oneself superior.

Because it disregards others, it differs from pride (*māna*). These six types arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*); being defiled in character and coarse, they are called "affliction-corruptions" (*kleśamala*).

Among these six affliction-corruptions, deceit (*śāṭhya*) and arrogance (*mada*) are outflows (*niṣyanda*) of greed; harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) and resentment (*upanāha*) are outflows of hatred; vexation (*pradāsa*) is an outflow of the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and guile (*māyā*) is an outflow of all [wrong] views.
As it is said that "crookedness" refers to various wrong views, guile is necessarily the outflow of those views.
Since these six also arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*), they receive the designation of "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), just like the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
The various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and defilement-stains (*kleśamala*) have already been explained; next, their antidotes for abandonment should now be analyzed.
Among these envelopments and stains, which are abandoned by what?
The verse says:
The envelopments of shamelessness, lack of dread, and torpor, along with lethargy and restlessness, are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation;
the remaining [envelopments] and the afflictive stains are abandoned only through cultivation because they function independently.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are universally associated with all unwholesome minds;
sleep (*middha*) in the desire realm arises universally with all mental consciousnesses;

and lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are universally associated with all defiled minds. Therefore, these five are all to be abandoned through both the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The remaining [afflictions]—envy (*īrṣyā*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and the outflows (*mala*)—arise independently; therefore, they are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and are associated only with those abandoned through cultivation.
Because they are associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) that functions through the power of others, they are termed "independently arising" (*svatantra*).
Because all ignorance associated with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*) that arise spontaneously is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding these various outbursts and impurities, which ones are common to which natures?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, three—sloth (*styāna*), torpor (*middha*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are of two natures; the others are unwholesome. In the higher realms, all are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The Commentary says:

The three—sloth, torpor, and restlessness—that are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) all pertain to both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) natures; all remaining [latent dispositions] are exclusively unwholesome.

These consist of the seven envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and six stains (*mala*) bound to the desire realm, as well as those that correspondingly exist within the two higher realms; all are comprised exclusively of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, namely: guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), arrogance (*mada*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
To which realms are these various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and stains (*mala*) bound?
The verse says:
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) and guile (*māyā*) belong to the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna; The other three belong to all three realms; the remainder belong to the Desire Realm.
The Treatise says:
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) and guile (*māyā*) exist only in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna.
How do we know that deceit and guile exist in the Brahma-world?
Because the Great Brahmā King concealed his true intentions and manifested deceptive signs to mislead the bhikṣu Aśvajit,
it is traditionally held that this [erroneous perception] arises only among ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and cannot manifest even for noble ones (*ārya*).
Stolidity (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and arrogance (*mada*) pertain to all three realms; all the remaining ones exist only in the desire realm.
That is to say, among the sixteen [defilements], five are as previously explained, while the remaining eleven pertain exclusively to the desire realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that have been explained, how many among them depend exclusively on the mental level (*manobhūmi*),
and how many arise depending on all six levels of consciousness?
The verse says:

The pride and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by seeing, as well as the autonomous secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), arise exclusively in the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*); the others pertain to all six consciousnesses.
The treatise says:

Among all the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) of pride (*māna*), torpor (*middha*), and those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), those that arise independently all rely upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), for there is no possibility for them to arise in dependence on the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*).

All remaining [afflictions] depend universally upon the six consciousnesses; that is to say, greed, hatred, and ignorance abandoned through cultivation, along with their associated secondary afflictions—namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—as well as other secondary afflictions subsumed under the "great ground of affliction" (*kleśamahābhūmika*), namely, heedlessness (*pramāda*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), because these are all capable of arising based on the six groups of consciousness.
In principle, all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) should be explained; however, for now, this is discussed based on those that are coarse and manifest.

Furthermore, one should investigate: as previously analyzed regarding the five faculties of feeling such as pleasure (*sukha*), which among all the primary and secondary afflictions discussed here are associated with which faculty?
Regarding this, one should first analyze the various afflictions.
The verse says:
The afflictions of the desire realm are associated with greed, joy, and pleasure.
Hatred is associated with all [mental factors] except joy; sorrow, suffering, and delusion are universal. False view is associated with sorrow and joy;
doubt is associated with sorrow; the remaining five are associated with joy. All are associated with equanimity.
In the higher stages, they are each associated according to their respective levels, universally corresponding to the various feelings of their own consciousness.
The treatise says:
Among the various afflictions bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), greed is associated with joy and pleasure, because it functions through a mode of elation and pervades all six consciousnesses.
Hatred is associated with sorrow and pain, because it functions through a mode of dejection and pervades all six consciousnesses.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is universally associated with the preceding four [mental factors], because it functions through both modes of joy and sorrow across all six consciousnesses, and because it is universally associated with the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).

False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with both sorrow and joy, because it functions through both modes of joy and sorrow exclusively in the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*), as one subsequently creates either sinful or meritorious karma according to these [respective states].

Doubt and sorrow are associated [with the mental factor of] dejection, because they proceed through a mode of dejection and exist solely on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*); for one who harbors hesitation seeks a definitive knowledge and thus experiences mental distress.
The remaining four views and pride are associated with joy, because they proceed through a mode of elation and exist solely on the level of the mental consciousness.

Generally speaking, all [afflictions] are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because it is taught that delusion (*moha*) increases in association with equanimity, and because delusion is universally associated with all afflictions.

When the continuity of afflictions reaches its ultimate point, they grasp their objects with laxity and give rise to a desire for the neutral state; as they gradually diminish, the continuity is severed. At that time, the afflictions accord with equanimity; therefore, they are all associated with the feeling of equanimity.
Since the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is neither joyful nor sorrowful, how can it be associated with the afflictions of joy and sorrow?
It is like a neutral person who is in conflict with neither; thus there is no contradiction.
If this is so for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), what is the case for the higher stages?
In all cases, they correspond universally with the various feelings that arise together with their own respective consciousnesses within their own stage, according to what is appropriate.

That is to say, if a particular stage contains all four consciousnesses, the afflictions arising from each of those consciousnesses correspond universally with the various feelings associated with their own respective consciousnesses.

If, within the various stages (bhūmi), there is only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), then the afflictions (kleśa) arising from that very mental consciousness are universally associated with all feelings (vedanā) of the mental consciousness.
How much consciousness is present in the higher stages?
That is to say, the first dhyāna possesses four [mental factors], while the remaining [levels] possess one each.
How many sensations (vedanā) are present?
That is to say, the first, second, third, and fourth [dhyānas] possess joy (prīti), pleasure (sukha), and equanimity (upekṣā) respectively.
One should know that joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and pleasure (*sukha*) are exclusively associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the afflictions present in each respective stage, they correspond accordingly with the consciousness and the feelings (*vedanā*) therein.
For what reason are both types of doubt (*vicikitsā*) indeterminate, yet the higher [levels] can be associated with joy and pleasure?

Doubt in the desire realm does not arise simultaneously with the feeling of joy; for when the various afflictions exist in a stage free from desire, although they are not definitive, one does not experience sorrow or distress, and even while caught in the net of doubt, the mind remains unclouded and serene.
Just as when one attains what is beloved in the human realm, one conceives a notion of pleasure despite much toil and fatigue;
some say that although doubt still persists in the form realm, one conceives a notion of wholesome qualities within that doubt, and therefore it can be associated with joy and bliss.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti*, Fascicle 27;
*Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, Fascicle 28, composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

Chapter Six: On the Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya), Part Four. Having already explained the association of the afflictions with the various feelings, we shall now further explain the secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
The verse says:

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), and resentment (*upanāha*) arise together with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*). Avarice (*mātsarya*) is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Deceit, guile, torpor, and concealment are associated with both sorrow and joy;
pride is associated with joy, pleasure, and equanimity; the remaining four are associated with all [mental states].
The commentary says:

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the six types beginning with envy (*īrṣyā*) are all associated with the faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyendriya*), because they function through a mode of dejection and belong exclusively to the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*).

Other masters say that vexation (*pradāsa*) is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), because it is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the view of grasping at excellence (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and should therefore function through a mode of elation.
Avarice is associated with joy (*saumanasya*), because it functions through a mode of gladness and belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
It functions through a mode of gladness because its characteristic is extremely similar to that of greed (*lobha*).

Deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), torpor (*middha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are associated with both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy, because they function through both modes of gladness and dejection and belong exclusively to the mental level.
Regarding those that proceed with joy or sorrow: some at times practice flattery and the like with a joyful mind, while at other times they do so with a sorrowful mind.
Other masters say:

since it has been stated that deception is an outflow of greed, it should only proceed with joy; one should not say it is associated with the faculty of sorrow, for as an outflow of joy, it ought not to be sorrowful.
Furthermore, because one should not feel dejection while actively deceiving, or else it should be said that deception is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of delusion (*moha*).

Pride (*mada*) is associated with joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and mental application (*saumanasya*); because its activity is exclusively mental, it is associated with pleasure in the third dhyāna, whereas in the lower stages it is associated with joy.

All the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) mentioned above are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because they abide in equanimity when the continuity [of consciousness] is interrupted, and because there are cases where they function exclusively in the stage of equanimity.
Abandonment (*upekṣā*) is universally associated with all [five] feelings without exception, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is universally associated [with all minds].

The remaining—lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are all universally associated with the five feelings; the first two are subsumed under the great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*), while the latter two are subsumed under the great afflictive mental factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
The mention of "two" and the word "and" (*ca*) indicates the objection and its resolution.

That is to say, regarding the objection raised concerning affliction (*daurmanasya*) and deception (*māyā*) as before, the logical response should state that the characteristics of the fruit and the cause are distinct. Just as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), though being outflows of greed (*lobha*), can still be associated with mental grief (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*), one knows from this that what is stated [in the sūtra] is indeed associated with feeling (*vedanā*).

It is not merely because they share the same cause that we allow for the existence of deceitful conduct based on the distinction of their characteristics; rather, it is because one who has a mental state of sorrow may nevertheless practice deceit.

Among the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) already mentioned, there are those that the Buddha taught as "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) according to different perspectives; these shall now be analyzed.
What are the characteristics of the hindrances?
The verse says:
The five hindrances exist only in the desire realm, Because their nutriment, antidote, and function are the same.
Although two [categories] are established as one hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), there are only five because they obstruct the aggregates (*skandha*).
The treatise says:
As stated in the Sūtra, if it is said that the five hindrances constitute a mass of unwholesomeness, this is a correct statement.
Why is this so? Because these five kinds constitute a purely complete aggregate of unwholesomeness. What are the five?

The five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are: first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and fifth, the hindrance of doubt.

Since the sūtras state that these hindrances are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is known that they exist only in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), and not in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) or formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Based on this evidence, we know that although the essential natures of torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) all pervade the desire, form, and formless realms, only those in the desire realm receive the designation of "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).

To demonstrate that the two types—torpor and restlessness—are established as hindrances only within the desire realm, they are established in conjunction with sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*), because sleep and regret are exclusively bound to the desire realm.

To show that only those forms of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) which are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) receive the designation "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*), it is established in conjunction with torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), because torpor and restlessness are exclusively of a defiled nature.
The nature of doubt should be understood as analogous to the preceding four [hindrances] and is to be found within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

For what reason are the hindrances of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) each established as a distinct hindrance based on a single constituent, whereas the two hindrances of lethargy-and-drowsiness (*styāna-middha*) and restlessness-and-remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) are each established as a hindrance based on two constituents combined?
Sensual desire, ill-will, doubt, and their respective nutriment and antidote are distinct; therefore, each is established separately as a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).

Because lethargy and sleep, as well as restlessness and remorse, share the same function regarding both their nutriment and their antidote, they are combined into single entities despite being different in substance.
The nutriment of the hindrance of sensual desire is the aspect of the attractive; its antidote is the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
The nutriment of the hindrance of ill will is the aspect of the repulsive; its antidote is the root of goodness of loving-kindness (*maitrī-kuśalamūla*).
The nutriment of the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) refers to the three periods of time, as stated in the Sūtra:
"One gives rise to such doubt regarding the past," and so forth, as explained at length.
The antidote to this hindrance is the ability to observe, in accordance with reality, the nature of conditions and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
