The nutriment for the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness consists of five factors: first, lethargy; second, lack of joy; third, yawning; fourth, irregularity of diet; and fifth, dullness and inferiority of mind. The antidote to this hindrance is the perception of light. The functional activity of this hindrance is that both [torpor and drowsiness] cause the nature of the mind to become sunken and obscured.

The nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and regret consists of four types of mental states: first, thoughts of relatives; second, thoughts of one’s native land; third, thoughts of immortality; and fourth, recollecting various past experiences such as laughter, play, amusement, and service. The antidote to this hindrance is *śamatha* (calm abiding). The functional activity of this hindrance is that both together cause the mind to lack tranquility.

For this reason, it is said that because their functions of nutriment and remedy are identical, torpor (*styāna*) and sleep (*middha*), as well as restlessness (*auddhatya*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*), are each combined into one.

Alternatively, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are full-fledged afflictions (*paryavasthāna*); each is capable of bearing the function of a single "enveloping" hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Lethargy-and-drowsiness and restlessness-and-regret are not independent afflictions; only when combined do they function as a single obscuration.
What is the meaning of these five being called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*)?
It means that they are definitively able to cover and obstruct the Noble Path and the preparatory practices for the Noble Path; therefore, they are designated by the name "hindrances."

If that were so, then all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like should be termed "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*), for they are all capable of obscuring and obstructing both the Noble Path and its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As the Blessed One told the bhikṣus:
"If one is obscured and obstructed by even a single dharma, one will not be able to realize that 'form is impermanent.'"
"A single dharma refers to greed," and so on, as explained at length.
Each is explained individually as in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
For what reason did the Blessed One teach that there are only five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)?

In principle, this is indeed so; however, when the Blessed One established the categories of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), he spoke of only five, because these alone are capable of acting as superior obstacles to the five aggregates (*skandha*).

That is to say, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) can obstruct the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), as they respectively cause one to distance oneself from sensual pleasures and from evil.
Lethargy and drowsiness can obstruct the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), for both cause one to distance oneself from vipaśyanā.
Excitement and remorse can obstruct the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), for both cause one to distance oneself from śamatha.

In this way, these four hindrances gradually cause one to transcend the white dharmas of renunciation; consequently, they subsequently give rise to doubt regarding karma and its results, as well as the Four Noble Truths. Because of this doubt, it prevents the arising of everything up to liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Therefore, only these five are established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

If that is so, the hindrance of restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) should have been mentioned before sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha*), since they are taught according to the sequence of the aggregates of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
It is not so. In this context, the sequential order is disrupted because the Blessed One intended to clarify a specific meaning.

That is to say, in the sūtras, the Buddha taught based on correct reasoning that the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*) is treated by insight (*vipaśyanā*) and not by serenity (*śamatha*), while the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) is treated only by serenity and not by insight. This is stated according to the method of suppression and abandonment, wherein the gates of insight and serenity are said to treat the two hindrances of torpor-drowsiness and restlessness-remorse separately.
However, if one relies on the perspective of permanent abandonment, there is no difference in the functional application of these gates of insight and serenity as antidotes for all [hindrances].
To manifest this principle, the sequential order is disrupted.
Why is ignorance (*avidyā*) not established as an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance)?
Because it is not stated that it is accomplished [as such].
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Enveloped by ignorance; the envelopment itself is an obscuration (nīvaraṇa).
Other masters say:
Among those who bear the burden established within the *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances), ignorance is the heaviest of what is borne; for this reason, it is not mentioned [here].
Furthermore, for what reason is pride (*māna*) not established as a *nīvaraṇa*?

Because there are those who, due to pride (*māna*), are able to cultivate superior dharmas, pride is inferior in its sense as an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*) and is therefore not established among the obscurations.
Other masters say:
That which constitutes an obscuration causes the mind to incline toward the lower; pride is not like this, for it can cause the mind to incline toward higher dharmas.
For what reason are the various views (*dṛṣṭi*) not established among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)?
This is because sentient beings who lack the view of non-self (*anātman-dṛṣṭi*), though they may cling to a self, are still able to become free from defilement.
Some say that because the nature of the views is swift and sharp, it does not accord with the meaning of a "hindrance," for the nature of a hindrance is dull and sluggish.
Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the others are not established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); this should be understood according to reason based on what was previously explained.
As for why the afflictions of the two upper realms are not established as hindrances: because they are free from the defilements of the three realms, they do not constitute an initial obstruction.

Furthermore, while those neutral hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), one must now investigate by what means the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth are abandoned. They are abandoned through the insight that perceives their objects (*ālambana*).
It is by means of the wisdom that contemplates and sees those objects that the latent dispositions and the rest are severed.

If that were so, then the universal defilements (*sarvatraga*) of the desire realm and other realms, as well as the outflow-afflicted afflictions (*sāsrava-kleśa*) in the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, would have no possibility of being abandoned;

for when the patience of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, it takes only the suffering and origin truths of the desire realm as its object, and when the various knowledges and patiences take the truths of cessation and the path as their objects, they take only the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their sphere.
There is no such fault, for I maintain that there are many methods for the permanent abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
How many kinds are there?
In total, there are four kinds.
What are these four?
The verse says:
Because of fully knowing the object of cognition, and because of abandoning that which cognizes it.
"By severing their objects of perception, and by the arising of their antidotes, they are abandoned.
The treatise says:
The afflictions to be abandoned through seeing are abandoned by means of the first three expedients.

First, abandonment occurs through the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the object (*ālambana*). This refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that take their own realm as an object and are abandoned by the insight into suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); it also includes all afflictions belonging to the form and formless realms abandoned by the insight into suffering and its origin. Furthermore, those [afflictions] of the two higher realms that take other realms or stages as objects are also abandoned through the thorough knowledge of the object, because when the receptivities to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arise, they are simultaneously able to observe the objects of all three realms.

Furthermore, this includes the untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) of the delusions abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path within the three realms; all such delusions are abandoned by means of fully knowing their objects.

Second, they are abandoned by means of abandoning their objective supports (*ālambaka*), namely, the delusions of the desire realm that take other realms as their objects. This is because the delusions of the desire realm abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin—which take their own realm as their object—can take those [other-realm delusions] as their objects. These [desire-realm delusions] act as the basis and support for them; when the basis and support are abandoned, the latter are abandoned accordingly.
It is like a weak and sickly person who stands supported by something; when one removes that support, the person falls down accordingly.
How, then, can it serve as a basis for that?
It is because it can act as the cause for it.
Is it not the case that this very point explains [the abandonment] by means of the cause of harm?
Indeed it is so; these two are merely different names for the same thing, yet this statement was made to prevent ambiguity.

This means that among the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, those taking objects within their own realm and those taking objects in other realms both possess the sense of being mutual causes for one another; however, there is no case where they take each other as objects in a reciprocal manner. Therefore, in this context, it is said that "the grasper is severed" in order to make it easy to understand that [only] those taking objects in other realms are meant; by severing this cause, the other [affliction] is consequently severed as well.

Third, they are abandoned by abandoning their objects; that is to say, the various defiled afflictions (*sāsrava-kleśa*) that take cessation and the path as their objects are abandoned because the undefiled-object-afflictions (*anāsrava-ālambana-kleśa*) can serve as their objects, and when those objects are abandoned, the former are abandoned accordingly.
It is like a weak and sick person walking with the aid of a staff; when that staff is removed, he falls down accordingly.
For what reason, among these abandoned afflictions (*kleśa*), is it said that the object of perception (*ālambana*) is abandoned because the capacity to perceive it has been severed?

For example, when one realizes the arising of suffering through its conditions (the origin) in relation to desire, there is an abandonment of the object; therefore, it is said that the subject which perceives it is abandoned.

Similarly, when one realizes cessation and the path, although both [the subject and the object] are indeed abandoned at that time, because there is a distinction between the superior and the inferior among those things to be abandoned, it is said that when the superior is abandoned, the inferior follows suit.

That is to say, if, within the objective referents (*ālambana*) of those afflictions, the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises and is able to act as an antidote, those afflictions are termed "superior," while the remainder are termed "inferior.
For what reason do those afflictions specifically receive the designation "superior"?
Untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) arises with respect to those objects, specifically because it exerts effort as an antidote to them.

If one allows that there are multiple means for the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*), some are abandoned through the abandonment of their subjective apprehension (*ālambaka*), while others are abandoned through the abandonment of their objective referent (*ālambana*).
Why was it previously stated that latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth are abandoned because they are observed through wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding their objects?
One should simply have established at the outset the thesis that the permanent abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) occurs through manifold means;
do not let the initial thesis and the subsequent explanation differ in meaning or contradict one another in sequence.

There is no difference between the initial establishment of the thesis and its subsequent explanation; the former is based on the necessity of observing the objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*), while the latter is based on the existence of distinctions within them.
Regarding the afflictions, the superior ones are presented first, followed by the explanation of the inferior ones; those that act as direct adversaries [to the path] are designated as "superior."
The three expedients for abandoning the afflictions abandoned through seeing have already been explained.
The abandonment of the afflictions abandoned through cultivation occurs by means of the fourth expedient; that is to say, they are abandoned solely because their antidotes arise.
When the path of antidote corresponding to a particular category arises, all the afflictions within that category are abandoned instantaneously.
For example, when the antidote of the lowest-of-the-low grade arises, the highest-of-the-high grade afflictions are all abandoned instantaneously.
When the path of cultivation of the highest-highest grade arises, the lowest-lowest grade of afflictions is immediately and simultaneously severed.
This principle will be discussed in detail later.
Is it not the case that when all afflictions abandoned by insight are severed, they too depend upon the arising of the path of counteraction?
Because when the path of antidote arises for a particular category [of defilements], the various afflictions within that category are severed.

This is indeed logically correct; however, it is stated here in order to demonstrate that among the afflictions of the three realms to be abandoned through cultivation, there are none that are not severed by the nine grades of the path, and that the path of antidote is thus determined. Therefore, these words were spoken.
Among those [afflictions] abandoned through seeing, only the afflictions of the Peak of Existence have a fixed antidote, as has already been explained previously.
When the various afflictions abandoned through seeing are severed, the three [types of] application are fixed; therefore, they are discussed separately.
Because the skillful means for abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are not fixed, this is stated in general terms.
One might ask: "Does not the fourth skillful means explained here fail to relate to the tenets of the preceding school?"

This means that during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) are able to sever the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms; however, this is because wisdom does not perceive the objects of these afflictions as views (*dṛṣṭi*).
This [objection] is actually irrelevant to the tenet under discussion, for the preceding tenet addresses exclusively those [afflictions] to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Even if they were to be subsumed collectively, there would be no contradiction, because one perceives that the objects of those delusions are the very things for which this antidote arises.
How many types of antidotes are there in total?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of remedies: namely, abandonment, maintenance, distancing, and aversion.
The treatise says:
In general, there are four types of remedial categories.

First, the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*): this refers to the path that is directly capable of abandoning the acquisition of various afflictions, namely the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Second, the counteractive of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*): this refers to the path that arises simultaneously with the initial acquisition of abandonment, namely the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); because such a path maintains the acquisition of abandonment, it prevents the acquisition of the afflictions from arising in succession.

Third is the antidote of distancing (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*): this refers to the path that causes the previously abandoned defilements to become even more distant; this is the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*). Any path arising after the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is termed "path of excellence," and even the acquisitions (*prāpti*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth that arise subsequently are given the name "path" because they cause the continuity of the various acquisitions to increase in opposition to the acquisition of the defilements.

Fourth is the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*). This refers to when, within whichever realm or stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*) the Path occurs, one perceives its faults and gives rise to profound revulsion; that is, to contemplate the meaning of those faults through various approaches. This is comprised solely within the collection of mental applications of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-manasikāra*).

By the power of this, even if one later encounters sublime objects, one will not become attached to them; it should be understood that for the most part, this belongs to the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), as it is not yet definitive.

The statement "mostly" (*bāhulyena*) at the beginning should be understood as indicating that within the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), those which take the truths of suffering and its origin as their objects also function as antidotes of aversion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*).
The antidotes to the afflictions have already been explained; now the principle of their abandonment shall be analyzed.
Is the permanent abandonment of all afflictions determined by way of their objects (*ālambana*), by way of their associations (*saṃprayoga*), or by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Why does doubt arise?
Because one perceives faults in all three of these positions.
Furthermore, it should not be said that abandonment occurs by means of the object; for if a given dharma is the object of another, there has never been a time when it was not its object.
Nor can it be said that abandonment proceeds from dissociation; for associated dharmas serve as causes for one another, and there is no time when this dharma is not of the nature of a cause.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of these afflictions that the mind becomes defiled, and there is no time when this mind is not defiled.
Nor can it be said that abandonment occurs from the perspective of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because a phenomenon cannot be divested of its own intrinsic nature.

Since, at the time of abandoning the afflictions, one cannot cause those phenomena which are to be abandoned to lose their status as "that which is to be abandoned," one must therefore consider from what [source] the afflictions are actually abandoned.
The verse says:
One should know that by means of the object of focus (ālambana), the various afflictions (kleśa) can be brought to cessation.
The commentary says:

The permanent abandonment of all afflictions necessarily proceeds from their objects; for, as previously stated, it is through the power of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the object that afflictions are rendered permanently abandoned.
Now, there are generally two kinds of objects of affliction: namely, things associated with bondage (*saṃyukta-vastu*) and things not associated with bondage (*asaṃyukta-vastu*).

The various afflictions that take as their object things bound by existence (*bhavasaṃyukta*), as well as those afflictions not taking such things as their object which are produced through the power of the former—
these two types of afflictions give rise to various acquisitions (*prāpti*) within the manifest continuum of a single sentient being.

Even when an undefiled mind is present, this acquisition (prāpti) continues to function constantly without interruption, serving as the cause for the fruits of the various afflictions (kleśa) in the past and future.

One should understand it thus: the same applies to the acquisitions of those afflictions that take unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) as their object, as well as to the concomitant active manifestations induced by the power of those afflictions, and to the acquisitions induced by those afflictions that do not take such phenomena as their object. The categories of these acquisitions are identical to what was stated previously.

Regarding the statement that they serve as the causes and effects of past and future afflictions: when these various acquisitions (*prāpti*) exist in the present, they are said to be "effects" because they are of the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of past afflictions;
they are said to be "causes" because they are of the nature of the conditions for the arising of future afflictions.

However, these various acquisitions (*prāpti*) are incompatible with the manifestation of the acquisitions that are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the antidotes to abandonment; they are able to maintain the past and future afflictions that have been acquired, thereby causing all afflictions that take this object as their basis, as well as those that take other objects, to continue in succession.

When the outflow (niṣyanda) of the various antidotes that abandon [defilements] with respect to these objective conditions arises, the acquisition (prāpti) of the defilements is immediately severed. Although the essence of those acquired defilements still exists with respect to their own objects, they can be said to be "abandoned" because the acquisition of both cause and effect has been permanently severed.

Because, regarding even a limited object, if the afflictions taking that object as their condition have not been fully understood, and because the afflictions taking other objects as their condition—which are induced by the power of those [first] afflictions—attain the causes and fruits of the induced past and future afflictions, they proceed without interruption within the present continuum.

When one attains thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding even a limited object, the acquisition (*prāpti*) induced by the afflictions no longer functions; thus, it is known that the abandonment of afflictions necessarily proceeds from their objects (*ālambana*).
Regarding the "distant counteractive" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) mentioned previously, how many kinds of "remoteness" (*dūratva*) are there in total?
The verse says: There are four kinds of remoteness— namely, by way of characteristic, antidote, location, and time—
such as the primary elements and ethical discipline, or things situated in different directions and two different times, respectively.
The treatise states:
There are, in total, four kinds of remoteness.

First is remoteness by way of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-prākaṭya*); for example, although the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise together within a single aggregate, they are also said to be remote because their characteristics are different.

Second is remoteness by way of mutual opposition (*pratipakṣa-viprakarṣa*): for example, the observance and violation of precepts, though both occur within a single body, are called "remote" because they are mutually opposed.

Third is remoteness by way of spatial location (*deśa-viprakarṣa*): for example, the two shores of the ocean; though both are situated on the edge of the same great sea, they are called "remote" because their locations are separated.

The nature of distance in terms of the four time periods is as follows: although the past and future worlds are both established based upon the same phenomena, they are also called "distant" because they are separated by temporal divisions.
Distant in relation to what?
The present world that has already ceased without interval and that which is currently arising are adjacent to the present;
how, then, can they be called "distant"?
It is because they are not objects of the eye and other [senses], or because they lack functional activity.
The unconditioned is not subject to time, so it cannot be challenged [as being distant].
Since the essence of space pervades both types of cessation, the Sūtra also describes them as "near.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) is used to clarify that the enumeration of dharmas is not exhaustive.
The distinctions among the antidotes to the afflictions have already been explained.
Within the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-bhāvanā*) that cultivates these antidotes, are the various afflictions to be abandoned abandoned again?
And is there a re-acquisition of the dissociation (*visamyoga*) already obtained?
The verse says:
Defilements are never severed twice; disconnection may be acquired repeatedly.
This occurs when the antidote arises, upon attaining a fruit, and during the six occasions of refining the faculties.
The treatise states:
Regarding the various afflictions to be abandoned, they are suddenly and permanently severed by attaining their respective paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Once they have been abandoned, there is no sense of re-abandoning them at a later time when one is free from regression; to abandon what has already been abandoned would be a futile exertion.

Regarding the dissociation (visamyoga) that has been attained, although there is no principle of gradual progression toward superior states in accordance with the path, it is possible for its superior acquisition (prāpti) to arise again when the path advances, because the acquisition of dissociation is subsumed under the path;
furthermore, since one both abandons and acquires it at the time of abandoning and acquiring the path, there is thus the principle of the repeated acquisition of various dissociations.
This is based on what is possible.
In total, there are six occasions: the arising of the path of remedy (*pratipakṣa*), the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*), and the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
The expression "the arising of the remedy" refers to both of these meanings.
If one refers to abiding in this [state] as being able to realize dissociation (*visamyoga*), it is termed the path of uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*);
if one refers to abiding in this [state] as actually realizing dissociation, it is termed the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
As for the phrase "attaining the fruits," it refers to attaining the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship (*arhat-phala*).

Regarding the term "refining the faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra*), it refers to the advancement of the faculties. This is because at these six moments, one attains paths not previously attained, and because there is the relinquishing of previously attained paths and the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga*).

Since the expression "attaining the fruit" (*phala-prāpti*) is used without distinction, the refinement of the faculties should be included within the inclusion of the four fruits, as the attainment of the fruit necessarily occurs at the time of the transformation of the faculties. Why, then, is it necessary to laboriously state this separate term "refining the faculties"?

In order to demonstrate that the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) differs from the attainment of the fruits through the abandonment of defilements, there is no fault in speaking of the refinement of the faculties as occurring outside of the attainment of the fruits.

However, regarding the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*), it may possess all six moments according to what is appropriate, down to the case of having only two; that is, for the dissociation obtained by abandoning the defilements of the desire realm associated with the four truths, as well as those of the form and formless realms associated with the [first] three truths, the acquisition of dissociation possesses all six moments.

Regarding the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) obtained through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that abandons [defilements] of the form and formless realms, it occurs at only five moments; this is because the fruit is attained precisely at the moment the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises.
Once the attainment of the fruit has been explained, the arising of the antidote is not mentioned separately.

The disjunction from the five categories [of afflictions] to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm is also attained at five moments, excluding the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry.
The attainment of the sixth disjunction occurs at only four moments, because there is no distinction between the moment of attaining the fruit and the moment when the antidote arises.
The seventh and eighth categories also consist of only four moments, because among the four fruits attained, the first two are excluded.
The acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*) in the ninth category consists of only three moments, because at the very moment the antidote arises, one simultaneously attains the fruit.

Among those [defilements] of the form and formless realms to be abandoned through cultivation, with the exception of the ninth disconnection of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the remaining disconnections likewise occur at only three times; this is because, among the four attainments of the fruits, the first three have been excluded.
The attainment of the ninth [dhyāna] of the Peak of Existence occurs at only two times, because the attainment of the fruit and the arising of the antidote occur simultaneously.
This is stated with reference to those of dull faculties.
If one considers those of sharp faculties, the attainment of the "refining of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is excluded from the aforementioned stages.

Is it not the case that since the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) can admit of worldly paths (*laukikamārga*), the abandonment [of defilements] should be divided into two types: that obtained through the path of antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and that obtained at the time of arising?
No; for this refers to attainment through gradual progression, or because this discussion pertains exclusively to attainment by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).

If one relies on the attainment of transcendence through skipping stages (*vyutkrāntaka*) that includes the contaminated (*sāsrava*), then for those who enter the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) from among the defilements of the eight stages by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), having abandoned a small or large portion [of these defilements], they attain dissociation (*visamyoga*). According to their respective cases, this may involve all six moments, or even just one, because of their sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), excluding the moment of refining the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).

This refers to one who, within the desire realm, first abandons five categories [of afflictions] and enters the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*). For such a person, the acquisition of the disconnection (*visamyoga*) from those five categories abandoned by vision occurs at six moments. There are two types: the time of one's own birth and the time of attaining the fruit; these, combined with four others, constitute the six.
The disconnection from the five categories abandoned through cultivation is attained at only five moments, excluding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

For one who has previously abandoned six categories and enters the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*), the disconnection from those six categories abandoned through vision is likewise attained at five moments, excluding one as before.

The disjunction from the six categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is attained only when the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) arises as its antidote; the supramundane antidote (*anāsravapratipakṣa*) certainly does not arise [at that time]. This is because it is subsumed under the path of the candidate for the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala-pratipannaka-mārga*). One does not give rise to the path of a candidate while abiding in the fruit, for one who abides in a superior fruit does not give rise to an inferior one.

Regarding those who enter the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*) after first abandoning eight categories [of afflictions], they also attain the dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the eight categories abandoned by vision during five moments, excluding one as previously stated.
Regarding the dissociation from the first six categories abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it should be understood that these are attained in a single moment, as before.
The disjunctions from the seventh and eighth categories are acquired at only four times: namely, through the arising of two antidotes and the attainment of two fruits.

For one who first abandons the nine grades [of afflictions] based on the *anāgamya* stage and enters the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*), those disjunctions from the nine grades of what is abandoned by vision are also acquired at four times; this should be understood as previously explained.

For one who enters the vision of the truths based on the fundamental dhyāna stage, the nine grades of dissociation from what is to be abandoned by vision are also attained simultaneously; this should be understood as previously explained, because the fundamental dhyāna is not the antidote for abandoning [defilements] of the desire realm.

Whether based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage or the fundamental (*maula*) stage, the dissociation from the nine grades of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation is also attained simultaneously; this should be understood as previously explained. It is certain that the untainted antidote for those [defilements] does not arise, because [this state] is subsumed under the path leading toward the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Regarding those who first sever the fetters of the upper seven stages and enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), they likewise attain the disconnection (*visamyoga*) from the seven stages through the vision of the three truths during four moments, as should be understood from what was previously stated.

For those who sever the fetters of the seven stages through the vision of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), the disconnection is attained in only three moments: namely, the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and the two attainments of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*). This is because the arising of the untainted antidote is itself the attainment of the fruit.
The disconnections from the seven stages abandoned through cultivation are attained at only three times: namely, the arising of two antidotes and the attainment of one fruit.

For one who enters the Noble Path having already abandoned the [afflictions] of the eight stages, the disconnections from the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) abandoned during the path of seeing—specifically those abandoned by the vision of the three truths—are attained at three times: namely, the arising of one antidote and the attainment of two fruits.
Regarding the disjunction from the abandonments of the path of seeing, there are two moments, because the fruit is attained at the very moment the antidote arises.
Regarding the eight grades of abandonment through the path of cultivation, there are also two moments: namely, one moment when the antidote arises and one moment when the fruit is attained.
The ninth disconnection is attained at a single moment, because the fruit is obtained precisely when its antidote arises.

Regarding the various [stages] where one is separated from defilement through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the further abandonment during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) should be explained by analogy with this.
By what reason is it proven that when one attains a subsequent fruit, one again acquires the dissociation from defilements previously abandoned?
It is because of the authoritative teaching (āptāgama).
That is to say, in the Sūtras, with reference to the correct attainment of the fruit of Arhatship, it is stated as follows:
"One should know thus, one should see thus: his mind is liberated from the outflow of desire," and so forth, as explained at length.

Because within this stage one also attains the dharmajñāna of the aśaikṣa, such as the antidote of revulsion toward the desire realm, it should be understood that the disjunction from those [defilements] is also attained again.

Regarding the preliminary statement that those who enter the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*) by abandoning six or nine grades of desire: for those who have previously cultivated the abandonment of the six or nine grades of disconnection (*visamyoga*), is their lack of untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) due to never attaining it at all, or merely due to a temporary non-attainment?
One must state with certainty that he will never attain it.

But is it not the case that when one realizes arhatship, one necessarily attains all untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of disconnection (*visamyoga*) from the defilements abandoned through seeing and cultivation that were previously present?

If there was previously an untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) for that which has been abandoned and separated from, and it is now relinquished, then one should now obtain an untainted acquisition for that [state].

If it did not exist previously, it likewise does not exist now; for at the time of attaining separation from bondage, it arises solely through self-cultivation, and because one relinquishes an inferior path while obtaining a superior one.

For those who previously entered the vision of the truths based on the fundamental dhyānas, how could their minds be liberated from the outflows of the desire realm at the time they attain the state of no-more-learning?

There is no error here, because this is said with reference to those who enter the vision of the truths based on the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) and those who follow the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*). Thus, the designation "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*) is applied to each respective stage of disentanglement (*visamyoga*), being established according to what is predominant.
There are two kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*): first, thorough knowledge as wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), and second, thorough knowledge as abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Thorough knowledge as wisdom has discernment (*prajñā*) as its essence and is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

The thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) is, in its essence, dissociation (*visamyoga*); because it is the fruit of wisdom, it receives the name "thorough knowledge," just as the term "liberation through action" denotes the fruit of liberation through action.
If this were so, then the fruits of the patiences (*kṣānti*) would not be thorough knowledges.
Because this knowledge is the retinue [of the path], it is called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) without error.
Alternatively, it may later transform into the fruit of knowledge.
Is a separate thorough knowledge established for each disjunction (visamyoga) obtained through each individual path of abandonment?
Is a single universal knowledge (parijñā) established for all disconnections (visamyoga) obtained through the path of abandonment?
Neither is the case, because both would entail the faults of being either excessively broad or excessively narrow. If so, how is it?
The verse says:

There are nine thorough knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*); in the desire realm, there is one for the first two abandonments, and one for each of the next two, totaling three; the same applies to the three [abandonments] of the higher realms.
The remaining five lower fetters, and the three [fetters] through the total abandonment of the form realm.
The treatise says:
All abandonments are collectively established as nine kinds; the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are likewise established based on nine conditions, as will be explained in detail later.
What are called the nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?

Briefly stated, six thorough knowledges are established based on the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*). Specifically, one thorough knowledge is established for the abandonment of the first two categories [of afflictions] belonging to the desire realm; then one each for the next two [categories]; the same applies to the higher realms, thus totaling six.

Regarding the abandonment of the remaining afflictions and so forth belonging to the other three realms that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), three universal knowledges (*parijñā*) are established. Specifically, the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation is established as one universal knowledge; it should be understood that this is the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*), as it was established previously.

The abandonment of the afflictions and so forth to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) establishes one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); it should be understood that this is precisely the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūpatṛṣṇākṣaya-parijñā*).

The abandonment of the afflictions and so forth to be abandoned through the path of cultivation pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) establishes one thorough knowledge; this is the thorough knowledge of the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādāna-parijñā*).
Since this is also combined with the preceding [categories] to establish a single [type],
one should now analyze how many among these nine established types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) constitute the fruits of the path.
The verse says:
Among these, six are the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*); the remaining three are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*).
All are the fruits of the *anāgamya* stage; five or eight are the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas;
one is the fruit of the preparatory stage of the formless realm (*ārūpya-sāmantaka*), and the same applies to the three fundamental stages of the formless realm.
The worldly fruits are two; for the noble ones, nine. Dharma-knowledge has three; subsequent knowledge has two.
The fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge are six; the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge are five.
The Treatise says:
Among these nine, one should first explain the distinctions regarding their being the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the path (*mārga*).

There are six fruits of patience, namely, the six kinds of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) consisting of the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) that are bound to the three realms.

There are three fruits of knowledge (*jñāna-phala*), namely: the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the fetters conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*), and the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana*). These three thorough knowledges are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
By this, the fruits of the paths of seeing and cultivation have already been explained.
Regarding the distinction from the dhyāna stages as fruits: the fruit of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) dhyāna possesses nine, because it serves as the basis for abandoning all [defilements].
The fruit of the fundamental dhyānas consists of either five or eight.
Regarding the statement that there are five, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"Because the fundamental dhyānas are not the antidotes for abandoning desire.
Regarding the statement that there are eight, the Venerable Ghoṣaka says:

Because the fundamental dhyānas also serve as antidotes for abandoning desire, the pervasive knowledges (*parijñā*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form and formless realms are excluded; this is because at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), the pervasive knowledges are collectively integrated.
The intermediate dhyānas are as described for the fundamental dhyānas.

Is it not the case that when one enters the vision of the truths (darśanamārga) by relying on a fundamental dhyāna, one also cultivates [the path] in the future? Since the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) that serves as the antidote to desire is obtained by relying on the stage of *anāgamya*, one should also realize the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*visamyogaprāpti*) from the abandonment of those factors to be abandoned by vision in the desire realm; why then is it said that the fundamental dhyānas obtain only five fruits?
This criticism is unfounded; for the path of abandonment cultivated at that time based on the *anāgamya* stage serves exclusively as the antidote to the abandonments of the form and formless realms.

Since the paths of the fundamental stages cannot serve as the antidote to the abandonments of the desire realm, how could they cultivate the path that acts as the antidote to the abandonments of the desire realm while they are manifest?
Because the cultivation of that *anāgamya* (uninterrupted path) serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for abandonment that treats only the higher realms, its fruits are only five.

As for the distinction regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as a fruit, there is only one fruit for the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realm; this is because, by means of the path of the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*), one attains the fruit of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*).

The stage where a noble one, relying on the mundane path, becomes free from all defilements is also termed "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*), because they have attained the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

The fruits of the first three fundamental [dhyānas] are likewise only one; that is, by relying on the first three fundamental dhyānas of the formless realm, one attains the fruit of the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of all [outflows].
By this, the distinctions regarding the number and types of the fruits of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) obtained through the dhyānas and formless attainments have already been explained.

As for the distinction between their fruits and those of the mundane and noble paths: there are two fruits of the mundane path; that is, by the power of the mundane path, one can only obtain the fruits of the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*).
There are nine fruits of the noble path; that is to say, by the power of the noble path, one is able to transcend even the two peaks of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Among these nine, it should be understood that two are common fruits and seven are uncommon fruits, because they are exclusively the fruits of the noble ones.

Regarding the differences in the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*): there are three fruits of the knowledge of phenomena, because the power of the knowledge of phenomena is able to abandon what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the three realms.
There are two fruits of the subsequent knowledge, because the power of the subsequent knowledge abandons what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.

Regarding the distinction of fruits for the categories of Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge: the fruits of the category of Dharma-knowledge are six, namely the six fruits obtained by the aforementioned Dharma-knowledges and Dharma-patience;
the fruits of the category of Subsequent-knowledge are five, namely the five fruits obtained by the aforementioned Subsequent-knowledges and Subsequent-patience.
The term "categories" (pakṣa) here comprehensively includes both knowledge (*jñāna*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
Among the six categories of dharmas, four are uncommon fruits: three belong to the patiences regarding the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and one belongs to the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*).
Two are common fruits; that is, the final two pairs belong to both the two types of knowledge: the knowledge of the dharma and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Among the five categories [of fruits], three non-common fruits belong to the *anvaya-kṣāntis*, while two are common fruits; the meanings of the latter two are as explained previously.
For what reason are the abandonments obtained through each individual path not each established as a separate *parijñā* (full knowledge)?
Because "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) is spoken of at the time of permanent abandonment. As the Sūtra says:
"I shall now proclaim thorough knowledge for you," and so on, up to the detailed explanation. In this context, what is called "thorough knowledge"?
This refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred, and the permanent abandonment of delusion.
The expression "permanent abandonment" is explained at length;
it indicates that only when the abandonment attained is entirely free from any further bondage can it be termed "thorough knowledge" (parijñā).
What is meant by "abandonment with residual bondage"?
What is meant by "abandonment without residual bondage"?
When abandonment is accomplished through three or four conditions, it is termed "without residual bondage."

It is called "non-endowment" because there may be some abandonments for which, although the acquisition of dissociation has been attained, other acquisitions are lacking; thus, it is possible to relinquish them again permanently.

Alternatively, even if other acquisitions have arisen for certain abandonments, they have not yet eliminated the robust head of saṃsāra; for although the defilements of the eight stages have been repeatedly abandoned, one has not yet eliminated them, and thus one falls back into the prison of the miserable destinies.

Furthermore, there may be an abandonment in which, although that [specific defilement] has been eliminated, other afflictive fetters have not yet been removed; thus, the sense of "complete abandonment" is not yet perfected.

Alternatively, there may be an abandonment in which the remaining fetters have also been removed, yet one is still unable to transcend the realm to which they belong; because the defilements of a similar class have not been abandoned without remainder, the sense of "complete abandonment" is likewise not yet perfected.
Since each of these various abandonments has its own corresponding fetter (*anuśaya*), they are not established as "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Only within the nine stages where the three or four conditions are complete and abandonment is free from such fetters can thorough knowledge be established.
What is meant by "possessing the conditions"?
The verse says:
One attains the acquisition of the abandonment of outflows, And the deficiency of the Peak of Existence.
Because one eliminates both causes and transcends a realm, nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are established.
The treatise states:
Because the abandonment of dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) possesses three conditions, thorough knowledge is established.
Because the abandonment of dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) possesses four conditions, it is only then that "complete knowledge" (parijñā) is established.

As for the abandonment of dharmas to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya), it possesses three conditions: namely, the attainment of the untainted acquisition of dissociation (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti), the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), and the extinction of both causes.

In this context, although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may also be said to have "extinguished both causes" by becoming free from the defilements of the eight stages, their abandonment does not constitute a full "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*), because they lack the other two conditions.

Regarding the abandonments in the second and third moments of the stage of seeing the noble truths (*āryasatya*), although there is the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*), universal knowledge (*parijñā*) is not established because the other two conditions are lacking.
Although the fourth and fifth moments also lack the two causes for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—which have not yet been extinguished—they likewise do not establish universal knowledge.
Because the causes to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) have not yet been extinguished.

At the stage of the dharma-knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), the two categories [of afflictions] of the desire realm are abandoned; because they possess three conditions, they obtain the designation "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*).

In the subsequent five moments—the stages of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)—the abandonments also possess three conditions, and thus all obtain the designation "universal knowledge."
Regarding the four conditions for the abandonment of dharmas through cultivation: three conditions are as described above, with "transcending the realm" as the fourth.
This means that when the Noble Ones have not yet transcended a stage within the various realms, the abandonment they attain possesses only two conditions;
if they have already transcended a stage but have not yet transcended the realm, the abandonment they attain still lacks one condition.
When one transcends a realm, four conditions must be fulfilled for that abandonment to be designated as "universal" (*parijñā*) according to its respective application.

Some say there are five conditions, adding "separation from both fetters" (*ubhaya-bandhana-vigama*); however, because this meaning differs from the former, it is not mentioned here, as it is stated that the cessation of the dual causes constitutes the accomplishment of separation from both fetters.
How many thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are accomplished when one is free [from defilements]?
The verse says:
In the stage of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), there are none; Or one may accomplish from one up to five.
The practitioner accomplishes six, one, or two; the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) accomplishes only one.
The commentary states:
Although an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) may become free from defilement even up to the eighth stage, they do not accomplish the full knowledge (*parijñā*).

Among those in the noble stages who enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, there is no complete knowledge (*parijñā*) from the beginning up to the stage of the *dharmajñānakṣānti* regarding suffering. Upon reaching the stage of the *dharmajñāna* regarding suffering and the *anvayakṣānti* regarding origin, one achieves only one. Upon reaching the *anvayajñāna* regarding suffering and the *dharmakṣānti* regarding cessation, one achieves two. Upon reaching the *dharmajñāna* regarding cessation and the *anvayakṣānti* regarding cessation, one achieves three. Upon reaching the *anvayajñāna* regarding cessation and the *dharmakṣānti* regarding the path, one achieves four. Upon reaching the *dharmajñāna* regarding the path and the *anvayakṣānti* regarding the path, one achieves five.

For one who enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) by relying on the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*), there is likewise no thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) up until the stage of the "patience regarding the subsequent cognition of origin" (*samudayānvayajñānakṣānti*); the subsequent stages should be analyzed accordingly as appropriate.

For one abiding in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) who has not yet abandoned desire, beginning from the "subsequent cognition of the path" (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and continuing until they have not yet attained complete freedom from the defilements of the desire realm or have regressed from that freedom from desire, they possess six [thorough knowledges].

Regarding those who have completely abandoned desire: starting from the ninth path of liberation of the abandonment of desire up to the final uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of abandoning the form realm—for those who previously abandoned desire—their possession consists of only one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely, the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-kṣaya*), from the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) until before the arising of the path that exhausts the form realm.

Falling away from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) and from the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) due to the arising of a defilement of the form realm (*rūpasaṃyojana*) is also exactly as described before.
For those who still possess craving for the form realm, [the falling away occurs] from the permanent exhaustion of that craving.
For those who have previously detached from the form realm, [the falling away occurs] from the arising of the path that exhausts the form realm.
Until one has completely abandoned craving for the formless realm, the exhaustion of the lower fetters is accomplished. When craving for the form realm is exhausted, two [parijñās] are accomplished.

When one falls back from the state of an Arhat (aśaikṣa) and gives rise to the fetters of the formless realm, two universal knowledges (parijñā) are accomplished; their names are as previously explained.
One who dwells in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) accomplishes only one [knowledge], namely, the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana*).

If, when entering right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the fundamental [dhyāna] during the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), that which has been abandoned therein is also designated as the "thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*), how can you maintain that the fruit of the fundamental [dhyāna] consists of only five?

Because one attains the designation "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) by means of abandoning those factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) within the realms of form and formlessness, there is no fault.
For what reason is this alone also given that name?
Regarding those who attain the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) by way of gradual progression, this name is established based on the abandonment [of the lower fetters] therein.

Furthermore, because the lower fetters previously abandoned by the mundane path are now rendered never to arise again through the power of the noble path (*āryamārga*), that abandonment attained is metaphorically designated as this fruit; however, at present, one does not actually obtain the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*parijñā*) regarding the realm of desire.
For what reason are the various abandonments of the Non-returner and Arhat fruits collectively established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
Because of transcending a realm and attaining a fruit, Thorough knowledges are collected in two places.
The treatise says:
Because two conditions are fulfilled, the abandonment thus attained is collectively established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, the transcendence of a realm; second, the attainment of a fruit.
What is called "accumulation" (samudaya) has the meaning of "conjunction.
If, within the formless realm, one attains the fruit of stream-entry by becoming detached from defilements partially, one attains arhatship by becoming detached from them entirely.

If one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm partially, one attains the fruit of a once-returner; if one becomes detached from them completely, one attains the fruit of a non-returner.
However, if one becomes detached from the form realm either partially or completely, one does not attain any such fruit.

Only in two cases are both conditions fulfilled: namely, when one attains the fruit, one simultaneously transcends a realm; therefore, for the Arhat and the Anāgāmin, the abandonment obtained through cultivation is established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), because at that time a single-flavored attainment (*ekarasalābha*) arises in its totality.

Regarding the other two fruits, although they are attained at a time when there is a single flavor (*ekarasa*), one has not yet transcended the realm (*dhātu*). At the stage when craving for the form realm is exhausted, although one has transcended the realm, there is no attainment of a single flavor. Therefore, the universal knowledge (*parijñā*) is not accumulated at those stages, because it must be accumulated as a whole only when both conditions are met.
Who abandons and who acquires how many types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
One abandons one, two, five, or six; Acquisition is likewise, except for five.
The treatise says:

Regarding the statement "abandoning one," this refers to falling away from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), or from the exhaustion of desire for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga-kṣaya*), or from the complete abandonment of desire.

Regarding the statement "abandoning two," this refers to non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who fall away from the exhaustion of desire for the form realm due to the arising of desire-entanglements (*kāma-paryavasthāna*), as well as those who, having previously abandoned desire by relying on the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) and entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), reach the stage of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) at the moment they attain arhatship.
Regarding the statement "abandoning five," the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) explains:

"This refers to the stage of the Knowledge of the Path (mārgajñāna) within the category of the Path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) for one who has previously abandoned desire. This, however, should have stated "at the time of the Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Path" (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti), because at the time of the Knowledge of the Path itself, those [fetters] have already been abandoned.
Regarding the statement that [the knowledges] are "attained and abandoned," this is based on what is about to be explained.

Furthermore, one must specify that this refers to those who enter the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration; for if one enters the vision of the truths by relying on the fundamental (*maula*) dhyānas, one does not obtain the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) regarding the abandonment of the desire realm. Consequently, one would not obtain the three types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) concerning the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned through vision in the desire realm. It cannot be said that these are "abandoned" now when they were not previously obtained.
Regarding the statement "abandoning six," this refers to when noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire attain the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Regarding "attaining likewise," this means that some attain one, some attain two, and some attain six.

To say "one is attained" refers to the nine stages beginning with the patience for the accumulation of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) during the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), as well as the falling back from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) due to the entanglements of the form realm (*rūpārūpya-saṃyojana*).
To say "two are attained" refers to the time when one falls back from the state of no-more-learning due to the various entanglements of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the statement that "six are attained," this refers to the case of falling back from the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
There is no attainment of five, because such a case is logically impossible.

This means that one who has previously abandoned desire by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration and enters the vision of the truths attains the fruit of non-returner at the moment of the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*, thereby relinquishing the five universal knowledges (*parijñā*).
If this fruit were subject to retrogression, one could attain five types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*);
since such retrogression does not exist, there is no possibility of attaining five. One might object:

"When attaining a superior fruit through spiritual progress, one gives rise to a superior acquisition (*prāpti*) regarding the various unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states; this may indeed be called 'attainment,' so why should thorough knowledge be relinquished?"
In terms of the actual state of abandonment, it is always accomplished;

however, for the time being, based on the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), if one obtains a different name, the original name is lost, which is termed "abandoning" (*tyāga*). There is no fault in this, because the establishment of thorough knowledge is distinct from that of abandonment.
*Abhidharmasamayasāra-śāstra*, Fascicle 28; *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā-samaya-śāstra*, Fascicle 29.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Seven: Distinguishing the Noble and the Holy (Bian Xian Sheng Pin), Part One. It has already been established that although afflictions are immeasurable according to their various categories, they are collectively classified into three realms and five divisions.

Although the objects to which the various afflictions are bound—and thus the instances of their abandonment—are likewise immeasurable, nine types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) are established based on their predominant stages.
Since abandonment must necessarily be attained through the power of the path, what are the characteristics of this path by which it is achieved?
The verse says:
It has already been explained that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
on the path of seeing, one sees the noble truths, while on the path of cultivation, one cultivates the nine grades.
The treatise states:

The World-Honored One taught that there are only two types of afflictions, distinguished by those to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
However, within the various treatises, these two are expanded into five, namely the five categories of what is to be abandoned, as previously explained.
To summarize briefly, there are only two [paths], as stated in the sūtra; the abandonment of those [afflictions] occurs solely through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
The path of seeing refers to the vision of the principle of the four noble truths, while the path of cultivation refers to the practice of the nine grades of distinctions.
The vision [of the truths] is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), while cultivation pertains to both types.
This has already been clarified by the preceding [explanation], and thus the verse does not mention it.
What are the characteristics of the Noble Truths that are seen?
The verse says:
The four truths have already been named—namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
their intrinsic natures are likewise so, following the order of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
The Treatise says:
In the sūtras, the Buddha taught that there are four truths: first, suffering; second, origination; third, cessation; and fourth, the path.

This has also been previously explained in this treatise: among conditioned phenomena, with the exception of the noble paths, those that function as results are all termed the truth of suffering, while those that function as causes are all termed the truth of origination.

Although the entities themselves do not differ, there is no loss in their numerical distinction, because the aspects (ākāra) of the various patiences (kṣānti) and knowledges (jñāna) established within the stage of clear realization (abhisamaya) are distinct, just as in the case of the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the [four] bases of liberation (niḥsaraṇa), and the [four] modes of investigation (vitarka).

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); both the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Since the cause precedes and the fruit follows as a matter of logical necessity, it is certain that these must be listed in this order according to their names.
Suffering is situated after its accumulation, and the Path precedes its cessation; why, then, is the fruit mentioned here before the cause?
It is explained according to the sequence of the stages of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
That is to say, in accordance with the practitioner’s stage of clear realization, what is realized first is explained first, and what is realized later is explained later.
However, some dharmas are taught in the order of their arising, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth;
others are taught according to convenience, such as the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) and so forth.
For what reason is the sequence of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) necessarily fixed?
Because one observes in this manner during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*). For what reason must one observe in this way during the stage of preparatory application?

It is because whatever phenomenon is most oppressive should, according to principle, be observed first during the stage of preparatory application; next, one seeks its cause; next, one seeks liberation from it; and finally, one should seek the means for that liberation.
For example, a skilled physician first observes the symptoms of the patient’s illness, next seeks its cause, then contemplates the cure, and finally seeks an effective medicine.
Thus, a sutra states:

"A king among physicians is one who possesses four qualities and is able to extract the poisonous arrow: first, he is well-versed in the symptoms of illness; second, he is well-versed in the causes of illness; third, he is well-versed in the cure of illness; and fourth, he is well-versed in effective medicines."

The Tathāgata is likewise a great king of physicians; because he has realized suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path exactly as they are, he relies on this sequence for contemplation during the stage of application (*prayoga*), and the sequence of contemplation is the same during the stage of direct realization (*abhisamaya*), as it is induced by the power of that prior application.
Just as one might recite previously memorized texts by rote, the names of the Noble Truths are listed according to the sequence of their realization (*abhisamaya*).
Because they are perfectly awakened to in succession, they are designated by the term "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).
Because it is the object of perfect awakening (*samyag-bodha*), it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because this awakening is truly pure, it receives the name "perfect" (*samyak*).
What is the meaning designated by the term "Noble Truth" (*ārya-satya*)?
They are called "Noble Truths" because they are truths for the Noble Ones.

That is to say, only the Noble Ones are able to contemplate these Four Truths through noble conduct and noble wisdom as they truly are; ordinary beings cannot do so, and therefore they are called Noble Truths.

Only one portion of sensation is the intrinsic nature of suffering; the remainder is not. How, then, can it be said that all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the Truth of Suffering?
The verse says:
Suffering arises from conjunction with the three types of suffering; All things are so according to their respective natures.
"Agreeable, disagreeable, and other contaminated conditioned phenomena.
The commentary states:

There are three types of suffering-nature: first, the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*); second, the nature of suffering as conditioning (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*); and third, the nature of suffering as change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).

Since all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are, as appropriate, associated with these three types of suffering, there is no error in considering them all to be the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Why is this so?
All conditioned phenomena associated with outflows are of three kinds:
agreeable, disagreeable, and the remainder.
What is the agreeable?
This refers to all pleasant feelings (*sukha-vedanā*) and their associated requisites; the other two categories are likewise.

Among these, agreeable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that are tainted (*sāsrava*) are called "suffering" because they are conjoined with the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); for those who have not yet abandoned defilement, sorrow and the like will inevitably arise when those things change.
For it is said in the sūtras of the Blessed One:
"All pleasant feelings are pleasant when arising, pleasant while abiding, and painful when perishing.
It should be understood that all formations conducive to pleasant feeling are like the pleasant feeling itself.
All unpleasing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) are called suffering because they are conjoined with the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkha*).
This is because when the essence of painful feeling itself, or phenomena conducive to pain, manifest, they inevitably afflict both body and mind.
For the Blessed One stated in a sūtra:
"All painful feelings are suffering when they arise, suffering while they persist, and pleasant when they cease.
It should be understood that all formations conducive to painful feeling are likewise like the painful feeling itself.

Aside from these, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called suffering because they are conjoined with the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Since everything produced by causes and conditions is impermanent, and nothing that is impermanent and with outflows is not suffering, all phenomena with outflows are of the nature of suffering.

Is it not the case that all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra-dharma*), based on this principle, can all be considered of the nature of the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)?
It should not be asserted that only non-painful-and-non-pleasant sensations (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*) and their requisite conditions constitute the nature of the suffering of conditioning.
Although this principle holds true, it is stated in this context as such because it relies upon what is unique [to suffering].
What is the essential nature of these three types of suffering?
One should definitively judge that their essence consists of the three feelings (*vedanā*), for it is by virtue of the three feelings that they exist.
The dharmas that accord with the three types of feeling likewise receive the names of the three types of suffering as appropriate.
Because the Path is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is not subsumed under the nature of suffering.
As has been analyzed above, among the Four Noble Truths, how many are conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and how many are ultimate (*paramārtha*)?
What are the characteristics of these two truths?
The verse says:
"That which ceases to exist when broken by cognition, and likewise that which [ceases] when analyzed by wisdom into its remaining parts,"
That which is like a jar or water is the conventional; that which differs from this is called the ultimate.
The treatise says:
Among all composite things, according to their respective natures, there are generally two types of categories:
First, it can be broken into minute parts by physical means; second, it can be analytically excluded from other phenomena by wisdom.

That is to say, when a collection of various forms is broken down into minute parts, the cognition of it ceases to exist; this is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), such as a jar and the like. This is because once a jar or the like has been broken into shards and so forth, one can no longer give rise to the cognition of a "jar" within those fragments.

There are composite aggregates which, though broken down into many parts, still give rise to that cognition; they are like water and other such things. If, by means of superior wisdom, one analyzes and removes other constituent dharmas, that cognition then ceases to exist; these too are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When water and so forth are analyzed away from form and other [elements] by means of wisdom, the cognition of "water" and so forth can no longer arise with respect to them.

Therefore, before those things have been broken down and analyzed, they are designated by worldly conventions and names; because they are established through such designation, they are called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

According to conventional reasoning, that which is said to exist as jars and so forth—being real and not false—is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because it is said to exist according to conventional reasoning.
If a thing differs from this, it is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

That is to say, when an object is broken, the cognition of it is not absent; furthermore, when it is analyzed away by wisdom, that cognition still persists. This is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

It is like form (*rūpa*) and so forth: for instance, when an object such as form is crushed into minute parts and gradually broken down until it reaches the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), or when taste and other qualities are analytically removed by superior wisdom, the cognition of that form and so forth remains constant, just as it was before.
