The same applies to sensation (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors]. However, because they are non-material (*arūpa-dharma*) and lack physical subdivisions, they cannot be broken down into parts down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Nevertheless, they can be analyzed by wisdom (*prajñā*) down to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), or the other factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) can be analytically excluded; yet the cognition of those sensations and so forth remains ever-present, just as it was originally.
This exists truly and is therefore called the ultimate (paramārtha), because its essence exists at all times.
Based on this ultimate principle, it is said that form and so forth exist as reality and not as falsehood; thus, it is termed the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).

Since they are said to exist according to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all four noble truths are subsumed within the ultimate truth, because when analyzed in detail, cognition does not abandon them.
Regarding conventional truths (*saṃvṛtisatya*), based on the principle of ultimate truth, is their own conventional nature existent or non-existent?
If one says it exists, then the truths should be only one;
if one says it does not exist, then the truths should not be two.
This should be definitively judged as existing, for the Venerable Vasumitra has said:
The name that non-erroneously reveals the meaning is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the meaning revealed by this name is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That the name is a substantial entity (*dravya*) has already been established as previously argued.
Has it not already been stated that the truths should be only one?
In principle, this is indeed so, for that which is emptiness in the ultimate sense cannot be designated as a "truth.
Why, then, are two established?
That is to say, within the ultimate sense, it is established as conventional based on a slight difference in principle, not because of a difference in essence.
The reason for this is that "name" is the basis of expression, for its nature is to circulate according to worldly convention.
Based on this principle, one should state as follows:
All that is conventional is necessarily ultimate, yet there is that which is ultimate but not conventional.

That is to say, when one sets aside mere names and considers the remaining truly existent objects, within the context of those objects existing by way of the ultimate, they are designated as "conventional truth" according to one aspect of reasoning, and designated as "ultimate truth" according to another aspect of reasoning.
That is to say, the principle of a unified whole (*piṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) apprehended as a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) without distinction is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

If there is an apprehension of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) through distinction—whether as a category or as a particular object—it is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). For example, within a single entity consisting of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), the apprehended sense of being an effect is termed the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), while the apprehended sense of being a cause is termed the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Alternatively, as in the case of a single entity consisting of mind and mental factors, which possess the nature of being endowed with the six causes and four conditions,
there is no contradiction or subversion of the truths taught by the Great Sage.
As it is said that there is but one truth and no second, and but one path and no other path, what is the general nature of these Four Noble Truths?

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) constitute the truths, because they are the objects of afflictions and the noble paths; because they possess the distinct natures of the causes and effects of defilement and purification; because non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) possess intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*); and because they are the objects of right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), which is itself an analytical discernment.

However, because it is not an object of the noble path, nor is it of the nature of the cause and effect of defilement and purification, nor is it an object of practice for those who feel aversion or delight, and because one does not become a noble one by awakening to it, it is not included among the Noble Truths discussed herein.
For what reason do the afflictions not arise taking those [uncontaminated phenomena] as their objects?
Because those two types of phenomena are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they cannot oppose or harm contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.

That is to say, craving takes only contaminated phenomena as its object; because delighting in uncontaminated phenomena opposes all forms of existence (*bhava*), it is not called "craving," but is instead termed "desire for wholesome phenomena" (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*).
If an object is extremely conducive to the arising of craving and attachment, that object is entirely an object-condition (*ālambana*) for the afflictions.
Because it is an object of craving, one consequently lacks the desire [to seek its cessation] and harbors doubt and slander regarding its cessation and the path to its cessation.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are the opposite of this; therefore, they certainly do not serve as objects for the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Is it not the case that even toward teachers such as those who employ the two similes, one may give rise to aversion, doubt, or slander? How then can it be said that afflictions do not arise by taking them as objects?

Ignorance, doubt, and wrong views that arise conditioned by those [objects] do not obstruct the realization of the cessation of suffering and the path leading to the cessation of suffering in the same way that [ignorance, etc.

become defiled when conditioned by suffering and so forth. For instance, even though an Arhat may still manifest ignorance, doubt, and slander regarding the path and other such matters, how could these be said to be defiled afflictions?
Therefore, these are all of an undefiled nature; for this reason, it is said that there are no afflictions which take them as objects.

Some say that this does not constitute a denial of emptiness or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), but rather a denial of their names while not taking their actual entities as objects.
These two are exclusively the objects of mundane wholesome knowledge; why is it not likewise so regarding the truths of suffering and the others?
Therefore, one should know that what was stated previously is without fault.
Now, one should investigate: for those who seek true vision within the Noble Truths, what practice should they first cultivate to seek the vision of the Noble Truths?

The conduct and practices cultivated during the stage of initial application are extremely extensive; those who wish to understand them thoroughly should seek them within the various treatises on contemplative practice compiled by the noble ones.

In brief, a beginner should possess a profound aspiration for liberation, contemplating the virtues of nirvana and the faults of saṃsāra; first, they should employ skillful means to draw near to virtuous friends, for virtuous friends serve as the foundation for all practices.

One who possesses the powers of hearing and so forth earns the name of "virtuous friend" (kalyāṇamitra); because they can discern the capacities of sentient beings and bestow the Dharma accordingly, drawing near to such a virtuous friend is called the "complete holy life" (brahmacarya).
Now that the practitioner has been taken into the care of a virtuous friend capable of expounding the true Dharma, what practice should they cultivate?
The verse says:
One who is about to enter the path of seeing the truths Should abide in ethical discipline and diligently cultivate That which is produced by hearing, reflection, and meditation;
Namely, the objects consisting of names, both [names and meanings], and meanings.
The Treatise says:

Those who have resolved their minds and are about to proceed toward the vision of the truths should first abide securely in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), and thereafter diligently cultivate the wisdoms consisting of hearing and so forth.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Abiding in and relying upon ethical discipline (*śīla*), one should diligently cultivate two things.
That is to say, having first established oneself in pure morality, one should further frequently associate with practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*)."
Following the instructions and exhortations of the yoga master, one diligently applies oneself to receiving teachings that accord with the vision of truth.

Having heard them, one zealously seeks the meaning of the Dharma as it was taught, so that the wisdom arising from the teacher’s instructions may increase, gradually becoming superior, increasingly clear, and ultimately reaching full maturity.

Not only does he give rise to a mind of contentment regarding this [attainment], but he further applies himself to the individual investigation of the meaning of the Dharma; in this way and that way, a definitive wisdom arises.

Once this definitive wisdom has arisen through the cause of his own reflection, he is able to diligently cultivate the two types of cultivation—the remedies for the specific characteristics and the general characteristics of the various afflictions.

To summarize the meaning herein briefly: it means that a practitioner, dwelling in ethical discipline and practicing diligently, gives rise to the wisdom arisen from reflection based on the wisdom arisen from hearing, and gives rise to the wisdom arisen from cultivation based on the wisdom arisen from reflection.
What are the distinctions between the characteristics of these three types of wisdom (*prajñā*)?

They are said, respectively, to take as their objects names (*nāman*), both name and meaning (*artha*), and meaning alone. In reality, when the three wisdoms reach full accomplishment, they all exclusively take meaning as their object; at that time, it would be difficult to distinguish their individual characteristics. Therefore, for now, we shall explain them according to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), stating that hearing, reflection, and cultivation take names, both name and meaning, and meaning as their respective objects. It is not the case that a determinate wisdom arises solely by taking names as its object; therefore, the wisdom consisting of hearing does not take only names as its object.

Nevertheless, by the power of the names, phrases, and syllables as taught by the master, there arises a definitive wisdom regarding the distinctions of meaning; this wisdom is called "wisdom accomplished through hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). In terms of the preparatory means for entry, it is said to take only names as its object.
Once the wisdom born of hearing has been accomplished for the sake of knowing specific meanings, one further applies diligent effort to personally examine and discern them.

To ensure that this discernment is free from error, one again recollects the teacher’s instructions regarding the sets of names, phrases, and syllables; through this, at a later time, a definitive wisdom arises concerning the distinctions of meaning, which is called the wisdom accomplished through reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).
At this stage of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), because the power of reflecting on the meaning induces mindfulness of names, it is said to take the combined object as its domain.

Once the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is perfected and meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) manifests, one realizes the distinctions of the meaning without depending on names or phrases; this definitive wisdom is called that "produced by cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī*).

Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* explains the characteristics of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), stating: if there is wisdom that, at the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*), produces an understanding of the meaning by the power of relying on names, this induced wisdom is called "wisdom consisting of hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

If, during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one induces mindfulness through the power of reflecting on the meaning, this is called "understanding" (*adhigama*); the certain wisdom (*niścaya-jñāna*) that subsequently arises from this is called "wisdom produced by reflection" (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).
If, without depending on names, one contemplates only the meaning and gives rise to internally realized wisdom, it is called "wisdom produced by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
Among these, the reason why the two types of wisdom are called "accomplished" (bhāvanā-mayī) is that they arise through the power of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).
As for the third, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), it is called "accomplished" in the sense that cultivation itself constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As it is said, the vessel of life is composed of precious food.
For those who wish to apply themselves with diligence to cultivation, how can they purify the vessel of the body so that their practice may be swiftly accomplished?
The verse says:
Possessing physical and mental seclusion, being free from lack and great desire—
namely, not seeking much for what has been obtained or what has not yet been obtained— is what is meant by "having nothing."
The three [roots] that counteract the discordant realms are untainted and have non-attachment as their nature;
the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are likewise. The first three consist solely of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*).
Three pertain to the requisites of life, while the last pertains to activity; they serve to counteract the arising of the four types of craving.
Because of the desire for "mine," "I," and "my affairs," [these] are temporarily stilled and permanently eliminated.
The treatise says:
The purification of the body-vessel is briefly due to three causes.
What are the three causes?
First, physical and mental seclusion; second, contentment and fewness of desires; third, abiding in the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
That is to say, if one wishes for cultivation to be swiftly accomplished, one must first diligently purify the vessel of the body and mind.
If one wishes to purify the vessel of the body, one must first cultivate physical and mental seclusion.

Physical seclusion means distancing oneself from evil companions; mental seclusion means abandoning unwholesome thoughts. Because the body and mind are thus separated from evil companions and thoughts, the vessel of the body becomes pure and the mind easily attains concentration.
By what means are these two easily accomplished? They are accomplished through contentment with robes and so forth, and through fewness of desires.
"Contentment" means the absence of discontent;
"fewness of desires" means the absence of great desire.

Those who have many desires for the requisites of life associate with evil companions by day and give rise to unwholesome discursive thoughts by night; consequently, they find no opportunity to bring their minds to meditative concentration.
What are the two kinds of distinctions regarding what is absent?
They are as follows: having already obtained excellent and abundant clothing and so forth, one does not wish for twice as much excellence or abundance;
because one further craves even more within that very state—manifesting a desire for equality or superiority—it is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).
If one seeks to obtain fine and abundant clothing and other such things that have not yet been acquired, it is called "great desire.
The meaning here is this: whatever possessions exist are sufficient to remedy suffering; if one seeks more than that, one transgresses the category of wholesome qualities.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"To whatever extent one attains physical ease and comfort, it makes the mind easy to concentrate and enables one to teach the Dharma.
Therefore, seeking objects that remedy suffering for this purpose serves as an aid to the Path and is not a fault.
Therefore, when one has already obtained the conditions for remedying suffering, yet further seeks after things of exquisite quality and great renown, this is called "lack of contentment.
When one excessively craves that which has not been obtained at all, it is termed "great desire."
These two are distinct characteristics.

Since contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) can counteract these [two faults], it should be understood that their characteristics are distinct from them by being their opposites;
that is, they counteract lack of contentment, which is the opposite of contentment.
This mark of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) serves as the antidote to great desire (*mahēcchā*); being contrary to great desire is the mark of fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*).
This is called contentment: the non-seeking of further objects once one has already obtained those things that serve as remedies for suffering.
Not seeking in excess what has not yet been obtained—specifically, objects that can remedy suffering—is the meaning of having few desires (*alpeccha*).
Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and having few desires pertain to all three realms; there are also those that transcend the three realms and are comprised within the untainted (*anāsrava*).

That is to say, contentment and fewness of desires associated with a wholesome mind bound to the desire realm are themselves bound to the desire realm; the two [types of] untainted [contentment and fewness of desires] pertaining to the [upper] two realms should be explained by analogy with this.
The two types of their opposites are bound exclusively to the desire realm.
By what is this known?

It is because even in the form and formless realms there exist the antidotes of contentment and fewness of desires; for we observe that when beings born in the desire realm give rise to [states] belonging to the form and formless realms and so forth, the two types of the discordant factors (the objects to be countered) are far removed from active manifestation, while the two types of the remedial factors (the antidotes) increase in their active manifestation.
The specific characteristics of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) have already been explained.
Their common characteristic is non-attachment (*alobha*), because both are capable of counteracting greed.
The common characteristic of that which is to be countered is sensual greed (*kāmarāga*).
The noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) should be understood as being explained according to their remedies; that is, they also pertain to all three realms.

They are untainted (anāsrava) and consist of non-attachment (alobha). Just as within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), although there is no object of resentment, the wholesome root of non-hatred (adveṣakuśalamūla) can still exist, so it is here.
Therefore, although clothing and such do not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*) can still be present there.
Just as one does not crave the body, one likewise does not crave the requisites for life; thus, the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are fully present in the formless realm.
Regarding the noble ones who experience sensual desires, they possess the *āśaya* (intentional disposition) within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) but lack the *prayoga* (actual application).
They are called "noble lineages" because they belong to the noble ones, and because the entire assembly of noble ones arises from these four.
Successive lineages of inheritance continue without interruption; that the former serves as the seed for the latter is universally established in the world.

The *dharmakāya* of all the Noble Ones is produced by the power of contentment with clothing and other requisites; thus, they belong to the noble clan and receive the name "noble lineage" (*āryavaṃśa*).

Among the four [noble lineages], the first three consist solely of contentment; that is, one gives rise to contentment with whatever robes, food, and bedding one obtains. These three forms of contentment are themselves the three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The wholesome root of non-attachment has many varieties. Among these, that which counteracts the greed for lack of contentment is designated as the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The fourth noble lineage refers to the delight in abandonment and cultivation—that is, the abandonment consisting of dissociation from defilements and the delight in the Noble Path.

This means that because one feels deep longing and admiration for those [two], taking joy in their abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is called "joy in abandonment and cultivation"; this is precisely the meaning of longing for cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

Alternatively, the cultivation of that which is joyful in abandonment is called "joy in abandonment and cultivation"; this is the meaning of longing for the path to cessation, because one cultivates the path with the desire to realize the cessation of afflictions.
Because this [state] is able to counteract craving for existence and non-existence, it likewise has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
But would it not follow that the fourth [immeasurable] also has non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and so forth as its intrinsic nature, since it too is able to counteract hatred and the like?

It is not that this meaning does not exist; however, because the first three serve as its provisions, because the first three are exclusively of the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*), and because this [fourth] is also able to counteract attachment by itself, it is explained in terms of its predominant characteristic.
For what reason is contentment alone established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), and not fewness of desires?
This is because one who possesses few desires may still harbor expectations regarding robes and other requisites.
That is to say, one whose disposition is not inferior does not dare to seek much for objects not yet obtained; even if they have already obtained much, they may still seek what is inferior or less.

Regarding contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*): one who is content does not seek further even when having obtained little, let alone when obtaining much; therefore, contentment alone is established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
Alternatively, it is to prevent the desire of those who practice asceticism that "fewness of desires" (*alpecchatā*) is not spoken of as a noble lineage.
It is not that those non-Buddhists possess superior desire; rather, it is because their mental continuum is constantly permeated by inferior desire.

Alternatively, to feel joy according to what one has obtained and no longer seek with further longing is called "contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*); the abandonment of the pleasure of desire is considered the most excellent of all.

Sentient beings of the desire realm mostly delight in sensual pleasures; this delight in sensual pleasures contradicts the mind of renunciation, causes the mind to become dull and obscured within the state of freedom from afflictions, and is able to obstruct the manifestation of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), constituting the deepest of faults.
Contentment is able to counteract [craving]; therefore, only contentment is established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).

It is not the case that the mind gives rise to joy when one entertains a longing for robes and other requisites not yet obtained—how much less so for those already few; thus, because having few desires is not the most excellent among the remedies for the delight in desire, it is not established as a noble lineage.
How can contentment arising from clothing and other such things be said to be untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Who says that such contentment is untainted?
If that were so, how could it be that all the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are universally associated with the untainted?

The noble path that arises through their predominance is named after them because it is induced by them; therefore, it is said that the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) all pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is not stated, however, that all contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) regarding robes and so forth pertains to the untainted.
The [terms] "fewness of desires" (*alpeccha*) and "absence of outflows" (*anāsrava*) should be explained according to this principle.
That is to say, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) arises through their predominance; because it is induced by them, it is named after them.
Since the Noble Path does not arise from conditions such as robes and other objects, for what reason did the Blessed One teach the four noble lineages (*catvāry āryavaṃśāni*)?

Because his disciples have abandoned worldly requisites and worldly occupations to go forth under the Buddha, he demonstrates to them that within the Buddha’s noble Dharma and Vinaya there exist requisites and occupations that can assist the path.
This means that for one who has developed weary detachment toward the household life of birth and death and has gone forth to seek liberation, what need is there for material requisites?

One should develop deep contentment with whatever clothing and other items are obtained, and engage in such activities as are conducive to the profound delight in abandoning and cultivating [the path], for apart from this, there is no way to realize nirvana.
For what reason are there exactly four, neither more nor less?
Because up to this point, the causes for the arising of the noble ones are fully satisfied.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of causes for the arising of the noble ones:
First, the abandonment of faults; second, the cultivation of virtues.
These correspond respectively to the first three and the fourth [of the four noble lineages]. Therefore, there are exactly four, neither more nor less.
Alternatively, all virtues produced through hearing, reflection, and meditation are the noble lineages, for they are the basis for liberation.
Nevertheless, in order to counteract the arising of the four types of craving, the Blessed One briefly explained these four; for the Sūtra states that there are four arisings of craving.
Thus the Sūtra says:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Craving arises when it should arise, persists when it should persist, and clings when it should cling, having clothing as its cause."
In this same way, craving for food, drink, bedding, and seats, as well as for existence and non-existence, is explained in all such cases.
To counteract these four, only the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are taught.
Why is contentment with medicine not considered a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*)?
It is because it is not said that craving arises therein.

Noble lineages are established as the antidote to the arising of craving; since the Sūtra states that craving arises in only four ways, contentment with medicine is not established as a noble lineage.

Alternatively, because they are already subsumed within the first three [noble lineages], it is said that medicinal substances may be included among clothing, food and drink, or bedding; therefore, contentment with medicine is not established as a separate noble lineage.
Alternatively, if one were to argue that pride and other such faults are induced therein, the Noble Lineages (āryavaṃśa) are established as their antidote.
Since no fault of inducing pride and so forth arises regarding medicine, there is no "contentment with medicine" among the Noble Lineages.

Alternatively, if it were the case that all people partake [of medicine], then contentment with that could be established as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa); however, this is not so, because those venerable ones such as Bakula did not at any time lack illness or the use of medicine.

Alternatively, those things that should be used at all times can be established as noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) based on contentment with them, because medicine is not something to be used at all times.

Furthermore, medical treatises also mention contentment with medicine; however, it is only within the Vinaya that contentment with robes and so forth is mentioned. This is because the noble lineages exist solely within the internal Dharma.
Some say that although there is contentment with medicine, it is not established as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa) because various medicines can be conducive to the holy life (brahmacarya).
That is to say, as is seen in the world, for one who delights in training in the precepts, contentment with medicine acts as an obstacle to the holy life.

Alternatively, because the Buddha wished to temporarily pacify and permanently eliminate the desire for things belonging to "self" (*ātman*) and "mine" (*ātmīya*), he taught the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Specifically, he taught the first three noble lineages in order to temporarily pacify the desire for things belonging to "mine."
The fourth noble lineage is taught for the sake of permanently eliminating both the self and the desire for things pertaining to the self (*mamakāra*).
Since the grasping at "mine" is designated by the term "desire," the Blessed One taught the first three noble lineages in order to temporarily pacify this grasping at "mine."

Because it brings about the permanent eradication of both contentment with robes and the like, as well as the noble path induced by that [contentment], along with the grasping at a self and its objects, the Blessed One taught the fourth noble lineage.
That is to say, delighting in abandonment and cultivation, as well as the noble path induced by their predominance, are all termed "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*).
The intent of this section is to show that the four noble lineages are taught in order to cause the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to temporarily cease and be permanently eliminated.
Thus, having already explained what should be practiced when about to enter the vision of the truths,

and what is to be practiced once that has been done— in order to swiftly purify the vessel of the body through cultivation— now that such provisions for the noble path have been gathered, by what door does one enter the actual practice?
The verse says:
There are two essential gateways for entering cultivation: the meditation on impurity and mindfulness of breathing.
Those in whom desire or discursive thought predominates should practice these respectively, in their proper order.
The treatise states:
Since the modes of conduct among various classes of sentient beings are manifold, the gateways for entering cultivation are likewise diverse.

Nevertheless, for the most part, they enter by means of two gateways: first, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); second, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Therefore, these two alone are designated as the essential gateways.
Do all sentient beings enter [the path] by means of both? No;
rather, they do so according to whether craving or discursive thought (*vitarka*) predominates.

Those for whom craving predominates enter by relying on the first gateway (the mindfulness of the body), while those for whom discursive thought predominates enter by relying on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Just as a single medicine cannot cure every variety of disease,

it should be understood that the teaching of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*)— expounded here from the perspective of immediate treatment— is capable of curing the disease of desire, even if it does not treat other afflictions; likewise,
the practice of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) for treating discursive thought (*vitarka*) should be understood in the same way.

However, because mindfulness of breathing takes as its object a subtle realm that is undifferentiated, and because its object is bound to one's own mental continuum, it is unlike the meditation on impurity which takes many external objects; thus, it is able to suppress distracted discursive thoughts.

Having already explained in general that those for whom desire and discursive thought are predominant enter into cultivation respectively by means of the two preceding gates, one should first here analyze the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
What are the characteristics of such a contemplation?
The verse says:
To serve as a general remedy for the four types of craving, one first contemplates the skeleton;
expanding the visualization until it reaches the ocean and then contracting it again is called the stage of a beginner in practice.
From the feet up to half the head is called "having already cultivated maturity";
binding the mind between the eyebrows is called "transcending the stage of mental attention.
The Treatise says:
The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity is specifically intended to counteract desire.
However, there are briefly four types of desire: first, desire for color; second, desire for shape; third, desire for exquisite touch; and fourth, desire for service and offerings.
To counteract the four types of craving, one relies on two kinds of analytical reflection: first, contemplating internal corpses; second, contemplating external corpses.
Those of sharp faculties initially rely on the former, while those of dull faculties initially rely on the latter.

This means that those of sharp faculties first take the skin of their own internal body as the limit, observing it from the soles of the feet upward to the crown of the head and downward to the base, thereby causing the mind to feel weary and repelled.

As for those of dull faculties, because their faculties are dull, their afflictions are fierce and difficult to subdue; they can only be subdued and treated by relying on the power of external conditions. Therefore, they first clearly observe an external corpse, gradually causing the afflictions of their own minds to be subdued.

This means that when one first wishes to contemplate an external corpse, one should first give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and go to the place where the body lies; one contemplates the characteristics of the external corpse to compare them with one's own internal body, thinking: "Since those characteristics are such, this [internal body] must also be thus."
One should cultivate eight perceptions to subdue and remedy the four types of craving.
To subdue and remedy craving for color (*varṇa-rāga*), one cultivates the perception of a livid corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*) and the perception of a discolored corpse (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*).
To subdue and remedy craving for shape (*saṃsthāna-rāga*), one cultivates the perception of a mangled corpse (*vikhādita-saṃjñā*) and the perception of a dismembered corpse (*vikṣiptaka-saṃjñā*).
In order to subdue and treat greed for exquisite tactile sensations, one cultivates the perception of disintegration and the perception of skeletons.
In order to subdue and treat greed for offerings and service, one cultivates the perception of bloating and the perception of festering pus.
It is permitted to cultivate the meditation on the impure by means of a chain of bones (*asthi-śaṅkalā*), as this is capable of subduing and treating these four types of craving.
Since a single chain of bones contains all the objects for abandoning these four cravings, one should now explain the cultivation of the meditation on the chain of bones.
However, when eliciting the various roots of virtue, there are three stages of the *pudgala* with respect to their practice: first, the beginner (*ādikarmika*);
second, the one who has already matured their practice (*kṛtaparicaya*); and third, the one who has transcended mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).

Furthermore, when a practitioner wishes to cultivate this contemplation of impurity, they should first bind the mind to a part of their own body—whether it be the toes, the space between the eyebrows, the bridge of the nose, or the forehead—focusing intently on whichever place they prefer without wavering, in order to make their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) firm and stable.
From the moment one has entered [the practice], it is called the stage of "initial cultivation.

The term "entry" is used to indicate the initial application of the mind, wherein one visualizes one's own body, starting from the toes and so forth, down to being able to see white bones the size of a coin; through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), this visualization gradually expands and increases until one fully perceives the entire skeleton of the body.

This refers to the stage where the practitioners of yoga, through imaginative contemplation, visualize the skin and flesh rotting and falling away, gradually purifying the bones until they are initially the size of a coin, and finally until the entire body consists of white bones.

In this stage, many types of perception arise; the phrase "perception arises" indicates that one does not abandon the focal object, but rather repeatedly generates other perceptions of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Other masters say:
because the practice of contemplation has not yet been perfected, mental attention (*manasikāra*) proceeds solely by the power of perception.
Once the practice of contemplation is accomplished, it proceeds by the power of wisdom;
since this stage has not yet been achieved, it proceeds through the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā*).

It should be understood that the term "attention" (*manasikāra*) used here generally indicates that all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) proceed in a continuous stream by the power of perception.

Having seen the entire body, one again employs skillful means to enter the gateway of the meditation on the impurity of external white bones. This is done in order to gradually increase one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*): one contemplates a skeleton outside oneself, situated by one’s side, and gradually extends this to fill one bed, one room, one monastery, one garden, one town, one district, one kingdom, and even the entire earth bounded by the oceans, with skeletons filling the space therein.

In order to cause resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) to gradually increase again, one contemplates the extensive objects by gradually abbreviating them, until finally contemplating only the skeleton of one's own body; when this gradual abbreviation of the contemplation on the impure (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is accomplished, it is called the stage of the beginner practitioner (*ādikarmika-yogācāra*).

In order to cause the increase of the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) through this abbreviated contemplation, one further removes the foot bones from within the white bones and dwells with the mind focused on the remaining bones. Gradually, one proceeds until half of the skull bone is removed, dwelling with the mind focused on that half-bone. Up to this point, the abbreviated *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity) is accomplished; this is called the stage where the practitioner of yoga has reached maturity in cultivation.

In order to attain mastery over concise contemplation and resolute conviction, one removes half of the skull-bone and fixes the mind between the eyebrows; by focusing single-mindedly on this single object and dwelling in profound stillness, the extremely concise meditation on impurity is perfected, and this is called the stage of the yoga practitioner who has transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*).
One should know that the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is perfected upon reaching this point, because all that was to be accomplished has been brought to completion.
Regarding mastery over the object of focus—whether it be small or large—one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), which should be reflected upon according to reason.
Because one contemplates according to one's desire in order to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is not called a perversion (*viparyāsa*) but is termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).

Regarding this contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): what is its nature? How many stages (*bhūmi*) does it comprise? What is its object (*ālambana*)? In what place does it arise? What is its mode of activity (*ākāra*)? To which time period (*adhvan*) does it refer? Is it outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)? Is it attained through detachment from defilement (*vairāgyalābha*) or through preparatory application (*prayogalābha*)?
The verse says:
Its nature is non-attachment; it exists in ten stages; it takes desire and form realms as its objects and arises in human beings;
it contemplates impurity and takes its own world as its object; it is with outflows and is acquired in two ways.
The Treatise says:
To answer in sequence the questions previously raised:

this contemplation has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature; it is induced by a mental orientation of opposition; it consists of revulsion and rejection, which is the reverse of attachment. One should know that this is termed the "contemplation of impurity."
To claim that it must be wisdom (*prajñā*) is also logically incorrect, because one must consider what it accords with.
That is to say, since the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) can directly counteract greed (*rāga*), it should properly have non-greed (*alobha*) as its essential nature.
The cause of greed—the perception of purity—is removed through the power of contemplation; therefore, it is said that non-greed is what is conformed to by contemplation.

While all impurity-contemplations (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) are forms of non-greed, not all forms of non-greed are impurity-contemplations. Only that which is able to suppress and remedy greed for visible form (*varṇa-rāga*) and so forth is designated as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this contemplation.
This is stated with respect to its essential nature (*svabhāva*). If accompanied by its concomitants (*anuvartin*), it has all four or five aggregates as its nature.

It universally relies upon ten stages—namely, the four dhyānas, the four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm—because this [state] can exist only within those stages.

This contemplation takes only the objective sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) within the desire realm as its object, because the manifest colors and shapes of the desire realm constitute the object of this contemplation.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"One who is protected by the restraint of the ear-faculty dwells in the contemplation of the foul," and so forth, at length?
This statement is made for those who are overcome by craving for forms; they will necessarily be overcome by craving for sounds and other objects that serve as conditions.

Therefore, one who wishes to overcome craving for forms as a condition must first abide in the restraint of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya-saṃvara*), and only through this can one abide in the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Some say that this contemplation relies solely on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is able to induce the remaining modes of perception associated with repulsive conduct.

Therefore, if one dwells in the restraint of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya-saṃvara*), one must necessarily first dwell in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); the power of this contemplation of impurity is capable of universally taking as its object all spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*) subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If it is argued that the Venerable Aniruddha was unable to contemplate the heavens as impure, and that Śāriputra and others were likewise unable to contemplate the Buddha’s physical body as impure, how then could this contemplation universally take both the desire realm and the form realm as its object?

This objection is not valid; for one who has attained mastery over non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*) can contemplate the color of celestial beings as impure, and the Buddha can contemplate his own subtle and wondrous physical body as impure. Therefore, this contemplation is certainly able to take the entirety of the desire realm and the form realm as its object.
By this, it has already been shown that the object of observation is not the name, and it has also been established that [this meditation] universally observes all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

A beginner can generate this contemplation only by relying on the human realm, and not the *Uttarakuru* continent; for among the celestial realms, there is no lividness (*vinīlaka*) and so forth, and thus it cannot be first initiated there.
Having first arisen here and subsequently being produced in that place, this aspect of the meditative cultivation also becomes manifest.
While its nature should be pure because it functions solely as the transformation of impurity, it is described as "impure" with respect to its mode of activity (*ākāra*).
This is subsumed under the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*); it is a preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and not fundamental (*maula*).

Although it is associated with the three faculties of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, it proceeds in conjunction with revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*). It is like the receptivities and knowledges regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-kṣānti-jñāna*), which, regardless of which time period they belong to, take as their object the realm of that same time period.

If the "non-arising" dharma takes all three time periods as its object, this aspect of the contemplation is not subsumed under the sixteen aspects such as impermanence and so forth; therefore, it is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

It is obtained both through preparatory application (*prayoga*) and through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*); at the moment one abandons the defilements of a particular stage and attains the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of that stage, one simultaneously acquires this contemplation of that stage.
Once it has been acquired through the abandonment of attachment (*vairāgya-lābha*), it may also be brought into manifestation at later times by means of application (*prayoga*).
For those who have not yet abandoned attachment, it is acquired solely through application.

Among these, all noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in their final existence (*caramabhavika*) possess both types—whether previously unacquired or previously acquired; others possess only that which was previously acquired.
Having explained the distinctions in the characteristics of the contemplation on impurity, one should next analyze mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
What are its distinctive characteristics?
The verse says:
Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) belonging to five stages; it takes wind as its object and relies upon a body in the desire realm.
It is acquired in two ways, exists in reality, and has no external counterpart. There are six types, namely counting (*gaṇanā*) and so forth.
The treatise says:
Regarding the term "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānasmṛti*), it refers to what is taught in the *Sūtras* as mindfulness of inhalation (*āna*) and exhalation (*apāna*).
"Inhalation" (*āna*) means holding the breath as it enters; it signifies the drawing of external wind into the body.
*Apāna* refers to holding the breath as it goes out; its meaning is that of drawing internal wind and causing it to exit the body.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'holding the breath as it enters' means inhaling external wind and causing it to enter within the body."
Regarding "retaining the exhalation": one expels the internal wind and causes it to exit the body.
Wisdom observes this as its object through the power of mindfulness; therefore, it is called *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
Other masters say:
"Āna" means that which can bring [air] in, and "apāna" means that which can carry [air] away.
The intent of these words is to reveal that inhalation and exhalation possess the sense of "bringing."
Because wisdom observes this through mindfulness, it receives the name "mindfulness.
Regarding the winds associated with the body, there are briefly six types:

first, the wind of inhalation; second, the wind of exhalation; third, the wind that initiates speech; fourth, the wind of elimination; fifth, the wind of movement; and sixth, the wind that moves the body.
This refers to when sentient beings are in the stages of the womb or the egg, a wind born of karma first arises at the navel, piercing the body to form a cavity like that of a lotus root or stem.

Initially, a wind enters the interior of the body; following this, other winds continue to enter through the mouth and nose. This initial wind and those that follow are called the winds of inhalation (*āśvāsa*).
When this wind of inhalation has just entered within the body, there arises a continuous wind called the wind of exhalation.
It is like the mouth of a bellows being opened by a goldsmith: wind enters naturally, for such is the nature of wind; wherever there is an aperture, it necessarily flows in.
Once it has entered, one presses upon it, and the wind exits again.
The sequence of inhalation and exhalation is likewise.

In reality, this wind neither enters nor exits; rather, its circulation alone can benefit or harm the body. Within the continuity of this process, "entering" and "exiting" are merely conventional designations.
When the inhalation proceeds, it can drive out the putrid, filthy, and foul-smelling substances within the body, increasing the fire element and causing the body to become light and buoyant.
When the exhalation proceeds, it can remove oppressive heat and diminish the fire element, causing the body to become heavy.
The wind that initiates speech refers to a distinct wind that, preceded by desire and successively induced, causes the mind that initiates speech to arise and become intensified.

At birth, [the wind] flows from the navel, surges up to strike the throat, and strikes the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the ripening-born (*vipākaja*) and developmentally nurtured (*aupacayika*) types; it induces the arising of the great elements of the wind-type that are of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*). It vibrates the distinctions of the teeth, lips, tongue, and palate, and by this power, it brings forth the future, manifesting the intrinsic nature of the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of names, phrases, and syllables.
That which resides within the mouth is called "speech" (*vāc*) and is also an action (*karman*); when it flows out externally, it is simply termed "speech.
It is a thoroughly established principle that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arise from the mind;
for instance, one observes that when a mind of greed, hatred, or delusion arises, the face exhibits abnormal colors such as glossiness, dryness, or agitation.

Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that those who harbor the poison of hatred have flames erupting from their faces and lack a compassionate heart; this is because the fire of greed arises and burns the body and so forth.

Regarding the "wind of expulsion," there is a distinct wind that moves along the pathways of the excretory organs and is able to clear away the two types of impurities. Because these impurities press upon the interior, painful sensations arise; because painful sensations arise, the desire for expulsion is triggered; and because of the desire for expulsion, the mind directed toward the wind is induced.
This mind gives rise to wind that performs the function of excretion; furthermore, the power of this wind brings peace and stability to the body.

As for the *anuvartaka* (concomitant) wind, it refers to a distinct wind that circulates throughout all the pores of the limbs of the body, and it is for this reason that it receives the name "concomitant wind."

This does not depend on the mind but relies solely on the power of karma; it flows naturally through the pores and cavities of the body, thereby able to eliminate all putrid filth and foul-smelling substances that dwell within those pores and cavities.
Regarding the "wind that moves the body," this refers to a distinct wind capable of striking and moving the body to initiate manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
It should be understood that the arising of this wind has the mind as its cause; it pervades all parts of the body and is able to effect this striking and movement.

Having introduced the meaning of "wind" (*vāyu*) by way of discussing the six winds, it is here that the two breaths are correctly elucidated, as the intention here is to explain mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
The intrinsic nature of this mindfulness is wisdom (*prajñā*) and nothing else, because the *Sūtra* speaks of it using the term "clear comprehension" (*parijñā*).

This chapter is named "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) because mindfulness is predominant; it is so called because the quantity of the inhalations and exhalations is maintained through the power of mindfulness.
To demonstrate that concentration and wisdom are accomplished by taking the breath as their object, it is said to be "mindfulness" due to the function of mindfulness.
Its concomitant nature should be understood according to the preceding section.

This mindfulness relies solely upon five stages: namely, the desire realm, the intermediate dhyāna, and the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first, second, and third dhyānas. Consequently, it is associated only with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), because this mindfulness is cultivated as an antidote for the body.

Pleasurable and painful feelings can facilitate the arising of discursive thoughts concerning kinsmen and the like; therefore, the antidote to such thoughts must occur when spontaneous feeling is manifest.
Some say that in the fundamental states of the first three dhyānas, while one is actually in meditative equipoise, there is also the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
He asserts that this mindfulness (smṛti) relies upon all eight stages, because the breath ceases when higher meditative absorptions manifest.
This mindfulness takes only the wind of the breath as its object; it does not universally take as its object the six types of winds mentioned above.
This mindfulness first arises based on a body in the desire realm, specifically within the human and celestial destinies, excluding Uttarakuru.
It is acquired solely through application (*prayoga*), not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).

This is because for one who has not yet abandoned defilements, it necessarily manifests through application; furthermore, it is not subsumed under any stage [of meditative attainment] that is acquired through the abandonment of defilements.

It has already been stated that these are all comprised within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and not the fundamental [dhyānas], because this mindfulness is induced solely by superior preparatory effort (*prayoga*). Therefore, one should not say that it is acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-prāpta*).
This is associated exclusively with the attention of reality (*tattvamanasikāra*).
Some say it also extends to the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanasikāra*); however, only sentient beings who possess the True Dharma are able to cultivate it.

Non-Buddhists do not possess it, because they lack a teacher [of this path], because they cannot awaken to subtle phenomena, and because this [attention] is utterly contrary to the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*).
Because that grasping at a self exists, this mindfulness is absent.
By possessing six causes, this characteristic becomes complete. What are these six?
First, counting; second, following; third, settling; fourth, observing; fifth, transforming; sixth, purifying.

Counting means binding the mind to count the inhalations and exhalations from one to ten, neither decreasing nor increasing, for fear that the mind might become excessively distracted or agitated regarding its object.
However, within this practice there may be three errors: first, the error of undercounting; second, the error of overcounting;
and third, the error of confusion. Furthermore, there are another three errors: first, the error of excessive laxity; second, the error of excessive tension; and third, the error of distraction.
If the mind becomes distracted during the counting of ten, one should again count from one in successive order, starting over from the beginning until concentration is attained.
When counting the breaths, one should first count the inhalations, because at the stage of birth, the inhalation occurs first, and so on until the exhalation is the last at the time of death.
By thus observing the stages of death and birth, one is gradually able to cultivate the perception of impermanence.

"Following" means binding the mind to follow the inhalation and exhalation, being mindful whether the inhalation and exhalation are short or long, how far they extend, and where they turn back; furthermore, one is mindful whether the inhalation pervades the entire body or occupies only a single part.
As the breath enters, follow it as it travels through the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, knees, calves, ankles, and the toes of the feet, with mindfulness constantly following along.
"Cessation" (śamatha) refers to binding the mindfulness exclusively to the tip of the nose, or between the eyebrows, or even down to the toes, settling the mind in whatever place one prefers.
One contemplates the breath abiding in the body like a thread within a pearl, observing whether it is cold or warm, and whether it is detrimental or beneficial.

"Contemplation" means that after having observed this wind of the breath, one simultaneously observes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) co-arising with the breath, as well as the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*) that abide dependent upon that matter; thus, one fully contemplates the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as the object of focus.

"Transformation" refers to shifting the awareness of the wind that is the breath-object and placing it within progressively superior wholesome roots, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness and culminating in the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
"Purification" refers to ascending into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth. Other masters say:

that which begins with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and ends with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is called "transformation," while the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth are what constitute "purification."
How should the distinctions among the characteristics of the breaths be understood?
The verse says:
Inhalation and exhalation follow the body; They proceed according to two types of distinctions.
The mental factors (*caitasika*) are not appropriated (*anupātta*); they are outflows (*niṣyanda*) and do not take lower stages as their objects.
The commentary states:
The breath belongs to the stage corresponding to the birth-place of the body, because the breath is comprised as a part of that very body.

The occurrence of this inhalation and exhalation depends on the distinctions between body and mind; therefore, the treatise states that the breath occurs in dependence upon the body and also in dependence upon the mind, for it is only when the four conditions are present as appropriate that the breath can occur.
Based on this principle, the phrase "as appropriate" is stated to show that the cessation [of breath] necessarily depends on the distinction between body and mind.

Regarding the four conditions: first, the body which is the basis for inhalation and exhalation; second, the opening of the pores; third, the unobstructed passage of the wind-channels; and fourth, the manifestation of a coarse state of mind belonging to the level of inhalation and exhalation.
Among these four, if any one is lacking, the breaths do not proceed.
These inhalations and exhalations are comprised within the category of sentient beings, because breath does not exist within a body devoid of perception.
Although these arise from the outside, they are connected to internal objects.
These inhalations and exhalations are not possessed of appropriation (*anupāttaka*), because breath lacks the characteristics of appropriation.
Although there are winds within the body that are appropriated (*upātta*), these breath-winds are exclusively non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
The substance of this inhalation and exhalation is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*), because it is a fruit produced by a cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Although there are winds of nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and maturation (*vipāka*) within the body, these respiratory winds are exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
This is because the breath diminishes when the body grows, whereas the breath increases when the body diminishes; therefore, it is not of the nature of nourishment.
Because it continues in succession after having been severed, it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*); other matter born of maturation lacks this characteristic.
It is observed only by a mind of its own level or a higher level, as it is not an object of perception for a mind of a lower level.

That is to say, when one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a mind of the desire realm, that body of the desire realm and the breath of the desire realm proceed in dependence upon that mind of the desire realm; thus, they are observed by that very mind.

If one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a mind of the first dhyāna, that body of the desire realm and the breath of the desire realm proceed in dependence upon that mind of the first dhyāna; thus, they are observed by that very mind.
The arising of the minds of the second and third dhyānas follows the same principle as before.

It should be stated that when one is born in the first dhyāna, the minds of the three levels arise; when born in the second or third, the minds of the two [lower] levels and their own level arise, following the same pattern as being born in the desire realm.

It should be explained according to principle: if one born in a higher realm gives rise to a mind belonging to a lower realm, that breath of the higher realm body depends upon the mind of the lower realm for its activity, yet it is not an object of observation for that [lower] mind.
Thus, the breaths of the desire realm are observed by the minds of four stages.
The breaths of the first, second, and third dhyānas are, respectively, observed by the minds of three, two, and one stage as their respective objects.
There are four stages with breath and five stages without breath.
When one dwells in a stage with breath and gives rise to a mind of a stage without breath, the breath necessarily ceases to function while one dwells there.
When one arises from a stage without breath and gives rise to a mind of a stage with breath, the breath likewise does not function.
When one dwells in a state with breathing and gives rise to a mind with breathing, inhalation and exhalation proceed accordingly.
What are the characteristics of the accomplishment and fulfillment of the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) as it has been explained?
One should say this:

If the practitioner focuses their attention to contemplate the breath flowing subtly and slowly—visualizing it as pervading the entire body like a single hole in a tube, with the wind of the breath continuing like a string of mani jewels—and is unable to move the body or produce tactile consciousness of the body, then up to this point, one should say that mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) has been accomplished.
Other masters say:
"The completion of this mindfulness is called 'attainment' when its increase and mastery have accomplished their task.

The initial mention of 'increase' indicates the successive establishment of the mindfulness of breathing through its lower, middle, and upper grades; it continues until the point where one can enter and emerge at will, which is termed 'mastery.'"
If, at this stage, one is able to benefit the body by distancing it from the basis of craving and discursive thought (*vitarka*), it is called "the completion of what was to be done.
Other masters say:

when one possesses the six characteristics and is free from the three faults, or when one fully cultivates the sixteen kinds of sublime mental aspects (*ākāra*), up to this point the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) should be said to be accomplished.

The Sūtra states that there are seventeen kinds of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*): namely, being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation; knowing "I am mindful of short inhalations and exhalations"; [knowing] long inhalations and exhalations; perceiving the whole body; calming the bodily formation; experiencing joy; experiencing pleasure; experiencing the mind; calming the mental formation; experiencing the mind; gladdening the mind; concentrating the mind; liberating the mind; contemplating impermanence; contemplating cessation; contemplating detachment; and contemplating extinction—thus, each of these is individually and personally known.

Among these seventeen, the first is a general contemplation, while the latter sixteen are specific contemplations; they should be understood as corresponding respectively to the four foundations of mindfulness, each consisting of four gates to form sixteen types.
How can mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) be subsumed under the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*)?
There is no fault here, as it is a case of applying the name of the effect to the cause.
It is not that "mental formations" refers to volition (*cetanā*) in this context; rather, one should understand that "sensation" is what is termed "mental formations" here.

This means that because of being attached to the flavor of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), one gives rise to a mind of volitional formation (*abhisamskāra-citta*) toward various objects; this is called mental activity (*cittābhisaṃskāra*).
Since feeling is the cause of volition (*cetanā*), there is no error in calling it mental activity.

Alternatively, for one who is able to perceive only the intrinsic nature of sensation (*vedanā*), it follows by implication that they can also sequentially perceive the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing within the intrinsic natures of volition (*cetanā*) and so forth.

Just as when one tastes a single drop of salt water from the great ocean, one thereby knows the taste of the entire ocean’s waters, thus perceiving sensation alone is termed "perceiving mental formations" (*cittasaṃskāra*).
The detailed explanation of each individual characteristic is as argued in the commentary on the Sūtra.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Exposition of the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Fascicle 29;
*Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (Exposition of the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Fascicle 30.
The Venerable Saṅghabhadra composed this;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
Chapter Seven: On the Analysis of the Noble Ones (II). Thus has been explained the entry into the two gates of cultivation; through these two gates, the mind attains concentration.
Having attained concentration, what should one further cultivate?
The verse says:
Relying on the already accomplished serenity (śamatha), One cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) for the sake of insight (vipaśyanā).
By means of their specific and general characteristics, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
These consist of the wisdoms of hearing and so forth, which have intrinsic natures; the others have mixed objects of focus.
They are taught in this sequence according to how they arise, and there are only four because they serve as antidotes to the [four] inversions.
The treatise states:

Having already cultivated and perfected *śamatha* as a basis, one cultivates the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) so that *vipaśyanā* may be swiftly accomplished; for it is not possible for one who has not attained meditative concentration to see things as they truly are.
How does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?
One contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, the practitioner, with a mind focused on a single object, cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness by contemplating each of these objects—the body and so forth—individually through both their specific and general characteristics.
To discern the meaning of the distinction between this phenomenon and other phenomena is called observing its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
To discern the meaning of the non-distinction between this phenomenon and other phenomena is called observing its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), observing its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) means examining the distinct characteristics of the various bases of the body.
Observing its general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) means observing that all these bases are equally the nature of the body and share the same characteristic of being material form (*rūpa*).
To contemplate specific characteristics means to contemplate the individual characteristics of the body.
To contemplate general characteristics means to observe that the body, like all other conditioned phenomena, is impermanent and so forth.
The applications of mindfulness regarding sensation and so forth should be understood accordingly.

Each of these four has three types, namely: essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so on. "Essential nature" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), which consists solely of the three—namely, that derived from hearing and the others.
"Associated" (*saṃprayukta*) refers to the other factors coexisting with this [wisdom].
The objects of focus refer to the objects of these three types of wisdom.
Why are these three all called "applications of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?

It is because mindfulness causes wisdom to abide upon its object; since mindfulness and wisdom mutually support one another through superior concentration and so forth, the name "application of mindfulness" is established for wisdom. Furthermore, because this involves mixed objects of focus, it is also called an application of mindfulness.
For what reason are three types of foundations of mindfulness taught?
They are taught as three for the sake of three kinds of sentient beings who are deluded regarding conduct, the provisions, and the objects of focus.
Alternatively, they are taught as three because there are three distinct states for each of the faculties and inclinations, as their capacities and dispositions differ.
Among these three, it is their mutual intermingling that can sever the afflictions; the two alone cannot sever them, as they would be either too deficient or excessive.
However, the term "intermingled" also encompasses the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*), because wisdom and its co-existent factors are mutually intermingled.
If one speaks of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it should not depend on anything else; however, because it is shown to depend on something else, the term "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) is used.

These [foundations of mindfulness] are comprised solely within those produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). They are able to sever afflictions only while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for they can sever delusions; thus, they take the four or five aggregates as their object, or they can sever delusions by taking *nirvāṇa* as their object.

Among the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) is capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas the attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) lacks this capacity because it takes only a limited portion of objects as its focus.
Within the four applications of mindfulness, the first three involve exclusively unmixed objects, while the fourth pertains to both.

However, regarding the wisdom of the three truths, only that which takes mixed objects can sever the afflictions; whereas the wisdom of the truth of cessation severs the afflictions even though it does not take mixed objects.
The applications of mindfulness, such as those of the body, each have three types, due to the distinctions of taking internal, external, or both as their objects.

Furthermore, among the three types of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), that which takes one's own continuum as its object is called "internal"; that which takes the bodies of others and so forth as its object is called "external"; and that which takes both types as its object is called "both internal and external."
For those who are lax due to self-love (*ātmasneha*), they should contemplate the internal body as being like the external.

Alternatively, that which is "internal" is as previously described; however, that which is taken as an object by non-appropriated [consciousness] is called "external," while that which takes another's continuum as its object is called "both internal and external," because it receives both names in relation to what is non-appropriated and in relation to one's own body.

Alternatively, they are called "three" because they take as their objects the faculties (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and both together. Alternatively, they are differentiated into three by taking as objects sentient beings (*sattva*), insentient things (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*), or both types.
Alternatively, they are differentiated into three by taking as objects sentient beings, external insentient things, and [insentient things such as] hair and body hair.
Because they all arise from within one's own body and yet exist apart from the sense faculties, they possess both names [internal and external].

Alternatively, those conditioned by sentient beings in the present are called "internal," while those conditioned by non-sentient things across the three times are called "external. Those conditioned by sentient beings in the past and future are said to be "both internal and external," because they belong to the category of sentient beings and yet fall within the enumeration of dharmas.

Furthermore, those that will fall into the category of sentient beings in the future and are currently falling into the category of dharmas, fell into the category of sentient beings in the past and were currently falling into the category of dharmas; for those dharmas that do not arise are of the same nature as those that do arise.
Each of the three [foundations], beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), likewise consists of three; they should be explained accordingly based on what precedes.
These four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are taught in the order in which they arise.
For what reason, moreover, do they arise in such a sequence?
Birth follows this sequence because it conforms to these characteristics.
Sentient beings, for the most part, delight in the enjoyment of various forms and thus fail to attain the sublime Dharma.
What serves as the condition for this delight in the enjoyment of forms?

This means that within sensation (*vedanā*), there is a deep-seated attachment and delight; this delight in sensation arises because the mind is undisciplined, and the mind’s lack of discipline is due to the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since the mind can be tamed through faith and other [wholesome factors], one contemplates this principle, whereby the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) arise.
Alternatively, it may be because they arise according to the coarseness or subtlety of their respective objects.
However, it is not for this reason that the mind [is considered the most subtle], because among the dharmas observed at the final stage, nirvāṇa is extremely subtle.

When those [mental factors] such as perception and volition observe feeling, one is already able to understand their characteristics through the logic that they arise based on the same mind and share its common welfare and peril.
Other masters say:

Form can be aggregated or dispersed, taken up or discarded; because its similar continuity, impurity, suffering, and so forth, are easily understood; because for the most part it is based on the body that greed and other afflictions arise; and because it is the locus where men and women mutually give rise to desire.

The three gateways for entering cultivation—contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), and analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhaṅga*)—all predominantly take the body as their object.

Therefore, at the stage of cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one should first practice this contemplation. This contemplation serves as the cause for the arising of the contact of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sparśa*); from the contact of pliancy, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is induced, for the Sūtra states that when the body is at ease, one experiences pleasure.
In this way, pleasant feeling arises dependent upon the mind; with a pure mind as its cause, one attains the fruit of liberation.
Because one contemplates feeling and the other aggregates in successive order, the applications of mindfulness arise in this specific sequence.
These four foundations of mindfulness neither increase nor decrease, for they serve as antidotes to the four inversions such as purity.
Contemplating the body as impure serves as the antidote to the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure.

Although the perception of purity regarding the inverted [notion of beauty] takes all five aggregates as its object, one can suppress it entirely simply by observing that the intrinsic nature of the body is impure.
It is like a person who, having observed that the substance of excrement is impure, no longer takes pleasure in anything produced from that excrement.
Having thus contemplated the impurity of the body, one no longer takes delight in what arises from the body.
Because of this contemplation of the body as impure, one finds no delight in any of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Those who are deluded by the perception of purity regarding the conditioned body will consequently take delight in that which arises based upon the body.
Therefore, one who contemplates the body as impure will likewise find no delight in what arises from the body.

Just as when one dwells in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), although one does not directly perceive sounds and other objects as sensory domains, one rejects songs and the like as if they were excrement;
