so too, when dwelling in the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), although one does not directly perceive feelings and other objects as domains, because one contemplates the very nature of the body as impure, one ultimately finds no delight in the three domains of feeling and the rest.

Furthermore, although one does not contemplate the objects of the form and formless realms as impure, these objects nonetheless give rise to the mental aspect of non-delight; therefore, even though the perversion of purity takes the five aggregates as its object, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is sufficient to suppress it entirely.

Although the latter three applications of mindfulness each observe their objects individually, one should reflect that, by analogy with this case, they possess the principle of being able to subdue [the afflictions] collectively.
Contemplating feeling as suffering can counteract the inversion of regarding suffering as pleasure.
If there is a phenomenon that can truly be desired and sought after, this constitutes the meaning of "pleasure.
To perceive excellent qualities worthy of desire within a course of action mired in manifold faults and afflictions is called the perversion of regarding suffering as pleasure.

This perversion necessarily takes attachment to feeling as its precursor; for only after becoming deeply attached to feelings does one falsely give rise to the perception of pleasure regarding all contaminated formations, which are the basis of all affliction.
Therefore, when one contemplates sensation as being of the nature of suffering, one is able to suppress, in its entirety, the perversion of conceiving it as pleasure.
When one contemplates the mind as impermanent, one can remedy the perversion of regarding what is impermanent as permanent.

This means that because the practitioner loathes and detests sensation (*vedanā*), they perceive within the dependent mind numerous categories of distinctions; this induces the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*) to manifest before them, whereby they no longer give rise to the notion of permanence regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Thus, they are able to comprehensively suppress the inversion of conceiving [conditioned things] as permanent.

Contemplating phenomena as non-self can remedy the perversion of regarding what is not self as self. This refers to a certain class of people who, upon hearing that the self does not exist, do not give rise to joy in their minds and instead think:
"Who causes this mind to have such manifold distinctions?"
"That [person] is precisely me.

To refute that conception, one must further contemplate with discernment that, apart from these three [aggregates], all else is likewise merely phenomena (*dharma*). Thus, one will no longer give rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*) regarding anything at all; consequently, one is able to completely subdue the perversion of conceiving a self.
Alternatively, the four applications of mindfulness, such as the body and so forth, are established in sequence as antidotes to the four nutriments—edible food, contact, consciousness, and volition;
their number is exactly four, neither more nor less.

Having thus thoroughly cultivated the two preparatory practices of the meditation on impurity and mindfulness of breathing, one is able to sequentially bring forth the unmixed applications of mindfulness regarding body, feeling, mind, and phenomena as objects of focus. Furthermore, immediately following the unmixed application of mindfulness regarding phenomena, one brings forth the mixed application of mindfulness regarding phenomena as objects of focus; next, one should cultivate the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena that takes general characteristics as its collective object.
What are the characteristics of this mindfulness of dharmas?
The verse says:
Abiding in that mindfulness of dharmas, One contemplates the four objects of focus collectively.
One cultivates the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The commentary states:

There are four types of the application of mindfulness on dharmas with mixed objects, distinguished by their taking two, three, four, or five aggregates as their respective objects; here, it refers specifically to that which takes all five aggregates collectively as its object.
Dwelling therein, he cultivates four modes of contemplation, observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as a whole—namely, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

However, when practicing this application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are other roots of goodness that serve as its preparatory application (*prayoga*); these should be cultivated in succession until they manifest.

That is to say, once one has already matured the practice of the application of mindfulness to phenomena with mixed objects (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), and is about to cultivate this [present] application of mindfulness, one should first cultivate the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) by taking all things as a general object; next, one contemplates arising and ceasing; and finally, one contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This is because practitioners first observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise and cease from causes; thus, they easily enter the gateway of observing the interconnectedness of cause and effect.

Alternatively, some wish to have them first observe dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), after which they give rise to the observation of the three meanings of conditions. Following this observation without interval, they cultivate the "skillfulness in the seven bases" (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*); by attaining skillfulness in these seven bases, they are able to establish the sequence of the truths of cause and effect regarding all previously perceived objects and observe them accordingly.

Having thus thoroughly cultivated wisdom and meditative concentration, one is then able to establish the truths conducive to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), namely, the specific sufferings of the desire realm and the higher realms. One contemplates these eight [truths] in their proper sequence, cultivating the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) never before cultivated.

Through the wisdom derived from hearing, he first initiates these sixteen modes of contemplation regarding the eight truths, seeing them as one would view various colors through a thin silk veil; up to this point, his wisdom derived from hearing is said to be perfected.
The wisdom derived from reflection should be explained accordingly.

Subsequently, one develops a profound sense of wearying revulsion toward saṃsāra and takes delight in the merit of the tranquility of nirvāṇa; thereafter, one frequently brings the contemplation of revulsion to manifestation.

Through skillful means, one diligently cultivates so that [the roots of goodness] gradually increase and become increasingly superior, thereby giving rise to such supreme roots of goodness comprised within the "thoughtfully accomplished" (*cintāmayī*) category that are conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Immediately following this cultivation of the mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) which takes general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its common object, what root of goodness arises?
The verse says:
From this arises the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata), which fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths through the cultivation of the sixteen aspects; the subsequent stage of Summits (mūrdhan) is likewise.
These two roots of goodness both consist of the first dharma and the subsequent four;
next, patience consists only of the mindfulness of dharmas. The lower and middle grades are the same as the "Summit" stage;
the upper grade contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm. Each consists of a single application and a single moment.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma is likewise; all are wisdom, with five [factors], excluding acquisition (*prāpti*).
The commentary states:

Following the mindfulness-establishment on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes general characteristics as its object and is produced by reflection (*cintāmayī*), there arises the first root of merit (*kuśalamūla*) belonging to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), which is named "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). This is a specific variety of the mindfulness-establishment on phenomena that takes general characteristics as its object.

That which thus arises is what should be cultivated; it is the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path that can burn the fuel of the afflictions, just as the initial sign of warmth appears during the process of drilling for fire. Because this dharma is identical to that warmth, it is called the "Dharma of Warmth" (*uṣmagata*).

Because the duration of this arising stage of the roots of goodness is extensive, one is able to fully observe the objects of the Four Noble Truths; by means of this, one fully cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
One observes the Noble Truth of Suffering and cultivates four aspects: first, impermanence (*anitya*); second, suffering (*duḥkha*); third, emptiness (*śūnya*);

and fourth, non-self (*anātman*). One observes the Noble Truth of Origination and cultivates four aspects: first, cause (*hetu*); second, origination (*samudaya*); third, production (*prabhava*); and fourth, condition (*pratyaya*).
One cultivates four aspects when contemplating the Noble Truth of Cessation: first, cessation; second, tranquility; third, excellence; and fourth, detachment.
One cultivates four aspects when contemplating the Noble Truth of the Path: first, the path; second, the right method; third, practice; and fourth, deliverance.
The distinctions between these characteristics will be explained later.

Although all levels of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) take the Four Noble Truths as their object, they are described for the most part as being accompanied by the practice of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*), because at the time of their arising, the perceptions of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃjñā*) predominate.

As the practitioner cultivates this root of goodness of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), it gradually progresses through the stages of inferior, middling, and superior; they develop a compliant faith in the Buddha’s teachings on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and they observe that all states of existence are constantly being incinerated by fierce and blazing flames.
Among the three jewels, faith is preeminent.

There is a stage of the roots of goodness called "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), which consists of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) produced through cultivation; it is a specific form of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes general characteristics as its object.
The term "summit" (*mūrdhan*) indicates that this is the most excellent stage; just as when an auspicious matter reaches completion, people in the world say that a person has "reached the summit.
This refers to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) subsumed within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), two of which are movable and two of which are immovable.
Among the two types of the movable [roots], the lower is called "Heat" (uṣmagata),
and the higher is called "Summit" (mūrdhan), because it is the highest among those that are movable.
Among the two types of the immovable [roots], the lower is called "Patience" (kṣānti), because it is extremely capable of enduring the objects of the Four Truths.
The highest stage is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), for it is the most excellent within the mundane world, just like clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Those who dwell in seclusion say:
because one cultivates these wholesome factors until their characteristic reaches its peak, it is therefore called the "Summit Dharma" (*mūrdhāna*).

The objects and modes of activity of this [stage] are the same as those of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage; that is, one contemplates the objects of the Four Noble Truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).

Thus, for these two types of wholesome roots—Heat and Peak (*mūrdhan*)—at the time they are first established, there is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*); in the subsequent stage of advancement, all four applications of mindfulness are present.
The phrase "initially placing the foot" indicates that, by means of its mode of activity (*ākāra*), one first traverses the tracks of the Four Noble Truths.
The subsequent phrase "further advancement" indicates that from this point onward, one practices them through the successive stages of weak, medium, and superior intensity.
Those roots of goodness previously attained do not manifest later, because one does not give rise to a sense of reverence toward them.
Since these roots of goodness are induced by superior preparatory effort (*prayoga*), one does not give rise to reverence for those already obtained.
Although this stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*) takes the Four Truths as its object, faith in the Three Jewels predominates in its manifestation.

As these wholesome roots of the Summit—whether inferior, middling, or superior—gradually increase until they reach their full development, there arises a superior wholesome root born of cultivation known as the "Stage of Patience" (*kṣānti*), which belongs to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). This is a specific form of the mindfulness-establishment (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the common characteristics of phenomena as its general object; it is so named because it is the most excellent among those [stages] capable of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding the principles of the Four Truths.
Furthermore, because there is no falling back from this stage of patience (*kṣānti*), it is called the "Dharma of Patience" (*kṣāntidharma*).

Although the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is also able to accept and affirm the Noble Truths, and because one will necessarily enter the Path of Seeing immediately thereafter, there is certainly no falling back; yet, it does not fully contemplate the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
Because this possesses [all four] contemplations, it specifically receives the name "patience" (kṣānti); therefore, it is specifically called "conformity-to-truth patience" (satyānulomikī kṣāntiḥ).
This root of goodness of patience—whether in its state of establishment or its further progress—is entirely the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
It differs from what preceded because it gradually resembles the path of seeing (darśanamārga), as in the stage of the path of seeing there is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena.

However, this dharma of patience (kṣānti) has three grades—lower, middle, and upper. The lower and middle grades are identical to the stage of the summits (mūrdhan), meaning they possess the observation of the objects of the Four Noble Truths and are capable of fully cultivating the sixteen aspects (ākāra).
The upper grade differs: it observes only the suffering of the desire realm, as it is immediately contiguous with the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma).

Based on this principle, it is established that the wholesome roots of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are all capable of fully taking the suffering and other truths of the three realms as their objects, as there is no distinction made [in the sūtras].
How, then, are the lower, middle, and upper stages of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) distinguished?

Furthermore, the lower grade of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) comprises eight types of mental states. That is to say, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects, this is called one type of mental state. In this manner, they successively contemplate the suffering of the form and formless realms; they likewise contemplate the truths of origin, cessation, and the path. These constitute the eight types of mental states known as the lower grade of patience.

In middle-stage patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*), the aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) are abbreviated. That is to say, the practitioner of yoga contemplates the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects, and so on, until they fully contemplate the path of the desire realm through four aspects; then, by reducing one aspect from the path of the higher realms, this is called the beginning of middle-stage patience.

In this manner, the aspects and objects of observation are gradually reduced and abbreviated until, with a minimum of only two moments of mind, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, as in the stages of *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* and *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*. Up to this point, it is called the fulfillment of medium-grade patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*).

The highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) contemplates only the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), cultivates a single aspect (*ākāra*), and lasts for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), because this root of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) arises without continuity.

Immediately following the highest patience, there is that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), which first opens the gateway to the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) and is the most excellent among worldly merits (*laukika-guṇa*).

This is the arising of the most supreme wholesome roots, which are comprised within the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and are distinguished as the mindfulness-establishment (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes general and common characteristics as its object; this is precisely what is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because this is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called "mundane" (*laukika*); because it is the most excellent, it is called "foremost.

It is called "foremost" because it arises through the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and is induced by the Noble Path, transcending its homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*). Therefore, it is named the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
As with the aforementioned "Patience" (*kṣānti*), this takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object and cultivates a single aspect (*ākāra*) for only a single moment.

In this way, by gradually reducing the aspects and objects of meditation, one draws closer and closer to the vision of the truths. Therefore, the "Supreme Worldly Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) take only the suffering of the desire realm as their object and cultivate only a single aspect for only a single moment; that is to say, because they enter the state of "entry into the certainty of liberation" (*niyāmāvakrānti*) immediately thereafter, there is no principle for continuity in this stage.

However, there are nine grades of wholesome roots associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): those termed "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) consist of the lowest-of-the-low, the low-middle, and the low-high; those termed "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) consist of the middle-low, the middle-middle, and the middle-high; those termed "Patience" (*kṣānti*) consist of the high-low and the high-middle; and the highest-of-the-high is termed "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
What constitutes the essence of the four dharmas, such as "heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth?

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of heat and the others has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence; if their associated factors (*sahāya*) are included, they are all subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), because that which is necessarily conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) must possess the concomitant matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*).
However, this excludes those who have already attained them, lest the wholesome roots such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth manifest again for noble ones (*ārya*).

For it is not admitted that those who have already seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*) would allow "Heat" and the others to manifest again; since the preparatory application (*prayoga*) would be rendered useless if it were to manifest for one who has already seen the truths.

In this context, when the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) is first established, among the three truths, whichever truth one contemplates, one cultivates the present application of mindfulness on phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) and the four future applications of mindfulness; whichever single aspect (ākāra) is present, one cultivates the four future aspects. One cultivates only those that are of the same category (sabhāga), not those of a different category (tatsabhāga).

Regarding the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna based on the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*): one currently cultivates one [of the four] in the future; according to one aspect (*ākāra*), one currently cultivates four in the future. It is not possible to cultivate the path that takes the aggregates as its object by first contemplating the cessation of the aggregates.

In the subsequent stage of advancement, regarding whichever of the three truths one contemplates according to conditions, one cultivates four future [knowledges] in the present based on each momentary dwelling; and regarding whichever aspect (ākāra) one contemplates, one cultivates sixteen future [aspects] in the present.

When the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna is cultivated in the present with the truth of cessation as its object, four [smṛtyupasthānas] are cultivated in the future; for each individual aspect (ākāra) cultivated in the present, sixteen aspects are cultivated in the future.

This initial establishment involves cultivating only those of the same category (sabhāga), because such a lineage has not been previously attained and because practice regarding the truths has not yet been extensive.
The subsequent stage of advancement is the opposite of this; therefore, it is able to cultivate both similar and dissimilar [factors].

When first establishing oneself in the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), whichever Truth among the Four Truths one contemplates, one cultivates the present mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and the four future ones; whichever single aspect (*ākāra*) is present, one cultivates all sixteen future aspects.

In the subsequent stage of advancement, whichever of the three truths one contemplates according to conditions, one cultivates four present and four future applications of mindfulness; and whichever single aspect one contemplates, one cultivates sixteen present and sixteen future aspects.

Regarding the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) cultivated in the present with respect to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), one cultivates the four [foundations] in the future; regarding any single aspect (*ākāra*) cultivated in the present, one cultivates all sixteen aspects in the future.

Whether it be the initial establishment or the subsequent progress within the four truths, whichever truth is being taken as the object, the mindfulness of phenomena cultivated in the present leads to the cultivation of the four in the future, and any single aspect cultivated in the present leads to the cultivation of the sixteen in the future.
This is stated according to the general characteristics of the categories of patience (*kṣānti*).
To speak of their specific distinctions: when the objects of focus are abbreviated, one follows that abbreviation of the objects and does not cultivate those respective mental aspects (*ākāra*).

That is to say, when taking all four truths as objects, one fully cultivates all sixteen aspects; if one takes three, two, or one truth as an object, one cultivates twelve, eight, or four aspects respectively.

Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), when it takes the suffering truth of the desire realm as its object, one cultivates the present mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and the future four [foundations of mindfulness]; according to whichever single aspect is present, one cultivates the future four [aspects].

Only those of the same category (*sabhāga*) are cultivated; the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) do not take other truths as their objects. Therefore, they cultivate only those aspects (*ākāra*) [of the Truth of Suffering]. Other masters say:
because they are proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and resemble the Path of Seeing, they cultivate only those [aspects].

That is to say, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) takes only the truth of suffering in the desire realm as its object and cultivates four aspects; the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) is likewise.
Having already explained the characteristics and essence of the roots of goodness that arise, one should now explain their specific distinctions.
The verse says:
These aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are all accomplished through cultivation;
they exist in six stages, or two or seven [according to some]; they rely on the body of the desire realm and consist of nine [minds].
Three [genders] and males obtain two; for the fourth, females likewise.
The noble ones abandon it by losing their stage; ordinary beings, by the end of life.
The first two also abandon it through falling away; based on the fundamental [attainment], one must necessarily see the truths.
"Once abandoned, they are not previously acquired; the two abandonments are of the nature of non-acquisition.
The commentary states:

These four superior roots of goodness—Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma—are called the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). As previously explained, they are divided into four types based on their degrees of inferiority, mediocrity, superiority, and supreme superiority.
"Decision" (*niścaya*) means decisive resolution; "discernment" (*pravicaya*) means analytical investigation.

Decisive resolution and analytical investigation refer to the various noble paths (*āryamārga*), because the noble paths are capable of severing doubt and are capable of discerning the characteristics of the four truths (*catuḥsatya*).
"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to a portion; it is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it is comprised within one part of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Since "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others act as conditions that induce the stages of penetration and are conducive to them, they receive the name "conducive" (*ānulomika*); therefore, these are called the "stages conducive to penetration."

These four types are all produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), not produced through hearing or reflection (*śruta-maya* or *cintā-maya*), because they are distant from the stages of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
These four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) all rely upon six stages, namely: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).
It does not exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it lacks the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
It also does not exist in the other higher realms, because it is an associate of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, the mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) does not take the desire realm as its object; the desire realm must first be fully known and abandoned; and among the three realms, the desire realm is the most coarse.

These four roots of goodness can serve as the cause for the full maturation (*vipāka*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in the form realm, but they cannot project a new homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), because they involve an extreme aversion toward all forms of existence (*bhava*) and a longing for parinirvāṇa.
Alternatively, the word "or" is used to indicate two differing explanations regarding the levels [of the aids to penetration], namely, the levels of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states:
they rely upon the six aforementioned levels and the seventh level of the Desire Realm.
The masters of the Abhidharma do not accept that [view], because these [four roots of merit] are not produced by hearing or reflection, but are factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

These four roots of merit arise based on a body in the desire realm; excluding Uttarakuru, they arise in nine locations among humans and gods. They rely exclusively on the nine bodies of the desire realm, as it is possible for them to enter the state of "entry into the certainty of correctness" (*niyāmāvakrānti*) therein.

Excluding the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the highest mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), the remaining three roots of goodness first arise in the three continents; they subsequently continue to manifest when one is born in the celestial realms. Those excluded [the supreme patience and the highest mundane dharmas] also first arise based on the celestial realms.
Other masters say:
If one has previously cultivated these four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), they may all first arise while in a celestial realm.

These four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) depend solely upon those who are male or female. Regarding the first three, both males and females can attain both types; as for the fourth, even a female body can attain both types, lest it be the case that one who later attains a male body would fail to achieve the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and the others.
Based on being male, one obtains only the roots of goodness of a male body; because even when a noble one (*ārya*) transmigrates to other lives, they do not become female.
Since those at the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) may undergo a change of gender, these two [stages] abide as mutually causal roots of goodness.

The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) based on a female body can serve as two causes, because once a woman has attained the state of an Arya, there is the possibility of subsequently attaining a male body through transformation.
That based on a male body serves as only one cause, because [for such a person] the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female body has already been attained.
The Noble Ones acquire these roots of goodness by depending upon this stage; they relinquish them only when they lose that stage.
The expression "losing the stage" indicates being reborn in a higher stage.

As for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whether or not they lose the stage, if they lose their homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), they necessarily relinquish these roots of goodness; this is because the bodies of the Noble Ones are sustained by the power of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
These four roots of goodness are not abandoned at the end of life.
How do we know that they are abandoned only by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not by noble ones (*ārya*) at the end of life?
Because the *Mūlaśāstra* states that an ordinary being within an egg or womb possesses only the body and does not possess bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Is it not the case that when ordinary beings first give rise to the "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and other stages based on a lower level, they must necessarily abandon those roots of goodness such as "heat" when later born into a higher level?
There is no such fault, because at that time those ordinary beings abandon the roots of goodness by virtue of abandoning their [previous] homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).

This means that one who dwells in the state of death-existence (*maranabhava*) lacks the support of the Noble Path; thus, they relinquish all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), not because of the arising of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of a higher plane.

If a noble one (*ārya*) dwells in the state of death-existence, they do not relinquish "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth due to the support of the Noble Path; rather, they relinquish the wholesome roots of a lower plane solely through the arising of the intermediate existence of a higher plane. Although the timing of the relinquishment is the same, the causes differ. Therefore, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have no relinquishing of the stages [of attainment], and for noble ones, there is certainly no relinquishing by way of the end of life.

Although a person of different lineage (pṛthagjana) abandons the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*) at the end of life, they certainly do not fall into the evil destinies nor undergo birth in those evil destinies, because [the seeds] have been rendered non-arising through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Since the body was previously the locus where the dharma of patience resided, the karma and afflictions capable of inducing birth in the evil destinies can no longer function within that body, just as various wild beasts do not dwell in a lion’s den.
The first two roots of goodness are also abandoned through falling away; such falling away applies to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not to noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the latter two, even for ordinary beings there is no falling away; having given rise to the roots of goodness such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) based on the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), they will certainly attain the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) in this very life.
Because their faculties are sharp and their revulsion toward existence is profound,

those who give rise to "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the subsequent stages based on the *anāgamya* or the intermediate dhyāna do not necessarily attain entry into the vision of the truths (*darśana-satya*) within this very life.
Other masters say:

Those who give rise to the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth based on the fundamental dhyānas will certainly attain nirvāṇa in this very life, because their revulsion toward existence (*bhava*) is profound.

If these stages are acquired again after having been previously abandoned, what is obtained is necessarily not that which was previously abandoned; for when they are acquired again after having been previously abandoned, they arise only through great exertion, and there is no reverence for what was previously abandoned—just as when one has previously abandoned the prātimokṣa vows and receives them again later, one obtains what was never before obtained.
The same applies to the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and subsequent stages:

what is attained later is not the same as what was attained previously. If one has already attained the wholesome roots of heat and so forth but loses them after passing through a rebirth, and then encounters a teacher who skillfully explains the Dharma regarding the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one will then give rise to the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) and the other stages;
if one does not encounter such a teacher, one must cultivate from the beginning once again.

The two types of relinquishment—loss and retrogression—have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as their nature. Retrogressive relinquishment necessarily arises due to the occurrence of faults, whereas relinquishment through loss may occur even when virtues are increasing.
What are the benefits of attaining these roots of goodness?
The verse says:
With "Heat," one will certainly reach nirvāṇa; With "Summits," one never again severs the roots of goodness;
With "Patience," one does not fall into the evil destinies; With the "Supreme Mundane Dharma," one enters the state beyond birth.
The treatise says:

Among the four roots of goodness, if one attains the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), although there may be regression, the severing of the roots of goodness, the commission of deeds of immediate retribution, or falling into the evil destinies, one will not remain in cyclic existence for long, as one is certain to reach nirvāṇa.
If that is so, how does this differ from the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)?

If there are no obstacles, one is close to the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*); for this [state] shares the same mode of activity as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because it comprises these superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) within meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).

If one attains the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan), although there may be regression and so forth, one increases toward the ultimate and never severs the roots of goodness; this is because, by taking the observation of the sublime qualities of the Triple Gem as the gateway, one gives rise to pure faith.
Once the "summit" (mūrdhan) has been attained, one does not sever the roots of goodness.
How then can it be said in the Sūtra that Devadatta regressed from the summit?
This was stated cryptically based on his having previously produced roots of goodness that were close to the summit, referring to a regression from what had not yet been fully attained.

If one attains the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), although at the end of life one relinquishes it and remains in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one increases in non-retrogression, does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), and does not fall into the evil destinies (*apāya*).

However, the verse mentions only the phrase "not falling into the evil destinies"; by implication, it is already known that one does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution, because those who commit such deeds necessarily fall into the evil destinies.
That there is no falling back from the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) has already been explained above.

One who has attained patience does not fall into the various evil states because they have distanced themselves from the karma and afflictions that lead there, and because they have attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of birth in the evil destinies.

By the power of the lower degree of patience (*kṣānti*), one has already attained the non-arising of all miserable destinies (*apāya*); by the power of the upper degree of patience, one further attains the non-arising of a small portion of births and so forth.
"A small portion of births" refers to birth from eggs and moisture-born birth, because these two modes of birth are characterized by much ignorance.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) is used to indicate that there are afflictions (*kleśa*) in certain abodes and bodies.

"Abodes" refers to the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the Great Brahmā realm, and Uttarakuru; for the realm of non-perception and the Great Brahmā realm are abodes of distorted views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and in Uttarakuru there is no realization through direct insight (*abhisamaya*).
"Body" refers to those such as *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others, because they possess manifold afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Existence" refers to the eighth [birth] and beyond, because noble ones (*ārya*) will certainly not undergo them again.
"Affliction" refers to afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), because they will certainly never arise again.

Having attained the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), although one still abides in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one is able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Although the verse does not explicitly state that it is abandoned at the end of life, since one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth immediately thereafter, it follows by implication that there is no abandonment at the end of life.
For what reason can only these [roots] enter the state of "leaving birth" (*niyāma*)?

Because one has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and because they can abandon the nature of an ordinary person just as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) does.
These four roots of goodness each have three grades, due to the differences in the lineages (*gotra*) of the Śrāvakas and others.
Once roots of goodness have arisen within any particular lineage, can they be shifted or redirected toward another vehicle?
The verse says:
The lineage of the Śrāvaka can be shifted; Two lead to Buddhahood, three to the rest.
The *qilin* (unicorn) is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s non-retrogression, because he attains enlightenment in a single sitting.
The commentary states:

One who has not yet planted the *mūrdhāna* and *uṣmagata* roots of goodness belonging to the vehicle of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) of the Buddha-vehicle, but has instead given rise to these roots based on the lineage (*gotra*) of the Śrāvaka, may still be capable of transforming [their destiny] to give rise to the *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhāna* stages of the Buddha-vehicle; however, this meaning can only be realized after a long period of time.

If one gives rise to that patience but does not incline toward the Buddha Vehicle, because their application to the Śrāvaka Vehicle has been most prolonged, their own fruit will necessarily be accomplished after sixty kalpas.

Because Bodhisattvas seek exclusively to benefit others, desiring to rescue and deliver infinite sentient beings, they adorn themselves with great vows and pass through immeasurable kalpas; thus, they enter the evil realms as if strolling through a garden.
If it were not so, there would be no possibility of attaining Buddhahood.

By giving rise to patience (*kṣānti*), one obtains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all miserable destinies; therefore, once that patience has arisen, there is no longer any turning toward the Buddha Vehicle, as it would sever numerous activities for the benefit of others.

When a bodhisattva has already planted the seeds of the Buddha-vehicle and follows the factors conducive to liberation, thereby obstructing rebirth in the evil destinies, they successively and firmly embrace the three—generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom; at that time, there is no need to laboriously give rise to the patience of other vehicles.

Therefore, while those at the stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit) among the Śrāvakas may turn toward the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*), once they have produced *kṣānti* (Receptivity), there is no possibility of their turning to become Buddhas.
Based on the Śrāvaka lineage, those who produce *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* may all turn to give rise to the path of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) belonging to the lineage of the śrāvaka, once it has arisen, does not possess the capacity to obstruct the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; therefore, by giving rise to that patience, one also becomes a pratyekabuddha.
Since this occurs outside the category of Buddhas, the verse refers to them as "others."
Regarding those who have attained the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* within the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna, is it possible for them to be diverted toward another vehicle?
Now, there are generally two types of Pratyekabuddhas:
first, those likened to a rhinoceros horn (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*), and second, those who were formerly Śrāvakas.
If they were previously śrāvakas, it is as explained for the śrāvakas.
Both the pratyekabuddha (the rhinoceros-like) and the Buddha cannot turn back from their path, because both attain enlightenment in a single sitting.

Since the fourth dhyāna is an immovable and most supremely lucid samādhi, it is capable of serving as the basis for the pratyekabuddha and the Greatly Awakened One; therefore, both rely upon the fourth dhyāna. From the foundation of mindfulness on the body up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, they are able to arise in successive order within that single sitting alone.
Therefore, the analogy of the rhinoceros horn and the Buddha-lineage, as well as the roots of goodness such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, are all irreversible.

Is it possible that one who has first planted the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) can, in this very same lifetime, give rise to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
The preceding stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) leads to liberation within at most three lifetimes;
it is accomplished through the three types of action—listening, reflection, and cultivation—and is planted by humans in the three continents.
The treatise says:
Regarding those who give rise to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in this life, they must have previously given rise to the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in a prior life.

For those who first plant the seeds of the aids to liberation, at the very fastest, they attain liberation within three lifetimes: in the first life they plant the seeds of the aids to liberation; in the second life they bring them to maturity; and in the third life they give rise to the aids to penetration and thereby enter the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

If it is claimed that one produces the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in the second birth and enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*) or even attains liberation in the third birth, such a statement would contradict what was previously stated.

Regarding those who give rise to the "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) stage and so forth based on the fundamental dhyāna stages, they will necessarily enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) in this very life.

Alternatively, one must admit that at most they require two births; that is, for one who gives rise to the "Heat" stage and so forth based on the fundamental stages in a second birth, they will necessarily enter the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) and attain liberation in their present life.

The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are produced through hearing and reflection, not through cultivation, because those who have not yet planted the seeds of the factors conducive to liberation are unable to plant them.

These factors conducive to liberation have the three types of action (*karman*) as their essence; however, the most excellent among them is exclusively the mental action (*manaskarma*) belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
When this power of intention and aspiration encompasses the actions of body and speech, it may also be termed "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
There are those who, through even a small portion of generosity, ethical discipline, or learning, are able to plant the seeds of what is conducive to liberation.
This refers to having a superior intention characterized by sincerity and continuity, characterized by aversion toward saṃsāra and delight in nirvāṇa;
conversely, even if one cultivates much merit, if one lacks these qualities, one cannot plant the factors conducive to liberation.

Because this root of goodness is planted through the predominance of mental action, it can only be planted among humans in three of the continents; this is because elsewhere, the wisdom of renunciation is inferior.
Whether a Buddha has appeared in the world or not, one is equally able to plant the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Having already discussed the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) as a digression, the actual subject at hand is the sequence of entry into meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

Within this, the various paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) have already been clarified, culminating in the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*). It now remains to be explained: what path arises from these?
The verse says:

Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object and gives rise to the untainted Dharma-patience; following this patience, the Dharma-knowledge arises.
Next, taking the suffering of the remaining realms as an object, there arise the Patience of Dharma-knowledge and the Knowledge of Dharma-knowledge;
likewise, taking the Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path as objects, four such moments arise for each.
These sixteen mental states are called the "Clear Realization of the Noble Truths."

This [receptivity] is generally of three kinds, namely: receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*), and receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*).
The treatise says:

Immediately following the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), there arises, with respect to the object of the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm, a state comprised within the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) category called "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*). This receptivity is termed *duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*.
How can it be known that this patience (kṣānti) is comprised within the untainted (anāsrava), arising immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma)?
For it is stated in the Sūtra:

"Immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one enters into the certainty of the right nature (samyaktva-niyāma) or the state of departure from birth (samyaktva-nyāma); at that time, one is said to have transcended the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-bhūmi)."

Since this patience (*kṣānti*) is definitively comprised within a portion of the stage of "separation from birth" (*viveka*), it is necessarily untainted (*anāsrava*). It arises immediately after the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The term "untainted" is used to distinguish it from the patience belonging to the world that follows the supreme mundane dharma.

This untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) takes the phenomena of suffering in the desire realm as its object and is thus called "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

This means that regarding the phenomena of suffering, which from time immemorial have been erroneously grasped by the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as "I" and "mine," one now for the first time perceives them as being solely the nature of suffering; this present state of patient acceptance is termed "patience regarding the dharma of suffering."

This is able to induce the arising of the subsequent *duḥkhe dharmajñāna*; as it is the antidote to the obstruction to the arising of that knowledge, it is further termed "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

This very state is called "entering into the determination of correctness" (*samyaktvaniyāmāvakrānti*) and is also called "entering into the departure from error" (*samyaktvanyāmāvakrānti*), because this is the first entry into the determination of correctness and is also the first entry into the departure from error.
The Sūtra speaks of "rightness" (samyaktva), which refers to nirvāṇa.

Alternatively, the term "rightness" may designate the various noble paths (āryamārga) because they are capable of definitively leading toward nirvāṇa, or because they definitively comprehend the characteristics of the truths; thus, the noble paths receive the name "definitive."
Reaching the attainment of certainty is called "entry.
If this is so, for what reason is the term "certainty" applied only to the initial vision of the truths within untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*)?
It is because at that time, one first attains a vision of the principles of the truths that is difficult to undermine and is definitive.
Alternatively, at that time, because there is a definitive characteristic not shared by other states of the path, it is called "arising" (*jāti*) as an affliction; as the Sūtra says:
"What is meant by 'putrid arising'?"
This refers to the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because one first transcends them at the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is called "birth-transcending" (*vairāgyaja*). Some say:
The Master Śrīlāta says that the faculty of sight is not yet mature;
because one first transcends this stage of seeing, it is called "leaving birth" (*vairāgya*).
Upon attaining this state of leaving birth, it is termed "entry."
Regarding the abandonment of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), various explanations differ:
some say it is the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), while others say it is the "dharma-knowledge patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Some say they are "concomitant abandonments," because these two types are like the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

This receptivity (*kṣānti*) is immediately followed by the arising of a dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) that takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object; this is called "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), because it is the wisdom that attains definitive certainty regarding the fact that this is exclusively suffering.
It should be understood that this wisdom is also comprised within the untainted (*anāsrava*), because the preceding mention of "untainted" applies throughout what follows.

Just as when taking the noble truth of suffering in the desire realm as its object, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arise; likewise, immediately following that knowledge of the dharma, taking the noble truth of suffering in the remaining realms collectively as its object, there arises the patience regarding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), which is called the patience regarding subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) taking this same object; it is called "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
Because it is the first direct realization of the true reality of all phenomena, it is called "dharma-knowledge" (*dharma-jñāna*).
Subsequently, because this object and cognition resemble those of the former [stage], it receives the name "of the same kind" (*jātīya*).
This means that the latter follows the former in realizing the nature of the object.
Alternatively, because it arises from the former, the latter takes on the name of the former's kind, just as in worldly parlance one says, "the son is of the father's kind."
This refers specifically to that which arises from the certainty of awakening regarding suffering in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The meaning of the certainty of awakening regarding suffering in the other realms is as follows: just as there are four conditions—the patience regarding the dharma of the category of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of the category of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)—arising from the truth of suffering in the desire realm and the others; likewise, for each of the remaining three truths, there are four such conditions.

Thus, for each [truth], there is the sense of four moments of mind; in this sequence, there are sixteen moments of mind, which are collectively termed the "clear realization of the noble truths" (*āryasatyābhisamaya*), because one contemplates the objects of the four noble truths within the three realms in their proper order, as they manifest before one, in accordance with reality.

Because one has already become thoroughly proficient through repeatedly circling through the objects of the various truths during the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*), one is now able to contemplate in this manner at this stage.
Other schools state that there is only a sudden realization (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*).
Since that statement is general in scope, it may not contradict reason, for there are three types of the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
What are these three? They are:
vision (*darśana*), object (*ālambana*), and matter (*vastu*).
Only untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that realizes the objects of the truths (*satya-viṣaya*) as they truly are is called "visionary clear observation" (*darśana-abhisamaya*).
This means that by means of vision clearly manifesting itself, one observes the objects of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*) in accordance with reality.

That is to say, untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) together with its associated factors, having a single common object of focus (*ālambana*), is called "contemplation through focusing" (*ālambana-abhisamaya*). This refers to the meaning that the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), such as vision (*darśana*) and so forth, collectively take the objects of the Four Noble Truths as their focal point.

That is to say, all those factors capable of being objects of cognition, together with the other co-existent factors that share a single activity, are termed "factual clear realization" (*vastv-abhisamaya*). This refers to the fact that, within the context of the [Four] Truths, the mental states and mental factors—such as vision (*darśana*) and so forth—along with the other co-existent factors such as morality (*śīla*) and the characteristics of birth (*jāti*) and so on, possess a common objective function.

The factors such as the arising of morality (*śīla*) are the causes of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); because they perform a functional role within clear realization, they are also designated by the name "clear realization.

Thus, one should understand that among the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*), there is only one type of clear realization; among the mental states and mental factors other than wisdom (*prajñā*), there are two types of clear realization; and only untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) possesses all three.

Regarding those who assert that "simultaneous clear realization" (sakṛt-abhisamaya) occurs: they claim that when one attains clear realization with respect to one truth, one also attains clear realization with respect to the remaining truths.
Therefore, concerning the school that asserts the aforementioned simultaneous clear realization, one should carefully investigate upon what basis this clear realization is established.
If one speaks in terms of the objective entity (*vastu*), one should praise it as "excellent.

This is because when one attains the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truth of Suffering, one possesses all three aspects regarding suffering, whereas regarding the others, there is only the objective entity.

That is to say, when first observing the Noble Truth of Suffering: because one exhausts the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the abandonment of the Origin; because one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is called the realization of Cessation; and because one gives rise to the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it is called the cultivation of the Path.

Because the stage of seeing suffering involves the actualization of the objects of abandonment, realization, and cultivation regarding the other three truths—origination and so forth—it is not erroneous to call this "simultaneous" (sakṛt) with respect to the actualization of the objects (*vastu-abhisamaya*).

However, if one speaks in terms of the vision (*darśana*), one must deny it and say it is not so; this actualization is necessarily gradual because the characteristics of the various truths are distinct, and a single vision of the principle does not possess multiple aspects (*ākāra*).
Because the Blessed One stated that each of these truths is to be seen individually according to their respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Having already established that the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) consists of sixteen moments of mind,
upon which basis do these sixteen moments of mind depend?
The verse says:
All are identical to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) in that they rely upon the same stage (*bhūmi*).
The commentary says:
One should know that the bases for these sixteen moments of mind correspond to the bases of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Those bases consist of six stages as previously explained: namely, the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).
For what reason must such patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) necessarily arise in this sequence, alternating one after the other?
The verse says:
Patience and knowledge follow their respective order, As the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The treatise states:

Among the sixteen moments of mind, the four *dharmajñānakṣāntis* and the four *anvayajñānakṣāntis* are called the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*); the four *dharmajñānas* and the four *anvayajñānas* are called the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Their names are as previously explained.

The initial moment of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that is able to accept and confirm the previously unseen suffering of the desire realm is called the "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
This is because the Blessed One himself stated in the *Sūtra*:
"If one examines and confirms this dharma with either inferior or superior wisdom, one is called a 'follower by faith' (*śraddhānusārin*) or a 'follower by dharma' (*dharmānusārin*)."
One should know that this patience (*kṣānti*) is precisely the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Where is this name "path of immediate succession" taught?
It is taught in the Sūtra:
One dharma is difficult to penetrate; it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) because of the mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"There is the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and there is the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*)," and so forth, as explained at length.

These two knowledges do not arise by taking the same objects—the suffering and so forth of the three realms—as their cognitive support, as explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*. Therefore, when a decisive understanding arises regarding the suffering of the desire realm as it was perceived during the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), this is termed the "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

The preceding forbearance (*kṣānti*) is able to sever the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the ten afflictions, while the subsequent knowledge (*jñāna*) arises simultaneously with the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from them.
The Sūtra states:
"Knowledge arises following the preceding forbearance."
Therefore, it is known that subsequent knowledge is called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Immediately following this, for one who has not yet seen the suffering of the form and formless realms, an untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises in the third moment; this is called the "subsequent patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*), because it belongs to the same category as the patience regarding the suffering of the desire realm.

Next, when the decisive understanding (*niścaya*) arises regarding the suffering observed by the subsequent patience of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayakṣānti*), it is called the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*).
Patience and knowledge sever the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) respectively; these are termed the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
Simultaneously with the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyogaprāpti*), they are termed the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*); this should be explained according to the preceding [analogy].
Regarding the other three truths, one should understand them by analogy with suffering.

Thus, the first eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the subsequent eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Furthermore, for what reason is that which is termed the "counteractive abandonment" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) called the path of uninterrupted transition, while the knowledge arising simultaneously with the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) is called the path of liberation?
Because there is no interval, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*); this uninterrupted state is itself the path, thus termed the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This path of the same category is capable of acting as an interval, in the sense that it does not serve as a condition for the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
All paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) consist of a single moment, whereas all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) may be continuous.

The path that arises simultaneously with the attainment of the abandonment (*prahāṇa-prāpti*) of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) to be countered by it—thereby attaining liberation from them—is called the path of liberation.
What meaning does the phrase "its own object of abandonment" intend to clarify?

It is to show that the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), such as the patience regarding the category of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), also arise simultaneously with the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from other objects of abandonment; this is so that they are not also designated as paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Since all sixteen moments of mind perceive the principle of the truths, are they all said to be comprised within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
The first fifteen [moments] constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees what has not been seen before.
The commentary says:
The vision of the principles of the Four Noble Truths, never before seen, is called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Therefore, among the sixteen moments of mind in the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the first fifteen moments are subsumed under the Path of Seeing, because at the stage of the Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā-kṣānti*), the vision of the Truths is perfected.

Upon reaching the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), although there is still one truth not yet previously known, there is no truth that has not already been seen; because all the patiences (*kṣānti*) are by nature seeing, for this reason, at that time, it is not called the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Is it not also the case that one sees what has never before been seen? This refers to the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path), because at that moment there is a single mental instant of the path associated with the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* (receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path).

While those who maintain that the "path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga*) consists only of seeing what has never before been seen would face this fault, in our view, at that time one sees both what has been seen before and what has not; therefore, this fault does not apply.

Alternatively, this refers to the truths (*satya*) and not to moments (*kṣaṇa*); it is not that one is contemplating a truth never before seen at that time, nor can a single moment among many moments of a single truth be called "a truth not yet seen."
Just as when one has harvested the rice in a field leaving only a single stalk, it cannot be said that this field is unharvested;
therefore, the designation "path of seeing" (darśanamārga) for what has been seen and what remains to be seen is well-established in its meaning as the characteristic of the path of seeing.

Therefore, our school maintains that the category of the subsequent path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) following the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because it involves the simultaneous cultivation of knowledge and aspects regarding distinct objects.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā*, Fascicle 30.3; *Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā*, Fascicle 31.

Chapter Seven, Part Three: Distinguishing the Noble Ones and Sages. Having already distinguished the differences in the arising of the paths of vision and cultivation, one should now establish the noble *pudgalas* (individuals) based on the specific stages of these paths.
Furthermore, regarding the establishment of distinctions among the noble ones based on the fifteen moments of mind during the path of seeing, the verse says:
They are named "Followers by Faith" and "Followers by Dharma," Due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties;
Having abandoned from one up to five categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, They are candidates for the first fruit.
"Having abandoned [the first three fetters], one is directed toward the second; having detached from the eight stages, one is directed toward the third.
The Commentary says:

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two types of noble ones (*ārya*): first, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), and second, those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*). These two names are established based on the distinction between dull and sharp faculties (*indriya*).
Those of dull faculties are called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*), because they cultivate and accumulate the preparatory application through the power of prior faith and reverence.
Those of sharp faculties are called "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*), because they cultivate and accumulate the preparatory application through their prior delight in analytical investigation.

The distinctions in the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) of sentient beings have existed as such by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) from the beginning; they differ in their capacity or incapacity to engage in various activities, whether viewing them with aversion or with delight. Thus, based on the difference in the degree to which the two noble ones (*ārya*) have abandoned the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), three paths (*trīṇi yānāni*) are established.
That is to say, if those two types of noble ones have not previously severed the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation by means of the mundane path, they are said to be "fully bound.

Alternatively, if they have previously severed from one to five grades of the desire realm, upon reaching this stage they are called "candidates for the first fruit" (*pratipannaka*), because they are proceeding toward the first fruit.
Regarding the "first fruit," this refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), as it is necessarily the first to be attained among all the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇya-phala*).

If one has previously abandoned six, seven, or eight categories [of afflictions] of the desire realm, upon reaching this stage, one is called a candidate for the second fruit (*dvitīya-phala-pratipannaka*), because one is proceeding toward the second fruit.
The second fruit refers to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), as it is the second among all fruits attained.

If one has previously abandoned the nine grades of the desire realm, or has previously severed even a single grade of the first dhyāna, up to having completely abandoned the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), then upon reaching this stage, one is called a candidate for the third fruit (*tṛtīyaphalapratipannaka*), because one is proceeding toward the third fruit.
The third fruit refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*); its enumeration follows the previous explanation.

Thus, for those who practice through faith and those who practice through dharma, there are seventy-three distinct types each, based on the differences in their prior possession of fetters and their abandonment of afflictions.
That is to say, beginning with one who is fully bound in the desire realm and ending with the abandonment of the ninth grade as the tenth;
proceeding in this manner up to the sphere of nothingness, there are nine grades for each stage, totaling seventy-three.

Since those who remain bound by all fetters at the later stages are the same as those previously described as having abandoned nine [categories of afflictions], there are no distinct "fully bound" individuals in the latter seven stages.

Next, regarding the establishment of distinctions among the noble ones based on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), the verse says:
Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, One abides in a fruit according to one's previous three inclinations.
They are named *śraddhādhimukta* and *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, distinguished by their dull or sharp faculties.
The treatise says:

Those who were previously practitioners following faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or following the dharma (*dharmānusārin*), upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind—the knowledge of the path-category (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*)—are called "abiding in the fruit" and no longer "striving toward it. Corresponding to the three previous paths of striving, they now abide in the three fruits.

This refers to one who was previously a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and now abides in the fruit of stream-entry; one who was previously a candidate for the fruit of once-returning and now abides in the fruit of once-returning; and one who was previously a candidate for the fruit of non-returning and now abides in the fruit of non-returning.

The fruit of arhatship can never be attained for the first time [by one who has already been an arhat], because an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) cannot possibly be separated from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), and because the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) cannot possibly abandon the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Upon reaching the stage of abiding in the fruit, one abandons two names and acquires two others: that is, one no longer bears the names of "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin) or "follower by dharma" (dharmānusārin), but instead acquires the two names of "resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) and "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta); this distinction also arises from the difference between dull and sharp faculties.

Those of dull faculties, who were previously called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*), are now called "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*), because their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is manifested through the predominant power of faith.

Those of sharp faculties, who were previously called "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*), are now called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), because their right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is manifested through the predominant power of wisdom (*prajñā*).

For what reason, when one has previously abandoned from one to five categories, or seven or eight categories, or even one category of the first dhyāna—extensively up to the ninth category of afflictions of the sphere of nothingness—at the sixteenth moment of the path-knowledge of subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), is one designated only as a stream-enterer, once-returner, or non-returner, and not as a candidate for once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship?
The verse says:
Among those who have attained the stages of fruition, because they have not yet attained the path to a superior fruit,
and thus have not yet given rise to that superior path, they are called "abiders in the fruition," not "candidates."
The treatise says:

The eight noble ones are established based on their attainment of the noble path; therefore, at the initial stage of attaining the fruit, one has not yet attained the path to the superior fruit, because the mind that has attained the fruit is not an antidote to the afflictions to be countered by the path to the superior fruit.
It is a settled principle that when the antidote to a particular state is present, one does not simultaneously attain the path that serves as the antidote to that very state.

Furthermore, at the moment of attaining a fruit, there is no arising of the acquisition of dissociation from the afflictions abandoned by the superior path, because the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* (subsequent patience regarding the path) cannot sever those acquisitions of bondage.

If the power of the path is able to sever the acquisition of those fetters, and this path induces the arising of the acquisition of disjunction from them, one may say that this path can realize that cessation; for at the time of attaining the preceding fruit, one has not yet attained the path of the superior fruit.

One who abides in the fruit, until the time when the path of superior fruit has arisen, is called merely "abiding in the fruit" even if they have previously abandoned one grade or more of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation; they are not called "progressing toward the subsequent [fruit]."
At what time later does one obtain the untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) of the dissociation from the previously abandoned afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation?
It is obtained at the time when the path of superior fruit (viśeṣa-mārga) manifests, for the sake of those [afflictions] previously abandoned.

After one has cultivated the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) to enter the stage of "entry into the state free from birth" (*vairāgya-bhūmi*) and attained the preceding fruit, will the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣa-mārga*) necessarily arise in this very life?
According to principle, it must be so;
for the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states:

For one born as an *ārya* in the fourth dhyāna or above, the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*) is necessarily accomplished; because their obstacles have been severed, they must certainly delight in that [attainment], and because the path through which obstacles are severed easily manifests before them.

Having thus established the distinctions among the noble ones based on the sixteen moments of mind for those who enter the vision of the truths—whether they previously possessed double-detachment from desire or were entirely detached from it—one should now explain the differences in the stages of the antidotal paths that arise gradually with respect to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
The verse says:
In each stage, there are nine faults and virtues; three each for the inferior, middling, and superior.
The commentary says:
"Loss" refers to faults, which are the obstacles to be remedied;
"virtue" refers to meritorious qualities, which are the remedial paths.

As previously explained regarding the nine grades of distinctions in the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, it should be understood that the same applies to the four higher dhyānas and the four formless attainments, because there is no part of saṃsāra that is not subsumed within these nine stages.

Just as each of the obstructions to be remedied within each stage consists of nine grades, so too do the remedial paths—the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and the liberation (*vimukti*) paths—consist of nine grades.
How is it that these faults are each divided into nine grades?

This means that within the fundamental category there are inferior, middling, and superior levels; each of these three is further divided into inferior, middling, and superior distinctions.
