Consequently, the faults and virtues are each divided into nine grades: namely, the inferior-inferior, inferior-middling, inferior-superior, middling-inferior, middling-middling, middling-superior, superior-inferior, superior-middling, and superior-superior.

It should be understood that herein, the power of the lowest-of-the-low path is able to sever the highest-of-the-high obstacles, and so on, until the power of the highest-of-the-high path is able to sever the lowest-of-the-low obstacles; for these remedial qualities, such as the highest-of-the-high, did not previously exist, and at this time, faults such as the highest-of-the-high have already ceased to exist.
It should be understood that herein, although wisdom surpasses the afflictions, because it has not yet become fully developed, the path is designated as "inferior.
Although the afflictions within the continuum are extremely difficult to sever, because they persist as subtle latent tendencies, the path is designated as "inferior."
Based on this principle, one should establish an analogy: just as when washing clothes, coarse stains are removed first, and only later, in successive stages, are fine stains gradually removed;
or as coarse darkness can be dispelled by a small light, but it requires a great light to dispel subtle darkness.
The same principle applies to the relative nature of faults and virtues.

For this reason, it can be said that the white [virtues] are superior and the black [faults] are inferior, because in a single moment the path of antidote arises and uproots the afflictions that have persisted since beginningless time.
Having already distinguished the nine grades of the faults and defects, we shall next establish the distinctions among the noble ones based upon them.

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for those in training (*śaikṣa*), they are collectively termed "those resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "those who have attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). Furthermore, there are many specific subdivisions according to their respective stages; first, we shall establish the case of those who have not yet abandoned any [defilements].
The verse says:
Having not yet abandoned the faults to be abandoned by cultivation, one who abides in the fruit [of Stream-enterer] returns at most seven times.
The commentary says:

Regarding those who abide in the fruit: when they have not yet completely abandoned any of the faults to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across all stages, they are called "stream-enterers" (*srotāpanna*), who are subject to at most seven returns.
The term "seven returns" indicates seven cycles of returning; this signifies the meaning of seven births each among gods and humans.
The expression "at most" is used to indicate that the maximum number of rebirths is seven; it does not mean that all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) are necessarily limited to exactly seven returns.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"At most seven times returning."
This refers to the meaning of being reborn at most seven times; the Sūtra’s explanation is no different from this meaning.
All untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are collectively termed "flows" (*āsava*), because by means of them as a cause, one proceeds toward Nirvāṇa.
The prophecy is given to manifest that one has first attained the state of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna); therefore, one is called a "stream-enterer.
To what meaning does this name "stream-enterer" refer?
If the initial attainment of the Path were what constitutes being a stream-enterer, then the name "stream-enterer" would have to refer to the eighth [person].

If one who first attains the fruit is named a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna), then those who have either partially or fully abandoned desire would also be named stream-enterers upon reaching the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna).
This name "stream-enterer" designates the initial attainment of the fruit.

However, those who have either partially or fully abandoned desire are not called "stream-enterers" (srotāpanna) until they reach the knowledge of conformity to the path (mārgānvayajñāna), because their respective fruits are established based on the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
A stream-enterer must necessarily depend upon the universal attainment of the fruit, as the name is established based on the first fruit attained.
The fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and Non-returner (anāgāmin) are not necessarily attained first; it is only this fruit [of Stream-enterer] that must necessarily be attained first.
For what reason is this name not applied to the eighth [stage]?

Because one has not yet fully acquired the untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) of both the candidate and the fruit; because one has not yet fully acquired the untainted paths of both seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); and because one has not yet universally reached the attainment of the flow of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are termed the "stream of clear realization" (*abhisamaya-srotas*); at the moment of the knowledge of the path-category (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one possesses the acquisition (*prāpti*) of all of them. For this reason, the eighth [moment] is not called "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*); thus, the stream-enterer is exclusively the first fruit.
From that point onward, they are to undergo seven births each among humans and devas. One might ask:
"If it should be stated as fourteen, why is it said that they undergo at most seven births?
This objection is invalid, because the number seven is equivalent, just as in the cases of the *saptaparṇa* tree and the "sevenfold excellence" (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*).

By the power of the Noble Path, one does not undergo more than seven existences; although the Noble Path may manifest during this interval, one does not realize parinirvāṇa because one is sustained by the force of residual karma, and because the Pratimokṣa restraint exists only in dependence upon the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

Regarding that seventh existence, if he does not encounter the Buddha-dharma, he will attain the fruit of arhatship while remaining a householder; yet once he has attained that fruit, he will certainly not remain in the household life, as it is the natural law for a bhikṣu’s deportment to be spontaneously perfected.

Although they do not encounter the teachings spoken by previous Buddhas, they develop an intense sense of revulsion toward further existence during their remaining lives and enter parinirvāṇa before long.
If one attains the fruit of a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) within the human realm, one will take seven full rebirths among humans; the same should be understood to apply to the heavenly realms.

Even those who are not noble (anārya) may have the sense of attaining nirvāṇa through the maturation of a continuity of births limited to seven returns; however, this is not certain, and for that reason it is not mentioned.

Thus, it has been explained that one who has not yet abandoned any of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) who will undergo at most seven returns.
Now, one should distinguish the noble ones according to their stages of abandonment; first, the candidate for and the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) shall be established.
The verse says:
Having abandoned the third or fourth category of desire, One is a "Family-to-Family" (kulaṃkula) with three or two more births remaining.
Having abandoned up to five [categories of afflictions], one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one attains the fruit of once-returner.
The commentary states:
When a stream-enterer further abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, if three conditions are met, they are designated as a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.

First, by means of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*): because one abandons three or four categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm; that is to say, either having abandoned them previously while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or abandoning them now while progressing in the stage of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

Second, by the accomplishment of the faculties, because one attains the untainted faculties that can counteract those [defilements]; that is to say, one has already accomplished the three or four grades of untainted faculties that constitute the path capable of counteracting them.

Third, by way of rebirth: because one undergoes three or two further births in the desire realm. That is to say, if one abandons three grades [of afflictions], one undergoes three more births; if one abandons four grades, one undergoes two more births.

These three and two births arise because, while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one performs and accumulates karma that brings about those three and two births. Noble ones (*ārya*), however, while in their noble state, can no longer newly create karma that draws them toward future existence (*punarbhava*), because they have turned their backs on birth and death and are oriented toward *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, the Sūtra states that noble ones only experience previously created karma and do not create new karma.
If any one, two, or all three of these conditions are lacking, one is not called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
Why, then, is it said that they possess faculties?

It is because the verse does not state that after the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one must further abandon afflictions; rather, it indicates that one possesses those untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) which serve as the antidotes to them.
Since the meaning has already been established by implication, it is not stated in full.
If that were so, one should not have mentioned the phrase "three or two births," because the meaning of abandoning three or four categories [of afflictions] would already be established.

This means that one who has already progressed in abandoning three or four categories of afflictions is certain to have only three or two remaining births; therefore, it is said that the characteristics of a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) are not yet complete. Thus, the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be added to the verse in order to fully encompass the three characteristics of a *kulaṃkula*, or else the mention of "three or two births" should not be stated.

However, regarding the statement in the verse that there are "three or two births," this is because there may be further progress, such that the births one undergoes may be fewer than three, or none at all, or even more than that.
One should know that, in general, there are two types of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family):

first, the *deva-kulaṃkula*, which refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) for three or two families—either in one celestial abode, or two, or three.

Regarding the "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) practitioners: this refers to those born within three or two households among the human realm who realize parinirvāṇa, whether in one continent, or two, or three.
If there are seven births, yet fewer than seven are completed, they do not belong to the stage of a house-to-house practitioner. To what category does such intermediate nirvāṇa belong?

These are subsumed under the seven births; because the term "maximum" (*parama*) within the phrase "seven at most" indicates the greatest number, this already implies that those who attain parinirvāṇa before their births are completed are also included therein.
Those with the most dull faculties may undergo up to seven births; however, those with sharp faculties do not necessarily complete all seven births.

Why then is one who has abandoned five [categories of defilement] also called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family)? Because at the time of abandoning the fifth, they must necessarily abandon the sixth; it is not that a single grade of affliction can obstruct the attainment of the fruit, just as one who is separated by only one interval has not yet transcended the realm.

That is to say, when a stream-enterer further abandons one grade of the afflictions of the desire realm up to five grades, it should be known that they are designated as being on the path toward the fruit of once-returning; if they abandon the sixth grade, they achieve the fruit of once-returning.
One who goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm before attaining parinirvāṇa is called a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*), because after this, there is no further rebirth.

By this very principle, it is proven that among those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), if one belonging to the heavenly *kulaṃkula* undergoes three more births, they will undergo two in the human realm and three in the heavenly realm.
Regarding those who undergo two births: one birth among humans and one among devas.
This should be explained by analogy with the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner among humans, as appropriate.
If this were not the case, what difference would there be between that fruit of once-returner and the "family-to-family" practitioner who undergoes two births?

Since his greed, hatred, and delusion remain only in their inferior forms, he is thus a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), designated as "one whose greed, hatred, and delusion are attenuated" (tanu-rāga-dveṣa-moha).
Having already distinguished the stages of the candidate for and the fruit of the Once-returner, one should next establish the candidate for and the fruit of the Non-returner (anāgāmin).
The verse says:
Having abandoned seven or eight grades, one who has one birth remaining is called an Ekābhisamayin;
this is the third stage of progress. Having abandoned nine grades, one attains the fruit of Anāgāmin.
The Treatise says:
When a Once-returner proceeds to further abandon remaining afflictions, if three conditions are met, they are designated as a "One-interval" (Ekavīcika):
first, by way of abandoning afflictions, because they have abandoned seven or eight categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
Second, by the attainment of faculties, because one acquires the untainted faculties of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) which serve as antidotes to those [defilements].
Third, by the taking of birth, because one takes yet another single birth among the gods of the desire realm or among humans.
If any one, two, or all three of these conditions are lacking, it is not called "one-interval" (ekavīcika), but rather constitutes the attainment of the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
These were not mentioned in the verse, yet they ought to have been mentioned.
The cause for [attaining] a single lifetime should be explained accordingly as in the case of the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).

What is called "intermediate" (*antara*) is a synonym for "gap" (*chidra*); it means that because there is a gap in that state sufficient to accommodate one more lifetime, one has not yet attained nirvāṇa.

Alternatively, this term "ekavicika" refers to the sense of being separated by an interval; that is, because at that stage there remains one more birth as an interval, one does not realize parinirvāṇa.
One who has such a single interval is called an "ekavicika."

How so? When there remains one final grade of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation that can act as an obstacle to prevent rebirth in the desire realm, one is called "one-interval" (ekavīcika).

If one who has not yet attained the fruit of non-returner eliminates this grade, they thereby transcend the ground of the two fruits—namely, the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the concordant fruit (*nisyandaphala*)—as well as the karma and afflictions bound to the desire realm.

Because he still possesses great hindrances that allow for further rebirth, and because he has not yet transcended that stage when the six grades [of defilements] are abandoned, there is no intermediate rebirth after abandoning five grades; thus, in his present body, he cannot realize the fruit of a Once-returner.

It should be understood that one who has abandoned seven or eight grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is likewise called a candidate for the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmipratipannaka*).

If one who previously abandoned three, four, seven, or eight grades of afflictions entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), at the time they subsequently attain the fruit, would they be designated as a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) or a "one-interval" (*ekavīcika*) practitioner?

This is not yet called "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula) or "one with one interval" (ekavicika), because the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that remedy those [defilements] have not yet been attained;
at the stage of first attaining the fruit, the path of the fruit (phalamārga) is present, but at that time, the path of superior fruit (viśeṣamārga) has not yet been cultivated.

Only upon reaching the subsequent stage and giving rise to the path of superior fruit can one be designated as a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) or a "one-interval" (ekavicika), for it is only at that time that the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) which counteract those [defilements] are attained.

As for one who has previously realized the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), when the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm are completely abandoned, one relinquishes the name of "once-returner" and attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin), because one will certainly not again undergo birth in the desire realm.
This may be called the severance of the five lower fetters; this statement is made in reference to their severance through the abandonment of the origin [of suffering].
There is certainly no principle by which all five fetters could be severed simultaneously, for two or three would have already been severed previously.
Based on the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), various distinctions are established through diverse approaches in the sūtras; we shall now explain the characteristics of those distinctions.
The verse says:
Among these, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or upon rebirth (*upapadya*).
If those who go upstream practice mixed meditation, they can proceed to the Akaniṣṭha heaven by leaping, half-leaping, or passing away entirely; others can proceed to the Peak of Existence.
There are four types of practitioners of the formless realm, some of whom attain parinirvāṇa while remaining here.
The treatise says: These non-returners (anāgāmin) are generally said to be of seven types. Briefly stated, there are five distinctions among those who proceed to the form realm (rūpadhātu):

first, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; second, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; third, one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion; fourth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion; and fifth, one who flows upward (ūrdhvasrotas).
Because this one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, it is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarā-parinirvāyin).
It should be understood in this way: this one [attains it] after being born, and this one by means of application (sābhisaṃskāra).
Because these attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*), they are designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) and so forth.
Because they are those who go upstream (*ūrdhva-srotas*), they are called "those who go upstream.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antara-abhava-parinirvāyin*): it refers to a certain class of *pudgalas* who have attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the fetters of rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*), but not so regarding the fetters of arising (*utpāda-saṃyojana*).

When he is oppressed by the conditions of affliction within the desire realm, he is able to exert himself to cultivate the superior application for abandoning the remaining fetters. Before his application is complete, he encounters the conditions for death and passes away; by the power of the fetters that have arisen, he receives a form-realm intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Because he loathes the abundance of suffering, he relies on the path previously generated to advance and abandon the remaining fetters, becoming an Arhat and attaining parinirvāṇa.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*): this refers to a certain class of individuals who, because they previously possessed and cultivated karma conducive to arising and rebirth, pass away from the desire realm and take birth in the form realm. Due to possessing the path of swift progress through diligent cultivation, they become arhats not long after being born; they attain parinirvāṇa only at the exhaustion of their lifespan. This is designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" with reference to the state of having a remainder of the basis (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
It is not that they attain parinirvāṇa without remainder immediately upon birth, because they lack mastery over the relinquishing of their life-span.

As for the terms "with exertion" (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) and "without exertion" (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), this refers to a certain class of *pudgalas* who become *aśaikṣas* only after a long time following their birth; among them, one who is courageous and diligent is called "with exertion," while one whose nature is slow and indolent is called "without exertion," respectively.

This refers to a certain class of persons who, while previously in the desire realm, rely on the power of samādhi through uninterrupted application to sever the five lower fetters and attain the fruit of non-returner; subsequently, having been reborn in the form realm, after the passage of much time, they are again able to advance and cultivate the path of the same kind to become an arhat—this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion" (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).
The one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*) is the opposite of this.

Alternatively, after having been born in the form realm for a long time, one who relies upon ascetic practices to liberate oneself from the remaining fetters is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion" (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), because they attain parinirvāṇa by practicing according to the path of effortful application.
That which is the opposite of this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion" (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin).

[Objection: Is it not the case that since the basis for those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, or in the present life also possesses such exertion, they too should be designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion" (sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) or "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion"?
There is no such fault, for although this meaning is the same, each of those [types of *parinirvāṇa*] possesses its own distinct stages.

That is to say, although those such as the "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*) also necessarily rely on either painful practice or pleasant practice to liberate themselves from the remaining fetters, each of them has different stages; in contrast to this, they are termed "unshared distinctions."

Since this [state] lacks such distinct stages, its differentiation is manifested through the diversity of the paths; how then can one use this to exemplify that and force them to be identical? Therefore, there is no fault in what has been argued here.

For this reason, some say that the distinction between the two lies in the fact that by relying on the noble path directed toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one attains nirvāṇa respectively.
One should know that this too is non-existent; other [arguments] suffer from the same fault.

However, there are sutras that state non-practice (*apravṛtti*) comes first, and there are also sutras that first state practice (*pravṛtti*). Since there is no difference in time, there is no contradiction in whichever is taught; yet, because practice is worthy of honor, I have spoken of it first.

Regarding those who are "Upstream-bound" (ūrdhva-srotas): this refers to a certain class of individuals (pudgala) for whom there is an upward progression; they do not attain parinirvāṇa at the very place of their initial birth.

That is to say, having passed away from the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and been born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), they do not attain parinirvāṇa therein, but must instead proceed to higher rebirths before entering parinirvāṇa.
There are two distinctions among these *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), based on differences in their causes and their results.
As for the difference in cause, it is due to whether or not there has been mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) within the dhyānas.
Regarding the distinction of the fruit: the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) constitute the ultimate limits.

This means that if one has practiced the "intermingled cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) within the dhyānas, one is able to go to Akaniṣṭha and there attain parinirvāṇa, because such intermingled cultivation can induce the fruit of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Furthermore, this [attainment] has three distinct varieties, distinguished by being "complete leapers," "half-leapers," and "those who die everywhere. Regarding the "complete leaper" (*skanda-gāmin*):

it refers to one who, having died from a certain location within the form realm, proceeds to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. This is because such a person had previously, while in a body within the desire realm, fully cultivated the four dhyānas through mixed practice; however, encountering conditions, they fell away from the upper three dhyānas and, with the relish for the first dhyāna as a condition, were reborn at the end of life in the Brahmakāyika heaven.
Due to the force of habitual tendencies from previous lives, they are further able to practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna; passing away from that state, they are reborn in Akaniṣṭha.

Because they pass away from the first location within the sixteen locations of the realm of form and are reborn in the final location, skipping all those in between, this constitutes the meaning of "complete leaping" (pluta).

Regarding "half-leapers" (ardhapluta): this refers to those within the form realm who die from the first heaven and so forth, gradually descending as far as the intermediate heavens, and only after skipping over one location are they able to proceed to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
To leap without passing through all stages is the meaning of "half-leaping.

As for the term "passing through all" (*sarvacyuta*), it refers to one who, because of a great abundance of craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), is born in every location. This is because throughout all sixteen locations within the four levels of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there exists a degree of inferior craving that serves as the condition for rebirth. Having died from each successive location starting from the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (*Brahmakāyika*) until finally reaching the Highest Heaven of Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), one then attains parinirvāṇa; therefore, this is called "passing through all."
By this principle of analogy, the abode of Mahābrahmā within the first dhyāna is not a separate location, but is included within the second Brahmakāyika heaven.
Were it otherwise, because the abode of Mahābrahmā is a place of heterodox views and there is but a single leader, no noble ones (ārya) would ever take birth therein.

There would be no distinction between those who die everywhere (*sarvacyuta*) and those who leap halfway (*ardhapluta*); therefore, it should be understood that among these two types of *ūrdhvasrotas*, this is because they possess the cause of mixed cultivation of the dhyānas.

Those who attain parinirvāṇa in Akaniṣṭha are distinct from those who lack the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas, as the latter can only attain parinirvāṇa after reaching the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

This means that because they previously lacked the practice of mixed meditative absorption (*miśrabhāvanā*), and due to their attachment to the flavors (*āsvāda*) of various concentrations, upon death they are reborn throughout all the levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), with the sole exception that they cannot go to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Having passed away from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and having been born successively in the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), one subsequently attains parinirvāṇa after being born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Between these two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), the former is one of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-carita*) and the latter is one of meditative stabilization practice (*samatha-carita*), due to the distinction between delighting in wisdom and delighting in concentration.
Regarding the two types of "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas), it is not contrary to reason that they may attain parinirvāṇa within the lower realms;
however, the statement that they proceed to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven or the Bhavāgra Heaven is made in reference to their ultimate destination.

There is no Non-returner who undergoes a second birth in a place where they have already been born, because such a person may seek further progress within that birth rather than remaining equal or inferior.

Only those who pass away from the Desire Realm and are reborn in the Form Realm—specifically those who attain Parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*)—are so described; this does not apply to those who pass away from the Form Realm and are reborn in the Form Realm, because there are no calamities within the Form Realm.

If one in the state of existence prior to birth (*pūrvakālabhava*) cannot attain nirvāṇa due to other obstructing conditions, the same applies to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), because the intermediate existence is inferior and not the prior existence.
Furthermore, if such [an intermediate existence] were to exist, it would have to belong to those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

There would be no distinction between those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), for there would be no causal basis whatsoever to make such a statement.

Only one who dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and attains parinirvāṇa upon receiving a form-realm intermediate existence (*rūpāvacara-antarābhava*) earns the name "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state," not one who dies in the form realm itself.
For what reason is there no one among those in training who has not yet abandoned desire and greed that attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
It is because the body upon which the intermediate state of the desire realm depends is weak and inferior, and thus lacks the capacity for many activities.

Even while abiding in the state of prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) in the desire realm, it is difficult to transcend its dharmas; how much more so in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), where one could transcend the desire realm and attain the fruit of arhatship?
One who performs many tasks refers to one who transcends the three realms, eternally abandons the two types of afflictions, and attains the realization of two or three fruits of the śramaṇa.
The state of abiding in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) lacks such capacity.
Furthermore, prior to this [existence], one has not yet repeatedly practiced the remedies for the nine grades of differentiated afflictions.

Moreover, the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and others cannot be attained by means of the intermediate body, because it is realized through the abandonment of predominant afflictions, and because it is extremely difficult to become free from the defilements of the three realms.

In the realm of no-desire (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are those capable of attaining parinirvāṇa; however, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the case is entirely different, as there are those who attain nirvāṇa therein.
Furthermore, those who attain parinirvāṇa in this specific stage [of the form realm] give rise only to the noble path (*āryamārga*) belonging to that very stage.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the stage of the first dhyāna, they manifest only the noble path (*āryamārga*) of the fundamental dhyāna of their own stage; they do not manifest the *anāgamya* or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because these are difficult to bring into manifestation. While in the intermediate state, the basis of the body is extremely weak; therefore, only that which is easily aroused can be manifested.
These five are called those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

There are four distinctions among those who proceed to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): namely, those who, while in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), become free from craving for the form realm, and upon passing away from there, are reborn in the formless realm. Within this category, there are only four types of distinction, due to the differences such as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) and so forth.
Together with the five previously mentioned, these constitute six types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, there are those who do not proceed to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), but instead attain parinirvāṇa while remaining right here; these are called those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*).
Including the previous six, there are seven.
Alternatively, one should establish nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) in total; that is, those who attain *nirvāṇa* in the present life are divided into two kinds:
first, those who were already well-versed in the noble intent (*āryārtha*) in their prior stage; second, those who are only able to become well-versed in it at the time of death.
Within the upward-streamers (*ūrdhvasrotas*), there are also two types:
those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those who proceed to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Together with the four preceding types, these constitute eight; when combined with the "transformative birth" (*parivṛtti-janman*), they total nine.

Regarding the term "transformational rebirth" (*paryāyanirvāṇa*): it refers to one who, having previously attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) or once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) in a prior birth, attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) only within this present life.
The expression "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present existence" (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin*) refers exclusively to the present life.

Those who first attain entry into the noble state and reach nirvana, or those who are non-returners (anāgāmin), are divided into nine types according to their differences in faculties (indriya) as appropriate; or they may proceed among the five types of non-returners within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Furthermore, there is another classification that divides them into nine types.
The verse says:
There are nine [types] of those who go to the form realm, namely, three each divided into three.
Because there are differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties, they are established as the three and nine distinctions.
The treatise says:
That is to say, the five types of non-returners in the form realm are collectively established as three; each of these is further divided into three types, thus forming nine types.

What are these three? They are distinguished as those who attain nirvana in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain it upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who ascend to higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
How is each of these three types further divided into three?

The parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāṇa*) is divided into three types because there is a distinction between attaining parinirvāṇa shortly after arising, at a distant point, or near the place of rebirth.

The parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāṇa*) is divided into three types because of the differences between those who attain it immediately upon birth, those who do so through effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*), and those who do so without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
All of these attain parinirvāṇa after being born; therefore, they should all be designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin).

As for the division of those who go upstream (ūrdhva-srotas) into three types, it is due to the differences between the "complete leaper" (pluta), the "half-leaper" (ardha-pluta), and the "one who passes away everywhere" (sarvasthāna-cyuta).
However, all three types are further divided into nine distinct categories without confusion, based on whether they attain parinirvāṇa quickly, not quickly, or after a long duration.

Thus, these three types and nine types of non-returners, due to differences in their karma, afflictions, and faculties, are distinguished as being swift, not swift, or taking a long time; in brief, they constitute three categories.

This is because there are differences in the karmic existence (*bhava*) that arises subsequently due to the prior accumulation of karma conducive to its arising; because there are distinctions in the manifestation of afflictions according to their sequence as inferior, middling, or superior; and because there are differences in the faculties as superior, middling, or inferior.
Each of these three [categories] is as it should be;
furthermore, because there are distinctions in karma, afflictions, and faculties, each has its own three subdivisions, thus forming nine types in total.
That is to say, the first two sets of three each consist of three types due to the distinctions in afflictions and faculties, not due to differences in karma.
The latter three are also divided into three types due to differences in karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*).

Thus, it is said that these non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who proceed to the form realm (*rūpaga*) are distinguished into nine types based on the differences in their karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).
If that is so, for what reason do the various sūtras state that the Buddha taught only seven destinies of the virtuous person (*satpuruṣagati*)?
The verse says:
The establishment of the seven destinies of the virtuous person is due to the lack of distinction among those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Because those who practice good or evil deeds go on and do not return, the treatise says:
there are three each for the intermediate and birth states, and one for the upward-streamer; based on this, the Sūtra establishes the seven destinies of the noble person (*satpuruṣagati*).
For what reason are the first two each divided into three, while the third, the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), is established as only one?
Because they move upward, they are called "Upstreamers"; since their meaning is thus the same, only one category is established.
Although the first two types are also identical in meaning, their specific characteristics are difficult to discern; therefore, each is divided into three to facilitate understanding.
As for the *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upwards), its three distinct characteristics are easily understood, so there is no need to establish further subdivisions therein.
Furthermore, because the first two [categories] are distinct and their objects are easily demonstrated, each is divided into three.
The third, the *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upward), has many distinct meanings that are difficult to demonstrate at once; therefore, it is established as a single category in total.

That is to say, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon initial entry exist only while about to be reborn; they are divided into three types due to differences in their faculties and the categories of their afflictions.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa after being reborn exist only once already born; they too are divided into three types due to differences in their faculties and afflictions.
Regarding those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), there are those who are about to be born and those who have already been born.

Those who go upstream and are about to be born are further divided into two types: those who practice the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in a mixed manner and those who practice them in an unmixed manner.
It is the same for those who go upstream and have already been born, as they are likewise divided into two.

Furthermore, among these two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who stream upward), if there is no mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), they may be reborn in both realms; if there is mixed cultivation, they are reborn in only one realm.

Those reborn in a single realm are further divided into three types based on the differences between the "complete leaper" (*pluta*), the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*), and the "one who passes through all" (*sarvasthānacyuta*).

Within the "half-leapers" (*ardhapluta*), there are many internal distinctions; because the specific characteristics of these various types of "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) would be too voluminous to detail, and because it would be difficult to provide a complete account for each one individually, they are collectively established as "Upstreamers" based on their common essential meaning.
Within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the distinctions in meaning are slight and easily discernible; therefore, it is divided into six.
Although each of these also possesses points of similarity, they are equivalent to the third [category].
Although there are differing interpretations regarding the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), it is equivalent to the previous two types.
Because they are established to mutually illustrate one another, only seven are posited.
Only these have abandoned sensual desire, hatred, and so forth, which are not the qualities of a true person (*satpuruṣa*) and are not yet the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Because the fruits of a great virtuous person (*mahāpuruṣa*) are extremely similar [to those of a Stream-enterer], the Sūtra speaks of this alone as the "destination of a virtuous person" (*satpuruṣagati*).
This does not mean that the Stream-enterer and Once-returner cannot at all be called "destinations of virtuous persons," for the Buddha also refers to them as "virtuous persons."
As stated in the Sūtra:
"What is a virtuous person?

It refers to one who is endowed with the right view of a trainee, up to being endowed with the right concentration of a trainee. To 'proceed upward' means to proceed toward higher fruits and to proceed toward higher rebirths."
Therefore, only seven are mentioned.
Alternatively, it is because only these seven are capable of practicing what is wholesome and refraining from what is unwholesome, whereas the others are not so.
Furthermore, only these seven are born into the higher realms and do not return again, while the others are not like this.
Therefore, it is based solely on this that the "destinies of the noble person" (satpuruṣagati) are established.
Is there also such a distinction among those who, while in the state of an ārya, have already undergone rebirth? No.
How so? The verse says:
An noble one who has taken birth in the desire realm does not go to take birth in another realm.
This and those who are reborn in the higher realms neither refine their faculties nor undergo retrogression.
The treatise says:

If one is in the state of an Ārya and undergoes birth in the Desire Realm, they will certainly not be reborn in the Form or Formless Realms; for having realized the fruit of Non-returner (Anāgāmin), they are certain to attain parinirvāṇa in that very same body.
If a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone rebirths in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) were to be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), such a possibility would exist.
However, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke as follows:
"I have heard that there is a heaven named Akaniṣṭha; when I eventually fall from my current state, I shall be born there."

Because they do not understand the characteristics of the antidote, those noble ones who have already undergone birth in the desire realm, as well as those who have already been born from here into the higher realms, will certainly never undergo the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) nor experience regression. This is because the Noble Path has been accumulated within their own mental continuum through having previously undergone such births, making it extremely firm, and because they have obtained a superior basis of existence (*āśraya*).

It was previously stated that the "upward-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), by taking the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas as a cause, is able to go to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. First, what dhyāna should one mix?
And by what stage is it known that the mixed cultivation has been accomplished?
Furthermore, for what reason does one practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?
The verse says:
First, one mixes the fourth [dhyāna]; its accomplishment arises from a single moment of mixing.
"For the sake of receiving rebirth, manifesting pleasure, and preventing regression through afflictions.
The commentary states:

Those who practice the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas must first practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, because that meditative concentration is most capable and is the most excellent among all practices leading to bliss.
Who is able to practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?

Only the noble ones, both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). Within the stage of training, this applies only to those of the faith-follower (śraddhādhimukta) and the vision-attainer (dṛṣṭiprāpta) types.

Within the stage beyond training, it applies to both those who attain liberation at specific times and those who attain it at any time. One must first practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna in the three continents; even one who has fallen away and been reborn in the form realm can still practice mixed cultivation, and having fallen away, may refine their faculties to become of the vision-attainer lineage.

Having passed away from the desire realm and been reborn in the form realm, one is able to further practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna based on previous training; therefore, all six spiritual lineages possess the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).
What expedient means are employed at the time of this mixed cultivation?

He must first enter the fourth dhyāna, wherein many moments of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) continuity manifest before him. From this, he induces many moments of contaminated (*sāsrava*) states; subsequently, many more moments of the uncontaminated manifest again. In this manner, they alternate, with each successive cycle gradually decreasing until finally there are two moments of the uncontaminated. Immediately following these, two moments of the contaminated manifest, and without interval, two moments of the uncontaminated arise once more; this is called the completion of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā-samādhi*).

From this point onward, without relying on deliberate effort, one spontaneously induces a single moment of contaminated [consciousness] to manifest from a single moment of uncontaminated [consciousness], followed immediately by the arising of another single moment of uncontaminated [consciousness].

In this way, because the intermediate moment of the contaminated state is interspersed with the preceding and succeeding moments of the uncontaminated state, it is called the fundamental perfection of the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā*).
Having thus cultivated the fourth dhyāna through mixed cultivation, by the power of this, one is also able to cultivate the lower three dhyānas through mixed cultivation as appropriate.
The meditative absorption of mixed cultivation has the five aggregates as its essence.
Within this, the various conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are those mixed with the four dharma-knowledges, the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*), and the eight knowledges.
Briefly, there are three conditions for the mixed cultivation of meditative absorption:
First, for the sake of taking rebirth; second, for the sake of manifesting happiness; and third, for the sake of preventing the arising of afflictions that lead to regression.

Among those who are Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), those of the lineage of "attainment through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) possess the first two conditions, while those of the nature of "liberation through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) possess all three conditions.

Among the Arhats, those who are liberated at any time (asamaya-vimukta) cultivate it solely for the sake of present happiness, while those who are liberated by time (samaya-vimukta) do so for the sake of the latter two conditions; furthermore, if they practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, it is for the purpose of being reborn in the five Pure Abodes.
For what reason are there only five abodes of the Pure Dwellers (*śuddhāvāsa*)?
The verse says:
"Due to the five grades of mixed cultivation, there arise five Pure Dwellers."
The treatise says:
Because the fourth dhyāna is cultivated through a mixture [of the mundane and supramundane] in five grades, there are only five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
What are these five grades?
This is due to the distinctions between the inferior, middling, superior, more superior, and most superior grades.

Among these, in the first grade, one attains fulfillment as soon as three moments of mind manifest: namely, first an untainted (anāsrava) mind, followed by an outflowing (sāsrava) mind, and finally another untainted mind.
The second middling grade is perfected only when six moments of mind have appeared, namely: two contaminated moments interspersed with four uncontaminated moments.
Likewise, for the remaining grades, they are perfected only when nine, twelve, or fifteen moments of mind have appeared in their respective order, as appropriate.
These five grades of mixed cultivation serve as the cause, sequentially bringing about the fruits of the five Pure Abodes.
Thus, these fifteen types of tainted and untainted minds are all for the first time attained now, having never been attained previously.
Other masters say:
Of these, the first five untainted [minds] are those not previously attained that are now attained; the remaining ten are all minds already previously attained.

Since the former five have already been cultivated in the future when they manifest, there are cases where one does not emerge from meditative absorption. For the mixed cultivation to reach completion, it is necessary to arise repeatedly before it can be fully perfected.
Other masters say:

"The five Pure Abodes are attained through the successive predominance of the five faculties beginning with faith; the attainment of these Pure Abodes results from the power of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) as well as from the mutual support of karmic forces."

However, it is only contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma that produces that maturation (*vipāka*), not the power of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because the latter turns its back on existence (*bhava*).
The Sūtra states that there is one who returns no more (*anāgāmin*) called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Based on what superior quality is this name established?
The verse says:
An *anāgāmin* who attains the meditative absorption of cessation is designated by the name "Body-Witness" (*kāyasākṣin*).
The commentary says:
The attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called "attaining the absorption of cessation.

Specifically, when a non-returner (anāgāmin) possesses the attainment of the absorption of cessation within their body, they are further designated as a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin). This means that because the non-returner has realized through the body a state resembling nirvāṇa, they are named a body-witness.
How is it said that they are merely "bodily witnesses" (*kāyasākṣin*)?
Because they lack mind.

Because [the attainment] arises in dependence upon the body, and because the power of the acquisition (*prāpti*) co-arises with the body, one is still said to possess that [attainment] even when it has already ceased.

For what reason does the Buddha state that those in training (*śaikṣa*) are fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), yet the one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*) is not included among their number?
It is because the World-Honored One told Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, you should know that there are two kinds of fields of merit:"
The first are those in training (śaikṣa) and the second are those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There are eighteen for those in training and only nine for those beyond training.
What are called the eighteen [factors] of those in training?

These are: the candidate for and the fruit of stream-entry; the candidate for and the fruit of once-returning; the candidate for and the fruit of non-returning; the candidate for arhatship; those who practice according to faith and those who practice according to the Dharma; those liberated through faith and those attained through vision; those who go from family to family; those with only one interval remaining; those who attain nirvana in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, with effort, or without effort; and those who ascend to the higher realms. These are called the eighteen.
What are called the nine types of those beyond training? They are:

the one subject to regression, the one who reflects, the one who guards, the one who abides, the one capable of penetration, the unshakable one, the non-regressing one, the one liberated by wisdom, and the one liberated both ways; these are the nine.

As for why the principle should have been stated but was not: it is because the Buddha perceived that those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess distinctions based on their abandonments (*prahāṇa*) and faculties (*indriya*); thus, they are able to produce superior fruits and are therefore called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).

However, because the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) attained by non-returners (anāgāmin) is still with outflows (sāsrava), it cannot be said to be "pure" on account of its intrinsic liberation (svabhāva-vimukti). Furthermore, because the physical body upon which that attainment relies still possesses afflictions that have not been eternally severed, it cannot be said to be "pure" on account of the liberation of the continuum (saṃtati-vimukti). Therefore, one does not establish them as a field of merit for those in training (śaikṣa-dakṣiṇīya) based on the accomplishment of that attainment.

The contaminated virtues within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), although not subsumed under liberation by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*), are termed "pure" because they are included within liberation of the continuum (*prabandha-vimukti*); for this reason, they are also capable of producing sublime fruits.
Therefore, based on conventional agreement and the distinctions among the faculties, all nine fruits of arhatship are called fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Having already explained the coarse distinctions of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), if analyzed in detail, their number amounts to many thousands.
In this context, we shall first rely on the five [categories] that practice within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), analyzing them according to five gates such as the various stages (*bhūmi*).
That is to say, these five, when categorized by stage, become twenty, because there are five types within each of the four dhyāna stages.
Fifth, when categorized by lineage (*gotra*), they number thirty, because there are five types within each of the six lineages.
Sixth, when categorized by birthplace (*upapatti-sthāna*), they number eighty, because there are five types within each of the sixteen birthplaces.

Fifth, when categorized by lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*), there are ninety types. This is because for each lineage—beginning with the *parihāṇadharman* (those subject to falling away)—there is a distinction of inferior, medium, and superior faculties, resulting in fifteen types; this applies likewise up to the *akopyadharman* (the immovable lineage).
Fifth, when categorized by stage (*bhūmi*) and lineage (*gotra*), they total one hundred and twenty, because there are thirty for each of the four stages.
Fifth, when categorized by stage, lineage, and faculty (*indriya*), they total three hundred and sixty, because there are ninety for each of the four stages.
Fifth, when categorized by birthplace (*janmasthāna*) and lineage (*gotra*), they number four hundred and eighty, because there are thirty for each of the sixteen birthplaces.
Fifth, when categorized by birthplace, lineage, and faculty (*indriya*), they number one thousand four hundred and forty, because there are ninety for each of the sixteen birthplaces.

Fifth, by calculating according to the distinctions of detachment from defilement (*vairāgya*), stage (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), and faculty (*indriya*), the total number of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) amounts to twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty. This is calculated by multiplying the previous one thousand four hundred and forty by the nine distinct grades of detachment from defilement.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Meaning of the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Fascicle Thirty-one. [Continued in] Fascicle Thirty-two.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Seven: Distinguishing the Noble Ones (Ārya-vibhāga), Part Four. Having already distinguished the differences between the third stage of the path and its fruition, one should next establish the fourth stage of the path and its fruition.
The verse says:

Among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms, from the abandonment of the first grade of the First Dhyāna up to the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence, one is in all cases a candidate for Arhatship.
The ninth path of immediate succession is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*);
together with the attainment of exhaustion, it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), whereby one becomes an adept (*aśaikṣa*) and attains the fruit of arhatship.
The treatise says:

The Non-returner who further proceeds to sever the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the form realm and the formless realm—beginning from the severance of the first grade of the first dhyāna and ending with the severance of the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)—should be known as being designated as one "progressing toward Arhatship" (arhattvapratipannaka).

Within this very context of the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvābhimukha*), the ninth uninterrupted path (*anantaryamārga*) that abandons the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is also called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropamasamādhi*). This concentration is as firm and sharp as a diamond because there is not a single latent tendency (*anuśaya*) that it cannot shatter, and because all have already been shattered by it.
Although nothing is actually destroyed [by the path], there truly exists the functional capacity to destroy everything.

Even though within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) there is also an untainted antidote capable of severing the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing can be treated as a single category, because the power of the nine categories [of afflictions] is too weak to be severed instantaneously.
Furthermore, because the non-substantial afflictions (*anupadhi-āsrava*) are easily severed, the antidote for them is not designated by the name "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).

The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) explained here serves as the antidote to the final, most subtle, and most difficult-to-sever grade among all substantial afflictions (*sopadhi-āsrava*); therefore, it is known to destroy all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
By this power, in a single kṣaṇa, one realizes the untainted attainment of disjunction (*anāsrava-visamyoga-prāpti*) through the abandonment of all afflictions.

This aforementioned diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is associated with only one of six types of knowledge—namely, the four subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna*). It takes the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the four noble truths as its object and relies upon all nine stages (*bhūmi*); this is established by implication.
Therefore, these distinctions are explained in many ways.

Briefly, there are fifty-two types subsumed under the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage; that is to say, when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) contemplate the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) through the aspects (*ākāra*) of impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth, as well as cause (*hetu*) and so forth, they form eight distinct types in association with those [mental factors].

The dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna) contemplates the cessation and the path of the desire realm through the aspects of "cessation," "calmness," and so forth, as well as "path" and so forth; the distinctions associated with these are also eightfold.

The subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) contemplates the cessation of each of the eight stages individually through four aspects; when associated with those, they constitute thirty-two.

The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) takes all paths of the eight stages as its collective object and performs four aspects (*ākāra*); when associated with these, it becomes fourfold through their distinctions.

Because the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge that counteract the eight stages must necessarily take them collectively as objects due to the causal relationship between similar types, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) takes them only individually, whereas the knowledge of the path does not; this has already been fully established in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
Just as there are fifty-two [mental applications] included in the *anāgamya* (preliminary stage), it should be known that the same applies to the four intermediate dhyānas.

In the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there are twenty-eight; that is to say, excluding the eight [applications] belonging to the category of the Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) regarding cessation and the path, and excluding the sixteen [applications] associated with the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) of the four lower stages. This is because, when relying on the formless realms, there is necessarily no Dharma-knowledge, and because one relies on the category of Subsequent-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) which takes the cessation of the lower stages as its object.
There is no logical obstruction to taking the stages of the lower paths as objects, for it has already been explained that the path necessarily takes [all] as its object;
since the rest is as previously stated, there are twenty-eight.
In the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, there are twenty-four.
In the sphere of nothingness, there are only twenty [mental applications].

That is to say, from the previous [set], one further excludes the four and eight aspects regarding the object of the Noble Truth of Cessation pertaining to the lower realm; these should be explained in sequence according to the preceding pattern.
Regarding those who maintain that the knowledge of the class of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) in the three formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*) takes the lower stages as its object, they state:

the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) adds sixteen [moments] to the preceding; the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) adds twenty to the preceding; and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) adds twenty-four.
Thus, in general, there are seventy-two types of diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) based on the formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*).
Alternatively, it is said that there are one hundred and thirty-two.
Other masters state:
The category of subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) also observes each of the eight paths individually; therefore, there are eighty [aspects] for each of the first six stages.

The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) has only forty, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) has thirty-two, and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) has twenty-four.

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that regarding the cessation of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across the eight stages, there is both a specific and a general contemplation; thus, within the first six stages, there are respectively one hundred and sixty-four [instances], fifty-two for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thirty-six for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and twenty-four for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Both of those views are unreasonable; the Path necessarily takes [all objects] collectively as its object, whereas Cessation takes them only individually, because of the presence or absence of causes.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka stated it thus:

"The Diamond-like Samādhi consists of thirteen moments in total, namely, the thirteen moments subsumed under the Uninterrupted Paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)."
This is also not the case, because the eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) preceding the four types of patience (*kṣānti*) are not of the highest degree.

Since this concentration (*samādhi*) is capable of severing the ninth grade of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it can induce the arising of the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) that accompanies the attainment of the total exhaustion of those afflictions; thus, it is called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*). Because this is the final uninterrupted path among those that sever afflictions, and because the knowledge of exhaustion arises from it as the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) among those that sever afflictions, it is said that the knowledge induced by this concentration arises simultaneously with the attainment of the exhaustion of the ninth grade.

Alternatively, the term "exhaustion" (kṣaya) here signifies the exhaustion of all [afflictions]; that is to say, because the ninth grade [of afflictions] and all remaining defilements attain analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it is called "exhaustion.

The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is able to induce the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), which occurs simultaneously with the attainment of the exhaustion of all afflictions; because this arises for the first time together with the attainment of the exhaustion of all afflictions, it is named the "knowledge of exhaustion."
Other masters say: Because this [knowledge] arises for the first time within the body when all afflictions have been exhausted, it is called "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).

When such knowledge of exhaustion has arisen, one then becomes an Arhat of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), because one has already attained the dharmas of the fruit of a Worthy One (*arhat*) who is beyond training.
Because there is no further training to be undertaken for the sake of attaining a distinct fruit, one receives the name "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Is it not the case that even those beyond training still aspire to a distinct fruit, since those beyond training also undergo the transformation of their faculties?
This objection is not valid, for it is not as if one who was previously a *śaikṣa* attains a distinct fruit [at that time].

Since it has been stated that one becomes a *aśaikṣa* Arhat fruit at the moment the *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) arises, it follows by implication that prior to the arising of the *kṣayajñāna*, the preceding seven noble ones are all called *śaikṣas*; they abide in their original state because they diligently cultivate training in order to attain a distinct fruit.
What is meant by "one in training" (śaikṣa)?
It is because their intention to train is not yet fulfilled, and because they are constantly accompanied by acquisitions resulting from training.
Why is one beyond training (aśaikṣa) called an Arhat?
Since one has already completed the training in all practices for one's own benefit, one should now act solely for the sake of benefiting others.
As it is said in a sutra:
"It is impossible for one who has not disciplined oneself to be able to discipline others."
Alternatively, they are called "Fruits of Worthiness" (*arhat*) because they are worthy of being venerated by all those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
What are the dharmas of training?
They are the untainted conditioned dharmas (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*) of those in training.
What are the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*)? They are the untainted conditioned dharmas (*anāsrava-saṃskṛtadharma*) of one who is beyond training.

Although all unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are untainted, they are not designated as dharmas of those in training or beyond training, because they are possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others as well.
If there were no attainment, they would not be connected to either the state of training (*śaikṣa*) or the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Thus, those in training and those beyond training together constitute the eight noble persons (*āryapudgala*), as there are four each for those proceeding toward the fruits and those abiding in the fruits.

Although there are eight names, there are only five actual entities: namely, those abiding in the four fruits and those in the path toward the first fruit; this is because those in the paths toward the latter three fruits are not separate from their preceding fruits.
This is stated with reference to those who attain the fruits through gradual progression.

If one who has either partially or fully abandoned desire dwells within the Path of Seeing, they are termed a "Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin) or a "candidate for the fruit of Non-returning" (anāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka), which is not subsumed under the preceding fruits.

Since the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), which path is capable of abandoning the defilements (*kleśa*) of which level?
When the two paths manifest and one becomes detached from the defilements of the various stages, how many acquisitions of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*) do they each induce?
The verse says:
The Peak of Existence is abandoned by the untainted [path]; The others are abandoned by both, through detachment.
The two noble paths and the eight stages of cultivation each possess two types of acquisition of dissociation from fetters.
The treatise says:
Regarding all afflictions within the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), only the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) can bring about their permanent abandonment.
Because these [contaminated paths] possess a powerful influence regarding the outflows (*sāsrava*), they are able to act as antidotes for their own level and all higher levels.

Only within the proximate stages (*sāmantaka*) immediately above can one give rise to a mundane path (*laukikamārga*) that acts as an antidote to the afflictions of the lower levels. Since there is no higher level for the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is no contaminated path capable of abandoning the defilements of that stage.
The various mundane paths do not eliminate their own afflictions, because those afflictions are increased by the latent tendencies (anuśaya) associated with them;
nor do they eliminate the afflictions of higher stages, because their power is inferior.

As for the afflictions belonging to the other eight stages, one can achieve permanent separation from them through both types of paths, because each of those stages possesses both a mundane path of the stage above and an uncontaminated (anāsrava) path of its own lower stage.

When the Noble One employs both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths to abandon the defilements to be eliminated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the lower eight stages, each path respectively brings about two acquisitions of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*). This is because the contaminated and uncontaminated paths of abandonment perform the same function across these eight stages.

Consequently, for one in training (*śaikṣa*) who has abandoned the eight [categories of] afflictions to be eliminated through cultivation, whichever of the mundane or supramundane paths manifests, they cultivate both the mundane and supramundane paths in their future state.
This is the general explanation.

When one abandons the first eight categories [of afflictions] of the seven higher stages by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), because one does not cultivate the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) of the upper limit, there is only the single acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) that is untainted.

Only upon abandoning the ninth category can both [types of acquisition] be possessed. Alternatively, one must admit that one cultivates the path while already possessing its acquisition; or else, one must admit that when severing defilements, one relies on a lower stage to cultivate a higher one.

Since it has been stated that for a noble one (*ārya*), both types of detachment (*visamyoga*) produced during the cultivation of the eight stages each induce the acquisition of two types of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*), we may infer accordingly that when a noble one attains detachment from the cultivation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) or at the time of abandoning what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), they employ the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to induce only the acquisition of untainted disjunction; furthermore, they do not cultivate the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) for the future, because this is a matter distinct from the mundane path.

Ordinary beings, being separated from the eight [levels of defilement] by means of the contaminated path, produce only the acquisition of disconnection (visaṃyoga-prāpti) that is itself contaminated; furthermore, they do not cultivate the uncontaminated path in the future, as this is established as a matter of course since they have not yet entered the state of a noble one (ārya).
Other masters say:

When one abandons the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the lower eight stages by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), on what basis is it known that one also produces the untied acquisition (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) of the tainted (*sāsrava*)?
Because if one were to abandon the untainted acquisition, the afflictions would not be established [as abandoned].

This means that when a noble one in training (śaikṣa) becomes detached from those defilements by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), if they were not to produce a contaminated acquisition of disconnection (saṃyojana-visaṃyoga-prāpti) that shares the same antidote, then even though they have already abandoned the defilements of the eight stages through the noble path, when they later attain the transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) based on dhyāna, they would suddenly discard all their previously possessed dull noble paths and acquire only the sharp fruit-noble paths of dhyāna. Consequently, the disconnection from the higher-level afflictions would fail to be established, and thus those afflictions would once again become manifest.
However, this is not what is accepted; therefore, it possesses both types of acquisition (*prāpti*).
This proof is invalid because it is not determinative.

For example, when one who has separated from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) undergoes the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), or when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is reborn in a higher realm and does not produce afflictions (*kleśa*), these two cases lack the acquisition of the abandonment of afflictions; yet, because they represent a superior advancement, the arising of the acquisition of afflictions is obstructed.
The same should apply to that case as well; therefore, the proof is irrational.

Consequently, one can only say this: because the two paths perform the same function within it, the manifestation of either one induces the arising of both acquisitions (*prāpti*); it cannot be said that this is for the purpose of accomplishing abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Having already explained that detachment from defilement occurs through different paths, we shall now explain it according to the distinctions of the stages (*bhūmi*).
By means of which path-stage does one become detached from the defilements of which stage?
The verse says:
The untainted path of the *anāgamya* stage can abandon all stages;
the remaining eight [stages] abandon their own and higher stages; the tainted path abandons the immediately lower stage.
The treatise says:

All untainted paths (anāsrava-mārga) rely upon nine stages: namely, the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and the three formless attainments (ārūpya).

If those included within the threshold concentration can abandon the defilements of the desire realm, then the remaining eight stages—up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra)—can each, as appropriate, abandon the defilements of their own stage and the higher stages, but they cannot abandon the defilements of lower stages.
Because when one has not yet become detached from a lower level, the path of a higher level cannot possibly manifest.
