All contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) are capable only of bringing about detachment from the level immediately below them, and not from their own level or higher levels; this is because [the latter] are augmented by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of their own level, because [the contaminated path] is weak in power, and because [those higher levels] have already been abandoned previously.

Regarding those [attainments] based on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) that abandon the defilements of the lower levels: just as all uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are included within the preparatory stages, are all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) also included within the preparatory stages?
Not necessarily.
How so? The verse says:
"The 'near-separation' [attainment] involves the abandonment of the defilements of the lower realm; it occurs during the first three and the final liberation."
The fundamental or the preparatory stage; for the higher stages, only the fundamental.
The treatise says:
There are eight preparatory stages that serve as the basis for the various paths, namely, the lower limits of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.

There are nine instances of abandonment: namely, the eight dhyānas; and during the first three stages of the preparatory (sāmantaka) concentrations, one abandons the defilements of the lower levels; and when the ninth liberation manifests, one either enters the fundamental concentration or remains in the preparatory stage itself.

Each of the five upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) is free from the defilements of the lower stage; when the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) manifests, one necessarily enters the fundamental [dhyāna] and not the preparatory stage itself, because the preparatory and fundamental stages are equal in terms of their faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Because the faculties of feeling differ between the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental states (*maula*) of the lower three dhyānas, there are cases where one cannot enter [the fundamental state].

This is because it is somewhat difficult to transition into a different type of feeling, and because when one becomes detached from the defilements of a lower level, one necessarily feels joy toward the higher level.
If the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are without distinction, they must necessarily enter the fundamental states (*maula*).

Regarding the paths of transcendence (*lokottaramārga*), both the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), since it has already been stated previously that they take the four truths as their objects and possess sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), this is established by implication.
By what conditions do the worldly paths arise, and what are their modes of activity?
The verse says:
The worldly paths and the uninterrupted paths, as well as the paths of liberation, respectively take the lower and the upper realms as their objects.
One forms the contemplations of coarseness, suffering, and obstruction, as well as the three of tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
The commentary states:

The mundane paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation respectively take the lower and higher stages as their objects, perceiving them as coarse, suffering, and obstructive, and as tranquil, excellent, and detached.

This means that the various uninterrupted paths take as their objects the contaminated phenomena of their own level or the immediately lower level, applying one of the three aspects—coarseness, suffering, and so forth.
The various paths of liberation take as their objects the contaminated phenomena of the immediately higher level, applying one of the three aspects—tranquility, excellence, and so forth.

It may be said, in a general sense, that each of the two paths possesses three aspects; however, it is not the case that every sentient being, at the stage of becoming free from defilement, necessarily possesses all three in both the immediate (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths.
Within the lower stages, because of excessive restlessness (*auddhatya*), tranquility (*śamatha*) is weak and inferior; therefore, they are termed "coarse" (*audārika*).
Although great exertion may temporarily cause agitation, its power is weak and inferior; it still cannot induce the arising of sublime bliss, and is therefore called "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

Furthermore, because there are many kinds of calamities and obstructions that can conceal and hinder one such that one lacks the capacity to perceive the means of transcendence, it is called an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*).
In the various higher stages, because there is no exertion of effort and agitation is subtle and weak, they are called "calm.
Because one does not undergo toil and agitation is subtle and weak, thereby inducing superior bliss, they are called "sublime."

Because one can definitively perceive all the calamities present in the lower stages, such that the mind does not give rise to delight in them, and because one is able to proceed toward those [higher stages], it is called "detachment" (*vairāgya*).

One should know that within this, the three aspects of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the three aspects of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are simultaneously indicated; they arise in their respective order as mutual opposites.
That is to say, in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the lower stage is perceived as coarse; in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the upper stage is perceived as calm.
The remaining characteristics arise in reverse order, which should be understood accordingly.
However, at the time of abandoning defilements (*vairāgya*), their arising is not fixed.

Because the mundane uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are able to abandon the nine grades of defilements of the lower realms and so forth, it should be understood that they likewise possess a ninefold distinction.

In this context, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) abandons the defilements of the desire realm, one of the three modes of activity—coarseness (*audārikatā*), etc.—manifests during each of the nine uninterrupted paths; furthermore, in each case, one cultivates the future attainment of all three modes of activity, namely coarseness and the rest.

In each of the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one of the three modes of practice—such as tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth—is manifested; in each case, one cultivates the six modes of practice, such as coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth, in the future.
In the subsequent paths of deliverance (*vimokṣa-mārga*), those cultivated in the present and future are as previously described.
Regarding the eight paths of liberation that differ from the preceding ones: one further cultivates the future aspects of infinite practice subsumed under the first dhyāna.
It should be understood that this continues in the same manner up to the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation cultivated upon becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.

If noble ones abandon the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path, in each of the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), one of the three aspects—coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth—is present; in each case, they cultivate nineteen aspects in the future, namely: the three aspects of coarseness and so forth (both contaminated and uncontaminated), the sixteen noble aspects, and the eight liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*).

When any one of the three [higher] practices—such as tranquility (*śamatha*)—is present, one cultivates twenty-two practices in the future for each; that is, the previous nineteen plus the three such as tranquility.
Regarding the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), those cultivated in the present and future are as previously described.

Regarding the eight paths of liberation that differ from the preceding [paths of uninterrupted transition]: one further cultivates nineteen aspects in the future—comprised within the first dhyāna—that are free from the defilements of the first dhyāna. In each of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition, one of the three aspects such as "coarseness" (audārika) manifests; for each, one cultivates nineteen aspects in the future, namely: the three aspects such as coarseness, and the sixteen noble aspects which are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
These sixteen modes of practice (*ākāra*) are subsumed under the lower stages (*adhobhūmi*), because the higher stages lack any noble practices (*ārya-caryā*).
It should be understood that the subsequent cultivation of noble practices follows this same principle.

In each of the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one of the three modes—calmness (*śānta*), etc.—manifests; in each case, twenty-two modes are cultivated in the future, namely the previous nineteen plus the three beginning with calmness.
Regarding what is cultivated in the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in both the present and future, it is as previously described for the eight paths of liberation.
The difference from the former is that one further cultivates, in the future, the two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) that comprise the infinite aspects (*ananta-ākāra*).
It should be understood that this applies even up to the path of liberation immediately following the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Other masters state:

"Both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) also cultivate the meditation on impurity (*aśubhā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) within the paths of liberation immediately following the abandonment of desire."

As previously explained, in the case of other higher stages, because the roots of goodness at the limit of the first dhyāna are extensive, one cultivates such practices; however, because the roots of goodness at the limits of the higher meditative concentrations are slight, what is cultivated is as previously described.

Furthermore, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there are many afflictions; in order to sever them, one cultivates many antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). This is not the case for the higher stages, and thus their cultivation is slight.

Regarding the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandon the defilements of the desire realm, the three modes of activity—coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth—which are cultivated in the future, take only the desire realm as their object. As for the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they likewise [take the desire realm as their object].

The three types of practice—coarse (*audārika*) and so forth—that are cultivated in the future [path] take the desire realm and the first dhyāna as their objects; the three types of practice—calm (*śānta*) and so forth—take the first dhyāna as their object.

Regarding the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the three types of practice—coarse and so forth—that are cultivated in the future take all three realms as their objects, while the three types of practice—calm and so forth—take the first dhyāna as their object.

Up to the point of becoming detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna while at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the three types of mental application—coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth—which are cultivated in the future during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), take the first dhyāna as their object.

During the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the three types of mental application—coarseness and so forth—which are cultivated in the future, take both the first and second dhyanas as their objects; the three types of mental application—calmness (*śānta*) and so forth—take the second dhyāna as their object.

Regarding the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the three modes of cultivation—coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth—which are cultivated in the future, take all three realms as their object; the three modes of cultivation—tranquility (*śāntatā*) and so forth—take the second dhyāna as their object, and this continues up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
For the abandonment of the defilements of the second and third dhyānas, it should be understood according to the previous explanation as appropriate for each case.

Regarding the separation from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition cultivate, for future attainment, the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—which take the fourth dhyāna as their object.

The eight paths of liberation cultivate, for future attainment, the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—which take both the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space as their objects; however, these do not occur in a single moment, because their respective realms are distinct.
The three modes of practice, such as tranquility (*śānta*), take only the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their object.

Regarding the subsequent path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), the three modes of practice—coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth—and the three modes of practice—tranquility and so forth—which are cultivated in the future, all take objects ranging from the sphere of infinite space up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

When one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space, the three types of cultivation—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated in the future during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition take only the sphere of infinite space as their object.

During the eight paths of liberation, the three types of cultivation—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated in the future take both the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness as their objects, while the three types of cultivation—tranquility and so forth—take only the sphere of infinite consciousness as their object.

Regarding the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—and the three modes of practice—tranquility and so forth—which are cultivated for the future, both take the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as their objects.
The detachment from the defilements of the sphere of consciousness and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) should, as appropriate, be understood according to what was previously explained.

For what reason, within the final path of liberation, do the three modes of practice—coarse and so forth—which are cultivated for the future, have as their objects all three realms when subsumed under the dhyānas, yet only the upper and self-realms when subsumed under the formless attainments?

Within the various dhyānas, there is wisdom that takes all things as its object; however, the fundamental stages of the formless realm necessarily do not take lower levels as their objects. Therefore, the objects cultivated by these two differ.
This incidental discussion is concluded; one should now analyze the primary subject matter.

This treatise explains the sequential arising of the various roots of goodness. Since it has already been stated that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) necessarily arises immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), what kind of knowledge arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion?
The verse says:
After the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) of an Immovable One, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) necessarily arises;
for others, it is either the knowledge of exhaustion or right view. These are possessed by all who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
The treatise says:

For those Arhats of the "unshakable dharma" type who have previously attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arises immediately after that knowledge of exhaustion; since this knowledge was what they originally sought, it is necessarily acquired simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion.
This means that when one seeks to obtain the understanding that accords with the prediction [of enlightenment], if this were absent, there would be an obstacle to entering nirvana.

When all Arhats simultaneously attain wisdom, they likewise aspire to seek the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); however, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) ought logically to arise first, as it was what was sought previously during the stage of the cause.

For one who was previously an Immovable [Arhat], after the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is attained, yet it has not yet manifested; it only arises manifest immediately following the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

With the exception of those previously immovable, for other Arhats, the knowledge of exhaustion arises immediately following the knowledge of exhaustion; or rather, it induces the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) rather than the knowledge of non-arising, because they may subsequently fall away from it.

That is to say, if one is of the nature of "liberation through timely effort" (*samayavimukta*), although they sought both types [of liberation] during the causal stage, because there is the possibility of falling away from the ultimate fruit, they do not attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is ceasing, but only attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Therefore, after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), either the knowledge of exhaustion manifests again, or it directly induces the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).

For those of the immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) who previously possessed the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), there subsequently arises either the knowledge of non-arising or the right view of one beyond training. This right view of one beyond training is common to all Arhats, just like the knowledge of exhaustion; thus, at the very moment when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is ceasing, everyone attains the right view of one beyond training.

However, this right view is not what is primarily sought; therefore, immediately following the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), it may either arise at once or remain unmanifest.

Regarding the general meaning of this stage: if one was previously immovable, the initial arising of the knowledge of exhaustion lasts for only a single moment, and the subsequent knowledge of non-arising likewise lasts for a single moment, though in some cases it continues in succession.
In the case of one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) first arises, it may occur for a single moment or as a continuous succession.

The unlearned right view (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) arising from these two states lacks the certainty of being either a single moment or a continuous succession, because, as previously stated, that [view] does not constitute a formal pursuit.
As it is said regarding the śramaṇa and the fruits of the śramaṇa: what is the nature of the śramaṇa?
What is the essence of these fruits?
And how many distinct categories of the stages of fruition are there in total?
The verse says:
The nature of a śramaṇa is the pure path; its fruits are both conditioned and unconditioned.
These consist of eighty-nine [moments]: the paths of liberation and cessation.
The treatise states:

One who is called a *śramaṇa* is so named because they are able to eternally extinguish and eliminate the demons of birth and death within the various realms, destinies, and modes of existence; or because they are able to diligently exert themselves to extinguish all faults and cause them to be eternally stilled. Therefore, they are named *śramaṇa*.
As the Blessed One himself has provided this explanation:

"Because one is able to exert effort to pacify and eliminate various evil and unwholesome states, and to distance oneself from the faults of defilement—and so on at length—one is therefore called a śramaṇa."
That which belongs to a śramaṇa is called the nature of a śramaṇa; this is precisely the perfuming dharma cultivated by a śramaṇa.
"Perfuming" (vāsanā) signifies the meaning of expelling and eliminating the stench of afflictions.
It takes the untainted noble path as its essence, rather than the mundane path, because it is capable of completely and ultimately bringing all faults to rest.

For this reason, although an ordinary person may have already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness, they are not a true śramaṇa; because their faults still remain, they merely rest in tranquility for a time rather than having attained the ultimate.

Since the untainted path constitutes the nature of a śramaṇa, and it takes both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as its fruits, the essence of the fruits of śramaṇaship thus encompasses both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The Buddha taught that these fruits are, in total, of four kinds: namely, from the first, stream-entry, up to the final, arhatship.

The category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is called the conditioned essence of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*); the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) is called the unconditioned essence of the fruit of stream-entry.

The category of the subsequent knowledge of the path, or the category of the sixth untainted path of liberation (*anāsravavimuktimārga*) for one who has become free from desire for the desire realm, is called the conditioned essence of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*);

the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by seeing, as well as the abandonment of the first six categories among those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the desire realm, is called the unconditioned essence of the fruit of once-returning.

The category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) or the category of the ninth untainted path of liberation (*anāsravavimuktimārga*) for one who has become free from desire for the desire realm—this is called the conditioned essence of the fruit of non-returning (*sopadhiśeṣa-anāgāmiphala*).

The abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm—this is called the unconditioned essence of the fruit of non-returning (*anupadhiśeṣa-anāgāmiphala*).

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the category of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) constitute the conditioned essence of the fruit of arhatship;
the abandonment of the factors to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation within the three realms constitutes the unconditioned essence of the fruit of arhatship.

However, in the sūtras, the Bhagavān speaks only of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as the essence and fruit of the state of a śramaṇa; for example, he says: "What is called the fruit of stream-entry? It is the abandonment of the three fetters," up to: "What is the fruit of arhatship? It is the permanent and complete abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion."
It should be understood that the term "abandonment" (prahāṇa) here includes the previously mentioned explanations of abandonment.
For what reason is only the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) mentioned in that context?
Because this unconditioned is exclusively a fruit (phala).

This means that while all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are exclusively fruits of the śramaṇa, the Path (*mārga*) is not mentioned here because it pervades both [the state of being a śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa].
Alternatively, since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are fruits but do not possess further fruits, and the Path pertains to both categories, it is omitted from this brief explanation.
Alternatively, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are free from the defects of the conditioned, they are taught specifically in order to inspire joy in them.

Or, this sūtra—which speaks only of unconditioned fruits—is an incomplete statement; one should not dogmatically adhere to the view that it teaches only the abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), for it does not universally teach the abandonment of all other afflictions (*kleśa*).
As stated in the Sūtra:

"The mind turns swiftly; through diligence one can realize unsurpassed bodhi, transcending the notion of physical food, surpassing all notions of form, and eliminating notions of sensory resistance—this is not possible for others."

One should know that this sūtra is likewise: just as it speaks of only the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as the fruits of śrāmaṇya by means of a specific intention, so too does it speak of only four kinds of fruits of śrāmaṇya by means of a specific intention.

If one sets aside specific intentions and discusses the characteristics of phenomena directly, there are eighty-nine fruits of the śramaṇa, all of which are paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) and have cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as their intrinsic nature.
This means that for the sake of permanently severing the afflictions of the three realms, eighty-nine uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) arise.

Those subsumed under the path of seeing (darśanamārga) number eight, because there are four instances each of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna);
those subsumed under the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) number eighty-one, because there are nine uninterrupted paths (ānantaryamārga) for each of the nine stages.
These eighty-nine [moments] constitute the nature of a śramaṇa alone.

The eighty-nine paths of liberation that arise immediately after these [paths of seeing] also constitute the conditioned fruits of śramaṇaship, because they are their outflow (niṣyanda) and virile (puruṣakāra) effects.

The analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) resulting from the abandonment of the eighty-nine afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the uninterrupted paths are exclusively unconditioned fruits of the śramaṇa; for they are the disjunction-fruits (*visamyoga-phala*) and the virile-activity fruits (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of those [paths], since those [paths] are able to abandon the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the obstacles to these [cessations].

Is it not the case that the nature of a śramaṇa also includes the path of liberation, since all paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) are also their outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and fruition fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*); therefore, the paths of uninterrupted transition should also be included within the conditioned fruits of the śramaṇa?
It is not so; furthermore, it is not the case that all uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are fruits of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Although there are such instances, one can only say that the path of liberation arises through the power of the uninterrupted path, because the power of the former is able to sever the obstacles to the arising of the latter, and because this [path of liberation] necessarily arises immediately after that path.

The power of the path of liberation does not induce the arising of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), because this [path of liberation] cannot sever the obscurations of that [uninterrupted path], nor is it the case that the latter necessarily arises immediately following the former.
This means that although there are instances where one arises immediately after the other, this is not always the case;
furthermore, it is not due to the power of the former, as it is induced by the power of other preparatory practices at other times.
Alternatively, because there is no further arising [in the case of the final fruit], there is no fault of lacking a corresponding category.
For what reason does the sūtra state that there are only four fruits of śrāmaṇya, rather than eighty-nine?
Has it not already been stated that the sūtra has a distinct meaning?
What is this distinct meaning?
For now, there is an explanation that says:
It is only within these four stages that practitioners of meditation give rise to clear, joyful, and awakened wisdom.
That is to say, only these four stages are supremely trustworthy and not others, because even if one should fall away from them, one will regain them before death.
Others further state:
"Only these four stages can, respectively, transcend the evil destinies, because they are demonstrated by the birth in the human and celestial destinies resulting from those [stages].
It is only through the power of superior and middling grades of greed and so forth that one goes to birth in the evil destinies, not through the inferior grade."

Alternatively, there are two bases: namely, the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Since two [results] transcend the peak of existence and two transcend the desire realm, only four are established as the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Alternatively, all afflictions can be categorized into two types: first, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and second, the unwholesome (*akuśala*). The first [stream-enterer] transcends both types; the latter [once-returner] transcends the indeterminate;
and the once-returner and non-returner transcend only the unwholesome. Because the unwholesome is difficult to transcend, only four [fruits] are established.
Other masters say:
It is not that the Blessed One did not directly realize the eighty-nine [moments]; however, he spoke of only four fruits of śrāmaṇya. As the verse says: "Four fruits are established by five causes:
Abandoning what was previously attained and obtaining a superior path; [The remaining three causes are] the abandonment of the path, the attainment of the fruit, and the completion of the task."
"Attaining the eight knowledges through the abandonment of the aggregates, one suddenly cultivates the sixteen aspects.
The Commentary says:

If the stage of the path of abandonment possesses five causes, the Buddha established in the sūtras that the abandonment itself and the attainment of that abandonment arise simultaneously with the pure path of liberation as the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
Regarding the five causes:
first, the relinquishing of the former path, which means relinquishing the previously attained paths of fruition and application;
second, the attainment of the superior path, which means attaining the distinguished paths subsumed within the fruition.
Third, the collective abandonment of defilements, meaning that one simultaneously attains the acquisition (*prāpti*) of all previously abandoned abandonments;

fourth, the attainment of the eight knowledges, meaning that within a single moment one collectively attains the four knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*);
fifth, the ability to suddenly cultivate the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), meaning that one can suddenly cultivate the aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth.
Those abiding in the four stages of fruition all possess these five causes, whereas those in other stages do not; therefore, only four are mentioned.

If the nature of a śramaṇa consists solely of the pure path (*anāsrava-mārga*), how can the two fruits obtained through the power of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) also be subsumed under the fruits of a śramaṇa?
The verse says:
That which is abandoned through the mundane path is also called a fruit of śrāmaṇya,
because it is mixed with that obtained by the noble ones, and because it is maintained by untainted acquisition.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, it is universally established that the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is subsumed within the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

When two fruits are attained, the analytical cessations obtained through various mundane paths (laukika-mārga) are very few in substance and number; they are unified with the analytical cessations obtained through numerous noble paths (ārya-mārga) by means of a single acquisition (prāpti). Therefore, in this context, the few follow the many, and both are collectively designated as the essence of the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

This means that when the two fruits are attained via the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), these fruits do not have as their nature of abandonment (*prahāṇaphala*) solely the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) obtained by the mundane path; rather, they also incorporate the analytical cessation obtained by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which intermingles with it to collectively constitute a single fruit, because both are acquired through the attainment of a single fruit-path.
Accordingly, this sutra states:
"What is the fruit of once-returning?
It is the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion."
What is the fruit of non-returning?
It refers to the abandonment of the five lower fetters.

Because the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the mundane path is mixed with that obtained through the untainted path, it is called a "fruit of the śramaṇa" by taking the name of the predominant factor.

Furthermore, the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained via the mundane path is also termed the essence of the fruits of śramaṇaship because it is sustained by the acquisition of the abandonment of outflows (anāsrava-prahāṇa-prāpti); because one does not die while falling away from it due to the support of this power; and because it is sealed by the seal of the acquisition of the abandonment of outflows.
Just as an object previously marked with the seal of a king is no longer called an object that can be accumulated [by others], so too should this be understood;
therefore, it is also called the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
Other masters say:
This cessation should be considered the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), because it is a true fruit of the śramaṇa; thus, it may also be designated by the name "fruit of the śramaṇa.

Although this cessation is not the disjunction-result (*visamyoga-phala*) of that [concentration], it is its result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); therefore, there is no error in calling it its fruit.
Others further state:
Because this unconditioned state is obtained through the predominant power of the nature of a śramaṇa, it should also be called a fruit of the śramaṇa.
This is because when one abandons the afflictions by means of the mundane path, one also cultivates and refines that very nature of a śramaṇa.

Thus, it has already been explained that when one abandons what is to be abandoned through cultivation by means of the mundane path and attains two fruits, the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) thus obtained is termed a fruit of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, the fruit of śrāmaṇya is the recompense for the nature of a śramaṇa.
This nature of a śramaṇa has already been explained as before; does it also have a distinct name? It does. What is it?
The verse says:
That which is called the nature of a śramaṇa is also named a brāhmaṇa,
and is also named the Brahma-wheel, because it is turned by the true Brahmā.
Among these, only the Path of Seeing is called the Wheel of Dharma;
it is so named because its swiftness and other qualities resemble a wheel, or because it possesses spokes and other such parts.
The Treatise says:
According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), śramaṇas are distinct from brāhmaṇas, as stated in the sūtras:
"One should give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.
According to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), however, all śramaṇas are indeed brāhmaṇas, as stated in the sūtras: [that śramaṇas are identical to brāhmaṇas].
Regarding these four types of śramaṇas, from the first up to the fourth, there are no true śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas outside of the True Dharma, and so forth, as explained at length.
Because they are able to eliminate evil and unwholesome dharmas, and because their nature is extremely similar to that of diligent cessation, the essence of a śramaṇa is itself that of a brāhmaṇa.
As it is said, one who is able to dispel evil and unwholesome dharmas— and as explained at length up to the point where he is therefore called a *brāhmaṇa*—
possesses the very nature of a *brāhmaṇa*, which is also termed the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahmacakra*), because it is turned by the power of the true Brahmā King.
The Buddha is endowed with unsurpassed Brahma-qualities; therefore, the World-Honored One alone deserves to be named Brahmā.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The Buddha is also called Brahmā, also called Tranquil, and also called Cool."
Quiescent silence, profound emptiness, and utter detachment are termed "Brahma"; because the Buddha possesses these virtues, he is given the name "Brahmā.
Having attained self-awakening, he causes others to awaken as well, transmitting this realization to them; therefore, it is called the "Brahma-wheel" (brahmacakra).

Within the Brahma-wheel (*brahmacakra*), it is based solely on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that the Blessed One in certain instances refers to it as the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*). This is because when the path of seeing arose for the group of five bhikṣus, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the gods of the earth and the sky immediately proclaimed that the Blessed One had turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma.
How is it that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called a "wheel" (*cakra*)?

Because it resembles a worldly wheel through its rapid movement and other qualities: just as the wheel of a noble universal monarch (*cakravartin*) revolves without ceasing, moving swiftly, abandoning what has been taken up, subduing what has not yet been subdued, crushing what has already been subdued, and revolving upward and downward; so too is the Path of Seeing. Therefore, it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
This means that just as the wheel of a noble cakravartin king revolves incessantly, so too is the path of seeing, for there is no interruption in its midst.
Just as the wheel of a noble cakravartin king functions with great speed, so too is the path of seeing, for each consists of a single moment of thought.

Just as the wheel of a noble cakravartin king takes up what is ahead and leaves behind what is behind, so too is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); for it abandons the objects of suffering (*duḥkha*) and the like, and takes up those of origination (*samudaya*) and the like.

This demonstrates that the vision of the four noble truths (*catur-āryasatya*) necessarily does not occur simultaneously; just as the wheel of the noble cakravartin king subdues what has not yet been subdued and suppresses what has already been subdued, so too is the path of seeing: it can see what has not yet been seen and can abandon what has not yet been abandoned, because there is no rapid falling back from what has already been seen and abandoned.

Just as the wheel of a noble cakravartin king revolves upward and downward, so too is the path of seeing (darśanamārga): having contemplated the suffering and other truths of the higher realms, one then contemplates the suffering and other truths of the lower realms.
For this reason, the path of seeing alone is designated as the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:

"Just as a worldly wheel has spokes, a hub, and a rim, the Noble Eightfold Path resembles it and is therefore called a 'wheel. Specifically, right view, right intention, right effort, and right mindfulness resemble the spokes of a worldly wheel; right speech, right action, and right livelihood resemble the hub; and right concentration resembles the rim. For this reason, it is named the Wheel of Dharma."

The fundamental intention of the Vaibhāṣika masters is that all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are collectively termed the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), because they are said to be subsumed within the three turnings and the three paths.
When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises in the mental continuum of another, it has already reached the beginning of the turning; therefore, it is called "already turned."
However, since only the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the beginning of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), it is said that the Wheel of Dharma consists solely of the Path of Seeing.
The various classes of celestial beings refer to the turning of the Wheel of Dharma based on this very first stage, and not upon the other two paths.

However, most masters maintain that only the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) is called the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), because the gods of the earth and sky speak only in reference to this, because it has never been taught that all three paths are called the Wheel of Dharma, and because only the Path of Seeing possesses the characteristics of a wheel as previously described.

Although all paths of vision (darśanamārga) are termed the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), because it was first turned within the person of Kauṇḍinya, the Sūtra states that when his path of vision arose, it was called "turning the wheel of dharma"; it is not that others did not turn it.

When Kauṇḍinya and others were said to have "set the wheel of Dharma in motion" at the moment the Path of Seeing arose, the intention was to show that they obtained the turning of the wheel of Dharma primarily through the Blessed One; thus, the credit was attributed to the Buddha so as to inspire reverence in those to be converted.
In this way, it is precisely the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma that is spoken of.
It is called "turning" because it is turned so as to reach another body.
If it were otherwise, the devas should have said that the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma beneath the Bodhi tree; they should not have proclaimed:
The World-Honored One is now in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
therefore, it is transmitted to others, and in this context, it is called "turning.
Some say that this teaching is called the "wheel of Dharma" because it is turned into the bodies of others to cause them to understand its meaning.
This is merely a provisional means and not the true Wheel of Dharma, because it lacks the superior capacity found in other [teachings] that are free from defilement.
Herein, we shall reflect upon and explain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Which fruit of śrāmaṇya is attained in which realm?
The verse says:

Three rely on the desire realm; the latter three do not, because the path of vision does not exist above, there is no hearing [of the Dharma] there, and they do not take the lower realms as objects, due to a lack of revulsion and according to the sūtras.
The treatise states:

The first three fruits are attained only by means of a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas the final fruit of Arhatship is attained by means of a body belonging to any of the three realms.
Since the first two fruits have not yet abandoned desire, it is logically plausible that they cannot be attained based on a higher realm.
Third, why is it not obtained by depending on a higher [stage]?
Because even one who has already abandoned desire can obtain it;
this is established by both reasoning and scripture.
Furthermore, what is the reasoning?
Because the path of seeing does not exist based on a body belonging to the higher realms, one cannot bypass the path of seeing.
For those who have already abandoned desire, there can be the sense of "leaping over" to realize the fruit of non-returner.
For what reason does the body in the higher realms necessarily not give rise to the Path of Seeing?
First, because in the formless realm there is no opportunity to hear the teaching on non-self;
and apart from hearing this teaching, there is certainly no possibility of entering the Path of Seeing.

Furthermore, because those born in that realm do not take the lower realms as an object, and because the Path of Seeing first takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object, the formless realm is therefore not a basis for the Path of Seeing.
Since there is no superior sense of revulsion toward the body in the form realm, one cannot enter the Path of Seeing without such superior revulsion.
This means that within the desire realm there are various painful sensations; even to produce a small amount of pleasure, one must rely heavily on arduous toil.

Furthermore, among humans and devas, the lifespan is short, wealth is lacking, illnesses are many, and one is separated from kinsmen and friends. Since such adverse conditions are numerous, the mind of renunciation increases in strength.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is the opposite of this.

That is to say, those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) therein indulge in the bliss of superior meditative concentration; they possess long life, freedom from illness, lack of poverty, and absence of separation [from loved ones]. Since such adverse conditions do not exist, their minds of renunciation are faint and weak.
It is not that a weak or inferior form of revulsion can enter the path of seeing or induce the path of seeing;
because a superior form of revulsion is absent, the path of seeing does not arise based on a body in the form realm.
One should not say that they lack revulsion altogether, for those born there do indeed possess revulsion.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Do not fear, O Great Sage!
It is impossible that those flames will come near here; having burned the Brahma palace, they shall be extinguished there."
In this context, the word "fear" (*bhaya*) refers exclusively to the essence of revulsion (*nirveda*).
Furthermore, in another place, there is a verse (*gāthā*) which says:
"Hearing that the long-lived gods possess exquisite forms and renown,"
"And with a mind harboring fear and aversion, like a deer facing a lion.
This expression "fear and aversion" indicates that fear is itself aversion.

As for the actual distinction between the characteristics of fear (*bhaya*) and aversion (*arati*): when one beholds an object and dreads it as a source of loss or harm, such that the mind becomes startled and timid, this is called fear.
If, upon observing those signs, the mind does not feel delight or desire, and one takes pleasure in relinquishing them, it is called "aversion" (*nirveda*).
This exists in its entirety within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), while in the higher realms it exists only as a single factor.
Furthermore, what is the distinction between the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these two?
Fear (*bhaya*) is defined as a state of mental agitation preceded by a lack of investigation;
aversion (*nirveda*) is defined as a lack of mental delight preceded by investigation.
Alternatively, fear refers to a state of mental timidity induced by delusion (*moha*), while aversion refers to a turning away induced by the intention of renunciation (*prahāṇa*).
Other masters say:
Fearing that it will cause one’s own mind to suffer decline, one desires to diminish or abandon it; this is called fear (*bhaya*).
Because one desires to diminish or abandon it, the mind does not give rise to delight toward that object; this is called aversion (*nirveda*).
In this sutra, the word "fear" (*bhaya*) has the sense of "dread of destruction," as when it is said, "Do not fear its breaking when it is thrown.
By this reasoning, it is proven that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) does not exist in the higher realms.
Furthermore, what does the scriptural teaching say?
This is because it is stated in the sūtras. The sūtra says:

"There are five types of persons who attain realization here and reach finality there; namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin), up to those who flow upwards (ūrdhvasrotas)."
This term "penetration" (prativedha) refers exclusively to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), as it is the initial application for realizing parinirvāṇa.
Since the Sūtra does not state that penetration occurs at those [higher] stages, we know that penetration definitely does not exist on the Path of Meditation (bhāvanāmārga).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā-nāma* (The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Meaning of the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Fascicle Thirty-two.

Chapter Seven: Distinguishing the Noble Ones (5). It has already been explained that there are many distinctions among those in training, such as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and so forth; are there likewise various distinct characteristics for Arhats?
There are also [cases where it is]. How so?
The verse says:
There are six types of arhats, ranging from the one subject to regression to the immovable.
The first five arise from the stage of "faith-understanding" (śraddhādhimukta) and are collectively termed "liberated by occasion" (samayavimukta).
The latter arises from the stage of "vision-attainment" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and is termed "not liberated by occasion" (asamayavimukta).
The treatise states:
In the sūtras, it is taught that there are six types of Arhats who abide in their respective lineages (*gotra*) due to differences in their spiritual dispositions:

first, those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*); second, those of the nature of reflecting (*cetayitadharman*); third, those of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*); fourth, those of the nature of abiding securely (*sthitākampyadharman*); fifth, those of the nature of being capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*); and sixth, those of the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).

However, other sūtras state that there are nine types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), namely: first, the one liable to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*); and last, the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
Among these, the "one not liable to fall away" (*aparihāṇadharman*) is subsumed under the "immovable" (*akopyadharman*) here;
and those two types of liberation are subsumed within these six [categories] here. Therefore, the Abhidharma speaks of only six types.

Regarding those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*): it means that they have acquired such faculties (*indriya*) and abide in these faculties; when they encounter conditions for falling away, they fall from what has been attained, whereas in the absence of conditions for falling away, they enter parinirvāṇa.

There are those who, through diligent application, have attained a superior nature, yet frequently regress when encountering conditions; therefore, they are called "those subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*).

As for "those who contemplate their own destruction" (*cetana-dharman*), this refers to those who have acquired such faculties and abide in them, whose power of mindfulness is firm, and who dwell much in contemplation of revulsion. Fearing they might lose their superior qualities, they exert themselves to rouse their own minds and frequently contemplate their own destruction; thus, they are called "those who contemplate their own destruction."

Regarding those who "guard the Dharma": this refers to a certain class of individuals who constantly maintain mindfulness directed toward the present within the liberation of mind through love; because they dwell with diligent protection and heedfulness, they are called "guardians of the Dharma."

One who abides in the state of stability (sthita-ka) is so called because, having been free from the conditions for falling back, they are able not to fall back even without guarding themselves; furthermore, though they lack superior application and do not refine their faculties, they dwell frequently in a state of intermediate [faculties], and are therefore named "abiding."

One capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*) refers to one whose nature is capable and who delights in training the faculties (*indriya*), thereby swiftly reaching the immovable state (*akopyadharman*) and being able to personally realize the benefit; thus, they are called "capable of penetration.

One of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) refers to a certain class of individuals whose faculty-nature is preeminent and whose resolve is not timid; even when encountering superior conditions for decline, the merits they have attained will certainly not regress; thus, they are called "immovable."
Others further explain:

these six distinct characteristics refer to the six types of lineages (*gotra*). Among them, the first two during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) lack both constant application and intensive application; however, upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), those of the "thought-dharma" (*cintā-dharman*) possess only slight effort, while those of the "protection-dharma" (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*) possess only constant application, and those of the "staying-dharma" (*sthitākampya*) possess only intensive application. Those of the "capable-of-reaching" (*prativedhanādharman*) possess both [applications] but are of dull faculties, whereas those of the "immovable" (*akopyadharman*) possess both and are of sharp faculties.
Some say: "One of the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharman) will necessarily fall back, and so on, up to one capable of reaching the immovable (prativedhanādharman) who will necessarily reach it.
If it were not so, the establishment of these names would be in vain."

They maintain that the desire realm possesses all six [types of faculties], whereas in the form and formless realms there are only the stable and the immovable; because those [higher realms] lack retrogression, self-harm, self-protection, and the cultivation of the faculties, they possess only two.

In reality, there is no fixed certainty regarding the regression of those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship; they regress only from their previously established lineage. This continues until one attains the state of the Immovable (akopya), which is defined solely by its capacity for penetration. Thus, the designations such as "regressing" are established based on what is possible. Consequently, all six types of Arhats exist throughout the three realms.

Among these six, the first five arise from liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); they are collectively termed "those liberated by love at all times" (*samayavimukta*), because they are liberated by love at all times.
They are also called "timely liberators" (*samayavimukta*) because they attain liberation only when there is a convergence of time, place, persons (*pudgala*), and requisites.
Because the functional capacity of the basis is weak and inferior, one must wait for a superior time before attaining liberation;
or alternatively, because all supreme meditative concentrations require a superior time prior to their manifestation, this is the meaning of "time."
Because it is free from fetters, it is called "liberation" (*vimukti*).
This refers to both the sense of "waiting for time" and "liberation"; the first term is omitted for brevity, as in the expression "butter-jar.
The immovable nature of reality is called the latter; this is termed the "immovable liberation of mind," because that liberation of mind cannot be moved by afflictions.
It is also called "liberation at any time" (*asamaya-vimukti*), because liberation is attained without depending on a specific time.

Alternatively, because the supreme concentration arises at any place, at any time, in response to any encountered condition, and according to one's desire, thereby being free from fetters, it is called "liberation."
This refers to the meaning of not depending on time and [not being subject to] liberation.
Other commentators explain the distinction between these two as follows:
one is called "liberation by time" (*samayavimukta*) because one attains liberation for a temporary duration and may subsequently fall away from it.

Because they have attained ultimate liberation, they are called "those liberated at any time" (asamayavimukta); since there is no possibility of falling back from this state, they arise from the nature of the "attained-through-insight" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) stage of the preceding level.
Regarding the lineages (gotra) of the six types of arhats thus explained, do they exist from the outset, or are they acquired only later?
It is not fixed. Why is this so?
The verse says:
Some possess this from their original lineage; some acquire it later through the refinement of the faculties.
The commentary says:

The lineage of the "one liable to fall away" (parihāṇadharman) must necessarily exist from the outset; however, the other five lineages, such as the "one who contemplates" (cetanādharman), may also be acquired later.

That is to say, there may be one who has been of the "contemplating" lineage from the beginning, up to one who was originally of the "liable to fall away" lineage but subsequently becomes "immovable" (akopyadharman) through the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra). One should reflect according to reason upon these various distinctions.
Among these six types of arhats, only the first five are subject to the possibility of falling away. From what do they fall, and by what means?
Is it from their nature (*prakṛti*) or from their fruit (*phala*)?
The verse says:
Fourth, there is falling away from the lineage; fifth, there is falling away from the fruit, but not from what was prior.
The Commentary says:
Since there is necessarily no principle for falling away from the immovable lineage, only the first five may involve the possibility of falling away.

Among these, the latter four possess the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), whereas the first type, that of the one liable to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*), does not possess the principle of such a nature, because this lineage occupies the very lowest position.

All five types possess the principle of falling away from the fruit; yet although all are subject to falling away, they are not all alike in their prior state. That is to say, within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), those of the lineage liable to fall away may cultivate the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) and transform into the lineage of the "thoughtful" (*cetana-dharman*) and so forth. These four [subsequent lineages] all possess the sense of being fruits that can be lost through falling away.

Although those of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage must necessarily have attained [the fruit] first, they are nonetheless of a nature subject to regression; thus, it is possible for them to fall away from the fruit.

Among all those in the stages of training (*śaikṣa*), when one cultivates the practice of refining the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) starting from the *parihāṇadharman* lineage and transforms it into the *cetana-dharman* lineage or others, as well as upon attaining the fruits of training, there is always the possibility of falling away.

Regarding those who are in the stage of no-more-learning, the spiritual lineage (gotra) in which they resided during their previous stage of learning cannot possibly be lost from that state, because it has been rendered firm by the paths of both learning and no-more-learning.

Regarding those in training who previously resided in the lineage during their stage as ordinary persons, there is likewise no possibility of falling away from that lineage, because it has been rendered firm by the mundane and supramundane paths.

In the two former stages, one who abides in the nature of *cetanā* (volition) and so forth necessarily does not undergo retrogression; this is because the fruit thus attained and that very nature are both firmly established by the two paths.

When such a person transforms from the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya*) through *cetanā* and so forth to attain the nature of *anurakṣaṇīya* (to be guarded), although they may retrogress from the nature thus transformed and attained, there is still the possibility of retrogression even when advancing to attain the fruit of a learner (*śaikṣa*), because this lineage is not formed by the two paths and is therefore not firm.

If one explains the meaning of "retrogression from the fruits" in terms of the four fruits, although all five lineages are capable of retrogressing from a fruit, that which was previously attained is necessarily never lost.

That is to say, among the four fruits, whichever was previously attained—namely, any one of the first three, such as stream-entry—is such that there is no possibility of retrogressing from that prior fruit; this is because it is a fruit obtained by abandoning the afflictions of the path of seeing, and because a noble one who has abandoned the afflictions of the path of seeing necessarily does not retrogress.
For what reason is there no falling back from the noble ones' abandonment of the afflictions of insight?
It is because those [afflictions] do not take the objects of grasping as their objective support.

That is to say, the manifestation of afflictions abandoned through insight never occurs without the power of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), for those afflictions arise with the view of self as their root.
Because of this, the delusions of view do not take that which is grasped as their object, since the entities thus grasped are entirely without substantial reality.

Nevertheless, because they do have the truths (*satya*) as their objective referents (*ālambana*), those grasped entities lack any seeds whatsoever; for they are utterly contrary to the objective referents [of the truths]. Furthermore, because the noble ones’ mental continuums are constantly accompanied by the realization of true selflessness, even if they momentarily lose mindfulness, there is no possibility for them to again grasp at a self. Since the delusions abandoned through vision arise based on the entity of a self, once the noble ones have severed them, there is necessarily no possibility of regression.

Although the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise in a distorted manner, they do not occur without seeds or without an object of grasping. That is to say, when they arise with the aspects of attachment, aversion, pride, or lack of understanding toward form (*rūpa*) and so forth, there is not a lack of some degree of purity, excellence, hostility, superiority, inferiority, or profundity within those forms; therefore, they do not arise in total contradiction with the objects themselves.

For this reason, although noble ones may at times lose mindfulness and give rise to afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation by grasping at signs such as purity and excellence, they do not regress in their vision regarding the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing.

This is because these latter afflictions are delusions concerning the principles of the truths—such as grasping at a self and so forth—which do not exist within those truths; since the principle is fixed and reliable, the noble one’s vision does not regress.

The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation arise from delusion regarding coarse objects; as these objects undergo transformation, they become difficult to rely upon, leading to lapses in mindfulness and regression.
Furthermore, the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing must arise from deliberation; when a noble one deliberates, such afflictions necessarily do not arise.
The afflictions abandoned through cultivation do not arise from deliberate reflection; thus, there is the possibility of regression when a noble one loses mindfulness.
For this reason, there is no regression from a fruit previously attained.
Within this context, there are three types of those who regress from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*):
First, those who advance their faculties; second, those who remain in the state of training after falling back; third, those who enter parinirvāṇa while abiding in their own stage.

There are four types of those who contemplate the Dharma (*cintāmayī*): three are as previously described, with the addition of one type—those who fall back and abide in a nature subject to falling back.
The remaining three [faculties] possess five, six, and seven [types of abandonment] respectively; this should be understood because each subsequent one increases by one.

For what reason do those who have refined their faculties through the faculty of reflection (*cetanā*) and so forth, when they fall back from that fruit of arhatship and abide in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), abide in their former nature of falling back rather than in a nature that is not subject to falling back?
Because the paths of volition and so forth that were attained have now been relinquished.

Is it not the case that when one transforms into the paths of volition and so forth during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), although one relinquishes what was attained at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), one nevertheless abides in the fruit of arhatship while possessing those paths of volition and so forth belonging to the stage of training?
The same should apply to the lineages of volition (*cetanā*) and so forth.

This example is not analogous, because that path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) subsumes the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) as its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). It is not possible for the volition and so forth abandoned at the stage of non-training to serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for this path of training, thereby inducing the lineage of volition and so forth belonging to the path of training; therefore, one must necessarily regress to and abide in what was previously abandoned.

Others have established a separate proof for this, stating: "If one were to regress and then abide [in a higher state], having attained a superior lineage from the lineage from which one regressed, it would therefore be an advancement rather than a regression."
This is not a valid logical reason (*sādhana*), for if the two meanings were absent, there would be the fallacy of advancing where there is no regression.
Nevertheless, although the attainment of a superior nature may be termed "advancing," it is also termed "regressing" because of the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, that objection is logically untenable.

Furthermore, such a person would give rise to factors that obstruct nirvāṇa; since the noble ones value nirvāṇa more than the noble path itself, even if they were to attain a superior nature, because they would still regress from nirvāṇa, they should only be called "regressive" and not "progressive."

Furthermore, for what reason do all Arhats, having equally abandoned the defilements of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and likewise not undergo further rebirth, yet among them some realize the state of non-arising regarding the afflictions while others do not?
Some say that this distinction arises from differences in the faculties (*indriya*);
however, this explanation is irrational, because the Sūtra states that those subject to regression and those not subject to regression are identical in their category of faculties (*indriya-varga*).
As it is said, one is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) because the five faculties are superior, sharp, and perfectly fulfilled;

however, there are those liberated in both ways who, because they belong to a nature subject to regression, do not realize the non-arising of afflictions due to a lack of excellence in their faculties.
If that is so, by what kind of gender are these six lineages (gotra) exclusively possessed by those in the state of fruition (phalastha),
or are they also found elsewhere?
The cultivation and refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) occurs only in the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), though it may also occur in other stages.
The verse says:
Learners and ordinary beings also have six; the refinement of faculties does not occur during the path of seeing.
The commentary says:
The lineages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise six, because the six types of fruition (*phala*) are preceded by them.
Due to the distinctions among the lineages in which one abides, there is the subsequent arising or non-arising of the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
At what time is the non-arising of the abandoned afflictions realized?
It is at the time one attains the superior path capable of suppressing these types of afflictions.
If that is so, this non-arising must be cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), not cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If it were non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), then non-analytical cessation would have to be the fruit of the Path; this would contradict the sacred teaching.
As it is said: "What are the dharmas that are not fruits?"
This refers to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*).

There is no fault of failing to produce analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because the superior path arises for other purposes and not for this one; since it is not that which is to be accomplished, it is not the fruit of the path.

Now, examining this in detail: the non-arising realized through the Path is certainly not obtained by means of the faculties, for if it were, everyone would necessarily attain it. Rather, it is obtained solely through the power of a distinguished spiritual lineage (*gotra*); therefore, for one who is immovable, afflictions will necessarily not arise.

It is not only those beyond training (aśaikṣa) who possess the capacity for the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra); those still in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) also have this quality.
However, only those outside the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) can cultivate the refinement of faculties, because within that stage there is no possibility of initiating preparatory effort (prayoga).
This means that because the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) proceeds with such rapid momentum, there is no leisure therein to further cultivate other matters.

Only during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who abides in faith and understanding (adhimukti) can one cultivate the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) as is done at the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is as stated regarding the case where an immovable [arhat] falls away from the bliss of the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra).
How can it be that there is also the sense of falling away (parihāṇi) admitted for those of immovable dharma (akopyadharman)?
There is no fault of contradiction. Why is this so?
The verse says:
One should know that there are three kinds of falling away: from what has been attained, from what has not yet been attained, and from enjoyment.
The Buddha possesses only the last; those of sharp faculties possess the middle and the last, while those of dull faculties possess all three.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that there are, in total, three kinds of retrogression:
first, retrogression from what has already been attained (*prāpti-hāni*), which refers to falling away from the superior qualities already acquired;
Second is retrogression from non-attainment, which means being unable to attain the meritorious qualities that ought to be attained;
third is retrogression from enjoyment, which means that the various already-attained, preeminent meritorious qualities do not manifest before one.
Among these three types of decline, the first two have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as their essence, while the third consists solely in the non-manifestation of those qualities.

Among these three forms of decline, the Blessed One possesses only the decline of enjoyment (*upabhogaparihāṇi*); because his mind is drawn toward his certain duties and activities, he lacks the leisure to give rise to the other immeasurable and uncommon Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), even though they exist.

With the exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, those of immovable dharma possess both non-attainment and enjoyment decline. This means that because they have not yet attained superior qualities such as the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) which they ought to attain, there is non-attainment decline;
and because their minds are distracted by other activities so that they lack the leisure to give rise to already attained qualities, there is enjoyment decline.
The other five types of lineage may possess all three [kinds of retrogression], as they are also susceptible to losing qualities already attained.

Regarding the *akopyadharman* (unshakable dharma), it is explained in terms of retrogression from enjoyment; thus, there is no contradiction in its retrogressing from the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Since it is admitted that Arhats may fall back from their fruit, will they be born again?
Since they pass away while still possessing afflictions during the state of retrogression, they ought to undergo further birth.
Furthermore, regarding those actions not performed while abiding in the fruit—does one perform them upon falling back?
Since he has already given rise to delusion, there ought to be further occurrences that contradict the nature of the fruit.
There is no such fault. Why is this?
The verse says:
All who fall away from fruition will certainly not die before they have regained it;
they do not perform what is incompatible with their state of fruition, for their sense of shame has increased and thus they do not act [unwholesomely].
The treatise says:
There is no falling away from the fruit followed by death in the interim, because once one has fallen away, they will necessarily regain it in an instant.
Furthermore, for those whose lifespan is about to end, there is no possibility of falling away, as they lack the loss of mindfulness.
There is the principle of falling away only when a remainder of life-span exists; once fallen away, one will certainly realize [the goal] again before long.
As the Sūtra says:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that such well-learned noble disciples may slowly lose right mindfulness, yet they quickly regain it, causing what has fallen away to be exhausted, subsided, extinguished, and departed."
If one were to say this is not so, then the fruit of practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) would not be a state of security that can be relied upon.
Furthermore, one who abides in the stage of fruition would not engage in actions contrary to that fruition, because their sense of shame (hrī) has increased.
Although afflictions may manifest due to a temporary lapse in mindfulness, there is no possibility that they would act as they do when abiding in the fruit [of the path].
This is like a person of noble lineage who, even when temporarily deprived of their rank, does not perform base or vulgar deeds equal to those of commoners.
Furthermore, who is subject to regression and who is not?

One who enters the Noble Path by practicing the contemplation of impurity may experience regression; one who enters the Noble Path by practicing mindfulness of breathing will certainly be free from regression.
When respect for śamatha and vipaśyanā increases without greed or delusion, one should understand accordingly that there is either falling back or no falling back.
In which realm and which destiny is falling back possible?
It occurs only among humans of the desire realm, specifically in the three continents.

Regarding those who attain the fruits of sainthood within the six heavens of the desire realm, some say that because they possess sharp faculties, there is no falling away; for they have superior wisdom capable of subduing the mind, causing it to turn away from exquisite objects and enter the noble path.
Some say that falling back occurs due to a lack of necessary conditions or because the physical basis (the body) is unbalanced.

In the abodes of the six heavens of the desire realm, neither of these two factors exists; therefore, although there are those of dull faculties who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), even if they attain the state of an *ārya* there, there is no possibility of falling back.

Regarding those who undergo retrogression, does it occur because they give rise to afflictions and thereby regress, or does it occur because they have already regressed first and the afflictions subsequently manifest?
If one maintains that retrogression occurs due to the arising of afflictions, how would one reconcile this with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?

As that treatise states: "The latent tendency of sensual desire arises from three conditions: first, because the latent tendency of sensual desire has not been abandoned or fully understood; second, because the phenomena conducive to its entanglement are currently present; and third, because improper mental attention directed toward them is arising. This is explained at length.
There is no contradiction. Why is this so?

Because there are briefly two types of manifest afflictions—those already abandoned and those not yet abandoned—and because of this distinction, what is discussed here refers specifically to those that arise when they have not been abandoned.

Furthermore, there are briefly two gateways for the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*), as they arise immediately following both defiled and non-defiled minds; herein, the discussion focuses specifically on those that arise immediately following a defiled mind.

Alternatively, there are generally three conditions for the arising of afflictions, yet the factors upon which their production depends are not fixed: some arise solely through the power of the object (*ālambana*), some depend on the object and its cause, and some additionally require the application of effort (*prayoga*). This statement of "three" refers to cases where all [conditions] are present.

When an affliction arises, these three conditions must necessarily be present: improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) must manifest before one, and the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned must necessarily re-emerge.
From which state of mind does one arise and fall back into affliction?

Furthermore, regarding one who falls away from the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) by giving rise to afflictions: if they fall away by giving rise to the fetters of the form realm or the formless realm, it occurs only immediately after a wholesome mind associated with the dhyāna of the regressive type belonging to their own level; it does not occur while dwelling in the desire realm with an unobscured-neutral mind subsumed under a higher level manifesting before them.
This excludes only the fruition-attaining mind (*abhisamaya-phala-citta*), yet there is no falling away from that state.

Is it not the case that the *anuloma-vairāgya-bhāga* (the part conducive to falling away) is abandoned at the time of detachment from the defilements of its own stage? If so, how can the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) manifest when they have not fallen away and have not yet given rise to afflictions?
The principle is indeed thus.
