However, there are three categories within the stage conducive to maintenance (*sthity-anuloma*): first, slightly conducive to decline; second, slightly conducive to progress; and third, maintaining its own position.

When it was previously stated that the concentration of one's own level conducive to decline refers to that which is slightly conducive to decline within the stage conducive to maintenance, it is because it is slightly conducive to decline that it receives the name "conducive to decline."
However, because this concentrated mind largely overlaps with that which maintains its own state, it is subsumed under the "part conducive to maintenance" (*sthity-anuloma-bhāgīya*).

For those who have not yet lost the "part conducive to decline" (*hāny-anuloma-bhāgīya*), afflictions manifest immediately after that mind; if one abandons that mind, it is then subsumed under the "part conducive to maintenance."
Regarding those who regress due to minor compliance, they regress because of the arising of afflictions; thus, there is no contradiction with the literal meaning of the text.

If one regresses by giving rise to the fetters of desire (*kāma-kaṣāya*), then from either of the two minds of one's own stage—the wholesome or the non-obscured neutral—either may immediately manifest.

Regarding those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) who fall away due to the arising of afflictions: when they fall away through the arising of afflictions of the form or formless realms, if they have previously completely abandoned the defilements of that level, then [the mind] arises immediately after only a wholesome mind associated with the *anuloma-pratyāgama-dhyāna* (the meditative absorption conducive to falling back) of that level;
if they have not yet completely abandoned the defilements of that level, then both wholesome and afflicted minds subsumed under that level may manifest immediately after one another.

Regarding those who fall away by giving rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm: if they have previously completely detached from the defilements bound to the desire realm, then immediately after either of the two minds belonging to their own level—the wholesome or the non-obscured-neutral—either may manifest.

If they have not yet completely detached from the defilements of the desire realm, then immediately after any of the three minds belonging to the desire realm—the wholesome, the defiled, or the non-obscured-neutral—any of them may manifest.

If one has not yet attained pure meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), it is impossible for them to lose what they have attained through the arising of fetters belonging to the realms of form or the formless; because those afflictions arise immediately from those states, they can only lose what they have attained through the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If one has attained pure dhyāna in the present but has not yet attained pure formless attainments (ārūpya) in the present, it is impossible for one to fall away by giving rise to the fetters of the formless realm; rather, one may fall away from what has been attained by giving rise to the fetters of the desire or form realms.

If one has already attained pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or formless absorption (*ārūpya*), and through the arising of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to the desire, form, or formless realms, loses what was attained—whenever such a loss of previously attained states occurs:
if one gives rise to a higher-level fetter and falls away from the present state, one does not lose the lower wholesome states nor does one produce the lower afflictions;
if one gives rise to a lower-level fetter and falls away from the present state, one certainly loses the higher wholesome states and certainly produces the higher afflictions.

Furthermore, if one were to claim that one must first fall away [from the fruit] before the afflictions manifest in relation to their objects at a later time, how would the *Prajñaptipāda-śāstra* explain it?
As that treatise states:
"When each of the three entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the formless realm manifests, one falls from the exhaustion of the formless realm and abides within the exhaustion of the form realm."
How, furthermore, is the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* explained?
As that treatise states:

"When a defiled mind associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) manifests, one abandons the wholesome mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and reconnects with the wholesome mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*); one falls away from the mind of one beyond training and abides in the mind of one in training."
These two are not mutually contradictory, as they are spoken of in reference to the state of awakening.

That is to say, although one has previously fallen back, this was not yet recognized; it is only at the time when afflictions subsequently arise that one realizes for oneself that one has fallen back.

For example, if one previously recited the four Āgamas and, having neglected them for a long time, forgot them without realizing it, only upon attempting to recite them later does one realize they have been forgotten.
This case should be understood in the same way; therefore, there is no contradiction or error.
Abiding in what kind of mind does one fall away and subsequently give rise to afflictions?

Abiding in the unobscured-neutral minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), or maturation (*vipākaja*) within the desire realm, one is only able to give rise to afflictions after having fallen away from that state.

However, regarding this unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm, there may be cases where it is entirely opposed to the afflictions of all three realms; when this mind is actually arising, there is no possibility of regressing and thereby acquiring the afflictions of the three realms.

There may be cases where one merely opposes the afflictions of the desire and form realms; when this mind is currently arising, it is possible that there is the sense of regressing from the attainment of the afflictions of the formless realm.

There may also be cases where one merely opposes the afflictions of the desire realm; when this mind is currently arising, it is possible that there is the sense of regressing from the attainment of the afflictions of all three realms.

Alternatively, there may be cases where this mind arises without contradicting the afflictions of the three realms; in such instances, it is possible for one to regress and lose the attainment regarding the delusions of the three realms.
Once all [attainments] have been lost, the preceding minds that give rise to the respective delusions follow the same principle as explained above.
Between these two explanations, the former is superior.

Regarding what was stated above concerning the attainment through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one should now investigate: how many paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and how many paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are there for the various noble ones who refine their faculties?
Is it by means of the contaminated path that one attains the uncontaminated?
Upon what body and in what stage does this rely?
The verse says:

In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) consists of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Because it has been practiced for a long time, that of the learner (*śaikṣa*) consists of only one. The untainted (*anāsrava*) [refinement] relies on three types of persons;
the no-more-learner relies on nine stages (*bhūmi*), while the learner relies only on six.
One abandons the path of the fruit and the path of the superior fruit, because one attains only the path of the fruit.
The commentary states:

For one who seeks a superior spiritual lineage and cultivates the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), when transitioning from each respective lineage within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for each, just as in the attainment of the fruit of arhatship.

Why is this? Because that dull faculty has been habituated for a long time; it cannot be transformed by a small amount of effort, as it is made firm by the paths of both training and no-more-training.

In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), when transforming from one nature to another, there is respectively one path of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as in the attainment of the first fruit; this is because these are not long-practiced.
For each of those stages of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), there is likewise one of each.

When those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) or the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivate the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra), they all gradually cultivate each subsequent lineage (gotra), attaining a superior lineage before abandoning the preceding inferior one.

Therefore, when various non-learners (aśaikṣas) cultivate the refinement of the faculties, the preparatory effort (prayoga), the immediate concentration (ānantarya), and the first eight liberations (vimokṣa) are, as appropriate, all subsumed under the category of "those subject to falling away" (parihāṇadharman); the ninth liberation is subsumed under the category of "those who reflect" (cetayitṛdharman).

When those in training (śaikṣa) cultivate the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra), the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga) and the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) are subsumed under "regression" and so forth; at the time of the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), it is termed "the cognition of thought" (cittajñāna) and so on.

All the great masters from whom I have received instruction unanimously state that the refinement of the faculties is entirely for the purpose of obstructing and dispelling the manifestation of non-obscured, non-defined (anivṛtāvyākṛta) ignorance (ajñāna) induced by the power of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation (darśana-bhāvanā-heya).
Therefore, the cultivation of the faculties (indriya) during the stage of training (śaikṣa) is primarily intended to eliminate that which is produced by the afflictions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa);
the cultivation of the faculties during the stage of no-more-training (aśaikṣa) is primarily intended to eliminate that which is produced by the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanā-kleśa).

Just as there are a certain number of uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths produced when those afflictions that give rise to it are severed, so too is the number of present paths of conduct that sever the ignorance produced by them.

Therefore, when one beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivates the faculties (*indriya*), nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are employed;
for one in training (*śaikṣa*), each of the two paths [of transformation] requires one [set].

However, because the ignorance produced by the afflictions of seeing and cultivation varies in its many categories according to the specific obstacles they present, when one transforms from the state of regression (*parihāṇa*) and so forth into the state of reflection (*cetanā*) and so forth, various paths manifest, each having its own specific object to be eliminated. Consequently, there is no such thing as "leaping over" to attain a superior nature.
Other masters say that all refinement of the faculties consists of a single application, followed by an uninterrupted path and a path of liberation.
The former explanation is superior, for the reasoning is as previously stated.

Thus, both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are comprised exclusively of the untainted (*anāsrava*) nature. It is logically impossible for a noble one (*ārya*) to transform their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by means of a tainted path, because the essence of worldly (*laukika*) phenomena lacks supremacy and functional capacity.

All preparatory applications (*prayoga*) pertain to both types [the contaminated and the uncontaminated]. What has been stated thus far refers only to those currently manifesting; however, there are further distinctions regarding their future cultivation.

Specifically, when one in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) cultivates the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*), the preparatory application in the future also pertains to the cultivation of both [types] for the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Furthermore, that which is cultivated in the future consists exclusively of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) ninth path of liberation.

In the future, one cultivates two [paths] while simultaneously cultivating all merits belonging to the three realms, because this is identical to what was cultivated during the initial *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion).

When one in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) cultivates the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) in the future also universally cultivates both the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and that which is cultivated in the future is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), just as when attaining the first fruit.

However, when one in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) cultivates the faculties (*indriya*), the number of paths cultivated is the same as that for abandoning the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

When one in the stage of learning (śaikṣa) cultivates the faculties, the number of paths cultivated is the same as that for abandoning what is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the higher realms; this is because they are merely similar to the paths at the time of attaining the neighboring fruit.

When training the faculties (indriya) during the stages of learning (śaikṣa) and no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), the preparatory applications (prayoga) pertain to both what has been previously attained and what has not; the uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) and paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) pertain only to what has not been previously attained. All of these pertain to both dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Those who cultivate the faculties (indriya) do so only as humans in the three continents, because it is only within this body that there is fear and the possibility of falling back.
For what reason is it called "cultivating the faculties"?
Because one trains and refines the faculties so that they may increase.

This means that by the power of the Path, the faculties (*indriya*) are made to continue in succession; one abandons the inferior to obtain the middling, and abandons the middling to obtain the superior. This gradual increase in excellence is called the "refining of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
Thus, the term "refining the faculties" signifies the meaning of "transforming the faculties" (*indriyaparāvṛtti*).

Although one gradually attains superior faculties through the eight liberations, because the fundamental mind seeks a state of excellence, one does not abandon the previous inferior state until that excellence is attained—just as one only abandons the prior path upon attaining the subsequent fruit.

Just as there are six lineages (*gotra*) in the noble stages (*ārya-avasthā*) that are capable of cultivating the faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*), it should be understood that the same applies to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The distinction is this: in the noble stages, if one attains a superior lineage, one necessarily abandons the previously held inferior one;

however, for those who cultivate the faculties during the stages of Heat and so forth, they merely attain the superior nature while the inferior nature ceases to function—this is called "transforming the faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra*), not the abandoning of the inferior to acquire [the superior].

The refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) relies upon all nine stages—namely, the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*)—because the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) exists only in these nine stages and not in others.
The training of the faculties by those still in training (śaikṣa) relies exclusively on six stages, excluding the three formless realms. Why is this?

Because one who transforms their faculties may relinquish either the fruit or the path of superior fruit; what is attained is only the fruit, not the path of superior fruit, because the mind delights in the fruit.

Since there is no fruit of training (*śaikṣa-phala*) included within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for those in training relies solely upon the six stages.

Even if one were to concede that a trainee might refine their faculties while relying on the formless realm, this would necessarily occur while abiding in the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣa-mārga*) as a non-returner (*anāgāmin*); however, since the fruit of non-returning itself is not included within the formless realm, one does not rely on the formless realm to cultivate the refinement of faculties and attain the fruit.
This is because the first two fruits are comprised solely within the *anāgamya* stage, whereas the fruit of non-return (*anāgāmin*) is comprised across all six stages.
Some say that the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) occurs only while abiding in the fruit, lest there be the fault of losing what has been gained and obtaining less than before.
There is no such fault, because one who refines their faculties (*indriya*) intends for a superior fruit and does not seek many [fruits].

Consequently, for one in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) who practices the refinement of faculties: if they abide in the three paths—the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), etc.—they are all subsumed under the path of the fruit (*phala-mārga*);

if they abide in the path of preparation for a superior path, they are subsumed under the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the superior fruit-path; and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is subsumed under the path of the fruit.

For those abiding in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who cultivate the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), the three paths—preparatory (*prayoga*) and so forth—are subsumed solely within the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*).

When those abiding in the stages of fruition cultivate the refinement of the faculties, they relinquish the fruition and attain a fruition while abiding in a superior path; when cultivating the refinement of the faculties, they relinquish two [paths] and attain a fruition.
Furthermore, when the various noble stages cultivate the faculties (*indriya*), they may be either the same as or different from the stage of the fruit originally attained.
That is to say, for the first two fruits, the stage upon which they rely must necessarily be the same, because both rely on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage.
The stage upon which the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) relies is not fixed; it may rely on its own original stage, or on a higher or lower one.
There is a distinction, however: if various non-returners refine their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) by relying on a lower stage, they do not attain a higher fruit;
the arhat is not like this, because he attains the fruit as originally established and has severed the fetters of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
When one sharpens the faculties (*indriya*) and attains a fruit, although one abandons those abandonments (*prahāṇa*), one does not incur those fetters (*saṃyojana*).

This is like an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in any of the seven higher stages; they abandon the abandonments of the lower stages as appropriate, yet do not incur the fetters of the lower stages, because in both cases it is a time of progress and not a time of regression.
How many types of individuals (pudgala) are there in total within the stage of those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
and by what distinctions are they differentiated?
The verse says:
Seven śrāvakas and two Buddhas—these distinctions arise from nine faculties.
The commentary states:
There are nine types of noble ones abiding in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), namely, seven śrāvakas and two awakened ones (buddhas).

The five types beginning with those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*), together with the two divisions of the immovable (*akopyadharman*), are called the seven śrāvakas because they are distinguished by their prior and subsequent [attainments].
The Pratyekabuddha and the Mahābuddha are called the two types of Awakened Ones (*buddha*).
Due to the differences in the nine grades of faculties—beginning with the lowest of the low—the noble ones beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are established as nine distinct categories.
All individuals, whether in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), are subsumed within seven categories without exception:

first, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth, those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); fifth, those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*); sixth, those liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*); and seventh, those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
On what basis are the seven established?
How many distinct entities are there?
The verse says:
The preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the faculties (*indriya*), the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and liberation (*vimokṣa*) thus constitute seven;
however, in terms of distinct entities, there are only six, because each of the three paths has two [aspects].
The treatise says:

The first two types are established based on differences in their preparatory application (*prayoga*); that is, because they are able to cultivate preparatory application toward all objects of pursuit—either by previously following the words of others through faith (*śraddhā*) or by following the Dharma for themselves—they are given the names "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) and "follower by Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).

The next two types are established based on differences in their faculties; that is, depending on whether the faculties of faith or wisdom predominate—whether dull or sharp—they are respectively named *śraddhādhimukta* (resolved through faith) and *dṛṣṭiprāpta* (attained through vision).

The name *kāyasākṣin* (body-witness) is established based on the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because one has personally realized the absorption of cessation through the body.

The latter two types are established based on differences in liberation: that is, one who is liberated from the hindrance of afflictions through wisdom alone is established as "liberated by wisdom," while one who additionally attains meditative concentration and is liberated from the hindrance to liberation is established as "doubly liberated."

Although these names are seven, the entities they designate are only six. This is because within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two types of noble persons: first, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, those who follow by the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

Upon reaching the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), these two are established with two different names: first, those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); second, those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
These [noble ones] at the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are further established with two names: namely, those liberated by time (samayavimukta) and those not liberated by time (asamayavimukta).

However, one should only say that there are two types of noble beings, because there is a distinction between those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
These two types, though established under different names according to the distinctions of the path, possess no separate essence.

Thus, the *pudgalas* described here—analyzed through various categories based on differences in faculties (*indriya*), lineage (*gotra*), paths (*mārga*), detachment from defilements (*vairāgya*), and supports (*niśraya*)—number in the thousands.
Furthermore, for example, the first type, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), becomes threefold by way of faculty (*indriya*), namely: weak, medium, and sharp;
it becomes fivefold by way of nature (*gotra*), namely: those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth;
and it becomes fifteenfold by way of the path (*mārga*), namely: the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the seven knowledges (*jñāna*).
Due to the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*), there are seventy-three types, meaning one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) abandons the defilements of the eight stages (*bhūmi*).
Due to the basis of the body (*āśraya*), there are nine types, namely the three continents and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

When these factors—the faculties (*indriya*), lineage (*gotra*), path (*mārga*), abandonment of defilements, and basis of the body—are multiplied together, they total one hundred and four million seven hundred and eighty-two thousand five hundred varieties.
One should reflect upon those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) and others as is appropriate.

There are immeasurable distinctions among such categories; if one were to analyze each one in exhaustive detail, the effort required would be immense while the practical utility would be extremely slight. Therefore, I have here briefly indicated the general direction; intelligent students should investigate and discern them extensively.
It was previously stated that the latter two types [of arhats] are established based on liberation. By what should the characteristics of these latter two types be known?
The verse says:
Both are established by attaining the meditative absorption of cessation; The others are called "liberated through wisdom."
The treatise says:

Those Arhats who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), because they are liberated from both the afflictions and the hindrance to liberation through the combined power of wisdom (*prajñā*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

The remainder, who have not yet attained the absorption of cessation, are called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*), because they attain liberation from the hindrance of afflictions through the power of wisdom alone.
What is the essence of the obstacle to liberation?
Although the minds of all Arhats are already liberated, they further seek liberation in order to liberate themselves from that obstacle.

This means that among the various liberations that are obstructed, there exists an inferior, non-cognizant, and unobscured-neutral nature capable of obstructing liberation; this constitutes the essence of the obstruction to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*).

Although one has already abandoned it without remainder at the time of attaining detachment from each respective realm and thus achieves liberation, it is only when that [nature] no longer functions that it is truly termed "liberation."
Other masters say: "The obstacle to liberation has as its essence the lack of mastery over the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Other masters say:
This obstacle to liberation has as its essence the failure to attain the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). Other masters say:

because one does not diligently seek their preparatory practices (*prayoga*), does not listen to them, and does not practice them repeatedly, liberation does not arise; this very [lack] is what is called the essence of the obstacle to liberation.
The first explanation is the reasonable one. Why is this so?
There must certainly be some slight force of dharma capable of acting as an obstacle, causing that person to lack mastery over meditative concentration.
If this were not the case, what would be the cause for their lack of mastery over the various meditative absorptions?

One who lacks mastery in concentration must have a specific cause; it cannot be said that the very cause of their lack of mastery is the lack of mastery itself, for a self-essence cannot logically take itself as its own cause.
Alternatively, one might also say that the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) should be explained as having the non-attainment of the fruit of arhatship as its nature.
Since that is not the case [for the obstacle of knowables], how could this be so?

For even the fruit of arhatship does not arise because of a lack of diligent seeking through preparatory application (*prayoga*); yet, does it follow that there is no distinct entity for the obstacle of afflictions?
Therefore, the latter three explanations are all unreasonable.

Furthermore, even the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is said to attain liberation from this [bondage], because liberation is spoken of in reference to its abiding in the body and its proceeding in the world; that is to say, it is only when one is liberated from the obstacles to liberation that the mind arises abiding in the body and proceeding in the world.
If there are Arhats who have the same names, do they also have the same faculties (*indriya*)? This should be analyzed in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the first permutation:

among those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), there are those liberated at times (*sāmaya-vimukta*) and those not liberated at times (*asāmaya-vimukta*); likewise, among those liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), there are these two types as well.
Regarding the second phrase: among those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), there are those liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*);

it is the same for those not liberated by occasion (*asamayavimukta*). Regarding the third phrase: within those liberated through wisdom, the two types of those liberated by occasion are mutually related; it is likewise for the two types of those not liberated by occasion and those liberated both ways.

Regarding the fourth phrase: within those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), there is the one liberated at times (*samayavimukta*); within those liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), there is the one not liberated at times (*asamayavimukta*).
These are to be understood in relation to one another. It should be known that the opposite cases are likewise.
As the Blessed One has said:
"One who has abandoned the five afflictions and cannot be led astray is not yet called one who has fulfilled the training.
By how many causes does each of the stages of training and beyond-training (śaikṣa and aśaikṣa) uniquely come to be designated as "fulfilled" within their respective classes?
The verse says:
One in training is called "perfected" By virtue of three factors: faculties, fruits, and meditative attainments;
One beyond training receives the name "perfected" By virtue of only two: faculties and meditative attainments.
The Treatise says:

Only those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) obtain the designation "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) by virtue of possessing three factors—namely, faculties (*indriya*), fruit (*phala*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, only the "attainer through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) are uniquely designated as "complete."
If one who lacks even a little is not yet considered a master of the training, how much less could one who lacks everything be called a master? What is meant by "lacking a little"?

It refers to those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation through faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*), or those who have reached the stage of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or non-returner (*anāgāmin*) but have not yet attained the absorption of cessation; or those who have reached the stage of vision but are not yet free from desire; or those who, being of faith-understanding or a non-returner, have not yet attained the absorption of cessation.
What is meant by "one who lacks everything"?
It refers to one who possesses faith and understanding but has not yet abandoned desire for existence; such a person is granted the designation "complete" despite having minor deficiencies.
They speak as follows:
There are those in training who receive the designation "complete" solely by virtue of their faculties; these are the *dṛṣṭiprāpta* who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.

There are those in training who receive the designation "complete" solely by virtue of their fruit; these are the *śraddhādhimukta* and *anāgāmin* who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

There are those in training who, by virtue of both their faculties and their fruit, also receive the designation "complete," namely: those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and non-returners (anāgāmin) who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

There are also those in training who, by virtue of their fruit and their meditative absorption, also receive the designation "complete," namely: those of faith-resolved (śraddhādhimukta) who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation.

There are those in training who, by virtue of all three factors, alone receive the designation "complete": namely, those who have attained the state of "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
There are also those in training who receive the designation "complete" by virtue of meditative absorption alone, as well as by virtue of both meditative absorption and faculties (indriya).
This cannot be relied upon.
How could one who is still in training (śaikṣa) be designated as "perfected" (paripūrṇa) when they have not yet fully realized the superior qualities of those in training?
Therefore, the principle stated previously is certainly what should be relied upon.
Within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there is nothing that is not the fulfillment of the fruit; therefore, the designation "fulfillment" is not established by means of the fruit.
For something to be uniquely termed "fulfilled" when compared within its own stage, it must possess two factors: namely, the faculties (*indriya*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, only those who are liberated neither by time nor simultaneously (asamayavimukta) receive the name "complete" (pūrṇa) in contrast to other arhats;
for if one lacks even one of these two qualities, they do not yet possess the status of a complete arhat, let alone how could one who lacks both be called a complete arhat?
What is meant by "lacking one"?

It refers to those who are liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) having attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or those who are not liberated by time (*asamayavimukta*) not having attained the meditative absorption of cessation.
What is meant by "lacking both"?

This refers to those who are liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) and do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Some maintain that even lacking one of these two, one may still receive the name "perfected" (arhat);
however, this cannot be relied upon, for the reasoning is as previously stated.
As stated in the sūtra:
"There are two types of arhats: first, those endowed with the three knowledges (trividyā);
second, those of non-retrogressive nature (avaivartika-dharman). Among the various fruits of arhatship mentioned previously, to which fruit do these two types of arhats belong?
Furthermore, those of the non-retrogressive nature are subsumed within the immovable; however, there are two distinctions regarding this immovability:
first, those who are only able to not retrogress from the fruit of arhatship; and second, those who do not retrogress from any of the supreme virtues.

Among these, the first is called merely "immovable" (akopya) because it is attained through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), such as by the Dhyāyins; yet, since there is still the possibility of falling away from the fruit of arhatship, it is distinguished from those [other types] and thus receives the name "immovable. Nevertheless, because one may still fall away from any of the supreme qualities of the state of fruition (*phala*), it is not called "non-retrogressive" (anivartin).
The second [stage] likewise lacks any regression from its superior qualities; therefore, the Sūtra establishes the name "non-regressive" (*avaivartika*) for it.

Since within the "immovable" (*akopya*) there may still be those who can regress from their superior merits, the Sūtra establishes the "dharma of non-regression" (*avaivartika-dharma*) within the immovable stage itself.

Regarding those who possess the three types of clear knowledge (*traividya*), some say they are included within both the "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*) and the "doubly liberated" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), because they generally have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Others say they are included only within the "doubly liberated," because the clear knowledge of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and the clear knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) rely upon the fundamental dhyānas, and one who gives rise to the fundamental dhyānas is termed "doubly liberated."

Now, examining the intent of the sutra: if the liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) and the liberation by both [wisdom and concentration] (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukti*) are fully perfected, their essential natures are distinct, because there is a vast interval between not yet having given rise to the fundamental dhyāna and having already attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Regarding those who are not perfected: since their two bodies are intermingled, either explanation applies.
However, if one wishes to distinguish them so that they are not confused, it should be explained in terms of whether the cessation-attainment has been attained or not yet attained.

Because those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), although the fundamental dhyānas do not manifest for them, they necessarily possess them in the future.
For this reason, it can be said that those who possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) are logically included within the two types of liberation.
The various distinctions among the paths are explained extensively as being immeasurable—namely, the mundane and supramundane paths, the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and so forth.
Now, one should investigate: how many paths, when briefly stated, can comprehensively encompass them all?
The verse says:
One should know that all paths, when briefly stated, are of only four kinds:
namely, the path of preparation, the uninterrupted path, the path of liberation, and the path of excellence.
The Commentary says:
The path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) refers to that which is immediately followed by the arising of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The uninterrupted path refers to that which is capable of eliminating the obstructions that ought to be abandoned.
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) refers to that which first arises once one has already been liberated from the obstacles that were to be abandoned.
The path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) refers to all paths other than the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), and the path of liberation.
In what sense is it called the "path" (*mārga*)?

It means it is the basis for seeking, because one relies upon this to seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Consequently, all cultivation of the knowledge of suffering and so forth is nothing other than the seeking of *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, this path is named the "Way to Nirvāṇa" because the noble ones of the three vehicles traverse this level road and swiftly reach the two types of nirvāṇic realms.
Elsewhere, this path is designated as the "Path of Skillful Practice" (*pratipad-kuśalā*) because it enables one to skillfully penetrate the truths and proceed swiftly toward the city of nirvāṇa.
How many kinds are there?
On what basis are they established?
The verse says:
There are four types of practice: those based on the fundamental dhyānas are pleasant, while those based on the remaining stages are painful;
these are further distinguished as slow or swift according to dull or sharp faculties.
The commentary says:

The Sūtra states that there are four types of practice leading to penetration (*pratipad*): first, the painful practice with slow progress; second, the painful practice with swift progress; third, the pleasant practice with slow progress; and fourth, the pleasant practice with swift progress.
Regarding the distinctions among these four modes of practice (*pratipad*), they are established based on differences in their respective stages (*bhūmi*) and faculties (*indriya*).
How are they established according to stage?
The noble path (*ārya-mārga*) arising within the four fundamental dhyānas is called the "easy mode of practice" (*sukhā pratipad*), because it proceeds spontaneously, like traveling by boat or raft.
"Spontaneous operation" means that in these stages, calm abiding and insight proceed together without increase or decrease.
Furthermore, all the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) belonging to these stages are established by way of encompassing five or four branches.

The noble path arising in dependence on the other formless attainments, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*) is called the "difficult practice" (*duḥkhā pratipad*). Although the path itself is not suffering, it is also termed "suffering" because it proceeds with difficulty due to its association with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*), just as traveling by horse or similar means over a land route proceeds with difficulty.

Because of this, although calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) coexist in these stages, they vary in their predominance; that is to say, in the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu), insight diminishes while calm abiding increases, whereas in the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), insight increases while calm abiding diminishes.
Furthermore, because the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) belonging to these various stages are not comprised of five or four branches (*aṅga*), other masters say:
"The path of the stage of *anāgamya* is difficult to accomplish; therefore, it is designated by the name 'suffering' (*duḥkha*)."
This refers to those who previously had not attained meditative concentration at all and must exert great effort for it to manifest.
Once this has manifested, it serves as a superior preparatory stage (*prayoga*), and because the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*) can then arise with ease, it is called "blissful" (*sukha*).

The intermediate dhyāna is subsumed under the same stage; because the cessation of one mental category and the arising of another mental category occurs with extreme difficulty, it is also called "suffering," just as, for example, splitting wood with wood is exceedingly difficult.
That is to say, within the first dhyāna, the coarse category of mind characterized by both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) ceases;
the subtle category of mind characterized by the absence of vitarka and the presence of only vicāra arises, requiring great effort.
Since the various formless attainments are likewise extremely difficult to accomplish, they are also termed "suffering" because they are exceedingly subtle.
This means that the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are so subtle as to be difficult to measure and hard to accomplish through cultivation.

Furthermore, when arising from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) into the formless realm, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) necessarily cease and the four aggregates necessarily arise; because this is extremely difficult to accomplish, it is designated by the name "suffering" (*duḥkha*).
How are the distinctions established based on the faculties (*indriya*)?
This means that within the two paths of practice—suffering and pleasure—the one with dull faculties is called "slow," while the one with sharp faculties is called "swift.
When these two modes of practice take a long time to penetrate their respective objects, it is termed "slow penetration" (*dhandhābhijñā*); the opposite is termed "swift [penetration]."
The path practiced by those who are dull-witted is called the "slow path," while the "quick" is its opposite.
Alternatively, there may be slowness or speed in the approach to nirvāṇa depending on whether the faculties are dull or sharp, as will be explained later.
This practice has the five aggregates or four aggregates as its nature, distinguished by whether it relies on the meditative concentrations of the form realm or the formless realm.
However, it is designated by the name "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) because insight is predominant.
This is just as, although the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) possesses all five aggregates, it is specifically given the name "seeing" because insight is predominant therein.

Just as the various conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) on the side of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) or four aggregates as their essence, and are thus designated by the names "knowledge" (*jñāna*) or "concentration" (*samādhi*), so too the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) takes the five or four aggregates as its essence, yet is established under the name of "concentration.

However, when certain sūtras state that the four paths of progress (*catasraḥ pratipadaḥ*) have the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as their nature, this is also stated from the perspective of what is predominant.
Because wisdom is the most excellent among excellences, it is established as the general name [for the faculty].
Although there are those of middling faculties, these are subsumed within the categories of sharp and dull, because within the sharp and dull there are degrees that are not yet ultimate.

However, what was stated previously—that based on the sharpness or dullness of the faculties, there is swiftness or slowness in approaching parinirvāṇa—was said in reference to those who practice with equal diligence in their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
If one does not rely on this equality, then the speed with which those of dull or sharp faculties proceed toward nirvana would be indeterminate.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that there are four distinct categories, such as "slow in the present life" and "quick upon the dissolution of the body," and so forth.

This is based on whether there is diligence or lack of diligence in the preparatory application (*prayoga*), and not based on the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) or falling away (*parihāṇi*).
This is because once noble ones (*ārya*) have already been born [in a certain stage], they do not fall away, do not transform their faculties, and do not take birth in a higher realm.

Regarding the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka who has reached the ultimate, by which path of practice (*pratipad*) do they enter the noble state and realize the supreme fruit?

The Greatly Awakened One relies solely upon the path of pleasant and swift progress (*sukhā pratipat kṣiprābhijñā*); that is to say, taking the fourth dhyāna as his basis, he enters into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of extremely sharp faculties and realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas, as the Great Awakened One has taught, they are fixed; others, however, are not so determined.

Among the two types of śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate, Śāriputra entered the noble state and realized the supreme fruit by means of both the path of swift progress through suffering and the path of swift progress through pleasure; he entered into right determination based on the *anāgamya* stage, and attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) based on the fourth dhyāna.

Maudgalyāyana relied solely on the path of swift progress through suffering; that is to say, he entered right determination based on the *anāgamya* stage and attained the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Both sages had previously delighted in wisdom and delight in meditative concentration, and thus they realized the ultimate fruit.

Since it is accepted that [the path] reaches its ultimate consummation based on the form and formless realms, and because it is the natural law for all great śrāvakas to attain the fruits only through gradual stages, those who enter the noble path do so entirely by relying on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* (The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Meaning of the Abhidharma-piṭaka), Fascicle Thirty-three [continued as] Fascicle Thirty-four,
composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: Distinguishing the Noble Ones and the Path. Section Six: These are also called the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
How many kinds are there?
What are their names and meanings?
The verse says:
The factors of enlightenment are thirty-seven, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
"Awakening" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising; because they accord with this, they are called "factors.
The treatise says:

The Sūtra states that there are thirty-seven factors of awakening, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

The knowledge of the exhaustion [of the outflows] and the knowledge of non-arising are designated as "awakening" (*bodhi*). According to the distinctions among those who possess this awakening, three types of awakening are established: first, the awakening of the śrāvakas; second, the awakening of the pratyekabuddhas; and third, the unsurpassed awakening. Because the sleep of ignorance has been forever severed, and because one knows according to reality that what was to be done has already been accomplished and there is nothing further to be done—these two aspects are called "awakening."
The thirty-seven factors accord with and lead toward enlightenment; therefore, they are all called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Are these thirty-seven distinct in their essential nature? No.
How so? The verse says:
These real entities are only ten, namely: wisdom, diligence, concentration, and faith;
Mindfulness, joy, equanimity, pliancy, as well as ethical discipline and investigation constitute their essence.
The Commentary says:
Although these factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) are thirty-seven in name, in actual substance there are only ten, namely: wisdom, diligence, and so forth.

That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, and right view have wisdom as their essence.
The four right endeavors, the faculty of vigor, the power of vigor, the factor of enlightenment of vigor, and right effort have diligence as their essence.

The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) have concentration as their essence.
The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*) have faith as their essence.
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the awakening factor of mindfulness, and right mindfulness have mindfulness as their essence.
The awakening factor of joy has joy as its essence.
The awakening factor of equanimity has the equanimity subsumed within the aggregate of formations as its essence.
The factor of enlightenment of pliancy has pliancy as its essence.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood have ethical discipline as their essence.
Right thought has applied thought as its essence.
Thus, regarding these factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), there are actually only ten real entities.

The first five are precisely the five faculties (*indriya*) beginning with faith; these are divided into thirty based on differences such as their objects. To these are added joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and the three divisions of morality (*śīla*) and investigation (*vitarka*). Together with the previous [five], they constitute thirty-seven types in total.

The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that there are eleven [factors], because bodily action and vocal action are distinct and thus the precepts are divided into two; the remaining nine are as previously stated.

Since the three names—mindfulness foundations (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth—do not have separate specific designations, why are they said to consist exclusively of wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*)?
The verse says:

The four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power are said to be, respectively, wisdom, diligence, and concentration; in reality, they are all wholesome states of application.
The Commentary states:

The three categories of wholesome dharmas, beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness, substantially encompass all preparatory wholesome qualities; however, they are designated as wisdom, diligence, and concentration respectively, according to their predominant wholesome roots within each corresponding category.
For what reason is the name "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) established for wisdom?
Because wisdom is maintained and made to abide by the power of mindfulness.
For what reason is diligence called "right abandonment" (samyakprahāṇa)?
In the stage of correctly practicing abandonment and cultivation, this diligence is called "right effort" (*samyakprahāṇa*) because it is capable of abandoning laziness;
or it is called "right exertion" (*samyagvyāyāma*) because it is the most excellent among the correct application and stimulation of body, speech, and mind.
For what reason is the name "basis of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*) established for meditative concentration?
Because it is the basis upon which all sublime and wondrous qualities depend.
For what reason are faith and the others established as "faculties" (*indriya*) and "powers" (*bala*)?
Because they are predominant and difficult to subdue.
For what reason are these five first called "faculties" (*indriya*) and later called "powers" (*bala*)?
It is because these five dharmas are distinguished as preceding and succeeding according to their division into lower and superior grades.

Furthermore, based on whether they can be overcome or cannot be overcome: because the power and function of inferior-grade faith and so forth are weak, they are still overcome by their counteragents and by factors of the same class; superior-grade [faith], being the opposite of this, receives the name "attaining power."
What is the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) that have been taught?
Their meaning is "that which can awaken," hence they are called factors of enlightenment.
If this were so, there would be only one factor of enlightenment.

It is not so; mindfulness and the others are factors of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*), and they are all named after their predominant quality because they accord with that investigation.
Alternatively, the meaning of "limb of awakening" (*bodhyaṅga*) is that which is a limb of awakening (*bodhi*).
If that were the case, one would have to admit that there are only six limbs of awakening.

It is not so; the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is both awakening (*bodhi*) and a limb of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), whereas the remaining six types are limbs of awakening but not awakening itself.
What is the meaning of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) that have been taught?
Seeking the basis for the meaning is called a "limb of the path" (*mārgāṅga*).
If that were so, there would be only one limb of the path.
This is not the case; the other seven are branches of right view, and they all receive their names based on their predominance in accordance with right view.
Alternatively, the meaning of "limb of the path" (*mārgāṅga*) is that it is a constituent part of the path.
If this were the case, one would have to admit that there are only seven limbs of the path.
This is not so; right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is both the path and a limb of the path, whereas the remaining seven types are limbs of the path but not the path itself.
At which stage should it be said that which factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) predominates?
The verse says:
In the stages of the beginner, the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), And the paths of cultivation and seeing.
The seven categories, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, should be understood to increase in sequence.
The treatise says:

In the stage of initial practice, it is said that the foundations of mindfulness increase; that is to say, in this stage, in order to eliminate inversions, one is able to discern clearly the specific and general characteristics of objects such as the body through the power of mindfulness. Because wisdom is predominant in its function, it destroys the two kinds of delusion.

Regarding the stage of *ūṣmagata*, it is said that the right exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*) increase; this means that within this stage, one perceives the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa, thereby being able to rouse courageous diligence and vigor, so as not to fall back into saṃsāra but to swiftly proceed toward nirvāṇa, because the application of effort is preeminent.

Regarding the stage of the "Dharma of the Summit" (*mūrdhāna-dharma*), it is said that the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) increase; this means that in this stage, one is able to master the mind and consciousness so as to advance toward the stage of non-retrogression without ever becoming deficient, because the application of the wholesome roots such as faith and the rest, as well as meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is preeminent.

Regarding the stage of the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*), it is said that the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) increase; for in this stage, one eternally ceases rebirth in the evil destinies and never again falls back, swiftly entering the state of "separation from birth" (*niyāma*), whereby the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) is established, as the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is preeminent.

It is said that the five powers (*pañca-balāni*) predominate in the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), because in this stage one is no longer overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus the meaning of "power" is preeminent.
Although such a state may also occur during the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*), it is not certain; therefore, it is not so described.
Alternatively, because one is not overcome by any other dharmas of ordinary beings within this stage, the meaning of "power" (*bala*) increases specifically in this stage.

In the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is proximate to the stage of enlightenment (*bodhi*), the factors that assist awakening (*bodhipakṣya*) are predominant; therefore, it is said that the limbs of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) increase.
Alternatively, because one repeatedly awakens to the fact that the nine grades of afflictions have been severed within this stage, the meaning of the "factors of enlightenment" (bodhyaṅga) increases.
Because all the meanings of the "path" (mārga) present in the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) are fully possessed here, the "factors of the path" (mārgāṅga) are said to increase.
It is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it possesses two meanings: it serves as the basis for seeking and it functions as the vehicle for proceeding toward [the goal].

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), these two meanings are most preeminent; that is, at the stage of the path of seeing, the noble wisdom first arises, which is superior in its authentic seeking of the principles of the truths (*satya*).
Furthermore, at this stage, one does not form a fixed resolve [to reach a specific limit], because one can proceed swiftly toward the superior state and because the number increases accordingly.
Thus, in the sūtras, the sequence is first seven and then eight; this is not the order of cultivation.
Others establish the following sequence here:

At the outset, through the power of wisdom, the practitioner truly understands the specific and general characteristics of objects such as the body, thereby guiding the arousal of all wholesome qualities. This is like a person with sight leading a group of blind people; therefore, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught first.

Having established the objects of focus through the four foundations of mindfulness, one is able to initiate right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) for abandoning evil and cultivating good; therefore, the four right efforts are taught in the second stage.

Through the power of right effort, faults are diminished and virtues are made to flourish within the mental continuum, thereby enabling the cultivation of sublime concentration (*samādhi*); thus, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are taught in the third stage.

With the supreme meditative concentration as their basis, they cause faith and the other faculties to serve as dominant conditions for supramundane dharmas; for this reason, these five faculties are designated as the fourth [set].

Once the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is established, one cannot be overcome by the evil karma and afflictions that lead to the miserable realms; for this reason, these five powers (*bala*) are designated as the fifth [set].

Since the meaning of the powers has already been established, and because one is now able to realize the objects of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are without doubt or hesitation, the seven factors of enlightenment are taught as the sixth [member].

Having realized the objects of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, one comes to weary of and relinquish saṃsāra while joyfully aspiring toward nirvāṇa; therefore, the factors of the path are taught as the seventh.
Within this, each point shall be analyzed in its proper sequence; one should seek to understand them correctly as they are explained in the sūtras and śāstras.
Since this treatise investigates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is no need for laborious elaboration on the logic of their sequence.
Among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), how many are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and how many pertain to both types?
The verse says:
Seven factors of enlightenment and eight members of the path are invariably untainted.
The three, four, five faculties, and powers all pertain to both types.
The commentary states:

Among these, the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight branches of the noble path are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are established only within the stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This means that at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) increase; being proximate to awakening (*bodhi*), they counteract the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Therefore, the essence of the factors of enlightenment is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). Although all factors of awakening assist toward awakening, these alone are specifically designated by the name "factors of enlightenment" because they are most proximate to the fruit of awakening.

By this principle, it should be understood that the realization of the seven factors of enlightenment is stated solely in reference to their being antidotes to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); as these serve as the primary antidotes for the lower stages, the name "factors of enlightenment" is established exclusively for those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
If this is not accepted, why would it not be admitted that [the factors] apply to both?
Alternatively, among all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), the designation "limbs of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) is established based on their proximity to enlightenment.

Within the path, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is proximate to enlightenment; since its nature is proximate to enlightenment and is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), it is only the untainted path of cultivation that is designated by the name "limb of enlightenment."

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are predominant; therefore, they are exclusively comprised within the nature of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Although right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the others may also be associated with the tainted (*sāsrava*), they do not receive the designation "factors of the noble path" (*āryamārgāṅga*), because the name "factors of the noble path" refers specifically to the untainted.

Furthermore, those who maintain various treatises agree that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) taught after the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are necessarily untainted (*anāsrava*).
If they were taught prior [to the limbs of enlightenment], they would pertain to both types [tainted and untainted].
Since the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are taught only after the limbs of enlightenment, the eight limbs of the path are exclusively untainted.
The remaining factors apply to both stages; this meaning is already established by implication.

That is to say, among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), those that increase in the earlier stage also increase in their functional power in the later stage, whereas those that increase in the later stage do not increase in the earlier stage.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"From the stage of initial practice until the stage of exhaustion and non-arising, the stages of mindfulness constantly increase," and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding these thirty-seven [factors], how many are present in which stages?
The verse says:
In the first dhyāna, all [factors] are present; in the *anāgamya* stage, the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*) is excluded;
in the second dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) is excluded; in the third, fourth, and intermediate [dhyānas], both [applied and sustained thought] are excluded.
In the first three formless stages, the two preceding types [of factors] excluding the precepts are absent;
in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence, the factors of enlightenment and the path branches are excluded.
The treatise says:

In the first dhyāna, all thirty-seven factors are present; however, in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) is excluded because one still harbors doubt regarding the factors of the lower stages and has not yet attained firm confidence, and thus joy does not arise.

Furthermore, when the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) first manifests, one has not yet been able to abandon the afflictions of the lower stages; even though they have subsequently been abandoned, the situation remains the same as before. Therefore, at the time of its arising, there is no joy (*prīti*) whatsoever.
Some say that all paths of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) proceed through strenuous effort; therefore, they lack the factor of joy (*prīti*).
In the second dhyāna, right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is excluded, because vitarka is already absent in that dhyāna.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"In those stages there is no vitarka, because the higher levels of samādhi become increasingly tranquil.
For this reason, each of these two stages consists of thirty-six [factors].
In the intermediate stage between the third and fourth dhyānas, both joy (*prīti*) and applied thought (*vitarka*) are eliminated, leaving thirty-five factors each.
In the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the three branches of morality (*śīla*) and joy and applied thought are eliminated, leaving thirty-two factors each.

In the Desire Realm and at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), excluding the factors of enlightenment and the path factors, there are twenty-two of each, as they lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) elements.
Thus, in these various stages, the number of awakening factors (*bodhipakṣa*) that manifest is not fixed, varying according to what is appropriate for each.

This means that according to their respective stages, a subsequent state necessarily includes the preceding ones; thus, while they may be conceptually distinguished as multiple types within a single entity, there is the sense that multiple types can arise simultaneously.

However, only the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) necessarily do not arise together, because they are divided into four based on their respective objects of observation (*ālambana*).
Since even two types of wisdom do not arise simultaneously, how much less could four types of wisdom arise at once?

It is impossible for a single wisdom to be divided into many based on its objects, because if it were to be subsumed under the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) through a general observation, there would necessarily be no instance of a single wisdom arising in a single moment with four objects and four aspects.

According to this principle, although the thirty-seven factors are present in their entirety within the first dhyāna in general, at most only thirty-four can manifest simultaneously within a single moment.
Thus, at most, there can be thirty-three [mental states] before reaching the second dhyāna;
thirty-two at most in the intermediate stage between the third and fourth dhyānas;
and twenty-nine at most in the first three formless attainments.
In the desire realm and at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there are at most only nineteen [factors], because all of them exclude three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Those that are reduced therein should be considered according to their respective stages.
Why is the mind-king (*cittarāja*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Reason (*yukti*) is also subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because they truly encompass all conditioned virtues of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

However, it is not established as a separate factor like wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others because, regarding the categories of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), the mind possesses an even and impartial functional capacity (*śakti-vṛtti*) without partiality, whereas the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) possess an intensified functional capacity exclusively within the category of purification; therefore, it is not established [as a separate factor].
Other masters say:

"The factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) mostly take the common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena as their objects, whereas the mind-king (citta-rāja) mostly takes its own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object; therefore, it is not established [as a factor of enlightenment].
Others further say:

The cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) is fundamentally intended as an antidote to all afflictions (kleśa). However, since the afflictions are mental factors (caitta) rather than the mind itself (citta), the remedial dharmas are likewise not the mind but merely mental factors; they are established through the mutual opposition between the obstacle and its antidote.
Some say that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) assist enlightenment (bodhi);

since enlightenment is a mental factor (caitta) with wisdom (prajñā) as its essence, it is impossible for the mind-king (citta-rāja) to assist a mental factor, just as a king cannot be assisted by his ministers; therefore, the mind-king is not established as a factor of enlightenment.
Other masters say:

"The mind leads the world through the cycles of rebirth across realms, destinies, and births without interruption; the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) serves to sever birth and death. For this reason, the sovereign mind (cittarāja) is not established as a factor of enlightenment."

Other masters say: Since beginningless time, the mind has been defiled by numerous afflictions; it scatters among various objects and is stubborn and difficult to tame. To tame the mind, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). That which is to be tamed is not itself the tamer; therefore, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is not established as a factor of enlightenment.
For what reason, among all the great mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), are only four established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
In reality, they are subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because those [foundations] truly encompass all conditioned wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*).

However, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are established separately because these three factors, being conducive to the class of purification (*vyavadāna-pakṣa*), possess such powerful efficacy that they can be established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) do not have separate establishments because their powerful efficacy is predominant within the class of defilement (*saṃkleśa-pakṣa*).

In the case of conceptual meditation (*parikalpita-bhāvanā*), resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) predominates; since the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) comprise only those meditations that accord with reality (*tattvārtha*), this resolute confidence is not included among the factors of enlightenment.

Other masters say: "Resolute confidence increases only upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)," because the Sūtra establishes it as a factor belonging exclusively to the state of no-more-learning.

The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) increase during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*); because they serve as the cause by which the power to bring forth the three types of enlightenment (*trividhabodhi*) is generated, resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is not included among the factors conducive to enlightenment.

The power of attention (*manasikāra*) can activate the mind, causing it to easily detach from its object and become unsettled; the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), however, examine the object with thorough discernment, causing the mind to become one-pointed.
Since it is the opposite of that [vitarka], this *manasikāra* (attention) is not subsumed under the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
If that is so, why then establish *vitarka* (applied thought) as a factor of enlightenment?

Although *vitarka* stimulates the mind toward its object, its purpose is to cause the mind to investigate the ultimate principle, rather than to cause the mind to be flighty or easily distracted from the object. It possesses the capacity to stimulate the observation of the truths, for it is said that this power stimulates right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Therefore, *manasikāra* cannot be cited as an analogy for *vitarka*.
Other masters say:

When the mind first grasps an object, whether it be defiled or pure, the power of attention (*manasikāra*) is predominant; therefore, it is said that [attention] is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

As for appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), because its force is weak during the initial stage of contacting the object, it is not established as a factor of enlightenment. This is because the factors of enlightenment must reach their full intensity precisely during the stage of continuous contact with the object.
Because its functional power increases within both the defiled and purified portions, it is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Consequently, it is established as the branch of sensation (*vedanā-aṅga*) among the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) pertaining to the process of transmigration, and as the factor of joy (*prīti-bodhyaṅga*) among the factors of enlightenment pertaining to the process of cessation.
Other masters say:

Although feeling (*vedanā*) is predominant in relation to defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it also possesses the capacity to perform a beneficial function for the category of purity (*vyavadāna*). Just as the nature of a *caṇḍāla*, though base and inferior, can perform a beneficial service for a noble clan, so too is feeling a limb of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*) within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and is thus established under the name of a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) among the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
For what reason do all three feelings pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*), yet among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), only joy (*prīti*) is included and not the other two?

This is because the mental modes (*ākāra*) of the factors of enlightenment are sharp and intense, whereas the mental modes of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are dull and sluggish; therefore, they are not included.
Other masters say:
The two sensations of pleasure and equanimity constitute the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*);
however, because they are obscured by the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*), their characteristics are not clearly manifest.
For this reason, they are not established [as such].
For what reason, among the great wholesome mental factors (*cittamahābhūmika-dharma*),
are only four factors established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
