This knowledge of others' minds does not exist within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because that path proceeds with extreme rapidity through a general contemplation of the principles of the Truths (*satya*). Nevertheless, all [beings] can potentially serve as objects for this knowledge of others' minds.

When the noble ones of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) give rise to this knowledge, those of the middle and lower vehicles must employ preparatory effort (*prayoga*); for Śrāvakas, the preparatory effort may be either superior or middling, while for the Rishyaputra-like [Pratyekabuddhas], only inferior preparatory effort is required. For the Buddha, there is no preparatory effort; it manifests at will.

If sentient beings are about to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas practice preliminary application (*prayoga*) in order to know the minds of those beings during the stage of the path of seeing.

When those sentient beings have entered the stage of the path of seeing, if the Śrāvakas' preliminary application regarding the category of phenomena (*dharmapakṣa*) is perfected, they know the first two moments of mind of that path of seeing.

If it is for the purpose of further knowing the categories of the mind, one separately cultivates the preparatory application until that application is perfected; he has then already transcended to the sixteenth moment of mind.
Although this mind is known, it is not the knowledge of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); therefore, it is said that he knows only two moments.
If the preparatory application for the dharma-part (*dharmajñāna*) is perfected, one knows the first two moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

If, in order to further know the subsequent category-part (*anvayajñāna*), one separately cultivates the preparatory application until it is perfected, one knows that eighth moment of the collective category-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Other masters say that he knows the fifteenth moment.
Some say that the Rṣabha knows four moments, namely: the first two moments, the eighth, and the fourteenth.
This statement is logical.
Why is this so? Because it is admitted that, after knowing the first two moments of mind, one knows the eighth mind by skipping over only five intervening moments.

If one further practices the preparatory application (prayoga) of the dharma-portion, the application should be accomplished within five moments of mindfulness; why, then, do you not allow that the fourteenth moment is known?
Others also say that four moments are known: namely, the first two minds and the eleventh and twelfth.
Because the Buddha’s mind is sovereign, all supreme qualities manifest according to his will; thus, he can know them sequentially within fifteen moments of thought.

Since the Blessed One diligently cultivated immeasurable provisions over three incalculable eons, he has attained inconceivable, supreme, and wondrous wisdom. Possessing great power and function, he can know whatever he desires; even as this wisdom arises, he also knows the mental factors associated with it.

However, the primary purpose of practicing the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) is to know the mind; thus, [knowing] the sphere of infinite space and so forth is termed "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:

"To induce the arising of this knowledge, one must first know the mind and only afterwards know its object; therefore, from the beginning, it is designated simply by the name 'knowledge of others' minds.'"
What preparatory application (*prayoga*) is cultivated when inducing this knowledge?
First, one should observe the physical appearance and the vocal expressions that indicate the distinctions of the mind.

That is to say, when a practitioner first begins their training, desiring to ascertain the distinctions within the minds of others, they first carefully observe their own physical appearance and the vocal expressions they prefer, investigating why these differences arise; thus, they come to know that such distinctions in appearance and so forth are caused by the mind.
Next, one further examines the manifest forms and so forth of others' bodies, seeing that their differences also arise from the variations of the mind.

Consequently, at a later time, when the body and mind are free from desire, become supple and pure, they induce the arising of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Based on this concentration, there arises majestic wisdom (*jñāna*); this wisdom truly perceives the minds of others.

Just as various colored threads within a bright pearl can have their distinct characteristics clearly perceived, this is called the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the conventional knowledge of others' minds (*saṃvṛti-paracittajñāna*).

When cultivating the uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*), the knowledge that contemplates [the four marks] such as impermanence and suffering serves as the preparatory practice; in this stage of preparation, it takes both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as its object, but upon reaching the stage of perfection, it takes only mind as its object, not form.

Furthermore, during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one takes both one's own and others' minds as objects; however, upon reaching the stage of fulfillment (*niṣpanna*), one takes only the minds of others as objects, not one's own.
What is the difference between the two characteristics of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
The verse says:
Regarding the four noble truths, the wisdom that "I have known what was to be known," "there is nothing further to be known," and so forth,
corresponds respectively to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The treatise says:
As stated in the treatise:
What is the knowledge of exhaustion?
It refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

If one correctly knows for oneself: "I have known suffering, I have abandoned its origin, I have realized its cessation, and I have cultivated the path"—the knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, wisdom, light, and contemplation resulting from this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of non-arising?

It is the correct self-knowledge that "I have already known suffering and need not know it again," and so on, as explained at length, up to "I have already cultivated the path and need not cultivate it again."
Based on all this, as explained at length up to the point where it is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*):

when these two knowledges function due to one's original intention (*āśaya*), they have the power to give rise to such a knowledge of understanding; however, when the two untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledges function, one does not form such an understanding, because they are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
This means that it is within the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which follows the two types of wisdom, that one performs these two kinds of conceptualization.

These two conceptualizations arise subsequent to the two wisdoms because they are induced by the power of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising; furthermore, these two conventional wisdoms are the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) resulting from those [two wisdoms].
The citation of two fruits serves to indicate the distinction between two types of knowledge; this must logically be so, as it is stated "by reason of this.
Based on this meaning, the expression "by reason of this" (tasmāt) signifies that which pertains to this very knowledge.

If that were not the case, one should say: "All such practitioners, at the time they originally engaged in their practice, certainly gave rise to this intentional resolve, thinking: 'When I realize arhatship, I must necessarily give rise to this wisdom of self-examination.'"
Therefore, when one now emerges from contemplation, this wisdom will necessarily arise.

To ensure that the wisdom thus produced is appropriately established under the names "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), it refers to the sense of being the basis upon which subsequent wisdom arises;
hence, it is said that this interpretation of the principle must necessarily be so.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of these ten knowledges: conventional knowledge includes one entire [knowledge] and a small portion of another; dharma-knowledge and inferential knowledge each include one entire [knowledge] and a small portion of seven others; the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation each include one entire [knowledge] and a small portion of four others; path-knowledge includes one entire [knowledge] and a small portion of five others; other-mind-knowledge includes one entire [knowledge] and a small portion of four others; and the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising each include one entire [knowledge] and a small portion of six others.
For what reason are the two knowledges established as ten?
The verse says:
By way of intrinsic nature and antidote, Aspects, and the objects of those aspects.
The preparatory application accomplishes the perfection of the cause; therefore, ten knowledges are established.
The treatise says:
Due to seven conditions, two are established as ten.
First, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is established by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because conventional knowledge constitutes its very nature.

Second, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are established by way of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), because they are fully capable of acting as antidotes to the desire realm and the higher realms, respectively.

3. The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination are established by way of their aspects (*ākāra*), because there is no difference in the essential nature of the objects of these two knowledges.

4. The knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are established by way of both their aspects and their objects, because both the aspects and the objects of these two [knowledges] are distinct.

Fifth, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is established on the basis of its preparatory application (*prayoga*). It is not that this [knowledge] does not know the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of others; rather, it is because one originally cultivated the preparatory application for the purpose of knowing the minds of others that, although at the time of its perfection one also knows the mental factors, it is designated by the name "knowledge of others' minds" in reference to its preparatory application.
The preparatory application (*prayoga*) has already been fully analyzed above.
Sixth, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is established because the task is accomplished, as it necessarily arises for the first time within a body in which the task has been completed.
Seventh, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is established because the causes are perfected, as it arises with all the noble paths (*āryamārga*) as its cause.

This means that there is knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) which arises not because it has the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) as its cause, and there is knowledge of non-arising which does not arise with the knowledge of exhaustion as its cause.

As stated above regarding dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), they are fully capable of counteracting the phenomena of the desire realm and the higher realms; is there also a partial counteraction of the higher [realms] by the [knowledge of] desire?
The verse says:
The dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path, within the stage of the path of cultivation, concurrently counteract the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms;
the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) lacks the power to counteract those in the desire realm.
The Treatise says:

The dharma-knowledge of cessation and the dharma-knowledge of the path, which are subsumed under the path of cultivation, are also capable of counteracting the afflictions of the upper realms to be abandoned through cultivation.
In relation to the dharmas of the desire realm, these dharma-knowledges of the four truths are fully capable of counteracting them.

Regarding the abandonment through insight into the desire realm, because dharma-knowledge also serves as a sustaining counteragent (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), both the counteragent and the countered obtain the designation "complete" (*sakala*); in contrast to the higher realms, both are deficient and thus designated "partial" (*pradeśika*).
For what reason do only the Dharma-knowledges of Cessation and the Path treat both their own spheres and those of the higher realms, whereas those of Suffering and Origin do not?
It is because their objects are identical in terms of being peaceful and constituting deliverance.
That is to say, the cessation and the remedial paths of the desire realm and the higher realms, when compared with one another, have no difference in their characteristics.

Since all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are both wholesome and eternal, and all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are capable of leading to liberation, their objects of focus differ—namely, suffering and its origin—with respect to the realms of desire and the higher realms, due to distinctions such as few versus many, subtle versus coarse, and lower versus upper.

Furthermore, the knowledge of the origin of suffering takes as its object that which is to be reviled; it is impossible to feel revulsion for that [object] while being free from craving for this [ground].
According to principle, when one feels revulsion toward a particular stage, one abandons the afflictions of that very stage.
If you allow that aversion and the detachment from craving are distinct, then detachment from craving and liberation must also be distinct.

If you allow that one can be detached from the craving for the form and formless realms without being averse to them, then the principle of practicing aversion to achieve detachment from craving would be destroyed.
The two knowledges of cessation and the path do not take objects of aversion as their cognitive objects; there is no fault in taking a lower realm as an object to counteract a higher one.

Furthermore, it is like the meditation on impurity and the aspiration for nirvana: the meditation on impurity takes the realm of desire as its object and is able only to cause the mind to feel revulsion toward and turn away from that realm of desire.
When the aspiration for *nirvāṇa* manifests before one, it is universally able to cause the mind to feel revulsion toward and turn away from the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Thus, when knowledge of suffering and its origin arises taking the desire realm as its object, it is only able to cause the mind to become detached from the defilements of the desire realm; when knowledge of cessation and the path arises taking the phenomena of the desire realm as its object, it is universally able to cause the mind to become detached from the defilements of all three realms.
Therefore, it is accepted that the category of Dharma-knowledge regarding cessation and the path increases until one attains the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).

Because the Great Sage clearly understood this through the gate of "complete mastery," he established the Knowledge of Dharmas (*dharma-jñāna*) and the Knowledge of Subsequent Categories (*anvaya-jñāna*) based on this principle. While a portion of Dharma-knowledge possesses the capacity to master the higher realms, the Knowledge of Subsequent Categories can never master the Desire Realm. Only when its own task within its own realm is fully accomplished can it simultaneously perform the task for other realms. Since it is not the case that when the Knowledge of Subsequent Categories has completed its own work but the work for others is not yet finished, there is a need for assistance, there is no instance where the Knowledge of Subsequent Categories masters the dharmas of the Desire Realm.

Is it not the case that when the sixteenth moment, the knowledge of the category of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), arises, one could, by virtue of this momentum, treat the afflictions of the desire realm?
However, when about to sever the afflictions of the desire realm, the knowledge of the category [of the path] does not function.

Even if it were granted that [the knowledge of classes] is currently active, because it is constrained by the obstacles of its own realm, it necessarily lacks the power to assist in the accomplishment of the functions of another dharma-knowledge; therefore, this knowledge of classes is incapable of counteracting [afflictions of] the desire realm.
Among these ten knowledges (*jñāna*), which possesses which aspects (*ākāra*)?
The verse says:
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) possess all sixteen aspects.
Conventional knowledge consists of this and others; the knowledges of the four truths each have four [objects].
Uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds takes only four as its objects, namely the Path;
contaminated knowledge takes specific characteristics as its objects, and both take only a single thing as their object.
The fourteen [aspects] of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising are said to be those excluding emptiness and non-self.
The commentary states:
Each of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge possesses the sixteen aspects, such as impermanence and suffering; these sixteen aspects will be explained in detail later.
Worldly wisdom (*loka-jñāna*) consists of this as well as others, because it is able to take the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its objects.
That is to say, conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) may sometimes fully exercise the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), as in the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*;
or it may not be complete, as in the "supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) concentration and the conventional wisdom at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

There are also other modes of activity that are not noble (*ārya*), such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The modes of activity of conventional wisdoms (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are infinite; however, each of the four wisdoms regarding suffering and so forth possesses four modes of activity, each taking its own respective truth as its object.

Within the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), if it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it possesses only four aspects (*ākāra*) that take the Path as its object, because this is subsumed under a portion of the knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñāna*).

If it is tainted (*sāsrava*), it apprehends the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the mind and mental factors that constitute its own objects; since its aspects are likewise identical to the specific characteristics of those objects, it is not included within the aforementioned sixteen [aspects].

In this way, these two types [of consciousness], at all times, take only a single object as their focal point within a single moment of thought; that is to say, when taking the mind (citta) as an object, they do not take mental factors (caitta), and when taking feeling (vedanā) and so forth as objects, they do not take perception (saṃjñā) and so forth.
If that is so, why did the Blessed One say:
"One understands as it really is a mind possessed of greed, and so forth"?
It is not that greed and the mind are apprehended simultaneously, just as a garment and its stain are not apprehended simultaneously.
How is it that while the knowledge of others' minds possesses both aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*), it is said not to observe its own object or aspects?
It is because it does not observe the object or aspects of the other person's mind.

This means that one only knows that the other person possesses a mind affected by defilement (*sāsrava*) and so forth, but does not know the objects (*ālambana*)—such as form—that color that mind, nor does one know the mental mode (*ākāra*) by which that mind takes its object.

Otherwise, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) would also have to take form and other [objects] as its domain; furthermore, it would incur the fault of being able to take itself as its own object. Moreover, untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) would have to take the Truth of Suffering and other [truths] as its objects, and thus one would also have to admit that it is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*).
Since this is not permitted, it is known that [this knowledge] does not observe both [the object and its characteristics].
All other-knowledge-of-minds (*paracittajñāna*) possesses a determinate characteristic:

namely, it can only take as its objective support the real, individual self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of present, homogeneous minds and mental factors within the mental continua of others, whether bound to the desire or form realms or unbound; it is dissociated from emptiness and signlessness; it is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising; it does not exist within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) or the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*); and it is not obstructed by anything else.

Just as it is possible for the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) to exist [in this way], excluding the aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*), each possesses the remaining fourteen aspects.
Because they are contrary to the mental orientation of the mind upon emerging from meditative absorption, these two aspects do not exist within the state of absorption.
This means that after emerging from meditative equipoise following the two types of knowledge, one necessarily realizes for oneself, "My births are exhausted," and so forth.

The intent here is to explain that although the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are ultimate truths, they involve conventional reality, because such expressions as "my births are exhausted" are themselves conventional.

"Emptiness and non-self are the ultimate truth (paramārtha)"; this necessarily involves the ultimate truth because, following this contemplation, one definitively realizes emptiness and non-self. By means of these two types of wisdom, one becomes detached from [the notions of] emptiness and non-self.
Are there any untainted (*anāsrava*) aspects that transcend these sixteen, which are further subsumed under other modes of activity (*ākāra*)?
The verse says:
The pure (*śuddha*) do not transcend the sixteen; others say they do, because of the treatises.
The treatise states:
Among the masters of the Abhidharma, there is one class who asserts that there are no more than sixteen aspects of untainted cognition (*anāsrava-ākāra*), for nothing else beyond these can be found.

Is it not said that one who possesses the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) must necessarily personally realize for themselves: "My births are exhausted," and so forth?
This is not contradictory, because it was already explained previously.

That is to say, it was already stated that after the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-darśana*), these modes of activity (*ākāra*) are performed within conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and not within untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

This turning of the aspect arises from the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), which induce conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). By attributing this merit to its source, it is said that the latter "comprehends" [the truth]. Therefore, it is accepted that this knowledge is free from [the aspects of] emptiness and selflessness. It is by the power of the original aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) that these two knowledges subsequently necessarily induce [the conventional knowledge] that "my births are exhausted," and so forth; it is not by contemplating this internal aspect within [the ultimate knowledges] that causes this aspect to arise at a later time.
Although the aspects of our practice do not exist when observed internally, we have not yet encountered the realization of self-liberation.

This implies that at this stage, there must already be the forceful influence (*ākāra-vaśitā*) of aspects such as "the birth of the self has been exhausted. Because these are induced by prior conventional aspects and are capable of inducing subsequent conventional aspects, one is free from the fourteen [categories of] inexhaustibility and non-arising.

If it is argued that this should be stated as "non-existent apart from the sixteen," this is not reasonable; for, with the exception of fourteen, the remaining [factors] exist, whereas their total non-arising is not universally established.

This means that apart from fourteen [factors], there is a cryptic teaching based on the [notion of] a self; because one reckons that "birth is exhausted" and so forth as the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*), it is said that these fourteen are excluded in order to negate that [view].
Since other [factors] are not universally established, how could they possibly serve as the basis for negating this?

If that were so, since there exists uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it would follow that there must be uncontaminated aspects (*ākāra*) beyond the sixteen, because all knowledge of others' minds takes the real, specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, whereas the aspects such as the Path take the collective, general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as their object. Since these two are distinct, one would have to admit that there definitely exist uncontaminated aspects separate from the sixteen. However, this is not accepted as a certainty.

The objection is not valid; for our position does not definitively maintain that the aspect of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) takes only a collection as its object, since we accept the existence of two applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), namely those of sensation (*vedanā*) and mind (*citta*). For example, when one contemplates a single entity of sensation as impermanent, it is universally established that at the moment this knowledge arises, it takes a single real particular characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) as its object by means of the aspect of common characteristics.

In this way, why not allow that untainted knowledge of others' minds takes a single real particular characteristic as its object through a universal characteristic aspect—namely, knowing another's mind to be "the true path" and so forth—which is to say, it takes the single real characteristic of being "the path" and so forth as its object?

If it is argued that, just as in the case of the mindfulness of feelings and the mindfulness of mind, one takes all feelings and minds of the three times as objects in their entirety with the aspect of universal characteristics such as impermanence, then the uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds would likewise take all uncontaminated minds and so forth of others across the three times as its object with aspects such as the Path; this would contradict your own school's tenets.

It is also incorrect to claim that when the knowledge of others' minds arises, it takes as its object only a single real particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the present; for their preparatory practices (*prayoga*) differ.

The preparatory practice for this knowledge is intended to know the specific distinctions of another's present cognitive mind, such as whether it possesses greed and so forth, whereas the preparatory practice for the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding impermanence and so forth is intended for the general purpose of cultivating revulsion toward all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).

Due to the distinction in the power of the preceding preparatory application, at the time of reaching fulfillment, there appears a synthesis of the particular; therefore, there is no fault of the fallacy of mutual analogy.
If it is argued that because it is neither impermanent nor the self-substance of feeling, one should contemplate feeling as impermanent at that time.
Since it does not take a single, real self-characteristic as its object, how can this be cited as an analogy for the knowledge of others' minds?
Consequently, one would have to admit that feeling is not impermanent, and thus one should not give rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding feeling.
Just as feeling and mind are distinct in their essential natures, there can certainly be no observation of feeling as being the mind.
Although one may observe feeling itself as impermanent, there is no fault of a single entity possessing multiple essences.
Because there is no distinct entity apart from experience, it is like [the cases of] harm or benefit, which do not exist apart from experience.
The same applies to the remaining mental factors (*saṃskāra*) and other phenomena (*dharma*).
If this were so, it would contradict the authoritative teaching (*āptāgama*).
As it is said: "Regarding the dwelling in the contemplation of the body as the body, one should say it is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)," and so forth, in detail.
Furthermore, it is said that contemplating old age and death should be called these four knowledges.
There is no contradiction between these two; however, what was stated first does not refer to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and so forth.

Apart from the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), one dwells in the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*), observing the body as body, but observing it only as it truly is—as impermanent and so forth.

I have already previously granted that the characteristic of being mutually traversed also takes the single, real specific characteristic as its object; therefore, what he has said does not contradict my position.
Furthermore, the term "old age and death" refers collectively to the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).
Contemplating the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent and so forth is subsumed under four knowledges; what contradiction is there in this?
If that is so, it is as when it is said: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows, as it truly is, that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling."
What is the knowledge of the path of mundane practice that is subsumed under the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge?
This should be investigated: when feeling is present, one necessarily does not cognize it, because it does not take itself as its object.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that one clearly knows [the feeling] while it is passing away or coming toward [the present], because the past and future are not designated as the time when pleasure is being experienced.
Yet the Sūtra says:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it really is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.'"
Therefore, one should know that this teaching has a distinct underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
To explain this intention: it is like the "exhaustion" and "non-arising," meaning that these modes of activity (*ākāra*) only arise at a later time, after one has emerged from meditative absorption.
Therefore, there are no aspects of untainted (anāsrava) practice outside of these sixteen.
A certain school asserts that there are those which exceed the sixteen, because the *Mūla-śāstra* states so.
As the *Mūla-śāstra* says:
Is it possible for a mind that is not bound [to any realm] to discern phenomena bound to the desire realm?
He replied:
It can discern them; namely, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self, as cause, as origin, as arising, and as condition. Such a case exists; such a thing occurs.
The proof based on "discerning as it is" (*yathābhūta-pravicaya*) is not established, for it misunderstands the intent of the treatise.

The treatise demonstrates that the aspects of the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) are manifold; among these, there are those that take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their object. It is with reference to this possibility that the expressions "there is such a case" (*asty etat sthānam*) and "there is such a thing" (*asty etad vastu*) are stated, showing that there is no error. For this very reason, these expressions are not found in the other [realms].
That is to say, that treatise further states:
"Is there a mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) that can discern phenomena associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It replies: "Yes."

It is able to discern [objects] by way of: the notion of "I," the notion of "mine," annihilationism, eternalism, causelessness, lack of action, denial, supremacy, excellence, superiority, being foremost, being capable of purification, being capable of liberation, being capable of transcendence, delusion, doubt, hesitation, greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance.

It is a discernment induced by what is not in accordance with reason; apart from this, there is no room for any other mental aspect (ākāra). For this reason, it is not said that "there is such a possibility" (*sthāna*);
because it proceeds entirely through perversion, it is not said that "such a thing exists" (*vastu*).
Therefore, the aspects of pure conduct do not exceed sixteen; this is consistent with both principle and scripture, and cannot be shaken.
As for what is called the "sixteen aspects of conduct," are they merely different names?
Is there indeed a difference?
What is meant by "aspect" (*ākāra*)? It refers to the agent of the activity and the object of the activity.
The verse says:
The aspects are truly sixteen; their essence is exclusively wisdom.
They are able to engage with objects of perception, and that which is engaged with consists of all existent phenomena.
The treatise says:
Some maintain that although the aspects (*ākāra*) are sixteen in name, they are only seven in substance.
Because they take the Truth of Suffering as their object and counteract the four inversions, both the names and the substances are fourfold.
Taking the three truths as objects, they are called "four realities and one.
If explained in this way, there are actually sixteen aspects, because the characteristics of the objects to be remedied and the practices undertaken are distinct.
Regarding the statement that the characteristics of the objects to be remedied are distinct: in order to remedy the view of permanence, one cultivates the aspect of impermanence.
One cultivates the aspect of suffering to counteract the attachment to pleasure in conditioned phenomena; one cultivates the aspect of emptiness to counteract the view of "mine";
one cultivates the aspect of non-self to counteract the view of self; one cultivates the aspect of cause to counteract the theory of no-cause;
and one cultivates the aspect of origination to counteract the theories of a single cause such as Īśvara. To counteract...

The aspect of cultivation regarding arising is practiced to counter the theory that there is a transforming cause or a permanent cause; the aspect of cultivation regarding conditions is practiced to counter the theory that knowledge is the precursor capable of producing [rebirth];
the aspect of cultivation regarding cessation is practiced to demonstrate that the eternal extinction of the aggregates is nirvāṇa, thereby countering the theory that returning to Īśvara is nirvāṇa;
and [the aspect of cultivation regarding the path] is practiced to counter the attachment to liberation as being inherent within one's own self, which is [actually] mixed with defilements.
One cultivates the aspect of tranquility (*śānta*) because of the afflictions of defilement, suffering, and incorrect views;

one cultivates the aspect of excellence (*pranīta*) to counteract the pernicious doctrine that clings to nirvāṇa as being like a curse resulting in total annihilation; one cultivates the aspect of detachment (*niḥsaraṇa*) to counteract the view that liberation can regress;
and one cultivates the aspect of the path (*mārga*) to counteract the clinging to the non-existence of a path to liberation.
The aspect of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is cultivated to counteract the view that asceticism is the true path and the false doctrine that slanders the true path;

the aspect of "practice" (*pratipatti*) is cultivated to counteract the notion that one need not cultivate the path because birth-and-death is naturally pure, or that worldly detachment from defilement is the true path;

and the aspect of "attainment" (*samyaktva*) is cultivated to counteract being deceived by those who have encountered a path that does not lead to the permanent abandonment of defilement, regarding it as the truth.
Because the Noble Path is also not [an object of] reverence, it cultivates the aspect of "going forth.
Regarding the statement that the aspects of the objects of practice are distinct: the Noble Truth of Suffering has four aspects:
first, impermanence; second, suffering; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self.

Because it is subject to arising and ceasing, it is impermanent; because its nature is oppressive and it contradicts the mind of the Noble Ones, it is suffering; because it lacks a sovereign master, it is empty; and because it contradicts the characteristic of a self, it is non-self.
The Noble Truth of Origination has four characteristics: first, cause; second, origination; third, production; and fourth, condition.

It is called "cause" because it is that which can produce phenomena; "origination" because it consists of many varieties; "production" because it constantly brings forth [phenomena]; and "condition" because each [factor] assists [the others] individually.
The Noble Truth of Cessation has four characteristics: first, cessation; second, tranquility; third, excellence; and fourth, detachment.
It is "cessation" because it brings an end to all suffering; it is "tranquility" because the three fires of the three conditioned marks have been extinguished.
Other masters say:
It is "tranquil" because all sufferings have ceased, as it is said: "O Bhikṣus, all conditioned phenomena are suffering; only Nirvāṇa is supremely tranquil.
It is "excellent" and "eternal," and thus "sublime," because it is forever liberated from all calamities and afflictions.
Because it is supremely peaceful and secure, it is free [from suffering].
The Noble Truth of the Path has four characteristics: first, the path; second, the correct; third, the practice; and fourth, the departure.

It is called the "path" because it enables one to seek out the nature and characteristics of all phenomena and reach liberation; it is called the "correct" because it does not turn back erroneously; and it is called the "practice" because it proceeds toward reality as it truly is.
Other masters say: They are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*) because they are capable of leading toward [a goal].
As it is said, "this path leads to purification," whereas other views certainly lack the principle of leading to purification, because these [formations] lead exclusively [toward that end].
Because they are capable of reaching their goal, they are called "exits" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Thus, because there is a distinction between the objects to be remedied and the objects traversed, there are actually sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).

These aspects have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence; that is to say, it is specifically when various forms of wisdom operate by discerning within the characteristics of an object that they are termed "aspects."

Is it not the case that both mind and mental factors are all termed "possessing an aspect" (*sākāra*)? If this were so, how could one say that wisdom possesses an aspect when there is no wisdom associated with [the mind]?
It is not that they possess an aspect.

When it is said that "only those mental states associated with wisdom are called 'possessing an aspect' (sākāra)," this means that these minds and mental factors possess the sense of being able to apprehend (grāhaka) the specific characteristics within the categories of their respective objects.

If the designation "having an aspect" (sākāra) were applied solely based on wisdom (prajñā), then the other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) accompanying wisdom would also be called "having an aspect" by virtue of sharing that same name; this would be analogous to how they are designated as "with-outflows" (sāsrava) because they share the same outflows, which signifies that they possess the same antidote (pratipakṣa) as the substance of the outflows themselves.

In this way, the remaining mental states and mental factors likewise engage their objects through their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*); they function simultaneously, meaning there is no sequence of before and after.

Alternatively, because many mental states and mental factors possess modes of activity—such as the faculty of "already-known" (*ājñendriya*)—they are collectively designated as "possessing modes of activity."
Alternatively, it is also said that there is sound based on the immediately preceding [moment], just as there is a basis (*āśraya*); therefore, there is no fault.

That is to say, just as the mind and mental factors are all called "having a basis," the various mental factors associated with the mental consciousness arise simultaneously with their supporting consciousness; however, the basis of that consciousness is exclusively that which has just ceased in the immediately preceding moment.
It should be understood that the same principle applies to the aspect (*ākāra*).
What capacity does a cognition that has just ceased have with respect to the present?
Its capacity regarding the present is like that of a mental consciousness (*manas*) that has just ceased.

If that were the case, then sensation (*vedanā*) and the others would also receive the designation "possessing sensation" (*sāvedana*), and while we would grant this without contradiction, it is not what is being discussed here.

Since wisdom (*prajñā*) and all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) possess objects (*sālambana*), they are all "capable of proceeding" (*saṃskāra*). However, since this term "capable of proceeding" should refer exclusively to the essence of the aspect of proceeding (*ākāra*) belonging to wisdom, how could the other mental states and mental factors—which are not themselves aspects of proceeding—be considered "capable of proceeding"?

If it is argued that the remaining [mental factors] are called "active" because they arise in association with the characteristics of activity, then wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others, being associated with feeling (*vedanā*), should likewise be called "feeling."
Although this statement exists, the reasoning is not so.

That is to say, "aspect" (*ākāra*) is a synonym for wisdom (*prajñā*), while "that which can proceed" (*sākāra*) is simply another name for the apprehension of an object; the term "that which can proceed" does not specifically denote wisdom alone.
One might raise this objection: "Since the essence of sensation (*vedanā*) and the others is not a mode of activity (*ākāra*), they should not be considered 'active' (*carita*).
Just as wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to discern within its object, we allow that wisdom is called 'active'."
Since the mental conception (*saṃjñā*) can grasp the image within the object and consciousness (*vijñāna*) can cognize it and so forth, how could these not be "active factors" (*pravṛtti*)?
Therefore, the designation "active factor" applies generally to the grasping of objects; thus, sensation (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] should also be considered active factors.

The "object of activity" (*gocara*) is defined as encompassing all existent phenomena (*dharma*), whether they be substantial (*dravya*) or nominal (*prajñapti*), because both are objects of activity.

Consequently, these three categories differ in their scope: wisdom (*prajñā*) functions as the aspect of activity (*ākāra*), the agent of activity (*sākārin*), and the object of activity (*ālambana*); other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) function only as the agent and the object of activity; and all other existent phenomena function solely as the object of activity.
This principle is well-established and cannot be shaken.

Having already analyzed the distinctions between the aspects and characteristics of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), one should now analyze their nature, their inclusion, their bodily basis, and their level of existence.
The verse says:
The mundane [knowledges] are three; the wholesome are nine. Regarding their stages, the mundane ones depend on all;
the knowledge of others' minds depends only on four. The Dharma-knowledge depends on six; the remaining seven depend on nine.
As for the bodies upon which they arise: the knowledge of others' minds depends on the desire and form realms.
Dharma-knowledge relies solely on the desire realm; the remaining eight pertain to all three realms.
The commentary states:
Regarding the inclusion of these ten knowledges within the three moral natures, conventional knowledge pertains to all three natures, while the other nine knowledges are exclusively wholesome.

Regarding the distinction of levels: conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) relies on all levels from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence; the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) relies only on the four fundamental dhyānas, not on the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), the intermediate dhyāna, or the formless realms, because the objects of this knowledge are extremely subtle.
The power of the path on those stages is weak and inferior; thus, one cannot fully comprehend the subtle, present minds and mental factors within the mental continuums of others.
Furthermore, it does not rely on the formless realms, as such preparatory application (prayoga) is absent there.
Furthermore, because it is universal in nature, other stages are not its basis; rather, the five supernormal powers (abhijñā) rely upon calm abiding (śamatha), insight (vipaśyanā), and so forth.

Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) universally relies upon six stages: namely, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas. It does not rely on the other access concentrations (sāmantaka), because those are exclusively contaminated (sāsrava).
Nor does it rely on the formless realms (*ārūpya*), because its object is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The remaining seven knowledges (*jñāna*) rely on nine stages, namely, the three lower formless realms and the six stages previously mentioned.
In general, it is so stated; however, there are distinctions.

Specifically, among these seven types of knowledge (jñāna) mentioned, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) definitely arises based on the nine stages (bhūmi). The knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), are subsumed under the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and take the six stages as their basis.
Those subsumed under subsequent knowledge, however, universally take the nine stages as their basis.

Regarding the distinction based on the body: the knowledge of others' minds can manifest in both the desire and form realms, but it does not depend on the formless realm, because that [knowledge] does not exist there of its own accord.

As for why the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage does not arise: this knowledge involves a concomitant form (*rūpa*), and since such form cannot possibly arise in those [formless realms], it does not occur.

The dharma-knowledge arises based solely on a body belonging to the desire realm; one does not enter into or emerge from this knowledge while in the two higher realms, because all contaminated minds exist only in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the support for the matter accompanying the dharma-knowledge are bound exclusively to the desire realm.

Furthermore, these [knowledges] can counteract the afflictions that give rise to the violation of precepts; since the violation of precepts pertains only to the desire realm and not the higher realms, when the other eight knowledges manifest, they universally rely on bodies belonging to all three realms.
Having already explained the nature and the categories of the knowledges, one should now explain their inclusion within the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The verse says:
The various knowledges are included within the applications of mindfulness; the knowledge of cessation is included in the last alone.
The knowledge of others' minds is included in the last three; the remaining eight knowledges pertain to all four.
The treatise says:
The knowledge of cessation is subsumed within the mindfulness-establishment of dharmas; the knowledge of others' minds is subsumed in the last three; and the remaining eight all pertain to all four.
Regarding these ten knowledges (*jñāna*), when they are mutually related to one another, it should be stated how many knowledges serve as the objects (*ālambana*) for each.
The verse states:

The knowledges take one another as their objects; The knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) each have nine [knowledges] as their objects.
The knowledges of suffering and origination each have two; all four have ten, while cessation does not.
The commentary states:
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) can take nine knowledges as its object, excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
The knowledge of types (*anvaya-jñāna*) takes nine knowledges as its object, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
The knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) takes nine knowledges as its object, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), because the latter is not subsumed under the category of the Path.

The two knowledges of suffering and its origin each can take two knowledges as their objects—namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and impure knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*): these four all take the ten knowledges as their objects.
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) does not take the various knowledges as its objects, because it takes only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object.
How many dharmas in total are the objects of the ten knowledges?
And which knowledge has how many dharmas as its objective sphere?
The verse says:
There are ten objects in total; namely, two each for the three realms and the untainted, and two for the unconditioned.
Conventional [cognition] takes ten as its object; the five dharmas take five.
The objects of the knowledge of types are seven; those of the knowledge of suffering and origination are six; those of the knowledge of cessation and the path are one and two respectively;
those of the knowledge of others' minds are three; and those of the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising are each nine.
The treatise says:
The objects of the ten knowledges comprise ten categories of phenomena in total.

That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are divided into eight types, because those bound to the three realms and the untainted conditioned phenomena each have both associated (*samprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*) varieties.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is divided into two types, distinguished as wholesome (*kuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) takes ten dharmas collectively as its object.
Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) takes five as its object: namely, the two [categories] of the desire realm, the two of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), and the wholesome unconditioned.

Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) takes seven as its objects: namely, the six consisting of the paths of the form realm, the formless realm, and the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as the wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The knowledges of suffering and origin each take the six belonging to the three realms as their objects.
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) takes one as its object: namely, the wholesome unconditioned.
The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) takes two objects as its conditions, namely, the untainted path (anāsravamārga).
The knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) takes as its conditions the associated dharmas of the three realms—desire, form, and the untainted.
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) take as their conditions the eight conditioned [dharmas] and the wholesome unconditioned.
Is there perhaps a single moment of wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object?
No, there is not. But would it not be the case that the wisdom of the contemplation of non-self knows that all phenomena are non-self?
This, too, cannot take all phenomena as its object.
What phenomena does it not take as its object?
What is the nature of this [consciousness]?
The verse says:
Conventional wisdom, excluding its own category, takes all phenomena as its general object;
it functions through the aspect of "non-self" and is produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The treatise states:

When one contemplates all phenomena as non-self by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), one still excludes those of its own category; "its own category" refers to the factors that are its own essence, its associated factors, and its co-existent factors.
Why does [a dharma] not take its own substance as its object?
The Abhidharmikas establish this reason, saying:
"Because no dharma ever depends upon its own substance."
Precisely for this reason, it does not take associated factors as its object, because it functions with the same object as those associated factors.
If one were to admit that it takes associated factors as its object, then one would necessarily have to admit that it takes itself as its object.
Nor can it take coexistent phenomena as its object, because such phenomena are too closely proximate, just as the eye does not see the matter that supports the visual faculty.
The Sūtra also states:
"The wisdom of a single moment cannot simultaneously know all phenomena as objects."
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who see and know all phenomena instantaneously. By this principle, it follows that [realization] is exclusively gradual.

This wisdom is comprised solely of the desire and form realms; although this type exists within the formless realm, it is of little scope regarding the objects of cognition (dharma) and is therefore not what is being elucidated here.
This [wisdom] encompasses the wisdoms produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as all are capable of eliminating their own respective categories while taking all phenomena as their objects.
The objects of focus have already been explained.
One should now further investigate: who possesses how many knowledges?
The verse says:
For ordinary beings and noble ones on the path of seeing, in the first moment one definitely achieves one [knowledge];
in the second moment, three knowledges are achieved; in each of the subsequent four moments, one knowledge is added respectively.
On the path of cultivation, seven are definitely achieved; for those free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds is added.
The non-learner (aśaikṣa) with dull or sharp faculties definitely accomplishes nine or ten [knowledges].
The Commentary says:

At the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and during the first moment of the noble path of seeing (darśanamārga), one definitely accomplishes one knowledge, namely, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
In the second moment, three knowledges are definitely established, namely those of dharma, suffering, and [the origin].
In the fourth, sixth, tenth, and fourteenth moments, respectively, the subsequent knowledges of class, collection, cessation, and the path are added.

In all stages prior to the increase [of faculties], the number of factors established is as previously stated; therefore, within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are also definitely seven.

In these various stages, if one has already become free from desire (*vītarāga*), each stage increases by one—namely, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)—with the sole exception of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

However, during the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one can only achieve conventional knowledge of others' minds; at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), both types are fully achieved, because at that moment one first attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), thereby simultaneously acquiring the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge to constitute the essence of that fruit.
In all other stages of cultivation, both types are fully present; however, one born in the formless realm abandons the conventional [knowledge].
At all times, those liberated through meditative concentration (samayavimukta) definitely possess nine knowledges, namely, the addition of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
One who is liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) definitely achieves ten [knowledges], namely, by adding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Chapter Eight, Part Two: On the Discrimination of Knowledge. In which stage are how many knowledges cultivated simultaneously?
Furthermore, one should investigate: what is meant by "cultivation" (bhāvanā)?
It refers to the practice of wholesome conditioned phenomena to bring them to fulfillment and mastery.
Non-defiled neutral states are excluded because they lack superior, desirable fruits.
That which is neither wholesome nor unconditioned does not exist within the continuum, and furthermore, the unconditioned has no fruit.
Having already explained the meaning of cultivation, the original question should now be answered.
Regarding the fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing, the verse says:
When the patiences and knowledges of the path of seeing arise, they are cultivated in the future;
the three types of subsequent knowledge are cultivated concurrently. The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations does not arise from its own or lower stages.
After the four [knowledges] regarding suffering and origin, and after cessation—
Regarding the aspects and objects of their respective truths, these are obtained solely through application (*prayoga*).
The treatise says:

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whichever patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) arise, they all cultivate their own corresponding types in the future; however, they fully cultivate the various aspects (*ākāra*) and applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) pertaining to their respective truths.
For what reason is the path of seeing cultivated only as its own kind?
Because both its function (*kārya*) and its object (*ālambana*) are fixed and distinct.

Some say that because this lineage has never been attained before, it is only at the time of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation that one can simultaneously cultivate the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) belonging to the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-antika*) in the future.
It is only at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of each individual truth that one can simultaneously cultivate both; therefore, this designation is established.
For this reason, in other stages one is unable to cultivate them simultaneously, because the tasks pertaining to one's own respective truth have not yet been fulfilled.

Some say: If this were cultivated at the stage of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), it should be called conventional knowledge within the direct realization (abhisamaya); the Sūtra would then not establish the designation "at the edge of direct realization" (abhisamayāntika).
Regarding the cultivation of these three [levels], which is superior and which is inferior?
If judged by the continuity of the stream, the latter is superior to the former, because they arise from the increase of the body.
If explained according to the realms (*dhātu*), those above are all superior to those below.
Therefore, that which was previously cultivated and bound to the form realm involves a superior realm but an inferior body;
that which is cultivated in the subsequent stage and bound to the desire realm involves an inferior realm but a superior body.
These constitute four permutations, which should be contemplated according to reason.
Why is this not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?

This knowledge belongs exclusively to the retinue of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereas that [subsequent knowledge] is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, it cannot be cultivated.

The meaning of this is that because the cultivation of the "skill in the seven bases" serves as the seed, the path of seeing arises; thus, when the path of seeing arises, those [seven skills] are described as its retinue.

Alternatively, because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has, from beginningless time, already known, abandoned, and realized the three truths, yet has never cultivated the path, it is not cultivated now.
Or, because one now perceives the true path, the false path is shunned with shame; therefore, it is not that which is to be cultivated.
Alternatively, one might cultivate this wisdom at the conclusion of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya-anta*). However, because the paths are infinite, this stage does not involve such cultivation.

That is to say, regarding the clear realization based on the phenomena within the [first] three truths, it is possible for a single practitioner to attain their entirety; yet there can never be anyone capable of cultivating all the paths, because one cannot cultivate the paths belonging to a different faculty or lineage (*gotra*).
Although it is possible for one to cultivate [the path] according to one's own faculties and nature, not even one part in a hundred thousand arises;

thus, although at the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) one has not yet universally abandoned the origin of suffering (samudaya) nor universally realized cessation (nirodha), within that specific stage, the task of abandoning the origin and realizing cessation is already complete.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), the afflictions deluded regarding the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) are not universally cultivated as their antidotes, because there are many grades of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*).
For this reason, the Blessed One spoke of "extremes" (*anta*) with respect to the [remaining] three truths.

As stated in the sūtras, there is the limit of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the limit of the origin of the view of a self-identity, and the limit of the cessation of the view of a self-identity.
Nowhere in the sūtras is there mention of a "limit of the path of the view of a self-identity," because it is impossible to cultivate the path to its ultimate limit.
This conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is a non-arising dharma, for there is no possibility of its arising at any time, as the body upon which it would depend is certainly not produced.

That is to say, while the bodies of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) may serve as a basis for inducing the arising of this knowledge, it has no possibility of arising while one is in the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, based on this abiding body, the dharmas do not arise; because they do not arise, they necessarily do not arise.
If this is so, in reliance upon what is there the meaning of "cultivation" (bhāvanā)?
It is called cultivation by virtue of the attainment of cultivation (pratilambha-bhāvanā).

This means that at that time, one attains mastery; although its substance does not manifest due to the obstruction of other conditions, it is for this reason called "attainment" (*prāpti*), because one has realized mastery over its arising.
Because there are certain dharmas that, upon being attained, manifest immediately, such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and others;
or there are certain dharmas that first attain and later manifest, such as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and others.
There are certain phenomena that can never manifest, such as this very wisdom;
there are also certain phenomena that manifest despite not being attained, such as external forms.

Since there are no phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings that can arise before one as objects of attainment, although [the path] does not arise [in the future], there is still the sense of "cultivation.
Whichever stage’s path of seeing manifests, one is able to cultivate the future [path] of that same stage and lower stages.

That is to say, this conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) takes seven stages as its basis, namely: the threshold stage (anāgamya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), the four dhyānas, and the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
If the path of seeing (darśanamārga) manifests based on the threshold stage, one is able to cultivate the path of seeing of one future stage and conventional knowledge of two stages.

Upon reaching the fourth [dhyāna] and the path of seeing (darśanamārga) becoming manifest, one is able to cultivate the future path of seeing of the six stages and the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) of the seven stages.

That which is cultivated at the limit of suffering and origination is subsumed under the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); that which is cultivated at the limit of cessation is exclusively the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Whichever truth one cultivates at the conclusion of its clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one takes that very truth as the object through those same mental aspects (*ākāra*).

That is to say, if one cultivates at the conclusion of the clear realization of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one does so by means of the four aspects associated with suffering. If it is bound to the desire realm and takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object, or if it is bound to the form realm, it takes the suffering of the higher realms as its object.

If one practices at the stage of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), one does so by means of the four aspects (*ākāra*) that take origination as their object; if it is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it takes the origination of the desire realm as its object, and if it is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it takes the truth of origination of the higher realms as its object.

If one practices at the stage of the clear realization of the truth of cessation, one does so by means of the four aspects that take cessation as their object; if it pertains to the desire realm, it takes the cessation of the desire realm as its object, and if it pertains to the form realm, it takes the cessation of the higher realms as its object.
This conventional knowledge is obtained solely through application (*prayoga*); that is, it is obtained by means of the application belonging to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

That which is comprised within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*), while that which is comprised within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*); it is not produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*), because the latter is too weak.

Because wisdom is predominant, it is designated by the name "wisdom. If the accompanying factors are included, its intrinsic nature consists of the four aggregates of the desire realm or the five aggregates of the form realm.
Next, regarding the stage of detachment during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the verse says:
"At the first moment of the path of cultivation, one cultivates six or seven knowledges."
In the uninterrupted path of the eight stages, as well as in the remaining paths involving desire,
and in the eight liberations of the Peak of Existence, one cultivates seven knowledges each;
in the subsequent uninterrupted paths and remaining paths, one cultivates six and eight respectively.
The treatise states:

At the first moment of the path of cultivation—namely, at the time of the sixteenth cognition, the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna)—one presently cultivates two knowledges, namely the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna); these differ in name but not in essence.

One who has not yet abandoned desire cultivates six future knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and those concerning suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
One who has abandoned desire cultivates seven, adding the knowledge of others' minds, because this serves as the antidote for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
One does not cultivate worldly [knowledge], having already abandoned desire.
For one who has entered the Noble Path, for what reason is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) not cultivated within the Path of Seeing?

Because the knowledge of others' minds is comprised within the qualities of investigative contemplation; it possesses the sense of being cultivated only by relying on the path of deliberate deliberation (praśrabdha-mārga).

In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for contemplating the principles of the truths is extremely rapid, one cannot cultivate this wisdom.
The same principle applies to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
Now, at the time of the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it is subsumed under the path of leisure (*vilambitamārga*); therefore, one cultivates this wisdom.

In the abandonment of desire through cultivation, one currently cultivates, as appropriate, nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the four conventional and four dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*).

In the abandonment of the seven higher stages, one currently cultivates, as appropriate, all paths of uninterrupted transition, the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*), the conventional knowledges, and the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-jñāna* and *mārga-jñāna*).

In the preparatory stage for abandoning desire, one currently cultivates the mundane, dharma, and subsequent knowledges as appropriate, along with the four knowledges of superior progress while still possessing desire.
Above this, in the future, one cultivates all seven knowledges—namely, the mundane, dharma, subsequent, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
When abandoning the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one should practice, as appropriate, the first eight liberations and the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*) along with the two dharmas.
Regarding these, in the future as well, only seven are cultivated; however, with the exception of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is added.

In the abandonment of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and four subsequent paths (*anvaya-jñāna*) and two dharma-knowledges (*dharma-jñāna*) are respectively cultivated in the present; as for future cultivation, one cultivates six: the dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
In the abandonment of desire through cultivation, one currently cultivates the ninth liberation, the conventional knowledge, and the four dharma-knowledges as appropriate.

In the abandonment of the seven higher stages, one currently cultivates all the paths of liberation, the four subsequent knowledges, the conventional knowledge, and the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path as appropriate.
Regarding the abandonment of desire through cultivation, during the ninth path of superior progress, one abandons the eight higher stages.

In these cases, the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the four types of knowledge—the dharmajñāna, anvayajñāna, and so forth—are cultivated as appropriate.

When abandoning the seven higher stages and the first eight categories of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the various paths of superior progress, the conventional knowledge, the four types of knowledge (dharmajñāna, anvayajñāna, etc.), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) are cultivated as appropriate; this is because the supernormal powers previously cultivated may manifest at that time.
From this point upward, one cultivates all eight knowledges in the future—namely, conventional, dharma, inferential, the four truths, and knowledge of others' minds.

Since the four types of inferential knowledge cannot sever the defilements of the desire realm, and the two dharma-knowledges (of suffering and origin) are not the antidotes for the higher realms, by what cause would they arise as antidotes for those?
This wisdom is cultivated in the future.

If one were to allow that what is not an antidote is also cultivated [simultaneously], then when becoming free from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and so forth, one would have to cultivate conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as well.
This objection is unreasonable, because it is not accepted that only those things which are identical in being antidotes are cultivated in the future.

This means that cultivation is also admitted because of the existence of a relationship [between factors], such as when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); or it is because of mutual support through the power of causes, such as when cultivating the four categories concurrently at the time of abandoning desire, or when cultivating the dharmas of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) during the stage of abandoning the defilements of the higher realms.

If one has severed the defilements of the desire realm but does not cultivate subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and having severed those of the higher realms, does not cultivate the two knowledges of suffering and its origin, then for one who attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) through gradual stages, there would be no possibility for subsequent knowledge to arise and manifest; likewise, an arhat would have no occasion to give rise to the knowledges of suffering and its origin, because those previously acquired would all have been relinquished, and those not previously acquired would not be objects of cultivation.

By way of category, if one has previously attained [a wisdom], it serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that draws forth the arising of a subsequent wisdom of similar outflow (*niṣyanda*); because this [subsequent] wisdom is drawn forth by the former wisdom, it can in turn serve as a cause for that same category of wisdom.
Therefore, when this knowledge arises, it is supported by the power of its cause; although it does not directly counteract the same afflictions, it is nonetheless cultivated in the future.
Next, the attainment of the stage of no-more-learning through the abandonment of defilements is explained.
The verse says:

In the first moment of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one cultivates nine or ten [paths], due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties; the same applies to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*).
The treatise says:

Regarding the first moment of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): it refers to the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) that severs the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). One should, as appropriate, presently cultivate the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). Because it takes the Peak of Existence as its object, one should, as appropriate, presently cultivate the ninety [moments] of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

In the future, one should cultivate nine or ten knowledges as appropriate; that is to say, those of dull faculties cultivate all except the knowledge of non-arising, whereas those of sharp faculties also cultivate the knowledge of non-arising.
Next, the number of knowledges cultivated in the remaining stages will be explained.
The verse says:
In the path of uninterrupted transition for refining the faculties, the learner has six and the non-learner seven;
for others, the learner has six, seven, or eight; the one beyond training has eight, nine, or all.
In the uninterrupted path of the mixed cultivation of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the learner (*śaikṣa*) cultivates seven, while the adept (*aśaikṣa*) cultivates eight or nine;
in other paths, the learner cultivates eight, and the adept cultivates nine or all [nine].
When a noble one (*ārya*) gives rise to other qualities, as well as in all stages of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), [the same applies].
The extent of the wisdom cultivated should all be considered according to reason.
The Commentary states:

In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), when refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one cultivates in the present, as appropriate, the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the four types of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

In the future, one cultivates six [knowledges], because the four dharma-knowledges and four subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) are similar to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). One does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), as it cannot sever the obstacles; nor does one cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Regarding the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one currently cultivates the four dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges as appropriate.
Those who have not yet abandoned desire cultivate six future knowledges—the four belonging to the truths and the two of dharma and subsequent knowledge.
