Those who have already abandoned desire cultivate seven future knowledges, namely those same six plus the knowledge of others' minds.
Other masters say:

In the stage of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one also cultivates the mundane paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); accordingly, the four mundane dharmas and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are cultivated in the present.
For those who have not yet abandoned desire, seven [knowledges] are cultivated in the future.
Those who have already abandoned desire cultivate eight [knowledges], namely, the path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) including the knowledge of others' minds.

If they have not yet abandoned desire, they should presently cultivate four conventional knowledges and either the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), as appropriate; in the future, they likewise cultivate seven.

If one has already abandoned desire, the four conventional knowledges, the knowledge of types (*jñāna-anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds are cultivated as appropriate in the present; in the future, eight are also cultivated.

When an Arhat refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), during the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the four knowledges of types and two knowledges of dharmas (*dharma-jñāna*) are cultivated as appropriate in the present, while seven are cultivated in the future.

The four truths, the dharma-knowledge, and the subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are exhausted; one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), as in the case of treating the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); thus there are five.

Regarding the first eight liberations, one cultivates four types of subsequent-knowledge and two types of dharma-knowledge as appropriate for the present cultivation, while in the future cultivation, one cultivates all eight.

Regarding the four truths, the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna), the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of exhaustion—these four are cultivated in the ninth liberation according to their respective applications. As for the future cultivation, nine knowledges are cultivated.
In the final liberation, one currently cultivates the path of suffering, the path of origin, the path of cessation, and the path of cultivation as appropriate; in the future, one cultivates all ten.
In all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one currently cultivates as in the case of a learner (*śaikṣa*); in the future, one cultivates nine.

Regarding the various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*): for those of dull faculties, nine knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated accordingly in the present, and nine are also cultivated in the future.
For those of sharp faculties, ten knowledges are cultivated accordingly in the present, and ten are also cultivated in the future.

Regarding the mixed cultivation of the stages of realization (*śaikṣa*), in all uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), the four dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are cultivated as appropriate in the present; seven are cultivated in the future.
In all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there are only the four dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges, with conventional knowledge added during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
In all paths of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is further added as appropriate in the present, while eight are cultivated in the future in all cases.

Regarding the mixed cultivation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are cultivated in the present as they are for one in training; as for those cultivated in the future, there are eight for those of dull faculties and nine for those of sharp faculties.
As for the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there are only four: the dharmajñāna and anvayajñāna categories.
The preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) increases conventional knowledge; it is cultivated in the present according to what is appropriate.
Regarding that which is cultivated in the future: for those of dull faculties, nine knowledges; for those of sharp faculties, ten.
All paths of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) are identical to the path of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

In the five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) during the cultivation of supernormal powers by one in the stage of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is cultivated in the present, and seven [knowledges] are cultivated in the future.

Regarding the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the supernormal power of the divine ear (*ṛddhiviṣaya*), conventional knowledge is cultivated in the present during both the two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the five paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

Regarding the liberation through knowledge of others' minds (*paracittavimukti*), one currently cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds; furthermore, all superior progressions (*viśeṣagamana*) and, as appropriate, the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation are cultivated.
Beyond this, in the future, one cultivates all eight knowledges.

When one beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivates the supernormal powers, in the five paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), the present cultivation is as in the case of one still in training (śaikṣa); as for future cultivation, those of dull faculties cultivate eight, while those of sharp faculties cultivate nine.

In the paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) and the preparatory paths (prayoga-mārga), the present cultivation is as in the case of one still in training; as for future cultivation, those of dull faculties cultivate nine, while those of sharp faculties cultivate ten.
The various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) are the same as those for refining the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
As for the two paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) regarding the divine eye and divine ear, because they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are not termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

When a noble one (*ārya*) gives rise to the remaining four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth, which are subsumed under the category of "attained through cultivation" (*bhāvanāmaya*), at the time of these impure virtues (*sāsrava-guṇa*), one cultivates in the present only one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
For those in training (*śaikṣa*), seven future [attainments] are acquired by one who has not yet abandoned desire, while eight are acquired by one who has already abandoned it.

For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), nine are acquired by one of dull faculties and ten by one of sharp faculties; this excludes the *sūkṣma-sūkṣma* mind, because this [attainment] cultivates only the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) in the future.
If one gives rise to other untainted virtues (*anāsrava-guṇa*) that are subsumed under the dhyānas, one should practice, as appropriate, the four dharmajñānas and anvayajñānas in the present;
if they are subsumed under the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), one should practice only the four anvayajñānas in the present, as appropriate.
The future cultivation is the same as before regarding the contaminated [paths].

When an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) becomes free from passion, they cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the present; this applies to the ninth liberation during the abandonment of the desire realm and the three dhyānas, as well as to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for becoming free from passion by means of the superior path (*viśeṣa-mārga*) arising from the four fundamental dhyānas.
In the future, two are cultivated, namely, with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds; for the remainder, only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated in the future.

When cultivating the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), conventional knowledge is cultivated in the present during all paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and the first two paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*); in one path of liberation, both conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds are cultivated in the present.
In all paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), two [types of knowledge] manifest as appropriate; in the future, one cultivates both types in their entirety.
In the five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), only conventional knowledge manifests and is cultivated in the future.
When cultivating other merits based on the fundamental dhyānas, conventional knowledge alone manifests and is cultivated; in the future, one cultivates both.
Only the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) necessarily do not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds, because they are the immediate attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
When cultivating other meritorious qualities based on concentrations of other stages, all are cultivated only as conventional (*saṃvṛti*) knowledge in the present and future.
Regarding the future cultivation (*bhāvanā*), how many stages (*bhūmi*) are cultivated?
And are all acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise considered cultivation?
The verse says:
When one attains these paths, one cultivates the outflow-tainted qualities (*sāsrava*) of this stage;
to achieve detachment from them, one cultivates the outflow-free qualities (*anāsrava*) of this and lower stages.
Only at the first moment of exhaustion does one universally cultivate the outflow-tainted virtues of all nine stages.
When born in a higher stage, one does not cultivate the lower; what was previously attained is not cultivated [further]. The Commentary says:

When various paths rely upon a particular stage and when that stage is attained, one can cultivate the future out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas of that very stage. That is to say, when mundane or supramundane paths manifest in reliance upon a certain stage, one cultivates only the future out-flowing dharmas of that stage. This is because out-flowing dharmas are firmly bound to their respective stages and are difficult to cultivate elsewhere; thus, whichever stage one relies upon to become detached from the defilements of a lower stage, one cultivates only those dharmas belonging to that specific stage.

When the ninth liberation manifests before one, one also cultivates the future acquired meritorious qualities—both the fundamental and preparatory stages—that are tainted (*sāsrava*) and pertain to the higher levels; for by being freed from the bonds of the lower levels, one necessarily attains the higher ones.

When an Ārya is about to leave a given stage (*bhūmi*) or has attained it, as well as when the various paths within that stage manifest, they are all able to cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) [paths] of that stage and those below.

That is to say, whenever the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated preparatory (*prayoga*) and other paths of any stage are present before one, if one wishes to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that stage, one cultivates in the future the uncontainted paths of that stage and those below; for the lower [paths] are equally capable of counteracting the defilements of the higher stages.

Although the various upper stages possess antidotes capable of counteracting the afflictions when one cuts them off through the lower noble path (*āryamārga*), because the bonds of the outflowing states (*sāsrava*) to those stages are firm, one cannot cultivate those [antidotes] as long as one has not yet abandoned the lower stage.
Some say that one also cultivates those [attainments], because one gives rise to the acquisition of their abandonment.

Whichever stage one relies upon to become detached from the defilements of a lower stage, at the moment the ninth liberation-attainment manifests, one also cultivates for the future the untainted merits of the higher stages as well as all the lower stages that have been acquired.
Whenever the mundane or supramundane paths of this particular stage manifest in the present, one cultivates in the future all the untainted virtues of this stage as well as those of the lower stages.

However, when the initial *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) manifests, its power enables the universal cultivation of immeasurable superior virtues—such as the contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and meditation—which are comprised within the tainted mental states of the nine stages.

That is to say, whichever stage the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests in, one universally cultivates [the qualities] of the future, as well as those of one's own and higher and lower stages.
For what reason is it that at the very first moment of this knowledge of exhaustion, its power is able to universally cultivate all contaminated virtues?
Because it is capable of utterly extinguishing all roots of merit and the enemies that are the afflictions which have existed since beginningless time—
just as when a common enemy of a kingdom is subdued, everyone comes together to rejoice, rely [on the victor], and praise his excellence.
Furthermore, because the bonds of affliction have been severed without remainder, just as when the binder is severed the breath of the bound flows freely;
moreover, as that King of Mind ascends to the station of sovereignty, all wholesome dharmas arise and come to court.
For example, when a great king ascends the throne through consecration, all territories come to pay tribute;
yet, once born in a higher state, he certainly does not cultivate the roots of goodness of lower states.

That is to say, while one in the desire realm attains arhatship, they cultivate the wholesome roots of all nine stages across the three realms; however, upon being born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they cultivate the wholesome roots of only that single stage.

The initial mention of "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) indicates that in the ninth path of liberation during the abandonment of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as well as in the five stages of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one abandons the preceding paths because one has newly attained the fruit.

Although one can also cultivate conventional knowledge of one's own stage and lower stages at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), this was already discussed previously and is therefore not treated here again.
Regarding all that is called "cultivation," it refers exclusively to what was previously unobtained and is now being aroused and obtained.
This constitutes both the object and the agent of cultivation;
that is to say, only that which was previously unobtained and is now obtained through the application of effort is truly what is cultivated.
If a dharma was previously acquired and then abandoned, even if it is acquired again now, it is not something that has been cultivated, because it was not realized through the exertion of effort.
If, however, a dharma arises that was not previously acquired, and it arises through the application of extreme effort due to its superior power, only then can one cultivate future merit.

If one has previously attained [a dharma] and it now arises and manifests, one cannot cultivate future merits therein; for it does not arise through great effort, its power is inferior, and its cultivation and function have ceased, thus one cannot cultivate the future.

If that which has already been attained and manifested can be cultivated for the future, then when the Bhagavat attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he would not yet have fully cultivated all meritorious qualities.

To fully realize them, he would have to cultivate further, in which case his meritorious qualities would be incomplete, just as those of the two vehicles. Is it then the case that "cultivation" is spoken of solely with respect to attainment?
It is not so. Why?
There are four kinds of cultivation: first, cultivation by acquisition; second, cultivation by practice; third, cultivation as an antidote; and fourth, cultivation by elimination.
Upon what basis are these four types of cultivation established?
The verse says:
The establishment of the cultivation of acquisition and the cultivation of practice is based upon wholesome conditioned phenomena.
Based upon all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), one establishes the cultivation of elimination (*prahāṇabhāvanā*) and the cultivation of purification (*viśodhanabhāvanā*).
The commentary states:

Because one attains through mixed cultivation both the manifestation of previously unattained qualities and the acquisition of remaining future qualities, these are all termed "cultivation by attainment" (*pratilambhabhāvanā*).
When previously unattained virtues arise for the first time and are currently cultivated, both are termed "cultivation through practice" (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*).
These two types of cultivation are established solely based on conditioned wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskṛta*).

Regarding future phenomena, there is only "cultivation through acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*); regarding present phenomena, both are fully present. Because one acquires the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for the body and other such factors, those body and other factors which are to be countered are termed "cultivation through antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).
Therefore, when one attains the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) regarding the body and so forth, it is said that one is practicing cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the body and so forth.
This should likewise apply to other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Because the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take the body and so forth as their objects are abandoned, the cultivation of the removal (*vibhāvanā*) of the dharmas such as the body is spoken of.
Therefore, when afflictions directed toward the body and so forth are abandoned, it is also said that one is "cultivating" the body and so forth.
This should likewise apply by analogy to other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
Since these two types of cultivation are established solely based on contaminated phenomena, wholesome contaminated phenomena possess all four kinds of cultivation.
Untainted conditioned phenomena and other tainted phenomena each possess both the two types of cultivation—prior and subsequent—respectively.
Within this context, some distinguish the number of cultivations possessed by various phenomena based on the sense of "that which is to be cultivated."

There are dharmas that possess all four [characteristics] and are termed "to be cultivated" (*bhāvanīya*); there are dharmas that possess three, some that possess two, some that possess one, and some that possess none at all.
Specifically, when wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas have not yet been permanently severed, they can be acquired and produced, thus possessing all four characteristics in their entirety.

Because this has not yet been permanently severed, one should fully cultivate it through the cultivation of remediation; because it can be attained, one should fully cultivate it through the cultivation of attainment; and because it is capable of arising, one should fully cultivate it through the cultivation of practice.
Those that have already been acquired possess three types of cultivation, excluding the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired (*aprāpti*).

Those that are not subject to arising possess three types, excluding the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), the cultivation of what has already been acquired, and the cultivation of what is not subject to arising or what is unobtainable (*aprāpti*).
Those that have already arisen possess two types, namely: the cultivation of counteracting and eliminating (*pratipakṣa-nirdhāvana-bhāvanā*) regarding defiled and neutral states.
The same applies to those that have not yet been abandoned.

When wholesome contaminated dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala*) have been permanently abandoned, there are two types of possession regarding those that can be acquired and can arise: namely, the possession of acquisition (*prāpti*) and the possession of cultivation (*vāsanā*). Regarding those that can be acquired but cannot arise, there is one type of possession, namely acquisition. Regarding those already acquired that can arise, there is one type of possession, namely cultivation.
It should be understood that the same applies to conditioned untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).

With the exception of those previously mentioned, all [other cases] are entirely non-existent; that is to say, among untainted phenomena, there are those already attained that do not arise, and so forth.

If one were to claim that a phenomenon which does not arise within the body is nonetheless called "cultivated" (*bhāvita*) merely by virtue of its attainment (*prāpti*), then one must also admit that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is likewise called "cultivated," for there is no distinction between the two cases.
This objection is irrational, because those factors of the same class (sajāti-dharma) abide within the body.
That is to say, although factors that are not destined to arise do not abide in the body, there is no error in designating them as "cultivated" (bhāvanā) when their counterparts do abide in the body.

Furthermore, because that [non-arising] abides as a result of having attained [the state of non-arising], it means that wholesome dharmas do not arise in the future; by causing them to arise, it is manifested as abiding as a result.
The meaning is: "We lack the necessary conditions and thus do not arise," rather than saying that they are not being summoned at this present time.
*Pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) is different from this and cannot be used as an analogy.
Furthermore, while future dharmas do not arise as wholesome phenomena, they are nevertheless sustained and benefited by the power of their causes;
this is not the case for analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and thus it lacks the sense of being "cultivated.
Moreover, because analytical cessation is solely a fruit, cultivation—which is fundamentally undertaken to obtain a superior fruit—is inappropriate for cessation, as it possesses no further fruit.

Furthermore, because analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is neither increased nor decreased, it cannot be cultivated. That is to say, the dharmas subject to cultivation may proceed from the inferior to the middling, or from the middling to the superior;
analytical cessation is not like this. Since it serves no purpose in cultivation, it cannot be cultivated.
Having thus already distinguished the various types of knowledge (*jñāna*), the virtues accomplished through that knowledge shall now be revealed.
Among these, the unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) of a Buddha shall first be discussed.
Specifically, at the moment of attaining the *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) upon initial enlightenment, there are eighteen kinds of unique Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*).
What are the eighteen?
The verse says:
The eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) are said to be the ten powers of the Buddha and so forth.
The treatise says:
The ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion—these combined are called the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
They are cultivated exclusively at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) by the Buddhas; since they do not exist in other noble ones (*ārya*), they are called "unique."
Furthermore, what are the distinctions among the Buddha’s ten powers?
The verse says:
The powers consist of ten [factors] regarding the possible and the impossible; [Of these], eight are the same as the [ten] paths of action, excluding cessation and the path.
The faculties, roots, inclinations, and elements are nine; the knowledge of the path leading everywhere is nine or ten.
The knowledge of past lives and of death and rebirth are conventional; the knowledge of exhaustion consists of six or ten knowledges.
The knowledge of past lives and of death and rebirth rely on the dhyānas; the remaining supernormal powers rely on the [four] meditative absorptions.
The male being of Jambudvīpa [perceives] the Buddha-body, because there is no obstruction regarding the object.
The treatise says:

Regarding the ten powers (*bala*) of the Buddha, the first is the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). It takes all ten knowledges of the Tathāgata as its nature. To know that the functional capacity and principle of all phenomena are definitively existent is called the knowledge of the possible (*sthāna-jñāna*).
Knowing that the functional nature and principle of all phenomena are definitively non-existent is termed the knowledge of the impossible (*asthānajñāna*).
This knowledge universally takes both sentient and insentient objects as its domain and is not in contradiction with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Fearing that it might be difficult to realize [the meaning] through a brief explanation due to its limited scope, he has further extracted the remaining nine from within this [chapter].

The power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma (*karmavipākajñānabala*) has eight knowledges as its nature, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). That is to say, the unimpeded knowledge that correctly discriminates how such types of karma produce such types of various matured fruits is called the power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma.

Alternatively, it is called the power of knowledge regarding one’s own karma (*karmasvakajñānabala*). This refers to the unimpeded knowledge that skillfully discerns how such a kind of fruit is summoned by the power of one’s own performed karma and cannot be taken away or given by others such as a wife or children; and that such a kind of karma will necessarily produce its own fruit and cannot be traded for another—this is called the power of knowledge regarding one’s own karma.

The third is the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*); the fourth is the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*) of beings; the fifth is the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (*adhimukti*); and the sixth is the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*dhātu*). These four powers all consist of nine types of knowledge, excluding only the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). That is to say, the unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the intrinsic natures of the meditative absorptions and so forth—such as their acquisition, skillful means, maintenance, relish (*āsvādana*), purity (*śuddha*), the untainted (*anāsrava*), and the stages of retrogression, stability, progress, and the factors conducive to penetration—is called the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions and so forth.
The characteristics of the dhyānas and so forth shall be explained in the section on concentration (*samādhi*).

If one knows, as it truly is, the distinctions among the categories of faculties (*indriya*) by which various classes of sentient beings can attain superior qualities, this is called the power of knowledge regarding the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriyaparāparajñānabala*).

Although there are those of medium faculties who depend upon superior or inferior [faculties], they are not separately identified because they are subsumed under the categories of inferior or superior.
What dharma does this term "medium faculty" refer to?
It refers to those such as faith (śraddhā) belonging to one who has severed the roots of virtue (samucchinna-kuśalamūla).
Within the total continuum, there are also past and future states; these include wholesome dharmas such as faith, or the faculties such as the mind.

If one possesses unimpeded knowledge that knows, according to reality, the differences in the inclinations and pleasures of various classes of sentient beings, this is called the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of superior resolutions (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*). This is because "inclination" and "pleasure" are designated as the specific distinctions [of those resolutions].

If one possesses unimpeded knowledge that, as they truly are, knows the various distinctions among the dispositions, latent tendencies, and natures of phenomena formed through the repeated practice of sentient beings since beginningless time, this is called the power of knowing the diversity of elements (*nānādhātu-jñāna-bala*).
It should be understood that herein, "elements" (*dhātu*), "dispositions" (*āśaya*), "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*), and "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) are merely different names for the same thing.
Since these four powers all take conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their object, they comprise only nine of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).

Regarding the seventh power, the knowledge of the paths leading to various destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*), the term "or" (*vā*) indicates that there are two interpretations of this meaning: if it is held that this power takes as its object only the various paths leading [to those destinations], it consists of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*);
if it is held that it also takes as its object the fruits toward which those paths lead, it has all ten knowledges as its nature.

That is to say, knowing the causes and effects of birth and death as they truly are, and possessing unimpeded knowledge of the path to their cessation, is called the power of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*).

The eighth is the power of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*), and the ninth is the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñānabala*); both of these powers are of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

Because there is a distinction between these two powers, it is said: the unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the differences in the past lives of oneself and others is called the eighth power;
if one possesses the unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the rebirths of all classes of sentient beings in future existences, this is called the ninth power.
A detailed discussion of these two is as found in the section on the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Regarding the tenth power, the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*), the word "also" (*vā*) indicates that there are two interpretations of its meaning. If it is held that this power takes only the destruction of the outflows as its object, it consists of six knowledges—excluding the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of others' minds.
If it is held that it also takes the means for the destruction of the outflows as its object, it has all ten knowledges as its nature.

This is indeed logical, for within the analysis of their characteristics, it is stated that both the knowledge regarding exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and the unimpeded knowledge regarding that which leads to exhaustion (*kṣayāya-dharmajñāna*) are termed the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).

These latter three powers are identical to the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); because these three among the six supernormal knowledges are particularly preeminent, they are established as the three clear knowledges (*vidyā*) in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and when residing in the body of a Tathāgata, they are likewise called powers.
The supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya*) and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), even when present in the body of a Buddha, do not have great utility;

therefore, they are not designated as "powers" (*bala*). For instance, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is able to perceive the differences in the maturation (*vipāka*) within the good and evil destinies of sentient beings. Because this can induce the arising of a distinguished wisdom and allows for the correct understanding of the karma that brings about those results, it is established under the name of the "knowledge of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).
The supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhi*) and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) do not possess such great utility; therefore, those two are not established as powers (*bala*).

However, the power of knowing others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is not mentioned separately because its meaning is already subsumed within the powers of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, since mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are included among the faculties of others.

Furthermore, the Bhagavān possesses all-encompassing wisdom and has attained mastery even in fields such as the arts and sciences; yet, since his buddha-activities are fully accomplished through these alone, other forms of knowledge have no distinct or superior utility therein. Therefore, although they exist, they are not mentioned separately, for it is solely by means of the ten objects of knowledge that the Buddha’s universal awakening fulfills all that he ought to do.

What are the ten objects of knowledge? They are: the meaning of cause and non-cause among all phenomena; the distinctions between the karmic fruits of the manifold scattered stages (*vicitra-vikṣipta-bhūmi*); the different categories of qualities in the meditative stages (*samāhita-bhūmi*); the differences in the faculties, inclinations, and elements of the sentient beings to be converted; the distinctions between the causes and effects of the remedial and the remediated; the different experiences of the past and future limits; and the diverse skillful means for the non-continuation of defilement. Since the Buddha’s work is accomplished solely by awakening to these, whether other things exist or not results in neither benefit nor loss; therefore, only these ten are designated as "powers" (*bala*).
Furthermore, when the Buddha observes the sentient beings to be converted, he establishes teachings according to their capacities; for this purpose, only ten knowledges are required.
That is to say, by means of the first knowledge, he observes whether the beings to be converted are capable or incapable within the various vehicles.
By means of the second knowledge, one observes the distinctions among karmic obstructions within the mental continuums of those to be converted;

by means of the third knowledge, one observes the distinctions in the lightness or heaviness of the afflictions—whether they possess flavor or are flavorless—that act as obstructions for those to be converted within their meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). By knowing these two causes, one also knows the ripening obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
By means of the fourth knowledge, one observes the distinctions in the functional capacities of the purified categories among those beings to be converted;
by means of the fifth knowledge, one observes the distinctions in the preparatory applications toward the categories of realization and purity among those beings to be converted.
By means of the sixth wisdom, one observes that the beings to be converted differ in their dispositions and inclinations regarding the category of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).

By means of the seventh wisdom, one observes the various beneficial and non-beneficial activities of those to be converted, and correctly contemplates and cultivates tranquility (*śamatha*) regarding these diverse distinctions.
By means of the eighth knowledge, one observes the distinctions accumulated by those beings to be converted throughout their past lives;
by means of the ninth knowledge, one observes the distinctions regarding their rebirth-linking in future lives.

Because the tenth wisdom observes that there are differences in the skillful means for attaining liberation by those beings to be converted, if any one of these ten wisdoms were lacking, the task of converting sentient beings would not be complete; furthermore, it would often be useless. Therefore, they are neither increased nor decreased.

The essential nature has already been explained. Regarding their distinction by way of the levels (*bhūmi*): the eighth and ninth [supernormal powers] rely on the four dhyānas; the remaining eight arise based on all eleven levels. These eleven levels consist of the desire realm, the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Such is the total number of levels upon which these various sublime qualities depend.

Having already distinguished them by their basis in terms of level (*bhūmi*) and physical body (*āśraya*), it should be understood that they all rely on the male body of a Buddha in Jambudvīpa, for only this serves as a fit basis for such power.

If these ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) exist among the followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*) as well, why is it that they receive the designation "powers" (*bala*) only when residing in a Buddha?

That which receives the name "power" (bala) is defined as unimpeded functioning; because the Buddha’s wisdom functions without impediment toward its objects, it is designated as a power, whereas others are not so. This is because even the followers of the two vehicles cannot perceive the roots of goodness conducive to liberation within the mental continuums of sentient beings, let alone know other profound and subtle matters.

For example, although Śāriputra abandoned his quest for liberation, he was unable to perceive the number of births of the pigeon being pursued by the hawk during its past and future limits; likewise, Mahāmaudgalyāyana could not perceive the distinctions among the various hungry ghosts led by the winds of karma. Therefore, the divine eye and other supernormal powers of the two vehicles differ from those of the Buddha regarding the distance and proximity of realms; because they are not unimpeded, they are not called "powers."
Since the two vehicles and the Buddha are alike in having exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), for what reason is that wisdom called "power" only in the case of the Buddha?
It is because only the World-Honored One possesses the specific wisdom that universally penetrates the distinct characteristics of the exhaustion of all outflows in all sentient beings.

This means that the Bhagavat possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding all categories and distinctions of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) among sentient beings; the two vehicles do not possess this. Therefore, the name "power" (*bala*) belongs exclusively to the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is because the wisdom of the Buddhas alone is fierce and sharp.
How is it fierce and sharp?

It is because the power of the Buddha’s wisdom can swiftly sever the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). This is like individuals of strong or weak strength using sharp or dull blades to cut grass and other vegetation.
Since the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) are no different among all classes of sentient beings, how does the Buddha perceive various realms (*dhātu*)?

Although the characteristics of the aggregates are the same for all sentient beings, there is nonetheless no lack of distinction within them. That is to say, while the substance of those aggregates is without difference, there are immeasurable varieties of dissimilarity; the Buddha knows these exactly as they are without any obstruction. Therefore, the World-Honored One possesses the power of knowledge regarding the various realms.

Furthermore, the names and reputations of the Tathāgatas are lofty and far-reaching; their rarefied wisdom and wondrous functions are boundless. Only a Buddha can know them—they are not to be fathomed by others. Since there are no distinct characteristics within what others perceive, how could it be surprising that the Tathāgata can perceive distinct characteristics?
Having already explained the general principles regarding the power of the Buddhas' minds, we shall now explain the physical power achieved by a Bodhisattva at that time.
The verse says:
The body has the strength of Nārāyaṇa, or else every joint possesses it.
The elephant and other [strengths] increase by multiples of seventy; this has the sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) as its nature.
The treatise says:
The physical strength of the Buddha’s birth-body is equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.
Other masters say:
"Each and every limb and joint of the Buddha’s body possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
In reality, the physical power of all Buddhas is boundless, just like their mental power, because it is able to sustain the great merit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

The Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), the Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha), and the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) have their limbs and joints connected in successive order, resembling a dragon’s banner-knots or interlocking chains; therefore, when these three are compared, there is a distinction in the superiority or inferiority of their strength.
What is the measure of the strength of Nārāyaṇa?
It is ten times greater than each of the seven strengths, beginning with the elephant, increasing tenfold at each stage.

These are: the ordinary elephant, the fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*), the mahānagna, the prasaṃkhyāta, the vāraṇa, the cāṇūra, and the nārāyaṇa; each subsequent one possesses ten times the strength of the preceding.
Some say that the preceding sixty [units] increase tenfold each time, such that they equal the strength of half a Nārāyaṇa; a thousand times this strength constitutes a full Nārāyaṇa.
Other masters say:
its measure is like the strength of a thousand Airāvaṇa celestial elephant-kings.
What is the measure of this elephant king’s strength?

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were about to go for recreation in the pleasure groves, the elephant king, having known this, manifested various heads adorned in diverse ways and proceeded to the celestial palace.

The retinues of these devas number in the thousands; mounted upon them, they soar into the air as lightly as if holding a birch leaf, swiftly arriving at pleasure gardens to enjoy themselves as they wish.
Such is the power and majesty of the great celestial elephant kings, a force a thousand times greater than that of Nārāyaṇa.
Among these various explanations, only the former is largely reasonable.
Thus, the nature of bodily strength consists of the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*); this should be understood as comprising all the varieties of tangibles.
Some say it consists solely of the distinctions among the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Some say it is a tangible derived from the primary elements, existing apart from the [other] seven;
others say that strength is heaviness, while weakness is lightness.
Such is called the power of the Buddha’s birth-body (*janmakāya*).
What are the specific characteristics of the four fearlessnesses of a Buddha?
The verse says:
The four fearlessnesses correspond in order to the first, the twelfth, and the seventh powers.
The treatise says:
The four fearlessnesses of the Buddha are explained at length in the sūtras.
First is the fearlessness of being perfectly awakened, which has the ten knowledges as its nature, just like the first power.
The second is the fearlessness regarding the permanent exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-vaiśāradya*), which has sixty cognitions as its nature, like the tenth power.
The third is the fearlessness regarding the teaching of obstructive dharmas (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*), which has eight cognitions as its nature, like the second power.
The fourth is the fearlessness regarding the path leading out [of suffering], which consists of ninety types of knowledge, as in the seventh power.
For what reason are there only four such fearlessnesses of the Buddhas?
It is because by this very measure, the perfection of both one’s own and others’ virtues is revealed to be ultimate in the Blessed Buddha.

That is to say, the first fearlessness reveals the perfection of the Buddha World-Honored One’s own wisdom, while the second fearlessness reveals the perfection of the Buddha World-Honored One’s own abandonment; these two demonstrate that the Buddha’s virtues for his own benefit are fulfilled.
To manifest the Blessed One’s perfection of altruistic virtue, the latter two fearlessnesses are further explained.

The third fearlessness prevents one from following wrong paths, while the fourth fearlessness leads one toward the right path; that is to say, the Buddha teaches his disciples in various places regarding obstructive factors so that they may be abandoned, which is precisely the means for cultivating the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, in various places he teaches the path of deliverance to his disciples and causes them to practice correctly; this is precisely causing them to cultivate the skillful means of the virtue of wisdom.
These two demonstrate that the Buddha’s virtue of benefiting others is perfected.

However, because these four, according to their respective applications, manifest the Buddha’s perfection of wisdom and abandonment—both for himself and for others—to their ultimate limit, only four are established.
How can it be said that fearlessness is itself wisdom? One should rather say that fearlessness is that which is accomplished by wisdom.
In truth, this is indeed so; however, it is to demonstrate that fearlessness has wisdom as its proximate cause that the essence of fearlessness is derived from wisdom.
Now, fearlessness means the absence of timidity or dread; because one does not fear others due to the possession of wisdom, wisdom serves as the causal nature of fearlessness.

Only the four sublime knowledges of the Buddha are the causes of the four fearlessnesses; that is to say, the sublime knowledge of all phenomena in all their aspects possessed by the Tathāgatas is the cause of the first fearlessness.
The sublime wisdom of all Tathāgatas that has severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies is the second cause of fearlessness.
The sublime wisdom of all Tathāgatas that knows whether the assembly of disciples will suffer loss or gain is the cause of the subsequent fearlessness.

Alternatively, the essence of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) consists of the four types of sublime wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*). "Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to timidity; it signifies the sense of harboring terror due to a lack of thorough comprehension regarding the Dharma. Wisdom possesses the capacity to directly counteract this fear and is diametrically opposed to it; therefore, it is called "fearlessness."
Is it not the case that the absence of wisdom (*ajñāna*) is itself the essence of fear? How then can you say that the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*) is itself fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*)?
This objection is not valid, because wisdom serves as the direct antidote to many factors, just as the absence of doubt (*niḥsaṃśaya*) does.

That is to say, just as wisdom (*jñāna*) can directly counteract ignorance (*ajñāna*), it also possesses the capacity to directly counteract fear; therefore, it receives the name "wisdom" and is also called "fearlessness.
Just as it counteracts ignorance, it can also counteract doubt; therefore, it receives the name "wisdom" and is also called "certainty" (*niścaya*).
Although the ignorance that is to be remedied is not itself doubt, since wisdom is free from doubt, these two are said to be identical in essence.

Likewise, although the absence of ignorance differs from fearlessness, the term "fearlessness" refers directly to the essence of wisdom; for a single wholesome factor is capable of severing many unwholesome states.
Some say that the essence of fearlessness also includes non-knowledge; therefore, one should not raise an objection regarding this point.
What is the difference between the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)?
There is no difference, for their essence is in both cases knowledge (*jñāna*).
However, within the essence of wisdom, it is designated as "power" (*bala*) based on one specific meaning, and established as "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*) based on another.
Specifically, the cause of not being overcome is called "power," while the cause of not being timid or afraid is called "fearlessness."
Alternatively, the initial establishment [of the teaching] is called "power" (*bala*), while remaining unshakable once established is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
Or, not being subdued by others is called "power," while being able to subdue others is called "fearlessness."
Other masters say:
For example, just as a skilled physician who thoroughly understands medical treatises is said to possess "power," and one who effectively cures various ailments is said to possess "fearlessness";
others say that being robust and agile is called "power," while being courageous and undaunted is called "fearlessness."
These two meanings are also distinct: the meaning of accomplishing tasks is the meaning of power (*bala*), and the meaning of being free from timidity is the meaning of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
What are the specific characteristics of the Buddha’s three foundations of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*)?
The verse says:
The three applications of mindfulness consist of mindfulness and wisdom, taking as their objects conditions that are favorable, unfavorable, or both.
The commentary says:
The Buddha’s three foundations of mindfulness are explained at length in the sūtras.

When the assembly of disciples is consistently respectful and able to correctly receive and practice the teaching, the Tathāgata does not give rise to joy on account of this; rather, he remains equanimous, dwelling in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. This is called the Tathāgata’s first foundation of mindfulness.

When the assembly of disciples is disrespectful and does not correctly practice what they have received, the Tathāgata does not give rise to sorrow or distress on account of this; rather, he remains equanimous, dwelling in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. This is called the Tathāgata’s second application of mindfulness.

Among the assembly of disciples, some are respectful and are able to correctly receive and practice [the teaching], while others are disrespectful and do not correctly receive and practice it; the Tathāgata, regarding this, gives rise to neither joy nor sorrow, but remains equanimous, dwelling in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension—this is called the Tathāgata’s third application of mindfulness.

Although those being transformed do not respectfully receive and practice [the teaching], the Buddha, the World-Honored One, still rains down the rain of Dharma; by means of this expedient, they or other sentient beings may at a later time enter the True Dharma.

It is not that what was previously stated as four is now restated as three; rather, one may say in total that there are seven applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This is because the present three are subsumed within the previous four, specifically being included within the application of mindfulness to external phenomena (*bahirdhā-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).

However, the substance of these three types [of faculties] generally comprises both mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*; i.e., correct awareness, *samprajanya*). This means that by abiding in right mindfulness and right awareness, one does not give rise to joy or sorrow regarding the three objects.

One cannot observe that certain great śrāvakas do not give rise to joy or sorrow regarding the three objects and then conclude that these three types are not the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Buddha; for it is only the Buddha who has abandoned them along with their habitual tendencies and who thoroughly understands the distinctions between the dispositions of sentient beings.

If a community of disciples were to belong to the Tathāgata, they would necessarily experience extreme joy or sorrow when encountering favorable or adverse circumstances; that the Buddha can remain unmoved by these is truly marvelous. However, for those who do not belong to the Śrāvakas, remaining unmoved is not considered extraordinary. Therefore, this quality is designated as "unshared" (āveṇika) exclusively with respect to the Buddha.
How do the various aspects of the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of all Buddhas differ?
The verse says:
Great compassion is exclusively conventional wisdom; It is distinguished by its provisions, its mode of activity, and its object.
Because it is impartial and of the highest degree, compassion differs [from great compassion] due to eight causes.
The treatise says:

The Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Tathāgata has conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as its nature; it takes all sentient beings universally as its object and functions with the three aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering, such as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), and so forth. Therefore, it is not untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*); such is the principle.
By what meaning is this name "Great Compassion" established?
It is established as "great" based on five meanings.
First, it is great by virtue of its provisions (*sambhāra*); that is, because it is accomplished through the vast provisions of merit and wisdom.
Second, it is great by way of its mode of activity (*ākāra*), meaning that this power is able to apply its mode of activity toward the objects of the three types of suffering.
Third, it is great by way of its object (*ālambana*), meaning that it takes all sentient beings of the three realms as its collective object.
Fourth, it is great by virtue of its equality, meaning that it brings about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings equally.
Fifth, it is great by virtue of its excellence, meaning that it is of the highest degree, such that no other compassion can equal it.
Other masters say:

It is designated as "Great Compassion" because it is realized through great application, because it is accomplished only by the body of a Great Being (mahāsattva), because it is included among the precious jewels of great merit, and because it is able to extract sentient beings from their great suffering and affliction.
What is the distinction between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
These two are distinguished by eight causes.
First, by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): they differ because their intrinsic natures are respectively non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and non-delusion (*amoha*).
Second, by way of the physical basis (*āśraya*): because they differ in that one is based on a body common to others, while the other is based on a body unique to a Buddha.
Third, by way of the aspect (*ākāra*): because one has the aspect of a single suffering, whereas the three have the aspects of the three types of suffering.
Fourth, by way of the object (*ālambana*): because one has a single realm as its object, while the three have all three realms as their objects.
Fifth, by way of the basis (*āśraya*), because it differs from others in that it pertains to the fourth *dhyāna*.
Sixth, by way of realization (*pratilambha*), because there is a difference in the realization of freedom from desire for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, there is a distinction between those who first cultivate compassion and then attain freedom from passion, and those who attain it through freedom from passion alone.
Seventh, by way of the difference in rescuing hopes for the accomplishment of goals, because the rescues differ;
eighth, by way of the difference in compassion toward those who are equal and those who are unequal, because the compassions differ.
Other masters say:

The great compassion of all Buddhas is far-reaching, subtle, pervasive, and capable of universally benefiting all; the compassionate minds arising in those such as the śrāvakas cannot extend pity to the form and formless realms, whereas the Buddhas give rise to a mind of supreme compassion toward the higher realms that exceeds the compassion of the two vehicles even for the Avīci hell.
Having already distinguished the qualities of a Buddha from those of other sentient beings,
are these qualities identical when Buddhas are compared with one another?
The verse says:
Regarding the provisions, the Dharma-body, the benefit of others, the Buddha-nature,
and the similarities [of Buddhas], there are differences among all Buddhas in terms of lifespan, lineage, and magnitude. The commentary says:

All Buddhas are equal by virtue of three factors: first, because their accumulations are equally perfected; second, because their dharma-bodies are equally accomplished; and third, because their benefit for others is equally consummated.
Due to differences in lifespan, lineage, physical stature, and so forth, there may be distinctions among the Buddhas when compared with one another.

"Difference in lifespan" means that the lifespans of Buddhas vary in length; "difference in lineage" means that Buddhas are born into the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes; "difference in clan name" means that Buddhas have surnames such as Gautama, Kāśyapa, and others; and "difference in stature" means that the bodies of Buddhas vary in size.

The word "etc. indicates that there are differences among the Buddhas regarding such matters as the duration for which their teachings remain; this is because the capacities and dispositions of the sentient beings to be converted differ according to the time of each Buddha's appearance in the world.
Those who possess wisdom, reflecting upon these three kinds of perfect qualities of the Tathāgata, will give rise to profound love and reverence.
What are these three? First, the perfection of causes; second, the perfection of results; and third, the perfection of benefits.
Regarding the first, the perfection of causes, there are again four kinds:
First, cultivation without remainder, because there is no omission in the cultivation of the two types of provisions—merit and wisdom;
second, cultivation over a long duration, because one cultivates without weariness throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
third, uninterrupted cultivation, because one cultivates with diligent vigor, moment by moment, without cessation.
Fourth is the cultivation of reverence, which consists of cultivating respect for what has been studied without any sense of attachment or stinginess, and practicing without pride.
Next, the excellence of the perfection of the fruit also comprises four kinds:

first, the excellence of the perfection of wisdom; second, the excellence of the perfection of abandonment; third, the excellence of the perfection of majestic power; and fourth, the excellence of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
The perfection of wisdom has four aspects:
first, teacherless wisdom; second, all-encompassing wisdom; third, wisdom of all modes; and fourth, effortless wisdom.
The perfection of abandonment has four aspects:

There are four kinds of abandonment: first, the abandonment of all afflictions; second, the abandonment of all obstacles to meditative concentration; third, ultimate abandonment; and fourth, abandonment together with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*). There are four kinds of the perfection of sovereign power (*vaśitā*):

first, the sovereign power of mastery over the transformation, manifestation, and maintenance of external objects; second, the sovereign power of mastery over the lifespan, whether shortening it or extending it; third, the sovereign power of mastery over traveling swiftly through space or obstructions, over great distances, and over the mutual entry of the small and the large; and fourth, the sovereign power that causes the various inherent natures of the world to become naturally superior, marvelous, and extraordinary.
The perfect virtue of majestic power further consists of four kinds:

first, the ability to transform those who are difficult to transform; second, the ability to resolve doubts when answering difficult questions; third, the ability to ensure liberation through the establishment of the teaching; and fourth, the ability to subdue evil factions.
The perfect virtues of the form body (*rūpakāya*) are fourfold:
first, being endowed with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*); second, being endowed with the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
Third, he possesses great power;
fourth, the bones within his body are as firm as adamant,
while the divine light radiating from his exterior surpasses that of hundreds of thousands of suns.

Subsequently, the virtue of perfected grace (*phala-sampad-guṇa*) also consists of four kinds: namely, causing [beings] to be eternally liberated from the three evil destinies and saṃsāra, or being able to establish them in the three vehicles within the good destinies.
Such, in brief, are the perfect virtues of the Tathāgata.

If analyzed individually, they are infinite; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know and explain them, for even if he were to maintain his life-force for many great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he could not finish explaining them all.
Thus, it is revealed that the body of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses boundless, extraordinary, and marvelous causes, effects, and virtues, like a great mountain of jewels.

Yet there are foolish people who, being themselves destitute of various virtues, cannot believe in or revere such a mountain of the Buddha’s merits and the Dharma he has taught, even upon hearing of them.
When those who possess wisdom hear such a teaching, they give rise to a profound faith that penetrates to the very marrow of their bones.
By means of that single moment of supreme and profound faith, they eliminate boundless indeterminate evil karma and embrace the excellence of human and celestial realms, as well as *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata appears in the world as the unsurpassed field of merit for all wise ones, because by relying upon him, one brings forth the empty, desirable, excellent, swift, and ultimate fruit.
As the Blessed One himself spoke in verse:
“If one can plant even a small portion of merit In the field of merit that is the Buddha,
One will first attain a superior realm of existence, And later shall certainly attain nirvāṇa.”
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle 36.
*Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, Fascicle 37. Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight, Part Three: On Discriminative Wisdom. Having already explained the unique qualities of the Tathāgata, the shared qualities shall now be analyzed.
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are other Buddha-qualities shared with other noble ones and ordinary beings, namely:
the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and other such virtues.
The treatise says:

The Blessed One further possesses immeasurable qualities in common with other noble ones and ordinary beings, namely: the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

According to what is appropriate: that is to say, the first three gates are shared only with other noble ones (*ārya*), while the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth, are also shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Although all the qualities within the Buddha’s body are superior in their purity, characteristics, and mastery compared to the qualities of the śrāvakas and others, they are nevertheless termed "shared" based on their commonality of category.
Furthermore, among the three qualities shared with other noble ones, what is the absence of conflict (*araṇā*)?
The verse says:
The absence of conflict is conventional knowledge, attained in the final dhyāna, and is unshakable.
In the three continents, with respect to those not yet arisen, there are the afflictions of the desire realm that possess objects.
The treatise says:

There are arhats who, recollecting many past lives, gave rise to afflictions of both self and others while assuming various types of bodies; because of this continuity, they experienced undesirable fruits, and thus they formed this thought:

If even a body possessed of afflictions gives rise to delusion when taken as an object and still invites bitter fruit, how much more so for a body free from afflictions and endowed with superior virtues?

Having reflected thus, one generates such a cognition of signs; through this skillful means, one causes other sentient beings not to give rise to attachment, aversion, or other defilements by taking one's own person as an object.

This knowledge has conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as its nature, because it takes as its object the future defilements to be abandoned through cultivation; it is not an outflow-free knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that operates with such a mode of activity (*ākāra*).
If the essence of the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) were subsumed under knowledge, how could one speak of "cultivating the meditative concentration of the absence of conflict"?
This is not contradictory, because a single category of associated factors possesses many qualities, and only one is mentioned according to the context.
It is like a mountain that contains various kinds of things, yet it is named after one particular kind as a designation for the whole.

In principle, non-contention (*araṇā*) should be subsumed under wisdom (*jñāna*), because it first employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya) to prevent the arising of future afflictions within the mental continuums of others before the matter is accomplished.

Nevertheless, all forms of contention (*raṇa*) are generally of three types, distinguished as those of the aggregates (*skandha-raṇa*), of speech (*vāda-raṇa*), and of afflictions (*kleśa-raṇa*). Contention of the aggregates refers to death; contention of speech refers to quarreling; and contention of afflictions refers to the one hundred and eight afflictions.
Because this power of conventional knowledge can suppress the strife of the afflictions, it receives the name "non-contention" (araṇā).
This knowledge relies solely upon the fourth dhyāna, as it opposes the causes of suffering.

Because the fourth dhyāna is the most excellent among the paths of ease (*sukha-pratipad*), only those who have attained the fruit of immovability (*akopya-arhat*) can give rise to it, and no others. Others are not even able to prevent the arising of their own afflictions, much less be able to suppress the afflictions of another's body.
This [self-view] relies solely upon the human bodies of the three continents, not those of the northern continent or others, because their natures are sharp and acute.
It arises in relation to objects of desire that have not yet arisen, so as not to cause the delusions of others to arise by taking oneself as an object.
The delusions regarding non-existent objects cannot be prevented, because they arise internally by taking their respective objects as a collective whole.
The "Knowledge of Non-contention" has already been explained.
What, then, is the "Knowledge of Vows"?
The verse says:
"The wisdom of aspiration can take all things as its object; the rest is as explained regarding the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
The commentary says:
Taking aspiration as the precursor, it induces the arising of sublime wisdom; because it realizes things exactly according to that aspiration, it is called "aspiration-wisdom" (*praṇidhijñāna*).

The intrinsic nature, stage, lineage, and body of this wisdom are identical to those of the "knowledge of non-contention" (*araṇājñāna*), but they differ in their objects of focus (*ālambana*), for this wisdom takes all phenomena as its object.
How does the wisdom of aspiration know the future?
It does so by examining the past and present and knowing through inference.
It is like observing that crops may be flourishing or stunted, whereby one infers that the field is either fertile or poor.
If that is so, why is it designated as "vow-knowledge" (praṇidhijñāna)?
For even those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are able to know [such things].
It is not so, because what is known is either determinate or indeterminate.

As for the reports that some of the great śrāvakas made predictions about future events that turned out to be uncertain, this error did not arise from their knowledge resulting from vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), but rather from other mundane knowledge (*laukikajñāna*) observing what was predicted.
Alternatively, there is no fault of uncertainty regarding what he prophesied, for he observed only the beginning and not the end, just as rain that has first fallen has not yet reached the ground.
He was cast aside by Rāhula; the child previously conceived was actually male, but at a later time it transformed into a female.
The spirits of Rājagṛha initially won the battle, but were later defeated by the spirits of Vaiśālī; this is because when humans intend to engage in combat, the spirits fight first.

Alternatively, while it is only through the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) that one truly perceives the future, at the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one first gives rise to inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*). By observing the past and present, one extrapolates to the future, thereby inducing the arising of the knowledge resulting from aspiration, which alone can bring about true perception.

It is precisely for this reason that one can know the formless realms (*ārūpya*). That is to say, by first observing the causal formations and their outflows (*niṣyanda*) therein, an inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*) arises which induces true *praṇidhi-jñāna* (knowledge resulting from aspiration).
Alternatively, by observing the mind at the time of death and rebirth in the desire or form realms, one infers the place of rebirth; only when this induces *praṇidhi-jñāna* can one truly know it.

Alternatively, there is no fault in knowing [the object] through inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*), because that which is realized and that which is the object of inferential cognition must necessarily be the same; if one does not know it through inference, how could one realize it?
In that case, one would have to say that the power of the "wishing-knowledge" (*praṇidhi-jñāna*) cannot universally take the three realms and the three periods of time as its object.

When an Arhat who is liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) wishes to correctly cognize a particular object, he first makes a formal resolve, vowing, "May I know this. Subsequently, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the limit (prāntakoṭika) as a preparatory application. Immediately thereafter, through the power of his prior resolve, correct knowledge arises, whereby he knows the intended object exactly as it is.
The term "limiting concentration" (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) will be explained later.
What is the difference between this power of the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) in knowing the past and the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*)?

The knowledge of aspiration knows both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), whereas the various knowledges of former abodes know only the general and nothing else.

One should understand that within common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) there are also distinctions; the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*) is clear and lucid, whereas the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) is not so.
Regarding the present objects of focus, one should reflect upon the distinctions between this [knowledge] and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) according to reason.
The knowledge resulting from prayer has already been explained. What, then, are the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?
The verse says:
There are four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), namely those of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence;
they have as their nature non-retrogressive knowledge regarding names, meanings, speech, and paths.
The [analytical knowledges] of phenomena and language consist only of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) and rely upon five or two stages respectively.
The meanings are sixteen; nine are explained, all based on every stage.
However, when attained, they must necessarily possess four; the rest is as explained in the section on the "Non-contentious" (*araṇā*).
The treatise says:

The analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are generally said to be fourfold: first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid); second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid); third, the analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid); and fourth, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).
These four are collectively explained as having, in their respective order, the non-retrogressive wisdom that takes names, meanings, speech, and the path as its objects as their intrinsic nature.
That is to say, non-retrogressive wisdom taking the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes—the designating dharmas—as its object is established as the first.
That which indicates the referent object is called a "name" (*nāman*); it is that which expresses the meaning of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
That which distinguishes the referent object is called a "phrase" (*pada*); it is that which clarifies the meaning of the specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*) among phenomena.

Cognition can arise independently, without depending on the sound of meaning; that which serves as its basis is called "phoneme" (*vyañjana*). This refers to [the consonants] *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so forth.

Logically, there must be a cognition that does not depend on the sound of meaning, and this cognition cannot be without an object of perception (*ālambana*); that object of perception is what is called "phoneme."
"Phrases" (vyañjana) refer to that which cannot directly perceive the meaning itself, but serves as the basis for the expression of meaning through names and phrases.
These three [names, phrases, and syllables] are able to sustain all expressed meanings and provide a model for generating understanding; therefore, they are called "dharmas."
The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are said to constitute the "body" (*kāya*), because there is a distinction between their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and their body.

Since the three [natures] and the word "nature" (*svabhāva*) are extremely closely intertwined in meaning, it is difficult to discern their distinct characteristics when they arise as objects of cognition; therefore, the term "body" is employed to manifest that they possess distinct entities.
If non-retrogressive knowledge takes all phenomena as its object, then the ultimate meaning (paramārtha) is established as the second meaning.

That is to say, although the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, as well as names and so forth, are also subsumed under "meaning" (artha), they are not the ultimate meaning because they involve manifold conceptualizations.

That is to say, there is that which accords with reality and that which does not accord with reality; there is that which possesses meaning and that which lacks meaning; there is that which functions based on the conventional and that which functions based on the ultimate. To comprehend these without interval, or at a later time, such that all subsequent evaluations are termed the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*), is for the purpose of demonstrating the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
The object of focus is neither speech nor names; therefore, this object of focus is called the ultimate (paramārtha).

This means that it apprehends only the meaning revealed by the name that arises dependent upon speech, rather than apprehending a mere generality; that which is the range of the mind is designated as "meaning" (artha).
If there is non-retrogressive knowledge that takes as its object the worldly and noble conventions of various regions, it is established as the third.
This is because one is able to understand worldly speech and canonical language across the diverse distinctions of various regions.

If one possesses non-retrogressive knowledge that accords with correct principle and is free from impediment when speaking, as well as mastery over the two paths of concentration and wisdom, this is established as the fourth [analytical knowledge].
Specifically, the ability to correctly proclaim the meaning of the texts and to employ unimpeded speech is termed *pratibhāna* (eloquence).
Furthermore, the sovereign capacity by which all attained merits manifest spontaneously without the need for further application is also called "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
Because this [capacity] gives rise to eloquence, it is designated by the name "eloquence."
The analytical knowledge that discerns and understands causes is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

This refers to the aforementioned capacity to correctly proclaim [the Dharma], skillfully responding to the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings without contradicting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); all such speech is termed "conforming to correct principle" (*yukti-anuloma*).
That which was previously described as unimpeded speech—being free from obstruction in its analytical discernment regardless of place, time, or sentient beings—is termed "unimpeded.
Furthermore, that which was mentioned above regarding the attainment of qualities—which manifests spontaneously without relying on deliberate application—is termed "mastery."

The two paths of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that constitute the knowledge of the conformity between the signifier and the signified are called the first two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

That is to say, the knowledge that realizes this name belongs to such a meaning, and that this meaning possesses such a name, is the knowledge of the conformity between the signifier and the signified; the verbal expression produced as an equal preparatory application at the time of such realization is called the third unhindered knowledge.
