The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is the fourth; it consists in the cause for attaining mastery over speech that accords with what one intends to express.

Furthermore, the six objects of knowledge, such as form (*rūpa*), are called "meaning" (*artha*). The distinctions among these—such as being conditioned or unconditioned, wholesome and so forth, or form and non-form—are called "phenomena" (*dharma*). The verbal expressions that designate these two are called "language" (*nirukti*).
The three types of knowledge are the first three analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), which consist of unimpeded knowledge regarding three objects; this is termed the fourth analytical knowledge.
Furthermore, the realization of the two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—is termed the first two analytical knowledges.
This is the perfection of the practitioner’s own benefit.
Being able to skillfully proclaim these two truths is called the third analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Skillfulness in answering difficult questions regarding these is called the fourth analytical knowledge.
This is precisely the practitioner’s perfection of altruistic virtue.
Some say that ignorance, hesitation, and distraction are the causes of obstruction in eloquent exposition.

By being liberated from these three, one attains abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), and by means of this, the practice of benefiting others is accomplished; this wisdom is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).

If one attains such concentration, one is able to proclaim [the Dharma] in accordance with correct reasoning and with unimpeded speech, as well as attain the merit of mastery in the presence [of the audience].

Furthermore, regarding names and so forth, and regarding words of ultimate meaning, one attains skillfulness in each within the midst of unimpeded exposition; these are established, respectively, as the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The first three types of skillfulness are termed "causes," which are differentiated by their distinct objects; the fourth is termed the "result," which is the unimpeded capacity for exposition.

Furthermore, because the accomplishment of the welfare of others is achieved through these four components—namely, being skilled in phrasing, thoroughly understanding the meaning, being proficient in phonology and prosody, and possessing mastery over concentration and wisdom—the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are established as being fourfold.
This is a general statement regarding the essence of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), while also revealing the distinctions among their four respective objects.
The sūtras briefly cite these numbers and names, whereas the Abhidharma treatises extensively elucidate their characteristics.
Furthermore, while the Sūtras present this with meaning (*artha*) first and phenomena (*dharma*) later, the Abhidharma treatises present phenomena first and meaning later.

This distinction between the Sūtras and the treatises is made to demonstrate that when the two types of knowledge arise, either meaning arises from names or names arise from meaning. Thus, the Sūtras and the treatises provide their respective explanations.

This means that the listener first discriminates names; having correctly understood the names, they next seek their meanings; once the meanings are correctly understood, they desire to explain them to others. Subsequently, they must seek the wisdom of unimpeded speech. Because it follows this sequence, "name" is mentioned first.
Among these four, however, the knowledge of meaning (*arthajñāna*) is supreme, while the others are its auxiliaries; therefore, meaning comes first.

That is to say, if one has correctly mastered the meaning, one should next employ skillful means to investigate its name. Once the name is known and one wishes to explain it to others, one must subsequently seek the wisdom of skillful means regarding that explanation. Thus, the sequence of these four is as follows.
If the analytical knowledge of non-obstruction (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid) takes speech as its object, how does it differ from the third, the analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid)?

The third [knowledge] thoroughly understands etymological definitions of words, such as "it is called 'form' (rūpa) because it possesses transformation and resistance" (*rūpaṇāt*); this [analytical knowledge of non-obstruction], however, is the unimpeded speech that realizes what is logically consistent.
Some say that *vyañjana* (phoneme/word) expresses the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, while *nirukti* (etymological analysis) is able to reveal their specific distinctions.

Others say that directly stating a phenomenon is called *vyañjana*, whereas analyzing it through successive, unimpeded stages is called *nirukti*. Based on these two types, there are distinctions among the three and four [categories].

Among these four, the analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as their nature, and not untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), because they take as their objective domain the names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), as well as worldly linguistic conventions.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena relies upon five stages: namely, the desire realm and the four fundamental dhyānas; for in the higher stages there are no names and so forth, and because those [higher stages] do not separately take lower names and so forth as their objects.

The analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence relies exclusively upon two stages, namely the desire realm and the fundamental first dhyāna; this is because in the higher stages there is no vitarka or vicāra, and in those stages there is necessarily no self-expression through speech.
This reason is illogical.

Why is that? It is not the wisdom that initiates speech that is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), lest it follow that the unimpeded analytical knowledge does not exist within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
On this basis, one should not say that [mental factors] are absent in the higher stages because they lack vitarka and vicāra;
there is no such fault, for the meaning of the "cause" (hetu) is different.
What is meant by the meaning of the cause?

This means that because the two factors of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) can give rise to speech, their characteristics are not tranquil and their intrinsic nature is coarse and agitated.
Since these do not exist in the higher [realms], they are tranquil and subtle.

The analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) takes external words as its object; furthermore, because it is categorized as being non-quiescent and coarse-movement in nature, this analytical knowledge does not exist in the higher stages.
Since there are still applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) within the first dhyāna, this analytical knowledge also exists within that concentration.

Thus, it is established that the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) relies solely on two stages and possesses the nature of sixteen knowledges. That is to say, if all phenomena (*dharmas*) are designated as "meaning," then it consists of ten knowledges; however, if only *nirvāṇa* is designated as "meaning," then it consists of six knowledges—namely, conventional, dharma, subsequent, cessation, exhaustion, and non-arising knowledges.

The analytical knowledge of non-obstruction (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid) has nine knowledges as its nature, namely, all except for the knowledge of cessation, because it takes the path and the truths as its objects.
These two [analytical knowledges] arise based on all stages, that is, from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

Regarding the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), since it is accepted that any one of its aspects may arise in accordance with conditions within the context of teaching the Dharma, there is no fault in its being based upon all stages (*bhūmi*).
However, among these, those that take only the "teaching" as their object rely solely on two stages, which is the same as the third [analytical knowledge].

Some say that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not included within the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), because the analytical knowledges are of the nature of vision (*darśana*).

According to their view, the second [analytical knowledge] consists of either four, eight, or—according to the fourth [position]—only seven; this should be understood by analogy with what was stated above.

These four should be understood as being like the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*): upon acquiring any one of them, one necessarily acquires all four; it cannot be called "acquisition" unless all four are possessed. Their actual manifestation, however, occurs according to one's desire, whether they are present in their entirety or not.
Other masters say:
there is an attainment that is incomplete; it is impossible for one to attain one [of these] without necessarily attaining all four.

Some say that when these four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) arise, they do so in sequence through the prior cultivation of arithmetic, Buddhist scripture (*buddhavacana*), grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), and logic (*hetu-vidyā*) as their preliminary practices (*pūrvaprayoga*); for if one has not attained skill in these four fields, one certainly cannot give rise to the analytical knowledges.

In reality, while all unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) arise, only through training in the Buddha’s word can one perform the preparatory application; it is by depending on the names and so forth practiced over many previous births that one is now able to cultivate the four kinds of skillfulness.
The term *pratisaṃvid* (unimpeded analytical knowledge) has multiple meanings: it is called *pratisaṃvid* because there is unimpeded comprehension regarding various respective objects;
or it is called *pratisaṃvid* because there is unimpeded decisive discernment regarding various respective objects.
Alternatively, the unimpeded knowledge regarding the correct exposition of various objects is called *pratisaṃvid*.
Other masters state that the non-erroneous knowledge regarding present objects is called *pratisaṃvid*.
These four differ from the *araṇā* (the state of non-conflict) in terms of their basis, intrinsic nature, and object.

Regarding the lineage (*gotra*) and the physical basis (*āśraya*), it has already been explained that they are as described for the *araṇā*: namely, one of immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) relies on a human body within the three continents. Concerning the aforementioned knowledge of non-conflict (*araṇā-jñāna*) and so forth, the verse states:
Six are obtained through the limit; the limit is the sixth dhyāna.
They range from being universal to being attained at the ultimate limit; for those other than the Buddha, they are acquired through applied effort (*prayoga*).
The commentary states:

The absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—these six types are all obtained by relying on the concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), because they are induced by the power of that ultimate concentration.

The essence of the *prāntakoṭika-dhyāna* (limit-dhyāna) consists of six types: the first six [categories], excluding the verbal [category], along with a portion of the remaining five, and furthermore, there is another superior dhyāna obtained through preparatory application (*prayoga*) which is called the limit-dhyāna; thus, there are six types in total.

Although the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is attained based upon those [dhyānas], its essence is not subsumed under those dhyānas; for the name "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) applies only to the fourth dhyāna. Because it conforms to all stages universally and increases until reaching the ultimate, it receives the name "limit."
For this reason, it should not be understood as applying to other stages [as well].
How is it that this is called "universally conformable"?

It means that when one correctly practices and trains in this dhyāna, one enters sequentially from the first dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and again descends sequentially from the Peak of Existence back down to the first dhyāna; furthermore, from the first dhyāna, one enters sequentially through each stage up to the fourth dhyāna. This is called being "universally conformable to all stages."
How is it that this is called "increasing to the ultimate"?

It refers to the exclusive cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, proceeding from the lower to the middle, and from the middle to the upper; these three grades are each further divided into three. When the "upper-of-the-upper" grade arises, it is called reaching the ultimate; thus, this dhyāna acquires the designation of being "limit-reaching."
In this context, the three vehicles are not without distinction, yet each attains the name "ultimate" within its own sphere.
Here, the term "limit" (*anta*) signifies the sense of being unsurpassed; since nothing else surpasses this, it is called a "limit."
The term "limit" (*koṭi*) expresses the sense of "category" (*jāti*) and "extreme" (*parama*), as in the expressions "four limits" (*catasraḥ koṭayaḥ*) and "the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).

These two terms indicate that this dhyāna is the most excellent category and the ultimate among meditative concentrations; for many sublime qualities are induced by it, and because it is the most preeminent among the paths of easy progress (*sukha-pratipad*).

Regarding the aforementioned non-contentious knowledge (*araṇā-jñāna*) and so forth, with the exception of the Buddha, other noble ones acquire them only through application (*prayoga-pratilambhika*) and not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-pratilambhika*), because they do not all necessarily attain them.
Only the Buddha acquires these even through the abandonment of defilements.

Regarding the merits of all Buddhas, at the initial moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they are all attained instantaneously through the abandonment of defilements; subsequently, they can be brought into manifestation according to one's wish without the need for preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, exercises sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
Having already explained that the first three [superknowledges] are exclusively shared with other noble ones (*ārya*),
one should now briefly explain those qualities shared even with ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
The verse says:

The six supernormal powers (abhijñā) are: the power of the base of psychic power (ṛddhi-viṣaya), the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya). They are subsumed under the wisdom of the path of liberation.
Four are conventional; the knowledge of others' minds consists of five [types of consciousness]; the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows is like the [ten] powers (bala).
Based on the four dhyānas, [the knowledge of others' minds] takes its own level and lower levels as its objects.
For Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, it extends to two thousand, three thousand, and incalculable worlds, respectively.
When not previously cultivated, it is attained through preparatory effort; when previously cultivated, it is attained through the abandonment of defilements.
Three bodies are one; the remaining three are one. The first dharma and the last dharma are four.
The divine eye and ear are indeterminate; the remaining four are exclusively wholesome.
The treatise says:

There are six kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the domain of psychic power; second, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the divine eye; third, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the divine ear; fourth, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the minds of others; fifth, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes; and sixth, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Although among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the sixth belongs exclusively to noble ones (*ārya*), the first five can also be attained by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); thus, speaking in terms of their general characteristics, they are also shared with worldlings.

These six supernormal powers are subsumed within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The term "path of liberation" (vimukti-mārga) signifies the meaning of emerging from an obstruction, as it is also possible for it to exist within the path of superior progress (viśeṣa-mārga).

Likewise, there is no path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) for such supernormal knowledge (abhijñā), because at this stage the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is necessarily excluded; otherwise, one would have to conclude that when an Arhat relinquishes the path of immediate succession, he would also be said to relinquish the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā).
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, the remaining four are subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

The supernormal power of knowing others' minds is subsumed under five knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds.
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) is as explained regarding the powers (*bala*): it consists of either six or ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
By this, the supernormal power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows has already been shown to rely on all stages (*sarvabhūmi*) and take all objects (*sarvaviṣaya*) as its domain.

The first five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) rely upon the four dhyānas, but not upon the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), because those states lack the meditative absorptions that serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers.

Only meditative absorptions that include the essential factors (*aṅga*) serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers. The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) does not rely on them either, because all stages (*bhūmi*) are capable of taking the exhaustion of outflows as their object, and because it does not require the contemplation of form (*rūpa*) as its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The objects of the first three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) cannot take the formless realm as their object, because these three supernormal knowledges exclusively take form as their object.
This is because the supernormal knowledge of others' minds takes form as its gateway for cultivation.

Furthermore, the supernormal knowledge of past lives is perfected only after one gradually recollects the distinctions between successive states; since one must necessarily observe form during its preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the formless stages lack such capacity.
If that were so, then since the intermediate dhyāna and the five preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) could also take form as their object, they too would possess the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

This is not the case, due to the reasons previously stated: namely, that only the dhyānas which include the [meditative] factors (*aṅga*) serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers. This is because those concentrations (*samādhi*) that do not include the factors are inferior, and furthermore, because in those states either calm (*śamatha*) or insight (*vipaśyanā*) is deficient.

If that is so, for what reason do the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) and the [supernormal powers of] pleasure, suffering, slowness, and speed differ in their stages?
Because all are capable of exhausting the outflows.
The [other] five are distinct cultivations of extraordinary merit; they can only be initiated at extraordinary stages.

When cultivating the first three supernormal powers, such as the power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya*), one takes lightness, radiance, and sound as the preparatory exercises (*prayoga*). Once accomplished, one acts with mastery according to one's desires.

Those who wish to cultivate the power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) first carefully observe the two characteristics of their own body and mind, noting how they change and transform in succession from moment to moment. Thereafter, they carefully observe the characteristics of another’s body and mind. Through these preparatory exercises, the power is gradually perfected; once accomplished, without observing the various forms of one's own mind, one is able to know the minds of others and so forth exactly as they are.

Those who wish to cultivate the supernormal power of recollecting past lives should first examine for themselves the consciousness that has most recently ceased; they then gradually look back in reverse through the various stages of this present life, observing each preceding distinction until reaching the mind at the moment of rebirth-linking, and even further back to the single thought-moment prior to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This is called "one's own past lives."
Once the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is perfected, the same applies to the application for recollecting others.

When this supernormal power first arises, it knows only in sequential order; however, when mastery through cultivation is achieved, one is also able to recollect various objects of memory by skipping over them.
Those who have previously experienced and remember the Pure Abodes do so because they have heard of them in the past.

For those who die in the formless realm and are reborn here, this supernormal power first arises based on the mental continuum of another; for all others, it likewise arises based on their own mental continuum.
Thus, the objects of these five supernormal powers (abhijñā) pertain only to one's own level or lower levels.

For instance, regarding the power of the supernatural bases (ṛddhi-viṣaya), regardless of which level it relies upon, one exercises mastery over movement and transformation within one’s own level and lower levels; this is not the case for higher levels, because one’s power is inferior there.
The same applies to the other four [supernormal powers] according to their respective natures; therefore, there is no capacity to take the formless realm as an object.

The supernormal powers of knowing others' minds and recollecting past lives serve as the objects for two [of the five] supernormal powers. Regarding the breadth or narrowness of the scope of these five supernormal powers within the world-realm, there are differences among the various noble ones (ārya).

This means that the great śrāvakas, the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas], and the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), when not applying intense attention (*anabhisaṃskāra*), are respectively able to exercise their sovereign functions—such as manifesting for the sake of conversion—within the spheres of one, two, or three thousandfold world systems;
however, when applying intense attention, they are respectively able to do so within two thousand, three thousand, or immeasurable world systems.

Regarding these five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), if there are those of superior efficacy and sharp intensity that have never been attained since beginningless time, they are acquired through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
If they have been previously practiced, even if they lack superior efficacy or belong to a different category [of practice], they are acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
If they arise and manifest, it is entirely through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
The Buddha has attained all [supernormal knowledges] free from defilement; they manifest according to his will without requiring preparatory effort.

Regarding the noble ones of the three vehicles, those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may attain them—whether previously attained or never before attained—whereas other ordinary beings can only attain what they have previously attained.

Regarding the explanation of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) in relation to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), there is a distinction between two meanings: that of their objects (*ālambana*) and that of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Some say that two of the powers are precisely the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), while the remaining four have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature.

That [tradition] asserts that the supernormal powers of the eye and ear are the objects of the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), while the remaining four are all objects of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

However, in reality, all six have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature; since the Sūtra states that they are all capable of thoroughly discerning their respective objects, they are therefore all objects of the mindfulness of phenomena.
If distinguished by way of their essential nature, then among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the first three pertain solely to the body, because they take only form as their object.

That is to say, the power of the miraculous realm (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) takes the four external bases as its object; the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) takes form as its object; and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) takes sound as its object.

If that is so, for what reason is it said that the knowledge of death and rebirth knows how classes of sentient beings accomplish various evil deeds of body, speech, and mind within their current existences? Is it not the case that this matter cannot be known by the supernormal power of the divine eye?

There is a distinct, superior knowledge that is an attendant of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); arising in dependence upon the body of an Ārya, it is capable of knowing in this way. Because it is induced by the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is combined with those powers and designated by the name "knowledge of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).

The supernormal knowledge of others' minds is subsumed under three applications of mindfulness—namely, those of sensation, mind, and phenomena—because it takes the mind and so forth as its object. The supernormal knowledge of past lives is subsumed under the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Although the sūtras state that one recollects such matters as having previously experienced pleasure and pain, this refers to the recollection of feelings such as pleasure and pain from previous births; since the objects experienced consist of various requisites, it is a "mixed" object of focus (*miśrālambana*).

The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) subsumes the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya); it is like the powers (bala), being either the power of phenomena or all four applications of mindfulness.
If the six supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) are distinguished according to categories such as the wholesome (kuśala), some masters state that all six are wholesome.
In reality, however, the divine eye and divine ear are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while the other four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are invariably wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) offers this explanation:
"The supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are subsumed under the indeterminate category, because they are wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the visual and auditory consciousnesses."

This explanation is incorrect, for all six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are subsumed within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and it is logically untenable that the two consciousnesses of eye and ear could constitute the path of liberation.

Therefore, one should state it thus: Within the four dhyānas, there exists a superior neutral wisdom (*avyākṛta-prajñā*) associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which can induce the superior great elements (*mahābhūta*) of its own level as its fruit. When this wisdom becomes manifest, it induces the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) of its own level to become present; these serve as the supporting faculties (*āśrayendriya*) from which the visual and auditory consciousnesses arise.
Therefore, the wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear is not supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*); it can only be said to be induced by supernormal knowledge.
As the Sūtra says: "The three types of supernormal knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
What constitutes the nature of those six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)?
The verse states:
The fifth, second, and sixth are the clear knowledges (*vidyā*), Because they counteract ignorance regarding the three time periods.
The latter two are real; the first two are conventional designations. In learning, there is darkness and not clarity. The treatise says:

There are those who possess the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): first, the clear knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past abodes; second, the clear knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth; and third, the clear knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*).
They are subsumed under the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in their respective order; the fifth, second, and sixth [knowledges] constitute their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Among these six, three alone are termed "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*) because they respectively counteract ignorance regarding the three time periods.

That is to say, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives remedies ignorance regarding the past; the supernormal power of knowledge of death and rebirth remedies ignorance regarding the future; and the supernormal power of knowledge of the destruction of the outflows remedies ignorance regarding the present. For this reason, these three alone are designated by the title "clear knowledges" (vidyā).

Furthermore, the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) recalls the suffering of oneself and others regarding the past; the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) observes the suffering of the bodies of others regarding the future. Because one thereby becomes weary of and turns away from the manifold sufferings of birth and death, one gives rise to the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) and contemplates the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. For these reasons, only these three types are specifically established as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, these three knowledges are established as "clear insights" (*vidyā*) because they can respectively abandon the views of eternalism, nihilism, and existence.
Moreover, they are specifically established as clear insights because they eliminate the three types of delusion regarding sentient beings, phenomena, and existence.
Other masters say:

The knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) can see that the aggregates (*skandha*) of the past have been transmitted in succession through mutual causality, entirely without a creator; by this, it can induce the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

The knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda*) can observe the birth and death of sentient beings as they revolve upward and downward like a waterwheel; thus, one does not long for the retributive fruits of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), and by this, it can induce the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).

Taking disenchantment as the gateway, one realizes the dharma of signlessness; thus, the liberation door of signlessness that exhausts the outflows arises. For this reason, these three supernormal knowledges alone are designated by the term "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*).
These three are all called the "clear knowledges of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa-vidyā*), because they all arise within the body of one who has reached the stage of no-more-learning.

Among these, only the last can truly be said to penetrate the untainted (*anāsrava*), because its nature and its continuity are both untainted; the other two are only metaphorically so called, as their substance is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
For this reason, only the last receives the name "non-learner" (*aśaikṣa*).

The first two types receive the designation of "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa) solely by virtue of their continuity (*saṃtāna*), not by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:

"There is a non-obscured, neutral wisdom associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which receives the designation of 'noble' (*ārya*) neither because it is wholesome nor because it is untainted (*anāsrava*)."
Because this can be attained within the body of an *ārya*, it is called "noble" (*ārya*).
This [state] should also be understood in the same way, and is therefore termed "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
Since the body of one in training (*śaikṣa*) contains the darkness of ignorance, although the former two [factors] are present there, they are not established as "clarity."
Although the darkness of ignorance may be temporarily suppressed, it will later be obscured again; therefore, one cannot establish it as "light.
Only when darkness is permanently absent can it be designated as "light.
Thus, it is said in the Sūtra:
There are three kinds of guidance.
Regarding those [powers], what is their intrinsic nature among the six supernormal knowledges?
The verse says:

Among the four types of guidance, the sixth is supreme; Instruction through admonition is the most honored, For it is accomplished through meditative concentration and supernormal powers, And because it leads to the fruits of benefit and happiness.
The Treatise says:

The three demonstrations (*prātihārya*) are: first, the demonstration of miraculous power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); second, the demonstration of reading the minds of others (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*); and third, the demonstration of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*).

In their respective order, these take as their intrinsic nature the first, fourth, and sixth of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Because these three alone are most excellent at inducing those to be converted to initially resolve upon the path, they are established under the name "demonstrations" because they can both show and lead.

Among the three kinds of guidance, the guidance of instruction is the most excellent, because it is necessarily accomplished through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and because it invariably leads to the fruits of benefit and happiness.
This is because the first two forms of guidance—such as spells and the like—can also be performed; they do not rely solely on supernormal powers, and thus they are not definitive.
For example, there is a mantra called Gandhārī; by holding it, one is able to soar through the air with ease.
Or there may be medicinal herbs possessing superior efficacy, such that by consuming or wearing them, one gains the power of flight at will.
Furthermore, there is a mantra called Icchanī; by holding this, one is able to know the thoughts in another's mind.
Alternatively, by observing physical signs or listening to their speech and sounds, one can likewise discern what another is thinking.
The instruction that guides toward liberation cannot be performed by anyone other than those possessing the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows; therefore, it is definitive.
Alternatively, while the first two types of guidance can also be performed by non-Buddhists, the third cannot, and for this reason it is called "definitive."
Furthermore, while the first two guides may only cause others to temporarily turn their minds [toward the Dharma], they cannot lead them to the fruit of ultimate benefit and peace.

The guide of instruction and demonstration, however, certainly causes others to attain future benefit and the fruit of peace, because it is able to explain through skillful means in accordance with reality.
Because this instruction is supreme and not otherwise,
what is the meaning intended by the two terms "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) and "domain" (*viṣaya*)?
The verse says:
The essence of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); its objects are twofold: movement and transformation. Movement is threefold:
by will, by mental impulse, and by the Buddha; it consists of bodily transport and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Transformation is twofold: belonging to the desire realm and the form realm; it has the nature of four or two external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Each of these is of two kinds, namely: resembling one's own body and another's body.
The treatise states:

That which is designated by the name "rddhi" (supernormal power) is exclusively superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because it is by means of this that one can perform the activities of miraculous transformation.
Yet the sūtras state: "The fruit of ṛddhi is called ṛddhi.

This is intended to indicate the coarse in order to reveal the subtle, and furthermore, to show that superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is its proximate cause; however, the actual substance of the miraculous feats (*ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa*) is not itself ṛddhi.
The various miraculous feats (ṛddhi-prātihārya) are designated as "objects" (viṣaya), and these are of two kinds: namely, movement (gati) and transformation (nirmāṇa).
Movement is further of three types:
first, the movement of the body (kāya-vikrīḍita), which refers to traveling through the air like a bird in flight.

Second is resolute confidence (*adhimukti*): that is, by directing one's thought toward an extremely distant place as being near, one can arrive there swiftly; likewise, if one directs one's thought toward the extremely distant Akaniṣṭha Heaven as being near, one is then able to reach it.
Since there is fundamentally no coming or going, what is meant by "swift movement"?
This is indeed movement; however, because the practice of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is extremely rapid due to its proximity [to the goal], it receives the name "resolute conviction.
Alternatively, the Blessed One said:
Because the domain of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is inconceivable, only a Buddha can fully comprehend it.
Third is the power of mental intent (*manojavitva*): when one directs the mind toward an extremely distant place, the body is able to arrive there immediately.
This power is "at will," thus it is given the name "power of mental intent" (*manojavitva*), because as the mind grasps an object, one arrives instantaneously at the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

Among these three types of movement, the power of mental intent belongs exclusively to the Buddha; however, the movement of the body through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) also extends to other vehicles.
It is said that my World-Honored One’s supernormal powers are swift; wherever one may be, far or near, he arrives as soon as the thought arises.
For this reason, the World-Honored One has declared:
"The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable, like the sun radiating its light."
The same applies to the aggregates (skandha) and the streams (srotas): because they can reach a distant point instantaneously, they are called "formations" (saṃskāra).
If this were not the case, then between passing away here and arising there, the stream would be severed, and the meaning of "formation" would be non-existent.

Alternatively, because the Buddha’s majestic power is inconceivable, he reaches his destination as soon as he directs his mind; thus, this mode of movement by mental impulse belongs only to the World-Honored One.
Superior resolve (*adhimukti*) is shared with other noble ones (*ārya*), while movement by bodily transport (*kāyavāhin*) is shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Transformation [bodies] are further of two kinds: those of the desire realm and those of the form realm.

If they belong to the desire realm, they consist of four external bases, excluding sound; if they belong to the form realm, they consist of only two, namely visible form and tangibility, because fragrance and taste do not exist within the form realm.
These emanations of the two realms each have two types, distinguished by whether they belong to one's own body or another's body.
There are four types of emanations when the body is in the desire realm, and the same applies when it is in the form realm; thus, there are eight in total.

Although one born in the form realm may manifest transformations belonging to the desire realm, there is no fault of producing smell or taste, because the manifested self consists of only two bases (āyatana).
Some say that four [bases] are also manifested, just as clothing and the like are not established [as real].

It is not the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya-abhijñā*) that can initiate the act of transformation; rather, it is the various transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) which are the fruits of this supernormal power.
How many characteristics do these transformative minds possess?
The verse says:
The transformative mind consists of fourteen types; as for the fruits of meditative concentration, they range from two to five.
They are acquired according to the concentration upon which they depend, and from the pure state, two arise spontaneously.
The activity of transformation occurs through its own level, while the power of speech extends through its own level and those below.
The emanation and the emanator— Their speech is necessarily neither [the same as] nor [different from] the Buddha.
Having first established a vow to retain the body, One subsequently gives rise to other minds and speech.
There are those who die while retaining a solid physical form; Others maintain that there is no such principle of retention.
Initially, many minds produce one transformation; its fulfillment is the opposite of this.
That which is acquired through cultivation is subsumed under the neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature; the remainder are acquired across all three natures.
The Commentary says:
There are fourteen types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) in total, which arise based on the four fundamental dhyānas.
Those arising from the first dhyāna consist of only two kinds: one subsumed under the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the other belonging to the first dhyāna itself.
In the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, there are respectively three, four, and five [results], as they do not depend on what is below; for the lower stages are inferior.
Regarding the fruits of a single dhyāna bound to upper and lower stages, there is superiority or inferiority in the stages of the basis, the practice, and so forth.

Regarding the stages of the fruits of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) bound to the first stage and those above or below it, although their bases are equal, there is a distinction between superior and inferior in terms of their activity (*caryā*).

When a fruit of a higher stage is bound to a lower stage, or a fruit of a lower stage is bound to a higher stage, they follow the respective inferiority or superiority of the stage as the basis for the superiority or inferiority of its activity.
The acquisition of the mind of transformation through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is likewise so, because the fruit and its basis are acquired simultaneously.

However, there are three general occasions for acquiring meditative absorption, distinguished by the differences between detachment from passion (*vairāgya*), rebirth (*upapatti*), and preparatory application (*prayoga*).
That is to say, when one is free from the defilements of a lower stage and attains a higher dhyāna, one also obtains the emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) produced by that concentration.

Furthermore, when one dies from a higher stage and is reborn in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), or when one gives rise to superior qualities through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), one newly acquires the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) that serves as the basis, and simultaneously acquires the emanation-mind produced by it.

When one attains the fruit of Arhatship based on a body in the desire realm, or when one attains the fruit of Arhatship during the stage of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), all fourteen transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) are acquired simultaneously.

Even when one’s body is in the fourth dhyāna and attains Arhatship, one acquires five transformation-minds; there is no principle whereby one could emerge directly from meditative absorption by means of a transformation-mind.

This arises from pure meditative concentration (*śuddhaka-samādhi*) and its own kind; it can immediately produce its own kind and pure meditative concentration. Therefore, it arises only from two and produces two, and not otherwise.
Only a transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of its own level gives rise to transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karma*) of its own level.

The speech produced by a transformation arises from a mind of its own level or a lower level. That is to say, the speech of a transformation in the Desire Realm or the First Dhyāna arises only from a mind of its own level;
however, when a transformation in a higher level produces speech, it does so from a mind of the First Dhyāna, because that higher level lacks a mind capable of producing manifest action (*vijñapti*).
If one is born in the desire realm or in the second dhyāna and so forth, how can informative action (*vijñapti*) arise when a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) occurs?

It is not possible for minds belonging to the paths of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*) to manifest based on a body of a different realm, because they must necessarily depend upon a body belonging to their own realm.
This is not faulty, because it takes as its basis the manifestation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) belonging to that realm which have been drawn forth.

That is to say, the primary elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are drawn forth and manifest, remaining in close conjunction with the body of the desire realm; based upon these, one gives rise to the mind capable of manifesting [vocal or bodily] intimation. Thus, there is no fault of a mind of the non-concentrated stage (*asamāpatti-bhūmi*) depending on a body of the scattered stage (*vyutthāna-bhūmi*).

Alternatively, there may arise a mind capable of producing manifest action based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such as the visual and auditory consciousnesses produced by relying on concentration.

If a single transformation-master produces many transformation-bodies, it is only when the master speaks that the transformation-bodies speak; the vocal expressions and their meanings are entirely identical for all.
Therefore, a verse says: "When the one who transforms speaks, all those who are transformed speak;
when the one who transforms remains silent, all those who are transformed do likewise."

This refers only to others; the Buddha is not like them. Because the power of concentration of all Buddhas is most sovereign, it is possible that his speech and that of those he transforms do not occur simultaneously, and what is expressed by their voices may also differ.

If, when speech is produced by a transformation being in the three higher realms, it is initiated by a manifest mind of the first dhyāna, then at the moment this mind arises, the transformation mind would have already ceased; thus, there should be no transformation body. How, then, could the transformation body speak?

By the power of a prior vow, one retains the manifested body while subsequently giving rise to other mental states that produce the vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*); therefore, there is no fault of lacking a physical basis for the manifested speech.

It is not only when the master of the manifestation is still alive that he can retain the manifested body to cause it to endure for a long time; he may also cause it to remain even after his life has come to an end.
For instance, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa left behind his skeletal body until the era of the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya).
Only a solid, enduring substance can remain for a long time; otherwise, Kāśyapa would have had to leave behind his flesh and other such parts.
Other masters say:

"The power of a vow to maintain the body can certainly not cause it to persist beyond death; as for the skeletal remains of the noble Mahākāśyapa that remained for a long time, they were sustained by various devas."
A beginner, by means of many transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*), must rely upon a physical basis to produce a single transformative act;
one who has perfected their practice, by means of a single transformation-mind, is able to produce numerous transformative acts without relying upon a physical basis.

In general, there are two types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*): first, those produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), and second, those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), etc.; the fruits of transformation (*nirmāṇa-phala*) they produce are likewise described as such.

Regarding the spheres (*āyatana*) subsumed under transformations produced through cultivation, they are as previously stated, because one cannot transform them into the bodies of sentient beings (*sattva-kāya*).
Regarding those obtained at birth and so forth, within the desire realm they transform into nine bases, and in the form realm they transform into seven.

Although it is said that they transform into nine based on the principle of not being separated from the sense faculties (*indriya*), in reality, there is no capacity to transform into actual sense faculties.

The fruit of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*) is without mind; however, other emanations may possess it. When the fruit of cultivation gives rise to informative action (*vijñapti*), it does so through the mind of the emanator; otherwise, it may arise from one's own mind as bodily or vocal informative action.
If the food and drink produced by the fruit of cultivation serves to sustain the body, it must necessarily be digested within the body of the emanator.

If, for some other purpose, one has swallowed gold, stone, or the like, these either remain within that transformation-body or are placed elsewhere as appropriate; the remaining transformed food and drink abide according to their respective supports.

The transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) resulting from cultivation is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); others, however, pertain to all three natures, namely the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.
Just as the transformative minds of devas, nāgas, and others can produce emanations, they are likewise able to manifest emanations of both their own bodies and those of others.
Regarding the terms "divine eye" and "divine ear," what do they signify?
Do they refer to the essence of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*), or do they refer to the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*)?
If they were wisdom, they should not be called the "divine eye" and "divine ear."
If it were a physical sense organ (*rūpīndriya*), it should not be called a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
This was stated previously.
What was stated previously?

This means that within the four fundamental dhyānas, there exists a superior neutral wisdom associated with meditative concentration which is termed the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear; the superior great elements produced by this [wisdom] are termed the "divine eye" and "divine ear."
What is their essential nature?
The verse says:
The divine eye and ear are faculties; they consist of pure matter belonging to the stage of meditative concentration.
Constantly of the same class and without deficiency, they apprehend what is obstructed, subtle, distant, and so forth.
The treatise says:
Their substance is precisely the divine eye and divine ear faculties, because they take sound and light as their preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Relying on the four dhyānas, one brings forth within the vicinity of the eyes and ears the two faculties of eye and ear—composed of the subtle primary elements (mahābhūta) of those stages and consisting of pure matter (rūpa-prasāda)—which see forms and hear sounds; these are called the divine eye and divine ear.
In this way, why are the eyes and ears called "divine"?
Their very substance is divine because they are subsumed within the meditative stages (*dhyāna-bhūmi*).
Because they are utterly pure, they are designated by the name "divine."
As stated in this sutra:
"The divine eye and ear are not composed of skin, flesh, sinews, or blood; they are merely pure matter (rūpa) derived from the sublime primary elements (mahābhūta).
Nevertheless, there are three types of divine eyes and ears:"
First, those acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*), which are as previously described.
Second, those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), meaning those possessed by those born among the gods.

Third, those resembling the divine (*tad-ākṛti*), meaning those produced in other realms of existence (*gati*) by the influence of superior karma and so forth, which enable distant seeing and hearing similar to the divine eye and ear—such as the "treasure-minister" (*maṇi-ratna*), Bodhisattvas, universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), various nāgas, spirits, and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The eyes and ears acquired through cultivation are always of the same class (*sabhāga*) throughout past, present, and future births; they persist until the present moment and are necessarily accompanied by consciousness.

Because they are capable of seeing and hearing, their sense bases must necessarily be complete, unobstructed, and without deficiency; thus, like all sentient beings born in the Form Realm who can, according to their respective capacities, perceive forms and sounds—even those that are obstructed, extremely subtle, or distant—in all directions.
Therefore, regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"The physical eye, in all directions, Lacks the capacity to see obstructed, subtle, or distant forms;
The divine eye perceives them all without exception."

It was stated previously that the transformation mind (nirmāṇacitta) is cultivated differently from others; is it the case that the five [supernormal powers], such as the power of psychic travel (ṛddhi), each have their own distinct cultivation? Yes, they do. How so?
The verse says:
The supernormal power of the base (*ṛddhi*) is fivefold—arisen from cultivation, birth, incantations, medicine, and karma;
the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is fourfold—arisen from cultivation, birth, incantations, and additionally, from divination by signs (*nimitta*).
The three [types of knowledge] are accomplished through cultivation and birth; excluding those cultivated, they all belong to the three natures.
Humans possess only that which is acquired without birth; those in hell can first know them.
The Commentary says:

There are five general types of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) knowledge: first, that acquired through cultivation; second, that acquired at birth; third, that accomplished through mantras; fourth, that accomplished through medicinal herbs; and fifth, that accomplished through karma.
The supernormal powers of King Mandhātṛ, those of beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and others are subsumed under the category of being accomplished through karma.
Other masters say:
There are four types of supernormal power (ṛddhi); that is, the three previously mentioned plus transformation (nirmāṇa) as one.
Regarding "transformation," as the Sūtra says:
"Dividing one into many," and so forth, as explained at length.
There are four general types of knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): the first three are as described above, with the addition of that accomplished through signs (*nimitta*).
Each of the remaining three types has three varieties, namely: those produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), those born of birth (*upapattija*), and those resulting from karma (*karmaja*).
Excluding those acquired through cultivation, all [types of mindfulness] pertain to the wholesome and so forth.
Because they are not the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do not receive the designation "universal" (*sarvatraga*).

Among humans, none possess that which is acquired at birth; however, for others, all [types] may exist, being subsumed under innate mindfulness according to their respective natures or as accomplished through karma.
Human beings, by virtue of their prior karma, are able to recollect the past.

At the very moment of first taking birth in the hell realm, they know the minds of others and their own past lives solely through the innate knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the recollection of former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); however, once they are oppressed by painful sensations, they no longer possess the capacity for such cognition.
By what means do they know their past? As stated in the sūtras, they recollect for themselves:
"In the past, we heard others speak of the faults of various sensual desires yet did not feel weary of them; therefore, at this present time, we undergo such intense suffering."
They can only remember their immediately preceding life; however, in other realms of existence, they possess knowledge as appropriate to their condition.
Animals know the past, such as the conch-shell-blower, the dog, and others.
The spirits know the past, as a verse says:
"I once accumulated great wealth, By means of both righteous and unrighteous acts;
Now others enjoy prosperity and happiness, While I alone endure poverty and suffering."
The deva knew the past, as it is said in a verse:
“I have offered the Jetavana Grove, Wherein the Great Dharma King dwells;
The noble Saṃgha enjoys its use, Therefore my heart rejoices.”
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"All those born in the heavens must, upon their initial birth, give rise to three thoughts:
'From where did I pass away?'"
"In what place did they live in their previous lives?
By virtue of what karma have they come to be born here?
Thus, one knows that the devas are able to recollect the past.
*Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle 37.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vyākhyā-śāstra*, Fascicle 38.
Composed by the Venerable Saṅghabhadra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine:

Analysis of Meditative Concentration (Dhyāna), Part One. Having thus analyzed the distinctions among the various types of knowledge (*jñāna*), we shall next distinguish the meditative concentrations upon which that knowledge relies.
Only the dhyānas can serve as a complete basis; therefore, among these, the dhyānas are explained first.

Alternatively, within the previously explained common qualities, those such as the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*) accomplished through wisdom have already been discussed; the other qualities accomplished [by the dhyānas] shall now be explained.
Among these, first we shall analyze the meditative concentrations that serve as the basis.
Now, regarding the dhyānas within the various concentrations, what are they?
The verse says:

The four dhyānas each have two [types]; among them, that which has already been explained is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), defined as being wholesome and one-pointed, with its attendants having the nature of the five aggregates.
The first possesses investigation (*vitarka*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*); the subsequent ones gradually abandon the preceding factors.
The treatise says:
Since all meritorious qualities largely depend upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should first analyze the distinctions among these concentrations.
There are four types in total, namely: the first, second, third, and fourth.

Is it not the case that the dhyānas possess unique designations and concepts, such as "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) and so forth, yet one now establishes distinct names for them only by way of the four numbers beginning with the first?

It is not that there are no unique designations and concepts here; however, there is no name that exclusively and universally encompasses a single stage (*bhūmi*), because each dhyāna has two types—namely, the distinction between meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and birth (*upapatti*).
The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the various classes have already been explained previously—namely, the fourth, the eighth, the first two, and the remaining three.
They have no distinct names; they are collectively designated as a single stage (bhūmi).

The general characteristics of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are without distinction; that is to say, when these four entities are considered as a whole, they are all comprised within the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*), consisting of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*), because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is wholesome concentration (*samādhi*).
If these are taken as being of the nature of the five aggregates together with their associated factors, then since these two are identical, it would be difficult to discern their distinction.

Although there is no difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is a difference in their stages (*bhūmi*). To manifest this difference in stage, they are designated by number; thus, they are called the first through the fourth.
In this regard, the Master of the Sūtras himself raises a question and provides an answer: "What is meant by 'one-pointedness' (ekāgratā)?
It means being focused on a single object.
His answer is irrational; if the visual consciousness and the mental consciousness were to have the same object, they ought to be termed "one-pointedness."
Therefore, one must seek a different principle in this regard.

That is to say, if one-pointedness (ekāgratā) were defined as relying upon a single foundational faculty while focusing exclusively on a single object, then since there is no shifting of objects within a single moment, would it not follow that one-pointedness exists in all states of mind?

In reality, all [mental states] possess it, because each momentary mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) operate upon a single object; however, not all of them receive the designation "concentration" (samādhi).

This is because, in this context, one-pointedness (ekāgratā) is taught merely to demonstrate that wholesome minds and mental factors continue to evolve through the power of superior meditative absorption (samādhi).

If that were so, when the mind itself functions based on a single sense faculty and induces the continuous arising of subsequent moments of mind directed toward its own object, this would be termed "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*); thus, there should be no separate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) apart from the mind itself.
This objection is not valid, for it has already been addressed previously.

Specifically, in the extensive analysis of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) presented earlier, it was already demonstrated that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) exists as something distinct from the mind itself.

If the essence of the mind were identical to *samādhi*, then that which causes the mind to become "equipoised" would likewise have no separate existence, as no causal basis for such a distinction could be found. Such objections have been fully set forth as before; therefore, it is not the case that the mind itself is designated as *samādhi*.
On what basis is the name "dhyāna" (meditative concentration) established?
It is because by relying on this tranquility (*śamatha*), one is able to engage in "discernment" (*pravicaya*).

Discernment has the meaning of "thoroughly knowing" (*parijñāna*); as it is said that when the mind is in meditative absorption, it can thoroughly know things as they truly are, because the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is placed within the sense of discernment.
According to the tenet of this treatise, the *vicāraṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of deliberation) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.

Based on the principles of etymological interpretation (*nirukti*), it receives the name "dhyāna" (meditative absorption) because it is a state of concentrated reflection upon an object; since it causes wisdom to arise, it is free from turbidity and distraction.
Some say that this meditative absorption (dhyāna) is called *dhyāna* because it maintains superior universal objects, reflects according to reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), and thus is tranquil.

The term "superior" excludes the desire realm; "universal objects" excludes the formless realms; and "reflecting according to reality" excludes that which is contrary to the truth and capable of maintaining [distraction].
This concentration is a sublime meditative absorption (samādhi), and this sublime meditative absorption is called dhyāna.
This statement indicates that śamatha and vipaśyanā proceed in equilibrium; only when meditative absorption is non-erroneous in this way is it termed dhyāna.
If that is so, how can the defiled states obtain this name?

Because they too are capable of improper deliberation (*vitarka*), this name is established for them by way of similarity, just as in the world one speaks of "rotten seeds" and the like; thus, there is no fault of applying the term "dhyāna" to everything.

If one posits the four dhyānas as consisting of the one-pointedness of mind that is virtuous in nature, together with its attendants, on what basis are the first, second, third, and fourth established?
That which possesses vicāra, prīti, and sukha is established as the first.
That is to say, when within a particular state there is virtuous one-pointedness of mind, fully associated with vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha, such a samādhi is called the first dhyāna.
Although the verse mentions only association with vicāra, it already implies the sense of being associated with vitarka as well.
Since any vicāra that is accompanied by prīti and sukha must necessarily not be dissociated from vitarka,
the verse states only that it "possesses vicāra but not vitarka" in order to clarify the establishment of the second [dhyāna] as being free from vicāra.
Otherwise, one should say that they possess vitarka, prīti, and sukha; since the presence of vicāra is established by the mention of vitarka, it is understood without being explicitly stated.

The four [dhyānas] are established by gradually abandoning the preceding factors: there are two [factors] when abandoning vicāra, there is sukha when abandoning those two, and there is one-factor possession when abandoning all three, according to their respective order; thus, one-pointedness of mind is divided into four types.
The dhyānas have already been explained.
What of the formless attainments?
The verse says:

The formless [attainments] are likewise: the four aggregates, detached from the lower stages and including the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher realms, are collectively termed "removal of the perception of form.
The formless is so called because there is no form; subsequent forms arise from the mind.
The three beginning with Infinite Space are named according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*);
Non-ideation and Neither-ideation-nor-non-ideation are named because they are dull and inferior.
The Treatise says:
These are identical in number and intrinsic nature to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), meaning there are two for each of the four.
As for their birth, it is as previously explained—that is, as stated in the *Lokadhātu* chapter—there are four types based on birth.

Regarding the essential nature of the meditative attainments of the formless realm (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), in summary, they are also comprised within the wholesome (*kuśala*) and consist of one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
It is on this basis that it is said, and likewise stated:
"However, among the accompanying factors, this excludes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), because in the formless realm there is no 'concomitant form' (*anuvartaka-rūpa*).

Although there is no difference between one-pointedness of mind and its accompaniments, they are divided into four types because they arise having transcended the lower stages: namely, when one has already transcended the fourth dhyāna, the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is established; and so on, up to when one has already transcended the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is established."
What is the meaning of "detachment" (*viveka*)?
It refers to the liberation from the afflictions of the lower stages by means of this path; thus, it signifies the detachment from the defilements of the lower realms.

These four fundamental [dhyānas], together with the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher [formless] realms, are collectively termed the "removal of the perception of form" (*rūpasaṃjñā-vyapagama*).

The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space does not yet receive this name because it gives rise to the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) by taking the forms of the lower stages as its object; thus, the designation "removal of form" cannot be established for that which takes the perception of lower forms as its object.
If this is so, for what reason is it said in the *Mahābhūta-skandha* that the removal of the perception of form constitutes the fourth dhyāna?
Because one gradually removes all forms existing within one's own body that take the desire realm as their object, this perception cannot exist in the formless realm.
Since this is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) preceding the removal of the perception of form, there is no error in establishing the name of the fundamental [attainment].
On what basis is the designation "formless" (ārūpya) established?
It is based on the fact that there is a total absence of all form (rūpa).
When one dies and is reborn there, form arises from the mind. We observe in the world both phenomena that possess form and those that do not.

Furthermore, there is also a process of mutual dependence and succession; that is to say, because the mind is diverse, the differentiation of form arises, and when the sense organs differ, the consciousness that arises becomes distinct.

Therefore, when one is about to descend from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to be born below, a mental continuum that accords with the production of form persists, and by its power, the production of form in the lower realm is induced.
However, it cannot be said that [present matter] arises solely from that [past matter].

It also takes the continuity of the mind associated with matter in previous lives as its condition, and takes matter that has long since ceased as its own seed, such that present matter now arises; this is because it is accepted that homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) function across both the past and the present.

Once the various Arhats have entered parinirvāṇa, because the continuity of the aggregates has been severed without remainder, there currently exists no condition for the arising of even a fraction of the aggregates; therefore, they cannot be compared to those who pass away from the formless realm.
Thus, the general name for the formless realms has been explained.
Why, then, are they specifically named "Infinite Space" and so forth?

Briefly, the names of the first three are derived from their preparatory practices (*prayoga*); for during the stage of cultivating these practices, one contemplates infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness.

If it is accomplished through the preparatory application of contemplating infinite space by means of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
That is to say, there may be phenomena that, although coexisting with form (*rūpa*), do not have their own essence dependent upon or belonging to form.
Those who seek liberation from form must first contemplate that principle:
although the essence of space coexists with form, it can only be clearly manifested by depending on the absence of form.

The external phenomena included therein are infinite in their characteristics; however, when one contemplates them, it is easy to become detached from form. Therefore, during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one contemplates space.
At the time of attainment, one may likewise take other phenomena as objects as appropriate, but this name is established based on the preparatory stage.

If it is accomplished through the application of meditative cultivation consisting of the contemplation of infinite consciousness by means of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

That is to say, having correctly grasped the signs within the pure sixfold body of consciousness capable of discernment, one dwells in resolute conviction and, through the power of mental construction (*parikalpa*), contemplates and examines the characteristics of infinite consciousness.

Because this is accomplished by taking preparatory effort as its precursor, it may also take other phenomena as its object according to the circumstances; however, this name is established based solely on that preparatory effort.
If, through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), one relinquishes all that was accomplished by preparatory effort, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

This refers to seeing that the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of the boundless [meditations] are coarse and agitated; one initiates this preparatory application (*prayoga*) with the desire to become weary of them and relinquish them.

For this reason, this stage is called "supreme equanimity" (*upekṣā*), because within it one no longer delights in producing the boundless mental aspects, and the mind dwells in tranquility, having relinquished all engagement with its objects.

The fourth name is established because perception (*saṃjñā*) is dull and inferior; that is to say, in this stage, perception is not clear or predominant, and thus it receives the name "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*), as it is like the state of non-perception.
However, since perception is not entirely absent, it is called "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*).

Because this stage still possesses dull and inferior perceptions, this statement indicates that it is the perception of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); since it is not like the seven lower stages, it receives the name "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*);
and since it is not like the three mindless states, it is called "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Is it not the case that during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), yogis also think:

"All perceptions are like a disease, like an arrow, like an abscess; the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is like delusion and like darkness; only the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the opposite of these, being tranquil and sublime."
Why is it that this [attainment] is not designated by the name of its preparatory stage (*prayoga*)?
In principle, this is indeed the case, because a practitioner must first cultivate revulsion toward both perception (*saṃjñā*) and non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).
However, someone might ask:
For what reason does the practitioner form such a thought while practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*)?

One must certainly cite this as the reason for answering the question; therefore, it is said that the establishment of the name [of "ignorance"] is due to the dullness and inferiority of perception (*saṃjñā*).
These four formless states are all called "abodes" (*āyatana*) because they are the places where various forms of existence (*bhava*) grow and develop.

That is to say, these four abodes serve as the grounds for the growth and development of various karmas and afflictions (*kleśa*), both existent and non-existent; furthermore, to refute the false reckoning that they constitute *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha taught them to be "abodes where existence grows."
The formless attainments have already been explained.
What, then, are the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*)?
The verse says:
These fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*) are eight in number;
the first seven each have three types—namely, the relishing (*āsvādana*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*). The last [attainment] has two types: the relishing and the pure.
"Relishing" refers to that which is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*); "pure" refers to mundane wholesomeness (*laukika-kuśala*).
"This is that which is tasted and clung to; the untainted is called supramundane.
The treatise says:

Of the eight fundamental attainments (samāpatti) of the dhyānas and formless realms (ārūpya) explained above, the first seven each possess all three types [of attainment]. The attainment of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) possesses only two types, because this stage is dull and inferior, being the root of birth and death; furthermore, as it lies at the extreme limit of all stages, it lacks the untainted state.

The first, "tasting attainment" (*āsvādana-samāpatti*), refers to that which is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Because craving is able to relish and become attached, it is called "tasting"; since this attainment is associated with that craving, it receives the name "tasting.
The phrase "associated with craving" is stated in terms of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), for this attainment has meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its essential nature.
If one were to include the associated factors (sahāya), one should say:
"The factors belonging to the category associated with craving (tṛṣṇā) are called the 'attainment of relish' (āsvādana-samāpatti).
This [definition], however, takes only those factors that are of the same fruit (eka-phala) as craving.
