The "pure" (*śuddha*) attainments are termed "worldly wholesome concentration" (*laukika-kuśala-samādhi*); because they are free from the defilement of afflictions, they are associated with non-attachment and other such pure, wholesome dharmas.

Because these are wholesome, they differ from those characterized by "tasting" (*āsvādana*); because they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), they are distinct from those that are without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is precisely the object previously relished; immediately upon its cessation, that relishing meditative absorption arises.

One deeply relishes the past purity, and at that time, although one is said to have emerged from the absorption that was relished, one is said to have entered the absorption that performs the relishing.
There are five general types of emergence from meditative concentration:
first, emergence from the stage; second, emergence from the moment; third, emergence from the mental aspect; fourth, emergence from the object; and fifth, emergence from the category.
To enter from the first dhyāna into the second and so forth is called "exiting the stage" (*bhūmi*).
To proceed through a continuous succession of mental states within the same stage, where the preceding moment immediately gives way to the succeeding moment, is called "exiting the moment" (*kṣaṇa*).
To enter from the aspect of impermanence into the aspect of suffering and so forth is called "emerging from the aspects.
To enter from taking the aggregate of form as an object into taking feeling and so forth as objects is called "emerging from the objects."
To enter the untainted from the tainted, or to enter the defiled from the undefiled, and so forth, is called "changing the category" (*visabhāga*).

Based on this change of category, it is said here that one "emerges from the savored object and enters the meditative absorption that savors it. Is this not a contradiction between the two statements?
The act of relishing is craving, not the meditative absorption entered;
that which is entered is the absorption, and it is not called "relishing.
How, then, can it be said that one enters an absorption characterized by relishing?

There is no fault of contradiction, for we observe their association; since any one name is cited to express the category of both, they receive both names because they are mutually intermingled—just as when a householder is exhorted to apply his attention, he receives both designations due to their mutual blending.

Because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with craving is termed "tasting" (*āsvādana*), and by the power of that concentration, craving itself receives the designation "concentration," there is no contradiction between these two terms.

Some say that when craving for concentration manifests in a continuous stream, each subsequent moment takes the preceding one as its object; thus, that which is tasted is the preceding moment that has already ceased, while the subsequently arising moment is called the "taster."

When this craving that experiences the flavor [of objects] manifests, it takes past objects as its objective support but does not take present factors—whether those of its own nature, associated factors, or co-existent factors—as its support, because it necessarily does not observe its own nature and so forth.
It does not take the future as its object, because it has never been experienced before.
Only when the mind is focused intently upon its object without wavering is it termed "concentration" (*samādhi*).
Although concentration associated with craving is likewise one-pointed toward its object and thus receives the name "concentration," this is not the case for those associated with other afflictions.

This means that other afflictions cannot cause the mind to focus single-mindedly upon their respective objects in the same way that craving can; therefore, when samādhi is accompanied by craving, its one-pointed concentration on an object resembles that of the wholesome.
Untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) refers to supramundane concentration; because craving does not take it as an object, it is not something to be relished.

Among the eight attainments thus described, the factors (*aṅga*) are included within the dhyānas but not within the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), because the formless attainments are extremely tranquil.

This means that while a yogin delights in cultivating wholesome qualities, if one were to establish individual factors (*aṅga*) within a vast accumulation of merit and diligently practice them, the mind and mental factors would become dull and weak due to the increase of tranquility (*śamatha*) in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therefore, no such factors are established therein.

Alternatively, it may be that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is predominant in those stages; however, a single predominance cannot justify the designation of a "limb" (*aṅga*), for a factor is called a limb only when multiple dharmas increase together.
For this reason, the dhyānas alone are established as having limbs, because in them concentration and wisdom proceed in equilibrium and many factors increase.

For this reason, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are also not established as having [meditative] factors (*aṅga*), because in the preparatory stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is only wisdom (*prajñā*) that increases. Other masters say:
"If there are distinct mental factors (*caitasika*) within certain stages, only when these others are completely eliminated can those factors be established for that stage, and not otherwise."

In the first dhyāna, mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*) are abandoned; in the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are eliminated without remainder; in the third, joy (*prīti*) is extinguished; and in the fourth, pleasure (*sukha*) is severed. Although there is a general and gradual reduction throughout the formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*), there is no complete abandonment of these factors within any specific stage.
This explanation fails to dispel the doubts of others as to why the factors (*aṅga*) are established only in these [four] cases;
therefore, the previous explanation is superior.
How many factors are there in each of the four dhyānas?
The verse says:
The first dhyāna has five factors: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi;
the second has four factors: adhyātmasaṃprasāda, prīti, sukha, and samādhi.
The third possesses five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and concentration;
the fourth has four factors: equanimity, mindfulness, neutral feeling, and concentration.
The commentary says:
Among the four pure, untainted dhyānas, the first possesses five factors: first, vitarka; second, vicāra; third, prīti; fourth, sukha; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).

One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is a synonym for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since concentration and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) are identical in essence though different in name, that which is called "concentration" is itself superior meditative absorption; it is here designated as one-pointedness of mind.
The second dhyāna possesses only four factors: first, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind. The third dhyāna possesses five factors:
first, equanimity; second, right mindfulness; third, right discernment; fourth, the experience of bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna possesses only four factors: first, purity of equanimity; second, purity of mindfulness; third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
For what reason do the first and third [dhyānas] each possess five factors, while the second and fourth possess only four?
It is because only that many factors are capable of being established as branches;
or alternatively, it is because the desire realm abounds in various unwholesome dharmas, and the five exquisite sensual pleasures are difficult to sever and difficult to relinquish.

The second dhyāna possesses the joy (*prīti*) of the moving stage; its characteristic is that of surging movement, the very pinnacle of joy, which draws forth the five classes of craving and is difficult to relinquish or sever.
To counteract this, the first and third [dhyānas] each possess five factors.
The first three are not so; therefore, the remaining [stages] each have four.

Alternatively, this is for the sake of conforming to the method of transcending meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); that is to say, when first arising in a transcendent attainment, it is difficult to enter a different category and easy to enter a similar category.

However, in the initial stage of arising from the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), one may enter the third from the first, or enter the fourth from the second; therefore, the second and fourth [attainments] each possess only four factors (*aṅga*), while the first and third each possess all five.
Since those that arise subsequently are easy [to cultivate], there are no factors above them.
Since the names of the dhyāna factors total eighteen, how many distinct entities are there among them in reality?
The verse says:
These actual entities are eleven: the first two are bliss and pliancy;
inner serenity is the faculty of faith; and joy is the sensation of gladness.
The Commentary says:
The actual entities (*dravya*) of these factors (*aṅga*) are only eleven: namely, the first five factors constitute five actual entities;
the three factors of the second dhyāna are as before, and with the addition of the factor of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), they total six.
The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the third dhyāna is as previously described, with four additional factors added to the previous ones to total ten.
The three factors of the fourth dhyāna are as previously described, with the factor of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure added to the previous ones to total eleven.

For what reason are the mind and other factors not branches of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)? This should be understood according to the previous analysis of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Those that differ from them shall now be briefly distinguished.
The three feelings that are neither-suffering-nor-joy are not [included] because suffering and joy are exclusively comprised within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The three feelings, according to their respective levels (*bhūmi*), serve as factors of benefit; because they accord with the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with great strength, they are all included among the factors (*aṅga*).
For what reason is diligence (*vīrya*) not established as a factor of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?

Because the factors of meditative concentration are conducive to excellence within their own stage (*svabhūmi*), whereas diligence is conducive to higher stages; therefore, it is not established as a factor.
Alternatively, the factors of meditative concentration provide a state of well-being and ease, whereas diligence seeks excellence through exertion, which is wearisome and painful.

Vitarka and vicāra both assist meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by restraining and directing the mind to distance it from coarseness and subtlety; because they counteract sensual desires and evil, they are established together as factors (*aṅga*).
For what reason is non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) not a factor of dhyāna?
The factors of the dhyānas assist in stabilizing the mind upon its object; since those [factors] do not take an object as their own support, they are not established as "factors.

Thus, although there are eighteen factors of dhyāna according to the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*), when sought among the actual categories of entities (*dravya-jāti*), there should be only nine types. However, because the characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*) differ, they are divided into eleven.
For this reason it is said: there are factors that constitute the first member but not the second member;
one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation refers to applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
The second phrase refers to internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
The third phrase refers to joy, bliss, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fourth phrase refers to all other factors remaining after excluding those previously mentioned.
The remaining members should be considered in relation to one another according to reason.
In this context, what is the meaning of the term "member" (*aṅga*)?
It signifies the sense of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
What is being demonstrated and established?
It means demonstrating and establishing that "this is the first dhyāna," up to "this is the fourth dhyāna.

Alternatively, these names for the factors (aṅga) follow their respective meanings; just as the citron and so forth are named after other factors, the eighteen factors each accord with their own respective stages.

Alternatively, the meaning of "requisite" (*upakaraṇa*) is expressed by the term "limb" (*aṅga*), as in the case of the limbs of a sacrifice, such as cattle and horses; that is to say, vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, mutually assist one another.
The Vaibhāṣika masters, wishing to manifest that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within the dhyāna stages is preeminent, have thus made this statement.
Samādhi is both dhyāna and a limb of dhyāna;
vitarka, vicāra, and so forth are limbs of dhyāna but are not themselves dhyāna.
How is it known that samādhi is the most excellent among the factors belonging to the stages of dhyāna?
For it is stated in the Sūtras: "One should know that the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) exists within the four dhyānas.

However, because the meanings of "mutual establishment" and "mutual protection" are similar, such a statement is made; there is no fault in this, just as with a fourfold army. Although the king and his retinue support one another, the king is preeminent among them.
Is it not the case that since the essential nature of the bliss in the three dhyānas is identical, there should not be eleven factors of meditative absorption?
The bliss of the third dhyāna has feeling as its essence, whereas the bliss of the first and second dhyānas is pliancy; therefore, the factors of meditative absorption actually number eleven.

Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) pervade all four dhyānas; for what reason are only pliancy established in the first two, while only equanimity is established in the latter two stages?
It is because these [qualities] are particularly conducive to those respective stages.
This means that in the desire realm there are various unwholesome dharmas, and in the stage of the first dhyāna there are vitarka, vicāra, and saṃjñā which afflict the mind like poisonous arrows.
Since the first two [dhyānas] are free from these, pliancy increases.

In the second dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is extremely agitated; in the third dhyāna, the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is excessively increased. Both can serve as superior bases for the arising of craving; therefore, in the third and fourth [dhyānas], one abandons them, and thus equanimity (*upekṣā*) increases.

Alternatively, the *dausthulya* (dysfunction) induced by desire and the sensory consciousnesses associated with the first level of form is more severe than in other stages; because the first two [stages] are free from these, *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) increases.
In the third and fourth stages, one is further removed from *dausthulya*, and as tranquility becomes increasingly superior, *upekṣā* (equanimity) increases.

This means that the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is like first laying down a heavy burden; because it becomes increasingly subtle as one shifts through the stages, pliancy is established only in the first two stages.
In the third and fourth stages, it proceeds spontaneously, and because its tranquility becomes even more superior, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established.
Alternatively, the first and second dhyānas possess pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as their condition, because joy (*prīti*) serves as the predominant condition for pliancy.
As the Sūtra says: "Because of joy, there is pliancy."
In the third and fourth dhyānas, because there is no object for joy (*prīti*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is weak and thus is not established as a factor (*aṅga*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) and pliancy mutually obscure one another; where one is present, the second is absent.

Pliancy (praśrabdhi) remedies sluggishness, its characteristic being buoyancy; equanimity (upekṣā) remedies restlessness, its characteristic being tranquility. Therefore, pliancy and equanimity mutually obscure one another.
What reasoning serves as proof that among the three factors of bliss, two are pliancy and the third is feeling (vedanā)?
It has already been stated that [the third dhyāna] exclusively conforms to that [pleasure].
That is to say, the pleasure of the third dhyāna is not pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), nor is pliancy a factor (*aṅga*) of that [third dhyāna].

Furthermore, it was previously stated that the pleasure of the first two dhyānas cannot possibly be a feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*); for it is illogical in both cases [to consider it either mental or physical feeling].

This means that the pleasure of the first two dhyānas cannot possibly be bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*), because while one is actually in meditative absorption, the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist.
Nor can it be mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*), for it would then be identical to joy (*prīti*).
Only when one has transcended both joy and pleasure can the mental gladness of the higher stages be established as a distinct "pleasure sensation" (*sukha-vedanā*) different from what preceded it.
Joy (*prīti*) is the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*); it is illogical for two feelings to coexist within a single moment of mind.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because joy and bliss arise alternately, this reasoning is also incorrect, for [the sūtras] speak of [the first dhyāna] as possessing five factors (*pañcāṅga*) and [the second] as possessing four factors (*caturaṅga*).

If it is argued that the numbers four and five are stated in terms of what is possible and do not necessarily imply simultaneous occurrence, this is also unreasonable, for it would follow that there must be a meditative absorption (dhyāna) possessing vitarka but lacking vicāra.
However, the Sūtra merely states that there are three types of sustained application (samādhi)—namely, that which possesses both vitarka and vicāra, and so forth, as explained at length.
If the factors of dhyāna do not necessarily arise together, for what reason is it not stated that there is a concentration with vitarka and without vicāra?
Furthermore, the three types of samādhi should also be fully present within the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
This would contradict what is taught in the sūtras.

One should now consider this: since the mental sensation of joy in the third dhyāna is already the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), it ought to be called "joy"; why, then, is it called "bliss" (*sukha*)?
This so-called "pleasure" also has its cause: it is because the various faculties of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) are not tranquil.
That is to say, joy surges and agitates the concentrated mind, like waves and billows that surge, overflow, and violently toss the water.
In the first and second dhyānas, the mental feeling of satisfaction possesses such characteristics that it receives the name "joy" (prīti).
In the third dhyāna, this same mental feeling of satisfaction becomes tranquil in its nature and thus acquires the name "bliss" (sukha).

Therefore, within this meditative absorption, the function of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is predominant; because joy (*prīti*) has been relinquished, it is established as the factor of "equanimity" (*upekṣā-saṃskāra*).
In the fourth absorption, pleasure (*sukha*) is further relinquished; thus, that equanimity is termed "pure."
For what reason, when mindfulness and wisdom exist in all stages, is mindfulness established as a factor only in the upper two dhyānas, and wisdom only in the third dhyāna?
Because it conforms excessively to what is appropriate for each case—

namely, that joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) within the three realms of existence are what sentient beings most intensely relish— the third dhyāna represents the ultimate limit of such relishing.

Since it contains the most excellent pleasure found within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it stands to reason that one should establish wisdom (*prajñā*) to observe and cultivate detachment from it.
If one lacks wisdom, one cannot even accomplish the wholesome roots of one's own stage, let alone progress toward higher ones.
To remedy such faults within one's own stage, wisdom is established as a factor in the third dhyāna; this is not the case for other stages, and thus wisdom is not established there.
In the second dhyāna, there is supreme joy (*prīti*), which is as flighty and distracting as a rākṣasa.
In the third dhyāna, there is supreme bliss (*sukha*), which is like the exquisite desires of the gods and is extremely difficult to relinquish.

In the third and fourth dhyānas, although the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*) has already been relinquished as appropriate to each stage, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is established to prevent its recurrence through the fear of falling back; this is not the case for other stages, and therefore mindfulness is not established there.

However, the power and function of the third mindfulness are firm and strong; it not only assists equanimity but can also assist wisdom, and is capable of universally preventing faults of both one's own stage and other stages.
The fourth is not so, as there are no faults of its own stage; for this reason, the factor of wisdom is not established for the fourth.

In the first and second dhyānas, although mindfulness and wisdom exist to prevent and illuminate, their function is slight due to the agitation caused by *vitarka* (applied thought) and *prīti* (joy). In the fourth dhyāna, they are obscured by the two types of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and because this state accords with ignorance (*avidyā*), the function of wisdom does not increase. Therefore, wisdom exists only in three [stages], while mindfulness extends through the upper two as well.

Alternatively, because the bliss of the third dhyāna is extremely subtle, the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) is not established; without it, there can be no clear discernment. If there is no clear discernment, one will neither feel revulsion toward the faults of one's own stage nor seek the merits of a higher stage.

However, because the lower levels seek joy while the higher levels are coarse, and although they illuminate renunciation and seeking, these are not considered extraordinary; therefore, wisdom is not established as a factor in the other three dhyānas.
Because the fault of pleasure in the third dhyāna is difficult to perceive, the Buddha said that it should be spoken of and known by the noble ones.

Because the faculty of wisdom (prajñā) is most preeminent within this meditative absorption (samādhi), it is established as a constituent factor (aṅga) since it is capable of discerning subtle faults;
although the wisdom at the limit of the fourth [dhyāna] can also comprehend them, it does so only in terms of general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) and is thus not considered extraordinary.

This means that because their associated levels (*bhūmi*) differ, this is the path of detachment which takes a general view of the faults of the lower realm; it is not like the wisdom of its own level, which, being bound by the same fetters, can only discern the faults of its own sphere as something marvelous. Therefore, it establishes its own factors (*aṅga*), whereas the wisdom of the higher level does not.

Furthermore, although there are those who have already attained the third dhyāna, they do not all possess mastery over its fourth limit; therefore, at the time when they are about to become detached from the defilement of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), that wisdom cannot be established as a constituent factor (*aṅga*). Consequently, wisdom is established as a constituent factor only in the [first] three dhyānas.

However, at the time of correct realization and when one has already become detached from the initial stage, both require guarding; thus, the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) must be established as a limb.
Why is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) established as a constituent body?
Because in the first and second dhyānas, the function of pliancy increases, reaching a distinguished state not previously encountered.

Through this power and function, one applies diligent effort without abandoning it, which enables the mental continuum to become capable and assists meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in drawing forth superior qualities; because it possesses such preeminent utility, it is established as a limb (*aṅga*).
What phenomenon does the term "internal serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) designate?
It designates the subsiding of vitarka and vicāra; its essence is the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya).

That is to say, when one realizes the second dhyāna, a profound faith arises even within the stage of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi) that allows for detachment from [vitarka and vicāra]; this is called internal serenity.
Therefore, although the faculty of faith exists in all stages, it can be established as a factor [of enlightenment] only in the second dhyāna.
This is because one now newly gains faith that the factors of the various dhyāna stages, like those of the non-concentrated (dispersed) stages, can both be abandoned.

Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, the presence of vitarka and vicāra within the aggregate of consciousness is like a hot mire that prevents faith from being clear and pure; in the latter two dhyānas, the function of equanimity (upekṣā) increases and eclipses the faculty of faith, and thus there is no internal purity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
This means that it increases precisely through the awakening power of faith; because it abandons its opposite, it is able to outshine it.

Since faith is characterized by purity, it is designated by the name "purity. Just as a water-clearing gem purifies the mind, this internal mental equanimity arises with that as its condition; therefore, the faculty of faith is called "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).

Alternatively, all the qualities belonging to the second dhyāna serve as equal conditions to induce this purity; it is for this reason that the name "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) is established.

It does not consist solely of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), because these [qualities] are all subsumed under mental factors (*caitta*), just as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) possess distinct substantial entities.
Other schools state: joy (*prīti*) is not the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
Joy belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and is subsumed under mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
The bliss within the three dhyānas is entirely the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
Therefore, joy (*prīti*) and the feeling of joy differ in their essential nature.
The bliss of the three dhyānas cannot be designated as the feeling of joy, for this is clearly proven by two Āgamas.
As stated in the *Viparyāsa-vibhaṅga-sūtra*:

"The five faculties, beginning with sorrow (*daurmanasya*), are gradually extinguished without remainder; in the third dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is extinguished without remainder; and in the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (*sukha*) is extinguished without remainder."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"In the fourth dhyāna, pleasure is abandoned and pain is abandoned; previously, joy and sorrow have subsided.
Therefore, the third dhyāna must certainly lack the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); thus, this feeling of joy is *prīti* (joy) rather than *saumanasya* (mental happiness).
Regarding the eight attainments previously mentioned, the first seven each have three types, while the eighth has two—namely, the defiled attainment.
How is it known that these exist?
This is because they are taught in both the sūtras and the śāstras.
This means that after the sūtra has explained the pure and untainted concentrations (anāsrava-samādhi), it further states that the Blessed One has not yet taught all concentrations.
Thus, we know that there remain other defiled concentrations (kliṣṭa-samādhi) that have not been taught.
The *Mūla-śāstra* also states that within the various dhyānas, all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of their own respective levels increase in accordance with them.

From these passages, one knows that there are defiled meditative absorptions; therefore, it is said that dhyānas are of two general types, distinguished by being either meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) or births (*upapatti*).
Furthermore, the meditative absorptions themselves are of two kinds: defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
The undefiled is further divided into two types: the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The untainted is further divided into two: that of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and that of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
Such distinctions, in principle, are manifold.
Are there factors (*aṅga*) within the defiled dhyānas?
Yes, but not all of them. Which ones are absent in which concentrations?
The verse says:
In the defiled [dhyānas], in order, from the first, there is no joy, bliss, inner purity, right mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, or mindfulness; others say there is no pliancy or equanimity.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, there is a certain class [of teachers] who speak according to the characteristics [of the states], asserting that the joy and bliss born of seclusion do not exist within the first dhyāna, because they are not produced apart from the afflictions.
Although defiled meditative absorption is also associated with joy (*prīti*), it is not included among the factors (*aṅga*) because it does not arise from seclusion (*viveka*).

This does not refer solely to the joy arising from the seclusion of desire; it also refers to the joy arising from the seclusion of the defilements of one's own stage (*svabhūmi*). For the Sūtra first states:
"Having become secluded from all desires and unwholesome, evil dharmas..."
It further states:
"joy and bliss born of seclusion.
Here, the term "born of seclusion" is repeated in order to show that there is also joy, which arises from being free from the afflictions of its own level.
To demonstrate that the factor of joy (*prīti*) is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*), the Blessed One has spoken of it in conjunction with pleasure (*sukha*).

Since that which is associated with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) must necessarily be wholesome, defiled meditative absorption (*samādhi*) can never possess the factor of joy; therefore, the first defiled dhyāna possesses only three factors.
In the second type of defiled [faith], there is no internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), because it is disturbed and turbid by afflictions.
Although worldly people speak of "defiled faith," it is not established as a factor because it is not subsumed under [true] faith.
Pleasure (*sukha*) is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and is comprised solely within the category of the wholesome; since it is analogous to the first dhyāna, it is not explicitly excluded here.
Therefore, these defiled factors consist of only two types.
It is accepted that the second defiled dhyāna possesses the factor of joy (*prīti*), whereas this is absent in the first defiled dhyāna. What serves as the proof for this?
The joy of the first dhyāna is said to arise from seclusion because the phrase "arising from seclusion" is absent in the description of the second [dhyāna].
Within the defiled third [dhyāna], there is no right mindfulness or wisdom, because it is deluded by defiled pleasure.

Although mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) exist within defiled meditative absorption (*kliṣṭa-samādhi*), they are termed "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*) and "lack of correct knowledge" (*asaṃprajanya*) respectively; therefore, these two factors do not exist within the defiled state.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is categorized exclusively as a wholesome factor (*kuśala-dharma*); since it is analogous to the fourth [dhyāna], it is not excluded here.
Therefore, these defiled factors consist of only two types.
Within the fourth defilement, there is no purity of equanimity and mindfulness, because it is defiled by the afflictions; for this reason, the fourth defilement consists of only two factors.
Other masters say:

In the first two defiled concentrations, there is simply no *praśrabdhi* (pliancy); in the latter two defiled states, there is simply no *upekṣā-saṃskāra* (equanimity of formation), because these are comprised within the great wholesome factors.
They further state that in the defiled states, *prīti*, *śraddhā*, *smṛti*, and *prajñā* are all included as factors (*aṅga*), because they all pertain to the defiled.
The Sūtra states:
"The three dhyānas are subject to movement; the fourth is immovable.
Based on what meaning is this said?
The verse says:
The fourth is named "Immovable," because it is free from the eight calamities;
these eight refer to vitarka and vicāra, and the four feelings along with inhalation and exhalation.
The treatise states:
The lower three dhyānas are called "subject to movement" because they possess calamities and afflictions;
the fourth dhyāna is called "unmoving" because it is free from calamities and afflictions.
There are eight calamities. What are these eight?
They are vitarka, vicāra, the four sensations, inhalation, and exhalation.
These eight afflictions are entirely absent in the fourth [dhyāna]; therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, described it as "unshakable" (*āneñja*).
However, when the sūtra states only that the fourth dhyāna is not shaken by vitarka, vicāra, prīti, or sukha, this is said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
According to the treatise on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the Blessed One has stated in certain passages:
"Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and with prior joy and sorrow having vanished, one dwells fully possessed of the fourth dhyāna."
Furthermore, it is said that in that concentration, bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) cease along with [the others].

Since inhalation and exhalation are called bodily formations, we know that this concentration does not merely avoid the four calamities of movement—namely, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*).
Other masters say:
The fourth dhyāna is called "unshakable" (āneñjya) because it is like a lamp in a sealed room that illuminates without flickering;
this is according to the *Upamā-sūtra*.
What fault do vitarka and vicāra possess that one seeks their cessation?
They cause the mind, even when constantly bound to its meditative object through mindfulness, to remain unsettled.
It is like the branches and twigs of a tree that, though resting upon the trunk, shake incessantly because they are joined with the wind.

Although practitioners of yoga do not desire for the mind to quickly shift its engagement with the aspects of objects, the power of vitarka and vicāra causes it to flow away; therefore, vitarka and vicāra are faults within meditative concentration.

Joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) can also stir the mind; it is because these four alone are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and are able to move the mind that the Sūtra speaks of them specifically.
However, in reality, the two breaths (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) and the two feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and pain (*duḥkha*) can also stir the mind; therefore, the Śāstra speaks of eight.
Since the two factors of vitarka and vicāra possess these faults, they should not be said to exist among the branches of dhyāna.
The Sūtra should simply state that vitarka and vicāra are stilled; how could it also say that [the first dhyāna] "possesses vitarka and vicāra"?

To clarify that although vitarka and vicāra are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they can act as afflictions within that concentration, it must be explained that they are not absent from it; therefore, they ought to be discussed.

Alternatively, these two serve as the initial provisions for concentration, acting as a remote antidote (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) to sensual and unwholesome thoughts; subsequently, they become afflictions within superior concentration. Thus, it is said that the function of vitarka and vicāra is not in vain.
It is the natural principle of the methods for abandoning conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) that even that which is to be abandoned must initially be relied upon.
Just as one who wishes to cross a river must first rely on a boat or raft, but once he has reached the other shore, it is logical that he should abandon them all; thus the Sūtra says:
"One relies on form to transcend desire, relies on the formless to transcend form, relies on the Path to transcend the formless, and upon attaining Nirvāṇa, one also transcends the Noble Path."
These two [minds] can coexist with a single mind, just as superior and inferior winds may converge upon a single branch.
If these two types of karma are said to be "agitating," how can they be described as being associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?

The mind in coarse and shallow concentration is only able to transcend the coarse defilements of the desire realm when spurred by vitarka and vicāra; therefore, this attainment is associated with the first dhyāna.

Because of this association, it is not yet pure, just as when both a lamp and the sun serve as conditions for seeing forms: though the lamp’s subtle light illuminates even in darkness, its clarity is not distinct, whereas the sunlight, being free from darkness, has a clearly manifest power of illumination.

Thus it should be understood: although the first dhyāna performs its own function while accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, it is without movement—unlike the fourth dhyāna—because it has not yet attained illumination.

If vitarka, when present in meditative concentration, can agitate and disturb the mind, then even its presence in untainted (anāsrava) concentration would constitute a defect; for what reason, then, is it established as a factor of the path?

It has already been stated that because these [factors] can stimulate right view, when a practitioner has not yet become habituated to meditative concentration, they are unable to recognize this as a defect; therefore, they have no desire to grow weary of or abandon this stage.
If one has already become habituated, one is then able to perceive that such calamities exist within the first dhyāna.
It is like when water is clear and still, one can see the submerged insects and small fish within the pool that cause turbidity and agitation.

Once the practitioner sees that the two factors of vitarka and vicāra within the first dhyāna are capable of causing agitation and distraction, they develop a general sense of weary detachment toward that entire stage, thinking: "Since this is coarse and shallow, it ought to be abandoned."
Just as vitarka and vicāra function in the first dhyāna, so too do joy and the other factors in the higher stages.
Is it the case that the distinctions among the various feelings in the dhyānas of meditative concentration are the same as those in the [resultant] births?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:

In the dhyānas born [of the form realm], from the first [dhyāna] onward, there are [the feelings of] joy and pleasure, joy and equanimity, and pleasure and equanimity; in the last, there is only the feeling of equanimity, respectively.
The commentary states:
Within the dhyānas of the realm of form, there are initially three feelings:
first, the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), which is associated with the mental consciousness;
second, the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*), which is associated with the [first] three consciousnesses.
The third is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which is associated with four consciousnesses.
The second [dhyāna] has two, namely joy (*prīti*) and equanimity, which are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) because there is no other consciousness [present], and because mental gladness (*saumanasya*) is coarse.
In the third [dhyāna], there are two, namely pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In the fourth [dhyāna], there is one, namely exclusively the sensation of equanimity, which is associated with the mental consciousness.
This is called the distinction in the experience born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Since the three higher dhyānas lack the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) and are devoid of vitarka and vicāra, how can one who is born there see, hear, touch, or produce manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*)?
It is not that those born in that stage lack eye-consciousness and so forth;
rather, it is that they are not bound by them.
Why is this? The verse says:

When one is born in the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna), the minds that give rise to the three types of informative [action] are all subsumed under the first dhyāna; they are exclusively non-obscured and do not arise [in those higher levels].
The treatise says:

When one is born in the three higher stages, the arising of the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) and the mind that initiates expression (*vijñapti-citta*) are all bound to the first dhyāna.
Just as one born in a higher stage may give rise to a lower [state], such as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), one is thus able to see, hear, touch, and initiate expression.

These four are exclusively non-obscured neutral; they do not give rise to defilements of a lower level because one has already abandoned such defilements, nor do they give rise to wholesome states of a lower level because those are inferior.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Sarvāstivāda School), Fascicle 38.

Chapter Nine: Analysis of Meditative Concentration (Dhyāna), Part Two. Having thus explained the matters concerning meditative concentration individually, how is the attainment (*prāpti*) of the various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*)?
The verse says:
The unwholesome is acquired through birth; the pure arises from the abandonment of defilement;
the untainted arises from the abandonment of defilement; and the defiled arises through birth and through falling away.
The treatise says:

Regarding the eight fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*), as appropriate to each case, if they are acquired without having been previously accomplished at all, the various pure attainments (*śuddhaka*) arise through two causes and conditions:

first, through detachment (*vairāgya*), which refers to the time when one becomes detached from the defilements of a lower stage while remaining in that same lower stage; [the second is through birth].
Second, by way of rebirth: this refers to when one is born from a higher level into one's own level.

This applies to all seven lower levels; however, it is not so for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because there is no higher level beyond it. Since one can only attain detachment through the absence of a superior level, there is no rebirth there from a higher level.

In this context, only the fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*) are mentioned because, regarding the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), when one has not yet abandoned defilement, there are cases where they are entirely unaccomplished and are acquired solely through application (*prayoga*).
What is being excluded by stating this?

The phrase "not at all" is used to exclude that which has already been accomplished, yet allows for the acquisition of a partial portion; for example, as one may obtain the pure fundamental meditative attainment (*mauladhyāna*) through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), or obtain its "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*) through falling away.
Based on this meaning, he poses the following question:

Is there any pure concentration that is acquired through the abandonment of defilement and relinquished through the abandonment of defilement; acquired through falling away and relinquished through falling away; and acquired through birth and relinquished through birth?
It is said:
Yes, namely the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*).

Furthermore, that which is subsumed under the stage conducive to decline in the first dhyāna is acquired when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm and abandoned when one becomes free from the defilements of its own level; it is acquired when one declines from freedom from the defilements of its own level and abandoned when one declines from freedom from the defilements of the desire realm; it is acquired when one is born from a higher level and abandoned when one is born from its own level into a lower one.
The inclusion of other stages should be understood through correct reasoning.

The untainted [attainments] are acquired solely through the abandonment of defilement; that is to say, when a noble one abandons the defilements of a lower stage, they acquire the untainted [attainments] of the higher stage. This also refers specifically to those who have not previously attained them at all.

If it has already been accomplished previously, it may also be attained at other times; that is, one attains the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) at the stage of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and one attains both the paths of learning (*śaikṣa*) and no-more-learning at the time of refining the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
Other cases, such as through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) or retrogression (*parihāṇi*), should all be considered according to reason.

Although there are cases where one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and thereby attains the fundamental uncontaminated meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samāpatti*), this is not necessarily through the gradual stages, because at that time one has not yet attained the fundamental dhyāna.

In this context, we discuss only those attainments that are certain: the noble ones necessarily obtain the fundamental untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the higher stages when they become free from the defilements of the lower stages.

As for the attainment of defiled states, it occurs through rebirth and through falling away (*parihāṇi*). That is to say, one obtains the defilements of a lower stage when dying in a higher stage and being reborn in a lower stage; and one obtains the defilements of a particular stage when falling away from the state of being free from the defilements of that stage.
It cannot be attained through detachment from passion (*vairāgya*) nor through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because it is at these two times that one is able to abandon passion.
Regarding which attainments (*samāpatti*) arise immediately after which:
the verse says:
The untainted (anāsrava) produces the wholesome (kuśala) of its own level, and those of the levels above and below up to the third;
the pure (śuddha) produces likewise, while also producing the defiled (kliṣṭa) of its own level.
The defiled produces the pure and the defiled of its own level, as well as the pure of the level immediately below.
The pure [state] gives rise to all; the defiled gives rise to its own level and those below it.
The commentary states:
Immediately following the untainted (anāsrava), one’s own level, the levels above, and the levels below give rise to the wholesome (kuśala).

The "wholesome" (kuśala) term fully encompasses both the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are diametrically opposed to the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), which necessarily does not arise from them.

However, within each [realm], one can only reach up to the third dhyāna; because it is too distant, there is no capacity to leap over and arise in the fourth. Therefore, among the seven untainted attainments (*samāpatti*), six arise immediately after the first *dhyāna*: namely, the pure and the untainted states of its own level, the second, and the third.

From the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), seven states arise in immediate succession: namely, the six levels from its own stage down to the lower ones, and the pure (*śuddhaka*) state of the higher level.
From the second dhyāna, eight states arise in immediate succession: namely, the six levels from its own stage upward, together with two states from the lower level—the two types of consciousness.
From the sphere of infinite space, nine states arise immediately: namely, the six from its own and lower levels, plus three from the higher levels.
From the third and fourth spheres of emptiness (ākāśānantya and vijñānānantya), ten states arise immediately: namely, the eight from the upper and lower levels, plus two from its own level.
Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) can immediately give rise to the formless realm,
whereas dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) cannot, because their bases and objects differ.
The same applies to what arises from pure meditative attainments (*śuddha-samāpatti*), though each also concurrently gives rise to the defiled states of its own level.

Therefore, from the pure [attainment] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), six arise in immediate succession: namely, its own pure and defiled [attainments], and the pure and untainted [attainments] of the lower realms.

From the first dhyāna, seven arise in immediate succession; from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), eight; from the second dhyāna, nine; from the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), ten; and from the remaining [spheres], eleven.
From an impure attainment (*samāpatti*), one gives rise to both an impure and a pure attainment of its own level, as well as a pure meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the immediately lower level.

This is because, when pressured by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of one's own level, one develops a sense of respect even for the pure absorption of a lower level; thus, there is the arising of a pure absorption of the next lower level from an impure one. However, because it is utterly incompatible with them, an untainted (*anāsrava*) absorption does not arise from an impure one.
If one can correctly understand defilement and purity, it is possible to transition from defilement to the arising of lower purity; in that case, this purity arises from purity itself.
Since correct understanding is subsumed under purity, and various defiled states are incapable of correct understanding, how could they give rise to purity from within defilement?
This is due to the power of prior vows;
that is, one previously vowed:
"I would rather attain the purity of the lower realms than require the defilement of the higher ones."
The power of a prior vow continues to function throughout the mental continuum; therefore, a subsequent pure meditative absorption arises from a state of defilement.
This is like first making a resolve before falling asleep, whereby one is able to awaken at the appointed time.

What has been stated regarding the production of defilement by the pure and the defiled refers only to the case of the pure and defiled states occurring while in meditative absorption (*samāhita*). As for the production of the pure and the defiled at the time of birth—specifically the production of defilement—it is not so;
that is to say, at the moment of death, from the pure state acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), every single [moment] is immediately followed by the arising of all types of defilement.

If, from each instance of defilement arising from birth, one can immediately produce all instances of defilement belonging to its own level and all those of lower levels— but not those of higher levels because one has not yet abandoned the lower—
then as for what was said regarding the production of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) from the pure (*śuddha*), are all types capable of producing it?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:

Pure concentration is of four kinds, namely: the part conducive to decline, the part conducive to maintenance, the part conducive to progress, and that subsumed under the part conducive to penetration.
These correspond respectively to the afflictions, to one's own level or a higher level, and to the untainted (anāsrava).
Mutually regarded, they arise in the sequence of two, three, three, and one.

The commentary states: There are four types of pure attainments (*śuddha-samāpatti*) in total: first, those categorized as conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*); second, those categorized as conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*); third, those categorized as conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*); and fourth, those categorized as conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). Each level (*bhūmi*) possesses all four; however, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) possesses only three, because there is no higher level to which one could proceed, and thus that level lacks those categorized as conducive to progress.
Among these four, only the fourth part can produce the untainted (*anāsrava*). Why is this? Because among these four types, they possess such characteristics:

the *parihāṇabhāgīya* (the part conducive to falling away) is conducive to the afflictions; the *sthityābhāgīya* (the part conducive to remaining) is conducive to its own level; the *viśeṣabhāgīya* (the part conducive to distinction) is conducive to a higher level; and the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (the part conducive to penetration) is conducive to the untainted. Therefore, all untainted states arise solely from this [last one].
Other masters say:

those of the stage conducive to decline (hāna-bhāgīya) abide in that state and may fall away; those of the stage conducive to maintenance (sthiti-bhāgīya) abide in that state neither falling away nor advancing; those of the stage conducive to distinction (viśeṣa-bhāgīya) abide in that state and are able to advance; and those of the stage conducive to penetration (nirvedha-bhāgīya) abide in that state and give rise to the Noble Path.
Some say that one abides in that state which accords with the penetration of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), from which one immediately thereafter enters the state beyond error (*niyāma*).

One should understand that the definitive meaning here is this: while the noble paths (*āryamārga*) necessarily arise immediately after this state, it is not the case that they must necessarily arise immediately after this state.
If it were otherwise, one would have to say that only the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is called the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Other masters state:

"The stage conducive to decline (*parihāṇabhāgīya*) is so called because afflictions of lower and higher degrees intermingle, such that defiled and pure states alternate in appearing before the mind."

The stage conducive to abiding (*ānukūlyāvasthāna-bhāgīya*) is that which, by means of various coarse (*audārika*) and other such aspects, rejects the lower stages and, by means of aspects such as tranquility (*śānta*), embraces its own stage.
The stage conducive to progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*) is that which contemplates the faults of its own stage and the merits of the higher stage.
Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*):
when the untainted (*anāsrava*) state arises immediately thereafter, which of these stages manifest?
Some say that all three [the first three] manifest, excluding the stage conducive to decline (*parihāṇabhāgīya*).

In reality, there are only two [types], namely the latter two kinds. This is because for those who cultivate the super-attainments (*samāpatti*) and so forth, these two alone are most firm and superior as they accord with the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The various yoga-practitioners state:

if a practitioner does not thoroughly master the meditative concentration of his own level, does not dwell in it constantly, and fails to aspire toward the concentrations of higher levels, repeatedly manifesting perceptions that accord with lower levels, his meditative equipoise is called the "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*). Alternatively, it is called the part conducive to decline when one falls away from detachment regarding one's own level; a person who achieves such a concentration is termed a "decliner."
Just as one who possesses ox-like behavior is called an "ox," so too, that which is stubborn and difficult to turn back is called "ox-like behavior.

When one is attached to and does not relinquish the meditative absorption of one's own level, yet is unable to aspire toward the meditative absorption of a higher level, such concentration is termed the "part conducive to maintenance" (*sthityanukūla-bhāga*).

Although one is able to dwell extensively in the meditative concentrations of one's own level without becoming attached to them, one feels aspiration for and is drawn toward the meditative concentrations of the higher levels; such concentration is called the "part conducive to progress" (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).

Because one does not become attached to the meditative attainments of one's own or higher stages and frequently dwells in the perception of revulsion, this concentration—which aims to bring about the abandonment of those [lower states]—is called the "Aid to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Those who abide in the "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*) have their minds largely bound to vast fruits.
Those who abide in the stage conducive to stability dwell frequently in their own meditative absorption and are unable to seek higher attainments.
Those who abide in the stage conducive to progress are able to successively seek further superior absorptions.

However, there are generally two kinds of factors conducive to progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*): first, the distinguished qualities of one's own stage; second, the distinguished qualities of higher stages. That which can lead toward these is called the factor conducive to progress.
This consists of two types: either aversion or aspiration.
Those who abide in accordance with the stage of penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) delight in severing all forms of existence and delight in cultivating the untainted (anāsrava); this is called "abiding."
The fourfold classification is distinct; that which accords with the afflictions is called the "part conducive to decline.
How could there be any possibility of regression for Arhats?
It is not that they still possess the meditative absorption conducive to decline such that it could be brought into manifestation, for they have abandoned it through detachment from defilements.

Although this objection exists, there is in fact no contradiction; for that which is conducive to abiding (*sthity-anuloma*) may also be designated as "conducive to decline" (*hāna-bhāgīya*) when it subsequently undergoes retrogression, as has already been explained previously.

Regarding the mutual production of these four in relation to one another: the first can produce two, namely the *anuloma-pratipakṣa* (conducive to decline) and the *sthiti-pratipakṣa* (conducive to maintenance).
The second produces three, excluding the *nirvedha-bhāgīya* (conducive to penetration).
The third produces three, excluding the stage conducive to decline;
the fourth produces one, namely its own [stage] and no others;
some say it also produces the stage conducive to superior progress.

As stated above, both the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) attainments can each leap over stages up to the third. How does the practitioner cultivate these leap-attainments (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), and what are the distinctions between their preliminary applications (*prayoga*) and their fulfillment?
The verse says:
There are two types of meditative absorption, practiced in forward and reverse order; they may be performed evenly, with intervals, in succession, or by skipping.
Mastery is attained through the "skipping" method; this pertains to those of sharp faculties who are beyond training, residing in the three continents.
The treatise states: The fundamental wholesome attainments (*samāpatti*) are divided into two categories: first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), and second, those without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Moving upward is termed "ascending" (*anuloma*); returning downward is termed "descending" (*pratiloma*). Being of the same category is termed "even" (*sama*); being of different categories is termed "intermediate" (*vyavakīrṇa*). Being adjacent is termed "sequential" (*krama*); skipping one level is termed "leaping" (*vilaṅghana*).

This refers to when a practitioner cultivates the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*): first, they repeatedly practice the contaminated (*sāsrava*) attainments of the eight stages in forward, reverse, even, and sequential order; next, they repeatedly practice the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) attainments of the seven stages in forward, reverse, even, and sequential order; next, they repeatedly practice the contaminated and uncontaminated attainments in forward, reverse, alternating, and sequential order; next, they repeatedly practice the contaminated attainments in forward, reverse, even, and leaping order; and finally, they repeatedly practice the uncontaminated attainments in forward, reverse, even, and leaping order. This is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application for the leap-concentration.

Subsequently, when one practices the meditative attainments (samāpatti), whether with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava), in forward, reverse, alternating, or skipping orders, it is called the accomplishment of the "leaping concentration" (vyutkrāntakasamāpatti).
Within this, "leaping" refers to skipping over two [levels] at once: first, leaping over stages (bhūmi); second, leaping over dharmas.
Because one can only leap over one stage at a time, one reaches the third; because it is too distant, one cannot leap over to enter the fourth.
The cultivation of the leap-attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*) occurs only in the three continents, excluding Uttarakuru, and applies to both men and women.

Among the Arhats who are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), only those who have attained the limit of meditative absorptions (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*)—such as the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*), the "wondrous knowledge of vows" (*praṇidhijñāna*), and so forth—are able to transcend [the realm of Māra], and no others; for they possess mastery over meditative absorption and are free from afflictions.
Those liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta), although free from afflictions, lack mastery over meditative concentration;

those who have attained vision through insight (dṛṣṭiprāpta), although they possess mastery over concentration, still have residual afflictions; therefore, neither of them is able to cultivate the "leap-over" attainments (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti).

Because the attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) is weak in its power, it cannot practice the leap-over meditative attainments (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) without interruption.
Upon what kind of body do these various meditative attainments arise?
The verse says:
The various meditative absorptions depend upon their own level or a lower one; they do not depend on a higher level because it would be useless.
Only an Ārya born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can give rise to a lower absorption to exhaust the remaining afflictions.
The Commentary says:

The arising of the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) depends upon a body belonging to one's own level or a lower level; it is impossible for them to arise in dependence on a body of a higher level. This is because there is no purpose in a higher level giving rise to a lower attainment, because one possesses superior concentrations of one's own level, because the power of the lower is inferior, because it has already been abandoned, and because it is subject to aversion and disparagement.

Although this is the general rule, if one explains it in detail: when an Ārya is born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they must necessarily transcend to the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). This is because, in their own level, there is no aspiration for the arising of the noble path; furthermore, since the sphere of nothingness is the most proximate [to the Peak of Existence], they bring that state into manifestation to exhaust the remaining afflictions of their own level. Without the untainted path, there is absolutely no way to sever those remaining delusions and become an Arhat.

Therefore, the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) relies on the bodies of nine stages; the tainted sphere of nothingness relies on the bodies of eight stages; the tainted and untainted sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) relies on the bodies of seven stages; the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) relies on the bodies of six stages; and so on down to the first dhyāna, which relies on the bodies of two stages, namely its own stage and that of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
If one achieves [a meditative attainment] based on the contaminated (*sāsrava*), it arises like the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [attainments], which rely on bodies belonging to all nine stages.
Among the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), what takes what as its object?
The verse says:
The taste-attainments take as their objects those things bound to their own level; the pure and the untainted take all things as their objects;
the wholesome fundamental formless attainments do not take lower tainted things as their objects.
The Commentary says:
The absorption of relishing (āsvādana-samādhi) takes as its object only the contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena of its own level, because contaminated phenomena are things that are bound.

The term "bound" indicates that these are comprised within the three realms of existence. It does not take uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena as its object, because it functions through the aspect of craving (tṛṣṇā).

If craving were untainted (*anāsrava*), it would not be an affliction (*kleśa*); for craving does not take dharmas of a higher stage as its object because the realms and stages are distinct, nor does it take dharmas of a lower stage as its object because one has already abandoned craving for them.

Both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) [knowledges] are able to universally take as their objects all levels—both those above and below themselves—because both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena serve as their spheres of cognition.

As for the distinction between them: the neutral unconditioned (*avyākṛtāsaṃskṛta*) is not an object of the untainted [knowledge], whereas regarding the [pure knowledge] of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it is said to be able to universally take everything as its object; there is nothing that is not its object, as has already been explained previously.

The wholesome formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) subsumed under the fundamental stages do not take the contaminated phenomena (sāsravadharma) of lower stages as their objects, because the phenomena of the lower stages are not tranquil, whereas these fundamental wholesome formless states are extremely tranquil.
For this reason, the sūtras state that in all cases of the formless realms (ārūpya), one "transcends" all lower stages.

This is not said regarding the dhyānas, because the formless states do not originally take lower levels as their objects; therefore, the term "transcendence" is applied to the lower levels in the case of the formless realms.
Since there is knowledge that takes all as its object within the various dhyānas, one does not speak of "transcending" with respect to the lower stages.
Since it is stated that one "transcends the perception of form" and so forth, we know that this is spoken of solely in terms of transcending the objects of cognition.

If this "transcending" (atikrama) is intended to manifest the state of being dissociated from fetters, then one should say it transcends *all* [objects], not merely the perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, within the dhyānas, one should speak of "transcending," for there is no phenomenon of a higher or lower stage that cannot be taken as an object.

Although it can also take the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of lower stages as its object, it takes only the *jñeya-jāti* (the category of "subsequent knowledge") and not the *dharma-jāti* (the category of "knowledge of phenomena"), because it can only take as its object that which constitutes its own complete antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
As previously stated, the *dharma-jāti* does not constitute a complete antidote.

Furthermore, although the path of the category of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) can act as an antidote within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is adventitious and not primary; thus, it cannot take the phenomena of lower stages as its object.

Since it has already been established that the fundamental levels of the formless realm do not take lower stages as objects, by logical extension, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) must have the capacity to take lower stages as objects, because their uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) necessarily take lower stages as their objects.
Among the three types of meditative attainments—the impure, the pure, and the untainted—which have the power to sever the various afflictions?
The verse says:
The untainted can sever the delusions, As well as the pure preparatory stages.
The treatise states:
All untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samādhi*) are capable of severing afflictions (*kleśa*).
If even the fundamental purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) lacks such power, how much less could the defiled states sever them?
That is to say, the fundamentally pure concentration (*prakṛti-viśuddha-samādhi*) cannot abandon the lower [stages], because one has already become free from defilement there;
it cannot abandon the higher [stages], because they are superior to itself;
it cannot abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of its own stage, because they share the same bondage, and furthermore, because it is not an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to itself.
If the pure preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) can also abandon the afflictions, it is because they are all capable of abandoning the afflictions of the immediately lower stage.
The pure [meditation] included within the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) cannot abandon them either.
How many such preparatory stages are there?
With which feelings (*vedanā*) are they associated?
Are all three—taste and so forth—fully present?
The verse says:
The eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are equanimous and pure; the first is also noble, and three are associated with delusion.
The treatise says:
There are likewise eight kinds of preparatory concentrations, as they serve as the gateways to the eight fundamental [dhyānas].
All [of these] are associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because they proceed through deliberate effort and because one has not yet abandoned fear of the lower realms.

These eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are all comprised within the pure meditative absorptions (*śuddhaka-dhyāna*); however, the first preparatory stage alone also includes the untainted (*anāsrava*). This is because all [of them] are paths for detachment through the absence of craving (*asvāda-vairāgya-mārga*).
The seven higher preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) state because they do not feel revulsion toward the phenomena of their own respective levels.
Only the first preparatory stage admits the untainted state because it is capable of feeling revulsion toward the phenomena of its own level.

Because this stage is extremely close to realms characterized by many calamities and afflictions, and because various desires and cravings arise from vitarka and vicāra, which still persist in this stage.
If that is so, for what reason does the *Vibhāṣā* state:

"The stages of preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka*) possess the mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*), for there is no principle whereby a mind free from defilement can effect rebirth-linking"?
Therefore, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) should indeed be associated with the flavor of attachment (*sāsvāda*).
Now, in this context, what is being excluded is defilement pertaining to meditative absorption (*samādhi-kleśa*), not defilement pertaining to rebirth (*upapatti-kleśa*);
thus, there is no contradiction. Alternatively, other masters have stated as follows:
The preliminary concentrations (*sāmantaka*) also possess defilement of meditative absorption, because even before the fundamental [dhyāna] has arisen, one still craves them.

For this reason, the *anāgamya* possesses all three types [of concentration]. Are the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the [four] dhyānas, and the various preliminary concentrations identical in meaning, or do they also have distinctions?

There is also a distinction in their meaning: namely, that all the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are paths for abandoning defilements and causes for entering the fundamental dhyānas, whereas the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is not so.
Furthermore, there is another specific point.
The verse says:
The intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka; it possesses the three [factors] and is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity.

The treatise says: The first fundamental and its preparatory stage are associated with both vitarka and vicāra. Within the seven higher meditative absorptions (samādhis), both vitarka and vicāra are entirely absent. Only the intermediate dhyāna possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka. Therefore, it excels the first dhyāna yet does not reach the level of the second; based on this meaning, it is designated by the name "intermediate."
For this reason, there is no intermediate dhyāna above [the first]; for there is no such ascending or descending between stages.

That is to say, the intermediate dhyāna is subsumed under the first dhyāna, yet it has a distinction: it is established as "intermediate" because it is diminished in its vitarka (applied thought) compared to the higher [levels].
By the reduction of what do they become distinct? Therefore, why does the first dhyāna of the intermediate state (dhyānāntara) exist above [the first dhyāna] but not below it?
Does the Sūtra not speak of the "seven bases of meditative concentration" (saptādhiṣṭhāna-dhyāna)?
How then can we know that there exists separately the "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) and the intermediate state?
This is because there are both sūtras and correct reasoning [to support it].
First, regarding the "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*), as a sūtra states:

"There are those who, though unable to enter the first dhyāna and so forth, yet fully abide therein and, by means of noble wisdom, attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) in this very life."
If the "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) concentration did not exist, upon what would noble wisdom rely?
Furthermore, the *Sūśmasa Sūtra* states:
"There are those liberated by wisdom who do not attain the fundamental dhyānas."
Is it not the case that one achieves liberation through wisdom by relying on meditative concentration?
From this, it is proven that there is the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration and the *dhyānāntara* (intermediate) concentration, as stated in the Sūtra:
There are three types of samādhi, beginning with those accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
The Sūtra states that the first dhyāna is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, while in the second and subsequent [dhyānas], both vitarka and vicāra have ceased.
If there were no intermediate dhyāna, who would possess vicāra without vitarka?
Because the mind and mental factors gradually cease, it stands to reason that there must be a state of concentration with vicāra but without vitarka.
Furthermore, since the Great Brahmā King is the sovereign of this world, what could serve as a superior cause for him other than the intermediate dhyāna?
From this it is proven that the intermediate dhyāna exists.

However, the Buddha did not explicitly enumerate the "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) and the intermediate stages because both are subsumed within the first dhyāna; thus, by speaking of the first dhyāna, he has already spoken of them.

Only the first preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is termed "unattained" (*anāgamya*) for the purpose of distinguishing it from the other preparatory stages; this preparatory stage does not arise by means of a preceding meditative absorption, nor does one experience craving (*āsvādana*) while abiding in it.
It is based on this meaning that the name "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) is established.

It is not the case that the borders of the higher meditative concentrations are also called "not-yet-attained," for all [of those] are induced by the power of a preceding concentration, and because the relish (*āsvādana*) has already arisen while abiding in them.
The *Vibhāṣā* masters explain it thus:
the name "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) is established because one has not yet reached the fundamental stage; this means that the virtues of that fundamental stage have not yet become manifest.
This intermediate absorption (*dhyānāntara*) possesses all three types, including the "tasting" (*āsvādana*), because it is specifically connected to a single place of rebirth.

This means that those who have extensively cultivated the intermediate dhyāna will, in the future, be born in the realm of Mahābrahmā; therefore, they also possess the three [characteristics] just as in the fundamental dhyānas.

It is not that one gives rise to craving for that state while in a non-fundamental stage, because just as there is a distinction in what is tasted (*āsvādya*), there is likewise a distinction in the taster (*āsvādaka*). Furthermore, because this state possesses superior qualities that are desirable to taste, and because even the arising of untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration gradually diminishes therein.

This [path] is also exclusively associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Because the three bodies of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*) are absent, there is no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); and because joy (*prīti-vedanā*) has already been excluded from the first [dhyāna], it is not associated with that either.
