For what reason do only these ten receive the name "totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
Because above these, there are no further modes of universal activity (*sarvatraga-ākāra*).
Only in the fourth dhyāna, as well as in the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness, can one speak of the existence of infinite modes of activity.

The first eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are like the liberation of purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*); their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is entirely the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*), and when including their associated factors (*sahabhū-saṃprayukta*), they consist of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The latter four spheres of mastery are induced by the preparatory application (*prayoga*), and therefore they are the same as those [first eight], just like the liberation of purity.
Furthermore, just as the pure liberation (*śuddha-vimokṣa*) relies upon the fourth dhyāna and takes the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as its object,
how is it that earth and so forth are also called the "form-sphere"?
This is because there are distinctions between earth and the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), and so on.

Since it has already been stated previously that "earth" and so forth refer to manifest form (varṇa-saṃsthāna), when the "bases of totality" (kṛtsnāyatana) of earth and so forth are taught, they do not refer to the "earth element" (pṛthivī-dhātu) and so forth; therefore, the first eight types take only the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) as their object.
Since wind and the wind-element are not distinct, how can it be said that [the wind] also takes the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) as its object?
This objection is unreasonable, for in common worldly usage one also speaks of "black winds" and "whirlwinds," and so forth.
By this, the principle that the first eight [totalities] take form as their object is established.

As for the latter two totalities, they are respectively the two purities of space and consciousness; having the formless [attainments] as their intrinsic nature, each takes the four aggregates of its own level as its object.
By what means are the merits of these three gates—liberation and so forth—attained?
Upon what body do they arise?
The verse says:
The attainment of cessation has been explained as before; all others are obtained through both [types of acquisition].
Those of the formless realm rely on the three realms; the rest arise only in the human destiny.
The treatise says:
The eighth liberation has already been explained previously, as it is identical to the preceding attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The remaining liberations and so forth are obtained through both means—that is, through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*) and through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)—because there are those that have been practiced before and those that have not.

When first practicing the first eight spheres of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one employs visual consciousness as the preparatory application (*prayoga*); the same applies to the initial practice of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), because it must initially take the form of the space-element as its object. Through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), when it later reaches fulfillment, it takes all four aggregates (*skandha*) of its own level as its object.

When first practicing the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*), one uses only the mental consciousness as the preliminary application (*prayoga*), because at the outset it must take consciousness as its object. Later, when it reaches fulfillment through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it likewise takes the four aggregates of its own level as its object.
The four formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) and the two formless totalities (*ārūpya-kṛtsnāyatana*) each arise based on bodies belonging to any of the three realms.
However, their initial arising mostly depends on a lower stage; it is permissible for them to arise subsequently based on one's own stage or a lower stage.
Only the state of non-existence (*akiñcanya*) relies on the higher realms; all others rely on bodies within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It exists only among humans, excluding the northern continent, because in other places the power of wisdom is inferior and the holy teachings are absent.
Because it is intended to remedy sensual desire, it does not exist in the two higher realms. Some say:
its initial arising occurs only within the human realm, because it must be induced by the power of the teachings.
The teaching exists among humans but not within the heavenly realms.

Even if one were to experience pleasure there, it could not be initially aroused; therefore, when one first arises [in the heavens] and subsequently falls back to be born in the desire heavens, it is by the power of past habituation that the subsequent arousal of the teaching occurs.
Furthermore, for what reason do the third dhyāna and so forth possess the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), yet lack the liberations (*vimokṣa*)?

The reasons for the absence of the liberations have already been fully explained; since the liberations do not exist [there], the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are likewise absent, because the spheres of mastery enter through the gates of the liberations.

Because the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) do not exist, the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) also do not exist, for one enters the spheres of totality by means of the spheres of mastery as their gateway.

Furthermore, because the third dhyāna is characterized by attachment to sublime bliss—and since this bliss is superior within the cycle of birth and death—it cannot give rise to the three [states], such as liberation.

Since these three all involve turning one's back on birth and death, they universally accord with immeasurable bliss; therefore, by relying on this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one can also cultivate and give rise to them.
Regarding the merits of these three gateways—the liberations and so forth—if one attains even one, does one attain them all?
This is not always the case.
What is the meaning? That which is attained later must necessarily have been preceded by what came before; however, that which comes before is not necessarily followed by what comes after.
This means that one who attains the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality bases) necessarily attains all three;
one who attains the *abhibhvāyatana* (mastery bases) necessarily attains the *vimokṣa* (liberations), whereas the attainment of the *kṛtsnāyatana* is not fixed—it may or may not be attained.
If one attains the *vimokṣa*, the other two are not fixed, because one enters the *kṛtsnāyatana* and *abhibhvāyatana* by way of the *vimokṣa*, and enters the *abhibhvāyatana* by way of the *vimokṣa*.
What are the distinctions between these liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth?

Merely being able to turn away from [objects] is called a liberation; when this is combined with the analytical discernment of the focal object (*ālambana*), it is called a sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); and when "boundlessness" is added to the attainment, it receives the name of a sphere of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). These three roots of goodness are cultivated in successive stages.
Other masters say:
These three roots of goodness are distinguished by being inferior, middling, and superior.
This is because they are capable of abandoning and overcoming their objects; since their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are boundless, there exists a gradation of inferiority and superiority.
Other masters say: "The liberations (vimokṣa) are exclusively causes; the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are exclusively effects; and the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) pertain to both.
Now this should be examined: since there are no such teachers in the two higher realms, by what cause do the meditative absorptions (samādhi) arise therein?
The verse says:
In the two realms, by means of causes and karma, One can give rise to the formless attainments;
In the form realm, one gives rise to the dhyānas, Also through the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
The Commentary says:
Birth in the two higher realms generally proceeds through three conditions that enable one to further induce the meditative attainments of the form and formless realms.
First, by the power of causes; that is to say, because in previous times one has practiced them both recently and repeatedly, thereby acting as the causal condition.

Second, by the power of karma: this refers to having previously created karma that results in birth in a higher realm and is to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*). When the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma is about to arise and manifest, its force is able to cause one to enter that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), because if one has not yet abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realm, it is absolutely impossible to be born in a higher realm.

Third is the power of natural law (*dharmatā-bala*). This refers to when the receptacle world is about to undergo destruction, sentient beings of the lower realms naturally (*dharmatā*) become able to give rise to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher realms; this is because, at that stage, all wholesome dharmas increase and flourish by the power of natural law.

Those beings born in the two higher realms who give rise to formless meditative attainments do so through the power of causes and karma, not by the power of natural law (*dharmatā*), because the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*) and other such heavens are not destroyed by the three calamities.
When one born in the form realm gives rise to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it occurs through the two aforementioned conditions and the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
When one born in the desire realm gives rise to a higher concentration, one should understand that each instance additionally involves the power of the teaching (*śāsana*).
Regarding those [who uphold the Dharma] by the power of the teaching, this refers to humans in the three continents;
although the gods also hear the teaching, they are not mentioned because their capacity is subtle.
All the preceding distinctions of various supreme dharma-gates were for the purpose of propagating and maintaining the True Dharma of the World-Honored One.
What is called the True Dharma?
For how long shall it remain?
The verse says:
The Buddha’s True Dharma is twofold, having both teaching and realization as its essence;
as long as there are those who uphold, explain, and practice it, it shall abide in the world.
The treatise says:
The essence of the World-Honored One’s True Dharma is twofold: first, the teaching; second, the realization.
The teaching refers to the sūtras, the vinaya, and the sublime dharma; the realization refers to all the untainted paths of the three vehicles.
If the realization of the True Dharma (dharmābhisamaya) remains in the world, then the teaching it upholds and propagates must likewise remain; this is logically necessary.

We observe that while the realization of the Dharma has declined in the East and much of the teaching has disappeared there, because the realization of the Dharma still flourishes in the North, the Blessed One’s authentic teaching is still widely disseminated.

Consequently, this unsurpassed realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—the Abhidharma, which is the dwelling place of all noble ones and possesses the unerring, true meaning—is widely prevalent in this country, and is not something that can be transmitted or practiced in the eastern regions and elsewhere.
What are those who support and sustain these two aspects of the True Dharma?
They are the teachers and the practitioners.
The teaching of the True Dharma abides by means of the teachers, while the realization of the True Dharma abides solely by means of the practitioners.
However, it is not that the realized Dharma alone is to be relied upon, for the taught Dharma should also be relied upon by practitioners.

This is because those who practice the Dharma without error can cause the realized Dharma to abide long in the world; when the realized Dharma abides, the taught Dharma also abides. Thus, the endurance of the taught Dharma depends upon the teaching of practitioners.
It is solely because practitioners cause the Dharma to abide that the Buddha’s True Dharma remains in the world for as long as those who practice according to his teachings remain.
This Abhidharma treatise is the basis upon which it relies; it compiles the essential, authentic meaning contained therein.
In that treatise, there are many ways of explaining its meaning; by what principle does this present treatise explain it?
The verse says:
The principles established by the scholars of Kaśmīra— I rely solely upon them to explain the Abhidharma.
"Whatever discrepancies there may be are my own fault; the adjudication of the correct principles of the Dharma rests with the Muni.
The commentary states:

The masters of the *Vibhāṣā* in the kingdom of Kaśmīra have well-established the principles of Abhidharma; I rely solely upon them to explain the tenets of the Abhidharma-piṭaka, and thus I have herein set forth my own original intention within these verses.

That is to say, relying upon this treatise on the principles of Abhidharma—the Great Vibhāṣā—composed by the sons of the Sugata of this land, we have initiated right effort and conducted thorough investigation; for the sake of causing the True Dharma to abide long in the world and to benefit sentient beings, we have composed this treatise.
The word "only" (kevalam) is used to indicate that there is no other path, as everything here relies upon the *Vibhāṣā*.

Nevertheless, the nature of all phenomena is vast and profound, and those who can explain it according to reality are extremely rare to encounter. Reflecting upon this, my own cognitive wisdom is exceedingly feeble, and I am too indolent to seek out such an authentic expounder; therefore, should there be any discrepancies within the principles established in this extensive treatise, these are my own faults.

The correct principles of all phenomena are vast and profound; only those who have previously approached and cultivated the provisions for true wisdom under immeasurable Buddhas will be entirely free from doubt regarding the realm of wisdom.

Even the *ṛṣabha*, who is likened to a *pratyekabuddha*, cannot definitively discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), let alone the *śrāvakas*, for the dharmas they realize are dependent upon the teachings of others.

Therefore, the definitive discernment of the correct principle of all phenomena resides solely with the truly Great Muni. Consequently, one should know with certainty that the Abhidharma is truly the word of the Buddha; it should be accepted with faith and practiced without error, as one diligently seeks liberation.
The truly wondrous meaning practiced by the Great Awakened One can only be realized by the sons of the Sugatas through the hook of the correct principles of the Abhidharma;
it is certainly not for those who are deluded by their own dogmatic attachments.
Those who wish to realize the truly sublime meaning must rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and correct reasoning;
it is not possible through mere attachment to the teachings alone, for one should also direct the mind toward correct reasoning.

Therefore, by following the Buddha’s words and the *Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa*, as well as the *Āgama* that accords with correct reasoning, one has sufficient grounds for proof and a basis for the wondrous meaning; why then persist in seeking perverse and difficult arguments?
The wise can rely solely upon this teaching; they will not suffer decline or fall by following anything else.
Therefore, in determining whether the meaning of the Dharma is true or false, only the Great Awakened One is the authoritative standard.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā: Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā, Fascicle Forty.
